items.term: What Machine Learning Actually Is

blocks.content:
Machine learning means writing programs that get better at a task by **learning from data**, instead of having a programmer spell out every rule.

**The question this lesson answers:** when does a program count as "learning", and what must you pin down before you can build one?

### The big picture

The figure below shows the whole idea in one picture: the arrow turns around.

```
Traditional programming:  data + rules    ->  program   ->  answers
Machine learning:         data + answers  ->  training  ->  rules (the model)
```

In SQL terms: with traditional code you write the `CASE WHEN` rules yourself. With machine learning you hand over rows where the answer is already filled in, and training works out the rule.

### 1 · Two definitions, one for the idea and one for the job

- **Arthur Samuel, 1959 (the informal one):** machine learning is the field of study that gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed.
- **Tom Mitchell, 1997 (the engineering one, far more useful in practice):** a program learns from experience *E* with respect to task *T* and performance measure *P* if its performance on *T*, as measured by *P*, improves with *E*.

### 2 · Mitchell's three blanks: T, E and P

Mitchell's version is useful because it forces you to name three things before you have a well-posed learning problem. Think of them as three required fields on a job spec:

| Letter | What you must name | In the spam filter |
|---|---|---|
| **T**, task | what you want done (flag spam, predict a price, group customers) | flagging spam |
| **E**, experience | the data it learns from: the training data, where one example is a *training instance* | the emails users have already flagged as spam or ham |
| **P**, performance measure | the yardstick you will judge it by (accuracy, error rate, and so on) | usually the ratio of emails classified correctly |

*Ham* is simply a normal email that is not spam.

The rule of thumb: if you cannot name all three, you do not yet have a machine learning problem; you have a wish. It is like a ticket that says "make the dashboard smarter" with no data source, no metric and no definition of done.

### 3 · What the definition rules out: data alone

Downloading a copy of every Wikipedia article gives your computer an enormous amount of data, but it has not learned anything. There is no task and no performance measure improving with that data. Loading a huge table into the lake does not make any report more accurate on its own either.

Data alone is not learning.

**One-liner for your notes:** a program learns when its score (P) on a task (T) improves with data (E); if you cannot name all three, you have a wish, not a machine learning problem.

items.term: Why Mitchell's definition is the useful one
items.text: Samuel's definition tells you what machine learning is; Mitchell's tells you whether you have a problem you can actually start. It turns a wish into three things you can go and fetch: a task, a dataset, a number. The test is destructive on purpose -- most 'let's use ML for this' requests die at E (nobody has the labelled data) or at P (nobody agrees what better means), and finding that out costs a conversation instead of a quarter.

items.term: The measure you choose is the thing you get
items.text: P is not a report you read afterwards; it is the target. The definition says performance improves as measured by P, so whatever P ignores, the system is free to be bad at. The spam filter's P here is the ratio of emails classified correctly, which counts letting one spam through and blocking one real email as the same mistake. For a mail system those are not the same mistake at all. Choosing P is a design decision, not a formality.

items.term: Data alone is not experience
items.text: The Wikipedia example draws the boundary precisely: E is experience with respect to a task. A pile of data becomes experience only once a task and a measure point at it. The same holds in a lake -- a table does not make anything smarter on the day it lands, and 'we have the data' is never on its own an argument that a model is possible.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Write Mitchell's definition out for a task you actually care about: name the T, the E and the P explicitly.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The spam filter's P is the ratio of emails classified correctly. When is that a bad performance measure, and what do people use instead?

Look up: the scikit-learn user guide section 'Metrics and scoring: quantifying the quality of predictions' (the classification metrics part), and chapter 3 of this book, which is the classification chapter and spends its opening on performance measures.

items.term: Why Use Machine Learning At All

blocks.content:
Machine learning earns its place when hand-written rules grow too long to maintain, cannot be written at all, or go stale as the world changes, and it can also show you patterns hidden in your data.

**The question this lesson answers:** if you can already build a spam filter with ordinary code, why train one instead?

### The big picture: one step swapped

The book builds the same spam filter two ways. The loop is the same; only the middle step changes.

```
Traditional (Figure 1-1):  study the problem -> WRITE RULES -> test -> repeat
Machine learning (1-2):    study the problem -> TRAIN       -> test -> repeat
                                                (learns from spam and ham examples)
```

### 1 · Why the rule-writing loop never ends

In the **traditional programming** route you study the problem and notice that words like "4U", "credit card" and "free" show up often in spam. You write detection rules for them, test, and repeat.

That loop never ends, because the rules are hand-written and the world keeps moving. The program becomes a long list of complex rules that is hard to maintain. If you have ever kept patching a `CASE WHEN` with new special cases every time a source system changed, you have lived this loop.

### 2 · What the machine learning route changes

The **machine learning** route replaces the rule-writing step with a training step. You feed examples of spam and ham to a learning algorithm, and it works out on its own which words and patterns are unusually predictive of spam. The program is shorter, easier to maintain, and usually more accurate.

### 3 · The four situations where ML earns its place

| Situation | Why ML helps |
|---|---|
| The existing solution is a long list of hand-tuned rules | ML shortens the code and simplifies maintenance |
| There is no good traditional solution at all | the best ML techniques can perhaps find a solution |
| Fluctuating environments | a trained model can be retrained on fresh data |
| Getting insight into large or complex datasets | inspecting a trained model can reveal correlations nobody suspected |

Three of them need a closer look.

**No good traditional solution.** Speech recognition is the standard example of a problem with no good traditional solution at all. You could hard-code a check for the high-pitch "T" sound that starts the word "two", but no reasonable set of hand-written rules distinguishes "one" from "two" across every speaker, let alone thousands of words, noisy rooms and dozens of languages.

**Fluctuating environments, the sharpest advantage over rules.** If spammers start writing "For U" instead of "4U", a rule-based filter needs a human to notice and patch it. A filter that is retrained on recent mail picks the new pattern up and flags it automatically. Figure 1-3 below shows that loop closing on itself.

**Insight into data.** Inspecting what a trained model learned often reveals correlations nobody suspected. It is like profiling a table and finding two columns that move together when nobody thought to query them. The card below shows how this works for a spam filter. Digging into large amounts of data to discover hidden patterns like these is called **data mining**, and machine learning excels at it.

**One-liner for your notes:** use machine learning when rules grow too long, cannot be written, or go stale; a retrained model keeps up with change by itself, and inspecting it can teach you about your data.

blocks.title: Data mining, and what inspecting a model shows
blocks.content: Many trained models can be opened up to see what they have learned, although this is tricky for some kinds of model. A spam filter is an easy case: once it has been trained on enough spam, you can inspect it and get the list of words and word combinations that it treats as the best predictors of spam. That list sometimes shows correlations or trends that nobody expected, which gives people a better understanding of the problem. The general activity of digging into large amounts of data to discover hidden patterns is called **data mining**, and machine learning is very good at it.

items.term: The real comparison is maintenance, not cleverness
items.text: Figures 1-1 and 1-2 differ by one step, but the cost that decides between them shows up over time. Hand-written rules are cheap to write once and expensive to keep correct. A trained model is expensive to set up and cheap to refresh. So the question is not 'is this problem hard' but 'how fast does the right answer change'. Where the rules are short and stable, hand-written rules are still the better engineering.

items.term: Why fluctuating environments is the sharpest of the four
items.text: In the other three situations ML is a better tool for the same job. Here it is a different operating model. A rule-based filter needs a human to notice that spammers now write 'For U' and to patch it; a retrained filter closes that loop itself (Figure 1-3). The trade you accept is that the system now changes without anyone deciding it should -- which is exactly why later lessons spend so long on bad data and on monitoring.

items.term: Inspecting a model feeds the other three reasons
items.text: Insight is listed as the fourth reason, but it is also how you improve the first three: the words a spam filter treats as its best predictors tell you which inputs are worth keeping and which were noise. Carry the card's caveat, though -- this is easy for a spam filter and tricky for some kinds of model, so do not plan a project on the assumption that you will be able to read what it learned.

items.term: Supervised Learning

blocks.content:
Supervised learning means every training example comes with its answer already filled in, and the model learns to produce that answer for new examples.

**The question this lesson answers:** what does "supervised" mean, and what are the two jobs it is used for?

### The big picture: where this lesson sits

ML systems can be sorted along several independent axes. This lesson opens the first one.

```
Axis 1  how much and what kind of supervision   <- this lesson and the next two
Axis 2  batch vs online learning
Axis 3  instance-based vs model-based learning
```

### 1 · Supervised means the answers come with the data

Supervised learning is the most familiar setting: the training set you feed the algorithm includes the answers, called **labels**.

In table terms, every row has its input columns plus one extra column holding the answer. Training teaches the model to fill that column in for new rows where it is still empty. Figure 1-5 below shows such a labelled training set for spam.

### 2 · The two jobs: classification and regression

The two tasks that dominate differ only in what the answer column holds.

| | Classification | Regression |
|---|---|---|
| Predicts | a class | a numeric value, called a *target* |
| Book example | a spam filter | a car's price |

**Classification.** The spam filter is trained on many emails, each labelled spam or ham, and must classify new ones.

**Regression.** Predicting a car's price from mileage, age and brand is regression; those input attributes are the *features*.

The two words are not as separate as they look. Logistic regression is commonly used for classification, because it can output a probability of belonging to a class, such as a 20% chance of being spam. And some regression algorithms handle classification perfectly well, and vice versa.

### 3 · Vocabulary: several words for the same thing

| Word | Other names | Note |
|---|---|---|
| feature | **predictors** or **attributes** | an input, such as a car's mileage |
| **label** | **target** | *target* is more common in regression, *label* in classification |

A feature is like a column, and the word works at two zoom levels:

- one cell: "this car's mileage feature is equal to 15,000"
- the whole column: "the mileage feature is strongly correlated with price"

### 4 · The price of supervision

The answer column does not fill itself. The practical cost of supervision is that somebody must produce the labels, and that is usually the expensive part of a supervised project.

**One-liner for your notes:** supervised learning trains on rows that already carry the answer (the label); predict a class and it is classification, predict a number and it is regression.

blocks.title: Features, predictors and attributes
blocks.content: In the book's vocabulary, *feature*, *predictor* and *attribute* are other names for the same thing: an input such as a car's mileage. The book does not use them to separate a data type from its value. Any of these words can talk about one sample or about all samples. The sentence "this car's mileage feature is equal to 15,000" is about a single car, while "the mileage feature is strongly correlated with price" is about every car in the data. The answers the model predicts have their own pair of synonyms: *label* and *target*.

items.term: Why the label column is the expensive part
items.text: The algorithms are free and the raw rows are often free. The answers are not. That is the whole content of section 4, and it sets the size of most supervised projects: the plan is really a labelling plan. It is also the reason the next lesson exists -- semi-supervised and self-supervised learning are both attempts to get the same answer column for less human work.

items.term: Classification and regression name the answer, not the toolbox
items.text: The two jobs differ only in what the answer column holds, which is why the same algorithm often does both: logistic regression outputs a probability and is used for classification, and the lesson says plainly that some regression algorithms handle classification and the other way round. So do not read the two words as two sets of tools. Read them as two questions about the label, and let the label decide.

items.term: One word, two zoom levels, and why it bites
items.text: Feature means both one cell and the whole column, and the book uses it both ways in consecutive sentences. Harmless in speech, dangerous when you act on it: 'the mileage feature is strongly correlated with price' is a statement about the column and can only be computed over every row, while 'this car's mileage feature is 15,000' is one value. Decide which zoom level a sentence means before you turn it into code.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Classification or regression: predicting tomorrow's electricity demand in megawatts. And predicting whether a transaction is fraudulent?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Labels are the expensive part. What does labelling a dataset actually cost in practice, and which techniques reduce how many labels you need?
Look up: the scikit-learn user guide section on semi-supervised learning (it documents self-training and label propagation), and read the next lesson in this chapter alongside it.

items.term: Unsupervised Learning

blocks.content:
In **unsupervised learning** the training data is unlabelled: the system has to find structure on its own, without anybody telling it what the right answer looks like.

**The question this lesson answers:** if the training data has no answer column at all, what useful jobs can a model still do?

### The big picture: four families, four questions

The rows look the same as in supervised learning; the label column is simply missing. Each family asks a different question of that same data.

| Family | The question it asks |
|---|---|
| Clustering | which groups of similar instances exist? |
| Visualisation and dimensionality reduction | how can the data be plotted, or simplified without losing much? |
| Anomaly and novelty detection | what does not belong? |
| Association rule learning | which attributes go together? |

### 1 · Clustering: groups nobody named

Given traffic to your blog, a clustering algorithm can detect groups of similar visitors without you naming the groups in advance. The book's example: it might notice that 40% of visitors are teenagers who love comic books and read after school, while 20% are adults who enjoy sci-fi and visit at weekends.

Think of a `GROUP BY` where the algorithm invents the grouping column itself. A *hierarchical* clustering algorithm can then subdivide each group further, into smaller groups.

### 2 · Visualisation and dimensionality reduction: fewer columns

- **Visualisation.** Feed a visualisation algorithm a lot of complex, unlabelled data and it produces a 2D or 3D layout you can plot, trying to preserve as much structure as possible (Figure 1-9 below).
- **Dimensionality reduction.** Simplify the data without losing too much information. Here a *dimension* is roughly one feature, one column. One way is to merge correlated features, features that tend to move together, into one.

The book's example: a car's mileage and its age are strongly correlated, so they can be merged into a single "wear and tear" feature. This is called **feature extraction**.

Why bother? Running it before a supervised algorithm often makes that algorithm faster and sometimes more accurate.

### 3 · Anomaly detection vs novelty detection

Both flag instances that do not fit. The difference is what they are trained on.

| | Anomaly detection | Novelty detection |
|---|---|---|
| Spots | unusual instances | instances that look genuinely *new* |
| Trained on | mostly normal instances | a training set completely free of the instance type it should flag |
| A new Chihuahua photo, when 1% of the thousands of training dog photos are Chihuahuas | may be flagged, as rare and different | not flagged: Chihuahuas were already in training |

Anomaly detection spots things like a defective product on a line or an odd credit card transaction, after being trained mostly on normal ones. Novelty detection is the close cousin: because it hunts for the genuinely new, it wants a training set completely free of the instance type it should flag. The Chihuahua row is the book's example of where the two part ways.

For a data engineer, anomaly detection is close to a data-quality check that flags a row far outside the usual range, except that the model learns what "usual" means from the data.

### 4 · Association rule learning: what goes together

Dig into large volumes of data to find relations between attributes. A supermarket log might reveal that people buying barbecue sauce and potato chips also tend to buy steak, which is an argument for putting them near each other. Picture it as discovering which products keep landing in the same basket across a huge sales log.

**One-liner for your notes:** unsupervised learning works on data with no answer column: it finds groups (clustering), shrinks columns (dimensionality reduction), flags what does not belong (anomaly and novelty detection) and finds what goes together (association rules).

items.term: There is no answer key, so 'good' has to be defined
items.text: With no label column there is nothing to compare a result against, so 'is this clustering correct?' has no answer the way 'is this email correctly classified?' does. That is the real difference from supervised learning, and it is why unsupervised results tend to be judged by whether they help something downstream -- the lesson's own justification for dimensionality reduction is that the supervised algorithm afterwards runs faster and is sometimes more accurate.

items.term: Dimensionality reduction is lossy on purpose
items.text: Merging mileage and age into one wear-and-tear feature throws away the ability to ask about either one separately, and you accept that to gain speed and sometimes accuracy. The word holding the whole idea up is correlated: features that move together carry overlapping information, so merging them costs little. It stops being safe when the two columns were only moving together in this particular sample.

items.term: Anomaly versus novelty is a decision about your training set
items.text: The two are the same job with different data hygiene. Anomaly detection is trained on mostly normal instances and tolerates a few odd ones being present. Novelty detection demands a training set completely free of the type it must flag. So the choice is made when you assemble the training data, not when you pick an algorithm -- and the Chihuahua row shows the consequence: rare-but-present in training gives 'may be flagged' for one and 'not flagged' for the other.

items: With no labels there is no right answer to check against, so how does anyone decide a clustering is good, or how many clusters to ask for in the first place?

Look up: the scikit-learn user guide section on clustering performance evaluation (the silhouette coefficient is the one to start with), and chapter 9 of this book, which is the unsupervised learning chapter.

items.term: Semi-supervised, Self-supervised and Reinforcement Learning

blocks.content:
This lesson covers the supervision styles between fully supervised and fully unsupervised: semi-supervised learning uses a few human labels, self-supervised learning makes its own labels, and reinforcement learning learns from rewards instead.

**The question this lesson answers:** when nobody labels every row, where does the learning signal come from?

### The big picture: where the learning signal comes from

| Style | Where the signal comes from |
|---|---|
| Supervised (see the Supervised Learning lesson) | a label on every training instance |
| **Semi-supervised learning** | a small labelled part; the rest stays unlabelled |
| **Self-supervised learning** | labels generated from the unlabelled data itself |
| Unsupervised | no labels |
| **Reinforcement learning** | the **rewards** and **penalties** that the agent's own actions earn |

The first four differ by how much human labelling they need. Reinforcement learning is a different shape entirely, as the figure at the end of this lesson shows.

### 1 · Semi-supervised: label a few, not all

Semi-supervised learning deals with data that is mostly unlabelled with a small labelled part, because labelling is usually time-consuming and costly.

Photo-hosting services are the everyday example:

```
1. unsupervised part: cluster the photos
      person A shows up in photos 1, 5 and 11
      person B shows up in photos 2, 5 and 7
2. your part: one label per person ("person A is ...")
3. the service names every cluster
```

The service clusters photos and works out unsupervised that the same person appears in several of them, and then all it needs from you is one label per person to name every cluster. Most semi-supervised algorithms are combinations of unsupervised and supervised ones underneath.

### 2 · Self-supervised: the data labels itself

Self-supervised learning generates a fully labelled dataset from a completely unlabelled one, then trains on it with ordinary supervised techniques.

The book's example: mask a random patch out of every image in a large photo set and train a model to reconstruct it. The masked image is the input and the original image is the answer (Figure 1-12 below: input left, target right). In table terms, it is like blanking out a value on purpose and training a model to put it back: the original value is the label, so nobody had to write one.

The trick is that the model learns representations useful far beyond that artificial task. A model trained to repair images turns out to be a good starting point for classifying them, once you fine-tune it, that is, train it a little more on the task you actually care about. Reusing a model this way is called **transfer learning**, and it is one of the most important ideas in modern ML.

### 3 · Reinforcement learning: learning from rewards

The learning system, called an **agent**, observes an environment, selects and performs actions, and gets **rewards** in return (or **penalties**, which are negative rewards).

```
agent ----- performs an action ----> environment
  ^                                      |
  +---- observation + reward or penalty -+
```

It must learn by itself the best strategy, the **policy**, to maximise reward over time. A policy defines what action the agent chooses in a given situation: think of it as the agent's rulebook of "in this situation, do this", learned rather than written.

Robots learning to walk and DeepMind's AlphaGo both work this way.

**One-liner for your notes:** semi-supervised learning needs a few human labels, self-supervised learning makes its own labels from raw data, and reinforcement learning has an agent learn a policy from the rewards its actions earn.

items.term: Three answers to one shortage, and one that is not
items.text: Semi-supervised and self-supervised learning both exist because labels cost money, and they buy them differently: one asks a human for a few and spreads them over clusters the machine already found, the other manufactures labels out of data it already has. Reinforcement learning is not on that spectrum at all. Its signal is produced by acting, so it needs an environment to act in, not a dataset to read. That is why the book draws it as a separate loop.

items.term: Why a made-up task teaches something real
items.text: Nobody needs image patches restored. The masking task is useful because filling the hole forces the model to learn what images are generally like, and that knowledge carries over to jobs you do care about after a little more training -- fine-tuning, and the general move is transfer learning. The limit follows from the same logic: the invented task has to demand the kind of understanding the real task needs, or nothing worth reusing gets learned.

items.term: A policy is a learned rulebook, and the reward is late
items.text: The policy is the mapping from situation to action, learned rather than written -- the agent's own version of the CASE WHEN nobody had to write. What makes it hard is timing: the reward for a good action can arrive long after the action, so the agent has to work out which of many earlier choices earned it. Walking robots and AlphaGo are the standard examples precisely because both take long chains of actions before any score arrives.

items: Why does a photo service's face-grouping feature count as semi-supervised rather than unsupervised?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: A reward can arrive many actions after the action that earned it. How does an agent work out which of its earlier choices to credit?
Look up: chapter 18 of this book, the reinforcement learning chapter, which is where this problem and its standard treatment are covered.

items.term: Batch Versus Online Learning

blocks.content:
Batch learning trains once on all the data and then stops learning; online learning keeps learning in small steps as new data arrives.

**The question this lesson answers:** can the system keep learning **incrementally from a stream of incoming data**, or must it be retrained from scratch every time? This is the second axis for sorting ML systems.

### The big picture: full refresh vs incremental load

You already know this split from loading tables.

| | Batch learning | Online learning |
|---|---|---|
| Like a | full refresh: rebuild from all the data | incremental load: apply new data as it comes |
| Trains on | all the available data at once, offline | instances one at a time, or small **mini-batches** |
| After launch | runs without learning any further | keeps learning on the fly |
| New data means | retrain a new version from scratch | one more fast, cheap learning step |
| Main risk | slow, costly retraining and **model rot** | bad data degrades the live system |

### 1 · Batch learning: train once, then freeze

**Batch learning** cannot learn incrementally. It must be trained using all the available data at once, offline, and then shipped and run without learning any further. This is called *offline learning*.

To teach it about new data you retrain a new version from scratch on the full dataset, old plus new, and swap it in. That is usually automatable, so batch learning is not automatically wrong. But it has two real costs:

1. **Time and compute.** Training on a full dataset can take hours and a lot of compute.
2. **Decay.** A batch model's performance decays over time simply because the world changes and the model does not. The book calls this **model rot** or *data drift*. It is like a snapshot table that was right the day it was built and quietly goes stale. Retraining daily or weekly is the mitigation.

Batch can also fail outright when the dataset is too large for memory, or when the system must run autonomously on limited resources, such as a smartphone app or a rover on Mars.

### 2 · Online learning: learn in small steps

**Online learning** trains the system incrementally, feeding it instances one at a time or in small **mini-batches**. Each learning step is fast and cheap, so the system can learn about new data on the fly.

The same incremental training can handle a dataset too large to fit in one machine's main memory. This is **out-of-core learning**:

```
dataset too large for memory
  -> load one part  -> training step
  -> load next part -> training step
  -> ... repeat until all of the data has been used
```

It is like processing a file bigger than your RAM one chunk at a time. Out-of-core learning is usually run offline despite the confusing name, which is why the card below suggests reading "online" as *incremental*.

### 3 · The learning rate: how fast it adapts

The critical knob is the **learning rate**: how fast the system adapts to changing data.

| Learning rate | What you get | What it costs |
|---|---|---|
| High | adapts quickly | forgets old data quickly |
| Low | less sensitive to noise | learns more slowly |

A high learning rate means it adapts quickly but forgets old data quickly; a low one means it learns more slowly but is less sensitive to noise. Too high, and a spam filter would flag only the latest kinds of spam it was shown.

### 4 · The risk: bad data gets in live

The matching risk is that bad data degrades the live system, like a broken upstream feed corrupting an incrementally loaded table. So you monitor input data closely and react to drops in performance.

**One-liner for your notes:** batch learning is a full refresh that goes stale between retrains; online learning is an incremental load that stays fresh, as long as the learning rate is sensible and bad data is caught early.

blocks.title: How out-of-core learning works
blocks.content: Sometimes a dataset is too large to fit in one machine's main memory. An online learning algorithm can still train on it: the algorithm loads part of the data, runs a training step on that part, and then repeats the process until it has run on all of the data. This is called **out-of-core learning**. It is usually done offline, not on the live system, which is why the book warns that the name *online learning* can be confusing and suggests thinking of it as *incremental learning* instead.

blocks.caption: Batch trains once on everything, offline, and the deployed model is frozen until you retrain it from scratch. Online learns incrementally from a stream — cheap and fresh, but bad data degrades it just as incrementally.

items.term: Batch is not wrong, it just moves the cost into the schedule
items.text: Retraining from scratch is usually automatable, so the choice is rarely capability. It is cadence. A batch model is exactly right on the day it ships and drifts until the next retrain, so the question to ask is how fast your world moves compared with how often you can afford to rebuild -- the same question you already answer when you pick a refresh interval for a derived table. Model rot lives entirely in that gap.

items.term: Online learning trades a build problem for a monitoring problem
items.text: With batch, a bad training set is caught before release and you keep serving the previous model. With online learning the bad data is already inside the parameters of the system that is serving traffic, and performance slides rather than failing. That is why the lesson's mitigation is not a better algorithm but an operational one: watch the input data closely and react to drops in performance.

items.term: The learning rate has no safe setting
items.text: High adapts quickly and forgets quickly; low is steadier and slower. There is no value that is good at both, so the right one depends on how fast the real pattern moves compared with how noisy the data is -- two properties of your data, not of the algorithm. The lesson's extreme case is the test to remember: turn it too high and a spam filter ends up flagging only the newest kind of spam it was shown.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Your model must run on a device that gets new data every second and cannot phone home. Batch or online? Why?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: How is a learning rate actually chosen, rather than guessed, and does it have to stay the same value for the whole life of an online system?

Look up: the scikit-learn user guide section on stochastic gradient descent, which is the incremental learner the library ships; it documents both the learning-rate schedules and the partial-fit call that makes online learning possible.

items.term: Instance-Based Versus Model-Based Learning

blocks.content:
This lesson is about the two ways a trained system handles a case it has never seen: compare it with remembered examples (instance-based), or run it through a model fitted to the examples (model-based).

**The question this lesson answers:** does money make people happier? Given a country's GDP per capita, predict its life satisfaction, for example for Cyprus, a country the life-satisfaction data has no score for.

### The big picture

The third axis for sorting ML systems is **how the system generalises**. To *generalise* means to perform well on instances the system has never seen. Almost every ML task is about prediction, so that is the real goal. Good performance on the training data is necessary but not sufficient, just as a report that is only right for the months you tested it on is not finished.

There are two ways to get there:

```
Instance-based:  keep examples -> compare new case with them
Model-based:     fit a model   -> apply it to the new case
```

| | Instance-based | Model-based |
|---|---|---|
| Learns by | memorising the training examples | building a model of the examples |
| Predicts by | a measure of similarity | applying the model |
| Algorithm in this lesson | k-nearest neighbours | linear regression |
| Cyprus | about 6.33, from the three closest countries | 6.30, from the fitted line |

### 1 · Instance-based learning: learning by heart

**Instance-based learning** is learning by heart. A spam filter built this way would flag emails identical to ones already flagged. Made slightly less trivial, it also flags emails that are similar to known spam, which requires a **measure of similarity**. A very basic one is the count of words two emails share.

The system memorises the training examples and generalises to new cases by comparing them with that measure. k-nearest neighbours is the standard algorithm here. The *k* is how many of the closest examples it looks at. For Cyprus, with k = 3, the whole prediction reads like a query:

```sql
SELECT AVG(life_satisfaction)              -- about 6.33
FROM (
  SELECT life_satisfaction
  FROM countries
  ORDER BY ABS(gdp_per_capita - 37655)     -- Cyprus: 37,655 USD
  LIMIT 3                                  -- k = 3
) AS nearest;
```

The "Worked out" card below names the three countries and does the arithmetic.

### 2 · Model-based learning: the four-step workflow

**Model-based learning** instead builds a model of the examples and uses the model to predict. The workflow is worth memorising, because the rest of the book is that workflow in more detail.

1. **Study the data.** Plot GDP per capita against life satisfaction and notice the trend.
2. **Select a model.** The plot looks roughly linear, so choose a linear model of life satisfaction with two parameters:

   $$\text{life satisfaction} = \theta_0 + \theta_1 \times \text{GDP per capita}$$

   **Why the formula looks like this**

   A straight line is the simplest rule that can say "more of this, more of that". It needs exactly two
   numbers: where to start, and how fast to climb. That is why there are two terms and not three, and
   why nothing is squared or multiplied together -- those would bend the line, and step 1's plot looked
   roughly linear, with no bend to follow.

   **Standard, or made up for this example?** Standard. This is the ordinary linear model, the same
   shape used everywhere, not a simplification invented for the life-satisfaction data. What changes in
   real work is the number of inputs, not the shape:

   | Inputs | The model |
   |---|---|
   | one (here) | theta zero + theta one times GDP |
   | two | theta zero + theta one times input one + theta two times input two |
   | many | theta zero plus one theta times input term per feature |

   Each extra input adds one more theta and one more multiply. The training step and the prediction step
   are unchanged, which is why this two-term version is worth understanding properly.

   **Two terms this uses:**

   - **Model parameter:** one of the blanks in the formula -- here theta zero and theta one -- that
   training fills in. You never choose them by hand; that is the whole point of training.
   - **Cost function:** a single number saying how badly one candidate line misses the real data points.
   Training searches for the parameter values that make it as small as possible. Step 3 below names it
   and its mirror image, the utility function, which is pushed up instead of down.

   For a straight line with one input, that search has an exact answer computed from the data in one
   pass -- no repetition, no randomness. That is why step 4 can work the two numbers out in five lines
   of arithmetic, and why running the training twice on the same data gives identical values.

   **Reading the formula, piece by piece:**

   | Piece | Say it as | What it is |
   |---|---|---|
   | life satisfaction | — | the number the model predicts, a 0–10 score |
   | $\theta_0$ | "theta zero" | the starting value: the prediction when GDP is 0 — the line's height at the left edge |
   | $\theta_1$ | "theta one" | the slope: how much the score rises for each extra dollar of GDP |
   | × | "times" | multiply |
   | GDP per capita | — | the input: money per person, in US dollars |

   In plain words: **prediction = starting value + slope × GDP**.

   $\theta_0$ (theta zero) sets the height of the line and $\theta_1$ (theta one) is its slope. The model is like a view with two blank parameters; training fills them in.

3. **Train it.** Training means finding the parameter values that make the model fit best, which requires a measure of fit: either a *utility function* measuring how good the model is, or a *cost function* measuring how bad. Linear regression minimises the distance between predictions and training examples. Here training finds $\theta_0 = 3.75$ and $\theta_1 = 6.78 \times 10^{-5}$.
4. **Apply the model to make predictions** on new cases. This is **inference**. For Cyprus: 3.75 + 37,655 × 6.78 × 10⁻⁵ ≈ 6.30.

   6.78 × 10⁻⁵ just means 0.0000678 (move the decimal point 5 places left).

   **How training gets those two numbers** (one input, so it can be done by hand):

   1. Average GDP of the 27 countries = 41,564.5. Average score = 6.5667.
   2. For each country, multiply (its GDP − 41,564.5) by (its score − 6.5667), then add the 27 results: **163,499.4**. This says how GDP and score move together.
   3. For each country, square (its GDP − 41,564.5), then add the 27 results: **2,411,886,717.9**. This says how spread out GDP is.
   4. θ₁ = step 2 ÷ step 3 = 163,499.4 ÷ 2,411,886,717.9 = **0.0000678**.
   5. θ₀ = average score − θ₁ × average GDP = 6.5667 − 0.0000678 × 41,564.5 = 6.5667 − 2.8176 = **3.749**.

   So 10,000 more dollars of GDP adds 0.0000678 × 10,000 = **0.68** points of life satisfaction.

| Measure of fit | It measures | Training pushes it |
|---|---|---|
| utility function | how good the model is | up |
| cost function | how bad the model is | down |

### 3 · Same question, two answers

The two approaches answer the same question differently, and they can disagree. Where the linear model predicts 6.30 life satisfaction for Cyprus, k-nearest neighbours with k = 3 predicts about 6.33 from the three closest countries. Close, but not identical.

**One-liner for your notes:** instance-based learning remembers the examples and predicts by similarity (k-nearest neighbours: Cyprus about 6.33); model-based learning fits parameters and predicts by applying the model (linear: Cyprus 6.30).

blocks.title: Worked out: the two predictions for Cyprus
blocks.content:
**Model-based (the linear model).** Training finds θ₀ = 3.75 and θ₁ = 6.78 × 10⁻⁵. Cyprus has a GDP per capita of 37,655 USD, so the model predicts 3.75 + 37,655 × 6.78 × 10⁻⁵ = 3.75 + 2.55 ≈ **6.30**.

**Instance-based (k-nearest neighbours, k = 3).** Look for the countries whose GDP per capita is closest to that of Cyprus. The closest is Israel (38,341 USD), with a life satisfaction of 7.2; using Israel alone would predict 7.2. The next two closest countries are Lithuania and Slovenia, and both have a life satisfaction of 5.9. The prediction is the average of these three values: (7.2 + 5.9 + 5.9) ÷ 3 = 19.0 ÷ 3 ≈ **6.33**, which is close to the linear model's 6.30.

blocks.caption: Two ways to generalise to a case you have never seen. Instance-based keeps the examples and measures similarity; model-based throws the examples away and keeps a fitted rule.

items.term: Why two methods can both be right and still disagree
items.text: The line says 6.30 for Cyprus and k-nearest neighbours says about 6.33. Neither is the answer; they answer slightly different questions -- what the overall trend says at 37,655 USD, versus what the most similar countries actually score. Close agreement is weak evidence that the pattern is real. A large disagreement would be telling you something about the shape of the data, not that one method is broken.

items.term: Scoring well on the training data proves very little
items.text: Generalising means performing well on instances never seen, and the lesson says training performance is necessary but not sufficient. That bites hardest for instance-based learning, which can look excellent on the training data for the trivial reason that the training data is what it memorised. This is the concrete reason the chapter later insists on holding data back before you believe any number.

items.term: With no model, the assumptions live in the similarity measure
items.text: Instance-based learning fits nothing, so every design decision sits in two places: how you measure similarity and how many neighbours you look at. The lesson's own measure for emails is the count of shared words; for countries it is distance in GDP. Change the measure and every prediction changes, with no training step to point at. The assumptions did not disappear -- they moved into the distance function.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Explain the difference between a utility function and a cost function in one sentence.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The slope says 10,000 more dollars of GDP goes with about 0.68 more points of life satisfaction. Does that mean money causes happiness, and what would you need before you could claim it?

Look up: the scikit-learn example titled 'Common pitfalls in the interpretation of coefficients of linear models', and the OECD Better Life Index, a real published source of life-satisfaction scores, to see how such a score is actually built.

items.term: The Whole Workflow in Ten Lines of Scikit-Learn

blocks.content: Example 1-1 is the entire model-based workflow compressed into one screen of code, and it is the only substantial code listing in this chapter. Read it as four moves, in order:

blocks.title: Figure 1-17
blocks.caption: Model-based learning
blocks.alt: Figure 1-17: Model-based learning

blocks.content:
### 1 · Load the data

`pandas` reads the life-satisfaction CSV. `X` is the input matrix — GDP per capita — and `y` is the label vector, life satisfaction. Note the double brackets: Scikit-Learn expects `X` to be 2D, one row per instance and one column per feature.

cells.source:
# Example 1-1, from ageron/handson-ml3 (Apache-2.0)
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # plotting
import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression  # the model

# Download the data: one row per country
data_root = "https://github.com/ageron/data/raw/main/"
lifesat = pd.read_csv(data_root + "lifesat/lifesat.csv")

# X = input feature (2-D: rows x 1 column), y = target
X = lifesat[["GDP per capita (USD)"]].values
y = lifesat[["Life satisfaction"]].values

lifesat.head()  # first 5 rows

items.term: `DataFrame`
items.text: pandas' table: named columns, one row per record. `lifesat` is 27 rows × 3 columns: `Country`, `GDP per capita (USD)`, `Life satisfaction`.

items.term: `pd.read_csv(url)`
items.text: Reads a CSV straight from a web address into a DataFrame. No separate download step.

Single brackets return one column as a `Series`, a bare list of values, shape `(27,)`. Double brackets pass a *list* of columns, like `SELECT` of one column, and keep a table: a `DataFrame`, shape `(27, 1)`.

items.term: `.values`
items.text: Drops the column names and row index and returns a NumPy array: a plain grid of numbers (`float64`).
27 rows × 1 column. scikit-learn always wants `X` 2-D (rows = samples, columns = features), even with one feature. That is why the double brackets.

items.term: `lifesat.head()`
items.text: The first 5 rows, like `LIMIT 5`. As the last line of a cell, the notebook shows it as a table.

blocks.content:
### 2 · Look at the data

The scatterplot is not decoration. It is what justifies choosing a linear model in the next step, and skipping it is how people end up fitting the wrong shape.

blocks.title: Figure 1-18
blocks.caption: Do you see a trend here?
blocks.alt: Figure 1-18: Do you see a trend here?

cells.source:
# Scatter plot: one dot per country
lifesat.plot(kind="scatter", grid=True,
             x="GDP per capita (USD)", y="Life satisfaction")
plt.axis([23_500, 62_500, 4, 9])  # KNOB: zoom window [x_min, x_max, y_min, y_max]
plt.show()

items.term: `plt`
items.text: `matplotlib.pyplot`, the plotting module. It tracks a *current* chart that the next calls change.

items.term: `lifesat.plot(kind="scatter", x=..., y=...)`
items.text: pandas draws with matplotlib. `x` and `y` name the column for each axis; one dot per row.

items.term: `grid=True`
items.text: Adds background grid lines so values can be read off the chart.

items.term: `plt.axis([x_min, x_max, y_min, y_max])`
items.text: Sets the visible window. It only zooms; the data is unchanged. The data spans GDP 26,456–60,236 and satisfaction 5.4–7.6, so every country is inside `[23_500, 62_500, 4, 9]`.

items.term: `plt.show()`
items.text: Finishes the chart and displays it. Here it arrives as a PNG under the cell.

blocks.content:
### 3 · Choose a model and train it

`LinearRegression()` picks the model class; `model.fit(X, y)` runs training, which finds the parameter values minimising the cost function.

blocks.title: Equation 1-1
blocks.caption: A simple linear model
blocks.explain:
**Reading Equation 1-1, piece by piece:**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is | In the code |
|---|---|---|---|
| life_satisfaction | — | the number the model predicts, a 0–10 score | `model.predict(...)` |
| $\theta_0$ | "theta zero" | the starting value: the prediction when GDP is 0 | `model.intercept_` = 3.749 |
| $\theta_1$ | "theta one" | the slope: score gained per extra dollar | `model.coef_` = 0.0000678 |
| × | "times" | multiply | |
| GDP_per_capita | — | the input: money per person, US dollars | `X` |

In plain words: **prediction = starting value + slope × GDP**.

**Cyprus, plugged in:** 3.749 + 0.0000678 × 37,655.2 = 3.749 + 2.5526 = **6.30**.

**How `fit` gets $\theta_0$ and $\theta_1$** (one input, so it can be done by hand):

1. Average GDP of the 27 countries = 41,564.5. Average score = 6.5667.
2. For each country, multiply (its GDP − 41,564.5) by (its score − 6.5667), then add the 27 results: **163,499.4** — how GDP and score move together.
3. For each country, square (its GDP − 41,564.5), then add the 27 results: **2,411,886,717.9** — how spread out GDP is.
4. θ₁ = step 2 ÷ step 3 = **0.0000678**.
5. θ₀ = 6.5667 − 0.0000678 × 41,564.5 = 6.5667 − 2.8176 = **3.749**.

blocks.title: Figure 1-19
blocks.caption: A few possible linear models
blocks.alt: Figure 1-19: A few possible linear models

blocks.title: Figure 1-20
blocks.caption: The linear model that fits the training data best
blocks.alt: Figure 1-20: The linear model that fits the training data best

cells.source:
# Pick a model
model = LinearRegression()  # model-based: fits a straight line

# Swap in instance-based learning: uncomment both lines
# from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor
# model = KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=3)  # KNOB: try 1, 3, 5

model.fit(X, y)  # train on all countries
print(model)  # which model was trained
if hasattr(model, "coef_"):  # linear models only
    print("intercept:", model.intercept_, "slope:", model.coef_)

items.term: Model object
items.text: `LinearRegression()` creates a model with settings but nothing learned yet, like a table with a schema and no rows.

items.term: `model.fit(X, y)`
items.text: Learns from the inputs `X` and the answers `y`, and stores the result on `model` itself. It changes the object in place.

items.term: `intercept_`, `coef_`
items.text: The learned $\theta_0$ and $\theta_1$ of Equation 1-1: `3.74904943` and `6.77889969e-05`. They print inside brackets because `y` is 2-D.

items.term: Trailing `_`
items.text: scikit-learn convention: an attribute ending in `_` exists only after `fit`.
Scientific notation: 6.77889969 × 10⁻⁵ = 0.0000678 per USD, about +0.68 satisfaction per extra 10,000 USD.

items.term: `hasattr(model, "coef_")`
items.text: Asks whether the object has that attribute. A k-nearest-neighbours model has no `coef_`, so the line is skipped instead of failing.

blocks.content:
### 4 · Predict for Cyprus

`model.predict(X_new)` performs inference for Cyprus's GDP per capita and returns roughly 6.30.

cells.source:
# Predict for a new country
X_new = [[37_655.2]]  # KNOB: Cyprus GDP per capita (USD, 2020)
print(model.predict(X_new))  # linear model: [[6.30165767]]

items.text: A list inside a list: one row with one column, the same 2-D shape as `X`.

items.term: `_` in numbers
items.text: Only a digit separator for reading. Python reads `37_655.2` as `37655.2`.

items.term: `model.predict(X_new)`

items.text: A NumPy array of shape `(1, 1)`: one row of predictions for the one input row.

blocks.content:
### 5 · Try another algorithm

The part worth internalising is how little of this changes between algorithms. Swapping the model-based approach for an instance-based one is two lines: replace the `LinearRegression` import and constructor with `KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=3)`. Everything around it — loading, shaping `X` and `y`, `fit`, `predict` — is identical. That uniform interface is Scikit-Learn's central design idea, and it is why the rest of the book can move quickly through many algorithms.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Change the code above to use k-nearest neighbours with k = 3. Exactly two lines change — which?
Step 3's cell has the two lines commented out (`# KNOB`): uncomment them, Run it, then Run step 4.

items.term: Same interface
items.text: Every scikit-learn model has `fit(X, y)` and `predict(X)`. That is why only the import and the constructor change.

items.term: `KNeighborsRegressor`
items.text: Instance-based: `fit` just stores the training rows. `predict` finds the `k` countries with the closest GDP and averages their satisfaction.

items.term: `n_neighbors`
items.text: How many neighbours to average. For Cyprus: k=1 → `[[7.2]]` (Israel); k=3 → `[[6.33333333]]` (Israel 7.2, Lithuania 5.9, Slovenia 5.9); k=5 → `[[6.26]]` (adds Italy 6.0, Spain 6.3).

items.term: Re-running
items.text: After editing step 3, Run step 4: step 3 changed, so it runs again first.

blocks.content:
### Recap

If the predictions are poor, the fixes are: use more attributes, get more or better-quality data, or select a more powerful model.

items.term: Bad Data: The First Four Challenges

blocks.content:
When a model disappoints, the book blames one of two things, **bad data** or **bad model**, and this lesson covers the four ways the data goes bad.

**The question this lesson answers:** before you blame the algorithm, what can be wrong with the data you trained it on?

### The big picture

```
What can go wrong
├── bad data    <- this lesson
│   ├── 1. insufficient quantity
│   ├── 2. nonrepresentative training data
│   ├── 3. poor-quality data
│   └── 4. irrelevant features
└── bad model   <- next lesson: overfitting and underfitting
```

These are data-quality problems of the kind you already chase in pipelines, with one nasty twist: the model still trains, still returns numbers, and is still wrong.

### 1 · Insufficient quantity

A toddler needs to be shown an apple a few times. ML algorithms need thousands of examples for simple problems and often millions for hard ones like image or speech recognition.

The Banko and Brill result the book cites is uncomfortable. On a natural-language disambiguation task (for example, choosing between "to", "two" and "too" from context), very different algorithms performed almost identically once given enough data (Figure 1-21 below). That prompted the famous argument that data matters more than algorithms.

The caveat matters too: small and medium datasets are still common, and getting more data is not always cheap or possible.

### 2 · Nonrepresentative training data

To generalise well, the training data must represent the cases you want to generalise to.

The book's check: the original life-satisfaction data had no country with a GDP per capita below 23,500 USD or above 62,500 USD. Adding a set of missing countries to the life-satisfaction data changes the model significantly (Figure 1-22 below) and shows the original linear fit was partly an artefact of who was in the sample. It is like testing a report on one region's partition and assuming it holds for every region.

A sample can fail to represent the real cases in two ways:

| Problem | What causes it |
|---|---|
| **sampling noise** | the sample is too small, so it is nonrepresentative by chance |
| **sampling bias** | the sampling method is flawed, so even a large sample is nonrepresentative |

The book's famous case of sampling bias: in 1936 the Literary Digest mailed a poll to about 10 million people, got 2.4 million answers, and predicted Landon would win 57% of the vote. Roosevelt won with 62%. A huge sample, picked the wrong way.

### 3 · Poor-quality data

Errors, outliers (instances far away from the rest) and noise make it harder to detect the underlying pattern, so cleaning is usually worth the time.

- **Clear outliers** are often best discarded or fixed by hand.
- **Instances missing a few features**, for example 5% of customers who did not give their age, force a choice:

| Option | In SQL terms |
|---|---|
| ignore the attribute | drop the `age` column |
| ignore those instances | `WHERE age IS NOT NULL` |
| fill the missing values, e.g. with the median age | `COALESCE(age, median_age)` |
| train one model with the feature and one without | build both, compare |

### 4 · Irrelevant features

Garbage in, garbage out. The cure is **feature engineering**: selecting the most useful existing features, extracting new ones by combining or reducing existing ones, and creating features from new data.

| Step | In SQL terms |
|---|---|
| select the most useful existing features | choose which columns go into the `SELECT` |
| extract new ones by combining or reducing existing ones | a derived column, like "wear and tear" from mileage and age |
| create features from new data | join in a new source |

**One-liner for your notes:** before blaming the algorithm, check the data: enough of it, representative of the real cases, clean, and made of relevant features.

blocks.caption: None of these are fixed by choosing a better algorithm. Each is a property of the data you fed in, and each fails quietly — the model still trains, still returns numbers, and is still wrong.

items.term: Bad data is worse than a bug because nothing fails
items.text: A broken pipeline usually fails loudly. Bad training data does not: the job succeeds, the model trains, the numbers come back, and the model is confidently wrong at exactly the inputs nobody sampled. Nothing in the run flags it. That is why the four checks in this lesson are about the data's coverage and cleanliness rather than about whether the job finished.

items.term: Only one of the two sampling problems is fixed by more data
items.text: Sampling noise is an accident of a small sample, so collecting more rows really does cure it. Sampling bias is in the method, so a bigger sample just makes the wrong answer more confident -- the Literary Digest got 2.4 million replies and still called the wrong winner. Before anyone proposes 'let's get more data', work out which of the two you have, because the same action fixes one and worsens the other.

items.term: The four missing-value options are not interchangeable
items.text: Dropping the column removes a feature for every row to deal with 5% of them. Filtering removes rows, and the customers who withheld their age may not resemble the ones who gave it. Filling with the median puts in a value nobody observed and quietly makes those rows look average. The fourth option -- train one model with the feature and one without -- is the only one that produces evidence instead of a preference, and it is cheap when the model is cheap.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: You have 30 rows of data and a model that fits them perfectly. Which of the four bad-data problems should worry you most?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The book lists four options for rows missing a feature and does not say which to pick. What does standard tooling actually do, and what does filling with the median do to those rows afterwards?

Look up: the scikit-learn user guide section 'Imputation of missing values', which implements three of the four options here and adds a fourth idea the lesson does not mention: an indicator column marking which values were filled in.

items.term: Overfitting and Underfitting

blocks.content:
The other two failures belong to the model, and they are opposites: overfitting is a model too complex for its data, underfitting is a model too simple for it, and their fixes run in opposite directions.

**The question this lesson answers:** the data is fine but the predictions are still bad. Is the model too complex or too simple, and what do you change?

### The big picture

```
too simple  <----- right balance ----->  too complex
UNDERFITTING                             OVERFITTING
inaccurate even on the         good on training data,
training examples              poor on new data
```

The figure at the end of this lesson draws the same three cases on six points.

### 1 · Overfitting: learning the noise

**Overfitting** means the model performs well on the training data but generalises poorly. It happens when the model is too complex relative to the amount and noisiness of the training data.

A high-degree polynomial fitted to the life-satisfaction data (Figure 1-23 below) will pass close to every training point and still make predictions you should not trust for a country it has not seen.

The book's clearest case: give a complex model uninformative attributes such as the country's name, and it may notice that every training country with a *w* in its name has a life satisfaction above 7: New Zealand (7.3), Norway (7.6), Sweden (7.3) and Switzerland (7.5). In SQL terms it has learned `CASE WHEN country LIKE '%w%' THEN 'above 7'`, true of every training country with a *w* in its name, and pure chance. Nothing says it holds for Rwanda or Zimbabwe.

The three fixes:

1. **Simplify the model:** fewer parameters, a simpler model class, or fewer attributes.
2. **Gather more training data.**
3. **Reduce the noise** in the training data by fixing errors and removing outliers.

### 2 · Regularization and hyperparameters

Constraining a model to make it simpler and reduce overfitting is called **regularization**, and its strength is controlled by a **hyperparameter**.

A hyperparameter is a parameter of the learning algorithm, not of the model: it is set before training and stays fixed during it.

| | Model parameter | Hyperparameter |
|---|---|---|
| Belongs to | the model | the learning algorithm |
| Example | $\theta_0$ and $\theta_1$ of the linear model | the regularization strength |
| Who sets it | training | you, before training |
| During training | tweaked to fit the data | stays fixed |
| Data-engineering picture | a value the job computes | a `--conf` setting you pass when you submit the job |

$\theta_0$ ("theta zero") is the line's starting value and $\theta_1$ ("theta one") is its slope — the two numbers training learns for the life-satisfaction model: 3.749 and 0.0000678.

Set the regularization hyperparameter very high and you get an almost flat model, which will not overfit but will also barely learn anything. The card below explains why, in terms of the line's height and slope. Tuning hyperparameters is a large part of building any ML system.

### 3 · Underfitting: too simple to learn

**Underfitting** is the mirror image: the model is too simple to learn the underlying structure, so its predictions are inaccurate even on the training examples. A linear model of life satisfaction is prone to it.

The fixes run the other way:

1. Select a more powerful model, with more parameters.
2. Feed better features, via feature engineering.
3. Reduce the constraints on the model by lowering the regularization hyperparameter.

### Side by side

| | Overfitting | Underfitting |
|---|---|---|
| Symptom | good on training data, poor on new data | inaccurate even on training data |
| Cause | too complex for the amount and noisiness of the data | too simple for the underlying structure |
| Fix the model | simplify it | a more powerful one |
| Fix the data | more data, less noise | better features |
| Regularization | constrain more | constrain less |

Stepping back, the summary is compact: your model must be neither too simple nor too complex, and your data must be sufficient, representative, clean and relevant.

**One-liner for your notes:** overfitting is a model too complex for its data (simplify, add data, remove noise), underfitting is one too simple (more power, better features, less regularization), and a hyperparameter is a setting you choose before training, not something training learns.

blocks.title: Parameters, degrees of freedom and regularization
blocks.content: The linear life-satisfaction model has two model parameters, θ₀ and θ₁. During training, the learning algorithm tweaks them to fit the data: θ₀ sets the height of the line and θ₁ sets its slope, so the algorithm has two degrees of freedom. If θ₁ were forced to 0, only one degree of freedom would be left: the algorithm could only move the line up or down, and it would end up around the mean. If θ₁ may change but must stay small, the algorithm has somewhere between one and two degrees of freedom, and that constraint is regularization. How strongly to constrain the model is set by the regularization hyperparameter, which belongs to the learning algorithm, is chosen before training and stays constant during it. A very large value gives an almost flat model, with a slope close to zero.

items.term: Complexity is always relative, never absolute
items.text: The definition says too complex relative to the amount and noisiness of the training data, and the word relative is load-bearing. No model is too complex on its own: a curve that overfits 27 countries could be exactly right with 27 million rows. That is why two of the three fixes -- more data, less noise -- change the data instead of the model. You are allowed to move either side of the comparison.

items.term: The w-in-the-name rule is the general shape of overfitting
items.text: Give a flexible model enough columns and few enough rows and it will always find some rule that holds across every training row. New Zealand, Norway, Sweden and Switzerland all score above 7 and all contain a w, so the rule is perfectly true of the training set and means nothing about Rwanda or Zimbabwe. The general lesson: a rule that is perfect on the training data is evidence about that data, not about the world -- which is precisely why the next lesson holds data back.

items.term: Regularization is a dial and both ends are failures
items.text: Constrain too little and the model traces the noise. Constrain so hard that the slope is pinned near zero and the line flattens out around the mean: it cannot overfit and it cannot learn either, as the card below works through in degrees of freedom. So the strength is something you tune and measure, never something you set once from principle -- and because it is a hyperparameter, training cannot choose it for you.

items.term: Testing, Validating and the Train-Dev Set

blocks.content:
To learn how a model will do on data it has never seen, you hold some data back and test on it, and you use each held-back set for one job only.

**The question this lesson answers:** how do you measure a model honestly, choose between models without fooling yourself, and tell overfitting apart from training data that does not look like production?

### The big picture: each set answers one question

| Set | Where it comes from | The question it answers |
|---|---|---|
| training set | most of your data | none: the model learns from it |
| validation set, also called dev set | held out from the training set | which candidate model is best? |
| test set | held out, used once at the very end | what error should you expect on new data? |
| train-dev set | held out from the training data, only when that data does not look like production | is the model overfitting? |

Think of the test set as a sealed reconciliation sample. You check the final result against it once. Keep tweaking until that one sample matches, and all you have proven is that it matches that sample.

### 1 · Training set and test set

The only way to know how well a model generalises is to try it on new cases. Putting it into production to find out works, but if it is bad your users will complain. So the standard practice is to split your data into a **training set** and a **test set** instead.

- The error rate on the test set is the **generalization error** (or *out-of-sample error*), and it estimates how the model will do on data it has never seen.
- A low training error with a high generalization error is overfitting, stated numerically.
- A common split is 80/20: 80% to train, 20% to test. With very large datasets far less than 20% is plenty in absolute terms. With 10 million instances, holding out 1% still gives a test set of 100,000, probably more than enough.

### 2 · Choosing between models without fooling yourself

Choosing between models is where people go wrong. Say you train 100 models with 100 different values of a hyperparameter and keep the one with the lowest test error. Tuning hyperparameters by repeatedly measuring on the test set means you are adapting the model to that particular test set, and the 5% error you measured becomes 15% in production.

The fix is **holdout validation**:

1. Hold out part of the training set as a **validation set** (also called the dev set).
2. Train candidate models on the reduced training set.
3. Pick the best one on the validation set.
4. Retrain that winner on the full training set.
5. Measure once on the test set.

In short: the test set is touched once, at the very end, after the winner has been retrained on the full training set (Figure 1-25 below).

The validation set has to be the right size:

| Validation set | What goes wrong |
|---|---|
| too small | the comparison is noisy, so you may pick a worse model by mistake |
| too large | the reduced training set is much smaller than the full training set, a poor basis for comparing candidates when the final model will be trained on the full set |

The book's picture for "too large": it is like selecting the fastest sprinter to run a marathon. Repeated **cross-validation** with many small validation sets addresses both, at the cost of training time: the training time is multiplied by the number of validation sets.

### 3 · Data mismatch and the train-dev set

One more trap: **data mismatch**, where lots of training data is available but not representative of production data. Andrew Ng's **train-dev set** diagnoses it. The card below walks through the book's flower-photo app.

Hold out part of the training data, train on the rest, and evaluate on the train-dev set first:

```
evaluate on the train-dev set (looks like the training data)
  |-- poor -> overfitting
  |-- good -> evaluate on the dev set (looks like production)
                |-- poor -> data mismatch
```

Poor performance on the train-dev set means overfitting; good performance there but poor performance on the dev set means data mismatch.

### 4 · The no free lunch theorem

The **no free lunch theorem**: with no assumptions about the data, no model is a priori better than any other. *A priori* means "in advance, before trying". Choosing a model is itself an assumption: pick a linear model and you are assuming the data is fundamentally linear. In practice you make reasonable assumptions and evaluate a handful of models.

**One-liner for your notes:** train on the training set, choose on the validation set, use a train-dev set to tell overfitting from data mismatch, and open the test set once at the end, or its error estimate stops meaning anything.

blocks.title: Why a dev-set failure means data mismatch
blocks.content: The book's example is a mobile app that identifies flowers from photos. You can download millions of flower pictures from the web, but perhaps only 1,000 pictures were actually taken with the app, and only those represent production. The validation (dev) set and the test set must be as representative of production as possible, so they are made only of app pictures: shuffle them and put half in each. The train-dev set is different: it is held out from the web pictures, so it looks like the training data. After training on the rest of the web pictures, evaluate on the train-dev set first. Poor results there mean the model has overfit the training set. Good results there but poor results on the dev set point to the mismatch between web pictures and app pictures; one remedy is to preprocess the web images to look more like app pictures and then retrain.

items.term: A set is spent the moment you make a decision from it
items.text: You do not have to train on a set to fit something to it. Pick the best of 100 hyperparameter values by test error and you have fitted one number -- the choice -- to that test set, which is how a measured 5% becomes 15% in production. The rule that falls out is mechanical and is the whole lesson: one set, one question, and the test set's question gets asked once.

items.term: Why the validation set has a size trade-off at all
items.text: Too small and the comparison is mostly noise, so you crown the wrong candidate. Too large and you are comparing models trained on far less data than the final model will get, which is the sprinter-picked-for-a-marathon picture. Cross-validation buys its way out of both by training many times over, and the price is stated plainly: training time multiplied by the number of validation sets. What you buy is a more trustworthy comparison, not a better model.

items.term: The train-dev set exists because two failures look identical
items.text: A bad dev score on its own cannot tell you whether the model memorised its training data or whether the training data simply does not resemble production. The train-dev set separates them by being held out from the data that looks like training: fail there and it is overfitting; pass there and fail on the dev set and it is data mismatch. Note the precondition -- you only need it when you knowingly trained on data that is not from production, as with web photos versus app photos.

items.term: The Eight-Step Project Checklist

blocks.content:
This chapter is one whole project from start to finish rather than a single concept: you play a newly hired data scientist at a fictional real estate company, and you build a model that predicts a district's median housing price from 1990 California census data.

**The question this lesson answers:** what are the eight steps a real ML project goes through, in what order, and why is it worth walking one of them end to end instead of studying algorithms one by one?

### The big picture

```
1 frame  ->  2 get data  ->  3 explore  ->  4 prepare
   ->  5 train  ->  6 fine-tune  ->  7 present
   ->  8 launch, monitor, maintain
```

That list is the chapter. Everything after this lesson is one pass along that arrow, using California housing as the worked example.

### 1 · The job, in one sentence

The company wants a model that predicts a district's median housing price from 1990 California census data — population, median income, housing age, and so on. A **district** is the book's word for a small geographic unit in that census, so one row of the data is one district, not one house.

In your terms: the input is a table with one row per district and a column per census attribute, and the column you are asked to produce is the district's median house value. Figure 2-1 below is what that data looks like plotted on a map.

### 2 · The eight steps

The order is: frame the problem, get the data, explore and visualize the data to gain insights, prepare the data for algorithms, select a model and train it, fine-tune it, present the solution, and finally launch, monitor, and maintain it in production.

Two things about the order are worth noticing now, because they both catch people out later:

| Step | Comes right after | Why the order matters |
|---|---|---|
| explore and visualize | get the data | you look before you clean, so cleaning is informed |
| launch, monitor, maintain | present the solution | the checklist ends in production, not in a notebook |

Exploration comes immediately after getting the data and before any preparation or modelling work begins. And the checklist **closes by launching, monitoring, and maintaining the system in production** — shipping is inside the job, not after it.

### 3 · Why messy, real data

Practise on real, messy, publicly available data — from places like OpenML, Kaggle, or the UC Irvine repository. It teaches things a clean toy dataset cannot: missing values, skewed distributions, capped attributes, and quirks that only show up when data was actually collected by an imperfect real-world process rather than generated for a textbook.

**Skewed** here means the values pile up at one end instead of sitting symmetrically around the middle. **Capped** means the collector clipped every value above some ceiling down to that ceiling. Both appear in this dataset, and both are found by looking, not by assuming.

You already know this instinct from ingest work: a source extract behaves nothing like a hand-written fixture, and the difference is exactly the quirks above.

### 4 · What you are supposed to take away

The value of reading this chapter is less about California housing specifically and more about internalizing the shape of the whole workflow. The dataset is a vehicle. The eight steps are the thing that transfers to the next project.

**One-liner for your notes:** eight steps — frame, get, explore, prepare, train, fine-tune, present, launch and maintain — and the point of the chapter is the shape of that list, not the housing data.

items.term: Why a checklist beats a clever method
items.text: The eight steps are ordered by what each one is allowed to assume. You cannot pick a performance measure before knowing what the business does with the number; you cannot clean data before seeing its quirks; you cannot trust a score from data that steered your choices. Most costly ML mistakes are order violations, not algorithm choices, which is why the list is worth memorising even though none of its items is difficult.

items.term: Why the project is worth more than the dataset
items.text: Every step here transfers unchanged to a different domain: the target changes, the framing questions do not. That is the argument for reading a full project once before studying algorithms — the algorithm is one box out of eight, and it is rarely the box that decides whether the project works.

items.term: Where 'messy' actually bites
items.text: Missing values, capped ceilings and skew are not cosmetic. Each one silently changes what a model can express: a capped target puts a hard ceiling on every prediction, missing values stop most algorithms outright, and skew makes scaling useless. A clean textbook dataset removes all three, which is exactly why it teaches you less.
