items.term: Framing the Problem

blocks.content:
Before writing any code you answer four questions about the problem itself: what the business actually wants, what it does today, what kind of learning problem this is, and which learning style fits.

**The question this lesson answers:** the company says "predict median house value". What has to be settled before a single line of code is written, and what does this particular project turn out to be?

### The big picture

| Question | The answer here |
|---|---|
| What is the business objective? | prices feed an investment-decision system |
| What is the current solution? | manual expert estimates, often off by 30% |
| What kind of problem? | supervised, regression, multiple, univariate |
| Which learning style? | plain batch learning |

### 1 · The model is never the goal

The first move is to understand the **business objective** — a model is rarely the end goal, it is an input to something else. Here, the predicted median house value will feed into a separate downstream system that decides whether a given area is worth investing in, so getting the number right actually affects revenue decisions. Figure 2-2 below draws that chain.

This is the same reasoning you already apply to a table: nobody wants the table, they want the report that reads it. Knowing the consumer tells you what accuracy is worth and what an error costs.

### 2 · Ask what exists today

It is also worth asking what the current solution looks like, because it sets a performance baseline and often hints at how to attack the problem. In this case, the current solution is manual: experts estimate district prices by hand using complex rules, and when checked against real numbers their estimates are frequently off by more than 30%. That gap is the opportunity for a learned model.

A **baseline** is the score you have to beat for the project to be worth anything. Without one, a model's number means nothing — "off by 15%" is a triumph against 30% and a disaster against 2%.

### 3 · Classify the problem

With the objective clear, the next job is to classify the learning problem along the axes from Chapter 1.

| Axis | Verdict | Because |
|---|---|---|
| supervised or not | supervised | every training example comes with the correct price |
| regression or classification | regression | the output is a number, not a category |
| how many inputs | multiple | many input features are used |
| how many outputs | univariate | one value predicted per district |

Since every training example comes with the correct price attached, this is **supervised learning**. Since the output is a number rather than a category, it is **regression** — specifically *multiple* regression, because many input features are used, and *univariate* regression, because only one value is predicted per district. Predicting several values per district would make it **multivariate** instead.

Two words that sound alike and are not: *multiple* counts the inputs, *multivariate* counts the outputs.

### 4 · Batch or online

Finally, because the data is small enough to fit in memory and there is no need to react to a live incoming stream, plain **batch learning** is the right call rather than online learning. Batch learning trains on all the data at once; online learning keeps learning in small steps as new data arrives. It is the full-refresh versus incremental-load choice, and here nothing forces the incremental version.

**One-liner for your notes:** frame first — objective, current baseline, problem type — and this project lands on supervised, univariate multiple regression, trained in batch.

items.term: Framing decides what 'good' means
items.text: The same predictions can be excellent or useless depending on the downstream consumer. If an investment system only needs a ranking of districts, being consistently 10% low costs nothing; if it feeds a price quoted to a customer, it is fatal. That is why the objective is settled before the metric, and the metric before the model.

items.term: A baseline is a decision tool, not a formality
items.text: The existing manual estimates are off by more than 30%. That single number tells you what success looks like, whether the project is worth funding, and when to stop improving. A model with no baseline cannot be called good or bad — only measured.

items.term: Why the four axes are worth classifying explicitly
items.text: Supervised or not, regression or classification, batch or online: each answer eliminates most of the library. Naming them turns 'which algorithm?' — an unbounded question — into a shortlist, and it exposes wrong assumptions early, while changing them is still free.

items.term: Choosing a Performance Measure — RMSE and MAE

blocks.content:
Before training anything you must pick the single number that says how wrong the model is, and for regression that number is usually RMSE.

**The question this lesson answers:** the model will predict a district's median house value and be wrong by some amount on every district. How do you turn thousands of individual misses into one score, and what does the choice of score change?

### The big picture

| Measure | Averages | Punishes big misses | Norm |
|---|---|---|---|
| RMSE | squared errors, then a square root | hard | ℓ2, Euclidean |
| MAE | absolute errors | evenly | ℓ1, Manhattan |

An **error** here is one district's prediction minus its true value. Both measures take the whole list of those errors and boil it down to one number; they differ only in how they treat the big ones.

### 1 · RMSE, step by step

For a regression problem the standard performance measure is the **root mean square error (RMSE)**: take the prediction error for every instance, square it, average those squares, then take the square root.

Read the recipe in that order, because the order is the name read backwards:

1. **error** — prediction minus truth, for one district
2. **square** — makes every error positive, and makes a big one count far more than a small one
3. **mean** — average those squares over all districts
4. **root** — undo the squaring, so the score comes back in the same units as a house price

Squaring means large errors count disproportionately more than small ones, so RMSE is a measure that punishes big misses hard. Equation 2-1 below is exactly those four steps written in symbols, with the explanation underneath it.

### 2 · MAE, and why you would want it

An alternative is the **mean absolute error (MAE)**, which just averages the absolute value of the errors instead of squaring them. **Absolute value** means drop the minus sign: a miss of −30 and a miss of +30 both count as 30. Equation 2-2 below is that one.

Because RMSE squares each error first, one wildly wrong district moves RMSE far more than it moves MAE. That is precisely why **RMSE is more outlier-sensitive than MAE**. An **outlier** is a value that sits far away from the rest of the data. When outliers are rare — which is typical for a bell-shaped distribution — RMSE is usually preferred; but if a dataset has many extreme outliers, MAE can be the safer choice.

### 3 · Both are distances, and there is a family

Both are ways of measuring the distance between two vectors — the vector of predictions and the vector of true values — and they correspond to different mathematical **norms**. A norm is just a rule for measuring length or distance.

- RMSE corresponds to the **Euclidean (ℓ2) norm**, the straight-line distance everyone is intuitively familiar with.
- MAE corresponds to the **ℓ1 (Manhattan) norm**, the distance you would travel along a city grid of blocks: no diagonals, so you add up the sideways and forwards moves.

The general pattern is the **ℓk norm**, and the higher k is, the more the measure is dominated by the largest values and the more it ignores small ones. RMSE at k = 2 already leans that way; MAE at k = 1 does not.

### 4 · The step people skip: check the assumptions

A smaller but important step: before writing any code, list out and double-check every assumption made so far.

Here that means confirming with the team downstream that they genuinely need continuous prices rather than, say, price *categories* ("cheap"/"medium"/"expensive") — because if categories were all they needed, this should have been framed as classification, not regression, and finding that out after months of work would be a disaster.

This is the contract conversation you would have before building a table: agreeing the grain and the data type with the consumer, while it still costs nothing to change.

**One-liner for your notes:** RMSE squares, averages and roots the errors (ℓ2) and punishes big misses hardest; MAE averages absolute errors (ℓ1) and shrugs at outliers — pick with your outliers, and check the downstream team really wants numbers at all.

blocks.title: Equation 2-1
blocks.caption: Root mean square error (RMSE)
blocks.explain:
**Why the equation looks like this**

The score has to turn thousands of separate misses into one number, and it has to end up in the same
units as a house price so a person can read it. Those two requirements produce the four operations in
Equation 2-1, in that order: subtract to get each miss, square so that a miss below and a miss above
cannot cancel out, average so the score does not grow just because you scored more districts, then
take the square root to get back out of "squared dollars" and into dollars.

**Is this standard?** Yes. RMSE is the default performance measure for regression and this is its
canonical form — nothing here was simplified for the housing example. Equation 2-2 (MAE) is the same
idea with the square-and-root pair replaced by absolute value.

**The general form.** Both belong to one family, the norms: raise each error to the power k, add them
up, then take the k-th root.

| k | Name | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | MAE, Manhattan | every miss counts in proportion |
| 2 | RMSE, Euclidean | big misses count far more |
| higher | the k-th norm | the single largest miss dominates |

**Terms this introduces:** an **instance** is one row being scored, here one district; a **vector** is
just an ordered list of numbers, so "the vector of predictions" means all the predictions in row
order; a **norm** is a rule for measuring the length of such a list.

**Every piece of Equation 2-1**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| RMSE(X, h) | R M S E of X and h | the score, for this data and this model |
| X | capital X | the inputs, one row per instance |
| h | h | the model itself (the book says hypothesis) |
| m | m | how many instances are being scored |
| i | i | which instance, counting 1 up to m |
| x⁽ⁱ⁾ | x superscript i | the inputs of instance number i |
| y⁽ⁱ⁾ | y superscript i | the true value for instance number i |
| h(x⁽ⁱ⁾) | h of x superscript i | what the model predicts for instance i |
| the sum sign | sum from i equals 1 to m | add the bracket up over every instance |
| the squared bracket | squared | multiply the bracket by itself |
| one over m | one over m | divide the total by m, giving the average |
| the root sign | square root | undo the squaring, back to price units |

**The formula in plain words**

RMSE = the square root of ( the average of ( prediction − true value ) squared ).

MAE = the average of the size of ( prediction − true value ), ignoring the sign.

**With real numbers**

This lesson is choosing the measure, so it has no predictions of its own yet. The first real ones
arrive later in the chapter: the linear model's first training district is predicted at 243,700
against a true label of 458,300, so that one instance's error is 458,300 − 243,700 = 214,600. Square
that, do the same for every one of the 16,512 training districts, average the squares and take the
root, and the chapter reports a training RMSE of roughly 68,600 USD.

The gap between one 214,600 miss and a 68,600 overall score is the squaring at work: a handful of
very large misses pull RMSE up far more than many small ones do.

---

blocks.title: Equation 2-2
blocks.caption: Mean absolute error (MAE)

items.term: Why squaring changes the model you end up with
items.text: The measure is not just a report card — tuning, model selection and often training itself chase whatever it rewards. Choosing RMSE means you have decided that one district wrong by 200,000 is worse than four wrong by 50,000. Choosing MAE means you have decided they are equally bad. Neither is objectively right; it depends on what a large error costs the business.

items.term: Outlier-sensitivity cuts both ways
items.text: RMSE's sensitivity is a defect when the extreme values are data-collection errors, and a feature when they are real and expensive. The question to ask is not 'are there outliers?' but 'are the outliers real, and do they matter more per unit than ordinary errors?'

items.term: Why the root is not cosmetic
items.text: Dropping the square root gives the mean squared error, which ranks models identically to RMSE — the ordering is unchanged. The root exists so the number is readable in the target's own units, which is what lets a stakeholder judge whether the error is acceptable. Same decision, communicable.

items.term: Fetching the Data with a Reusable Function

blocks.content:
Do not download the data by hand: write a small function that checks for the file, downloads and extracts it only if it is missing, and returns a DataFrame.

**The question this lesson answers:** the housing data is one compressed `housing.tgz` archive containing a single CSV. Why wrap fetching it in a function instead of just clicking download once and moving on?

### The big picture

```
call function
   -> is datasets/housing.tgz already there?
        yes -> just read the CSV
        no  -> download, extract, then read the CSV
   -> return a DataFrame
```

### 1 · Where the code runs

The chapter uses **Google Colab**, a free hosted Jupyter environment, so nobody needs to install anything locally. A **notebook** is a document where code cells and their output live together; Figures 2-3, 2-4 and 2-5 below show the notebook list, a notebook, and how files move in and out of a Colab session.

That is a convenience, not the lesson. The lesson is the design habit in the function below.

### 2 · Why a function and not a manual download

Rather than manually downloading and unzipping a file once, you write a small function that does the whole job — check whether the data is already present, download it if not, extract it, and load it into a DataFrame.

This matters for reasons that go beyond this one dataset:

| A function gives you | What that means in practice |
|---|---|
| rerunnable | the source data changes, you just call it again |
| schedulable | it can be run automatically at intervals |
| portable | a new machine, a teammate, a server: one line |

A function like this is trivially rerunnable when the source data changes, it can be scheduled to run automatically at intervals, and installing the same dataset on a new machine becomes a one-line operation instead of a manual multi-step ritual anyone could get wrong. This is the same argument you would make for putting an extract in a job rather than in someone's shell history.

### 3 · Idempotent, from the start

Notice the function is **idempotent**: calling it again after the data already exists does nothing destructive, it just loads what is on disk. That property — safe to call repeatedly — is worth building into any data-fetching code from the start rather than bolting it on later.

You know the property from reruns: a job you can fire twice without doubling rows or deleting yesterday's output. Same idea, three lines of Python.

### 4 · Reading the code card below

The card below is that function. Three details carry the whole idea:

1. `tarball_path.is_file()` is the guard — the archive is downloaded and extracted **only when that local file is missing**.
2. `urllib.request.urlretrieve` fetches the archive; `tarfile` unpacks it into `datasets`.
3. The last line calls `pd.read_csv()` on the extracted CSV, so the function **returns a Pandas DataFrame** built from it.

Nothing in it is specific to housing data. It is the same shape of function you would write for almost any dataset that lives behind a URL.

**One-liner for your notes:** fetch data with a guarded, idempotent function that returns a DataFrame, so the same one line works on any machine and can be rerun or scheduled safely.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
import tarfile
import urllib.request

def load_housing_data():
    tarball_path = Path("datasets/housing.tgz")
    if not tarball_path.is_file():
        Path("datasets").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        url = "https://github.com/ageron/data/raw/main/housing.tgz"
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, tarball_path)
        with tarfile.open(tarball_path) as housing_tarball:
            housing_tarball.extractall(path="datasets")
    return pd.read_csv(Path("datasets/housing/housing.csv"))

housing = load_housing_data()
```

items.term: Idempotence is a correctness property, not a convenience
items.text: A fetch that is safe to call twice can be retried after a failure, run on a schedule, and placed at the top of a notebook that gets re-executed dozens of times. Without it, every one of those becomes a decision someone has to make correctly each time. The same reasoning is why reruns are designed into a pipeline rather than avoided.

items.term: What this function deliberately does not do
items.text: It never checks whether the remote file changed. Presence of the local tarball is the only test, so a refreshed source is invisible until someone deletes the local copy. That is a reasonable trade for a book dataset and a real hazard in production, where the usual answers are a version in the filename or a checksum comparison.

items.term: Code as the installation instruction
items.text: A written procedure drifts from what people actually do; a function cannot. Putting the fetch in code makes the dataset reproducible on a new machine at the same moment it makes it schedulable — one artifact, two problems solved.

items.term: A First Look at the Data

blocks.content:
Four cheap Pandas calls and one grid of histograms tell you most of what is wrong with a dataset before you touch it.

**The question this lesson answers:** the housing CSV is loaded into a DataFrame. What do you look at first, and what does looking actually catch in this particular dataset?

### The big picture

| Call | Answers |
|---|---|
| `head()` | what are the columns and what does a row look like |
| `info()` | how many rows, how many non-nulls, what types |
| `value_counts()` | what values does this text column really take |
| `describe()` | how is each numeric column distributed |
| `hist()` | what shape is every numeric column, all at once |

### 1 · The four calls

`head()` shows the first few rows so you can see the ten columns firsthand: longitude, latitude, housing age, room and bedroom counts, population, household count, median income, the target (median house value), and one text column, ocean proximity. Figure 2-6 below is that output. The **target** is the column you are trying to predict.

`info()` gives row counts and per-column non-null counts and types in one shot — here it immediately surfaces that `total_bedrooms` is missing 207 values out of 20,640, something you must decide how to handle before training. **Non-null** means present; the gap between 20,640 and 20,433 is the missing ones, and the card below does that subtraction.

`value_counts()` on the one text column shows it is really a small set of repeating categories, that is, a **categorical attribute** in disguise — a column whose values come from a short fixed list, like an enum, not free text.

`describe()` summarizes each numeric column's count, mean, min, max, standard deviation, and percentile cut points — the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles. A **percentile cut point** is the value below which that percentage of the data falls: the 25th percentile is the value below which 25% of the data falls. Figure 2-7 below is that table.

If you have ever opened a new source table with a row count, a `COUNT(*)` per column for nulls, a `GROUP BY` on the one suspicious string column and a min/max sweep, you have already done all four. These are the same checks with shorter names.

### 2 · The histogram grid

Plotting a histogram of every numeric attribute at once is often the fastest way to build intuition. A **histogram** buckets a column's values and draws how many rows land in each bucket, so its shape shows you the distribution rather than a summary of it. Figure 2-8 below is the grid for all of them.

Doing that here reveals real data quirks that would otherwise cause silent problems downstream:

| Quirk | What it means |
|---|---|
| income is rescaled and capped | the numbers are not dollars |
| housing age and the target are capped | a hard ceiling was applied |
| attributes sit on wildly different scales | one column dwarfs another numerically |
| many histograms are skewed | values pile up on one side |

**Capped** means every value above some ceiling was clipped down to that ceiling. That is the dangerous one here: because the target is capped, **the model can never learn to predict a genuine price above that ceiling unless something is done about it**. **Skewed** means the distribution leans rather than sitting symmetrically around its middle, which some algorithms handle poorly.

### 3 · The income scale, spelled out

Median income is not raw dollars but a rescaled and capped value. The card below records what the team who collected the data said: the values were scaled and capped at 15 (actually 15.0001) for higher incomes and at 0.5 (actually 0.4999) for lower ones, and they represent roughly tens of thousands of dollars — so a value of 3 means about 30,000 dollars.

Note how that was found: the histogram looked wrong, and then somebody *asked the source owner*. No amount of staring at the column would have produced the multiplier.

### 4 · Notice now, fix later

None of this is fixed yet — the point of this pass is just to notice it. Missing values, capping, scale differences and skew each get their own lesson later in the chapter. Writing them down now is what stops them being discovered by a model that quietly learns the artifact instead of the pattern.

**One-liner for your notes:** `head`, `info`, `value_counts`, `describe` and a histogram grid cost nothing and surface the 207 missing bedrooms, the rescaled capped income, the capped target, mixed scales and skew — notice them now, fix them later.

blocks.title: Worked out: the 207 gaps and the income scale
blocks.content: The `info()` output reports 20,640 entries, but the `total_bedrooms` column shows only 20,433 non-null values, so 20,640 − 20,433 = 207 districts are missing that feature. `describe()` ignores the nulls, which is why its count for `total_bedrooms` is also 20,433. For median income, the team that collected the data explains that the values were scaled and capped at 15 (actually 15.0001) for higher incomes and at 0.5 (actually 0.4999) for lower incomes. The numbers represent roughly tens of thousands of dollars, so a value of 3 means about 30,000 dollars. That is why the median income histogram does not show raw US dollars.

items.term: Why looking precedes cleaning
items.text: Every cleaning decision later in the chapter is answering something found in this pass: the 207 gaps set up imputation, the capped target sets up a conversation with the business, the mixed scales set up feature scaling, the skew sets up log transforms. Cleaning before looking means guessing which problems you have.

items.term: A capped target is a business problem, not a code problem
items.text: No transformation recovers a value that was clipped before the data reached you. The real options are to get proper labels for the capped districts, or to remove them and state that the model is not valid above the ceiling. Both require a decision from whoever owns the requirement, which is why it is raised now and not silently patched.

items.term: Summary statistics hide shape
items.text: `describe()` gives a mean, a spread and percentiles — all of which can be identical for distributions that look nothing alike. The histogram grid is cheap precisely because it shows shape rather than summarising it, and shape is what tells you whether scaling or a log transform is needed.

items.term: Data Snooping Bias and Setting Aside a Test Set

blocks.content:
Cut off a test set now, before you have properly looked at the data, because your own brain leaks information from data you have seen into decisions you make later.

**The question this lesson answers:** why carve off 20% of the rows before exploring them, and what goes wrong with the obvious way of doing the split?

### The big picture

```
all rows -> shuffle -> first 20%  = test set (locked away)
                    -> the rest   = training set (you work here)
```

### 1 · Data snooping bias

It feels backwards to carve off part of the data before you have even really looked at it, but there is a sharp reason to do it early: your own brain is a powerful pattern detector, and if you eyeball the full dataset (including what will become the test set) you may notice a pattern that steers your model choice — and then your later measurement of generalization error on that same data will be **too optimistic**. That failure mode has a name, **data snooping bias**, and it is entirely self-inflicted.

**Generalization error** is how wrong the model is on data it has never seen. That is the only number anyone actually cares about, and it can only be measured on data that influenced nothing.

The closest thing in your world is tuning a transformation until one reconciliation sample matches. Afterwards that sample proves nothing, because it is no longer independent of the thing it is checking.

### 2 · The simple fix

The conceptually simplest fix is to randomly shuffle the rows and slice off, say, 20% as a test set, set it aside, and never touch it again until the very end.

The function in the card below is that idea in four lines:

1. `np.random.permutation(len(data))` shuffles the row positions, not the rows themselves
2. `test_set_size = int(len(data) * test_ratio)` is how many rows the test set gets — multiply the row count by the ratio and drop the fraction
3. the first `test_set_size` shuffled positions become the test set
4. the rest become the training set

On the full housing dataset that is int(20,640 × 0.2) = 4,128 test rows and 16,512 training rows, which the card below works through.

### 3 · The flaw in it

A naive implementation of this idea works, but has a real flaw: run it again — say, after fetching updated data — and you get a *different* random test set each time.

`np.random.permutation()` is called without a fixed **seed**, the starting number that makes a random sequence repeatable, so **calling the function twice on the same dataset produces two different splits**. That matters because over repeated runs your model quietly gets exposed to instances that were supposed to stay held out. Nothing errors. The held-out set simply stops being held out, one rerun at a time.

| Run | Test set | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| first | a random 20% | fine so far |
| second | a different random 20% | rows from run 1 are now training rows |
| after many | a moving target | the model has effectively seen everything |

The next lesson covers the more robust fixes to this different-split-every-run problem.

**One-liner for your notes:** split before you look, because looking biases your choices; and a shuffle with no fixed seed leaks the test set back into training one rerun at a time.

blocks.title: Worked out: how many rows go to the test set
blocks.content: The line `test_set_size = int(len(data) * test_ratio)` multiplies the number of rows by the test ratio, and `int()` drops any fraction. The book runs the function on the full housing dataset, which has 20,640 rows, with a ratio of 0.2: int(20,640 × 0.2) = 4,128. The first 4,128 shuffled indices become the test set, and the remaining 20,640 − 4,128 = 16,512 indices become the training set. That matches the book's output, where `len(train_set)` is 16512 and `len(test_set)` is 4128.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import numpy as np

def shuffle_and_split_data(data, test_ratio):
    shuffled_indices = np.random.permutation(len(data))
    test_set_size = int(len(data) * test_ratio)
    test_indices = shuffled_indices[:test_set_size]
    train_indices = shuffled_indices[test_set_size:]
    return data.iloc[train_indices], data.iloc[test_indices]
```

items.term: Why the leak is in you, not the code
items.text: Data snooping needs no bug. You look at the whole dataset, spot a pattern, pick a model that exploits it, and the test set that later scores that model already contributed to choosing it. The score is then a measure of fit to data you used, dressed up as a measure of generalization. No code review catches it, which is why the split comes first.

items.term: What 'held out' has to mean
items.text: The test set must not influence any decision: not the model family, not the features, not the cleaning rules, not the thresholds. Every decision you make with a look at those rows spends a little of the honesty of the final number, and nothing spends it back.

items.term: Why a moving split is worse than a bad split
items.text: A fixed but unlucky split gives you a skewed estimate you can reason about. A split that changes on every run gives you an estimate that improves for the wrong reason, run by run, with no moment where anything looks wrong. Slow, invisible failures are more expensive than loud ones.

items: Name the failure this naive shuffle-based split has when you rerun it after fetching a refreshed dataset.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The book later replaces this shuffle with a split based on hashing an identifier. What problem does hashing an identifier solve that a fixed random seed does not?
Look up: the "Create a Test Set" section of this chapter, and the scikit-learn user guide section "Common pitfalls and recommended practices" on data leakage.

items.term: Stratified Sampling for a Representative Test Set

blocks.content:
Do not trust luck to give you a representative test set: bucket the most predictive attribute and draw the test set proportionally from each bucket.

**The question this lesson answers:** a purely random 20% could, by chance, contain too few low-income districts. How do you force the test set to mirror the full dataset on the attribute that matters most?

### The big picture

```
income (continuous)
   -> pd.cut into 5 buckets  = strata
   -> draw 20% from EACH bucket
   -> test set mirrors the full income distribution
```

### 1 · Two different ways a sample goes wrong

Purely random sampling for the test set is fine when the dataset is large relative to the number of attributes, but it carries a real risk otherwise: a test set that ends up skewed relative to the true population purely by chance.

| Name | Cause | Cured by |
|---|---|---|
| sampling noise | pure chance in a small sample | a bigger or stratified sample |
| sampling bias | a flawed sampling method | fixing the method |

Chapter 1 calls this chance-driven skew **sampling noise** and keeps the name **sampling bias** for skew caused by a flawed sampling method, although this chapter warns that a sample skewed this way would still leave the results quite biased.

The book's analogy is a phone survey — if the true population is 51.1% female, a well-run survey deliberately keeps that ratio in its sample rather than trusting pure luck to land close to it.

### 2 · Choosing what to mirror

Since experts believe median income is unusually predictive of housing price, the test set should mirror the full dataset's income distribution rather than risk a random skew. You mirror the attribute that drives the answer; mirroring everything at once is not possible.

Because income is continuous, the first step is to bucket it into a small number of categories using `pd.cut()`, creating discrete **strata** — a stratum is just one bucket that sampling will treat as its own pool. The card below cuts income at 1.5, 3.0, 4.5 and 6.0 into five labelled categories, and Figure 2-9 below is the histogram of them.

Care is needed here, because too many strata (or ones that are too small) make the per-stratum estimate noisy. A bucket with four rows in it cannot be sampled proportionally in any meaningful way.

### 3 · Stratified sampling

With the strata defined, **stratified sampling** draws the right proportion of instances from each income bucket rather than sampling the whole dataset uniformly, so the resulting test set's income distribution closely tracks the full dataset's, unlike a purely random split. Figure 2-10 below compares the two side by side.

Scikit-Learn's `train_test_split()` accepts a `stratify` argument that does exactly this in one call — pass it the column to stratify on, and it **guarantees the same category proportions land in both the train and test halves**.

If you have ever sampled a fact table for testing with a `GROUP BY` and a proportional take per group, rather than a flat `LIMIT`, this is that, with one argument.

### 4 · Drop the scaffolding

Once the split is made, the temporary income-category column itself is dropped, since **it was only a means to a representative split, not a modelling feature**. Leaving it in would hand the model a coarse copy of a column it already has.

**One-liner for your notes:** bucket the most predictive attribute into strata, pass it to `stratify` so both halves keep the same proportions, then drop the bucket column — it was scaffolding, not a feature.

blocks.caption: Histogram of income categories
blocks.alt: Figure 2-9: Histogram of income categories

blocks.title: Figure 2-10
blocks.caption: Sampling bias comparison of stratified versus purely random sampling
blocks.alt: Figure 2-10: Sampling bias comparison of stratified versus purely random sampling

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
housing["income_cat"] = pd.cut(housing["median_income"],
                               bins=[0., 1.5, 3.0, 4.5, 6., np.inf],
                               labels=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

strat_train_set, strat_test_set = train_test_split(
    housing, test_size=0.2, stratify=housing["income_cat"], random_state=42)
```

items.term: Noise and bias need different fixes
items.text: Sampling noise shrinks as the sample grows; sampling bias does not, because the method itself is wrong. Doubling a badly drawn sample gives you twice as much of the same skew. Knowing which one you have tells you whether to collect more data or to change how you collect it.

items.term: Why you stratify on one attribute and not all of them
items.text: Strata multiply: stratifying on two attributes with five buckets each gives twenty-five cells, and some will be nearly empty. So you spend the budget on the attribute most predictive of the target — here median income — and accept that the rest are only balanced on average.

items.term: The bucket boundaries are a judgement
items.text: Too few strata and the split is barely better than random; too many, or too small, and each stratum's proportion is itself noisy. The cut points here were chosen to leave every bucket with a workable number of districts, which is a design decision, not something the data dictated.

items.term: Visualizing Geographical Data

blocks.content:
The data has latitude and longitude, so the first exploration plot is a map — and three plotting arguments turn that map from a shapeless outline into a picture of where the money is.

**The question this lesson answers:** every district has coordinates. What can a scatterplot of them tell you that a table of numbers cannot, and how do you get it to show more than the outline of California?

### The big picture

```
plain scatter      -> the shape of California, little else
+ low alpha        -> density becomes visible
+ size and colour  -> population and price on the same map
```

### 1 · Explore the training set, only

With the test set safely set aside, **exploration begins on a copy of the training set only**. A copy, so that anything you scribble onto the data during exploration cannot damage the original; the training set only, so the held-out rows stay genuinely unseen.

Because this dataset carries latitude and longitude, the natural first plot is a scatterplot of every district's location — which, unsurprisingly, traces the outline of California, but on its own does not reveal much more than that. Figure 2-11 below is that first attempt.

### 2 · Fix the plot, not the data

The fix is tuning the plot's visual parameters rather than the data. Setting the point transparency (**`alpha`**) low makes overlapping points visually accumulate, so dense clusters of districts become visibly darker than sparse ones.

That single change turns a shapeless scatter into a clear picture of where districts are concentrated — the Bay Area, the Los Angeles and San Diego corridor, and a line of moderately dense districts running through the Central Valley. Figure 2-12 below is the result.

The trick is worth remembering generally: when a plot of twenty thousand rows looks like a solid blob, the blob is data, not noise. Transparency is how you read it.

### 3 · Four variables on one picture

Going further, two more variables are encoded into the same plot:

| Plot argument | Carries | Reads as |
|---|---|---|
| `s` | population | circle size |
| `c` | median house value | circle colour |

In the `housing.plot()` call in the card below, `s` maps population to each circle's size and `c="median_house_value"` maps the target to **the colour of each circle**. Using a blue-to-red colour map, that produces a single figure — Figure 2-13 below — that visually links price to both location and density: **prices run noticeably higher near the coast and in high-population areas**. Red is expensive, blue is cheap, larger circles are more populated areas.

So position, size and colour carry four columns at once: longitude, latitude, population and price.

### 4 · A hint, not a proof

This kind of finding is a **hint, not proof**, but it is exactly the sort of signal that later informs **feature engineering** — inventing new input columns from the ones you have. For instance, it is why proximity to the ocean, or a computed distance-to-cluster-centre feature, might matter for the model. Both of those show up later in this chapter.

A map that shows price rising near the coast does not establish that the coast sets prices. It tells you where to look next, which is all an exploration plot is ever for.

**One-liner for your notes:** explore on a copy of the training set, use low `alpha` to reveal density and `s`/`c` to add population and price, and treat what you see as a hint that guides feature engineering, not as proof.

items.term: Plots are for generating hypotheses, not confirming them
items.text: The map shows price rising near the coast. It cannot tell you whether the coast causes the price, whether both follow income, or whether the effect is really about density. Its whole job is to point at a feature worth engineering — and the engineered feature is then judged by the model, not by the picture.

items.term: Why over-plotting is a real failure mode
items.text: Twenty thousand opaque dots draw the same black shape whether the data is uniform or piled into three cities. Transparency, sampling or binning are the standard answers, and choosing none of them is choosing to see nothing. The first plot in this lesson is exactly that mistake, kept in deliberately.

items.term: Encoding more variables has a ceiling
items.text: Position, size and colour carry four columns on one map, which is close to the limit before the picture stops being readable. Past that you split into small multiples rather than adding channels — a limit of human vision, not of the plotting library.

items.term: Looking for Correlations

blocks.content:
The correlation coefficient scores how strongly two columns move together in a straight line, and reading those scores points you at the attribute that matters most.

**The question this lesson answers:** which of the ten attributes actually relate to median house value, how strongly, and what does the correlation number fail to tell you?

### The big picture

| Coefficient near | Means |
|---|---|
| +1 | strong positive linear relationship |
| −1 | strong negative linear relationship |
| 0 | no *linear* relationship — possibly still a relationship |

### 1 · Reading the number

Because this dataset is small enough to work with directly, it is cheap to compute the standard (**Pearson**) correlation coefficient between every pair of attributes and then read off how strongly each one correlates with the target.

A coefficient near +1 means a strong positive linear relationship — as one goes up, so does the other. Near −1 means **a strong negative linear relationship**. Near 0 means no *linear* relationship — and importantly, that last case does not mean no relationship at all, only that it is not linear. Two columns can be locked together in a U-shape and still score 0, because the measure is blind to anything but a straight-line trend. Figure 2-16 below shows several datasets with their coefficients, including exactly that trap.

### 2 · What the housing numbers say

Here, **median income comes out as by far the strongest positive correlate with house value**, while latitude shows a mild negative one — **prices trend slightly downward moving north**.

The card below has the sorted list: median income at about 0.69, then total rooms at about 0.14, and latitude at about −0.14. Two things fall out of those numbers:

| Reading | Why |
|---|---|
| income dominates | 0.69 is five times the next positive value |
| the north trend is mild | −0.14 is a long way from −1 |

Strength is distance from 0, whatever the sign. The sign only tells you the direction.

### 3 · The scatter matrix

A **scatter matrix** — a grid plotting every chosen numeric attribute against every other one — is a faster way to eyeball many of these relationships at once than reading a table of numbers. Figure 2-14 below is it.

With many attributes the number of plots explodes, so it pays to first narrow down to a handful of the most promising ones: the data now has 11 numerical attributes, and plotting every pair would take 11² = 121 plots, so the book plots only four.

### 4 · What the number hides

Zooming in specifically on median income versus house value — Figure 2-15 below — confirms the trend is real and reasonably tight. But the plot also exposes something the correlation number alone hides: **flat horizontal bands of oddly identical price values**. One is the capped 500,000 USD ceiling noticed earlier; there are a few other suspicious flat lines too.

That is a pattern worth investigating or removing before training, since a model could otherwise learn to reproduce these artifacts of the data rather than genuine price behaviour. A row of hundreds of districts sharing one exact price is a collection artifact, and a model has no way of knowing that.

**One-liner for your notes:** correlation scores straight-line agreement only — median income at about 0.69 dominates here — and you still plot it, because the plot shows the capped price bands the number cannot.

Median income, at about 0.69, is far above the next positive value (total_rooms, at about 0.14), so it is by far the strongest positive correlate. Latitude is negative but only about −0.14, a long way from −1, so the link is mild: prices have a slight tendency to go down as you go north. items.term: What a correlation of zero does and does not license
items.text: Zero means no straight-line trend. A perfectly deterministic U-shaped relationship scores zero, and dropping that attribute because of the number would throw away a strong predictor. This is why the coefficient is read next to a scatterplot, never instead of one.

items.term: Correlation with the target is a starting shortlist
items.text: It ranks attributes one at a time, so it misses features that only matter in combination and over-rewards features that duplicate each other. It is a cheap way to decide what to look at first — the model's own importance scores, later in the chapter, are the real verdict.

items.term: Artifacts are the dangerous kind of pattern
items.text: The flat price bands are a property of how the data was collected, not of the housing market. A model has no way to tell those apart and will happily learn to reproduce the ceiling. Finding them now is the difference between a documented limitation and a confident wrong prediction.

items.term: Engineering New Attributes from Ratios

blocks.content:
A ratio between two existing columns can carry more signal than either column on its own, and here one invented ratio beats both of its ingredients.

**The question this lesson answers:** total rooms per district correlates only weakly with price. What do you do about a raw count that is nearly meaningless on its own?

### The big picture

| New attribute | Built from | Why it is better |
|---|---|---|
| rooms per house | total rooms ÷ households | size per home, not district size |
| bedrooms ratio | total bedrooms ÷ total rooms | share of rooms, not a raw count |
| people per house | population ÷ households | crowding, not district size |

### 1 · Why a raw count says little

Raw attributes are sometimes less informative than a ratio between two of them. **The total number of rooms in a district is not very meaningful on its own — a district with many rooms could simply have many households.** What actually matters more is rooms *per household*.

The same logic applies twice more: bedrooms are more informative expressed relative to the total number of rooms in a district than as a raw count, and population is more informative expressed per household than as a raw total.

The habit is one you already have. A count column is usually a size column in disguise, and the interesting number is the count divided by whatever makes districts comparable — the same reason you report errors per million rows rather than errors.

### 2 · Three divisions

All three of these are computed as simple elementwise divisions of existing columns and stored as new attributes. **Elementwise** means row by row: each district's own numerator divided by its own denominator, the way a derived column works in a `SELECT`.

The card below is the three lines. `people_per_house` divides the **population column by the households column**; `rooms_per_house` divides total rooms by households; `bedrooms_ratio` divides total bedrooms by total rooms.

### 3 · The payoff, in numbers

Recomputing the correlation matrix afterward shows the payoff directly: **the new bedrooms-to-rooms ratio correlates with the target more strongly than either of the two raw columns it was built from**, and in the opposite direction — **districts with a lower ratio of bedrooms to rooms tend to be more expensive**. Rooms-per-household also edges out the raw room count.

The card below has the numbers: bedrooms ratio at −0.256397 against total rooms at 0.137455 and total bedrooms at 0.054635, and rooms per house at 0.143663 against total rooms at 0.137455.

Two readings, kept apart:

| From the number | Reading |
|---|---|
| 0.256 beats 0.137 and 0.055 | the ratio is the stronger signal |
| the sign is negative | fewer bedrooms per room, higher value |

### 4 · How far to take this

This is the core idea behind **feature engineering by combination**: a derived attribute can carry more predictive signal than either of its ingredients, and finding these combinations is not something an algorithm hands you automatically — it comes from actually looking at the data and asking what raw numbers actually mean in context.

The book is explicit that this exploration pass does not need to be exhaustive; **the goal is a reasonably good starting point, not a final answer**, since you will return to explore further once a working prototype exists.

**One-liner for your notes:** divide raw counts by what makes districts comparable — the bedrooms-to-rooms ratio at −0.26 beats both columns it came from — and stop at a reasonable starting point, not an exhaustive one.

blocks.title: Worked out: the ratio correlations
blocks.content: After adding the three ratios, the book recomputes each attribute's correlation with `median_house_value`. The raw counts give total_rooms 0.137455 and total_bedrooms 0.054635, while the new bedrooms_ratio gives −0.256397. The strength of a correlation is its distance from 0, whatever the sign, and 0.256 is larger than both 0.137 and 0.055, so the ratio is much more strongly correlated than either raw column. The minus sign gives the direction: as the bedroom-to-room ratio goes down, the house value tends to go up, so districts with a lower ratio tend to be more expensive. In the same output, rooms_per_house at 0.143663 edges out total_rooms at 0.137455, and people_per_house comes out at −0.038224.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
housing["rooms_per_house"] = housing["total_rooms"] / housing["households"]
housing["bedrooms_ratio"] = housing["total_bedrooms"] / housing["total_rooms"]
housing["people_per_house"] = housing["population"] / housing["households"]
```

items.term: Why a ratio can beat both of its inputs
items.text: Raw counts here mostly measure district size, which is shared by nearly every count column, so they all say the same uninteresting thing. Dividing removes the size and leaves the composition — and composition is what varies between an expensive district and a cheap one. Normalising by a common denominator is the general move.

items.term: Reading a correlation's sign and size separately
items.text: Strength is distance from zero; the sign only gives direction. A value of −0.26 is a stronger signal than +0.14, even though it looks smaller. Mixing these up leads people to discard good negative predictors.

items.term: Why this step resists automation
items.text: Nothing in the data says 'divide rooms by households'. That comes from knowing what a room count means for a district. Some of it can be brute-forced by generating many combinations and testing, but the search space is enormous and mostly nonsense, which is why domain reading still wins here.

items.term: Handling Missing Values with SimpleImputer

blocks.content:
Most algorithms cannot handle a missing value at all, so you fill the gaps — and you fill them with a tool that remembers what it filled them with.

**The question this lesson answers:** 207 districts have no `total_bedrooms` value. What are the options, which one does the chapter take, and why use `SimpleImputer` instead of one line of Pandas?

### The big picture

```
separate X and y
   -> three options for the gaps: drop rows / drop column / fill
   -> fill (impute) with the median
   -> learn the median ONCE, reapply it everywhere
```

### 1 · Split the inputs from the answers first

Before touching transformations, the predictors and the labels are separated — `drop()` on the target column creates a copy, leaving the original training set untouched, and the label column is copied out on its own.

A **predictor** column here is an input; the **label** is the answer column, median house value. They are separated because **the label should generally not go through the same feature transformations as the inputs**. Scaling or imputing your answer column by accident is a silent, expensive mistake.

### 2 · Three options, one least-destructive

Most ML algorithms simply cannot handle missing values, and this dataset has some in `total_bedrooms`. There are three general options:

| Option | What it costs |
|---|---|
| drop the affected rows | you lose 207 otherwise-usable districts |
| drop the whole attribute | you lose the column for all 20,640 |
| fill (impute) the gaps | you invent a value, but keep everything |

Dropping is destructive and throws away potentially useful rows or a whole feature, so **filling the gaps (imputation) is the least destructive choice**; this chapter fills them with the median. **Imputing** just means substituting a stand-in value — zero, the mean, or the median.

The median is the middle value when the column is sorted. It is preferred over the mean here for the same reason MAE resists outliers: one absurd value drags a mean and barely moves a median.

You have met all three options before, as drop the column, `WHERE ... IS NOT NULL`, and `COALESCE`.

### 3 · Why `SimpleImputer` and not `fillna`

Rather than compute the median with plain Pandas, Scikit-Learn's `SimpleImputer` is the better tool, because **it remembers the value it computed**.

Its `fit()` step learns and stores each column's median, and that stored value can then be reapplied consistently to the validation set, the test set, and any brand-new data the model sees later, so nothing is imputed with a different reference value than what training used.

That is the whole argument, and it is an argument about production, not convenience:

| Approach | On new data |
|---|---|
| `fillna(df[col].median())` | recomputes a new median from that batch |
| fitted `SimpleImputer` | reuses the median learned during training |

A batch of a hundred new districts has its own median, which is not the training median, so the same raw row would be filled differently depending on what it arrived alongside. The fitted imputer removes that.

### 4 · What it is fitted on, and applied to

Since a **median only makes sense for numeric columns**, the imputer is fit only on the numeric subset of the data, excluding the one text column — that is what `select_dtypes(include=[np.number])` does in the card below.

And it is applied to *all* numeric attributes, not just the one currently missing values, **since future data could have gaps anywhere**. Today only `total_bedrooms` has holes; nothing promises that tomorrow's extract will be as tidy.

**One-liner for your notes:** separate labels first, impute rather than drop, and use a fitted `SimpleImputer` so every future row is filled with the median training learned — not with its own batch's median.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer

imputer = SimpleImputer(strategy="median")
housing_num = housing.select_dtypes(include=[np.number])
imputer.fit(housing_num)
X = imputer.transform(housing_num)
```

items.term: The real argument for a fitted imputer is train-serve consistency
items.text: A median recomputed per batch means the same raw row is filled differently depending on what arrived alongside it, so predictions become dependent on batch composition. Freezing the statistic at training time is what makes a single row's prediction reproducible — the same property you want from any reference data used in a transformation.

items.term: Imputation is a guess, and it leaves a trace
items.text: Filling with the median makes the column usable at the cost of shrinking its variance and inventing values that were never observed. A common refinement is to keep a flag column marking which rows were filled, so the model can learn that missingness itself carries information.

items.term: Why fit on every numeric column, not just the broken one
items.text: Fitting only the currently-broken column hardcodes today's data quality into the pipeline. The moment a different column arrives with gaps, the pipeline fails in production rather than degrading. Preparing for gaps everywhere costs one statistic per column and removes a whole class of outage.

items.term: Scikit-Learn's Design: Estimators, Transformers, Predictors

blocks.content:
Scikit-Learn has only a handful of roles, and once you know the three words — estimator, transformer, predictor — an unfamiliar class in the library stops being a mystery.

**The question this lesson answers:** the library has hundreds of classes. What vocabulary lets you predict what any one of them can do before reading its documentation?

### The big picture

```
estimator          learns from data            .fit()
  |- transformer   also changes data           .transform()
  |- predictor     also makes predictions      .predict()
```

Every object is an estimator first. The other two names say what it can do *in addition*.

### 1 · Estimator: anything that learns

An **estimator** is anything that can learn (estimate) parameters from data. `SimpleImputer` is one, since fitting it means computing and storing a median.

The `fit()` method always does the learning, and it takes the dataset — plus, for supervised algorithms, the labels too.

Any extra setting that is not learned from data but instead configures *how* learning happens, like `SimpleImputer`'s `strategy` argument, is a **hyperparameter**, and it is **set through the constructor before fitting ever runs**. That is the split worth holding on to:

| Kind of value | Who sets it | When |
|---|---|---|
| hyperparameter | you | in the constructor, before fit |
| learned parameter | fit(), from the data | during fit |

A hyperparameter is the `--conf` you pass when submitting the job: chosen before the run, fixed during it.

### 2 · Transformer: learns, then changes data

A **transformer** is an estimator that can also transform data — its `transform()` method takes a dataset and hands back a modified one, typically using whatever it learned during `fit()`.

Every transformer also gets a convenience **`fit_transform()`** for free, which just **chains the two steps** — fit, then transform — and is sometimes faster than calling them separately.

### 3 · Predictor: learns, then answers

A **predictor**, by contrast, is an estimator that can make predictions. **It exposes `predict()`**, and usually a `score()` method to judge prediction quality against labelled data.

So the three roles are not three separate hierarchies, they are a base plus two capabilities:

| Object | fit | transform | predict |
|---|---|---|---|
| estimator | yes | not necessarily | not necessarily |
| transformer | yes | yes | no |
| predictor | yes | no | yes |

**Not every estimator is a transformer.** Estimator is the broad category; transformer and predictor are the two things an estimator might additionally be able to do.

### 4 · Three conventions that finish the picture

A few more conventions round this out:

1. Hyperparameters and learned parameters are both exposed as plain public attributes. **Learned ones get a trailing underscore**, like `imputer.statistics_`. So the underscore is a readable signal: this value came from the data, during fitting, and did not exist before.
2. Datasets are represented as ordinary NumPy arrays or SciPy sparse matrices rather than custom container classes, so nothing forces you into a library-specific type.
3. Sensible defaults mean most classes work reasonably well out of the box, without exhaustive configuration.

**One-liner for your notes:** estimator learns with `fit`, transformer adds `transform`, predictor adds `predict`; hyperparameters go in the constructor and learned values come back with a trailing underscore.

items.term: Why one vocabulary makes a big library learnable
items.text: Every estimator shares the same three verbs, so a class you have never seen still has a predictable surface. That is what makes pipelines, cross-validation and hyperparameter search possible at all — they manipulate estimators without knowing what any of them do.

items.term: The hyperparameter and parameter split is the whole design
items.text: Anything you choose goes in the constructor; anything the data determines appears after `fit()`. That separation is what lets a search tool enumerate and set the first group while leaving the second alone, and it is why the trailing underscore is a convention worth taking seriously.

items.term: Duck typing over inheritance
items.text: The library checks for methods, not for base classes, so your own class becomes a first-class citizen by implementing three methods. Open by construction — with the trade-off that a typo in a method name fails later and less clearly than a missing override would.

items.term: Encoding Categorical Attributes

blocks.content:
A text column has to become numbers, and the naive way of doing that invents an ordering the data does not have.

**The question this lesson answers:** ocean proximity is a text column with a handful of repeated values. How do you turn it into numbers without telling the algorithm something false about it?

### The big picture

| Encoder | Output for one row | Implies an order? |
|---|---|---|
| OrdinalEncoder | one integer, say 3 | yes — often wrongly |
| OneHotEncoder | one column per category, one of them 1 | no |

### 1 · Why integers are a trap

The one text column in this dataset, ocean proximity, only ever takes on a handful of repeated values, which makes it a **categorical attribute** rather than free text — and most ML algorithms want numbers, not strings, as input.

`OrdinalEncoder` is the simplest fix: it assigns each distinct category an integer. But that introduces a subtle and often wrong assumption: **an algorithm reading those integers will treat category 0 and category 1 as closer than category 0 and category 4**, purely because of the numbers assigned, even when there is no real ordering to the categories at all.

That is fine for genuinely ordered categories — "bad", "average", "good" — but wrong for something like ocean proximity, where the categories have no natural rank.

This is a mistake you cannot make in SQL, because a string stays a string. Here the encoding silently hands the model a distance between categories, and the model believes it.

### 2 · One-hot encoding

The standard fix is **one-hot encoding**: create one binary column per category, each equal to 1 exactly when a row belongs to that category and 0 otherwise — only one column is ever "hot" per row.

So with five distinct categories, each encoded row becomes **five binary columns with exactly one of them set to 1** and the other four 0. No category is numerically nearer to another; they are simply different columns.

`OneHotEncoder` does this and, **because the resulting matrix is mostly zeros for datasets with many categories, returns a memory-efficient sparse matrix by default** rather than a dense array. A **sparse matrix** stores only the non-zero entries and their positions, which is the difference between storing one number per row and storing five.

### 3 · Why not `pd.get_dummies()`

Pandas has its own `get_dummies()` that looks similar, but it lacks a crucial property: **it only knows about the categories present in whatever DataFrame you pass it**.

So a batch of new data missing a category — or containing an unfamiliar one — **produces a different set of output columns than training did**, a silent mismatch that would corrupt a live model. The model was trained on a fixed column layout; hand it a different one and it either errors or, worse, reads the wrong column as the wrong feature.

| Tool | New batch missing a category |
|---|---|
| `pd.get_dummies()` | fewer output columns; layout changes silently |
| fitted `OneHotEncoder` | same columns as training, every time |

`OneHotEncoder`, once fitted, remembers the exact categories it was trained on and either raises an error on an unseen category or, **with `handle_unknown="ignore"`, encodes it as all zeros** — either way, the output column layout stays identical to what training produced.

This is the schema-stability argument you would already make about a contract: the consumer's column list must not depend on which rows happened to arrive today.

**One-liner for your notes:** one-hot encode unordered categories so no false distance is invented, and use a fitted `OneHotEncoder` rather than `get_dummies()` so the column layout never shifts under new data.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
cat_encoder = OneHotEncoder()
housing_cat_1hot = cat_encoder.fit_transform(housing_cat)
```

items.term: Encoding is where false assumptions get injected
items.text: An integer code silently asserts order and distance. Most algorithms will use both. The failure is invisible in the data and shows up only as slightly wrong predictions, which is why the safe default for unordered categories is one column each, even at the cost of width.

items.term: What one-hot encoding costs
items.text: One column per category means a high-cardinality attribute explodes the feature count, which slows training and thins the data per column. Sparse storage handles the memory; the statistical cost is real, and it is why alternatives exist for attributes with hundreds of categories.

items.term: Fitted encoders are a schema contract
items.text: The fitted encoder pins the output column layout so training and serving agree by construction. `get_dummies()` derives the layout from whatever rows it was handed, which is the same class of bug as a consumer whose column list depends on today's data.

items.term: Feature Scaling and Heavy-Tailed Transformations

blocks.content:
Columns on wildly different scales confuse most algorithms, so you rescale them — and which rescaling you pick depends entirely on your outliers.

**The question this lesson answers:** room counts run into the tens of thousands while median income tops out around 15. What does that do to a model, and what are the two standard fixes?

### The big picture

| Method | Formula in words | Range after | Outliers |
|---|---|---|---|
| min-max scaling | subtract min, divide by range | fixed, usually 0 to 1 | one bad value ruins it |
| standardization | subtract mean, divide by std dev | not fixed | barely affected |

### 1 · Why scale at all

Most ML algorithms perform badly when input attributes sit on very different scales — here, room counts range up into the tens of thousands while median income tops out around 15.

Without correction a model can end up effectively ignoring income and fixating on room counts purely because of their larger raw magnitude. Nothing about the data says rooms matter more; the units do. Scaling removes the units from the argument.

### 2 · Min-max scaling

**Min-max scaling**, often called **normalization**, rescales every value into a fixed range, typically 0 to 1, by subtracting the minimum and dividing by the range.

In words: take the value, subtract the smallest value in the column, then divide by the largest minus the smallest. So a column running from 10 to 60 maps its value 35 to (35 − 10) ÷ (60 − 10) = 25 ÷ 50 = **0.5** — halfway along the column's span.

`MinMaxScaler` does this and lets you pick a different target range via `feature_range`.

### 3 · Standardization, and the outlier argument

**Standardization** instead subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation, so the result has **zero mean and unit variance** — but, unlike min-max scaling, **it does not confine values to a fixed range**.

The **standard deviation** is the typical distance of a value from the mean; **unit variance** means that typical distance has been rescaled to 1.

That lack of a fixed range turns out to be an advantage with outliers: **a single wildly wrong value can crush min-max-scaled data into a tiny sliver of its range, while standardization barely notices it.**

The card below works the book's example: incomes normally run 0 to 15, one district is recorded as 100 by mistake, and under min-max scaling that 100 becomes 1 while a genuine top income of 15 becomes 0.15 — every real value squeezed into the bottom 15% of the range.

### 4 · Fit on training data. Only.

`StandardScaler` implements standardization, and crucially, **scalers must only ever be fit on the training data** — the already-learned scaling is then just *applied* to validation, test, and future data, never refit on them.

| Dataset | Call |
|---|---|
| training set | `fit_transform()` |
| validation, test, future data | `transform()` only |

Calling `fit_transform()` on the test set would compute the test set's own mean and standard deviation and quietly fold them into your preprocessing — the same leak as the imputer's median, and the same fix.

### 5 · When scaling is not enough

Scaling alone is not enough for **heavy-tailed distributions** — ones where extreme values are not exponentially rare, so big values keep showing up instead of dying off. In that case both scaling methods **squash most values into a narrow band**, because the few huge values own the range.

The fix is to reshape the distribution first:

1. a square root or logarithm for a right-skewed positive attribute — Figure 2-17 below shows a feature pulled closer to a bell shape this way
2. for a distribution with multiple distinct peaks, bucketize it into ranges
3. or add features measuring similarity to each peak using a **radial basis function** — a similarity score that is highest at a chosen centre and falls away from it, as in Figure 2-18 below

**One-liner for your notes:** rescale so no column wins on units alone — min-max for a fixed range, standardization when outliers exist — fit the scaler on training data only, and reshape a heavy tail before scaling it.

blocks.title: Worked out: one outlier under min-max scaling
blocks.content: Min-max scaling turns each value x into (x − min) / (max − min): subtract the minimum, then divide by the difference between the maximum and the minimum. In the book's example, median incomes usually range from 0 to 15, but one district has a median income of 100 by mistake. That outlier becomes the maximum, so it maps to (100 − 0) / (100 − 0) = 1, while a genuine top income of 15 maps to (15 − 0) / (100 − 0) = 0.15. All the real incomes are crushed into the range 0 to 0.15. Standardization instead subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation; it does not restrict values to a fixed range, and the book says it would not be much affected by the outlier.

items.term: Scaling is about the algorithm, not the data
items.text: Nothing is wrong with a column that runs to tens of thousands. The problem is that distance-based and gradient-based algorithms read magnitude as importance. Tree-based models are largely indifferent, so scaling is a requirement of the model you picked, not a universal cleaning step.

items.term: Why a fixed range is a liability with outliers
items.text: Min-max ties the whole transformation to two single observations — the min and the max. One bad value replaces one of them and rescales everything else. Standardization uses the mean and standard deviation, which every row contributes to, so no single value can dominate.

items.term: Reshaping, then scaling, in that order
items.text: Scaling is a shift and a stretch: it moves and resizes a distribution without changing its shape. A heavy tail is a shape problem, so no scaler fixes it. A log or a square root changes the shape; scaling afterwards puts it on a comparable range. Reversing the order accomplishes nothing.

items.term: Writing Custom Transformers

blocks.content:
When no built-in transformer does what your project needs, you write one — and Scikit-Learn asks for surprisingly little before it treats your class as a first-class citizen.

**The question this lesson answers:** the housing project needs transformations nobody shipped, like "how close is this district to each price hotspot". What is the least amount of code that makes a custom step behave like a real transformer?

### The big picture

| Does it need to learn from data? | Use |
|---|---|
| no — stateless | `FunctionTransformer` wrapping a plain function |
| yes — fit then reuse | a small class with fit, transform, fit_transform |

### 1 · Stateless: wrap a function

Scikit-Learn's built-in transformers cover a lot, but real projects always need something bespoke — a custom cleanup rule, or a way to combine specific columns.

For a **stateless** transformation, meaning **nothing needs to be learned from data**, `FunctionTransformer` wraps a plain function as a transformer with almost no ceremony. Wrapping `np.log` turns it into a proper transformer. Passing an `inverse_func` lets that transformation later be undone, which is useful when the *target*, not just the inputs, gets transformed — you predict on the transformed scale, then invert to get a price back.

Stateless is the test. Taking a logarithm needs nothing from the data; filling a median does.

### 2 · Stateful: a small class

When a transformer genuinely needs to learn something during `fit()` and reuse it in `transform()`, a full custom class is needed.

Scikit-Learn relies on **duck typing** here — it checks what methods your object has, not what it inherits from. There is no required base class, only three expected methods: `fit()` — which **must return `self`** — `transform()`, and `fit_transform()`.

Two mixins save you writing two of them:

| Inherit from | You get for free |
|---|---|
| `TransformerMixin` | `fit_transform()` |
| `BaseEstimator` | `get_params()` and `set_params()` |

**Inheriting from `TransformerMixin` gives `fit_transform()` for free**, and **`BaseEstimator` adds `get_params()`/`set_params()`, which hyperparameter search tools rely on** — the tuning tools later in the chapter read and set a step's settings through exactly those two methods. The one condition is that your constructor avoids `*args` and `**kwargs`, so the parameters stay inspectable by name.

### 3 · A custom transformer can contain a model

A custom transformer can also lean on other estimators internally. The `ClusterSimilarity` class in the card below does exactly that:

1. its `fit()` runs **k-means** — an algorithm that finds a chosen number of centre points in the data — to locate cluster centres in the training data, weighted here by median house value, so pricier districts pull cluster centres toward them
2. its `transform()` **measures each row's Gaussian RBF similarity to every cluster centre it found**, one output column per centre
3. `return self` is marked in the code with the comment "always return self!", because forgetting it breaks every pipeline the class is used in

**Gaussian RBF similarity** is a score that is 1 at the centre and falls off smoothly with distance. So a district's row of ten similarity scores says how close it is to each of the ten hotspots.

That turns raw geographic coordinates into a richer set of "how close is this district to each price hotspot" features that a model may find more useful than raw latitude and longitude alone. Figure 2-19 below draws the similarity to the nearest centre across the map.

Raw latitude on its own is nearly useless to a model — two coasts at the same latitude are hundreds of miles apart. A distance-to-known-hotspot column is the kind of derived column you would build in a `SELECT` for exactly the same reason.

**One-liner for your notes:** stateless transformations go in a `FunctionTransformer`; anything that learns needs a class with `fit` returning `self`, plus `TransformerMixin` for `fit_transform` and `BaseEstimator` for the tuning tools.

items.term: Why fit and transform are separate methods
items.text: Splitting them is what makes train-serve consistency expressible: learn once on training data, apply many times everywhere else. A single do-everything function cannot distinguish the two, and that is exactly the distinction every leak in this chapter comes down to.

items.term: A transformer that contains a model
items.text: `ClusterSimilarity` blurs the usual line: k-means is a model, and here it is preprocessing. That is legitimate, and it has a consequence — the number of clusters is now a hyperparameter of the preprocessing, tunable alongside the forest's own settings later in the chapter.

items.term: Why raw coordinates are weak features
items.text: Latitude and longitude are only useful in combination, and their relationship to price is sharply nonlinear. Converting them into distances from learned hotspots hands the model something monotonic it can actually use. Turning raw coordinates into a distance-to-known-place feature generalises well beyond this dataset.
