items.term: Chaining It All Together with Pipelines

blocks.content:
Every preprocessing step so far becomes one object: a pipeline that takes the raw DataFrame in and hands a fully prepared array out, in one call.

**The question this lesson answers:** imputing, log-transforming, ratio-building, one-hot encoding and scaling all have to run in the right order on the right columns. How do you make that one reproducible object instead of a script you must not run out of order?

### The big picture

```
raw DataFrame
   -> ColumnTransformer  (a different pipeline per column group)
        ratios | logs | cluster similarity | one-hot | rest
   -> concatenate side by side
   -> 24-column array, ready for a model
```

### 1 · Pipeline: steps in order

With several transformation steps that must run in a specific order — impute, then scale, for instance — **`Pipeline` chains them into a single object**.

Its constructor takes a list of (name, estimator) pairs. **Every step except the last must be a transformer, and the last can be anything** — transformer or predictor. That rule is not arbitrary: each step's output feeds the next, so each step must be able to *produce* data, and only the final step is allowed to end the chain with a prediction instead.

Calling `fit()` on the pipeline **runs `fit_transform()` on every step in sequence, feeding each step's output into the next, and finishes by just calling `fit()` on the last one.** There is nothing to transform after the last step, so it only needs fitting.

If you do not care about naming steps yourself, `make_pipeline()` auto-generates names from each class name.

### 2 · ColumnTransformer: different treatment per column group

Since numeric and categorical columns need entirely different treatment, **`ColumnTransformer` applies a different pipeline to a different subset of columns and concatenates the results side by side.**

Its constructor takes a list of (name, transformer, column-list) triples. **`make_column_selector()` can pick columns by dtype automatically instead of naming them by hand** — handy, since hardcoding a long column list is brittle: add a column upstream and a hardcoded list quietly stops covering it.

One more argument matters. By default, columns nobody mentions are **dropped**; passing a transformer to `remainder` overrides that and routes the leftovers through it instead. Here `remainder=default_num_pipeline` catches the single leftover column, `housing_median_age`, so it is **kept and standardized rather than discarded**.

### 3 · The full preprocessing object

The full preprocessing pipeline in the card below is the payoff of everything explored so far. It:

1. computes the bedroom/room, room/household and population/household ratios via a small reusable `ratio_pipeline()` helper
2. log-transforms the heavy-tailed count columns
3. adds the ten cluster-similarity features from the custom transformer
4. one-hot encodes the categorical column
5. standardizes whatever is left over — just the housing age — through the `remainder` argument

One single object that turns a raw DataFrame into a fully prepared, 24-column NumPy array ready for a model, all with one `fit_transform()` call.

Where the 24 come from, per the card below:

| Step | Columns |
|---|---|
| three ratio pipelines | 3 |
| log pipeline | 5 |
| cluster similarity, ten clusters | 10 |
| one-hot ocean proximity | 5 |
| remainder, housing age | 1 |

3 + 5 + 10 + 5 + 1 = 24, and the result's shape is (16512, 24): one row per training district, one column per feature.

### 4 · Why this shape is worth the trouble

A pipeline is the same discipline as putting transformation logic in a job rather than in a sequence of notebook cells someone must remember to run in order. It is reproducible, it applies identically to the test set and to production rows, and — as the tuning lesson later shows — because preprocessing and model live in one object, a search can tune both at once.

**One-liner for your notes:** `Pipeline` runs steps in order with only the last one exempt from being a transformer, `ColumnTransformer` gives each column group its own pipeline and joins the results, and together they turn the raw DataFrame into 24 prepared columns in one call.

blocks.title: Worked out: where the 24 columns come from
blocks.content: The book lists the output names with `preprocessing.get_feature_names_out()`, and they add up as follows. The three ratio pipelines give 3 columns: `bedrooms__ratio`, `rooms_per_house__ratio` and `people_per_house__ratio`. The log pipeline gives 5 columns, one each for total_bedrooms, total_rooms, population, households and median_income. The `ClusterSimilarity` step, built with `n_clusters=10`, gives 10 cluster-similarity columns. The one-hot encoder gives 5 columns, one per ocean-proximity category (`<1H OCEAN`, `INLAND`, `ISLAND`, `NEAR BAY`, `NEAR OCEAN`). The remainder pipeline gives 1 column for housing_median_age. In total, 3 + 5 + 10 + 5 + 1 = 24, and the shape of the result is (16512, 24): one row per training district and one column per feature.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
def column_ratio(X):
    return X[:, [0]] / X[:, [1]]

def ratio_name(function_transformer, feature_names_in):
    return ["ratio"] # feature names out

def ratio_pipeline():
    return make_pipeline(
        SimpleImputer(strategy="median"),
        FunctionTransformer(column_ratio, feature_names_out=ratio_name),
        StandardScaler())

log_pipeline = make_pipeline(
    SimpleImputer(strategy="median"),
    FunctionTransformer(np.log, feature_names_out="one-to-one"),
    StandardScaler())
cluster_simil = ClusterSimilarity(n_clusters=10, gamma=1., random_state=42)
default_num_pipeline = make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median"),
                                     StandardScaler())
preprocessing = ColumnTransformer([
        ("bedrooms", ratio_pipeline(), ["total_bedrooms", "total_rooms"]),
        ("rooms_per_house", ratio_pipeline(), ["total_rooms", "households"]),
        ("people_per_house", ratio_pipeline(), ["population", "households"]),
        ("log", log_pipeline, ["total_bedrooms", "total_rooms", "population",
                               "households", "median_income"]),
        ("geo", cluster_simil, ["latitude", "longitude"]),
        ("cat", cat_pipeline, make_column_selector(dtype_include=object)),
    ],
    remainder=default_num_pipeline) # one column remaining: housing_median_age
```

items.term: A pipeline is a leak-prevention device
items.text: Because only `fit` learns and every later call is `transform`, wrapping preprocessing in a pipeline makes it structurally hard to fit anything on the test set. Cross-validation then refits the whole chain inside each fold, which is the only way fold scores stay honest when preprocessing learns from data.

items.term: Why the last step is the exempt one
items.text: Each step feeds the next, so every step but the last must be able to produce data. The last has nothing downstream, so it may be a predictor — which is what lets one object hold the entire path from raw DataFrame to prediction, and lets a search tune every stage of it.

items.term: Column-wise composition beats a cleaning script
items.text: `ColumnTransformer` makes the column-to-treatment mapping explicit and re-applicable, instead of spreading it across cells that must run in order. Selecting columns by dtype rather than by name is the same instinct as writing a transformation against a contract rather than a frozen column list.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: In a Pipeline's list of (name, estimator) steps, which steps must be transformers and which one is exempt from that rule?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Preprocessing inside the pipeline is refitted on every cross-validation fold. What would go wrong if it were fitted once on all the training data instead?
Look up: the scikit-learn user guide page "Pipelines and composite estimators", plus its "Common pitfalls and recommended practices" section on data leakage.

items.term: First Models: Underfitting and Overfitting in Action

blocks.content:
The first two models fail in opposite directions: the linear one is too weak to fit even its own training data, and the tree fits it perfectly, which is worse.

**The question this lesson answers:** with preprocessing wrapped in one pipeline, trying a model is two lines. What do the first two attempts score, and why is the better-looking score the more alarming one?

### The big picture

| Model | Training RMSE | Diagnosis |
|---|---|---|
| LinearRegression | about 68,600 USD | underfitting |
| DecisionTreeRegressor | exactly 0.0 | severe overfitting |

Neither number is a result you can ship. They are two different failures, and telling them apart is the whole lesson.

### 1 · The linear model underfits

With preprocessing wrapped into one pipeline, trying a model is now almost trivial: chain the preprocessing pipeline with `LinearRegression` and call `fit()`.

The resulting model's predictions on the training data are visibly imperfect — one prediction is off by over 200,000 USD, two are off by about 25%, and two are off by less than 10%. The card below has the five predictions and the five true labels, with each miss worked out.

Measuring RMSE on the training set confirms it numerically, at roughly 68,600 USD. Since typical house values in this data run from about 120,000 USD to 265,000 USD, **an average error near 68,600 USD is a poor result**.

That is a textbook case of **underfitting**: **the model's predictions are not accurate even on the data it was trained on**. Being wrong on data you have already seen cannot be blamed on novelty. It points at one of two causes:

| Possible cause | Ruled out here? |
|---|---|
| features are not informative enough | no — still open |
| the model is underpowered | no — still open |
| the model is over-constrained | **yes** — it was not regularized |

**Regularization** is a deliberate restriction placed on a model to stop it fitting too closely. **Since this model was not regularized, an over-constrained model is not the explanation here.**

### 2 · The tree overfits

Swapping in a `DecisionTreeRegressor` — **a substantially more flexible model capable of capturing complex nonlinear patterns** — and repeating the same fit-and-measure routine produces a **training RMSE of exactly 0.0**.

That is not a triumph. **A model with zero error on the data it was trained on almost certainly memorized that data** rather than learning a generalizable pattern, which is the signature of severe **overfitting**.

Perfect agreement with the input is the giveaway. A lookup table also scores zero on the rows it contains, and a lookup table predicts nothing about a district it has never met.

### 3 · Why the training score cannot settle it

The catch is that **training-set error alone cannot distinguish a genuinely excellent model from one that has simply memorized its training examples.** Both come back with a small number; only one of them will survive contact with a new district.

So the score you have is the score you cannot trust, and the test set is still locked away until the very end. Which is precisely why the next step is proper held-out evaluation rather than trusting the training score.

**One-liner for your notes:** a big error on training data is underfitting, a zero error is memorization, and training error alone can never tell a good model from a memorizing one.

blocks.title: Worked out: the first five predictions
blocks.content: The book compares the linear model's first five training predictions, rounded to the nearest hundred, with the true labels. The predictions are 243,700, 372,400, 128,800, 94,400 and 328,300; the labels are 458,300, 483,800, 101,700, 96,100 and 361,800. The first prediction misses by 458,300 − 243,700 = 214,600, which is over 200,000. The second misses by 483,800 − 372,400 = 111,400, about 23% of its label, and the third by 128,800 − 101,700 = 27,100, about 27% of its label, so both are off by roughly 25%. The fourth misses by 1,700 (under 2%) and the fifth by 33,500 (about 9%), so both are off by less than 10%.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

tree_reg = make_pipeline(preprocessing, DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=42))
tree_reg.fit(housing, housing_labels)
```

items.term: Two failures, opposite fixes
items.text: Underfitting and overfitting both show as poor predictions on new data and are repaired in opposite directions: more capacity or better features for one, less capacity or more data for the other. Guessing wrong makes it worse, so the training score is read first to tell which one you have.

items.term: Why a perfect score is evidence against you
items.text: Real data contains noise, and two districts with identical features can have different prices. A model that reproduces every training label exactly has fitted the noise as well as the signal, which is only possible by memorising. Perfection on training data is a symptom, never a result.

items.term: What flexibility buys and costs
items.text: A decision tree can express shapes a straight line cannot, and that same freedom lets it carve the training data into single-row regions. Capacity is not good or bad in itself — it is a quantity you match to the data you have, which is what the rest of the chapter is doing.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: A model scores a training RMSE of exactly 0.0. Should that be read as success? Why or why not?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The linear model underfits. Of the two remaining explanations — weak features or a weak model — how would you tell which one you have without simply trying both?
Look up: the scikit-learn user guide section "Validation curves: plotting scores to evaluate models", which covers learning curves for exactly this diagnosis.

items.term: Better Evaluation Using Cross-Validation

blocks.content:
Cross-validation gives you an honest score without touching the test set: train and evaluate ten times on ten different slices of the training data.

**The question this lesson answers:** the tree scored a perfect 0.0 on its training data and the test set is off-limits until the end. How do you find out what these models are actually worth?

### The big picture

```
training set -> 10 folds
round 1: train on folds 2..10, score on fold 1
round 2: train on folds 1,3..10, score on fold 2
...
round 10: ...                       -> 10 scores
```

### 1 · K-fold cross-validation

The decision tree's perfect training score is meaningless without touching the untouched test set, but the test set is off-limits until the very end — so a way is needed to estimate generalization performance using only the training data.

**K-fold cross-validation** does this: split the training set into k non-overlapping chunks called **folds** (10 in this example), then repeat a train-and-evaluate cycle k times, each time holding out a different fold for evaluation and training on the remaining **k − 1 folds** — that is **9 folds when k is 10**. The payoff is k separate performance scores instead of one.

Two things follow immediately, and people get both wrong:

| It does | It does not |
|---|---|
| train the model 10 separate times | train once and score 10 times |
| hold out a different fold each round | sample 10 random test sets |

Because the model is trained from scratch on every fold, **cross-validation costs roughly k times the compute of a single fit.** That is the trade-off you are buying the honesty with.

### 2 · What it says about the tree

Running this on the decision tree produces a very different picture than the earlier 0.0: a **mean RMSE around 66,868 USD with a standard deviation around 2,061 USD**.

In other words, once evaluated on data it was not trained on, the tree performs barely better than plain linear regression, whose cross-validated mean RMSE is around 69,858 USD. That **confirms the earlier suspicion of overfitting**: the 0.0 was memorization, and it evaporates the moment the model meets an unseen fold.

The card below also explains why the raw scores come back negative — Scikit-Learn's cross-validation expects a utility function where greater is better, so `neg_root_mean_squared_error` returns the negative of each fold's RMSE, and the minus sign in front of `cross_val_score(...)` flips it back.

### 3 · What ten scores give you that one cannot

Having ten separate scores also delivers something a single train/validation split cannot: **a sense of how precise the estimate itself is, via that standard deviation.**

A single split hands you one number with no idea whether re-splitting would have given you something wildly different. Ten scores with a spread of about 2,061 USD around 66,868 USD tell you the estimate is stable. A spread of twenty thousand would tell you it is not, and that is worth knowing before anyone quotes it.

### 4 · A third model

A third model, `RandomForestRegressor`, **trains many decision trees on random data subsets and averages their outputs** — a strategy the book calls an **ensemble**, meaning many models voting instead of one deciding.

It comes out clearly ahead, with a **mean cross-validated RMSE around 47,020 USD**:

| Model | Cross-validated mean RMSE |
|---|---|
| linear regression | about 69,858 USD |
| decision tree | about 66,868 USD |
| random forest | about 47,020 USD |

Though its own training-set RMSE, much lower still, shows some overfitting remains even here. Better is not the same as fixed.

**One-liner for your notes:** k-fold cross-validation trains k times on k − 1 folds and scores on the held-out one, which costs k fits and buys both an honest mean and a standard deviation saying how much to trust it.

blocks.title: Why the cross-validation scores come out negative
blocks.content: Scikit-Learn's cross-validation features expect a utility function, where greater is better, rather than a cost function such as the RMSE, where lower is better. The scoring option `neg_root_mean_squared_error` therefore returns the opposite of each fold's RMSE, which is a negative number, and the minus sign in front of `cross_val_score(...)` switches it back to a positive RMSE. Calling `pd.Series(tree_rmses).describe()` on the 10 decision-tree scores gives a mean of 66,868.03 and a standard deviation of 2,060.97, which the book rounds to about 66,868 and 2,061. The same summary for the random forest gives a mean of 47,019.56 and a standard deviation of 1,033.96. For the linear model, the book reports a mean RMSE of 69,858 and a standard deviation of 4,182.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

tree_rmses = -cross_val_score(tree_reg, housing, housing_labels,
                              scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error", cv=10)
```

items.term: Cross-validation buys an estimate of your own uncertainty
items.text: One held-out split gives a number with no error bar. Ten folds give a spread, which answers a different and more useful question: how much would this score move if the data had been split differently? A small mean with a huge spread is not a better model than a slightly larger mean with a tight one.

items.term: The folds are not independent, so read the spread carefully
items.text: Each round trains on nine-tenths of the same data, so the ten scores share most of their training rows and are correlated. The standard deviation is a useful stability signal, not a textbook standard error, and it tends to look tighter than the truth.

items.term: Why averaging many trees fixes the tree
items.text: A single tree overfits because it commits hard to every split it makes. Training many trees on different random subsets makes their individual mistakes partly independent, and averaging cancels a good share of them. That is the general ensemble argument, and it is why the forest beats its own building block here.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Scikit-Learn's cross_val_score with scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error" returns negative numbers. What do you have to do with them to get the actual RMSE, and why is the scoring function negative in the first place?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Ten folds cost ten fits. How do people choose k, and what do they do when a single fit already takes hours?
Look up: the scikit-learn user guide page "Cross-validation: evaluating estimator performance", including its cross-validation iterators and `cross_validate`.

items.term: Fine-Tuning with Grid Search and Randomized Search

blocks.content:
Stop hand-tweaking settings: hand a search tool the values you want tried and let it cross-validate every combination, or a random sample of them.

**The question this lesson answers:** the random forest has hyperparameters, and so does the preprocessing pipeline. How do you find a good combination without guessing one setting at a time?

### The big picture

| Tool | Tries | Cost you control |
|---|---|---|
| GridSearchCV | every listed combination | no — the grid decides |
| RandomizedSearchCV | a chosen number of random combinations | yes — you pick it |
| halving variants | many candidates cheaply, then survivors | yes — by round |

### 1 · Grid search

Hand-tweaking hyperparameters one at a time is slow and easy to do badly, so `GridSearchCV` automates it: give it a dictionary (or list of dictionaries) naming which hyperparameters to try and which values for each, and **it cross-validates every combination**, keeping track of scores along the way.

Grid search multiplies the value counts. The card below counts the book's grid: **3 values for `n_clusters` times 3 values for `max_features` gives 9 combinations** for the first dictionary, 2 × 3 = 6 for the second, 15 in total — and with 3-fold cross-validation that is 15 × 3 = 45 rounds of training.

After the search finishes, `best_params_` names the winning combination and `best_estimator_` gives the refitted best pipeline. **By default the winning combination is automatically retrained on the entire training set**, since more data generally helps — during the search each candidate only ever saw k − 1 folds at a time.

### 2 · Tuning preprocessing and model together

Because the preprocessing steps and the model both live inside one combined pipeline, the search can tune **preprocessing hyperparameters — like the number of clusters in the custom `ClusterSimilarity` transformer — at the same time as model hyperparameters**.

That is addressed by a double-underscore path like `preprocessing__geo__n_clusters`, which **names the step and then the parameter within it**:

| Part | Means |
|---|---|
| preprocessing | the pipeline step called "preprocessing" |
| geo | the step called "geo" inside it |
| n_clusters | the hyperparameter of that transformer |

This matters because these hyperparameters can genuinely interact: the right number of clusters may depend on how many features the forest is allowed to consider per split, and vice versa. Tuning them separately, one after the other, would miss that.

### 3 · Why grid search runs out of road

Grid search's weakness is that it must exhaustively try every listed combination, which becomes impractical fast as the search space grows.

The book's larger example: **6 hyperparameters with 10 possible values each give 1,000,000 combinations**, so grid search has no choice but to train the model a million times.

`RandomizedSearchCV` instead **samples a fixed, chosen number of random combinations** from given value ranges or probability distributions. Two consequences:

1. you set the compute budget directly, rather than letting the size of the grid set it for you
2. adding an unimportant hyperparameter to the search costs nothing extra — it just gets sampled a few times — unlike grid search, where it multiplies the total combinations

### 4 · Halving variants

Scikit-Learn also offers **halving** variants of both searches, which **spend limited resources on many candidates in an early round and progressively hand more resources only to the survivors of each round.**

It is a tournament rather than a full round-robin: cheap short evaluations eliminate the obviously bad candidates before anything expensive is spent on them.

**One-liner for your notes:** put preprocessing and model in one pipeline so a search can tune both through double-underscore names — grid search for a small space, randomized search when the grid would explode past a million.

blocks.title: Worked out: counting grid-search combinations
blocks.content: Grid search multiplies the number of values listed for each hyperparameter. The book's first dictionary lists 3 values for `n_clusters` and 3 for `max_features`, which gives 3 × 3 = 9 combinations; the second lists 2 and 3 values, which gives 2 × 3 = 6. In total the search explores 9 + 6 = 15 combinations, and with 3-fold cross-validation each one is trained 3 times, for 15 × 3 = 45 rounds of training. The same rule explains the book's larger example: 6 hyperparameters with 10 possible values each give 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000,000 combinations, so grid search has no choice but to train the model a million times, whereas random search can run for any number of iterations you choose.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV

full_pipeline = Pipeline([
    ("preprocessing", preprocessing),
    ("random_forest", RandomForestRegressor(random_state=42)),
])
param_grid = [
    {'preprocessing__geo__n_clusters': [5, 8, 10],
     'random_forest__max_features': [4, 6, 8]},
    {'preprocessing__geo__n_clusters': [10, 15],
     'random_forest__max_features': [6, 8, 10]},
]
grid_search = GridSearchCV(full_pipeline, param_grid, cv=3,
                           scoring='neg_root_mean_squared_error')
grid_search.fit(housing, housing_labels)
```

items.term: Why random search wins as dimensions grow
items.text: Grid search spends its budget evenly across every hyperparameter, including the ones that do not matter, and its cost multiplies with each one added. Random search spends the same budget sampling across the whole space, so it tries many distinct values of the hyperparameters that do matter. The advantage grows with the number of unimportant dimensions.

items.term: Tuning is another way to overfit
items.text: Every combination evaluated is another look at the validation folds, and the winner is partly selected for luck on those folds. That is why the final test-set score is often a little worse than the best cross-validated score, and why the test set stays untouched until after tuning.

items.term: Interaction is the reason to tune jointly
items.text: If hyperparameters were independent you could optimise them one at a time for a fraction of the cost. They are not: the best number of clusters depends on how the forest uses features, and vice versa. Joint search is what makes the combined preprocessing-plus-model pipeline worth building.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: You have 6 hyperparameters to explore, each with 10 possible values. Why would RandomizedSearchCV usually be the more practical choice over GridSearchCV here?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Random search samples from distributions rather than lists. Which distribution would you give a hyperparameter that spans several orders of magnitude, and why not a uniform one?

Look up: "Random Search for Hyper-Parameter Optimization" by Bergstra and Bengio (Journal of Machine Learning Research, 2012), and the scikit-learn user guide page "Tuning the hyper-parameters of an estimator".

items.term: Final Evaluation, Launch, and Ongoing Monitoring

blocks.content:
The test set gets used once, at the very end, and whatever number comes out is the number you report — going back to improve it destroys the only honest measurement you have.

**The question this lesson answers:** the model is tuned and looks good. What are the last checks before launch, what does the test set finally say, and what does "done" actually mean once it is in production?

### The big picture

```
inspect what mattered  ->  ONE test-set evaluation
   ->  report with a confidence interval
   ->  launch  ->  monitor for model rot  ->  retrain
```

### 1 · Look at what the model actually used

Before declaring victory, it is worth inspecting *why* the best model performs the way it does. A random forest exposes **`feature_importances_`**, a score per input feature showing how much it actually contributed to predictions.

Sorting these often reveals that a whole category of engineered feature barely matters. Here, **most of the one-hot-encoded ocean-proximity columns turn out close to useless**, while median income and the engineered ratio features dominate — which is a legitimate reason to consider dropping the unhelpful ones.

The card below has the sorted scores: median income at about 0.187, more than twice any other feature, with two ocean-proximity categories at the bottom at about 0.00015 and 0.00007. Only one of those categories is really pulling its weight.

Dropping dead features is not just tidiness — it is fewer columns to compute, validate and monitor in production, for no loss of accuracy.

### 2 · The one evaluation

Only once a model is genuinely considered finished does it ever touch the test set — **one single evaluation**, computing the final RMSE on data that has never influenced any decision up to this point. Here that number is 41,424.

Because that RMSE is a **single point estimate** — one number from one sample, which would have come out slightly differently on a different sample — it is good practice to also compute a **confidence interval** around it, using a t-distribution over the squared errors. A confidence interval is a plausible range for the true value. So a stakeholder sees not just "41,424" but a range around it: the card below gives 39,275 to 43,467.

### 3 · The rule that makes the number mean anything

Critically, however that final number lands, **you never go back and retune hyperparameters to chase a better test-set score**, since doing so would just refit the model to the test set by another name and destroy the honesty of the estimate.

| After a disappointing test score | Legitimate? |
|---|---|
| report it honestly, with the interval | yes |
| investigate whether tuning overfit the validation folds | yes |
| accept it as the final generalization estimate | yes |
| retune hyperparameters to raise the test number | **no** |

The test set is a one-shot measuring instrument. Use it twice and you no longer have one.

### 4 · Launch is not the finish line

Getting the model into production is not the finish line either. Figure 2-20 below shows it deployed as a web service behind an application.

A model needs monitoring for **model rot**, also called **data drift** — **slow, easy-to-miss performance decay as the real world diverges from what the model was trained on**. Sometimes it is inferred through downstream business metrics, sometimes through human review of samples. It is the snapshot table that was right the day it was built and quietly goes stale.

Sensible automation includes:

1. scheduled retraining on fresh data
2. automatically comparing a new candidate against the currently deployed model before replacing it
3. monitoring the *inputs* themselves for drift or new unseen categories
4. **keeping backups of every model and dataset version, so a bad rollout can be reverted quickly**

That list should read familiar. It is the operational discipline you already apply to a pipeline — freshness checks, a candidate compared before promotion, input validation, and versioned artifacts you can roll back to.

**One-liner for your notes:** inspect feature importances, spend the test set exactly once and report it with an interval, never retune against it, and treat launch as the start of monitoring for model rot.

blocks.title: Worked out: importance scores and the interval
blocks.content: Sorting the tuned random forest's `feature_importances_` puts `log__median_income` first at about 0.187, followed by `cat__ocean_proximity_INLAND` at about 0.075, `bedrooms__ratio` at about 0.069, `rooms_per_house__ratio` at about 0.054 and `people_per_house__ratio` at about 0.053. Median income scores more than twice as high as any other feature. At the bottom of the list sit `cat__ocean_proximity_NEAR BAY` at about 0.00015 and `cat__ocean_proximity_ISLAND` at about 0.00007, so the book concludes that only one ocean-proximity category is really useful and that you could try dropping the others. For the final test RMSE of 41,424, `scipy.stats.t.interval()` gives a 95% confidence interval from 39,275 to 43,467, with the point estimate roughly in the middle.

```python
X_test = strat_test_set.drop("median_house_value", axis=1)
y_test = strat_test_set["median_house_value"].copy()

final_predictions = final_model.predict(X_test)

final_rmse = mean_squared_error(y_test, final_predictions, squared=False)
```

items.term: The test set is a budget of exactly one look
items.text: It measures generalization only while it has influenced nothing. Retuning after seeing it turns it into a second validation set, and there is no third set to catch that. This is why the number is reported as it is, even when disappointing.

items.term: A point estimate invites false precision
items.text: One RMSE comes from one particular sample of districts; a different test set would give a somewhat different number. Reporting an interval alongside it tells the stakeholder how much of the difference between two models is real and how much is sampling.

items.term: Importance scores are a hint, not a verdict
items.text: A low importance can mean a feature is useless, or that another feature already carries the same information. Correlated features split their credit between them. So the scores are a good reason to try dropping something and re-measure, and a bad reason to drop it without measuring.

items.term: Why monitoring is part of the model, not of operations
items.text: Model rot has no error message. Accuracy decays while every service stays healthy, so the only detections are a held-out stream of fresh labels, human review of samples, or a business metric moving. Input drift monitoring catches a subset earlier, which is why it is listed separately.

items.term: The MNIST Dataset and Scikit-Learn's Dataset Helpers

blocks.content:
This chapter swaps chapter 2's number-prediction problem for a class-prediction one, and the dataset it uses is MNIST: 70,000 handwritten digit images, each one flattened into a row of 784 numbers.

**The question this lesson answers:** given 70,000 pictures of handwritten digits, what shape does that data arrive in, and which loader settings do you have to get right before any training can start?

### The big picture

```
70,000 images, 28 x 28 pixels
  X: 784 columns, one per pixel, 0-255
  y: one label per row, the string '5'
  60,000 train (shuffled) | 10,000 test
```

### 1 · An image is just a very wide row

Chapter 2 predicted values (a district's median house price). That is **regression**. This chapter predicts **classes** — which of a fixed set of answers a thing belongs to. Here the classes are the ten digits.

Each image is 28x28 pixels, and **each pixel becomes one feature**, so every image is represented as a row of 784 numbers between 0 (white) and 255 (black). That is where 784 comes from: 28 times 28. If you think in tables, `X` is a table with 70,000 rows and 784 columns, and every column holds one pixel position's darkness.

The answer column is different from chapter 2's in one small but load-bearing way: **each row's label is the digit it depicts, stored as a string like '5' rather than an integer**. A comparison you will use later in the chapter will therefore be `y_train == '5'`, with quotes, not `y_train == 5`.

MNIST has been studied so much that the book calls it the "hello world" of machine learning — whenever someone invents a new classification algorithm, they try it on MNIST.

### 2 · Three families of dataset helper

Scikit-Learn's `sklearn.datasets` module groups its dataset helpers into three families, and the prefix tells you where the data comes from:

| Family | Where the data comes from |
|---|---|
| `fetch_*` | downloads a real dataset from the internet |
| `load_*` | small toy datasets bundled with the library |
| `make_*` | synthesizes fake data for quick tests |

**`make_*` functions synthesize fake data for quick tests** — useful when you want a dataset of a known shape and do not care what it means.

Downloaded and loaded datasets typically arrive as a **`Bunch`** — a dictionary-like object exposing a description, the input matrix, and the target array as attributes. In practice that means three entries worth knowing: `"DESCR"` (a description of the dataset), `"data"` (the inputs) and `"target"` (the labels). Being *dictionary-like* just means you can reach a field either as `mnist["data"]` or as `mnist.data`.

### 3 · The one flag to remember

`fetch_openml()` has one quirk worth remembering: it defaults to returning a Pandas DataFrame and Series, which is convenient for tabular data but awkward for image pixels, so **passing `as_frame=False` gets you plain NumPy arrays instead**.

A **DataFrame** is pandas' table object, with named columns. A **NumPy array** is a plain grid of numbers with no column names. For 784 anonymous pixel positions, named columns buy you nothing and cost you a reshape every time you want to draw the picture back as a 28x28 grid — hence the flag.

### 4 · The split is already done, and already shuffled

The MNIST split returned by Scikit-Learn is already divided into a **60,000-image training set and a 10,000-image test set**, so there is no `train_test_split` call in this chapter.

The training portion is also already shuffled, and that matters for two separate reasons: algorithms that are sensitive to instance ordering need a mixed stream rather than a thousand 0s in a row, and cross-validation folds need a representative mix of digits rather than one fold missing a class entirely. Both depend on that shuffle having already happened.

If you have ever loaded a table that arrived sorted by one key and then taken "the first 20%" as a sample, you already know the failure this avoids.

**One-liner for your notes:** MNIST is 70,000 digit images as 784 pixel columns with string labels, split 60,000/10,000 and pre-shuffled, and `fetch_openml(..., as_frame=False)` is how you get it as arrays instead of a DataFrame.

items.term: What flattening an image into 784 columns throws away
items.text: Once the picture is a row of 784 independent numbers, the model has no idea that pixel 100 sits next to pixel 101. A linear model simply assigns a weight per class to each pixel and sums the weighted intensities, which is why later in this chapter it confuses 3s and 5s that differ by a few pixels, and why it is sensitive to an image being shifted or rotated. Keeping spatial structure is what convolutional networks exist for (book page index 186 names the shift problem and points at chapter 14).

items.term: A pre-shuffled set is a convenience, not a rule
items.text: In chapter 2 you shuffled the data yourself; here the provider did it. When a dataset is not already shuffled you have to do the equivalent — Scikit-Learn's own cross-validation code carries the comment 'add shuffle=True if the dataset is not already shuffled'. The habit worth keeping is to ask how a dataset is ordered before you slice it, because 'the first 60,000 rows' is only a fair sample if nothing sorted them first.

items.term: Why MNIST being famous cuts both ways
items.text: Because everyone benchmarks on it, a strong MNIST score is a sanity check rather than evidence your method is good in general — the dataset is clean, balanced across ten classes, small, and already split. Real problems usually break at least one of those, which is exactly why this chapter has to spend most of its length on how to measure a classifier rather than on the classifier itself.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Explain in your own words why fetch_openml() needs as_frame=False for MNIST but not necessarily for a typical tabular dataset.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: fetch_openml() downloads from OpenML.org, so the exact bytes you get depend on what is hosted there today. How do you pin a specific dataset version so a rerun in six months loads the same data?
Look up: the scikit-learn user guide, "Downloading datasets from the openml.org repository", and the `version` and `data_id` parameters of `fetch_openml`.

items.term: Framing and Training a Binary Classifier

blocks.content:
Before tackling ten digits, the chapter builds a classifier that answers one yes-or-no question: is this image a 5, or not?

**The question this lesson answers:** how do you turn a ten-class digit problem into the simplest possible first model, and which classifier does the book reach for to train it?

### The big picture

```
y_train: '5' '0' '4' '5' ...   ten possible answers
   |  (y_train == '5')
   v
y_train_5: True False False True ...   two answers
   |  SGDClassifier.fit
   v
sgd_clf.predict(one image) -> [True]
```

### 1 · Narrowing ten classes to one decision

To get started without tackling all ten digits at once, the chapter narrows the problem to **a single binary decision: is this image a 5, or not?** A **binary classifier** is one that distinguishes between exactly two classes.

Building that "5-detector" starts with turning the multiclass label array into a boolean one: `y_train_5` is `True` wherever the original label is '5' and `False` everywhere else. Note what that array does *not* hold — the digit's actual value is gone. It is a derived boolean column, the same way `is_weekend` is derived from a date and does not let you recover the date.

The classifier then only ever has to answer yes or no. Every measurement in the rest of the chapter — precision, recall, the confusion matrix — is defined for exactly this yes/no shape, which is why the book sets it up first.

### 2 · Why SGDClassifier

For the model itself, the book reaches for `SGDClassifier`, built on **stochastic gradient descent**. The reasoning is practical rather than about raw accuracy:

| Property | What follows from it |
|---|---|
| deals with training instances independently, one at a time | efficient on very large datasets |
| never needs the whole dataset in one step | naturally suited to online learning |

**SGD deals with training instances independently, one at a time**, instead of using the whole dataset at once. That is what makes it efficient on very large datasets and, as a side effect, naturally suited to **online learning** — the topic from chapter 1 where new instances can be incorporated as they arrive rather than requiring the whole training set to be reprocessed. In lakehouse terms that is the incremental load, not the full refresh.

The book passes `random_state=42`, which is the tell that this procedure has randomness inside it: fix the seed and two runs agree.

### 3 · One correct answer proves almost nothing

Once `sgd_clf.fit(X_train, y_train_5)` has run, `predict()` on a single reshaped instance returns **a one-element boolean array** — `[True]`, not a bare `True`, because `predict` is built to score many rows at once and one row is just the smallest batch.

Getting a correct answer on one hand-picked digit feels satisfying, but **it says nothing about how the model performs in general**. One matching row is not a reconciliation. That gap is exactly what the rest of the chapter exists to close.

**One-liner for your notes:** `y_train_5` turns ten labels into one yes/no column, `SGDClassifier` learns it one instance at a time (so it scales and suits online learning), and a single correct prediction is not evidence of anything.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
y_train_5 = (y_train == '5')   # True for all 5s, False for all other digits
y_test_5 = (y_test == '5')

from sklearn.linear_model import SGDClassifier

sgd_clf = SGDClassifier(random_state=42)
sgd_clf.fit(X_train, y_train_5)
```

items.term: Why narrow to one class first, beyond convenience
items.text: Every metric in this chapter — the confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1, the ROC curve — is defined for one positive class against everything else. Reducing ten digits to '5 versus not 5' is not a teaching shortcut, it is what makes those definitions applicable at all. The multiclass sections later have to reintroduce them class by class.

items.term: What 'one instance at a time' buys and costs
items.text: Updating from a single instance means the memory cost does not grow with the dataset and new data can be folded in without a rebuild — the incremental load rather than the full refresh. The cost is that each step is taken on one noisy piece of evidence, so the procedure has randomness in it. That is why the book pins `random_state=42`: without it, two runs on identical data give different models.

items.term: When a binary frame is the wrong frame
items.text: A 5-detector answers a question nobody actually has; the real task is 'which digit is this'. The binary frame is a scaffold for learning the metrics, and the chapter dismantles it later. The general trap is shipping the scaffold: a yes/no model whose 'no' hides nine different answers will look fine on every binary metric and still be useless to the consumer.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Why would framing '5 vs not-5' make this an easier first classifier to build than jumping straight to all ten digits?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: SGDClassifier has a `loss` hyperparameter, and its default is not the one that gives you probabilities. Which loss would you choose if you wanted probability outputs from this same model, and what changes about training?
Look up: the scikit-learn API reference for `sklearn.linear_model.SGDClassifier`, the `loss` parameter and its list of supported values.

items.term: Why Accuracy Lies: Cross-Validation on a Skewed Dataset

blocks.content:
Accuracy looks great on the 5-detector and is still the wrong number, because a classifier that never detects a single 5 scores almost as well.

**The question this lesson answers:** cross-validated accuracy on the 5-detector comes back above 95%. Is that good? And what cheap test tells you whether a score like that means anything?

### The big picture

| Classifier | Cross-validated accuracy | 5s it detects |
|---|---|---|
| SGD 5-detector | above 95% | some |
| DummyClassifier | above 90% | none at all |

Two numbers five points apart; one model works and the other does nothing.

### 1 · The obvious metric, and the baseline that breaks it

The obvious way to score a classifier is **cross-validated accuracy** — the fraction of predictions that are correct. Running `cross_val_score` with three folds on the SGD 5-detector returns numbers above 95%.

**Cross-validation** here means splitting the 60,000 training images into three folds, training three times, each time holding one fold out to score on. It is how you get a score without touching the test set.

That 95% looks outstanding until you build a deliberately useless baseline: `DummyClassifier`, which **always predicts the single most frequent class regardless of the input**. Fitted on the 5-detector labels, the most frequent class is "not a 5", so it answers "not a 5" every single time and never once detects an actual 5.

Its cross-validated accuracy also comes in above 90%.

### 2 · Why the floor is so high

Because **only around 10% of MNIST images are actually 5s**, always guessing "not a 5" is correct roughly 90% of the time.

That is the trap: on a **skewed dataset**, where one class vastly outnumbers the other, accuracy rewards a model for doing the easy, lazy thing. A 95%-accurate detector and a 90%-accurate detector that never fires are not nearly as far apart as the numbers suggest, and accuracy alone cannot tell them apart.

The useful habit is the one this section demonstrates: build the do-nothing baseline first, so you know what the floor is before you read your model's score. A row count that matches 90% of the time tells you nothing if 90% of the rows are the same value.

### 3 · What `cross_val_score` is actually doing

The chapter also shows how to hand-roll the same cross-validation loop, using two pieces:

| Piece | Job |
|---|---|
| `StratifiedKFold` | splits so each fold keeps a representative mix of the two classes |
| `clone` | produces an untrained copy of the classifier for each fold |

**`StratifiedKFold` splits the data so each fold keeps a representative mix of the two classes** — which matters exactly because the data is skewed: an unstratified split could hand one fold far fewer 5s than the others, and that fold's score would be mostly noise. **`clone` produces an untrained copy of the classifier for each fold**, so fold three is not quietly benefiting from fold two's training.

Seeing the mechanics spelled out makes it clear that `cross_val_score` is doing nothing exotic — just repeated train/evaluate splits — which is useful once a project needs more control than the built-in function offers.

**One-liner for your notes:** on a skewed dataset accuracy flatters anything that predicts the majority class, so measure the do-nothing baseline first and then reach for a metric that can tell the two apart.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier

dummy_clf = DummyClassifier()
dummy_clf.fit(X_train, y_train_5)
print(any(dummy_clf.predict(X_train))) # prints False: no 5s detected
```

items.term: Build the floor before you read the score
items.text: The dummy classifier is not a joke, it is the measurement that makes the other number interpretable. Any metric that cannot separate your model from a model that does nothing is the wrong metric for that problem. This generalises to every rare-event problem: fraud, equipment failure, rare disease, defect detection.

items.term: Accuracy is not broken, it is answering a different question
items.text: Accuracy weights every row equally, so on 90/10 data it mostly reports how well you predict the majority. If the classes were balanced and both kinds of mistake cost the same, accuracy would be a perfectly good choice. The defect is in the match between metric and problem, not in the formula.

items.term: What stratification actually protects
items.text: With roughly 10% positives split into three folds, an unstratified split can hand one fold far fewer 5s than the others. That fold's score is then mostly noise, and the average of three folds quietly inherits it. Stratifying keeps each fold's class ratio representative so the three scores are measuring the same thing.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Describe a real dataset you've worked with where accuracy alone would have been a misleading metric.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: DummyClassifier has several strategies besides always predicting the most frequent class. Which baseline is the right one when your model outputs scores or probabilities rather than hard labels?
Look up: the scikit-learn user guide, the "Dummy estimators" section of "Metrics and scoring: quantifying the quality of predictions".

items.term: The Confusion Matrix, and Where Precision and Recall Come From

blocks.content:
The confusion matrix replaces one flattering number with four honest counts, and precision and recall are both built straight out of those four.

**The question this lesson answers:** accuracy hid the fact that the 5-detector misses most 5s. What do you look at instead, and where exactly do precision and recall come from?

### The big picture

```
                 predicted no     predicted yes
  actual no   |  true negative  |  false positive
  actual yes  |  false negative |  true positive
```

Four cells. Precision reads the right-hand column; recall reads the bottom row.

### 1 · What a confusion matrix is

Its idea is simple: **count how often instances that actually belong to class A get predicted as class B, for every pair of classes.**

**Each row in a confusion matrix is the actual class, and each column is the predicted class.** Keep that orientation in your head — half the mistakes people make reading one come from having it backwards.

Building one requires predictions that were never seen during training. Instead of touching the held-out test set early, the book uses `cross_val_predict`, which runs the same k-fold mechanics as `cross_val_score` but **returns each instance's out-of-sample prediction rather than a score**. *Out-of-sample* means the model that predicted a given row had never been trained on that row — so you get a clean prediction for all 60,000 training images without spending the test set.

### 2 · Four outcomes, and their other names

For the binary 5-detector, the resulting 2x2 matrix has a row for the actual negative (non-5) and actual positive (5) classes, and a column for each predicted class. Reading it names four outcomes:

| Cell | Means | Also called |
|---|---|---|
| true negative | actual non-5, called non-5 | — |
| false positive | actual non-5, called a 5 | type I error |
| false negative | actual 5, called non-5 | type II error |
| true positive | actual 5, called a 5 | — |

True negatives and false positives sit in the negative row; false negatives and true positives sit in the positive row. **False positives are also called type I errors, and false negatives type II errors.**

A flawless classifier would have entries only along the diagonal, since every prediction would match the true class — everything else would be zero. The card below works through the real numbers.

### 3 · Precision and recall, from those four counts

From these four counts come two of the chapter's central metrics.

**Precision is the fraction of positive predictions that were actually correct** — of everything the model called a 5, how much really was one. Equation 3-1 below.

**Recall is the fraction of actual positives the classifier managed to catch** — of all the real 5s in the data, how many it found. Equation 3-2 below. So recall divides the true positives by the real 5s: the 3,530 it caught, over the 1,891 it missed plus those same 3,530.

The two are not interchangeable. Precision ignores the 5s you never flagged; recall ignores the non-5s you wrongly flagged. Neither one uses the true negatives at all.

### 4 · Why precision is never quoted alone

The chapter is careful to note that **precision alone can be gamed: a classifier that makes exactly one very confident positive prediction, and gets it right, technically has 100% precision** while predicting negative for everything else — and is obviously useless.

That is why precision is always read alongside recall. One of them can be driven to a perfect score by refusing to do the job; together they cannot.

**One-liner for your notes:** rows are the actual class and columns the predicted one, the four cells are TN/FP/FN/TP (false positive = type I, false negative = type II), precision is TP over everything you called positive, and recall is TP over everything that really was.

blocks.title: Worked out: reading the 5-detector's confusion matrix
blocks.content:
In `[[53892, 687], [1891, 3530]]`, the first row holds the actual non-5s: 53,892 were correctly classified as non-5s (true negatives) and 687 were wrongly classified as 5s (false positives). The second row holds the actual 5s: 1,891 were wrongly classified as non-5s (false negatives) and 3,530 were correctly classified as 5s (true positives).

Putting these counts into the two equations gives precision = 3,530 / (687 + 3,530) ≈ 0.837 and recall = 3,530 / (1,891 + 3,530) ≈ 0.651. A perfect classifier on the same 60,000 training images would give `[[54579, 0], [0, 5421]]`: all 53,892 + 687 = 54,579 non-5s and all 1,891 + 3,530 = 5,421 5s land on the main diagonal.

blocks.title: Equation 3-1
blocks.caption: Precision
blocks.explain:
**Why the equations look like this**

Both come straight out of the four counts in the confusion matrix, and each one asks a different
question about the same set of predictions. Precision asks: of everything I called a 5, how much
really was one — so its denominator is everything the model flagged, TP plus FP. Recall asks: of all
the real 5s, how many did I catch — so its denominator is everything that really was a 5, TP plus FN.
The numerator is the same in both because true positives are the only thing either question counts as
a success.

That is why neither equation contains TN. Precision and recall are both about the positive class, and
the true negatives — 53,892 of them here — say nothing about it.

**Is this standard?** Yes. These are the canonical definitions used everywhere; nothing was simplified
for the MNIST example. The only thing that varies between projects is which class you declare
positive, and that choice changes what both numbers mean.

**The general form.** For more than two classes there is no single precision or recall — you compute
one pair per class, treating that class as positive and everything else as negative, and then decide
how to average them. The multilabel lesson later in this chapter meets exactly that choice as
`average="macro"` versus `average="weighted"`.

**Terms these introduce:** a **true positive (TP)** is an actual 5 that was called a 5; a **false
positive (FP)** is a non-5 that was called a 5; a **false negative (FN)** is an actual 5 that was
called a non-5. The bar in each fraction is ordinary division.

**Every piece of Equations 3-1 and 3-2**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| precision | precision | the share of positive calls that were right |
| recall | recall | the share of real positives that were caught |
| TP | T P, true positives | actual 5s called 5s — here 3,530 |
| FP | F P, false positives | non-5s called 5s — here 687 |
| FN | F N, false negatives | actual 5s called non-5s — here 1,891 |
| TP + FP | T P plus F P | everything the model called a 5 |
| TP + FN | T P plus F N | everything that really was a 5 |
| the fraction bar | divided by | ordinary division |

**The formulas in plain words**

precision = the 5s you got right, divided by everything you called a 5.

recall = the 5s you got right, divided by every 5 that was actually there.

**With real numbers**

From the 5-detector's confusion matrix, TP = 3,530, FP = 687 and FN = 1,891.

1. Precision: everything called a 5 is 687 + 3,530 = 4,217. Of those, 3,530 were right.
3,530 divided by 4,217 is about 0.837, so 83.7%.
2. Recall: every actual 5 is 1,891 + 3,530 = 5,421. Of those, 3,530 were caught.
3,530 divided by 5,421 is about 0.651, so 65.1%.

The same 3,530 sits on top of both. Only the denominator changes, and that alone is the difference
between an 84% score and a 65% one.

---

blocks.title: Equation 3-2
blocks.caption: Recall

blocks.title: Figure 3-3
blocks.caption: An illustrated confusion matrix showing examples of true negatives (top left), false
blocks.alt: Figure 3-3: An illustrated confusion matrix showing examples of true negatives (top left), false

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_predict

y_train_pred = cross_val_predict(sgd_clf, X_train, y_train_5, cv=3)

from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix

cm = confusion_matrix(y_train_5, y_train_pred)
cm
# array([[53892,   687],
#        [ 1891, 3530]])
```

items.term: Why four counts and not one
items.text: Every binary result lands in exactly one of the four cells, so the matrix is the complete record and any single-number metric is one particular way of squeezing four numbers into one. Knowing that lets you see what each metric ignores: precision never looks at the false negatives, recall never looks at the false positives, and neither one touches the true negatives at all. Accuracy uses all four but treats them as interchangeable.

items.term: Why out-of-sample predictions on the training set, not the test set
items.text: `cross_val_predict` gives you a clean prediction for every training row while leaving the test set untouched, so you can iterate on error analysis as many times as you like. Spending the test set early turns it into another training signal: every decision you make after looking at it has been fitted to it, and the final number stops being an estimate of new-data performance.

items.term: 'Positive' is a choice you make, and all four names follow it
items.text: Type I and type II are borrowed from hypothesis testing, and like the words 'false positive' they only mean anything once you have declared which class is positive. Flip the positive class from 'is a 5' to 'is not a 5' and every cell changes name, precision and recall swap character, and the same model gets different scores. Declare the positive class explicitly before quoting any of these numbers.

items: cross_val_predict stitches together predictions from k different models. Scikit-Learn's own documentation warns that this makes it unsuitable for some measurements — which ones, and why does stitching break them?

items.term: Precision, Recall and F1 in Practice

blocks.content:
The 5-detector's real scorecard is 83.7% precision and 65.1% recall, and the F1 score is how you squeeze those two numbers into one without letting a bad one hide.

**The question this lesson answers:** you now have two numbers instead of one. What do they say about the 5-detector in plain words, how do you combine them for comparing classifiers, and when should you deliberately not combine them?

### The big picture

| Number | Value | Read as |
|---|---|---|
| precision | about 83.7% | when it says "5", it is right 84% of the time |
| recall | about 65.1% | it finds about two-thirds of the real 5s |
| F1 | the harmonic mean | high only if both are high |

### 1 · The two headline numbers

Scikit-Learn's `precision_score` and `recall_score` turn the confusion-matrix counts into the two headline numbers for the 5-detector: roughly **83.7% precision and 65.1% recall**.

Read plainly: whenever the classifier claims an image is a 5 it is right about 84% of the time, but **it only manages to find about two-thirds of the 5s that actually exist in the data**. That is a much less flattering picture than the 95%-plus accuracy from earlier suggested — and it is the same model, on the same data. Only the question being asked changed.

### 2 · F1, and why the harmonic mean

Because juggling two numbers is awkward when comparing classifiers, the chapter introduces the **F1 score** — it **turns precision and recall into one number**, so two classifiers can be ranked.

The design choice that matters is that F1 is the **harmonic mean** of precision and recall, rather than their ordinary average. A harmonic mean is what you get by averaging the *reciprocals* and flipping the result back; the practical effect is all you need here. **It punishes a low value in either precision or recall far more severely than an arithmetic mean would, so a classifier only earns a high F1 score if both numbers are genuinely good** — it cannot hide a weak recall behind a strong precision. Equation 3-3 below is the formula, with the explanation underneath it.

### 3 · When one number is the wrong answer

But a single balanced number is not always what a project needs. The book contrasts two real scenarios:

| System | Lean toward | Because |
|---|---|---|
| videos safe for kids | high precision, low recall | better to reject good videos than pass a bad one |
| shoplifters on camera | high recall, low precision | a few false alarms beat missing real cases |

**A camera system flagging shoplifters should lean toward high recall even at low precision.** The book is blunt about how lopsided that is willing to be: 30% precision is fine there as long as recall reaches 99%, because the security guards can absorb a few false alerts and almost every shoplifter gets caught.

Notice what decided each case: not the data, but the cost of each kind of mistake. That is a conversation with the people who own the consequences, not a modelling choice.

### 4 · The catch that sets up the next lesson

You cannot simply push both numbers as high as you like, because **raising one of them reliably tends to lower the other**. That is a property of how the classifier makes its decision, not a limitation of these two formulas, and it has its own name and its own section next.

**One-liner for your notes:** 83.7% precision and 65.1% recall for the 5-detector, F1 is their harmonic mean so both must be good to score well, and when one error type costs more than the other you deliberately pick a side instead of combining them.

blocks.title: Equation 3-3
blocks.caption: F score
blocks.explain:
**Why the equation looks like this**

The job is to fold two numbers into one in a way that cannot be gamed by pushing only one of them up.
An ordinary average fails that: 100% precision with 0% recall averages to a respectable-looking 50%.
The harmonic mean does not — it is built from the reciprocals of the two numbers, and a reciprocal
explodes as its input approaches zero, so one very low input drags the whole result down with it. A
high F1 is therefore evidence that both inputs are high, which is exactly what you wanted the single
number to certify.

The three expressions in Equation 3-3 are the same value written three ways: the definition (two
divided by the sum of the reciprocals), the form that is easiest to compute from precision and
recall, and the form written straight from the confusion-matrix counts.

**Is this standard?** Yes, this is the canonical F1 score, not a simplification for this example. The
subscript 1 exists because there is a general version that lets you declare recall more important
than precision by some factor; this chapter only uses the balanced case.

**Terms this introduces:** the **harmonic mean** of two numbers is two divided by the sum of their
reciprocals — the same average you use for speeds over equal distances, where the slow leg dominates.
A **reciprocal** of a number is one divided by it.

**Every piece of Equation 3-3**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| F1 | F one | the combined score |
| precision | precision | TP over TP plus FP, from Equation 3-1 |
| recall | recall | TP over TP plus FN, from Equation 3-2 |
| 1 over precision | one over precision | the reciprocal of precision |
| 1 over recall | one over recall | the reciprocal of recall |
| the 2 on top | two | there are two quantities being averaged |
| TP | T P | true positives — actual 5s called 5s |
| FN + FP over 2 | F N plus F P, over two | the average of the two mistake counts |

**The formula in plain words**

F1 = two, divided by (one over precision plus one over recall).

Equivalently: F1 = twice the product of precision and recall, divided by their sum.

**With real numbers**

The 5-detector has precision 0.837 and recall 0.651.

1. Multiply them: 0.837 times 0.651 is about 0.545.
2. Add them: 0.837 plus 0.651 is 1.488.
3. Twice the product divided by the sum: 2 times 0.545, divided by 1.488, is about 0.733.

Scikit-Learn's `f1_score` reports about 0.7325 for this classifier. Compare that with the plain
average of the two, which would be about 0.744 — the harmonic mean sits below it, and the gap widens
the further apart precision and recall are. If recall fell to 0.10 with precision unchanged, the
plain average would still read 0.47 while F1 would drop to about 0.18.

---

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.metrics import precision_score, recall_score

precision_score(y_train_5, y_train_pred) # == 3530 / (687 + 3530)
recall_score(y_train_5, y_train_pred) # == 3530 / (1891 + 3530)

from sklearn.metrics import f1_score

f1_score(y_train_5, y_train_pred)
```

items.term: Why a harmonic mean rather than taking the minimum
items.text: You want a single number that collapses when either input is bad. Taking the minimum would do that too, but it would then ignore any improvement in the other number entirely. The harmonic mean punishes the low one hard while still responding to the high one, which is what makes it usable for ranking classifiers rather than just rejecting them.

items.term: F1 is one point on a family, not the only balance
items.text: The subscript 1 in F1 is a hint: the general form lets you declare that recall is some multiple more important than precision, which is how you would encode the shoplifter case as a single number instead of abandoning single numbers. This chapter only uses the balanced version — flagged here as the honest answer to 'why is there a 1 there', not as something chapter 3 establishes.

items.term: The metric is chosen from the cost of each mistake
items.text: Nothing in the videos-for-kids or shoplifter examples came from the data. Both were decided by what a false positive costs versus what a false negative costs, which is a conversation with the people who live with the consequences. A metric picked before that conversation is a guess about someone else's priorities.

items: Give an example project where you'd deliberately choose low precision to keep recall high, and explain why.

items: F1 never looks at the true negatives at all. When does ignoring them give a misleading comparison, and what does the Matthews correlation coefficient do differently?
Look up: the scikit-learn user guide, "Matthews correlation coefficient" under Classification metrics.

items.term: The Precision/Recall Trade-off and Choosing a Threshold

blocks.content:
The precision/recall trade-off is not a law of nature — it is one number you get to choose, the decision threshold.

**The question this lesson answers:** why does pushing precision up always pull recall down, and how do you pick a threshold on purpose instead of accepting whatever `predict()` happens to use?

### The big picture

```
scores:  low ............................ high
                    ^ threshold
  left of it  -> called negative
  right of it -> called positive
  move right: precision up, recall down
  move left : recall up, precision down
```

### 1 · The mechanism underneath

`SGDClassifier` assigns every instance a **decision score** and compares that score to a **threshold** to decide positive or negative. The score is just a number saying how strongly the model leans positive; the threshold is the line you draw across it.

**Raise the threshold and precision tends to go up while recall goes down.** Fewer instances clear the higher bar, and the ones that do are more likely to be real positives — but some real positives now fall short and are missed. Move the threshold down and the effect reverses.

This is why the trade-off is real and unavoidable: both quantities are read off the same ranked list, separated by the same line. You are not tuning two dials, you are sliding one.

### 2 · Scikit-Learn will not set it for you

**Scikit-Learn does not expose a way to set this threshold directly through `predict()`** — there is no threshold argument to pass. What it gives you instead is `decision_function()`, which hands back the raw score for any instance, so you can compare it to whatever threshold you choose yourself.

So the recipe for a custom threshold is: call `decision_function()`, compare the scores to your own number, and use that comparison as your prediction. `predict()` is just that comparison with the threshold fixed at 0.

### 3 · Choosing a threshold on evidence

To pick one deliberately rather than by guesswork, the workflow is three steps:

1. Get out-of-sample decision scores for every training instance via `cross_val_predict(..., method="decision_function")` — **the same cross-validation as before, but returning decision scores rather than predictions or a single score.**
2. Feed those scores into `precision_recall_curve()`, which reports the precision and recall that would result at every possible threshold.
3. If you have a target precision in mind — say 90% — search the precision array for the first threshold that clears it.

Step 3 uses `argmax()` on a boolean condition, which works because **`argmax` returns the index of the first `True` value**. A boolean array is read as 1s and 0s, so "the largest value" is the first `True`. It is the same trick as taking the first row of an ordered result that passes a test.

Figures 3-5 and 3-6 below plot the two views of this: precision and recall against the threshold, then precision directly against recall. The card below walks the actual numbers, including the 2,164-ish score of the example digit.

### 4 · The follow-up question to always ask

Here is the catch the chapter is careful to flag: hitting a chosen precision is easy — just raise the threshold far enough. But the resulting recall might be unacceptably low. In the book's example, the threshold that reaches 90% precision leaves recall at 48%.

**A precision number quoted alone is close to meaningless; the recall at that same threshold is what tells you whether the trade-off is actually livable for your use case.** If someone says they hit 99% precision, the question is "at what recall?".

**One-liner for your notes:** the classifier scores every instance and a threshold turns scores into yes/no, so precision and recall move in opposite directions as you slide it — choose the threshold from `precision_recall_curve` and always quote the recall that came with it.

blocks.title: Worked out: how the threshold changes the numbers
blocks.content:
In Figure 3-4 the digits are ranked by score. With the threshold at the central arrow, 4 true positives (actual 5s) and 1 false positive (a 6) sit to its right, so precision is 4 out of 5, or 80%. Of the 6 actual 5s, 4 are detected, so recall is 4 out of 6, or 67%. Moving the threshold to the right arrow turns the 6 into a true negative and one 5 into a false negative: precision rises to 100% and recall drops to 50%. Precision can dip on the way, though: one digit to the right of the central arrow it goes from 4/5 (80%) down to 3/4 (75%).

`SGDClassifier` uses a threshold of 0. The example digit scores about 2,164, so it is called a 5, but with a threshold of 3,000 it is missed. The lowest threshold giving at least 90% precision is about 3,370, where precision is 90.0% and recall only 48.0%.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
y_scores = cross_val_predict(sgd_clf, X_train, y_train_5, cv=3,
                             method="decision_function")

from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve

precisions, recalls, thresholds = precision_recall_curve(y_train_5, y_scores)

idx_for_90_precision = (precisions >= 0.90).argmax()

threshold_for_90_precision
```

items.term: The threshold is not part of the model
items.text: The model produces an ordering of instances by score; the threshold turns that ordering into decisions. They are separable, which means you can change the operating point — become stricter or more permissive — without retraining anything. That is a genuinely useful property in production: the same trained artifact can serve two consumers with different tolerances.

items.term: Why precision wobbles while recall only falls
items.text: Raising the threshold can only take instances out of the positive set, so the count of caught positives can only shrink: recall moves in one direction, smoothly. Precision is a ratio whose numerator and denominator both shrink, so it can dip — the book's own example is precision going from 4/5 to 3/4 when the threshold moves one digit to the right (book page index 170).

items.term: A threshold chosen on your scores is fitted to your scores
items.text: The 90%-precision threshold was picked by scanning the same cross-validated scores it is then evaluated on, so the realised precision on genuinely new data will usually be a little worse than the 90.0% quoted. The chapter does not make this point; it is the same selection effect as tuning a hyperparameter on your validation set, and the fix is the same — keep a set you did not choose on.
