items.term: The ROC Curve and AUC

blocks.content:
The ROC curve is the same trade-off plotted against a different denominator, and its one-number summary, AUC, can look brilliant on a rare positive class when the model still has real room to improve.

**The question this lesson answers:** there is a second standard curve for binary classifiers. What does it plot, what does its area under the curve mean, and when should you use it instead of the precision/recall curve?

### The big picture

| Curve | Vertical axis | Horizontal axis | Prefer when |
|---|---|---|---|
| PR | precision | recall | positives are rare |
| ROC | true positive rate | false positive rate | otherwise |

Both are the same ranked list read at every threshold; only the denominators differ.

### 1 · The two rates

The ROC curve is the precision/recall curve's close cousin, built from a different pair of rates. Instead of precision, it plots the **true positive rate** against the **false positive rate**.

**The true positive rate is recall by another name** — the fraction of actual positives correctly caught. **The false positive rate measures the fraction of actual negatives that get wrongly flagged as positive.**

The false positive rate is also 1 minus the **true negative rate**, the fraction of actual negatives correctly left alone, which goes by the name **specificity**. Recall, in the same vocabulary, is called **sensitivity**. So the ROC curve is really sensitivity plotted against 1 minus specificity — three names for two quantities you already know.

### 2 · Reading the curve and its area

`roc_curve()` computes matching false-positive-rate and true-positive-rate pairs across every threshold, in the same spirit as `precision_recall_curve()`.

Plotted, **a genuinely useful classifier's curve bows up and to the left**, away from the diagonal line. That diagonal is the ROC curve of a classifier making pure random guesses — the same idea as the `DummyClassifier` baseline from earlier: know the floor before you read the score.

Collapsing the whole curve into a single number gives the **area under the curve (AUC)**, computed with `roc_auc_score()`:

| Classifier | ROC AUC |
|---|---|
| perfect | 1.0 |
| purely random | 0.5 |

**A perfect classifier gets a ROC AUC of 1.0, and a classifier that makes purely random guesses gets 0.5.** So the number is read against that floor of 0.5, not against zero. The 5-detector's own number is in the card below.

### 3 · The rule of thumb, and why it bites here

The chapter's rule for choosing between the two curve types matters more than it might first appear: **prefer the precision/recall curve when the positive class is rare, or when false positives matter more than false negatives; otherwise the ROC curve is fine.**

The reason is concrete here. With 5s being a small minority of MNIST, the false positive rate divides by a very large number of non-5s, so several hundred wrong flags barely move it. Precision divides by the much smaller set of things the model actually called a 5, so the same wrong flags dominate. That is why the ROC AUC can look impressively close to 1 even though the PR curve, plotted over the same data, makes clear there is real room left to improve.

Same predictions, two denominators, two very different impressions. Pick the denominator that matches what your users will feel.

**One-liner for your notes:** ROC plots recall against the false positive rate and summarises to AUC (1.0 perfect, 0.5 random), but on a rare positive class it flatters the model — reach for the PR curve there.

blocks.title: Worked out: the 5-detector's ROC numbers
blocks.content:
For the SGD 5-detector's cross-validated scores, `roc_auc_score(y_train_5, y_scores)` returns about 0.9605, close to the 1.0 of a perfect classifier. On the ROC curve, the threshold chosen for 90% precision sits at 48% recall, and the curve shows the same kind of trade-off as before: the higher the recall (TPR), the more false positives (FPR) the classifier produces.

The high AUC is mostly because there are few positives (5s) compared with the negatives (non-5s). The precision/recall curve for the same scores tells a different story: it could really be closer to the top-right corner, so the classifier still has room for improvement.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve

fpr, tpr, thresholds = roc_curve(y_train_5, y_scores)

from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

roc_auc_score(y_train_5, y_scores)
```

items.term: Why the two curves disagree on the same predictions
items.text: The false positive rate divides by all the negatives, and in the 5-detector's confusion matrix there are 54,579 of them, so several hundred wrong flags barely move it. Precision divides by the much smaller set the model actually called positive, so the same wrong flags dominate. Rarity of the positive class is exactly what makes those two denominators diverge, which is why the rule of thumb keys on it.

items.term: AUC is threshold-free, which is both the point and the catch
items.text: A single AUC summarises the ordering across every threshold, so it answers 'is the ranking any good' without committing to an operating point. That makes it a fair way to compare two models. It does not tell you what precision and recall you will actually ship with, because that still requires choosing a threshold.

items.term: The diagonal is the same idea as the dummy classifier
items.text: Both are floors. The dummy gave the accuracy a do-nothing model reaches; the diagonal gives the ROC curve a coin-flipping model traces. Reading any score without its floor is how a 90% accuracy and a 0.96 AUC both end up sounding better than they are.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Explain why a high ROC AUC score can be misleading on a dataset where the positive class is rare.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: ROC AUC has a probabilistic reading: it is the chance a randomly chosen positive scores higher than a randomly chosen negative. Does the area under the precision/recall curve have a comparable plain-language meaning, and why is average precision usually reported instead of its trapezoidal area?
Look up: the scikit-learn user guide, "Receiver operating characteristic (ROC)" and the note on `average_precision_score` under "Precision, recall and F-measures".

items.term: Comparing Classifiers: Random Forest vs SGD

blocks.content:
A random forest beats the SGD 5-detector on every measure the chapter has built, and scoring it takes one substitution: estimated probabilities in place of decision scores.

**The question this lesson answers:** the evaluation toolkit is finished. What does it cost to point it at a second, different classifier, and what does it say?

### The big picture

```
SGDClassifier   -> decision_function() -> raw score
RandomForest    -> predict_proba()     -> probability
        both are just an ordering
        -> precision_recall_curve() -> compare
```

### 1 · The forest has no decision function

To see whether the SGD 5-detector can be beaten, the chapter brings in `RandomForestClassifier` and compares its precision/recall behavior directly. The comparison hits one snag immediately: **`RandomForestClassifier` has no `decision_function()` method**, so there is no raw score to threshold.

Instead you use `predict_proba()`, which returns an estimated probability for each class. **Since the two classes' probabilities always sum to 100%, the probability assigned to the positive class works as a perfectly good substitute score** for building a precision/recall curve: knowing one of the two tells you the other, so one column carries all the information. It is obtained the same way as before, via `cross_val_predict(..., method="predict_proba")`.

What the curve actually needs from a score is only an **ordering** — which instances the model is more confident about than which others. A probability supplies that ordering whether or not its exact value is trustworthy, which is the next point.

### 2 · Estimated probabilities are not measured ones

Before trusting those numbers too far, the book adds an important caveat: **these are estimated probabilities, not verified ones.**

Looking at every instance the model called positive with 50-60% estimated confidence, roughly 94% of them turned out to actually be positive — **meaning the model was, in that band, considerably more accurate than its own stated confidence implied.** Its probabilities were too low there; the book notes models can be overconfident just as easily.

Scikit-Learn's calibration tools exist specifically to correct this kind of mismatch between estimated and real probabilities. The practical point for you: a column labelled "probability" is a model output like any other, not a measurement, and it should be checked against outcomes before anyone downstream treats 0.55 as meaning 55%.

### 3 · The verdict, and the actual payoff

Plotting the random forest's PR curve alongside the SGD classifier's makes the difference visible at a glance: **the forest's curve sits much closer to the ideal top-right corner across the board**, and its F1 score and ROC AUC both come out clearly higher. Figure 3-8 below is that plot; the card below has the numbers.

This is the payoff of building reusable evaluation tooling in the first half of the chapter — once PR curves, F1, and ROC AUC are working for one classifier, comparing a second one is nearly free. The work was never in the model; it was in deciding how to judge one.

**One-liner for your notes:** use `predict_proba()`'s positive-class column as the score when a model has no `decision_function()`, remember those probabilities are estimates rather than measurements, and note that the forest wins on PR curve, F1 and ROC AUC alike.

blocks.title: Worked out: the forest's probabilities and scores
blocks.content:
For the first two training images, `y_probas_forest[:2]` returns `[[0.11, 0.89], [0.99, 0.01]]`. The model says the first image is positive with 89% probability and the second is negative with 99% probability, and each row adds up to 100%. The second column holds the positive-class probabilities, so `y_probas_forest[:, 1]` is the score given to `precision_recall_curve()`.

Calling an image a 5 when that probability is at least 50% gives the forest an F1 score of about 0.9242, against about 0.7325 for the SGD 5-detector, with about 99.1% precision and 86.6% recall. Computed from the probabilities themselves, the forest's ROC AUC is about 0.9983, against about 0.9605 for SGD.

blocks.caption: Comparing PR curves: the random forest classifier is superior to the SGD classifier
blocks.alt: Figure 3-8: Comparing PR curves: the random forest classifier is superior to the SGD classifier

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

forest_clf = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42)

y_probas_forest = cross_val_predict(forest_clf, X_train, y_train_5, cv=3,
                                    method="predict_proba")
```

items.term: Ranking well and being calibrated are different properties
items.text: A model can order instances perfectly — a near-1.0 AUC — and still state probabilities that are systematically wrong, which is exactly what the 50-60% band being 94% correct shows. Curves, F1 and AUC only need the ordering, so they stay valid. Anything that consumes the number itself — a cost calculation, an expected-value threshold, a figure shown to a user — needs calibration first.

items.term: Why a vote share works as a score at all
items.text: A precision/recall curve never uses the magnitude of a score, only which instances score higher than which others. So the positive-class probability is a legitimate substitute for a decision function even though its values are estimates: it supplies an ordering. That is also why the curve stays correct while the probabilities themselves are miscalibrated.

items.term: The work was in the judging, not the modelling
items.text: Swapping SGD for a random forest was three lines. Deciding what 'better' means — which curve, which average, which operating point — took the first half of the chapter. That ratio holds in real projects, and it is the argument for building the evaluation harness before collecting a shortlist of models.

items: The chapter points at calibration tools without saying how they work. The two standard methods behave differently with small data — which one overfits, and how much data does each need?

items.term: Multiclass Classification: OvR and OvO

blocks.content:
Ten digits, not one: two standard strategies build a ten-class classifier out of binary ones, and Scikit-Learn picks between them for you.

**The question this lesson answers:** the 5-detector only answers yes or no. How do you get from binary classifiers to a system that names all ten digits, and what does that cost?

### The big picture

| Strategy | Trains | Decides by |
|---|---|---|
| OvR, one-versus-the-rest | one per class, so 10 | highest confidence score wins |
| OvO, one-versus-one | one per pair, so 45 | most duels won |

### 1 · Two ways to build ten answers out of yes/no

**One-versus-the-rest (OvR)** trains one binary classifier per class — a 0-detector, a 1-detector, and so on — and classifies a new instance by running it through all of them and **keeping whichever classifier reported the highest confidence score**.

**One-versus-one (OvO)** instead trains a separate classifier for every pair of classes. For 10 digits that means **45 classifiers**, and a new instance is classified by having every pair "vote" and counting which class wins the most duels. The card below shows where 45 comes from.

### 2 · When OvO is worth 45 models

OvO's real advantage shows up **for algorithms that scale poorly as the training set grows**, such as support vector machines: training 45 classifiers, each only on the two classes it needs to tell apart, ends up cheaper than training a smaller number of classifiers on the full dataset. Each of those 45 sees a small slice of the data instead of all of it.

For most other algorithms, OvR is the default. Scikit-Learn detects when a naturally-binary classifier is handed a multiclass target and picks OvO or OvR automatically, though `OneVsOneClassifier` and `OneVsRestClassifier` exist to force one strategy explicitly. Worth knowing that the automatic choice is happening — otherwise you can be training 45 models without ever asking for them.

### 3 · Reading the winner back out

`classes_` stores the trained classifier's class labels in order. That is needed **to translate a raw index — the one `argmax()` returns for the highest decision score — back into an actual digit label.**

`argmax()` gives you a position in an array, not an answer; `classes_[position]` is the answer. For MNIST the index happens to match the digit, which hides the step, so get in the habit of writing the lookup anyway.

### 4 · The biggest win came from the data

One practical detail closes the section, and it is the most transferable thing here: simply **standardizing the pixel values** before training — nothing about the model itself — lifted `SGDClassifier`'s cross-validated accuracy from around 86% to around 90%.

**Standardizing** means rescaling each feature so the values sit in a comparable range, which is the chapter-2 `StandardScaler` step. Nothing was changed about the algorithm, its hyperparameters or the amount of data. It is a reminder that scaling is not just a chapter-2 regression trick, and that the input pipeline is often where the cheap gains are.

**One-liner for your notes:** OvR trains one detector per class and takes the highest score, OvO trains one per pair (45 for ten digits) and counts duels won, Scikit-Learn chooses for you, and scaling the pixels alone bought roughly four points of accuracy.

blocks.title: Worked out: counting classifiers and reading the scores
blocks.content:
With N classes, OvO trains one classifier per pair of classes, which is N × (N – 1) / 2. For the 10 digits that is 10 × 9 / 2 = 45 classifiers. OvR trains one classifier per class, so 10, and `len(ovr_clf.estimators_)` indeed returns 10.

For the example digit, the SVC (which used OvO) returns 10 scores from `decision_function()`, one per class. Each score is the number of duels that class won, plus or minus a small tweak of at most 0.33 to break ties. The highest score is 9.3, at index 5, and `svm_clf.classes_[5]` is '5'.

For the ten-digit `SGDClassifier`, the three cross-validation folds scored 0.87365, 0.85835 and 0.8689 accuracy. After scaling the inputs with `StandardScaler`, the folds scored 0.8983, 0.891 and 0.9018.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.svm import SVC

svm_clf = SVC(random_state=42)
svm_clf.fit(X_train[:2000], y_train[:2000]) # y_train, not y_train_5
```

items.term: The cost arithmetic behind 45 models
items.text: Forty-five classifiers sounds worse than ten until you notice each one only ever sees the two classes it must separate, so its training set is a small slice rather than the whole 60,000. When training cost grows faster than linearly with the number of rows — the support vector machine case the book names — many small fits beat a few large ones. When cost grows about linearly, that advantage disappears and OvR's simpler bookkeeping wins.

items.term: The biggest gain in this section came from the data
items.text: Scaling the pixels changed no model, no hyperparameter and no amount of data, and it moved accuracy about four points — more than switching strategies would have. Worth noticing honestly: the chapter states the result and does not explain the mechanism, so treat it as an empirical prompt to try scaling, not as a theory you can quote.

items.term: Automatic strategy selection hides a real cost
items.text: Handing a binary estimator a ten-class target silently trains 10 or 45 models depending on the algorithm. That is convenient until you are measuring training time, memory or reproducibility. Checking `len(estimators_)` and `classes_` is how you find out what actually got built.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Would you expect OvR or OvO to train faster for a small dataset with just 3 classes and a model that scales well with dataset size? Why?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The book says support vector machines scale poorly with training-set size, which is the whole argument for OvO. What is the actual growth rate, and roughly where does the dataset get big enough for it to matter?
Look up: the scikit-learn user guide, "Support Vector Machines", the "Complexity" section.

items.term: Error Analysis With the Confusion Matrix

blocks.content:
The same confusion matrix that exposed the 5-detector, now 10x10, is how you find out what your model actually gets wrong — as long as you read the percentages against the right denominator.

**The question this lesson answers:** you have a promising ten-digit model. How do you find out which mistakes it makes, and what do you do about them?

### The big picture

| Setting | Each cell divided by | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| raw counts | nothing | how many, absolutely |
| normalize="true" | its row total (the true class) | of the real 5s, where did they go |
| normalize="pred" | its column total | of the things called 8, what were they |
| errors only | row total, correct ones zeroed | of my mistakes on 7s, which mistake |

One matrix, four questions. The denominator *is* the question.

### 1 · Raw counts mislead

`ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_predictions()` turns the 10x10 grid into a picture where a strong diagonal signals mostly-correct predictions at a glance. But raw counts alone can mislead: a darker cell for the digit 5 might mean more errors on 5s, or it might just mean there are fewer 5s in the dataset to begin with.

That ambiguity is the same one a raw count always has when the groups are different sizes. You cannot compare a count across classes until you divide by something.

### 2 · Normalizing by row

**Setting `normalize="true"` divides every cell by its row's total — the true class — so every row reads as a percentage of that class rather than a raw count**, comparable across digits regardless of how many examples of each exist.

That normalized view shows only about **82% of 5s were classified correctly**, with the most common mistake being 8: **10% of all 5s were called 8s, while only 2% of 8s were called 5s.** Read that pair again — it is the same two digits, and the two numbers are nowhere near each other. **Confusion matrices are not symmetric.** The confusion has a direction, and a fix aimed at "5s and 8s look alike" would miss it.

### 3 · Making faint errors visible

To make faint-but-real error patterns visible, the book also zeroes out every correct prediction with a `sample_weight` before normalizing. The diagonal disappears and only mistakes remain, so the shape of the errors stops being drowned out by the correct answers.

It can also normalize by predicted column instead of true row. **With `normalize="pred"`, each cell is divided by the total of its predicted column**, which asks the complementary question: of everything the model called an 8, what were those things really?

### 4 · The care point that changes the meaning

One thing matters more than it looks: **a normalized error percentage describes a slice of the errors, not the whole class.**

In the errors-only, row-normalized plot, 36% at row 7, column 9 means **36% of the mistakes made on 7s were called 9 — not that 36% of all 7s were.** Out of all the 7s, only 3% were misclassified as 9s. Two very different statements from one cell, and only the denominator tells them apart. The card below works both through.

### 5 · From diagnosis to next steps

Reading that difference correctly is what turns this analysis into concrete next steps, and the chapter names two:

- **gather more training data** resembling the true source of confusion — digits that look like 8s but are not;
- **engineer features that separate the confused digits, such as counting closed loops** — 8 has two, 6 has one, 5 has none.

Note that both act on the inputs, not the metric. The confusion matrix does not tell you to change models; it tells you where the model cannot see a difference that is really there.

**One-liner for your notes:** normalize the 10x10 matrix by row to compare classes fairly, by column to ask what a predicted label really contained, and remember an errors-only percentage is a share of the mistakes, not of the class.

blocks.title: Worked out: the percentages in the error plots
blocks.content:
The errors-only plot passes `sample_weight = (y_train_pred != y_train)`, which puts zero weight on every correct prediction, so only the errors are left when each row is normalized. That is why the 36% at row 7, column 9 is a share of the errors made on 7s. Out of all 7s, only 3% were misclassified as 9s, as the full row-normalized plot (Figure 3-9, right) shows.

With `normalize="pred"`, each column is divided by its own total instead. For example, 56% of the images wrongly classified as 7s are actually 9s. In the errors-only plot, the column for class 8 is really bright: many digits get misclassified as 8s, which is why the chapter suggests spending effort on reducing the false 8s.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.metrics import ConfusionMatrixDisplay

y_train_pred = cross_val_predict(sgd_clf, X_train_scaled, y_train, cv=3)
ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_predictions(y_train, y_train_pred,
                                        normalize="true", values_format=".0%")

```

items.term: Normalising is choosing a denominator, and the denominator is the question
items.text: By row: of the real 5s, where did they go. By column: of everything called an 8, what was it really. Errors only, by row: of my mistakes on 7s, which mistake was it. One matrix, three questions, three different pictures — the same discipline as deciding what a rate is divided by before you quote it.

items.term: Asymmetry is information, not noise
items.text: Ten percent of 5s becoming 8s while only two percent of 8s become 5s says the confusion has a direction. A symmetric reading ('5s and 8s look alike') would send you looking for a feature that separates the pair; the asymmetric reading points at what makes a 5 look like an 8 specifically, which is a narrower and more actionable question.

items.term: Diagnosis points at inputs, not at metrics
items.text: The bright column for 8 in the errors-only plot says too many things are being called 8 — a statement about the predicted side. Both fixes the chapter suggests act on the inputs: more data resembling the confusers, or a feature that makes the difference visible. A confusion matrix never tells you to change the metric; it tells you where the model cannot see a difference that is really there.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Why can normalizing a confusion matrix by row (normalize='true') tell a different story than normalizing it by column (normalize='pred')?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The chapter suggests engineering a feature such as counting closed loops. How would you measure whether a new feature actually helped, beyond watching overall accuracy move?
Look up: the scikit-learn user guide, "Permutation feature importance".

items.term: Multilabel Classification

blocks.content:
Some instances deserve several answers at once, and multilabel classification is the shape that allows it: one independent yes/no tag per label, not one choice out of many.

**The question this lesson answers:** a photo contains two people your model recognises. How does a classifier output both of them, and how do you score a model that produces several answers per instance?

### The big picture

```
single-label:  one image  -> one class   '5'
multilabel  :  one image  -> [large?, odd?]
                            [False, True]
```

Think of it as several boolean columns rather than one enum column.

### 1 · Several tags, not one choice

Not every classification problem has exactly one right answer per instance. A face-recognition system shown a photo of two specific people should tag both of them, not force a single label. **That is multilabel classification: the output is a set of independent binary tags rather than one class choice**, one tag per thing it might recognise.

The card below works through the book's Alice, Bob and Charlie example, where `[True, False, True]` means Alice and Charlie are recognised in the picture but Bob is not.

The chapter's toy version tags each MNIST digit with two labels at once: whether it is **large (7, 8, or 9)** and whether it is **odd**. The two are combined into a two-column array and fed to `KNeighborsClassifier`, which is one of the classifiers that actually supports multilabel targets natively — not all do.

So the digit 8 gets `[True, False]`: large, and not odd.

### 2 · Scoring several labels at once

Scoring a multilabel classifier means picking a way to combine per-label scores into one number, and the choice matters:

| Averaging | Treats each label as |
|---|---|
| macro | equally important, however rare |
| weighted | important in proportion to its support |

Averaging each label's F1 score with `average="macro"` treats every label as equally important. **`average="weighted"` instead weights each label's contribution by its support** — how many instances actually carry that label — which is the more honest choice when the labels are not evenly represented in the data.

This is a values decision, not a technical one: under `weighted`, a rare label's poor performance nearly vanishes from the headline number; under `macro`, it counts as much as a common one.

### 3 · When labels are not independent

Classifiers that cannot handle multilabel targets natively, like SVC, can still be pressed into service by training one independent binary model per label — but that throws away any relationship between the labels. The chapter's own example: **large digits are twice as likely to be odd as even**, and the "odd" model has no way to know what the "large" model decided.

`ClassifierChain` fixes this by **feeding each model in the chain not just the input features but also the predictions from every model earlier in the chain.** The chain turns independent models into a sequence where later ones can use earlier answers.

It can optionally be trained on cross-validated out-of-sample predictions, so the chain learns from the kind of predictions it will actually receive at run time rather than from the true labels it will not have.

**One-liner for your notes:** multilabel means independent binary tags per instance, macro vs weighted averaging decides whether rare labels count equally, and `ClassifierChain` passes earlier predictions forward so later models can use label relationships.

blocks.title: The Alice, Bob and Charlie example
blocks.content:
The chapter's face-recognition example uses a classifier trained to recognize three faces: Alice, Bob and Charlie. It outputs one True/False tag per person, in that order. Shown a picture of Alice and Charlie, it should output `[True, False, True]`, meaning "Alice yes, Bob no, Charlie yes".

The digit version works the same way with two tags, large (7, 8 or 9) first and odd second. For the example digit, a 5, `knn_clf.predict([some_digit])` returns `[[False, True]]`, because a 5 is not large but is odd. Among the large digits, 7 and 9 are odd and only 8 is even, which is why a large digit is twice as likely to be odd as even.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

y_train_large = (y_train >= '7')
y_train_odd = (y_train.astype('int8') % 2 == 1)
y_multilabel = np.c_[y_train_large, y_train_odd]

knn_clf = KNeighborsClassifier()
knn_clf.fit(X_train, y_multilabel)
```

items.term: Independent tags versus one choice
items.text: Multilabel is N yes/no columns; single-label is one column with N possible values. In table terms that is several boolean columns versus one enum column, and the modelling question is whether the booleans are really independent. When they are not — large digits being twice as likely to be odd — separate models leave information on the floor.

items.term: Macro versus weighted is a values decision
items.text: Macro says a rare label matters as much as a common one; weighted says a label matters in proportion to how often it occurs. Under weighted, terrible performance on a rare label almost vanishes from the headline number. Neither is more correct — but whichever you pick is a claim about whose errors count, so state it.

items.term: What the chain costs
items.text: A chain is a sequence, so the label order is a choice, and a model late in the chain is consuming predictions that may be wrong. The book's cross-validation option exists to stop a subtler problem: trained on true labels, later models learn to rely on inputs they will never see at prediction time. Training on out-of-sample predictions makes training conditions match run-time conditions.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Explain why ClassifierChain can capture label dependencies that training one independent model per label cannot.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: A ClassifierChain's result depends on the order the labels are chained in, and the book picks one order without discussing it. How do people choose an order, or avoid choosing?
Look up: the scikit-learn user guide, "Multiclass and multioutput algorithms", the "Classifier Chain" section.

items.term: Multioutput Classification: Denoising Images

blocks.content:
The last generalization in the chapter lets each label carry more than two values, and the example is an image denoiser: 784 labels per instance, each one a pixel intensity.

**The question this lesson answers:** multilabel gave each instance several yes/no tags. What happens when each of those "tags" can take 256 different values instead of two — and is that still classification?

### The big picture

```
multilabel   : 2 labels  x  2 values each (True/False)
multioutput  : 784 labels x 256 values each (0-255)
   input : noisy 28 x 28 image
   output: clean 28 x 28 image
```

### 1 · The example first, the definition after

Multioutput classification is best understood through a concrete example rather than a definition: an **image-denoising system**. Feed the model a noisy digit image, and ask it to predict the original clean image back.

The noisy inputs are built by **adding random pixel-level noise to real MNIST images** — the clean image plus a random amount on each of its 784 pixels. The training label for each instance is **the original clean image, as an array of 784 pixel intensities**. Input and target are both pictures; the model learns to get from one to the other.

That gives one label per pixel, and **each of those 784 labels can take any value from 0 to 255, not just true or false.** That is what makes it multioutput rather than plain multilabel: **multilabel assumes each label is binary, and here each "label" is really its own miniature multiclass problem.**

### 2 · Where classification stops being the right word

The book is candid that this blurs the line between classification and regression — predicting a pixel's intensity looks a lot more like regression than like picking a class.

The reason is worth spelling out, because it is the difference between the two families. A classifier treats its possible answers as unrelated names: to it, intensity 200 and intensity 201 are two different classes with nothing in common, exactly as 200 and 10 are. A regressor treats them as numbers on a line, so being off by one is nearly right and being off by 190 is badly wrong. Pixel intensities are obviously the second kind, which is why the label "classification" sits awkwardly here.

The book also notes multioutput systems in general are not restricted to classification tasks at all; a system could just as easily mix class labels and numeric labels together.

### 3 · Mechanically, nothing new

The point of ending the chapter here is that none of the machinery changed. The same `KNeighborsClassifier` used for the earlier multilabel example is trained on noisy inputs paired with their original clean versions as targets, and calling **`predict()` on a noisy test image returns a full reconstructed image** of 784 pixels — Figure 3-13 below — rather than a single tag.

Same `fit`, same `predict`, same library. Only the target column changed shape.

That closes out the chapter's tour by showing that the classification toolbox — from picking metrics to comparing models — scales to problems that do not look like classification at first glance.

**One-liner for your notes:** multioutput classification is multilabel where each label can take many values, the denoiser's target is the clean 784-pixel image, and the only thing that changed from earlier examples is the shape of `y`.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
np.random.seed(42) # to make this code example reproducible
noise = np.random.randint(0, 100, (len(X_train), 784))
X_train_mod = X_train + noise
noise = np.random.randint(0, 100, (len(X_test), 784))
X_test_mod = X_test + noise
y_train_mod = X_train
y_test_mod = X_test

knn_clf = KNeighborsClassifier()
knn_clf.fit(X_train_mod, y_train_mod)
clean_digit = knn_clf.predict([X_test_mod[0]])
```

items.term: Only the shape of y changed
items.text: Same KNeighborsClassifier, same fit, same predict, same library. Single-label, multilabel and multioutput differ only in what sits in the target: one value, several booleans, or several many-valued numbers. That is the chapter's closing argument — the tooling generalises because it was never specific to the target's shape.

items.term: Why this is barely classification
items.text: A classifier treats its possible answers as unrelated names, so intensity 200 and 201 are as different to it as 200 and 10. A regressor treats them as points on a line, so being off by one is nearly right. Pixel intensities are plainly the second kind, which is exactly the book's own reason for calling the line blurry (book page index 189).

items.term: Denoising by nearest neighbours is really retrieval
items.text: The k-nearest-neighbours idea from chapter 1 — find the closest training rows and answer from them — is doing the work here: the reconstructed image is assembled from the clean targets of the training images that most resemble the noisy input. That reframes 'the model removed the noise' as 'the model found images it had already seen', which is a useful way to think about what such a system can and cannot do on a digit unlike anything in its training set.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Why does the book describe the line between classification and regression as 'blurry' in the denoising example?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Scikit-Learn also ships MultiOutputClassifier and MultiOutputRegressor. Given the book admits predicting pixel intensity is closer to regression, what would change if the denoiser were built as multioutput regression instead?
Look up: the scikit-learn user guide, "Multiclass and multioutput algorithms", the "Multioutput classification" and "Multioutput regression" sections.

items.term: End-of-chapter exercises

blocks.title: 4 book exercises
items: Exercise 1: Try to build a classifier for the MNIST dataset that achieves over 97% accuracy on the test set. Hint: the KNeighborsClassifier works quite well for this task; you just need to find good hyperparameter values (try a grid search on the weights and n_neighbors hyperparameters).

Exercise 2: Write a function that can shift an MNIST image in any direction (left, right, up, or down) by one pixel. Then, for each image in the training set, create four shifted copies (one per direction) and add them to the training set. Finally, train your best model on this expanded training set and measure its accuracy on the test set. You should observe that your model performs even better now! This technique of artificially growing the training set is called data augmentation or training set expansion.

Exercise 3: Tackle the Titanic dataset. A great place to start is on Kaggle. Alternatively, you can download the data from https://homl.info/titanic.tgz and unzip this tarball like you did for the housing data in Chapter 2. This will give you two CSV files, train.csv and test.csv, which you can load using pandas.read_csv(). The goal is to train a classifier that can predict the Survived column based on the other columns.

Exercise 4: Build a spam classifier (a more challenging exercise):
a. Download examples of spam and ham from Apache SpamAssassin's public datasets.
b. Unzip the datasets and familiarize yourself with the data format.
c. Split the data into a training set and a test set.
d. Write a data preparation pipeline to convert each email into a feature vector. Your preparation pipeline should transform an email into a (sparse) vector that indicates the presence or absence of each possible word. For example, if all emails only ever contain four words, "Hello", "how", "are", "you", then the email "Hello you Hello Hello you" would be converted into a vector [1, 0, 0, 1] (meaning ["Hello" is present, "how" is absent, "are" is absent, "you" is present]), or [3, 0, 0, 2] if you prefer to count the number of occurrences of each word. You may want to add hyperparameters to your preparation pipeline to control whether or not to strip off email headers, convert each email to lowercase, remove punctuation, replace all URLs with "URL", replace all numbers with "NUMBER", or even perform stemming (i.e., trim off word endings; there are Python libraries available to do this).
e. Finally, try out several classifiers and see if you can build a great spam classifier, with both high recall and high precision.

items.term: The Linear Regression Prediction Equation

blocks.content:
A linear regression model predicts by multiplying every input by its own weight, adding those products together, and adding one flat constant on top.

**The question this lesson answers:** given n input numbers for one row, what arithmetic turns them into a single predicted number — and why does the chapter write that same arithmetic three different ways?

### The big picture

```
each input × its own weight ─┐
                             ├─> add up ─> ŷ
the bias θ₀ (always × 1) ────┘
```

Equations 4-1, 4-2 and 4-3 below are three views of that one picture: the long way of writing it, the short way, and the score that says how wrong it came out.

### 1 · The weighted sum

A linear model makes a prediction by computing a **weighted sum** of the input features, plus a constant. A **feature** is one input column — mileage, GDP per capita, petal width. Its **weight** is the number saying how much that column matters. Multiply the two and you get that column's contribution to the answer.

If you have written a `SELECT`, the shape is `w1*col1 + w2*col2 + ... + const`. The difference is that you do not choose the numbers: training does.

### 2 · The bias term

The extra constant is the **bias term**, also called the **intercept**. It is the prediction the model would make if every feature were zero.

The two kinds of number move the prediction differently:

| Change this | And this happens |
|---|---|
| one weight | every prediction shifts along that one feature's direction |
| the bias | every prediction shifts by the same flat amount, whatever the inputs are |

### 3 · One prediction, done by hand

Take a model whose bias is θ₀ = 2 and whose feature weights are θ₁ = 3 and θ₂ = 0.5, and feed it a row with x₁ = 4 and x₂ = 10. The prediction is the bias plus each weight times its feature value: 2 + 3 × 4 + 0.5 × 10 = 2 + 12 + 5 = 19.

That is the whole model. Everything else in this chapter is about how the weights get chosen.

### 4 · Why the chapter switches to a dot product

Written out with n features, the prediction ŷ is θ₀ (the bias) plus θ₁x₁ plus θ₂x₂, and so on through θₙxₙ. That is a lot of terms to write for every single prediction, so the chapter switches to a compact **vector** notation. A vector is just an ordered list of numbers.

Pack the weights, bias out front, into one vector θ; pack the feature values into another vector x with a fixed 1 slotted in for the bias; and the whole weighted sum collapses into one **dot product**, θ·x. A dot product multiplies two equal-length lists position by position and adds up the results.

The fixed 1 is the trick that makes this work: θ₀ × 1 = θ₀ puts the bias back inside the very same operation used for every other weight, so there is no special case to write. Equation 4-2 below is that form.

Nothing about the model changed — it is still the same weighted sum — only the notation got shorter. This dot-product view is what the rest of the chapter reuses everywhere.

### 5 · What "training" means here

Training a linear model always means searching for the vector θ that makes θ·x land as close as possible to the true target y across every training example.

"As close as possible" is not a feeling; it needs a score. Equation 4-3 below is that score: the **mean squared error (MSE)**, the average of the squared gaps between prediction and truth. Every method in this chapter — the one-step formula, the three gradient descent variants — is a different way of hunting for the θ that makes that one number as small as it can go.

**One-liner for your notes:** a linear model is one weighted sum plus a bias, θ·x is the same sum written shorter, and training is the search for the θ that minimises the MSE.

blocks.title: Equation 4-1
blocks.caption: Linear regression model prediction
blocks.explain:
**Why these equations look like this**

Equation 4-1 is a weighted sum because that is the simplest rule in which every input
gets its own independent say. Each feature is multiplied by exactly one number and the
results are added. Nothing is squared and no two features are multiplied together —
either of those would bend the surface or let one feature change another feature's
effect, and a linear model deliberately does neither. The lone extra constant exists
because without it every prediction would be forced to be zero when the inputs are
zero, which is almost never what real data does.

Equation 4-2 is not a second model. It is Equation 4-1 with the terms packed into two
lists so the whole sum can be written as one symbol.

Equation 4-3 is a score, not a prediction. It squares each gap so that a miss above and
a miss below cannot cancel each other out, and it averages so the score does not grow
just because you scored more rows.

**Standard or simplified?** All three are canonical. Equation 4-1 is the general
n-feature form — chapter 1's life satisfaction model, a start value plus a slope times
GDP per capita, is this same equation with n = 1. Equation 4-3 is the ordinary MSE; the
book chooses it over RMSE only because it is simpler to minimise and lands on the same
θ, since whatever minimises a positive quantity also minimises its square root.

**The general form.** Equation 4-1 already is the general form. Going from one feature
to many adds one θ and one multiply per feature and changes nothing else:

| Features | The model |
|---|---|
| one | θ₀ + θ₁x₁ |
| two | θ₀ + θ₁x₁ + θ₂x₂ |
| n | θ₀ plus one θ times x term per feature |

**Terms these equations introduce**

- an **instance** is one row being predicted or scored
- the **target** y is the true answer for that row
- **h** is the model itself; the book calls it the hypothesis, and writes h with θ
underneath to stress that the model is decided entirely by the vector θ
- **m** is how many instances are being scored; **n** is how many features there are
- the small **T** raised after θ is the **transpose**, which flips a column of numbers
onto its side so it can be multiplied against another column. It changes no value

**Every piece of Equation 4-1**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| ŷ | y hat | the predicted value |
| θ₀ | theta zero | the bias, added with no feature attached |
| θ₁x₁ | theta one x one | feature 1 multiplied by its own weight |
| the dots | and so on | the same pattern for every remaining feature |
| θₙxₙ | theta n x n | the last feature times its weight |

**Every piece of Equation 4-2**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| h with θ under it | h theta of x | the model, run on the row x |
| θ | theta | the whole list of weights, bias first |
| x | x | the row's feature values, with a 1 in front |
| the centre dot | dot | multiply position by position, then add |

**Every piece of Equation 4-3**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| MSE of X and h | M S E | the score for this data and this model |
| m | m | how many instances are being scored |
| the sum sign | sum from i equals 1 to m | add the bracket up over every instance |
| θ transpose x | theta transpose x of i | what the model predicts for instance i |
| y of i | y superscript i | the true value for instance i |
| the squared bracket | squared | multiply the bracket by itself |
| one over m | one over m | divide the total by m, giving the average |

**The formulas in plain words**

- Equation 4-1: prediction = bias + (weight × feature) added up over every feature.
- Equation 4-2: prediction = the dot product of the weight list and the feature list.
- Equation 4-3: score = the average of (prediction − truth) squared.

**With real numbers**

Take the lesson's own model: bias θ₀ = 2, weights θ₁ = 3 and θ₂ = 0.5, and a row with
x₁ = 4 and x₂ = 10.

1. feature 1's contribution: 3 × 4 = 12
2. feature 2's contribution: 0.5 × 10 = 5
3. add the bias: 2 + 12 + 5 = 19

Equation 4-2 does the identical arithmetic with the lists θ = [2, 3, 0.5] and
x = [1, 4, 10]: 2 × 1 + 3 × 4 + 0.5 × 10 = 19. The leading 1 is what turns the bias into
an ordinary term.

Equation 4-3 has no worked value in this lesson, because scoring needs true targets and
none have been introduced yet. The next lesson supplies them: fitting the 100 noisy
points minimises exactly this quantity and returns θ = [4.215, 2.770] where the rule
that generated the data was [4, 3]. The leftover gaps — 4.215 − 4 = 0.215 and
2.770 − 3 = −0.230 — are what is left after the MSE is as small as it can be.

---

blocks.caption: Linear regression model prediction (vectorized form)

blocks.title: Equation 4-3
blocks.caption: MSE cost function for a linear regression model

items.term: Why a weighted sum, and what it cannot express
items.text: A weighted sum is the most constrained useful model there is: every feature contributes independently and by a fixed amount per unit. That constraint is what makes the model fast to train, easy to read off (a weight IS the answer to 'how much does this column matter') and hard to overfit. The price is that it cannot express anything that bends, and it cannot express an effect that depends on another feature's value. Both of those limits are real and both are worked around later in this chapter, not by changing the model but by changing the columns.

items.term: The fixed 1 is a pattern, not a trick
items.text: Slotting a constant 1 into the feature vector so the bias becomes an ordinary weight is a move you will see repeatedly: it removes a special case from the code by making it a normal case in the data. The cost is that you must remember the column is there when you count features, and the regularization lessons later in the chapter have to go out of their way to exempt it again.

items.term: A weight is only interpretable if the columns are comparable
items.text: It is tempting to rank features by the size of their weights. That only works if the features share a scale, because a column measured in millions needs a tiny weight to have a large effect and a column measured in fractions needs a huge one. The same fact is what makes feature scaling matter for gradient descent and for ridge later on — three different consequences of one cause.

items.term: Training by Formula: The Normal Equation

blocks.content:
For plain linear regression you do not have to search for the best weights at all — one formula, the Normal equation, computes them directly from the data in a single step.

**The question this lesson answers:** the model is a weighted sum and the score is the MSE. Is there a way to jump straight to the weights that make that score smallest, and what does the library actually run when you call `fit`?

### The big picture

| Route | How it gets θ | Breaks when |
|---|---|---|
| Normal equation | one matrix formula, one step | XᵀX is not invertible |
| SVD pseudoinverse | matrix factorisation, one step | never — always defined |
| gradient descent | many small steps downhill | next lesson |

### 1 · What "as close as possible" means

Training a linear regression model means finding the θ vector that makes predictions land as close as possible to the true targets, and "as close as possible" is measured by the **mean squared error (MSE)**: average the squared gap between each prediction and its true value, so a few big misses hurt the score far more than many tiny ones.

Squaring is doing the work there. A gap of 10 contributes 100; ten gaps of 1 contribute 10 in total. The score is deliberately not democratic.

### 2 · The shortcut

For plain linear regression there is a shortcut: instead of searching for the best θ by trial and error, one formula — the Normal equation — computes it directly from the data in a single step. Equation 4-4 below is that formula, with the full walkthrough underneath it.

"Closed-form" is the word for this: a finite recipe of ordinary arithmetic that hands back the answer, with no loop and no stopping rule. Think of a single deterministic query that returns the result, rather than a job that iterates until it is happy.

### 3 · Running it on data whose answer we already know

Running it on a small synthetic dataset (y = 4 + 3x plus random noise) makes the abstraction concrete. Generate 100 points from that rule, plug the feature matrix and the targets into the formula, and the result comes out close to but not exactly [4, 3] — something like [4.215, 2.770].

That gap is entirely the noise: with perfectly clean data the equation would recover [4, 3] exactly, and the smaller or noisier the dataset, the further the estimate tends to drift. **Noise** here means the random wobble added to each point, the part of the target no rule could have predicted. The formula fits the noisy points it was given, not the clean rule hiding behind them.

### 4 · What scikit-learn really runs

Scikit-Learn's `LinearRegression` class does not actually run this literal matrix-inversion formula under the hood — it uses a matrix factorization technique (SVD) that computes a pseudoinverse instead. **SVD** (singular value decomposition) splits a matrix into three simpler ones; the **pseudoinverse** is a stand-in for an inverse that is defined even when a true inverse is not.

That route is more efficient and, unlike the raw Normal equation, it never breaks: the Normal equation can fail outright when X-transpose-X is not invertible (which happens with more features than instances, or duplicated features), while the pseudoinverse is always defined.

Duplicated features are the everyday case: ship the same column twice under two names and the raw formula has no single answer to give, because the two copies can trade weight freely.

### 5 · What each one costs

Both approaches share one limitation: inverting a matrix that grows with the number of features gets expensive fast.

| If you double the features | Time goes up by |
|---|---|
| raw Normal equation | about 5 to 8 times |
| SVD route in scikit-learn | about 4 times |

Put as one sentence: doubling the feature count roughly multiplies the compute time by 5 to 8 times for the raw inversion, and by about 4 times even for the faster SVD route.

Neither approach cares much about the number of training instances, so both stay fast on huge datasets as long as the data fits in memory. In your terms: rows are cheap, columns are not — the opposite of the instinct a big-table background gives you. The card below has the exact complexity figures.

**One-liner for your notes:** the Normal equation solves linear regression in one step, scikit-learn runs the safer SVD version of it, and both scale fine with rows but badly with columns.

blocks.title: Worked out: where the 5.3-to-8 and 4 times figures come from
blocks.content:
The Normal equation inverts XᵀX, which is an (n + 1) × (n + 1) matrix, where n is the number of features. Inverting a matrix of that size typically costs about $O(n^{2.4})$ to $O(n^3)$, depending on the implementation. Doubling n therefore multiplies the computation time by roughly $2^{2.4} = 5.3$ up to $2^3 = 8$. The SVD approach used by Scikit-Learn's `LinearRegression` class is about $O(n^2)$, so doubling the features multiplies the time by roughly $2^2 = 4$.

The number of instances behaves differently: both approaches are linear in it, $O(m)$, so twice as many instances take roughly twice as long. That is why they handle large training sets efficiently, provided the data fits in memory, yet both get very slow when the number of features grows large, for example 100,000.

blocks.title: Equation 4-4
blocks.caption: Normal equation
blocks.explain:
**Why the equation looks like this**

Equation 4-4 is the answer to a question you can ask directly: where is the bottom of
the MSE bowl? For a weighted sum scored by squared error, that bottom can be worked out
exactly with ordinary matrix arithmetic, so there is no need to walk downhill looking
for it. That is what makes it a **closed-form** solution — a finite recipe of constants,
variables and standard operations, with no loop, no stopping rule and no tolerance.

The two halves of the formula have readable jobs. Xᵀy measures how strongly each feature
moves together with the target: features that rise when the target rises get a large
entry. If features never overlapped, that alone would be the answer. But they do
overlap, and XᵀX is the table of how strongly every feature moves with every other one.
Inverting it is what shares the credit out fairly between features that carry the same
information, instead of paying both of them in full.

**Standard or simplified?** Standard, and famous. This is the closed-form least squares
solution, and the book does not derive it — it presents it as a given and moves to using
it, so treat the formula as something to read and apply rather than to re-derive. The
name shows up in the library too: scikit-learn's LinearRegression is built on a function
called lstsq, which stands for least squares.

**The general form.** There is no smaller or larger version. Equation 4-4 already covers
any number of features and any number of rows. What changes in practice is which
*implementation* computes it: the literal inversion here, or the SVD pseudoinverse that
scikit-learn actually runs, or Equation 4-9 later in the chapter, which is this same
formula with a regularization term added.

**Terms this equation introduces**

- **X** is the whole training set as a grid: one row per instance, one column per
feature, with the fixed 1 column added in front for the bias
- **y** is the column of true targets, one per row
- **transpose** (the small raised T) flips a grid onto its side, turning rows into
columns; it moves no numbers, it only changes which direction they line up in
- **inverse** (the raised −1) is the matrix version of dividing. A matrix times its
inverse leaves things unchanged, the way multiplying by 3 then by one third does
- **singular** is the word for a matrix that has no inverse, which is when the raw
formula has nothing to return

**Every piece of Equation 4-4**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| θ with a hat | theta hat | the θ that minimises the cost |
| X | capital X | the training inputs, one row per instance |
| X transpose | X transpose | X flipped onto its side |
| X transpose X | X transpose X | how every feature overlaps every other |
| the raised minus one | inverse | undo that overlap |
| X transpose y | X transpose y | how each feature lines up with the target |

**The formula in plain words**

Best weights = (undo the overlap between the features) applied to (how each feature
lines up with the target).

**With real numbers**

The demo generates 100 points from y = 4 + 3x plus random noise, feeds X and y into the
formula, and gets back θ = [4.215, 2.770].

1. the rule that made the data had a start value of 4 and a slope of 3
2. the formula returned a start value of 4.215 and a slope of 2.770
3. the leftovers are 4.215 − 4 = 0.215 and 2.770 − 3 = −0.230

Those two gaps are the noise, not an error in the formula. The formula is exact for the
data it was handed; the data itself was not exact.

---

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import numpy as np

np.random.seed(42) # to make this code example reproducible
m = 100 # number of instances
X = 2 * np.random.rand(m, 1) # column vector
y = 4 + 3 * X + np.random.randn(m, 1) # column vector

from sklearn.preprocessing import add_dummy_feature

X_b = add_dummy_feature(X) # add x0 = 1 to each instance
theta_best = np.linalg.inv(X_b.T @ X_b) @ X_b.T @ y
```

items.term: When a closed form is the right answer, and when it is a trap
items.text: One formula, no tuning and an exact answer is genuinely better than an iterative search — when you can afford it. The cost is cubic-ish in the number of columns and it needs the whole dataset in memory, so the closed form quietly stops being available as a problem grows, and nothing warns you: it just takes longer and longer. Knowing which axis is the expensive one is what lets you predict that before it happens.

items.term: Why 'not invertible' is a data problem, not a maths problem
items.text: The Normal equation fails when two columns carry the same information, or when there are more columns than rows. Both are statements about your data, not about the algebra: in the first case the model genuinely cannot tell which of two identical columns deserves the credit, and in the second there are more unknowns than equations, so infinitely many weight vectors fit perfectly. The SVD route does not solve that ambiguity — it just returns one particular answer instead of failing, which is convenient and worth knowing about.

items.term: Fitting the noise is the correct behaviour, not a bug
items.text: The formula returns 4.215 and 2.770 rather than 4 and 3, and it is right to. It was asked for the best fit to the points it was given, and those points include the noise. Any method that recovered exactly 4 and 3 from noisy data would have to be using information it was not given. This is the honest version of what the rest of the chapter calls variance.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Your dataset has 500 training instances and 50,000 features. Would the Normal equation's per-feature cost or its per-instance cost dominate the runtime?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The pseudoinverse returns an answer even when infinitely many weight vectors fit the data perfectly. Which one does it return, and why that one?
Look up: the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse (numpy.linalg.pinv) and the minimum-norm solution it selects; the book names it on the same page as np.linalg.lstsq.

items.term: Gradient Descent: Feeling Your Way to the Minimum

blocks.content:
Gradient descent is the general-purpose alternative to the one-step formula: start from a random guess and keep nudging the weights in whichever direction the cost is falling fastest.

**The question this lesson answers:** the Normal equation only works for linear regression's exact MSE formula, and it gets expensive as the number of features grows. What do you do instead — and what are the two things that make it go wrong?

### The big picture

```
random start ─> feel the slope ─> step downhill ─> repeat
                       ↑                            │
                       └────────────────────────────┘
```

### 1 · Feeling your way downhill

Instead of solving for the best θ in one step, gradient descent starts from a random guess and nudges θ a little at a time, always moving in whichever direction most reduces the cost function right now — like feeling your way downhill in thick fog by sensing the slope under your feet.

The **cost function** is the single number saying how badly the current weights fit the data; for linear regression that is the MSE from the last lesson. Figure 4-3 below shows the walk.

Nothing about this is specific to linear regression, which is the point: the same loop trains almost every model in the rest of the book.

### 2 · The one dial: the learning rate

The size of each step is set by a single hyperparameter, the **learning rate**. A **hyperparameter** is a setting you fix before the run and that training never changes — the equivalent of a `--conf` value passed at submit time, not a value the job computes.

| Learning rate | What happens | Figure |
|---|---|---|
| too small | an enormous number of tiny steps; safe but slow | 4-4 |
| too large | each step overshoots and lands higher up the far side | 4-5 |

Make it too small and the algorithm needs an enormous number of tiny steps to reach the bottom, which is safe but slow. Make it too large and each step can overshoot the minimum and land higher up the opposite side of the valley than where it started — repeat that a few times and the algorithm diverges, wandering farther from a solution rather than closer.

**Diverge** is the important word: this is not "slower to finish", it is "getting worse every step and never stopping".

### 3 · Why it is safe here: the bowl has one bottom

Two extra facts make gradient descent tractable for linear regression specifically.

First, the MSE cost function is **convex** — picture one smooth bowl with no dips or ridges — so there is exactly one minimum to find, and gradient descent is guaranteed to reach it eventually as long as the learning rate is sane.

That guarantee is not general. Figure 4-6 below shows the pitfalls on a cost surface that is *not* a clean bowl: a **local minimum** is a dip that is lower than everything nearby but higher than the true bottom, and a **plateau** is a near-flat stretch that takes forever to cross. Linear regression has neither.

### 4 · Why feature scaling matters so much

Second, the bowl's shape depends on how the features are scaled. If one feature's values are far larger than another's, the bowl becomes a long narrow trench, and descent crawls sideways before finding the way down.

Scaling every feature to a similar range (with something like `StandardScaler`) turns that trench back into a round bowl and speeds up convergence dramatically. Figure 4-7 below is the two cases side by side.

This is the single most common reason a correctly written training loop is mysteriously slow, and it costs one preprocessing step to remove.

**One-liner for your notes:** gradient descent walks downhill on the cost function; the learning rate decides whether it crawls or diverges, and unscaled features turn the bowl into a trench.

items.term: Why a generic optimiser is worth more than an exact formula
items.text: Gradient descent gives up exactness and gains reach: it needs only that you can measure the cost and its slope, so the same loop trains linear regression, logistic regression, and every neural network in the later chapters. The Normal equation is better at exactly one problem. Learning the general tool once is why this lesson sits in the middle of the chapter rather than at the end.

items.term: The convexity guarantee is the exception, not the rule
items.text: Everything reassuring in this lesson — one minimum, guaranteed arrival, no dependence on where you started — comes from the MSE bowl being convex, which is a property of this particular cost with this particular model. Most models later in the book have none of it: the random starting point matters, two runs give two answers, and 'the minimum' becomes 'a good enough minimum'. Read the guarantee as a fact about linear regression, not about gradient descent.

items.term: Feature scaling is not preprocessing hygiene, it is geometry
items.text: Unscaled features do not make the answer wrong; they make the path to it long. The cost surface is stretched along the axis of the small-valued feature, so the steepest-descent direction points almost sideways relative to where the minimum is. That is why the fix is a rescale rather than a smarter step rule — you are changing the shape of the problem, not the algorithm.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Sketch, in words, what happens to gradient descent's path if the learning rate is 100x too large versus 100x too small.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The learning rate has to be guessed and then tuned. Are there methods that adapt the step size automatically as training runs, and what do they cost?
Look up: the scikit-learn user guide section on Stochastic Gradient Descent, specifically its Tips on Practical Use, and the learning_rate options it lists.

items.term: Batch Gradient Descent: One Step, the Whole Training Set

blocks.content:
Batch gradient descent measures the slope of the cost using every training row, then takes one step in the opposite direction — and repeats that for a fixed number of passes.

**The question this lesson answers:** "step downhill" is a picture, not an instruction. What exactly does the algorithm compute to know which way downhill is, and how much does that computation cost?

### The big picture

```
whole training set ─> gradient (points uphill) ─> step −η
        ↑                                           │
        └────────── repeat, one epoch each ─────────┘
```

### 1 · The slope, one parameter at a time

To actually move θ downhill you need to know which direction is downhill, and that means computing the **partial derivative** of the cost function with respect to every parameter — how much the MSE would change if you nudged that one weight slightly.

"Partial" just means: hold every other weight still and wiggle this one. It is the slope of the mountain if you face exactly east, then again facing north, and so on once per parameter. Equation 4-5 below is that single slope.

### 2 · Stacking the slopes: the gradient vector

Stack all of those partial derivatives together and you get the **gradient vector**, which points uphill; step in the opposite direction and you are heading toward lower cost. Equation 4-6 below computes the whole stack in one matrix expression instead of one parameter at a time.

The sign is the part people get wrong. The gradient is the direction of steepest *increase*, so the algorithm subtracts it. Equation 4-7 below is that subtraction, and it is the entire update rule.

### 3 · Why it is called "batch"

Batch gradient descent computes that gradient using every single training instance at every step — hence "batch" — then updates all of θ at once: subtract the gradient vector, scaled by the learning rate η (eta), from the current θ.

Note what "batch" does *not* mean here. It is not a chunk of rows, the way a batch job or a micro-batch is in your world; it is the whole table, every step. The book itself remarks that *full* gradient descent would probably be a better name — see the card below.

### 4 · The loop, and what it returns

The code that implements this is short: initialize θ randomly, then repeat a fixed number of times (each full pass through the data is called an **epoch**): compute the gradient over the whole training set, then take one step of size η in the opposite direction.

Run it for 1,000 epochs with η = 0.1 on the same noisy linear data used for the Normal equation, and θ converges to the exact same answer the Normal equation found — which makes sense, since both are hunting for the minimum of the same convex bowl. The card below prints both results digit for digit.

Figure 4-8 below shows what three different learning rates do to the first 20 steps.

### 5 · What it costs, and when you would want it

| | Batch gradient descent |
|---|---|
| Big training set | slow — the whole set is rescanned every step |
| New data arriving | cannot be updated on the fly |
| Many features | scales far better than the Normal equation |

The catch is cost: recomputing the gradient over the entire training set at every single step is why batch GD is painfully slow once the training set is large. It also cannot be updated on the fly as new data streams in — every step needs the whole dataset in hand.

On the plus side, it scales far better with the number of features than the Normal equation does, so it is the better choice when there are hundreds of thousands of features. That is the exact axis where the one-step formula falls over, which is why both methods exist.

**One-liner for your notes:** the gradient vector is one slope per weight and points uphill; batch GD builds it from the whole training set and steps the other way by η, every epoch.

blocks.title: Worked out: what the batch GD loop returns
blocks.content:
Each pass of the loop does two things. First it computes the whole gradient vector at once, `gradients = 2 / m * X_b.T @ (X_b @ theta - y)`, which is Equation 4-6 applied to all the training instances. Then it steps the other way, `theta = theta - eta * gradients`, with η = 0.1, which is Equation 4-7.

After 1,000 of these epochs, starting from random values, `theta` comes out as [[4.21509616], [2.77011339]]. The Normal equation's `theta_best` on the same data was also [[4.21509616], [2.77011339]], so the two methods agree on every printed digit. Because every step uses the whole batch of training data, the book remarks that full gradient descent would probably be a better name for the algorithm.

blocks.title: Equation 4-5
blocks.caption: Partial derivatives of the cost function
blocks.explain:
**Why these equations look like this**

Equation 4-5 exists because "downhill" is not a single direction when there is more than
one weight. You have to ask the question once per weight — if I nudge only this one, does
the cost go up or down, and how fast? — and that one-weight-at-a-time slope is what a
partial derivative is. Its shape is worth reading rather than memorising: for each
instance it takes the error (prediction minus truth) and multiplies it by that instance's
value for the feature in question. So a row that is badly wrong contributes a lot, and it
contributes most to the weights of the features that were large for that row. That is
exactly the blame assignment you would want.

Equation 4-6 is the same thing stacked. Writing n separate sums is slow to read and slow
to run, so the equation stacks all the partial derivatives into one column — the gradient
vector — and then shows that the whole stack equals one matrix expression. One matrix
multiply replaces the loop.

Equation 4-7 is the update, and it is subtraction for one reason: the gradient points in
the direction the cost *increases* fastest. Going the other way is the whole algorithm.
The learning rate η in front is simply how far you commit to that direction before
re-measuring.

**Standard or simplified?** Canonical, and not specific to linear regression. Equation
4-7 is the gradient descent step used to train nearly every model in the rest of the
book, including neural networks; only the cost function inside it changes. Equations 4-5
and 4-6 are the MSE-specific gradient, so those two do change when the cost changes —
compare Equation 4-18 later in this chapter, which is the same shape for a different cost.

**The general form.** Equation 4-6 is already general over the number of features. The
generalisation that matters here is which rows go into it, and it is the subject of the
next two lessons:

| Rows used to build the gradient | Name |
|---|---|
| all of them | batch gradient descent |
| one random row | stochastic gradient descent |
| a small random subset | mini-batch gradient descent |

**Terms these equations introduce**

- a **partial derivative** is the slope of the cost with respect to one weight, holding
every other weight still
- the **gradient vector** is all of those slopes stacked into one column; it points in
the direction of steepest increase
- the upside-down triangle in front of MSE is the symbol for that gradient vector; read
it as "the gradient of"
- **η** is the Greek letter eta, and here it is the learning rate
- **epoch** is one full pass over the training data

**Every piece of Equation 4-5**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| the curly d over curly d theta j | partial derivative with respect to theta j | slope of the cost in weight j's direction |
| two over m | two over m | the averaging factor, with the 2 left in from squaring |
| the sum sign | sum from i equals 1 to m | add over every training instance |
| theta transpose x of i | prediction for instance i | what the model currently says |
| minus y of i | minus the true value | the error on that instance |
| x j of i | x sub j superscript i | instance i's value for feature j |

**Every piece of Equation 4-6**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| the upside-down triangle | gradient of | the whole stack of partial derivatives |
| the tall bracket | the column | one row in it per model parameter |
| X transpose | X transpose | the training inputs flipped onto their side |
| X theta minus y | X theta minus y | every instance's error, in one column |

**Every piece of Equation 4-7**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| theta next step | theta, next step | the updated weights |
| theta | theta | the weights right now |
| the minus sign | minus | go the opposite way to the gradient |
| η | eta | the learning rate, the step size |

**The formulas in plain words**

- 4-5: slope for one weight = average over rows of (error × that row's feature value),
doubled.
- 4-6: gradient = the same thing for every weight at once, as one matrix multiply.
- 4-7: new weights = current weights − learning rate × gradient.

**With real numbers**

The loop runs with η = 0.1 for 1,000 epochs on the same 100 noisy points the Normal
equation used, starting from randomly chosen weights.

1. each epoch computes the gradient over all 100 rows, which is Equation 4-6
2. each epoch then does new θ = old θ − 0.1 × gradient, which is Equation 4-7
3. after 1,000 of those, θ is [4.21509616, 2.77011339]

The Normal equation returned [4.21509616, 2.77011339] on the same data. The two agree on
every printed digit, which is what "both are hunting the bottom of the same convex bowl"
means in practice — one solved for it, one walked to it.

---
