blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
eta = 0.1 # learning rate
n_epochs = 1000
m = len(X_b) # number of instances

np.random.seed(42)
theta = np.random.randn(2, 1) # randomly initialized model parameters

for epoch in range(n_epochs):
    gradients = 2 / m * X_b.T @ (X_b @ theta - y)
    theta = theta - eta * gradients
```

items.term: Why the gradient is the right direction and not just a direction
items.text: Of all the ways you could move θ, the negative gradient is the one that reduces the cost fastest per unit of distance travelled. That is what makes it worth computing rather than, say, trying each weight in turn. The catch is that 'fastest right now' is local advice: on a stretched bowl the steepest direction can point almost at right angles to the minimum, which is exactly the unscaled-features problem seen from the algorithm's side.

items.term: Every step costs a full scan, and that is the whole trade-off
items.text: Batch GD's one weakness generates the next two lessons. The gradient is an average over rows, and an average can be estimated from a sample — so the obvious question is how few rows you can get away with. One row gives stochastic GD, a handful gives mini-batch. Everything after this lesson is that one question being answered three ways.

items.term: Agreeing with the Normal equation is a test, not a coincidence
items.text: Two completely different methods landing on the same digits is the strongest evidence available that both are implemented correctly, because they share no code path. This is worth borrowing as a habit: when a cheap exact method exists for a small case, run it alongside the scalable method and compare, then trust the scalable one on the cases where the exact one cannot run.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: If you cut the learning rate eta in half in the batch GD code above but keep n_epochs the same, will theta likely end up closer to or farther from the optimum?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The loop runs a fixed 1,000 epochs. How would you decide to stop earlier without knowing the answer in advance?

Look up: the tolerance idea the book raises right after this code (stopping when the gradient vector's norm becomes tiny), and the tol and n_iter_no_change arguments in scikit-learn's SGDRegressor reference.

items.term: Stochastic Gradient Descent: One Random Instance at a Time

blocks.content:
Stochastic gradient descent takes the opposite bet from batch GD: one random row per step, which is nearly free but noisy.

**The question this lesson answers:** batch gradient descent rescans the whole training set for every single step. What if you used exactly one row instead — what do you gain, what breaks, and how do you fix it?

### The big picture

| | Batch GD | Stochastic GD |
|---|---|---|
| Rows per step | all of them | one, picked at random |
| Step cost | high | nearly free |
| Path | smooth, stops at the minimum | bounces, never settles |
| Memory | whole dataset | one instance |

### 1 · One random row at a time

Batch gradient descent's biggest weakness is needing the whole training set for every single step. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) fixes that by going to the opposite extreme: at each step it grabs one random training instance, computes the gradient from that single example alone, and takes a step based on just that.

**Stochastic** simply means random. Each step is nearly free computationally, which makes SGD fast even on datasets too big to fit in memory, since only one instance needs to be loaded at a time. That is the same idea as streaming a file bigger than RAM through a job one chunk at a time, except the chunk is a single row.

### 2 · The price: noise

The cost of that speed is noise: instead of gliding smoothly toward the minimum, the cost bounces around erratically, decreasing only on average. It ends up near the minimum but keeps jittering around it forever rather than settling. Figure 4-9 below is that jagged path; Figure 4-10 below is its first 20 steps.

That randomness has one silver lining — an irregular cost surface with bumps and local minima is much easier for SGD to escape than for batch GD, since a wild step can leap right out of a shallow dip. Linear regression's bowl has no dips, so this buys nothing here; it matters for the models in later chapters that do.

### 3 · The fix: a learning schedule

The standard fix for the settling problem is a **learning schedule**: start with large steps (which helps escape bad local spots early) and shrink the learning rate as training goes on, so steps get smaller and the final position lands closer to the true minimum instead of jittering around it.

The demo's schedule is `t0 / (t + t1)` with `t0 = 5` and `t1 = 50`, where `t` counts steps taken so far. At the very first step t = 0, so the learning rate is 5 / (0 + 50) = 5 / 50 = 0.1 — the same rate batch GD used — and it shrinks from there on every step.

The demo code runs only 50 epochs (versus batch GD's 1,000) and still lands close to the Normal equation's answer. The card below has both sets of digits.

### 4 · The requirement that is easy to break by accident

One requirement that is easy to violate accidentally: the instances fed to SGD need to look independent and identically distributed over the run, which is usually guaranteed simply by shuffling.

**Independent and identically distributed** means each row you draw should look like a fair sample of the whole dataset, unrelated to the rows drawn before it. Feed it data sorted by label instead, and SGD will fixate on optimizing for one label at a time and never settle near the true optimum.

This is a real trap for a data engineer, because tables arrive sorted all the time — by load date, by partition key, by the label column itself. Sorted input does not error; it silently trains the wrong model.

### 5 · The library version

Scikit-Learn's `SGDRegressor` does the same job: it defaults to optimizing the MSE cost function and uses its own default learning schedule (different from the demo's), while the book's example switches regularization off explicitly with `penalty=None`. Regularization is the subject of several later lessons in this chapter; here it is simply turned off so the comparison is fair.

**One-liner for your notes:** SGD steps from one random row, which is fast and out-of-core but never settles — a shrinking learning schedule and shuffled data are what make it land near the answer.

blocks.title: Worked out: how close SGD and SGDRegressor get
blocks.content:
The demo loop picks a random instance m times per epoch, so some instances may be picked several times in an epoch while others are not picked at all. After only 50 epochs it returns `theta` = [[4.21076011], [2.74856079]], against [[4.21509616], [2.77011339]] from the Normal equation: a good solution, but not the optimal one.

Scikit-Learn's `SGDRegressor(max_iter=1000, tol=1e-5, penalty=None, eta0=0.01, n_iter_no_change=100, random_state=42)` runs for at most 1,000 epochs, or until the loss drops by less than $10^{-5}$ during 100 epochs. It starts from a learning rate of 0.01 and uses its own default learning schedule. It finds an intercept of 4.21278812 and a weight of 2.77270267, again quite close to the solution of the Normal equation.

blocks.title: Figure 4-9
blocks.caption: With stochastic gradient descent, each training step is much faster but also much more stochastic
blocks.alt: Figure 4-9: With stochastic gradient descent, each training step is much faster but also much more stochastic

blocks.title: Figure 4-10
blocks.caption: The first 20 steps of stochastic gradient descent
blocks.alt: Figure 4-10: The first 20 steps of stochastic gradient descent

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
n_epochs = 50
t0, t1 = 5, 50 # learning schedule hyperparameters

def learning_schedule(t):
    return t0 / (t + t1)

np.random.seed(42)
theta = np.random.randn(2, 1) # random initialization

for epoch in range(n_epochs):
    for iteration in range(m):
        random_index = np.random.randint(m)
        xi = X_b[random_index : random_index + 1]
        yi = y[random_index : random_index + 1]
        gradients = 2 * xi.T @ (xi @ theta - yi) # for SGD, do not divide by m
        eta = learning_schedule(epoch * m + iteration)
        theta = theta - eta * gradients
```

items.term: Noise as a feature, not only a defect
items.text: SGD's bouncing is usually described as the price of speed, but on a cost surface with local minima it is also the mechanism that escapes them — a deterministic method walks into the nearest dip and stops there forever. Linear regression's bowl has no dips, so here the noise is pure cost; in later chapters it is part of why the method works at all.

items.term: The learning schedule is a bet, and it can be lost either way
items.text: Shrinking the step size is what lets a noisy method settle, but the shrink rate is itself a choice with two failure modes: too fast and the run freezes short of the minimum or in a bad spot, too slow and it is still bouncing when you stop. There is no default that is right for every dataset, which is why the library's schedule and the demo's schedule differ.

items.term: Sorted input is the silent failure to look for
items.text: SGD assumes each row it draws is a fair sample of the whole. Data arriving sorted — by date, by partition, by the label itself — breaks that assumption without raising an error or looking unusual in any log. The model simply optimises for one region at a time and never settles. Anywhere a pipeline hands ordered data to an incremental learner, shuffling is a correctness step, not a tidiness one.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Your training data happens to be sorted so all label=0 rows come first, then all label=1 rows. Why is this dangerous for stochastic gradient descent specifically?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The demo shuffles by drawing a random index each step, which means some rows are drawn several times per epoch and others not at all. When would you prefer shuffling the whole set once per epoch instead, and does it actually help?
Look up: the book's own note on that alternative in this section, and the shuffle argument in scikit-learn's SGDRegressor API reference.

items.term: Mini-Batch Gradient Descent and Choosing Among the Three

blocks.content:
Mini-batch gradient descent computes each step from a small random handful of rows, which is the middle setting between batch GD's whole table and stochastic GD's single row.

**The question this lesson answers:** with five ways to train a linear model now on the table — Normal equation, SVD, batch, stochastic and mini-batch GD — which one do you reach for, and on what evidence?

### The big picture

```
rows used per step:
  1 ────────── a few ────────── all
 SGD        mini-batch        batch GD
 noisy       steadier         smoothest
```

### 1 · The middle setting

Mini-batch gradient descent sits between the other two: instead of using the whole training set (batch) or a single instance (stochastic) at each step, it computes the gradient over a small random subset — a **mini-batch** — of instances.

This keeps each step reasonably cheap while giving hardware, especially GPUs, enough data per step to exploit fast matrix-multiplication routines, a speed advantage stochastic GD cannot get from working one row at a time.

That is a real engineering reason, not a mathematical one: the arithmetic for 32 rows at once is one matrix multiply, which specialised hardware does far faster than 32 separate single-row multiplies. Processing a set at a time beats processing a row at a time, for the same reason it does in your own jobs.

### 2 · How its path looks

In terms of behavior, mini-batch GD's path through parameter space is less erratic than pure stochastic GD — with a large enough mini-batch it walks a steadier line toward the minimum — but because it is still not using the full dataset at every step, it can end up wandering around the minimum rather than stopping exactly on it, the same trade-off stochastic GD has.

Figure 4-11 below draws all three paths on the same picture. **Parameter space** is just a plot with one axis per weight, where a point is a candidate model and the walk is training.

### 3 · Choosing among all five

Comparing all three algorithms against the closed-form options:

| | Normal equation / SVD | Batch GD | Stochastic / mini-batch GD |
|---|---|---|---|
| Works for | linear regression only | any model with a gradient | any model with a gradient |
| Many features | slow | fast | fast |
| Data larger than memory | no | no | yes |
| Hyperparameters to tune | zero | learning rate | learning rate |
| Final answer | exact | exact | near, with residual noise |

The Normal equation and SVD only work for linear regression and are the only ones with zero hyperparameters to tune, but both get slow as the number of features grows large and neither supports learning from a streaming data source.

The three gradient descent variants all scale to huge numbers of features, and (aside from plain batch GD) support learning from data too large to hold in memory all at once — the price is a learning rate to tune and, for stochastic and mini-batch, some residual noise around the final answer rather than a clean stop exactly at the minimum.

### 4 · Reading the table as a decision

Two columns decide almost every real case. If the data fits in memory and the features are few, the closed-form route wins on simplicity: nothing to tune, nothing to converge. The moment either of those stops being true — hundreds of thousands of columns, or rows arriving faster than you can hold them — you are in gradient descent territory, and the only remaining question is how many rows you can afford per step.

**One-liner for your notes:** mini-batch GD trades a little of SGD's noise for hardware speed; closed-form wins on small wide-enough problems, gradient descent wins the moment features or rows stop fitting.

blocks.caption: Gradient descent paths in parameter space

items.term: Batch size is a hardware decision as much as a statistical one
items.text: More rows per step means a less noisy gradient, which is a statistical argument, and one larger matrix multiply instead of many small ones, which is a hardware argument. The two usually point the same way, which is why mini-batch has become the default in practice even though neither extreme is wrong. When they disagree, the hardware argument tends to win, because a step that is ten times better but a hundred times slower is not a bargain.

items.term: Zero hyperparameters is an underrated column in that table
items.text: The closed-form methods are the only ones with nothing to tune, and that is worth more than it looks: no learning rate means no divergence, no schedule, no run that silently produces a worse model because a setting was off. Every gradient method buys scale by taking on a tuning obligation. On a problem small enough for both, the one with no dials is the safer engineering choice, not merely the simpler one.

items.term: Out-of-core is the property that actually decides the architecture
items.text: Whether a method can learn from data it never holds in full is the difference between a job that fits on one machine and a job that does not. It is the same distinction as a full refresh versus an incremental load, and it has the same consequence: it determines the shape of the pipeline around the model, not just the runtime of the model.

items: Mini-batch size is not in Table 4-1 as a tuned hyperparameter, but it clearly matters. How do people choose it, and what breaks at the extremes?
Look up: the scikit-learn guide Strategies to scale computationally: bigger data, which covers out-of-core learning and the partial_fit API.

items.term: Polynomial Regression: Fitting Curves with a Straight-Line Model

blocks.content:
You can fit a curve with an ordinary linear regression model by adding powers of your inputs as extra columns — the algorithm never changes, only the data handed to it does.

**The question this lesson answers:** the scatterplot bends, so a straight line cannot fit it. Do you need a different algorithm, or is there a way to reuse the one you already have?

### The big picture

```
x ─> [ x , x² ] ─> ordinary linear regression ─> a curve
      PolynomialFeatures     still linear in θ
```

### 1 · The trick

A straight line cannot fit curved data, but you do not need a fundamentally different algorithm to handle it — you can trick a linear model into fitting curves by handing it extra features. Take your one feature x, add x² (and x³, and so on) as additional columns, and train an ordinary linear regression on the expanded set.

This is the same move as adding a derived column to a table before the query runs. The query stays simple; the column does the work.

### 2 · Why this is still a linear model

The model is still **linear in its parameters**; it is just being handed a nonlinear transformation of the original input.

That phrase is worth unpacking, because the name looks like a contradiction. "Linear" does not mean the picture is a straight line. It means the prediction is a plain weighted sum of whatever columns it was given — each column multiplied by one weight, then added up, exactly as in Equation 4-1. Feed it a column holding x² and the weighted sum is still a weighted sum; plotted back against the original x, it draws a curve.

This is polynomial regression, and Scikit-Learn's `PolynomialFeatures` class does the transformation for you: give it `degree=2` with one input feature, and every row grows a second column holding that feature's square. So an input of 3 becomes [3, 9], exactly as the demo turns −0.75275929 into [−0.75275929, 0.56664654].

### 3 · Does it actually recover the truth

Fit an ordinary `LinearRegression` on this expanded data, generated from a true quadratic relationship (y = 0.5x² + x + 2 plus noise), and the recovered coefficients land close to the real ones. A **quadratic** is an equation of the form ax² + bx + c — one bend, no more.

The card below lines up each learned number against the number that generated the data. As with the Normal equation demo, the gap is the noise, not a flaw in the method. Figure 4-12 below is the raw data; Figure 4-13 below is the fitted curve.

### 4 · What changes with two or more features

With more than one original feature, `PolynomialFeatures` does something linear regression alone never could: it also generates every cross-combination up to the chosen degree — for two features a and b at degree 3, that is not just each feature's own square and cube, but also every mixed product between them — letting the model discover **interactions** between features.

An interaction is an effect that only shows up when two inputs move together — the effect of a is not the same at every value of b. A plain weighted sum cannot express that, because each column contributes independently. Give it the product column and it can.

### 5 · The bill

That power has a cost worth remembering: the number of features `PolynomialFeatures` produces grows combinatorially with the degree and the number of original features, so a large degree on many features can explode into an unmanageable number of columns fast.

**Combinatorially** means it grows by counting every possible combination, which gets out of hand much faster than doubling. The card below gives the exact formula and the worked example for two features at degree 3. Remember from the Normal equation lesson that columns are the expensive axis — this is the fastest way to manufacture them by accident.

**One-liner for your notes:** polynomial regression is plain linear regression fed extra columns of powers and products; it fits curves and finds interactions, at a column count that explodes with the degree.

blocks.title: Worked out: the fitted coefficients, and the feature count
blocks.content:
Fitting `LinearRegression` to `X_poly` (the feature and its square) gives `intercept_` = 1.78134581 and `coef_` = [0.93366893, 0.56456263]. The first weight belongs to x₁ and the second to x₁², so the model estimates ŷ = 0.56x₁² + 0.93x₁ + 1.78. The data came from y = 0.5x₁² + 1.0x₁ + 2.0 plus Gaussian noise, so each learned value lands close to the true one without matching it: 0.56 against 0.5, 0.93 against 1.0, and 1.78 against 2.0.

The growth in columns also has a formula: `PolynomialFeatures(degree=d)` turns an array of n features into (n + d)! / d!n! features, where n! = 1 × 2 × 3 × ⋯ × n. For two features a and b with degree=3, it adds a², a³, b² and b³, and also the combinations ab, a²b and ab².

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
np.random.seed(42)
m = 100
X = 6 * np.random.rand(m, 1) - 3
y = 0.5 * X ** 2 + X + 2 + np.random.randn(m, 1)

>>> from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
>>> poly_features = PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False)
>>> X_poly = poly_features.fit_transform(X)
>>> X[0]
array([-0.75275929])
>>> X_poly[0]
array([-0.75275929, 0.56664654])
```

items.term: Changing the data instead of changing the model
items.text: Polynomial regression is a template worth recognising: rather than build a more powerful algorithm, transform the inputs so a simple algorithm becomes sufficient. The whole toolchain around linear models — the closed form, the convexity guarantee, the regularizers later in this chapter — keeps working, because from the algorithm's point of view nothing happened. Several later chapters are variations on this same move.

items.term: Degree is a complexity dial, and it is the one that overfits
items.text: Choosing degree 2 versus degree 10 versus degree 300 is choosing how much freedom the model has to bend. The data in this chapter was generated by a quadratic, so degree 2 is right and the book's degree 300 fit is a demonstration of what too much freedom does. In real work you do not know the true degree, which is precisely why the next lesson is about diagnosing that from the learning curves rather than guessing.

items.term: The column explosion is a real operational limit
items.text: The count grows by combinations, so a modest degree on a wide table produces a number of columns that is not merely inconvenient but fatal for the closed-form methods, whose cost scales badly in columns. Polynomial expansion is therefore also a decision to move to gradient descent, and to regularize — which is why these lessons sit next to each other in the chapter.

items: PolynomialFeatures adds powers and products of the existing columns. What other kinds of derived column let a linear model fit a curved relationship, and when would you prefer them?

items.term: Learning Curves and the Bias/Variance Trade-off

blocks.content:
A learning curve plots training error and validation error against training-set size, and the shape of the two lines tells you whether the model is too simple or too flexible.

**The question this lesson answers:** cross-validation gives one number for how well a model generalizes. That number is bad — but is it bad because the model is too simple, or because it memorised the training data? And will more data help?

### The big picture

| The two curves | Diagnosis | The fix |
|---|---|---|
| both flat, close together, both high | underfitting, high bias | a better model or better features |
| training low, a persistent gap above it | overfitting, high variance | more training data |

### 1 · What a learning curve is

Cross-validation tells you a model's overall generalization score, but learning curves show you how that score got there. A learning curve plots two lines — training error and validation error — as the model is trained on progressively larger slices of the training set.

**Training error** is how wrong the model is on the rows it learned from; **validation error** is how wrong it is on held-out rows it has never seen. The gap between those two lines is the whole diagnostic.

### 2 · The underfitting signature

For a plain linear model fit to curved data, the training error climbs to a plateau while the validation error slowly falls to one, and the two end up close together, but both plateau high: the model cannot do well even on the data it was trained on, because a straight line genuinely cannot represent the underlying curve. Figure 4-15 below is exactly this shape.

That pattern — both curves flat and both bad — is the signature of **underfitting**, and the fix is not more data (more data will not help a shape the model structurally cannot represent) but a better model or better features.

This is the most useful thing on the page. Adding rows is usually the first instinct and here it is simply wasted work: a straight line fed a million curved points is still a straight line.

### 3 · The overfitting signature

Now retrain a 10th-degree polynomial on the same data: the training error drops much lower, but a visible gap opens up between the training curve and the validation curve — the model does noticeably better on data it has already seen than on new data. Figure 4-16 below shows the gap; Figure 4-14 below shows what an extreme version of that wiggling looks like.

That gap is the signature of **overfitting**, and it shrinks as more training data is added, because a model with too many **degrees of freedom** — the number of independent knobs it can turn, roughly its parameter count — needs more examples before it can no longer just memorize idiosyncrasies of a small sample.

The card below explains why each curve starts where it does and moves the way it does.

### 4 · The theory underneath: three kinds of error

A model's generalization error decomposes into three sources.

| Source | Comes from | Too much means |
|---|---|---|
| bias | wrong assumptions, like fitting a line to curved data | underfitting |
| variance | over-sensitivity to the exact training sample seen | overfitting |
| irreducible error | noise in the data itself | nothing a model can do |

**Bias** is error from wrong assumptions (fitting a line to curved data) — high bias means underfitting. **Variance** is error from the model being overly sensitive to the exact training sample it saw (a wiggly, many-parameter model) — high variance means overfitting. **Irreducible error** is baseline noise in the data itself that no model can remove; only cleaning the data helps that part.

Note that this "bias" is a different word from the bias *term* θ₀ in Equation 4-1. Same word, unrelated meaning.

### 5 · Why it is a trade-off and not a to-do list

Making a model more complex trades bias for variance — complexity reduces bias and increases variance, and simplifying does the reverse — so tuning model complexity is really tuning this trade-off, never eliminating both sides at once. Push complexity up and you buy a better fit at the price of sensitivity; push it down and you buy stability at the price of a fit the model cannot reach. The learning curve is how you find out which side you are currently paying on.

**One-liner for your notes:** both curves high and together means underfitting and more rows will not help; a persistent gap means overfitting and more rows will.

blocks.title: Why the curves move, and which way the trade-off goes
blocks.content:
With just one or two training instances, a model can fit them perfectly, so the training error starts at zero. As new instances are added, the noise and the curve in the data make a perfect fit impossible, and the training error rises to a plateau. The validation error does the opposite: a model trained on very few instances cannot generalize, so the error starts large and then slowly goes down to a plateau.

The trade-off has a fixed direction. Increasing a model's complexity typically increases its variance and reduces its bias; reducing its complexity increases its bias and reduces its variance. So an underfitting, high-bias model needs a better model or better features, and a simpler model would only add bias. An overfitting model can be improved by feeding it more training data until the validation error reaches the training error.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.model_selection import learning_curve

train_sizes, train_scores, valid_scores = learning_curve(
    LinearRegression(), X, y, train_sizes=np.linspace(0.01, 1.0, 40), cv=5,
    scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
train_errors = -train_scores.mean(axis=1)
valid_errors = -valid_scores.mean(axis=1)

plt.plot(train_sizes, train_errors, "r-+", linewidth=2, label="train")
plt.plot(train_sizes, valid_errors, "b-", linewidth=3, label="valid")
[...] # beautify the figure: add labels, axis, grid, and legend
plt.show()
```

items.term: Why the shape of the curves beats the value of the score
items.text: One cross-validation number tells you the model is bad; the two curves tell you what to do next, and the two answers are opposites. Underfitting says buy a better model; overfitting says buy more rows. Acting on the wrong one wastes the more expensive resource — collecting data to fix a model that structurally cannot use it is the classic version of that mistake.

items.term: The decomposition is a way of thinking, not a measurement
items.text: You cannot run a command that prints your model's bias, variance and irreducible error separately. The three-way split is a framework for reasoning about where error is coming from and what kind of change could reduce it. Its practical payoff is knowing that some of the error is not yours to remove at all, so a model that is not perfect is not automatically a model that is badly built.

items.term: More data has a ceiling, and the curves show you where it is
items.text: The overfitting gap narrows as rows are added, but both curves are heading for a plateau. Once the validation curve has flattened, further rows buy nothing and the remaining error is bias plus irreducible error. That makes the learning curve a budgeting tool as much as a diagnostic: it is the evidence for whether another month of data collection is worth funding.

items.term: Ridge Regression: Keeping the Weights Small

blocks.content:
Ridge regression fights overfitting by adding a penalty on the size of the feature weights, so training has to fit the data *and* keep the weights small.

**The question this lesson answers:** the learning curves say the model is overfitting. How do you take freedom away from a model without changing which model you are using?

### The big picture

| α (alpha) | The pull on the weights | The model becomes |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | none | plain linear regression |
| moderate | weights squeezed a bit | flatter, more reasonable |
| very large | weights near zero | a flat line through the average |

### 1 · What regularization is

**Regularization** is the general fix for overfitting: constrain the model so it has less freedom to contort itself around the training data's noise.

The last lesson framed overfitting as too many degrees of freedom. Regularization does not remove parameters — it makes large ones expensive, which amounts to the same thing.

### 2 · What ridge adds

Ridge regression regularizes a linear model by adding a penalty term to the cost function equal to a scaled sum of the squared feature weights — so training is no longer just "fit the data as closely as possible" but "fit the data closely while also keeping the weights small." Equation 4-8 below is that cost, with the full walkthrough underneath it.

Crucially, the bias term θ₀ is left out of the penalty; only the feature weights are pushed toward zero. The bias just sets the overall level of the predictions, so shrinking it would drag every prediction toward zero for no benefit.

### 3 · The one dial: α

The strength of this pull is set by a hyperparameter, α (alpha).

Set α = 0 and ridge regression is just ordinary linear regression — no constraint at all. Crank α up and the weights get squeezed closer and closer to zero, until at a very large α the model flattens into roughly a constant line through the data's average, regardless of the inputs — heavily regularized, low variance, but high bias.

Read that last clause against the previous lesson: α is a direct handle on the bias/variance trade-off. Turning it up buys stability and pays in bias.

### 4 · Two ways to solve it

Ridge can be solved either by a closed-form equation (a small variant of the Normal equation) or by gradient descent, and Scikit-Learn exposes both: the `Ridge` class with a Cholesky-based solver for the closed form, or `SGDRegressor` with `penalty='l2'` for the gradient descent route. Equation 4-9 below is the closed form; the card below explains the matrix A inside it and why the SGD version is passed a divided alpha.

Cholesky is a matrix factorisation technique, the same class of tool as the SVD from the Normal equation lesson — a faster, sturdier way to compute the same answer.

### 5 · The correctness detail: scale first

One detail matters for correctness: ridge, like most regularized models, is sensitive to feature scale, so the inputs need to be scaled (for example with `StandardScaler`) before fitting, or the penalty will not treat features fairly.

The reason is direct. A feature measured in small units needs a large weight to have any effect, and a large weight is exactly what the penalty punishes — so an unscaled model is penalised for its units rather than for its complexity. Note this is a *second*, independent reason to scale: gradient descent already wanted it for speed, and ridge wants it for correctness.

Applied to a high-degree polynomial fit, increasing α visibly flattens the wiggly overfit curve into something far more reasonable — trading some bias for a large drop in variance. Figure 4-17 below shows that at several values of α.

**One-liner for your notes:** ridge adds a squared-weight penalty scaled by α, leaves the bias alone, needs scaled inputs, and turns α into a direct bias-for-variance dial.

blocks.title: Worked out: the matrix A, and why SGD gets alpha=0.1 / m
blocks.content:
In the closed-form Equation 4-9, A is the (n + 1) × (n + 1) identity matrix except with a 0 in the top-left cell, the cell that corresponds to the bias term, so the bias is not regularized.

The ridge cost in Equation 4-8 adds α/m times the sum of the squared feature weights. `SGDRegressor(penalty="l2")` adds alpha times the square of the ℓ2 norm of the weight vector, with no division by m. To make the two penalties equal, the code passes `alpha=0.1 / m`, which gives the same result as `Ridge(alpha=0.1)`. That is why the two predictions for an input of 1.5 nearly match: 1.55325833 from the Cholesky solver and 1.55302613 from SGD. For batch gradient descent, add 2αw / m to the part of the MSE gradient vector for the feature weights w, and add nothing to the gradient of the bias term.

blocks.title: Equation 4-8
blocks.caption: Ridge regression cost function
blocks.explain:
**Why these equations look like this**

Equation 4-8 is a sum of two things because the model is now being asked to satisfy two
demands at once: fit the data, and stay modest. MSE(θ) is the fit; the second term is the
modesty. Adding them means the optimiser can trade one against the other, and α decides
the exchange rate.

Why squared weights, specifically? Squaring makes the penalty blind to sign — a weight of
−8 is exactly as expensive as +8 — and makes large weights disproportionately expensive,
so the pressure falls hardest on the few extreme weights that a wiggly overfit model
relies on. It is the same reason MSE squares its errors, applied to a different quantity.

Notice where the sum starts: at i = 1, not 0. That single index is what leaves the bias
term out of the penalty.

Equation 4-9 is the Normal equation from earlier in the chapter with one addition inside
the bracket. That is not a coincidence — ridge changes the cost by adding a term, so it
changes the closed-form solution by adding a term. A has a 0 in its top-left cell, again
so that the bias escapes the penalty.

**Standard or simplified?** Standard. Ridge regression is also known as Tikhonov
regularization, and this is its usual form. One detail is a convention rather than a law:
the penalty here is divided by m, the number of instances. Lasso's penalty in Equation
4-10 is not divided by m — it is multiplied by 2α instead — and the book says plainly
that these factors were chosen so that the best α does not depend on how big the training
set is. Different penalty shapes need different factors to achieve that. The card below
shows the practical consequence: to make SGDRegressor match Ridge, the code has to pass
alpha divided by m by hand.

**The general form.** The whole regularization family is one shape — cost = fit +
α × (some measure of weight size) — and the three members differ only in the measure:

| Penalty measures | Name | Effect on a useless weight |
|---|---|---|
| squared weights | ridge | small, rarely exactly zero |
| absolute weights | lasso | driven to exactly zero |
| a blend of both | elastic net | some of each |

**Terms these equations introduce**

- **J(θ)** is the book's general name for a cost function with no shorter name; here it
is the ridge cost
- **α** (alpha) is the regularization strength; it is a hyperparameter, fixed before the
run
- **A** in Equation 4-9 is an identity matrix with one cell changed. An **identity
matrix** is all zeros except for 1s down its main diagonal, and multiplying by it
changes nothing — which is why altering exactly one of its cells is a precise way to
exempt exactly one parameter
- **variance** and **bias** here are the two error sources from the learning curves
lesson, not the bias term θ₀

**Every piece of Equation 4-8**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| J of theta | J of theta | the total cost being minimised |
| MSE of theta | M S E of theta | the ordinary fit term |
| the plus | plus | the two demands are added, not traded by hand |
| alpha over m | alpha over m | the strength, averaged over the instances |
| the sum from i equals 1 | sum from one, not zero | every feature weight, bias excluded |
| theta i squared | theta i squared | one weight, multiplied by itself |

**Every piece of Equation 4-9**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| theta with a hat | theta hat | the weights that minimise the ridge cost |
| X transpose X | X transpose X | the feature overlap table, as before |
| plus alpha A | plus alpha A | the ridge term, added along the diagonal |
| A | A | identity, except a 0 in the top-left cell |
| the raised minus one | inverse | undo the overlap, as before |
| X transpose y | X transpose y | how each feature lines up with the target |

**The formulas in plain words**

- 4-8: total cost = how badly it fits + α ÷ m × (the sum of every squared feature weight).
- 4-9: best weights = the Normal equation, with α added along the diagonal and the bias
cell left alone.

**With real numbers**

The lesson's example fits the same data with α = 0.1 and asks for a prediction at an
input of 1.5.

1. the closed-form route, Ridge with the Cholesky solver, returns 1.55325833
2. the gradient descent route, SGDRegressor with an l2 penalty, returns 1.55302613
3. the two differ by 1.55325833 − 1.55302613 = 0.0002322

They agree to four decimal places only because the code passed alpha as 0.1 divided by m,
matching the two different scaling conventions described above. Skip that division and
the two routes solve genuinely different problems and return genuinely different numbers.

---

blocks.content:
```python
>>> from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
>>> ridge_reg = Ridge(alpha=0.1, solver="cholesky")
>>> ridge_reg.fit(X, y)
>>> ridge_reg.predict([[1.5]])
array([[1.55325833]])

>>> sgd_reg = SGDRegressor(penalty="l2", alpha=0.1 / m, tol=None,
...                        max_iter=1000, eta0=0.01, random_state=42)
>>> sgd_reg.fit(X, y.ravel()) # y.ravel() because fit() expects 1D targets
>>> sgd_reg.predict([[1.5]])
array([1.55302613])
```

items.term: Why penalising size works at all
items.text: Overfitting shows up as extreme weights, because that is how a model makes a smooth function pass exactly through scattered points — large opposing coefficients that nearly cancel except near the training rows. Charging for weight size makes that strategy unaffordable, which is why a size penalty reduces wiggle even though it never mentions wiggle. It is an indirect fix, and the indirectness is why it generalises to models whose shapes you cannot picture.

items.term: Alpha is a dial on a trade-off you cannot escape
items.text: There is no value of α that reduces both bias and variance. Turning it up buys stability at the cost of systematic error; turning it down does the reverse. This is the bias-variance trade-off from the previous lesson made adjustable, which also means α is exactly the kind of setting that must be chosen by validation rather than by argument.

items.term: Regularize during training, evaluate without it
items.text: The penalty is part of the training objective, not part of the model's quality. When you report how good the model is, you report the plain error on held-out data — the penalty was a device for finding good weights, not a component of the score. Confusing the training loss with the reporting metric is a common and quietly misleading error.

items: If alpha in ridge regression is set extremely high, what happens to the model's predictions, and is that closer to underfitting or overfitting?

items: The lesson mentions the Cholesky solver, but Ridge offers several others. What does each solver assume about the data, and when does the choice change the answer rather than just the runtime?

items.term: Lasso Regression: Zeroing Out the Useless Features

blocks.content:
Lasso uses the same idea as ridge with one change — it penalises the absolute size of the weights instead of their squares — and that single change makes it delete features outright.

**The question this lesson answers:** ridge shrinks every weight a little and never quite kills one. What if you want the model to tell you which features do not matter at all?

### The big picture

| | Ridge | Lasso |
|---|---|---|
| Penalty sums | squared weights | absolute weights |
| A useless weight ends up | small, rarely exactly zero | exactly zero |
| Cost contours are | round | cornered on the axes |
| Result | all features kept | a sparse model |

### 1 · The one-character change

Lasso regression regularizes the same way ridge does — by adding a penalty on the feature weights to the cost function — but swaps the penalty shape: instead of the sum of squared weights, lasso penalizes the sum of the absolute values of the weights. **Absolute value** means drop the minus sign, so a weight of −3 and a weight of +3 both count as 3. Equation 4-10 below is that cost.

### 2 · What that change buys

That single change produces a strikingly different behavior: where ridge shrinks every weight a little, lasso tends to shrink the least useful weights all the way to exactly zero, effectively deleting those features from the model.

The result is a **sparse** model — one where most weights are exactly zero — that has done its own **feature selection** along the way. A weight of exactly zero means that column contributes nothing to any prediction, so the model has told you, in its own output, which columns to stop collecting. Figure 4-18 below shows lasso fits at several values of α.

### 3 · Why exactly zero, and not merely small

The geometric reason is worth holding onto: this penalty's cost contours have sharp corners right on the axes, so as gradient descent minimizes the combined cost it gets pulled directly into those corners — where one or more weights are exactly zero — rather than sliding smoothly toward the origin the way ridge's round contours do.

A **contour** here is a line joining every pair of weights that costs the same, like a contour on a map joining points of equal height. Ridge's are circles; lasso's are diamonds, and a diamond's points sit exactly on the axes. Figure 4-19 below draws all four pictures, and the card below walks the descent step by step.

### 4 · The side effect: it keeps bouncing

This also means the penalty does not smoothly flatten out near zero the way ridge's does, so gradient descent tends to keep bouncing slightly around the optimum unless the learning rate is gradually shrunk as training proceeds.

The card below gives the mechanism: lasso's penalty gradient is either −1 or +1 whatever the weight already is, so the pull never eases off near the bottom. Ridge's eases off, which is why it settles on its own. This is the same shrinking-learning-rate fix that stochastic gradient descent needed, for the same underlying reason — steps that do not get smaller cannot land precisely. Equation 4-11 below is the vector gradient descent uses to cope with the corner, where the ordinary slope is undefined.

### 5 · When to reach for it

In Scikit-Learn, the `Lasso` class fits this directly, and `SGDRegressor` with `penalty='l1'` gives the gradient-descent equivalent.

Because lasso actively drops features rather than merely shrinking them, it is the natural choice when only a handful of the features actually matter and you want the model itself to tell you which ones — at the cost of being less stable than ridge when there are more features than instances or when several features are strongly correlated with each other.

**Correlated** means two columns carry much the same information. Lasso then has no principled way to choose between them, so it picks one somewhat arbitrarily, and a small change in the data can flip the choice.

**One-liner for your notes:** lasso penalises absolute weights, so useless ones land on exactly zero and the model selects its own features — at the price of bouncing, and of instability when features are correlated or outnumber the rows.

blocks.title: Worked out: lasso's path to a zero weight
blocks.content:
Figure 4-19 walks through two parameters. The ℓ1 loss |θ₁| + |θ₂| drops linearly as you get closer to either axis, and its gradient is either –1 or 1 for each parameter, however small that parameter already is. Start at θ₁ = 2 and θ₂ = 0.5: gradient descent decrements both parameters equally, so θ₂ reaches 0 first, because it began closer to 0. Gradient descent then rolls down the gutter along θ₂ = 0 until θ₁ = 0, with a bit of bouncing, since the ℓ1 gradients never get close to 0.

With the ℓ2 penalty of ridge, the gradients get smaller as the parameters approach the optimum, so gradient descent naturally slows down and bounces less. Increasing α moves the ridge optimum closer to the origin, but the weights never get eliminated entirely.

blocks.title: Equation 4-10
blocks.caption: Lasso regression cost function
blocks.explain:
**Why these equations look like this**

Equation 4-10 is Equation 4-8 with exactly one change: the squared weight is replaced by
its absolute value. Every difference between lasso and ridge comes out of that swap.

Here is why the swap deletes features. Think about what the penalty charges for shrinking
a weight by one more notch. With squares, the charge shrinks as the weight shrinks — going
from 0.1 to 0 barely saves anything, so the optimiser stops bothering and leaves a small
non-zero weight. With absolute values, the charge is the same size at every distance from
zero, so the last notch is worth as much as the first. There is nothing to discourage
going all the way, and the weight lands exactly on 0.

Equation 4-11 exists because of the price of that shape. At exactly zero, an absolute
value has a corner, and a corner has no single slope — which is a problem for an algorithm
whose entire method is reading slopes. A **subgradient** is the standard patch: at the
corner, pick any value between the two slopes on either side, here 0. Away from the
corner it is just −1 or +1, the sign of the weight.

**Standard or simplified?** Both are the canonical forms. The name is an acronym: lasso
stands for least absolute shrinkage and selection operator, which is the method described
in the equation read out loud. The factor of 2α, rather than ridge's α over m, is the
convention described in the previous lesson, chosen so the best α does not move when the
training set size changes.

**The general form.** Ridge and lasso are the k = 2 and k = 1 members of one family, the
norms — the same family RMSE and MAE belong to:

| Penalty | Norm | Geometry | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|
| absolute weights | ℓ1 | diamond, corners on the axes | deletes weights |
| squared weights | ℓ2 | circle, smooth everywhere | shrinks weights |

**Terms these equations introduce**

- the **absolute value** bars mean take the size and drop the sign
- **sign(θ)** returns −1 for a negative weight, +1 for a positive one, and 0 at exactly
zero — it keeps only the direction and throws the size away
- a **subgradient** is a stand-in for a gradient at a point where the true slope is
undefined
- **sparse** means most of the weights are exactly zero

**Every piece of Equation 4-10**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| J of theta | J of theta | the total lasso cost |
| MSE of theta | M S E of theta | the ordinary fit term |
| two alpha | two alpha | the strength, with lasso's own scaling factor |
| the sum from i equals 1 | sum from one, not zero | every feature weight, bias excluded |
| the bars around theta i | absolute value of theta i | the weight's size, sign dropped |

**Every piece of Equation 4-11**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| g of theta and J | g of theta, J | the subgradient the optimiser actually uses |
| the gradient of MSE | gradient of M S E | the ordinary fit gradient, unchanged |
| two alpha | two alpha | the same strength factor as in 4-10 |
| the tall column of signs | sign of theta one, and so on | one direction per weight |
| the three-case bracket | minus one, zero, plus one | negative, exactly zero, positive |

**The formulas in plain words**

- 4-10: total cost = how badly it fits + 2α × (the sum of the sizes of the feature
weights, signs ignored).
- 4-11: the search direction = the ordinary fit direction + 2α × (which side of zero each
weight is on).

**With real numbers**

The card below works the book's two-parameter walk. Start at θ₁ = 2 and θ₂ = 0.5.

1. the penalty's pull is the same size on both, because the sign part of Equation 4-11 is
−1 or +1 whatever the weight already is
2. both are decremented equally, so θ₂ — which started 1.5 closer to zero — arrives first
3. once θ₂ = 0, the walk rolls along that axis until θ₁ reaches 0 as well, bouncing,
because the pull never eases off near the bottom

Ridge, on the same walk, eases off as the weights shrink, slows down, bounces less, and
never quite reaches zero. And the fitted lasso model in this lesson predicts 1.53788174
at an input of 1.5, against ridge's 1.55325833 on the same data.

---

blocks.content:

>>> from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso
>>> lasso_reg = Lasso(alpha=0.1)
>>> lasso_reg.fit(X, y)
>>> lasso_reg.predict([[1.5]])

items.term: Selection versus shrinkage is a decision about what you want back
items.text: Ridge returns a model that uses every column a little; lasso returns a model that uses some columns and genuinely ignores the rest. If the deliverable is a prediction, shrinkage is usually fine. If the deliverable is an answer to 'which of these 200 inputs actually matter', only selection gives it to you — and that answer has operational value, because a column no model uses is a column no pipeline has to keep collecting.

items.term: Do not read a zero weight as proof of irrelevance
items.text: When two columns carry nearly the same information, lasso keeps one and zeroes the other, and which one survives can flip with a small change in the data. The zero means 'not needed given the column that was kept', not 'unrelated to the target'. Treating lasso's output as a ranking of true importance is the most common way this tool is misused.

items.term: The corner is the mechanism, and it generalises
items.text: The reason lasso produces exact zeros is geometric: a penalty whose level sets have corners on the axes pulls solutions onto those corners. That idea reappears well beyond linear models — whenever you want a method to make a hard choice rather than a soft compromise, a non-smooth penalty is the usual way to ask for it, and paying for it with a subgradient is the usual price.

items: You have 200 features and strongly suspect only 5 of them matter for the prediction. Why might lasso be more useful here than ridge?

items: Ridge divides its penalty by m while lasso multiplies its own by 2. The book says these factors keep the best alpha independent of training-set size. What goes wrong if you use the same factor for both?

items.term: Elastic Net: Splitting the Difference, and Choosing a Regularizer

blocks.content:
Elastic net uses both penalties at once, with one dial deciding how much of each — and the lesson ends with the practical rule for choosing among all four options.

**The question this lesson answers:** ridge shrinks everything, lasso deletes things, and lasso misbehaves in two known situations. Which do you actually pick, and is there something in between?

### The big picture

```
r = 0 ──────────── r ──────────── r = 1
ridge         elastic net          lasso
shrink all    both at once     delete some
```

### 1 · The blend

Elastic net regression does not pick a side between ridge and lasso — it blends both penalties into one cost function, weighted by a **mix ratio** r. Equation 4-12 below is that cost, with the walkthrough underneath it.

Set r = 0 and elastic net behaves exactly like ridge; set r = 1 and it behaves exactly like lasso; anywhere in between gives a combination of the two effects — some shrinkage toward zero everywhere (ridge's contribution) plus some outright feature elimination (lasso's contribution). Scikit-Learn's `ElasticNet` class exposes this mix as `l1_ratio`.

Note that r and α are two separate dials doing two separate jobs: α sets *how hard* the model is penalised, r sets *which kind* of penalty that pressure is made of.

### 2 · The choosing rule

With four regularization options on the table — none, ridge, lasso, elastic net — the practical guidance is straightforward:

| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| any linear model at all | almost never plain unregularized |
| no reason to think features are useless | ridge, the default |
| only a subset of features matters | lasso or elastic net |
| that subset case, features correlated or outnumbering rows | elastic net |

Almost never use plain unregularized linear regression, since a little regularization essentially always helps generalization. Ridge is the sensible default when there is no particular reason to think most features are useless.

Reach for lasso or elastic net instead when only a subset of features is suspected to matter, since both can drive irrelevant weights to zero and hand back a simpler, more interpretable model.

### 3 · Elastic net over plain lasso

Between those two, elastic net is generally the safer choice over plain lasso: lasso's feature-selection behavior can become erratic specifically when there are more features than training instances, or when several features are strongly correlated with each other — situations where elastic net's blend of both penalties behaves more predictably.

Both of those are ordinary conditions, not exotic ones. A polynomial expansion can manufacture more columns than you have rows in one call, and correlated columns are the normal state of any table built by joining related sources.

### 4 · The part worth remembering

The takeaway is less about memorizing a flowchart and more about the underlying logic: the ridge penalty tames all weights uniformly, the lasso penalty actively deletes weights, and mixing the two buys controlled deletion without lasso's instability.

If you hold those three sentences, you can re-derive the table above rather than recall it — which is the difference between knowing the rule and being able to defend it when a dataset does not match the example.

**One-liner for your notes:** elastic net mixes the ridge and lasso penalties with a ratio r; always regularize something, default to ridge, and prefer elastic net over lasso when you want deletion without the instability.

blocks.title: Equation 4-12
blocks.caption: Elastic net cost function
blocks.explain:
**Why the equation looks like this**

Equation 4-12 is the two previous cost functions added together with a slider in front of
each. The two multipliers, r and (1 − r), always add up to 1, so the slider moves weight
from one penalty to the other without changing the total amount of pressure. That is the
whole design: r chooses the *kind* of regularization, α chooses the *amount*.

Reading the endpoints is the fastest way to trust it. At r = 0 the lasso half is
multiplied by zero and vanishes, and the ridge half is multiplied by 1, so what is left is
Equation 4-8 exactly. At r = 1 the reverse happens and what is left is Equation 4-10
exactly. Nothing had to be redefined for those two cases; they fall out of the arithmetic.

**Standard or simplified?** Standard. Note that each half keeps its own scaling factor
from its own equation — 2α on the lasso term, α over m on the ridge term — rather than
being tidied into a single shared constant. That looks untidy and is deliberate: those
factors are what keep the best α independent of training-set size, and changing them to
match each other would break that property.

**The general form.** Equation 4-12 is the general case, and the other two are corners of
it:

| r | What survives | Equivalent to |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | the squared-weight term only | ridge, Equation 4-8 |
| between | both terms, mixed | elastic net |
| 1 | the absolute-weight term only | lasso, Equation 4-10 |

**Terms this equation introduces**

- **r** is the mix ratio; scikit-learn's ElasticNet calls it l1_ratio, because r is the
share going to the ℓ1 (absolute value, lasso) penalty
- **α** is still the overall strength, unchanged in meaning from ridge and lasso
- **interpretable** — used in the lesson's guidance — means you can read off which
features the model actually uses, which is exactly what a weight of zero tells you

**Every piece of Equation 4-12**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| J of theta | J of theta | the total elastic net cost |
| MSE of theta | M S E of theta | the ordinary fit term |
| r times the bracket | r times | the share of pressure given to lasso |
| two alpha, sum of the bars | the lasso penalty | deletes the least useful weights |
| one minus r, times | one minus r times | the share of pressure given to ridge |
| alpha over m, sum of squares | the ridge penalty | shrinks every weight a little |

**The formula in plain words**

Total cost = how badly it fits + r × (the lasso penalty) + (1 − r) × (the ridge penalty).

**With real numbers**

The lesson fits the same data with α = 0.1 and l1_ratio = 0.5, so half the pressure is
lasso's and half is ridge's, and asks for a prediction at an input of 1.5.

1. pure ridge on this data predicted 1.55325833
2. pure lasso on this data predicted 1.53788174
3. elastic net at r = 0.5 predicts 1.54333232

The blend lands between the two it is made of, which is what the equation says it should
do. It does not land on the exact midpoint of those two numbers, 1.545570035 — a mix ratio of
one half splits the pressure evenly between the two penalty terms, which is not the same
thing as landing halfway between the two models' predictions.

---

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
>>> from sklearn.linear_model import ElasticNet
>>> elastic_net = ElasticNet(alpha=0.1, l1_ratio=0.5)
>>> elastic_net.fit(X, y)
>>> elastic_net.predict([[1.5]])
array([1.54333232])
```

items.term: Two dials that are genuinely independent
items.text: Alpha sets how much pressure is applied and r sets what kind. Keeping them separate is what makes the family searchable: you can tune the amount on a log scale and the mix on a short list, rather than exploring one tangled parameter. Recognising when a design has separated concerns like this is worth more than memorising the three names.

items.term: Why 'a little regularization always helps' is a defensible default
items.text: The unregularized fit is the corner case α = 0, and nothing about it is special except that it is what you get by accident. Any small penalty trades a tiny, known amount of bias for a reduction in variance, and on finite noisy data that trade is favourable far more often than not. The advice is a prior, not a theorem — but it is a prior that costs one line to act on.

items.term: The guidance is a starting point for a search, not a verdict
items.text: Ridge-by-default and elastic-net-when-sparse are reasonable opening bets, and neither is evidence. Each of these models is cheap to fit, so the honest procedure is to try the candidates on a validation set and let the numbers choose. The value of the rule of thumb is that it tells you which two or three candidates are worth the compute.

items.term: Early Stopping: The “Beautiful Free Lunch”

blocks.content:
Early stopping regularizes a model without touching its shape or its weights — it simply stops training at the epoch where validation error was lowest.

**The question this lesson answers:** every regularizer so far changes the cost function. Is there a way to stop an iterative model overfitting that costs you nothing at all?

### The big picture

```
validation error:  falls ... reaches its low ... climbs
                                  ↑
                     keep THIS epoch's model
```

### 1 · A different kind of regularizer

Every regularization technique so far has worked by constraining the model's shape or weights before or during training. Early stopping takes a completely different angle: it regularizes an iterative algorithm like gradient descent simply by deciding when to stop.

It is so cheap and so effective that Geoffrey Hinton called it a "beautiful free lunch", which is where this lesson's title comes from.

### 2 · Watching overfitting happen live

Watch a complex model's error on a held-out validation set as training proceeds epoch by epoch — early on, both training and validation error fall together, but eventually the model starts memorizing quirks of the training set specifically, and validation error turns around and starts climbing back up even as training error keeps falling.

That upturn is overfitting happening in real time, and the fix is simply to stop training right before it — at the point where validation error was at its lowest. Figure 4-20 below is those two curves.

Two lessons ago the same phenomenon appeared as a *gap* on a learning curve, plotted against training-set size. Here it is the same failure plotted against time instead, which is what makes it actionable while a run is in progress.

### 3 · What the code actually does

The book's implementation does not literally halt training partway through; it runs the full schedule but keeps a saved copy of whichever epoch's model produced the best validation RMSE seen so far, then hands back that snapshot at the end rather than whatever the final epoch produced.

| | Naive version | The book's version |
|---|---|---|
| Behaviour | stops the loop at the first rise | runs every epoch to the end |
| Returns | wherever it happened to stop | the best-scoring snapshot seen |
| Cost | none saved in practice | one model copy held in memory |

### 4 · Why a deep copy, not an epoch number

The copy has to capture both the learned weights and the model's hyperparameters, which is why a full deep copy is used rather than just remembering an epoch number to retrain later.

A **deep copy** duplicates the object and everything inside it, so the saved snapshot is not a reference that keeps changing as training continues. Remembering "epoch 213 was best" would mean retraining to get back there — and a run with any randomness in it is not guaranteed to land in the same place twice.

### 5 · Do not react to the first tick

This matters because with stochastic or mini-batch gradient descent the validation curve is noisy rather than smooth, so a single upward tick does not necessarily mean training has truly started overfitting — it is often better to wait for a sustained rise before rolling back to the best-seen checkpoint, rather than reacting to the very first uptick.

That is the same noise the stochastic gradient descent lesson described, showing up in the metric rather than in the path. The keep-the-best-snapshot design handles it for free: if the tick was noise, a later epoch simply beats the saved score and replaces it.

**One-liner for your notes:** early stopping regularizes by when you stop, not by what you penalise — keep a deep copy of the best-validation-RMSE epoch and ignore single upticks on a noisy curve.

blocks.title: Figure 4-20
blocks.caption: Early stopping regularization
blocks.alt: Figure 4-20: Early stopping regularization

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from copy import deepcopy
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

X_train, y_train, X_valid, y_valid = [...]            # split the quadratic dataset

preprocessing = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(degree=90, include_bias=False),
                              StandardScaler())
X_train_prep = preprocessing.fit_transform(X_train)
X_valid_prep = preprocessing.transform(X_valid)
sgd_reg = SGDRegressor(penalty=None, eta0=0.002, random_state=42)
n_epochs = 500
best_valid_rmse = float('inf')
for epoch in range(n_epochs):
    sgd_reg.partial_fit(X_train_prep, y_train)
    y_valid_predict = sgd_reg.predict(X_valid_prep)
    val_error = mean_squared_error(y_valid, y_valid_predict, squared=False)
    if val_error < best_valid_rmse:
        best_valid_rmse = val_error
        best_model = deepcopy(sgd_reg)
```

items.term: Regularization by time, and what it generalises to
items.text: Every other regularizer in the chapter changes the objective; early stopping changes the search. A partially trained model has effectively explored less of the parameter space, so it is a simpler model in the sense that matters, without anything being penalised. That framing is why the technique transfers unchanged to models where writing a sensible weight penalty would be hard, which is most of the later chapters.

items.term: Keep the best snapshot instead of detecting the turn
items.text: The naive implementation has to answer a hard question — has the curve really turned? — and pay for a wrong answer immediately. The book's version never answers it: it records the best score seen and lets later epochs overrule a false alarm for free. Converting a detection problem into a bookkeeping problem is a pattern worth stealing whenever the signal you are watching is noisy.

items.term: The validation set is now part of training
items.text: Choosing the stopping point using validation error means that set has influenced the model, so its score is no longer a clean estimate of how the model will do on genuinely unseen data. The effect is small for one decision, but it is the same mechanism as tuning on the test set, and it is why a separate final test set exists.

items.term: Logistic Regression: From Weighted Sum to Probability

blocks.content:
Logistic regression is a linear model with one extra step bolted on the end: the weighted sum is squashed into a probability between 0 and 1, and that probability is compared to a threshold.

**The question this lesson answers:** a weighted sum can return any number at all. How do you turn that into "the probability this email is spam", and what cost function do you train it with once no squared error makes sense?

### The big picture

```
features ─> weighted sum t ─> sigmoid ─> p̂ ─> is p̂ ≥ 0.5?
```

### 1 · The extra step

Logistic regression starts exactly like linear regression — compute a weighted sum of the features plus a bias — but instead of outputting that number directly as the prediction, it squashes it through the **logistic (sigmoid) function**, which maps any real number into a value strictly between 0 and 1. *Sigmoid* just means S-shaped; Figure 4-21 below is the curve.

That squashed value is read as the estimated probability that the instance belongs to the "positive" class. Equations 4-13 and 4-14 below are the two halves of this: the model, and the squashing function itself.

### 2 · From a probability to a yes or no

To turn a probability into a definite yes/no prediction, logistic regression compares it to a threshold, 50% by default: at or above 0.5 it predicts the positive class, below it predicts the negative class. Equation 4-15 below is that rule.

Because the sigmoid crosses 0.5 exactly where its input, the raw weighted sum, is zero, this is equivalent to a simpler rule: predict positive whenever the weighted sum itself is positive, negative otherwise.

So a weighted sum of −1.3 predicts the negative class, and you never had to compute a probability to know that. The sigmoid earns its keep when you want the *confidence*, not the label.

### 3 · Scoring one prediction

Training means choosing θ so the model outputs high probabilities for true positives and low probabilities for true negatives, and that goal is captured by a per-instance cost: the cost is the negative log of the predicted probability when the true label is 1, and the negative log of one minus that probability when the true label is 0. Equation 4-16 below is those two cases.

Both halves punish confident wrong answers severely — as the predicted probability for the correct class approaches zero, its negative log shoots up toward infinity — while confident correct answers cost almost nothing.

Concretely: a model that says 0.02 for an instance whose true label is 1 pays a large cost, because the cost in that case is the negative log of the predicted probability and −log(0.02) is a big number. Saying 0.98 instead would have cost almost nothing.

### 4 · The log loss

Averaged over the whole training set, this is called the **log loss**. Equation 4-17 below writes both cases as one expression — the label y, being 0 or 1, switches one half of it off.

Squared error is not used here. A probability that is wrong by 0.9 is not merely nine times worse than one wrong by 0.1; it is catastrophically worse, and the logarithm is what encodes that.

### 5 · No formula, but a guarantee

Unlike linear regression, there is no closed-form, Normal-equation-style shortcut for minimizing log loss — but the good news is that it is convex, so gradient descent, whether batch, stochastic, or mini-batch, is guaranteed to reach the global minimum given a reasonable learning rate and enough time.

That is the same convexity argument from the gradient descent lesson, doing the same job: one bowl, one bottom, no local minima to get trapped in.

The partial derivatives it needs look almost identical in shape to linear regression's: for each instance, take the difference between predicted probability and true label, multiply by that feature's value, and average across instances. Equation 4-18 below is that derivative — compare it to Equation 4-5 and the resemblance is the point.

**One-liner for your notes:** logistic regression is a weighted sum squashed by the sigmoid into a probability, thresholded at 0.5, trained on the convex log loss by gradient descent because no closed form exists.

blocks.title: Equation 4-13
blocks.caption: Logistic regression model estimated probability (vectorized form)
blocks.explain:
**Why these equations look like this**

Equation 4-13 is a linear model with a wrapper. Everything inside the brackets is the
weighted sum from Equation 4-2; σ around it is the only new thing. The wrapper exists
because a weighted sum can return 8,000 or −3, and a probability has to land between 0
and 1. Something must do that conversion, and the sigmoid is the standard choice.

Equation 4-14 is that converter. Read it in three steps and it stops being mysterious.
Negate the input, so a big positive score becomes a big negative one. Exponentiate, which
turns a big negative into something near 0 and a big positive into something huge. Then
take one over (1 + that). Huge denominator gives an answer near 0; a denominator near 1
gives an answer near 1; and at an input of exactly 0 the exponential is 1, so the answer
is one over two, exactly 0.5. That last fact is the whole reason 0.5 is the natural
threshold rather than an arbitrary one.

Equation 4-15 is the threshold written out, and it is a two-case bracket rather than
arithmetic because a class label is a choice, not a computed quantity.

Equation 4-16 is where the reasoning matters most. Squared error is wrong here, and not
just inconvenient: being 0.9 wrong about a probability is not nine times worse than being
0.1 wrong, it is catastrophically worse, and squaring does not say so. The negative
logarithm does. It is near 0 when the predicted probability for the correct class is near
1, and it climbs without limit as that probability approaches 0. So the cost is small when
the model is confidently right, moderate when it hedges, and enormous when it is
confidently wrong — which is the ranking you actually want from a classifier.

Equation 4-17 folds the two cases of 4-16 into one line. The trick is the label y: since
y is 0 or 1, the term y × log(p) disappears whenever y = 0 and the term (1 − y) ×
log(1 − p) disappears whenever y = 1. Exactly one half survives per instance. It is a
switch written as arithmetic, and it is the same device as the leading 1 in the feature
vector back in Equation 4-2.

Equation 4-18 is the gradient, and its resemblance to Equation 4-5 is the point: error
times feature value, averaged. The only change is what "error" means — predicted
probability minus true label, instead of predicted number minus true number.

**Standard or simplified?** All six are canonical, and none is simplified for teaching.
Two honest caveats the book makes. First, the 50% threshold in Equation 4-15 is the
default, not a law; it can be moved when one kind of mistake costs more than the other.
Second, the log loss is not arbitrary: the book notes it can be shown, through Bayesian
inference, that minimising it gives the model with the maximum likelihood of being
optimal — under an assumption about how the data is distributed, and the more wrong that
assumption is, the more biased the model will be. That is stated in the book as a warning,
not derived, and is worth knowing exists rather than working through here.

**The general form.** Equation 4-17 is the two-class case of a more general cost. The
many-class version is Equation 4-22 later in this chapter, cross entropy, and with two
classes it collapses back to exactly this.

**Terms these equations introduce**

- **σ** is the Greek letter sigma, and here it names the logistic function
- **p with a hat** is the estimated probability of the positive class
- **exp(−t)** means e raised to the power −t, where e is about 2.718; all you need from
it is that it turns large negatives into near-zero and large positives into very large
- **log** here is the natural logarithm, the inverse of exp
- the **positive class** is the one labelled 1, the **negative class** the one labelled 0;
neither word means good or bad
- **convex** means one bowl with one bottom, as in the gradient descent lesson

**Every piece of Equation 4-13 and 4-14**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| p with a hat | p hat | the estimated probability of the positive class |
| sigma of something | sigmoid of | squash it into the range 0 to 1 |
| theta transpose x | theta transpose x | the ordinary weighted sum, the score |
| t | t | whatever number is being squashed |
| exp of minus t | e to the minus t | huge when t is very negative, near 0 when large |
| one over one plus that | one over one plus | turns that into a value between 0 and 1 |

**Every piece of Equation 4-15 and 4-16**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| the tall curly bracket | in the case that | two cases, pick the one that applies |
| p hat below 0.5 | p hat less than nought point five | predict the negative class, 0 |
| p hat at or above 0.5 | p hat greater than or equal | predict the positive class, 1 |
| c of theta | c of theta | the cost for one single instance |
| minus log p hat | minus log of p hat | the cost when the true label is 1 |
| minus log of one minus p hat | minus log of one minus p hat | the cost when the true label is 0 |

**Every piece of Equation 4-17 and 4-18**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| J of theta | J of theta | the log loss over the whole training set |
| minus one over m | minus one over m | average, and flip the sign so lower is better |
| y of i times log p of i | y i log p i | live only when the true label is 1 |
| one minus y of i, times log | one minus y i, log | lives only when the true label is 0 |
| the curly d over curly d theta j | partial derivative for theta j | the slope for one weight |
| sigma of theta transpose x, minus y | predicted probability minus the label | the error on one instance |
| x j of i | x sub j superscript i | that instance's value for feature j |

**The formulas in plain words**

- 4-13 and 4-14: probability = squash(the weighted sum), where squash sends any number
into the range 0 to 1 and sends 0 to exactly one half.
- 4-15: predict 1 if the probability is at least a half, otherwise 0.
- 4-16: cost for one row = minus the logarithm of the probability the model gave the
correct answer.
- 4-17: log loss = the average of that cost over every row.
- 4-18: slope for one weight = the average over rows of (predicted probability − true
label) × that row's feature value.

**With real numbers**

The lesson's own two cases, worked through.

1. a weighted sum of −1.3. Negative, so the sigmoid returns something below 0.5, so
Equation 4-15 predicts the negative class. No probability needed to decide.
2. a predicted probability of 0.02 on an instance whose true label is 1. Equation 4-16
uses the first case, minus the logarithm of 0.02, which is a large number — this is a
confident wrong answer and it is charged accordingly.
3. had the model said 0.98 instead, the same formula would use minus the logarithm of
0.98, which is very close to 0 — confidently right, charged almost nothing.

The whole training run is the search for the θ that makes the average of those per-row
charges as small as possible.

---
