items.term: Why not just threshold the weighted sum directly
items.text: You could classify by the sign of the score and skip the sigmoid entirely — the predictions would be identical, as this lesson points out. The sigmoid earns its place at training time, not prediction time: a hard yes/no has no useful slope to descend, so there would be nothing for gradient descent to work with. Squashing gives a smooth, differentiable stand-in for a step, and as a side benefit the output is readable as a confidence.

items.term: Why squared error is wrong for a probability
items.text: Squared error treats a miss of 0.9 as ninety times worse than a miss of 0.01 — but a model that says 0.001 for something that happens is not somewhat wrong, it is asserting near-impossibility for an event that occurred. The logarithm charges unboundedly for that, which is the behaviour a probability estimate deserves. Using MSE here also costs the convexity guarantee, so the choice buys a better-behaved search as well as a better-shaped penalty.

items.term: The three gradients in this chapter are one gradient
items.text: Linear regression's Equation 4-5, logistic regression's Equation 4-18 and softmax's Equation 4-23 all reduce to: error times feature value, averaged over rows. Different models, different definitions of error, same assembly. Noticing that is what turns four pages of equations into one idea you can carry into the neural network chapters, where the same pattern appears again with an extra layer of bookkeeping.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: A logistic regression model outputs p_hat = 0.02 for an instance whose true label is 1. Is the cost for this instance large or small, and why?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The book warns that minimising log loss assumes something about how the data is distributed, and that the model gets more biased the more wrong that assumption is. What exactly is being assumed, and how would you notice it failing?
Look up: maximum likelihood estimation for logistic regression, and the scikit-learn user guide section on Logistic regression.

items.term: Decision Boundaries: Classifying Iris Flowers

blocks.content:
A decision boundary is the set of inputs where the model's estimated probability is exactly 50% — one point when you have one feature, a straight line when you have two.

**The question this lesson answers:** a logistic regression model trained on iris petal width outputs a probability for any width you give it. Where exactly does its answer flip from "no" to "yes", and how sure is it near that line?

### The big picture

| Petal width | What the detector says |
|---|---|
| below about 1 cm | highly confident: not virginica |
| about 1.65 cm | the decision boundary — 50 percent either way |
| above about 2 cm | highly confident: virginica |

### 1 · The dataset

The iris dataset makes logistic regression concrete: 150 flowers, each with sepal and petal length and width, labeled as one of three species. Figure 4-22 below shows the three.

In table terms it is 150 rows, four numeric feature columns and one label column — small enough to hold in your head, which is why it is the standard teaching set.

### 2 · A one-feature detector

Train a logistic regression model to detect just one species, Iris virginica, from a single feature, petal width, and you can plot the model's estimated probability as petal width varies from 0 to 3 cm. Figure 4-23 below is that plot.

Turning three species into one yes/no question is the move that makes a binary classifier applicable at all: the label becomes "is virginica" versus "is not virginica", and the other two species are both simply "not".

Below about 1 cm the model is highly confident the flower is not virginica; above about 2 cm it is highly confident it is; in between, it is genuinely unsure.

That unsure band is not a defect. The card below gives the reason: virginica petal widths run from 1.4 cm to 2.5 cm while the other irises run from 0.1 cm to 1.8 cm, so the two groups genuinely overlap and no rule on petal width alone can separate them cleanly.

### 3 · The boundary itself

Somewhere in that uncertain zone sits the **decision boundary** — the exact petal width where both probabilities equal 50%, which the book's example puts at about 1.65 cm. The card below shows the three lines of code that locate it.

Feed the model a petal width above that boundary and `predict()` returns True (virginica); below it, False — even when the model's confidence right at the edge is barely better than a coin flip.

That last clause is the practical warning. `predict()` hands you a hard label and throws the confidence away, so a 51% case and a 99% case come back looking identical. When the cost of being wrong is not symmetric, read the probability instead.

### 4 · Two features, same idea

Add a second feature, petal length, and the same logic scales up: the decision boundary is no longer a single point on a number line but a full boundary line through the two-dimensional feature space, again the set of points where the model estimates exactly 50% probability. Figure 4-24 below is that picture.

**Feature space** is a plot with one axis per feature, where each flower is a dot. With one feature the boundary is a point on a line; with two it is a line on a plane; with more features it keeps going, and stops being drawable long before it stops being a boundary.

### 5 · Why the boundary is straight

Because the underlying weighted sum is linear, that boundary is a straight line, and the further an instance sits from it in either direction, the more confident the model's probability estimate becomes — flowers well beyond one side sit above 90% confidence, and flowers well beyond the other sit below 15%.

Those parallel lines of equal confidence are the sigmoid seen from above: the weighted sum grows steadily as you walk away from the boundary, and the sigmoid turns that steady growth into a confidence that closes in on certainty without ever arriving.

**One-liner for your notes:** the decision boundary is where the estimated probability equals 50 percent — about 1.65 cm of petal width here — and it is straight because the score behind the sigmoid is a plain weighted sum.

blocks.title: Worked out: finding the 1.65 cm boundary
blocks.content:
The book computes the boundary in three lines. `X_new = np.linspace(0, 3, 1000).reshape(-1, 1)` makes 1,000 evenly spaced petal widths from 0 cm to 3 cm. `y_proba = log_reg.predict_proba(X_new)` gives two columns per width: column 0 is the probability of not Iris virginica, and column 1 is the probability of Iris virginica. `decision_boundary = X_new[y_proba[:, 1] >= 0.5][0, 0]` keeps the widths whose virginica probability is at least 0.5 and takes the first one, 1.6516516516516517. So `log_reg.predict([[1.7], [1.5]])` returns `[True, False]`: 1.7 cm lies above the boundary and 1.5 cm below it.

The unsure zone matches the data: virginica petal widths range from 1.4 cm to 2.5 cm, while the other irises generally range from 0.1 cm to 1.8 cm, so the two groups overlap.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
>>> from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
>>> iris = load_iris(as_frame=True)
>>> list(iris)
['data', 'target', 'frame', 'target_names', 'DESCR', 'feature_names',
  'filename', 'data_module']
>>> iris.target_names
array(['setosa', 'versicolor', 'virginica'], dtype='<U10')

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X = iris.data[["petal width (cm)"]].values
y = iris.target_names[iris.target] == 'virginica'
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=42)

log_reg = LogisticRegression(random_state=42)
log_reg.fit(X_train, y_train)

>>> decision_boundary
1.6516516516516517
>>> log_reg.predict([[1.7], [1.5]])
array([ True, False])
```

items.term: A hard label throws away the most useful output
items.text: The classifier knows the difference between 51% and 99%, and predict discards it. Where the two kinds of mistake cost different amounts — and they usually do — the right move is to read the probability and set your own threshold, rather than accept the default of one half. The decision boundary is a consequence of the threshold you chose, not a property of the data.

items.term: Overlap is a property of the features, not a failure of the model
items.text: Virginica petal widths run from 1.4 to 2.5 cm and the other species run up to 1.8 cm, so on petal width alone some flowers simply cannot be separated. No model, however flexible, can fix that — it is irreducible error from the previous lesson, created by a feature choice. The fix is another feature, which is exactly what the second half of this lesson does.

items.term: Straight boundaries are a limit you will want to break
items.text: The boundary is straight because the score behind it is a plain weighted sum. If the true separation curves, this model cannot draw it — the same limit linear regression had. And the same fix applies: feed it polynomial features and the boundary in the original feature space bends, while the model stays linear in its parameters.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: A flower has a petal width of exactly 1.6516516516516517 cm, the book's computed decision boundary. What probability does the model estimate for it belonging to Iris virginica?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The default threshold is 50%. How do you choose a different one deliberately, and what do you measure to defend the choice?
Look up: the scikit-learn user guide sections on Probability calibration, and on TunedThresholdClassifierCV for post-hoc threshold tuning.

items.term: Softmax Regression: Logistic Regression for Many Classes at Once

blocks.content:
Softmax regression handles many classes in one model: score every class, turn the scores into probabilities that add up to 1, and predict whichever class scored highest.

**The question this lesson answers:** logistic regression only separates two classes. How do you classify an iris into one of three species with a single model, rather than training three separate yes/no classifiers and stitching them together?

### The big picture

```
one score per class ─> softmax ─> probabilities ─> argmax
    θ⁽ᵏ⁾ · x          exp, then     they sum to 1    winner
                      normalise
```

### 1 · One parameter vector per class

Logistic regression as covered so far only handles two classes. Softmax regression, also called **multinomial logistic regression**, generalizes it to handle several classes directly, in one model, without training and combining several separate binary classifiers.

The idea: for an instance x, compute one score per class — each class gets its own parameter vector, and each score is just that class's weighted sum of the features, exactly like a linear regression prediction. Equation 4-19 below is that score.

So a three-class iris model is not one θ but three, stacked as rows of a matrix. Each row is a complete linear model in its own right, asking "how much does this row look like *my* class".

### 2 · Turning scores into probabilities

Then run all the class scores through the **softmax function**, which exponentiates each score and divides by the sum of all the exponentials. Equation 4-20 below is that function.

The result is a full probability distribution across every class: every value between 0 and 1, the whole set summing to 1. Summing to 1 is the property that separates this from running three independent sigmoids — the classes are competing for one fixed budget of probability, so pushing one up pushes the others down.

### 3 · Picking the answer

By default, the predicted class is simply whichever one got the highest score, equivalently the highest probability — that is the **argmax** operation. Argmax means "give me the position of the largest value, not the value itself". Equation 4-21 below states it three equivalent ways.

Given `predict_proba` output of [0, 0.04, 0.96], argmax returns 2, because 0.96 sits at index 2 — the third class, Iris virginica. Figure 4-25 below draws the resulting boundaries for all three species.

### 4 · Training: cross entropy

Training minimizes a cost function called **cross entropy**, the natural multi-class generalization of log loss: it penalizes the model whenever it assigns a low probability to an instance's true class, averaged across the whole training set, and with only two classes cross entropy reduces exactly to the log loss from ordinary logistic regression. Equation 4-22 below is the cost; Equation 4-23 below is the gradient used to minimise it.

As with plain logistic regression, there is no closed-form shortcut here either — gradient descent on the parameter matrix does the job, using a gradient vector for each class's own parameters.

### 5 · The library, and the one constraint

Scikit-Learn's `LogisticRegression` class switches into softmax mode automatically the moment it is trained on more than two classes, applies ℓ2 regularization by default, and lets you control that regularization strength through `C` — higher C means less regularization, the opposite direction from the alpha used elsewhere.

| Hyperparameter | Used by | Turning it up |
|---|---|---|
| alpha | Ridge, Lasso, ElasticNet | more regularization |
| C | LogisticRegression | less regularization |

That inversion catches people out constantly, because the two names sit in the same library and mean opposite things.

One constraint worth remembering: softmax regression assumes the classes are mutually exclusive, so it is the wrong tool for tagging one image with multiple labels at once. **Mutually exclusive** means exactly one can be true. A picture that is both outdoor and daytime needs two independent yes/no models, not one softmax that must choose.

**One-liner for your notes:** softmax scores every class, normalises the exponentials into probabilities summing to 1, predicts the argmax, trains on cross entropy — and only works when exactly one class can be true.

blocks.title: Equation 4-19
blocks.caption: Softmax score for class k
blocks.explain:
**Why these equations look like this**

Equation 4-19 is the same weighted sum as Equation 4-2, run once per class. Nothing new
is invented for the multi-class case; the model is simply K copies of the linear score,
each with its own parameter vector, all reading the same row.

Equation 4-20 is the piece that does the real work. The scores can be any numbers at all,
including negatives, and they do not add up to anything in particular — so they cannot be
probabilities as they stand. Two problems, two fixes. Exponentiating makes every score
positive, which is the first fix. Dividing each one by the sum of all of them forces the
set to add up to 1, which is the second. That division is why the classes compete: raising
one score lowers every other class's share automatically, without anyone coordinating it.

Why exponentiate rather than simply shifting the scores up until they are all positive?
Because the exponential preserves the *order* of the scores while widening the gaps
between them, so a clear winner comes out as a clear winner rather than a narrow one. It
is also the step that makes the two-class case line up with ordinary logistic regression —
the book states that equivalence at the level of the cost function, where cross entropy
with K = 2 is the log loss of Equation 4-17.

Equation 4-21 looks long only because it says one thing three times: the class with the
highest probability, the class with the highest post-softmax value, and the class with
the highest raw score are all the same class. The exponential-and-divide step never
reorders anything, so you can pick the winner before computing any probabilities at all.

Equation 4-22, cross entropy, is Equation 4-17 with an extra sum over the classes. The
target y for class k is 1 when the row really is class k and 0 otherwise, so once again
exactly one term per row survives and the rest are multiplied away. What survives is minus
the logarithm of the probability the model gave to the true class — the same log loss
charge, applied in a room with more doors.

Equation 4-23 is the gradient, and it is the same shape yet again: predicted probability
minus the target, times the feature values. Equations 4-5, 4-18 and 4-23 are three
instances of one pattern, which is the single most useful thing to carry out of this
chapter.

**Standard or simplified?** All five are canonical. The book adds one piece of history
worth knowing: cross entropy comes from Claude Shannon's information theory, where it
measures the average number of bits you spend per message when your assumed distribution
is not the true one, and the excess over the ideal is the Kullback–Leibler divergence.
That is context, not something this chapter uses.

**The general form.** This *is* the general form; logistic regression is its K = 2 case.
The book states that directly — with two classes, Equation 4-22 is equivalent to the log
loss of Equation 4-17.

| Classes | Squash with | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | sigmoid, Equation 4-14 | log loss, Equation 4-17 |
| K | softmax, Equation 4-20 | cross entropy, Equation 4-22 |

**Terms these equations introduce**

- **K** is the number of classes
- **k** indexes one particular class; **j** in the denominator of Equation 4-20 runs over
all of them, which is why the same letters appear twice in that formula
- **theta with a superscript k in brackets** is that one class's own parameter vector;
stacked together they form the parameter matrix, written as capital Theta
- **s(x)** is the vector of all K scores for one row
- **logit** is another name for a raw score before squashing
- **argmax** returns the position of the largest value, not the value

**Every piece of Equation 4-19 and 4-20**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| s k of x | s sub k of x | class k's score for the row x |
| theta superscript k | theta k | class k's own weight vector |
| p hat sub k | p hat k | the probability the row belongs to class k |
| exp of s k | e to the s k | make that score positive, keeping the order |
| the sum over j from 1 to K | sum over all classes | add up every exponentiated score |
| the division | divided by | force the whole set to add up to 1 |

**Every piece of Equation 4-21, 4-22 and 4-23**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| argmax over k | arg max over k | which k gives the largest value |
| J of capital Theta | J of Theta | the cross entropy over the training set |
| the double sum | sum over rows, then classes | every row, every class |
| y sub k of i | y k superscript i | 1 if row i really is class k, else 0 |
| log of p hat k of i | log of p hat k i | how surprised the model was to be right |
| the gradient for theta k | gradient for class k | the slope stack for one class's weights |
| p hat k minus y k | predicted minus target | the error on that class for that row |

**The formulas in plain words**

- 4-19: class score = the ordinary weighted sum, using that class's own weights.
- 4-20: probability of a class = its exponentiated score ÷ the total of all exponentiated
scores.
- 4-21: the prediction = whichever class has the largest score.
- 4-22: cost = the average over rows of minus the logarithm of the probability given to
the true class.
- 4-23: slope stack for one class = the average over rows of (that class's predicted
probability − its target) × the row's feature values.

**With real numbers**

The lesson's iris flower, 5 cm long and 2 cm wide, run through the trained model.

1. three classes, so Equation 4-19 produces three scores, one per species
2. Equation 4-20 exponentiates and normalises them, giving [0, 0.04, 0.96] to two
decimal places
3. those three add up to 0 + 0.04 + 0.96 = 1.00, which is the property the division buys
4. Equation 4-21 takes the argmax, and 0.96 sits at index 2, so predict returns 2 —
Iris virginica, with Iris versicolor at 4% as the runner-up

---

```python
X = iris.data[["petal length (cm)", "petal width (cm)"]].values
y = iris["target"]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=42)

>>> softmax_reg.predict_proba([[5, 2]]).round(2)
```

items.term: One model with K heads versus K separate models
items.text: You can classify into three classes by training three yes/no models and picking the most confident, and chapter 3 does exactly that. Softmax differs in that the classes share one normalisation step, so their probabilities are forced to add up to 1 and are directly comparable. Separate binary models give you three unrelated confidences that may all be high or all be low, with no principled way to compare them.

items.term: Mutually exclusive is a modelling assumption with teeth
items.text: The sum-to-one constraint is not a formatting nicety, it is a claim that exactly one class is true. When that claim is false — a photo that is both outdoor and daytime — the model is not merely imprecise, it is being forced to express something the data does not mean. The fix is independent binary classifiers, one per label, each free to be confident on its own.

items.term: C versus alpha, and why inverted hyperparameters persist
items.text: LogisticRegression's C raises regularization as it falls, the opposite of alpha everywhere else in the same library. The reason is historical — C comes from the support vector machine literature, alpha from the statistics literature — and it survives because changing it would break every existing call. Inherited conventions that cannot be fixed without breaking callers are a familiar shape; the defence is to check the direction rather than assume it.

items.term: End-of-chapter exercises

blocks.title: Recap: the facts these review questions rely on
blocks.content:
- **Feature scales:** gradient descent needs all features on a similar scale (for example with a `StandardScaler`), or it converges much more slowly.
- **Logistic regression:** the log loss is convex, so gradient descent finds the global minimum if the learning rate is not too large and you wait long enough.
- **Noisy curves:** with stochastic and mini-batch gradient descent the validation curve is not smooth, so stop only once the error has stayed above its minimum for a while, then roll back to the best model.
- **Ridge:** training and validation errors that are close and fairly high mean underfitting (high bias). A larger α adds bias, so reduce α.
- **Softmax:** it handles several classes in one model, estimates a probability for each class and is trained with gradient descent, but it predicts only one class at a time. A picture that is both outdoor and daytime needs two labels, so two logistic regression classifiers fit better.

Exercise 2: Suppose the features in your training set have very different scales. Which algorithms might suffer from this, and how? What can you do about it?
Exercise 3: Can gradient descent get stuck in a local minimum when training a logistic regression model?
Exercise 4: Do all gradient descent algorithms lead to the same model, provided you let them run long enough?

Exercise 5: Suppose you use batch gradient descent and you plot the validation error at every epoch. If you notice that the validation error consistently goes up, what is likely going on? How can you fix this?
Exercise 6: Is it a good idea to stop mini-batch gradient descent immediately when the validation error goes up?

Exercise 7: Which gradient descent algorithm (among those we discussed) will reach the vicinity of the optimal solution the fastest? Which will actually converge? How can you make the others converge as well?

Exercise 8: Suppose you are using polynomial regression. You plot the learning curves and you notice that there is a large gap between the training error and the validation error. What is happening? What are three ways to solve this?

Exercise 9: Suppose you are using ridge regression and you notice that the training error and the validation error are almost equal and fairly high. Would you say that the model suffers from high bias or high variance? Should you increase the regularization hyperparameter α or reduce it?

items.term: Large-Margin Classification and Support Vectors

blocks.content:
An SVM classifier does not settle for *any* line that separates two classes — it looks for the line that leaves the widest possible empty corridor between them, and only the handful of points touching that corridor's edges decide where it ends up.

**The question this lesson answers:** many different straight lines separate two classes perfectly on the same training data. Which one should the classifier pick, and which training rows actually decide it?

### The big picture

```
 ● ● ●             class A
────────────  edge of the street
     ↕  margin = the street's width
════════════  DECISION BOUNDARY (centerline)
     ↕
────────────  edge of the street
 ▲ ▲ ▲             class B
```

### 1 · Why the widest street, and not just any line

Picture it as a **street**: the boundary is the centerline, and the width of that street is the **margin**. A classifier that only cares about separating classes correctly, without worrying about how close it hugs the nearest points, can score perfectly on the training set and still fail on new data, because a small shift in an unseen point is enough to land it on the wrong side. Maximizing the margin builds in a buffer against exactly that kind of noise, and the book calls this **large margin classification**.

Figure 5-1 below shows the contrast in one picture. Its left plot holds three candidate lines: one so bad it does not even separate the classes properly, and two that work perfectly on this training set but run so close to the instances that they will probably do worse on new ones. The right plot is the SVM's answer — the same separation, but as far from the closest instances as it can get.

### 2 · Support vectors: the few rows that decide everything

The points that actually pin down where the widest possible street sits are called the **support vectors** — the training instances sitting right on the edge of the margin, circled in Figure 5-1. Once those support vectors are fixed, every other training instance could be moved around freely, or deleted entirely, as long as it stays off the street, and the decision boundary would not budge; the model's fit is fully determined by that small subset.

That is a strange property if your instinct comes from aggregates. An `AVG` over a column moves a little whenever any row moves. This is more like `MIN` and `MAX`: each is decided by one row at the edge, and the thousands of rows in between can be shuffled around all day without changing the answer, right up until one of them becomes the new extreme.

### 3 · Why scaling is not optional here

This is also why SVMs are unusually sensitive to **feature scaling** — the step of putting every column on a comparable numeric range. If one feature ranges over thousands of units and another over single digits, the geometric notion of a "wide street" is dominated by whichever feature has the larger raw scale, and the resulting boundary can be close to useless.

Figure 5-2 below shows exactly that: on the left the vertical scale is much larger than the horizontal one, so the widest street the model can find is nearly horizontal — it is measuring width almost entirely in the big column's units. Standardizing every feature first (for example with Scikit-Learn's `StandardScaler`) fixes it, which is why scaling is close to mandatory for SVMs, not just good practice.

**One-liner for your notes:** an SVM picks the boundary with the widest empty street around it, that street is pinned down only by the support vectors on its edges, and because "wide" is measured geometrically you must scale the features first.

blocks.caption: Large margin classification
blocks.alt: Figure 5-1: Large margin classification

blocks.title: Figure 5-2
blocks.caption: Sensitivity to feature scales

items.term: Why 'widest' is a stand-in for 'generalises'
items.text: The model cannot see future data, so it cannot optimise generalisation directly. What it can optimise is a geometric property that stands in for it: distance from the boundary to the nearest points, which is exactly the room an unseen point has to move before it is misclassified. That substitution is the whole idea, and it is also its limit — a wide margin on an unrepresentative sample is still a confidently wrong boundary, because margin measures robustness to small movement, not to a biased sample.

items.term: A model decided by a few rows cuts both ways
items.text: Being determined by the support vectors alone gives you a compact model and total indifference to bulk changes far from the boundary. The same property makes the fit hypersensitive to a handful of edge rows, so one mislabeled point near the boundary can move everything — which is precisely the failure the next lesson has to fix.

items.term: When scaling is a modelling decision, not cleanup
items.text: Any algorithm whose objective is a distance in feature space inherits the units of its columns, so the column with the biggest raw numbers quietly wins. That is why SVMs, k-nearest neighbours and k-means all need scaling while tree-based models do not. The question to ask of a new algorithm is not 'should I scale?' but 'does its objective measure distance?'

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: In your own words, why does maximizing the margin — not just finding any separating line — help a classifier generalize to new data?

items: The book standardises features here. Would min-max scaling to a 0-to-1 range give the same SVM boundary, and what changes if one feature has heavy outliers that stretch its range?

items.term: Soft Margin Classification and the C Hyperparameter

blocks.content:
Insisting that every training instance stay completely off the street is called hard margin classification, it breaks on real data, and the fix is to allow a controlled number of violations — with C as the dial that sets how many.

**The question this lesson answers:** real data has outliers and overlapping classes, so a perfectly empty street often does not exist. What does an SVM do then, and which knob decides how strict it is?

### The big picture

| | Low C | High C |
|---|---|---|
| The street gets | wider | narrower |
| Margin violations | more are tolerated | very few allowed |
| Instances supporting it | more | fewer |
| Failure mode | underfitting | overfitting the noise |

### 1 · Hard margin, and its two real problems

Requiring every single training instance to sit fully off the street and on the correct side is called **hard margin classification**, and it has two real problems: it only works on linearly separable data, and it is extremely sensitive to outliers.

1. **It only works when the classes are genuinely linearly separable** — *linearly separable* means a single straight line can put every instance of one class on one side and every instance of the other on the other side. If they are not, there is no valid street to find at all.
2. **It is extremely sensitive to outliers** — an **outlier** being a point that sits far away from the rest of its class. A single mislabeled or oddly placed point can make a valid margin impossible to find, or force the boundary into a shape that generalizes badly to everything else.

Figure 5-3 below is the same iris data as the previous lesson with exactly one extra outlier added. On the left, no hard margin exists at all; on the right, one is found but the boundary ends up very different from the clean version, and it will probably not generalize as well.

This is the failure mode of any rule written as "every row must satisfy this". The single worst row decides the outcome — the same reason one bad record can fail an entire zero-tolerance load.

### 2 · Soft margin: allow violations, but budget them

**Soft margin classification** relaxes the rule. Instead of a hard either/or, the training objective now balances two competing goals: keep the street as wide as possible, and keep the number of **margin violations** — instances that end up inside the street or on the wrong side entirely — as small as possible.

Notice what a margin violation is *not*: an instance sitting just outside the street on its correct side is perfectly fine, however close it is.

### 3 · C, the knob that sets the balance

The knob that sets this balance is the regularization hyperparameter **C**. A **hyperparameter** is a setting you fix before training, not something training learns — the `--conf` flag you pass when you submit the job, rather than a value computed by it.

A low C tolerates more margin violations in exchange for a wider street; because more instances effectively help define that street, the model is less likely to overfit, but push C too low and it starts underfitting instead. A high C insists on very few violations, which narrows the street and increases the risk of overfitting to noise in the training data.

The practical rule of thumb: if an SVM is overfitting, try lowering C first.

Figure 5-4 below is the book's own demonstration, and it is worth reading carefully because it cuts against the rule of thumb: the low-C model on the left (C = 1) has the wider street, the high-C model on the right (C = 100) has fewer violations, and on this particular dataset the book judges that C = 100 looks like it will generalize better — the low-C model appears to be underfitting. Both directions are real failure modes; neither value is safe by default.

**One-liner for your notes:** hard margin demands a perfectly empty street and dies on outliers or non-separable data; soft margin trades a few margin violations for a wider street, and C sets the trade — lower C for a wider street and less overfitting, too low and it underfits.

items.term: Why one bad row can destroy a hard margin
items.text: The hard margin constraint is written over every instance, so the solution is decided by the single hardest row. Any rule of the form 'this must hold for all rows' inherits that property — its outcome is set by its worst record, and one mislabeled point is enough to make it unsatisfiable. Soft margin is the standard escape: keep the rule, price the exceptions, and let the optimiser buy the cheapest set of them.

items.term: C runs backwards from how people usually say 'regularisation'
items.text: Here a *larger* C means *less* regularisation, because C is the price charged for each violation. That is the opposite direction from most regularisation settings you will meet, which get stronger as the number grows. It is worth pinning down now, because the book's advice 'reduce C to regularise' sounds wrong until you know which way the dial points.

items.term: Both ends of the dial are real failure modes
items.text: It is tempting to read 'lower C is safer' out of the rule of thumb. The book's own Figure 5-4 shows the opposite case, where the low-C model underfits and the high-C one looks like the better generalizer. Neither end is a safe default, which is the actual argument for searching the value rather than reasoning it out.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Your SVM classifier is overfitting on a small, slightly noisy dataset. Would you raise or lower C, and why?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Soft margin counts every margin violation the same, whichever class it came from. What happens when one class has far fewer instances than the other, and what does changing the per-class weight actually change in that trade-off?
Look up: the class_weight parameter in the scikit-learn documentation for sklearn.svm.SVC, and the 'Unbalanced problems' section of the user guide's Support Vector Machines page.

items.term: Training and Reading a Linear SVM Classifier in Scikit-Learn

blocks.content:
Training a linear SVM in Scikit-Learn is the usual two-step pipeline, and the thing worth slowing down for is what comes *out* of it: a bare class, plus a signed score that is not a probability.

**The question this lesson answers:** given petal length and width for an iris flower, how do you train a model that flags *Iris virginica*, and what can you actually read back out of it afterwards?

### The big picture

| What you call | What comes back |
|---|---|
| .predict(X_new) | True or False per flower, nothing more |
| .decision_function(X_new) | a signed distance to the boundary |
| .predict_proba(X_new) | nothing — LinearSVC has no such method |

### 1 · The two lines that make it an SVM

Scikit-Learn's usual pattern applies almost unchanged from the rest of the book — the two lines that make this an SVM (rather than, say, logistic regression) are the import of `LinearSVC` and its constructor call. Everything is wrapped inside a single `make_pipeline`, chaining `StandardScaler()` before `LinearSVC(C=1)`.

That ordering is not cosmetic: because SVMs are sensitive to feature scale, scaling has to happen as part of the same fitted object, so that any new data run through `.predict()` gets scaled exactly the same way the training data was.

A `StandardScaler` is *stateful* — during training it learns each column's mean and spread, and it has to reuse those same learned numbers later. Scaling X by hand first and fitting the model separately leaves those numbers sitting outside the model, and nothing forces the next caller to apply them. It is the same reason you put a cast inside a view definition instead of asking every consumer to remember it.

### 2 · What predict gives you, and what it withholds

Once fit, `svm_clf.predict(X_new)` returns a plain `True`/`False` classification per instance — no probability, just a class. In the card below, the first plant is classified as an *Iris virginica* and the second is not.

Digging one layer deeper, `svm_clf.decision_function(X_new)` reveals the number actually driving that classification: the **signed distance** between the instance and the decision boundary. A positive score means the positive class, and a larger magnitude means the instance sits further from the boundary (more confidently classified); a negative score flips both.

Read the card's two scores that way. The first flower scores about 0.66 — positive, so *virginica*, and further from the boundary. The second scores about −0.22 — negative, so not *virginica*, and closer to the boundary than the first one is. Neither number is a percentage; 0.66 is not "66% likely".

### 3 · Probabilities cost extra, and here is exactly what they cost

Note what is *not* available here. Unlike `LogisticRegression`, plain `LinearSVC` has no `predict_proba()` — it was never trained to output a calibrated probability, only a decision score.

Getting probabilities out of an SVM means switching to the `SVC` class with `probability=True`, which under the hood runs 5-fold cross-validation to generate out-of-sample scores and then fits a separate `LogisticRegression` on top of them — a real slowdown, paid only if probabilities are actually needed. That extra fit is what makes `predict_proba()` and `predict_log_proba()` appear on the model afterwards.

**One-liner for your notes:** scale inside the pipeline so serving matches training, read `decision_function` as a signed distance rather than a probability, and pay for real probabilities only by switching to `SVC(probability=True)`, which quietly trains a second model on 5-fold cross-validated scores.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.svm import LinearSVC

iris = load_iris(as_frame=True)
X = iris.data[["petal length (cm)", "petal width (cm)"]].values
y = (iris.target == 2) # Iris virginica

svm_clf = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                        LinearSVC(C=1, random_state=42))
svm_clf.fit(X, y)

>>> X_new = [[5.5, 1.7], [5.0, 1.5]]
>>> svm_clf.predict(X_new)
array([ True, False])

>>> svm_clf.decision_function(X_new)
array([ 0.66163411, -0.22036063])
```

items.term: A decision score is not a probability, and the difference is not pedantic
items.text: The score orders instances by how far they sit from the boundary, which is enough to rank them or to pick a cut-off by trial. It carries no calibration: 0.66 does not mean a 66% chance, and the same score means different things on two differently scaled datasets. The moment a decision depends on an absolute threshold with a cost attached, an uncalibrated score stops being usable and you have to pay for probabilities.

items.term: Why a fitted transformer belongs inside the model object
items.text: A scaler learns numbers from the training data and must reuse exactly those numbers later. Leaving it outside the model means every future caller has to remember to apply it, with the same parameters, in the same order — and the failure when they do not is silent, because the model still returns predictions, just wrong ones. Packaging the transform with the estimator makes the contract impossible to get wrong.

items.term: Probabilities are a second model, not a formatting option
items.text: Setting probability=True does not reinterpret the SVM's output; it trains an additional model on cross-validated scores from the first one. That is why it is off by default and why it costs real time. It is a good reminder that some model 'features' are extra fitting work hiding behind a keyword argument.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Why does the code above wrap StandardScaler and LinearSVC together in a single pipeline instead of scaling X first and fitting LinearSVC separately?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Turning decision scores into probabilities by fitting a second model on cross-validated scores is a named, published technique with known weaknesses. Which technique is it, and when is it unreliable?
Look up: the 'Scores and probabilities' section of the scikit-learn user guide's Support Vector Machines page, which names the method and cites its source papers.

items.term: Handling Nonlinear Data: Extra Features and the Polynomial Kernel

blocks.content:
When a dataset cannot be split by a straight line, the first fix is not a different algorithm — it is more columns; and the kernel trick is a way to get the effect of those columns without ever building them.

**The question this lesson answers:** the two interleaving crescents of the moons dataset cannot be separated by any straight line. How does a *linear* classifier end up drawing a curved boundary around them, and why is the obvious way to do it too slow?

### The big picture

| Route | Builds the extra columns | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| PolynomialFeatures then LinearSVC | yes, really, in memory | explodes at high degree |
| SVC with kernel="poly" | no, never built | same power, far cheaper |

### 1 · More features can straighten a boundary

Plenty of real datasets are nowhere near linearly separable, and the fix does not have to be a fundamentally different algorithm — it can be extra features. Take a dataset with a single feature x₁ that is not linearly separable; adding a second feature x₂ = x₁ squared can be enough to make the resulting 2D version perfectly separable by a straight line. Figure 5-5 below shows both views of the same data.

Nothing about the model changed there. The classifier is still drawing one straight cut; the data simply moved into a space where a straight cut is enough. In query terms, you did not swap the engine — you added a derived column and the same simple predicate started working.

Generalizing that idea, running `PolynomialFeatures` ahead of `StandardScaler` and `LinearSVC` in a pipeline lets an otherwise linear classifier handle a nonlinear boundary, and it works reasonably well on the classic "two interleaving moons" toy dataset (`make_moons`), shown in Figure 5-6.

### 2 · The catch is cost

The catch is cost. At a low polynomial degree this approach cannot represent very complex boundaries, and at a high degree the number of generated features explodes, making training slow. **Degree** here is the highest power used: the higher it goes, the more combinations of the original features get generated, and the book's word for what follows is a combinatorial explosion.

### 3 · The kernel trick, stated without the maths

This is exactly the gap the **kernel trick** closes: it lets `SVC(kernel="poly", degree=3, coef0=1, C=5)` behave as if the training data had been expanded with high-degree polynomial features — even a very high degree — without Scikit-Learn ever constructing those extra columns.

Note carefully what it does *not* claim. The kernel does not give the model powers that explicit features could not; it gives the identical model at a fraction of the computational cost. How that trick actually works mathematically gets its own explanation later in this chapter; for now, treat it as: the same modeling power as adding the features by hand, without the bill.

Figure 5-7 below shows this kernel at work — a third-degree polynomial kernel on the left, and a 10th-degree one on the right, where the boundary is visibly more contorted.

### 4 · Its two knobs

Two hyperparameters tune the polynomial kernel:

- **`degree`** — raise it if the model underfits, lower it if it overfits. That is the same logic as with explicit polynomial features, because it is the same quantity.
- **`coef0`** — controls how much the fitted model is swayed by high-degree terms relative to low-degree ones.

**One-liner for your notes:** adding polynomial features can make an unseparable dataset separable by a straight line, but the column count explodes at high degree, so `SVC(kernel="poly")` buys the same modeling power without ever materializing those columns — tuned by `degree` and `coef0`.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures

X, y = make_moons(n_samples=100, noise=0.15, random_state=42)

polynomial_svm_clf = make_pipeline(
    PolynomialFeatures(degree=3),
    StandardScaler(),
    LinearSVC(C=10, max_iter=10_000, random_state=42)
)
polynomial_svm_clf.fit(X, y)

from sklearn.svm import SVC

poly_kernel_svm_clf = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                                    SVC(kernel="poly", degree=3, coef0=1, C=5))
poly_kernel_svm_clf.fit(X, y)
```

items.term: Why extra columns can straighten a curved boundary
items.text: A boundary that curves in two dimensions can be a flat cut in three. Nothing about the model changes — it is still fitting one straight separator — only the space it fits in. That is the general pattern behind every 'linear model plus engineered features' setup, and its cost is that you have to guess a transformation that helps. Blind high-degree expansion is the guess-free version, and you pay for it in variance and compute.

items.term: Capacity knobs all behave the same way
items.text: degree, C and gamma are different mechanisms with an identical user-facing rule: underfitting means turn capacity up, overfitting means turn it down. Recognising which direction a new knob points is a more transferable skill than memorising any particular one, and it is why the book keeps restating the same sentence for each.

items.term: The kernel trick buys cost, not power
items.text: It is easy to read 'kernel' as 'stronger model'. It is not: the kernelised model is the same model you would get by building the features explicitly and fitting a linear SVM on them. What changes is that you never build or store the columns. Keeping that straight matters, because it means a kernel cannot rescue a model whose explicit-feature version would also have failed.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: You added third-degree polynomial features by hand and the model got slow. What does switching to SVC(kernel='poly', degree=3) get you that plain PolynomialFeatures did not?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: coef0 is described as trading high-degree terms against low-degree ones. Where does it sit in the polynomial kernel's actual formula, and what does the gamma in that same formula do for a polynomial kernel rather than an RBF one?
Look up: Equation 5-7 later in this chapter, which prints the polynomial kernel, and the 'Kernel functions' section of the scikit-learn user guide's Support Vector Machines page.

items.term: Similarity Features and the Gaussian RBF Kernel

blocks.content:
The second way to make a curved problem linear is to stop using an instance's position as its features and start using how much it resembles a few chosen reference points.

**The question this lesson answers:** the same 1D dataset that no straight line could split — how do you rebuild its columns so that a straight line *can* split it, and what does that cost when you scale it up?

### The big picture

```
similarity
  1 |    ▁▄█▄▁       1 exactly at the landmark
    |  ▁▀     ▀▁
  0 |▀▀         ▀▀▀  toward 0 far away
    +-----▲---------  distance from the landmark
       landmark
```

### 1 · Landmarks and a similarity function

A second way to make a nonlinear dataset linearly separable is to measure how much each instance resembles a handful of chosen reference points, called **landmarks**, using a **similarity function** — a function that turns "how far is this row from that reference point" into a score.

Géron's running example places two landmarks on a 1D dataset and uses the **Gaussian RBF** as the similarity function — a bell-shaped curve that outputs 1 exactly at the landmark and decays toward 0 the further away an instance sits. RBF is short for *radial basis function*: *radial* because only the distance matters, not the direction you travelled to get there.

Replacing each original feature with its similarity score to every landmark can turn an inseparable 1D dataset into a perfectly separable one, at the cost of adding a new feature per landmark. Figure 5-8 below shows the before and after, and the card below it walks one instance through the arithmetic with the book's own numbers.

You have met this shape before if you read Chapter 2: the geographic similarity feature there is the same move — replace a raw coordinate with "how close is this district to San Francisco", and a messy 2D position becomes one meaningful column.

### 2 · Reading the similarity score

The similarity of an instance to a landmark is a bell curve over the distance between them, with one tuning number in it:

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| d | the distance | how far the instance sits from the landmark |
| γ | gamma | how fast the score falls off with distance |
| the score | similarity | 1 at the landmark, decaying toward 0 |

In plain words: **similarity = 1 when you are standing on the landmark, and it shrinks the further away you get, with gamma deciding how quickly.** The card below plugs in the book's example — two landmarks, gamma of 0.3, and one instance sitting a distance of 1 from the first landmark and 2 from the second — and gets 0.74 and 0.30, the nearer landmark scoring higher.

### 3 · Where to put the landmarks, and what it costs

The simplest way to choose landmarks is to place one at every single training instance. That guarantees plenty of dimensions to work with, which raises the odds of linear separability, but it also means a training set with m instances turns into a training set with m *features* — brutal for a large training set if computed explicitly.

That is a genuinely alarming shape for anyone used to tables: the width of your dataset now grows with its height. A million rows would mean a million columns.

Once again, the **kernel trick** sidesteps the explicit computation: `SVC(kernel="rbf", gamma=5, C=0.001)` gets the effect of similarity features against every instance without Scikit-Learn ever materializing them.

### 4 · gamma, the width of the bell

The RBF kernel's own hyperparameter, **gamma**, controls how narrow that bell curve is.

- **Higher gamma** narrows it, so each instance's zone of influence shrinks and the decision boundary starts wiggling tightly around individual points — a classic overfitting shape.
- **Lower gamma** widens the curve, spreads each instance's influence further, and produces a smoother boundary that can underfit if pushed too far.

Gamma behaves like an inverse regularization knob, the same role C plays elsewhere: reduce gamma if overfitting, raise it if underfitting. Figure 5-9 below varies gamma and C together, which is the honest way to look at them — they interact.

**One-liner for your notes:** replace positions with similarity-to-landmark scores and a hopeless dataset becomes separable; one landmark per instance is the simple choice and would cost m features, so `SVC(kernel="rbf")` fakes it — with gamma as the bell's width, narrower meaning more overfit.

blocks.title: Worked out: RBF similarity features for one instance
blocks.content:
The book's example uses a 1D dataset with two landmarks, one at $x_1 = -2$ and one at $x_1 = 1$, and the Gaussian RBF with $\gamma = 0.3$ as the similarity function. The similarity of an instance to a landmark is $\exp(-\gamma \times d^2)$, where $d$ is the distance between the instance and the landmark (the Gaussian RBF kernel in Equation 5-7 has the same form).

Take the instance $x_1 = -1$. It sits at a distance of 1 from the first landmark and 2 from the second landmark.

- First new feature: $x_2 = \exp(-0.3 \times 1^2) \approx 0.74$
- Second new feature: $x_3 = \exp(-0.3 \times 2^2) \approx 0.30$

The nearer landmark gives the score closer to 1. Computing both features for every instance, and dropping the original feature, gives the transformed dataset in Figure 5-8, which is linearly separable.

blocks.caption: Similarity features using the Gaussian RBF
blocks.alt: Figure 5-8: Similarity features using the Gaussian RBF

blocks.title: Figure 5-9
blocks.caption: SVM classifiers using an RBF kernel
blocks.alt: Figure 5-9: SVM classifiers using an RBF kernel

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
rbf_kernel_svm_clf = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                                   SVC(kernel="rbf", gamma=5, C=0.001))
rbf_kernel_svm_clf.fit(X, y)
```

items.term: Why resemblance makes a hopeless dataset separable
items.text: Swapping 'where is this row' for 'how much does it resemble these reference points' re-coordinates the data. Classes that interleave along a raw axis can be pulled apart because they sit near different landmarks, even though neither class occupies a contiguous stretch of the original feature. The catch is that the landmarks carry the whole burden: put them somewhere uninformative and the new columns say nothing.

items.term: gamma and C both add flexibility, which is why you cannot tune them separately
items.text: Raising gamma and raising C each let the model fit the training data more closely, so a low value of one can hide a high value of the other. That is why the book's Figure 5-9 varies both at once rather than showing a tidy one-at-a-time sweep, and why a search over the pair beats two sequential searches.

items.term: Where the kernel trick stops being an optimisation
items.text: One landmark per instance means the transformed dataset has as many columns as it has rows: the work grows with the square of the dataset before training even begins. At that point not building the features is no longer a speed-up, it is the only version that runs at all. Any method whose feature count grows with the data has this same cliff.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Your RBF-kernel SVM wiggles tightly around individual training points. Is gamma too high or too low, and what would you do about it?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: A landmark at every instance would mean m features, but a trained RBF SVM only keeps its support vectors. How many does it actually end up keeping on a given dataset, and what makes that number grow?
Look up: the support_vectors_ and n_support_ attributes in the scikit-learn documentation for sklearn.svm.SVC.

items.term: Choosing Among LinearSVC, SVC, and SGDClassifier

blocks.content:
Scikit-Learn gives you three different classes that all do large-margin classification, and you pick between them on how big your data is and whether you need the kernel trick — not on accuracy.

**The question this lesson answers:** you have a classification problem and a row count. Which of `LinearSVC`, `SVC` and `SGDClassifier` should you reach for, and what does each one refuse to do?

### The big picture

| Class | Training time | Out-of-core | Kernel trick |
|---|---|---|---|
| LinearSVC | about O(m × n) | no | no |
| SVC | O(m² × n) to O(m³ × n) | no | yes |
| SGDClassifier | about O(m × n) | yes | no |

Here m is the number of training instances (rows) and n the number of features (columns). Table 5-1 in the book adds one more column, and its answer is the same for all three: **scaling required, yes**.

### 1 · LinearSVC — the fast one

`LinearSVC` is built on the `liblinear` library: it has no kernel-trick support, but it scales close to linearly in both the number of instances (m) and features (n) — roughly O(m × n) — which makes it the fastest option by a wide margin on large datasets, especially compared to `SVC(kernel="linear")`.

Read those complexity classes the way you would read a query plan. O(m × n) is one pass over the data. O(m² × n) is the shape of work that compares every row with every other row — a self-join, and it behaves like one as the table grows.

### 2 · SVC — the flexible, expensive one

`SVC` is built on `libsvm` and is the one that supports the kernel trick (polynomial, RBF, and friends). The price for that flexibility is steep: training time complexity runs from roughly O(m² × n) up to O(m³ × n), so it becomes painfully slow once the training set reaches the hundreds of thousands of instances.

It is the right tool specifically for small-to-medium nonlinear datasets, and it does scale well with the number of *features*, especially when those features are sparse. **Sparse** means most values in a row are zero — a one-hot-encoded text column is the usual example — and `libsvm`'s cost then tracks the average number of non-zero features per instance rather than the full width.

### 3 · SGDClassifier — the one that streams

`SGDClassifier` trains via stochastic gradient descent and, with the right hyperparameters (`alpha`, `penalty`, `learning_rate`), approximates the same large-margin behavior as the linear SVM classes.

Its real advantage is that SGD training works incrementally — it can learn from a stream of mini-batches without ever holding the full dataset in memory, making it the only one of the three suited to true **out-of-core learning**, while still scaling at roughly O(m × n). Out-of-core is the incremental-load story rather than the full-refresh one: the data arrives in chunks, each chunk nudges the model, and nothing ever needs to fit in RAM at once.

### 4 · The rule of thumb

As a starting rule of thumb: try the linear kernel first, reach for RBF-kernel `SVC` if the data is nonlinear and not too large, and fall back to `SGDClassifier` when the dataset simply will not fit.

**One-liner for your notes:** `LinearSVC` is the fast linear default at about O(m × n), `SVC` is the only one with kernels but costs O(m² × n) to O(m³ × n) so it suits small-to-medium nonlinear data, and `SGDClassifier` is the only one that learns out-of-core from a stream — and all three need scaled features.

items.term: The choice here is a throughput decision, not an accuracy one
items.text: All three classes do large margin classification and, on data that suits them, land on similar models — the book's own exercise asks you to make them agree. What separates them is what they can physically get through: rows per unit time, and whether the data has to be in memory. Sizing first and shaping second is the order that saves you from discovering the cost after the modelling.

items.term: The kernel trick is what costs you the scalability
items.text: The reason SVC grows so much faster than linearly is that kernelised training works with comparisons between pairs of instances, not with features one at a time. The very property that lets you skip building columns forces you to weigh rows against rows — which is why the one class with kernels is also the one that dies on large datasets.

items.term: Out-of-core is a property of the training algorithm, not of the model
items.text: Nothing about a large margin classifier requires the whole dataset in memory; it is the solver that does. Stochastic gradient descent updates from one mini-batch at a time, so it can stream — incremental load rather than full refresh. The catch is the same one incremental pipelines have: each batch has to be representative, so streaming data that arrives sorted will mislead the model.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: You have 5 million training rows that don't fit in memory. Which of LinearSVC, SVC or SGDClassifier can even attempt this, and why?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: liblinear and libsvm are separate C libraries with different algorithms inside them. Which algorithm does each actually run, and why does that difference produce the complexity gap in the table above?

Look up: the two papers the book cites for them — Chih-Jen Lin et al., 'A Dual Coordinate Descent Method for Large-Scale Linear SVM' (ICML 2008) for liblinear, and John Platt, 'Sequential Minimal Optimization: A Fast Algorithm for Training Support Vector Machines' (Microsoft Research technical report, 1998) for libsvm.

items.term: SVM Regression and the Epsilon Hyperparameter

blocks.content:
SVM regression keeps the street and flips what it is for: instead of an empty corridor between two classes, it is a tolerance band you try to fit the data *inside*.

**The question this lesson answers:** the same street machinery, pointed at a continuous target instead of two classes — what changes, and what does the hyperparameter epsilon actually set?

### The big picture

| | SVM classification | SVM regression |
|---|---|---|
| The street should hold | nothing, keep it empty | as many instances as possible |
| Its width is | maximised by training | fixed by you, via epsilon |
| A violation is | an instance inside it | an instance outside it |

### 1 · The flip

Flip the SVM classification objective around and you get SVM regression. Instead of maximizing the street's width between two classes while limiting how many points fall inside it, SVM regression tries to fit as *many* training instances as possible **inside** a street of fixed width, while limiting how many fall outside it.

The street's width is set by the hyperparameter **epsilon**: a small epsilon (say 0.5) carves out a narrow street, a larger one (say 1.2) a wider one. Figure 5-10 below shows both of those fits on the same linear data.

### 2 · Epsilon-insensitivity, and why it matters

The consequence of this flip is a property called **epsilon-insensitivity**: once a training instance already lands inside the margin, adding more instances there or moving them around within it has zero effect on the fitted model's predictions. Only instances that would fall outside the margin — and so become new support vectors — actually change the fit.

This is the behaviour of a tolerance band in a reconciliation check. Any row whose difference falls inside the agreed tolerance contributes nothing at all; only the breaches drive anything. Rows inside the band are not weighted less, they are ignored outright.

### 3 · Shrinking epsilon regularizes

That also explains why shrinking epsilon tends to *increase* the number of support vectors: a narrower street leaves fewer instances safely inside it, so more of them end up defining the boundary, which regularizes the model further. Run it the other way and the same logic holds — widen the street and fewer instances stick out to be support vectors.

### 4 · Which class to use

`LinearSVR` handles the linear case, mirroring `LinearSVC`'s scaling behavior. For nonlinear regression, `SVR` supports the kernel trick the same way `SVC` does for classification — the code below fits a second-degree polynomial kernel to a quadratic dataset, with `C` controlling regularization strength exactly as it does for classification: a small C regularizes more, a large C lets the model hug the training data more tightly. Figure 5-11 below shows exactly that pair, the regularized fit on the left and the loose one on the right.

The cost story carries over unchanged too: `LinearSVR` scales linearly with the size of the training set, while `SVR` gets much too slow once the training set grows very large.

Note that epsilon and C are not two names for the same dial. Epsilon decides which misses count as errors at all; C decides how hard the remaining ones are punished.

**One-liner for your notes:** SVM regression fits as many instances as possible inside a street of width epsilon, ignores anything already inside it (epsilon-insensitivity), and a smaller epsilon means more support vectors and more regularization — `LinearSVR` for linear, `SVR` for kernels.

blocks.caption: SVM regression

blocks.title: Figure 5-11
blocks.caption: SVM regression using a second-degree polynomial kernel
blocks.alt: Figure 5-11: SVM regression using a second-degree polynomial kernel

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.svm import LinearSVR

X, y = [...] # a linear dataset
svm_reg = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                        LinearSVR(epsilon=0.5, random_state=42))
svm_reg.fit(X, y)

from sklearn.svm import SVR

X, y = [...] # a quadratic dataset
svm_poly_reg = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                             SVR(kernel="poly", degree=2, C=0.01, epsilon=0.1))
svm_poly_reg.fit(X, y)
```

items.term: A loss that is exactly zero inside a band changes what the model learns
items.text: Instances inside the street are not down-weighted, they are ignored: they contribute nothing to the fit. So the model is decided entirely by the breaches, which makes it compact and indifferent to the bulk of the data. The price is that epsilon is a modelling assumption — you are declaring which errors do not matter — and it is a width on the same axis as the target, so a value that is tiny for one target is enormous for another.

items.term: Epsilon and C pull on different things
items.text: Epsilon decides which misses count as errors at all; C decides how hard the errors that remain get punished. They can be confused because both change how tightly the fit follows the data, but only one of them alters the definition of an error. Knowing which is which is what makes a search over the pair interpretable.

items.term: Fewer support vectors means a smaller model, not just a looser one
items.text: A kernelised SVM stores its support vectors and uses them at prediction time, so epsilon quietly sets how much model you end up shipping and how much work each prediction costs. A hyperparameter that changes the deployed artifact's size, not only its accuracy, is worth noticing before you tune it purely on a validation score.

items: Explain in one sentence why increasing epsilon in SVM regression tends to reduce the number of support vectors.

Look up: the epsilon parameter description in the scikit-learn documentation for sklearn.svm.SVR and sklearn.svm.LinearSVR.

items.term: Under the Hood: The Margin Objective and Hinge Loss

blocks.content:
Everything so far described the street in pictures; this is the same street written as an optimization problem — and the whole of it comes down to one fact: a smaller weight vector means a wider street.

**The question this lesson answers:** "maximize the margin" is a sentence, not something a computer can solve. What exact quantity does training actually minimize, and how does the C from earlier get into it?

### The big picture

```
 wide street   ⇄   small ‖w‖      b only slides
 narrow street ⇄   large ‖w‖      the street sideways
```

### 1 · Predicting is the easy half

Making a prediction with a linear SVM is simple: compute the decision function (a weighted sum of the features, w·x + b) and check its sign. **w** is the weight vector, one number per feature; **b** is the bias, a single number added at the end. (Chapter 4 wrote the same thing with every parameter in one vector θ; from here the book splits the bias out as b and keeps the feature weights in w.)

Training — finding the weight vector w and bias b that make that rule good — is where the real machinery lives.

### 2 · The one geometric fact everything rests on

The key geometric fact is that the margin's width is controlled entirely by the size of w, not by b. Shrink the norm of w (written ‖w‖) and the two lines marking the edges of the street — the points where the decision function equals exactly −1 or +1 — move further apart. A **norm** is just a measure of a vector's length; here it stands for how big the weights are overall.

The bias b only shifts the whole street left or right without changing how wide it is. So "maximize the margin" becomes, mathematically, "make ‖w‖ as small as possible", while still forcing every training instance onto the correct side of the street. The card below works this through with the book's own numbers from Figure 5-12: weight 1 gives a margin of 2, weight 0.5 gives a margin of 4.

### 3 · Hard margin, written down

That constrained minimization of half the squared norm of w (rather than the norm directly) is the **hard margin** objective — Equation 5-1 below, with its full explanation underneath it.

Why the squared norm and not the norm itself? Because the squared norm has a clean, simple derivative, while the plain norm is not differentiable at w = 0, and optimizers strongly prefer differentiable objectives. **Differentiable** means the function has a well-defined slope everywhere, which is what a solver follows downhill; the plain norm has a sharp corner at zero where no single slope exists.

### 4 · Soft margin, and where C enters

The **soft margin** version adds one **slack variable** per training instance, measuring how far that instance is allowed to poke into (or past) the margin. The objective now balances two conflicting things — keep the slack variables small (fewer violations) and keep the squared-norm term small (wider margin) — and the hyperparameter **C** sets that trade-off explicitly. That is Equation 5-2 below.

So the C from the soft-margin lesson was never a vague strictness dial: it is literally the multiplier in front of the summed slack. A big C makes violations expensive, so the solver buys fewer of them by accepting a smaller margin — which is why raising C shrinks the street.

### 5 · Two ways to actually solve it

Both the hard and soft margin problems are convex quadratic optimization problems (**QP problems**), solvable by an off-the-shelf QP solver. *Convex* means the objective has a single bottom with no other dips to get stuck in, so a solver that keeps going downhill is guaranteed to land on the one right answer.

Another way to train is gradient descent on the **hinge loss** (used by `SGDClassifier`) or the smoother **squared hinge loss** (the `LinearSVC` default): the loss is zero once an instance is correctly outside the margin on the right side, and grows the further it strays — linearly for hinge, quadratically for squared hinge, which makes squared hinge more sensitive to outliers but often faster to converge on clean data. Figure 5-13 below draws both curves; both classes expose the choice as a `loss` hyperparameter.

Note the shape of that loss: it is flat at zero for every instance that is already safely correct. Just like epsilon-insensitivity in SVM regression, most of your rows contribute nothing, and the fit is decided by the ones near or across the line.

**One-liner for your notes:** training a linear SVM minimizes half the squared norm of w (small w equals wide street, b only slides it) subject to every instance being on its own side; soft margin adds one slack per instance with C as its price, and you solve it either with a QP solver or by gradient descent on the hinge loss.

blocks.title: Worked out: why a smaller w gives a wider street
blocks.content:
Figure 5-12 shows this with a single feature. The edges of the street are the points where the decision function equals $-1$ or $+1$.

- In the left plot the weight $w_1$ is 1, so $w_1 x_1 = -1$ or $+1$ at $x_1 = -1$ and $x_1 = +1$. The margin's size is 2.
- In the right plot the weight is 0.5, so $w_1 x_1 = -1$ or $+1$ at $x_1 = -2$ and $x_1 = +2$. The margin's size is 4.

The smaller weight put the edges further apart, which is why training keeps w as small as possible. Changing the bias b only shifts the street without changing its size.

In Equations 5-1 and 5-2, $t^{(i)}$ is $-1$ for a negative instance ($y^{(i)} = 0$) and $1$ for a positive instance ($y^{(i)} = 1$). So the hard margin constraint $t^{(i)}(\mathbf{w}^\intercal \mathbf{x}^{(i)} + b) \ge 1$ puts every instance off the street on its correct side.

blocks.title: Figure 5-12
blocks.caption: A smaller weight vector results in a larger margin
blocks.alt: Figure 5-12: A smaller weight vector results in a larger margin

blocks.title: Equation 5-1
blocks.caption: Hard margin linear SVM classifier objective
blocks.explain:
**Why the equation looks like this**

Training needs a single number it can push downhill, and "make the street as wide as possible" is
not one. The lesson above supplies the conversion: the street's width is set by the size of w, so
"widen the street" and "shrink w" are the same instruction. Equation 5-1 is that instruction plus the
one thing that stops it cheating — on its own, the smallest possible w is all zeros, which would mean
no decision function at all. The "subject to" line is what keeps the answer honest: every training
instance must still sit off the street, on its own side.

**Is this standard?** Yes. This is the canonical hard margin SVM objective, not a simplification made
for this example. The ½ and the squaring are conveniences rather than modelling choices: any w that
minimises ½ wᵀw also minimises ‖w‖, so the winner is unchanged, but the squared form has a clean
derivative (it is just w) while ‖w‖ has a sharp corner at w = 0 that optimisers handle badly.

**The general form.** Equation 5-2 below is this same objective with one slack variable ζ added per
instance and C in front of their sum — the soft margin version, and the one Scikit-Learn actually
fits. Adding features changes nothing structural: with n features, wᵀw is just w₁² + w₂² + … + wₙ².

**Terms this introduces:** a **norm** (‖w‖) is a measure of a vector's length, here how big the
weights are overall; **wᵀw** is w multiplied by itself column by column and summed, which is that
length squared; a **constraint** is a condition the answer must satisfy, not a cost it can trade away;
**m** is the number of training instances; **convex** means the objective has a single bottom, so a
solver going downhill cannot get stuck anywhere else.

**Every piece of Equation 5-1**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| minimize over w, b | choose w and b | this is training's whole job |
| ½ | one half | a constant kept so the derivative comes out clean |
| wᵀw | w dot w | the squared length of the weight vector |
| subject to | while obeying | what follows binds for every instance, no exceptions |
| t⁽ⁱ⁾ | t for instance i | −1 for a negative instance, +1 for a positive one |
| wᵀx⁽ⁱ⁾ + b | the decision function | instance i's weighted feature sum, plus the bias |
| ≥ 1 | at least one | in other words, off the street and on the correct side |
| i = 1, 2, …, m | for every instance | m is the number of training instances |

**The formula in plain words:** pick the smallest weight vector that still puts every training row at
least one full street-half away from the centerline, on its own side.

**Real numbers, using Figure 5-12 and the card above.** That example has a single feature, so w is
the one number w₁.

1. With w₁ = 1 the street's edges sit where w₁x₁ equals −1 and +1, that is at x₁ = −1 and x₁ = +1, so
the margin's size is 2. The quantity being minimised is ½ × 1 × 1 = 0.5.
2. With w₁ = 0.5 the edges sit at x₁ = −2 and x₁ = +2, so the margin's size is 4. The quantity being
minimised is ½ × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.125.
3. 0.125 is smaller than 0.5, so minimising this expression is literally what picks the wider street.
That comparison is the whole equation in one line of arithmetic.

**And the constraint, checked on one point.** Take the w₁ = 0.5 model with b = 0 and an instance
sitting exactly on the edge at x₁ = 2. Its decision function is 0.5 × 2 = 1, so for a positive
instance (t = +1) the constraint reads 1 ≥ 1: satisfied, and only just. Instances that sit exactly at
that limit are the support vectors.

blocks.title: Equation 5-2
blocks.caption: Soft margin linear SVM classifier objective
blocks.latex: \begin{aligned} &\underset{\mathbf{w},b,\mathbf{\zeta}}{\text{minimize}} && \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{w}^\intercal \mathbf{w} + C \sum_{i=1}^m \zeta^{(i)} \\ &\text{subject to} && t^{(i)} \left( \mathbf{w}^\intercal \mathbf{x}^{(i)} + b \right) \ge 1 - \zeta^{(i)} \quad \text{and} \quad \zeta^{(i)} \ge 0 \quad \text{for } i = 1, 2, \dots, m \end{aligned}

blocks.title: Figure 5-13
blocks.caption: The hinge loss (left) and the squared hinge loss (right)
blocks.alt: Figure 5-13: The hinge loss (left) and the squared hinge loss (right)

items.term: Rewriting a goal into an equivalent, easier goal
items.text: 'Make the street as wide as possible' cannot be handed to a solver; 'make the weight vector as short as possible, subject to these constraints' can. The two are the same instruction because of one geometric fact. Most of applied optimisation is this move — find a quantity that is provably equivalent to what you want and is also differentiable, then minimise that instead. The risk is that the equivalence is only exact under the stated constraints, which is why the 'subject to' line is not decoration.

items.term: Why squared terms keep turning up
items.text: Squaring buys a smooth derivative and a convex problem with a single minimum, which is what makes off-the-shelf solvers reliable. It charges for that in outlier sensitivity, since a distant point contributes the square of its distance. You are seeing both sides in one lesson: the squared norm gives a well-behaved objective, and the squared hinge loss gives faster convergence on clean data and worse behaviour on dirty data.

items.term: Two routes to the same model, and why both exist
items.text: A QP solver solves the constrained problem directly and exactly, but it needs the whole problem at once and scales badly. Gradient descent on the hinge loss only approximates it, but it works one mini-batch at a time — which is exactly the property that made SGDClassifier the only out-of-core option in the class-comparison lesson. The objective is shared; the solver decides what the class can do operationally.
