items: Why does increasing C tend to shrink the margin rather than widen it?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Both the hard and soft margin problems are convex quadratic programs solved by off-the-shelf solvers. What does a QP solver actually do to find the answer?
Look up: Stephen Boyd and Lieven Vandenberghe, 'Convex Optimization' (Cambridge University Press) — the reference this chapter cites for quadratic programming.

items.term: The Kernel Trick: Why It Avoids Computing New Features

blocks.content:
The kernel trick is one sentence with a lot of machinery behind it: if an algorithm only ever touches your data through dot products between pairs of rows, you can swap that dot product for a function that returns what it *would* have been in a much bigger feature space — and skip building that space entirely.

**The question this lesson answers:** the last two lessons kept saying "you get the effect of the extra features without computing them". How is that possible at all, and why does it only work for SVMs written a particular way?

### The big picture

```
primal:  find w and b        ← no dot products exposed
  dual:  find one α per row  ← data appears ONLY as xᵢ·xⱼ
                               so swap that for K(a, b)
```

This is the single hardest idea in the chapter, so it's worth being explicit about *why* it works, not just that it does. The book's own comment after the derivation is "if you are starting to get a headache, that's perfectly normal".

### 1 · Two ways to write the same training problem

The SVM training problem has two equivalent formulations: the **primal** problem (worked with directly in the previous block — weight vector w and bias b) and its **dual** problem. Both reach the same solution, but the dual is written entirely in terms of dot products between pairs of training instances — and that single fact is what makes the kernel trick possible at all. The primal never exposes dot products this way, so the trick cannot attach to it.

A **dot product** of two rows is just multiply-matching-columns-and-add: it is one number saying how aligned two instances are. The dual's variables are one number per training row rather than one per feature, which is also why the book notes the dual is faster to solve when you have fewer instances than features.

### 2 · The substitution, on the book's own example

Suppose you apply some transformation, call it phi, to every training instance before computing that dot product — say, a second-degree polynomial mapping applied to a two-dimensional training set such as the moons dataset. Equation 5-5 below is that mapping: two columns in, three columns out.

For certain transformations, the dot product of two transformed vectors collapses down to a simple, closed-form expression built only from the *original*, untransformed vectors — for the second-degree polynomial case, it is exactly the square of the original dot product. Equation 5-6 below does that collapse line by line.

Put numbers on it. If two instances have an original dot product of 3, then the dot product of their transformed versions is 3 squared, which is 9 — one multiplication, instead of building two three-component vectors and multiplying those out.

A **kernel function**, written K(a, b), is exactly this: it computes what the dot product of the transformed vectors would equal, using only the original vectors a and b, without ever constructing the transformed versions. Equation 5-7 below lists the common ones — linear, polynomial, Gaussian RBF and sigmoid — and you have already used two of them by name.

### 3 · Why the substitution is legitimate

Since the dual problem — and the prediction formula built from it — only ever needs this dot product, never the transformed vectors on their own, substituting K(a, b) everywhere gives exactly the answer you'd get from actually transforming every instance and training a plain linear SVM in that blown-up feature space — without ever paying to build or store it.

**Mercer's theorem** licenses this substitution in general: if K satisfies a short list of mathematical conditions — the book's examples are that K must be continuous, and symmetric so that K(a, b) equals K(b, a) — then some transformation phi is guaranteed to exist with K(a, b) equal to the dot product of phi(a) and phi(b), even when nobody can write phi down explicitly.

The Gaussian RBF kernel is the extreme case: its phi maps into an *infinite*-dimensional space that could never be computed directly, yet K(a, b) evaluates the equivalent dot product in closed form. Which is the real punchline of the previous two lessons — "we never build the columns" is not an optimization there, it is the only option.

Worth knowing as a caveat: some frequently used kernels, the sigmoid among them, do not respect all of Mercer's conditions and are used anyway because they generally work well in practice.

### 4 · Predicting the same way

Predictions follow the same pattern: plugging the dual solution into the decision function replaces every transformed vector with K, so scoring a new instance means comparing it against the stored support vectors through K — never against the full training set, and never through an explicit transformed feature vector. The card below walks that substitution in three steps, and Equations 5-8 and 5-9 below are the result for the score and for the bias term.

That is also why the trained model has to keep its support vectors around: they are not diagnostics, they *are* the model at prediction time.

**One-liner for your notes:** the dual form touches the data only as dot products between pairs of rows, so replacing that dot product with a kernel K gives exactly the model you would have got by expanding the features — Mercer's theorem says a matching phi exists even when it is infinite-dimensional, and prediction only ever compares a new row against the stored support vectors through K.

blocks.title: Worked out: why predictions need only the support vectors
blocks.content:
Equation 5-4 builds the weights from the dual solution: $\hat{\mathbf{w}} = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \hat{\alpha}^{(i)} t^{(i)} \mathbf{x}^{(i)}$. With the kernel trick, each $\mathbf{x}^{(i)}$ becomes $\phi(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})$, so $\hat{\mathbf{w}}$ would have as many dimensions as $\phi(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})$, which may be huge or even infinite, and it cannot be computed.

Equation 5-8 avoids that in three steps:

1. Plug the formula for $\hat{\mathbf{w}}$ into the decision function for the new instance $\mathbf{x}^{(n)}$.
2. The result contains only dot products $\phi(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})^\intercal \phi(\mathbf{x}^{(n)})$, and each one is replaced by $K(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{x}^{(n)})$.
3. The value $\hat{\alpha}^{(i)}$ is nonzero only for support vectors, so every other term is zero and the sum keeps only the support vectors.

The bias $\hat{b}$ in Equation 5-9 uses the same trick, and the $n_s$ in Equations 5-4 and 5-9 is the number of support vectors.

blocks.title: Equation 5-3
blocks.caption: Dual form of the linear SVM objective
blocks.latex_truncated_removed: \underset{\mathbf{\alpha}}{\text{minimize}} \quad \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \sum_{j=1}^{m} \alpha^{(i)} \alpha^{(j)} t^{(i)} t^{(j)} \mathbf{x}^{(i)\top} \mathbf{x}^{(j)} - \sum_{i=1}^{m} \alpha^{(i)} \quad \text{subject to } \alpha^{(i)} \ge 0 \text{ for all } i = 1, 2, \dots, m \text{ and } \sum_{i=1}^{m}

KaTeX would render the incomplete form happily, showing a WRONG constraint. Removing `latex` makes assetPanel fall back to the book's own crop eq-5-3.png -- the renderer's stated rule: a wrong formula is worse than a picture. 17-09-26.
blocks.explain:
**Why the equation looks like this**

The primal problem hunts for w, one number per feature. The dual hunts for α, one number per training
instance. That swap is the whole point. Once the unknowns are attached to instances instead of
features, the instances can only enter the objective by being compared with one another — and the
comparison used is the dot product x⁽ⁱ⁾ᵀx⁽ʲ⁾. Nothing else about this equation matters as much as
that: x appears **only** inside a dot product, and that is the slot the kernel is dropped into.

**Is this standard?** Yes, this is the standard dual form of the linear SVM objective. The book
deliberately does not derive it here and points at the chapter's notebook for the derivation, so it is
meant to be read for its shape rather than reproduced.

**The general form.** Replace every x⁽ⁱ⁾ᵀx⁽ʲ⁾ in this equation with K(x⁽ⁱ⁾, x⁽ʲ⁾) and the same
equation trains a kernelised SVM — polynomial, Gaussian RBF, or any other kernel from Equation 5-7
below — with no other change anywhere. That one substitution is the kernel trick.

**Terms this introduces:** an **instance** is one training row; a **dot product** of two rows
multiplies matching columns and adds the results, giving a single number that says how aligned they
are; **α⁽ⁱ⁾** (alpha i) is the weight the solver gives row i, and it comes out zero for every row
except the support vectors; a **QP solver** is the off-the-shelf optimiser from the previous lesson,
and it is what actually finds α.

**Every piece of Equation 5-3**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| minimize over α | choose the alphas | one number per training instance |
| the double sum | for every pair i and j | every instance weighed against every instance |
| α⁽ⁱ⁾ α⁽ʲ⁾ | alpha i times alpha j | how much this pair is allowed to matter |
| t⁽ⁱ⁾ t⁽ʲ⁾ | t i times t j | +1 when the pair shares a class, −1 when it does not |
| x⁽ⁱ⁾ᵀx⁽ʲ⁾ | x i dot x j | how aligned two instances are — the kernel's slot |
| ½ | one half | the same derivative convenience as Equation 5-1 |
| minus the sum of α | take the alphas back off | pulls the alphas up, against the first term |
| α⁽ⁱ⁾ ≥ 0 | alphas are never negative | a row can push on the answer or not at all |
| m | m | the number of training instances |

**The formula in plain words:** score every pair of training rows by how alike they are and whether
their labels agree, then choose per-row weights that keep that total small without simply setting
every weight to zero.

**Real numbers, in the slot that matters.** Under the second-degree polynomial mapping of Equation 5-5
below, a 2-feature instance turns into a 3-feature one. If two instances have an original dot product
of 3, Equation 5-6 below shows that the dot product of their transformed versions is 3 squared, which
is 9. So wherever this training problem asks for a pair's dot product, you write 9 — one squaring —
instead of building both three-component vectors and multiplying them out. With the Gaussian RBF
kernel the transformed vectors would be infinite-dimensional, so writing the kernel's value straight
into the slot is not a shortcut: it is the only way the equation can be evaluated at all.

**How α turns back into a model.** Equation 5-4 below adds up α⁽ⁱ⁾ t⁽ⁱ⁾ x⁽ⁱ⁾ across the instances to
get the weight vector, and averages t⁽ⁱ⁾ minus its predicted value over the support vectors to get the
bias; nₛ there is the number of support vectors. The card above shows why, once a kernel is involved,
prediction skips the weight vector entirely and goes straight to K.

blocks.caption: From the dual solution to the primal solution

blocks.title: Equation 5-5
blocks.caption: Second-degree polynomial mapping

blocks.title: Equation 5-6
blocks.caption: Kernel trick for a second-degree polynomial mapping
blocks.latex: \begin{aligned} \phi(\mathbf{a})^{\text{T}} \phi(\mathbf{b}) &= \begin{pmatrix} {a_1}^2 \\ \sqrt{2} a_1 a_2 \\ {a_2}^2 \end{pmatrix}^{\text{T}} \begin{pmatrix} {b_1}^2 \\ \sqrt{2} b_1 b_2 \\ {b_2}^2 \end{pmatrix} = {a_1}^2 {b_1}^2 + 2 a_1 b_1 a_2 b_2 + {a_2}^2 {b_2}^2 \\ &= (a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2)^2 = \left( \begin{pmatrix} a_1 \\ a_2 \end{pmatrix}^{\text{T}} \begin{pmatrix} b_1 \\ b_2 \end{pmatrix} \right)^2 = (\mathbf{a}^{\text{T}} \mathbf{b})^2 \end{aligned}

items.term: 'Only dot products' is the entire trick
items.text: Any algorithm that touches its data solely through a pairwise comparison can have that comparison swapped for a different valid one, and it will behave as though it were running in whatever space the new comparison corresponds to. That is why the primal-versus-dual distinction is worth the headache: it is not a mathematical detail, it is the difference between an algorithm the trick can attach to and one it cannot.

items.term: Infinite dimensions is not a figure of speech, and not a problem
items.text: With the Gaussian RBF the transformed space genuinely cannot be written down, and the model is perfectly usable anyway, because the space is never visited. The cost does not vanish, it moves: instead of paying to build columns at training time, you pay to store support vectors and to evaluate K against each of them for every prediction. Deciding which of those costs you can afford is a real design choice.

items.term: The dual is not free
items.text: It trades one unknown per feature for one unknown per training instance, so the problem now grows with rows. That is the same fact, seen from the other side, as the O(m²) to O(m³) training cost of the kernelised class — and it is why the book notes the dual wins specifically when there are fewer instances than features.

items.term: Training and Visualizing a Decision Tree

blocks.content:
A decision tree is a model made of yes/no questions, and the same structure handles classification, regression and even tasks with several outputs at once — so this chapter builds one small enough that you can look at it rather than just trust its score.

**The question this lesson answers:** what is a decision tree for, what will this chapter cover, and how do you get an actual picture of a trained tree instead of only a number?

### The big picture

```
train ─> look at it ─> CART ─> regularize
                            └─> regression ─> limits
```

That left-to-right order is the chapter. Each box assumes the one before it.

### 1 · One structure, three kinds of task

Decision trees are versatile algorithms: the same structure handles **classification** (predict which category a row belongs to), **regression** (predict a number) and even **multi-output** tasks, meaning tasks with several outputs at once.

They are also powerful enough to fit very complex datasets — sometimes too well, which is exactly what happened back in Chapter 2 when a `DecisionTreeRegressor` fit the California housing data perfectly and overfit it in the process. **Overfitting** is learning the training rows so closely that the model stops working on rows it has not seen; it is the failure this chapter keeps coming back to.

Trees also matter beyond themselves: they are the building block inside **random forests**, one of the strongest model families around, covered next chapter. So even if you never ship a single tree, you will ship things made of them.

### 2 · The chapter's arc

| Step | What you get out of it |
|---|---|
| train and visualize | a picture of a tree, and how it predicts |
| the CART algorithm | how the tree was grown in the first place |
| regularization | the settings that stop a tree overfitting |
| regression | the same tree predicting numbers |
| limitations | where one tree stops being enough |

Two things are worth naming right now. The algorithm Scikit-Learn actually uses to grow its trees is **CART**, and unpacking it is the second step above. And a **hyperparameter** is a setting you fix before training that training itself never changes — in your terms, a `--conf` flag passed when you submit the job, not a value the job computes.

### 3 · The running example

The running example fits a `DecisionTreeClassifier` on the iris flowers using only two measurements, petal length and width, capped at a depth of two splits. Two features and two levels is a deliberate choice: the whole tree then fits on one page, so every claim in the next few lessons can be checked by eye.

### 4 · How you actually see a tree

To actually look at the result rather than just trust it, Scikit-Learn's `export_graphviz()` writes a `.dot` file — a plain-text graph description, not an image — which the open-source **Graphviz** package (or its Python wrapper here) can then render, including straight to PDF or PNG from its bundled `dot` command-line tool.

So it is two steps, not one, the same shape as writing a `.sql` file and then running it through a client: the first step only produces text, and a separate tool turns that text into the thing you look at. Figure 6-1 below is what comes out at the end.

**One-liner for your notes:** one tree structure covers classification, regression and multi-output work, and `export_graphviz()` writes a `.dot` text file that Graphviz renders into the picture you read.

blocks.title: Figure 6-1
blocks.caption: Iris decision tree
blocks.alt: Figure 6-1: Iris decision tree

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

iris = load_iris(as_frame=True)
X_iris = iris.data[["petal length (cm)", "petal width (cm)"]].values
y_iris = iris.target

tree_clf = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=2, random_state=42)
tree_clf.fit(X_iris, y_iris)
```

items.term: Why one structure covers three different jobs
items.text: A tree does not model a relationship at all — it partitions the input space into regions and stores one answer per region. That is why swapping classification for regression changes only what is stored in a region, never how regions are found. Any model whose output is 'which bucket does this row fall into' can be made to do any prediction task, and the cost is that it can never express something smooth between buckets.

items.term: Why a model you can look at is worth the detour
items.text: Most of this book's models cannot be inspected by eye, so their failures have to be diagnosed indirectly through metrics. A tree can be printed and read, which makes it the right place to learn what overfitting physically looks like — you can literally see the splits carved around individual points. The lesson transfers to models where you will never get that view.

items.term: Trees matter mostly because of what is built on them
items.text: A single tree is rarely a final answer in production; random forests and gradient boosting are. Both are made of trees, and both inherit the tree's properties — no feature scaling needed, axis-aligned splits, fast prediction. Understanding one tree properly is what makes the next two chapters cheap rather than mysterious.

items.term: How a Tree Actually Makes a Prediction

blocks.content:
Reading a trained tree is a walk, not a calculation: you answer one yes/no question per level until you land on a leaf, and the leaf is the answer.

**The question this lesson answers:** given the trained iris tree, how does a single flower get turned into a predicted class — and what do the numbers printed inside each node actually mean?

### The big picture

```
root: petal length < 2.45 cm ?
  yes -> leaf: setosa (done)
  no  -> petal width < 1.75 cm ?
           yes -> versicolor    no -> virginica
```

Three questions at most, and usually two. Nothing is multiplied, summed or scored along the way.

### 1 · The walk

Every walk begins at the root, depth 0, which asks a single yes/no question about one feature — for the iris tree, whether petal length is under 2.45 cm.

A yes routes you to the root's left child; if that child has no children of its own it is a **leaf**, it asks nothing further, and the class written on it is the answer. A no instead sends you to a **split node** one level down that asks a second question, this time about petal width, and the branch you land on next gives the final class.

The vocabulary is worth pinning down once, because the rest of the chapter uses it constantly:

| Word | Means |
|---|---|
| root | the top node, where every walk starts |
| split node | a node that still asks a question |
| leaf | a node with no children, so it only answers |
| depth | how many questions deep a node sits |

### 2 · The three numbers on every node

Each node on the way carries three numbers worth reading.

- **samples** is how many training rows reached that node at all.
- **value** breaks those rows down by class — a node might apply to 0 setosa, 1 versicolor and 45 virginica rows, for instance.
- **gini** is the **Gini impurity**: it hits exactly 0 when every row at that node shares one class, meaning the node is "pure" and cannot be made any more decisive by a further split.

The impurity of a node is one minus the sum, over every class present, of that class's squared share of the node's rows. Equation 6-1 below is that sentence in symbols, with the walkthrough underneath it, and the card below works it out for the depth-2 left node.

The shape will feel familiar: `samples` is a `COUNT(*)` at that node, `value` is the same count with a `GROUP BY class`, and `gini` is one derived number summarising how mixed that group-by came out. A pure node is a group-by that returned exactly one row.

### 3 · Two branches, always

One structural fact worth knowing: Scikit-Learn's CART only ever builds binary trees, so every question has exactly two branches. Other algorithms such as **ID3** allow a node to fork more than two ways.

This is not a limitation in practice — a three-way choice is just two binary questions stacked — but it does mean tree depth and question count are not the same thing, so a "shallow" tree can still ask a lot of questions in total.

### 4 · Why a tree counts as a white box

A separate but important label: because a tree's reasoning can be read off and checked step by step, it counts as a **white box model**, unlike a random forest or neural net, whose accurate predictions come with no comparably simple account of which input features actually drove a given answer — which is exactly the gap **interpretable ML** tries to close.

The practical version of that: you can hand this tree to someone with no ML background and they can apply it by hand with a ruler. That is a real property, and most stronger models do not have it.

**One-liner for your notes:** prediction is a root-to-leaf walk over binary yes/no questions, each node reports samples, value and gini, and gini = 0 means every row there is one class.

blocks.title: Worked out: Gini impurity of the depth-2 left node
blocks.content:
In the iris tree, 100 training instances have a petal length greater than 2.45 cm (the depth-1 right node), and 54 of those have a petal width smaller than 1.75 cm, so they reach the depth-2 left node. That node's value is 0 setosa, 49 versicolor and 5 virginica. To get its Gini impurity, take each class's share of the 54 rows, square it, and subtract every square from 1:

G = 1 − (0/54)² − (49/54)² − (5/54)²

The squared shares are 0, about 0.823 and about 0.009, so G ≈ 1 − 0 − 0.823 − 0.009 ≈ 0.168. The node is not pure, because a pure node, where every row belongs to one class, has a Gini impurity of exactly 0.

blocks.title: Equation 6-1
blocks.caption: Gini impurity
blocks.explain:
**Why the equation looks like this**

You need one number per node that says "how mixed are the classes here", and it has to be 0 when
every row agrees. Squaring each class's share and adding the squares gives a total that is largest
(exactly 1) when a single class holds everything, and smaller as the rows spread across classes.
Subtracting that total from 1 flips it round, so a pure node scores 0 and a well-mixed node scores
high. Squaring is what makes a dominant class count for much more than a rare one.

**Is this standard?** Yes. This is the canonical definition of Gini impurity, used the same way
everywhere, not a simplification written for the iris example.

**The general form** is already general: the sum runs over however many classes n the node has —
2, 3 or 300. Nothing else changes.

### Piece by piece

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| Gᵢ | G sub i | the Gini impurity of node number i |
| 1 − … | one minus | flips the score so that pure means zero |
| Σ from k=1 to n | sum over k from 1 to n | add one term per class at the node |
| n | n | how many classes exist |
| pᵢ,ₖ | p sub i k | class k's share of node i's rows |
| pᵢ,ₖ squared | p squared | that share multiplied by itself |

### In plain words

impurity = 1 − (share of class 1)² − (share of class 2)² − … one subtraction per class.

### With real numbers

The depth-2 left node of the iris tree holds 54 rows: 0 setosa, 49 versicolor, 5 virginica.

1. shares: 0 ÷ 54 = 0, 49 ÷ 54 ≈ 0.907, 5 ÷ 54 ≈ 0.093
2. squares: 0, about 0.823, about 0.009
3. subtract them all from 1: 1 − 0 − 0.823 − 0.009 ≈ **0.168**

Two sanity checks with the same formula. A node where all rows are one class: that class's share is
1, its square is 1, so G = 1 − 1 = **0** — pure. A node split evenly between two classes: both shares
are 0.5, both squares are 0.25, so G = 1 − 0.25 − 0.25 = **0.5**.

blocks.title: Figure 6-2
blocks.caption: Decision tree decision boundaries
blocks.alt: Figure 6-2: Decision tree decision boundaries

items.term: Why impurity is a squared sum and not just a count
items.text: You could score a node by 'how many rows are in the minority class', and it would also be 0 for a pure node. Squaring the shares instead makes the score respond smoothly as a split shifts a few rows across, which is what lets the growing algorithm compare two near-identical candidate splits and pick one. A score that jumps in whole rows would tie constantly.

items.term: What binary-only actually costs you
items.text: Forcing every question to have two answers looks limiting, but any n-way choice can be built from n−1 binary questions, so nothing becomes inexpressible. What changes is the shape of the tree: a categorical feature with many values gets shredded into a deep chain of yes/no tests rather than one wide fork, which makes the tree deeper and each split's row counts smaller.

items.term: White box is a property you can lose
items.text: A depth-2 tree is readable. The same algorithm with max_depth unset on a large dataset can grow thousands of nodes, and 'you could check the reasoning step by step' stops being true in any useful sense. Interpretability here is a consequence of keeping the tree small, not a guarantee the model type hands you — which is worth knowing before you promise it to anyone.

items: A node has samples=54, value=[0, 49, 5]. Is this node pure? Compute its Gini impurity to check your answer.

items: Gini impurity has a second reading: it is the chance that two rows drawn at random from a node belong to different classes. Can you show that this is the same quantity the formula computes?

items.term: Estimating Class Probabilities

blocks.content:
A trained tree gives you more than a single class guess for free: it can report a probability per class, and it does so by reading counts that were already worked out during training.

**The question this lesson answers:** for a flower with 5 cm long, 1.5 cm wide petals, where do the numbers 0%, 90.7% and 9.3% come from — and why does a visibly different flower get exactly the same three numbers?

### The big picture

| Step | What the tree does |
|---|---|
| walk | the same root-to-leaf walk as a prediction |
| read | the share of that leaf's rows in each class |
| pick | the class with the largest share |

No arithmetic happens at prediction time beyond reading three stored numbers.

### 1 · Nothing is recomputed

To estimate how likely a new instance belongs to class k, the tree runs the same root-to-leaf walk it would for a prediction, lands on one leaf, and reports the fraction of that leaf's training rows that belonged to class k — nothing is recomputed, the answer was already baked in during training.

If you have built a summary table, this is the same trade: the expensive counting happened once when the table was built, and a query is now a lookup. The tree's leaves are the pre-aggregated buckets, and `predict_proba` is the lookup.

### 2 · The worked flower

Take a flower with 5 cm long, 1.5 cm wide petals. It lands on the same leaf that held 54 training flowers split 0 setosa / 49 versicolor / 5 virginica, so the tree reports roughly 0%, 90.7% and 9.3% for the three classes, and picks versicolor as its single answer because that share is the largest.

That is the whole mechanism: 49 out of 54 is 90.7%, 5 out of 54 is 9.3%, 0 out of 54 is 0%. The card below walks the two questions that get the flower to that leaf, and the code card below that shows `predict_proba` returning exactly those three numbers.

### 3 · The part worth sitting with

The detail worth sitting with is what happens elsewhere in that same leaf's region. A flower with 6 cm long, 1.5 cm wide petals — which intuitively feels more clearly virginica — gets exactly the same three probabilities, because it falls in the identical rectangle of petal-length/petal-width space and the tree cannot distinguish positions within one leaf.

A tree's output is a **step function** over its leaves' regions, not a smooth score that keeps refining as an instance moves further from a decision boundary. A step function is one that holds a constant value across a whole region and then jumps at the edge, rather than sliding gradually.

So the probability is flat inside a leaf and jumps at the boundary:

```
prob  ────────┐
              └──────────  (one jump, no slope)
     leaf A      leaf B
```

The consequence in practice: you cannot read a tree's probability as confidence about *this particular* row. It is the historical class mix of a bucket, and every row in the bucket is handed the same answer.

**One-liner for your notes:** a tree's class probabilities are the class shares of the leaf you land in, counted during training, so every instance in one leaf gets identical probabilities no matter where it sits inside that leaf.

blocks.title: Worked out: the walk and the probabilities for a (5, 1.5) flower
blocks.content: The flower's petals are 5 cm long and 1.5 cm wide. The root asks whether petal length is smaller than 2.45 cm; 5 cm is not, so the walk moves to the depth-1 right node. That node asks whether petal width is smaller than 1.75 cm; 1.5 cm is, so the walk ends at the depth-2 left leaf. This leaf holds 54 training flowers: 0 setosa, 49 versicolor and 5 virginica. Dividing each count by 54 gives 0/54 = 0%, 49/54 ≈ 90.7% and 5/54 ≈ 9.3%, and `predict` returns class 1, versicolor, because 90.7% is the largest share. A flower with 6 cm long, 1.5 cm wide petals gives the same two answers (not smaller than 2.45 cm, then smaller than 1.75 cm), so it reaches the same leaf and gets the same probabilities.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
>>> tree_clf.predict_proba([[5, 1.5]]).round(3)
array([[0.   , 0.907, 0.093]])
>>> tree_clf.predict([[5, 1.5]])
array([1])
```

items.term: Why these probabilities are not really confidence
items.text: The number reported is the historical class mix of one bucket, so it says how mixed the training rows in that region were — not how sure the model is about this particular row. A leaf holding 3 rows of one class reports 100%, and a leaf holding 3,000 rows split 2,999 to 1 reports 99.97%. The first is far less trustworthy and the output gives you no hint of that.

items.term: The step function is the whole trade-off
items.text: Flat-inside-a-region is what buys the tree its speed, its readability and its freedom from assumptions about shape. It is also what costs it the ability to say 'this one is further from the boundary, so I am more sure'. Logistic regression gives you that gradient and gives up the readable rules; you cannot have both from one model.

items.term: Where the coarseness actually bites
items.text: Any decision that thresholds a probability — approve above 0.8, review below — inherits the leaf's granularity. With few leaves there are only a few distinct probabilities the model can ever output, so a threshold either catches a whole leaf or none of it. Deeper trees give finer probabilities and overfit more, which is the same tension as everywhere else in this chapter.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Explain why a flower at (6, 1.5) and a flower at (5, 1.5) get identical class probabilities from this tree, even though they clearly are not the same flower.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: A leaf with 3 rows and a leaf with 3,000 rows can both report 100%. How do practitioners make a model's probabilities trustworthy enough to threshold on?
Look up: the "Probability calibration" page in the Scikit-Learn user guide, and its reliability diagrams.

items.term: The CART Algorithm — Greedy, and Why That's Unavoidable

blocks.content:
CART grows a tree by repeatedly picking the single feature and threshold that splits the current rows into the purest pair of groups, and it never looks further ahead than that one step.

**The question this lesson answers:** nobody hand-wrote the iris tree's two questions. What procedure chose "petal length under 2.45 cm" as the first question, and why does it settle for a merely good tree instead of the best one?

### The big picture

```
pick best (feature, threshold) ─> split in two
        ^                              |
        └──── repeat on each half ─────┘
              until a stop rule fires
```

### 1 · The loop

Growing a tree with CART means repeatedly picking one feature k and a threshold tₖ and splitting the current set of rows into two groups on that test.

The pair chosen at each step is whichever one produces the purest pair of subsets once you weight each subset's impurity by how many rows landed in it — that weighted-impurity total is the quantity CART is minimizing at every split. Equation 6-2 below is that sentence written in symbols, with the walkthrough underneath it.

Weighting by size is the part people skip past, so be explicit about it: a tiny very-pure group is worth less than a large fairly-pure group, because the score cares about how many rows actually got tidied up, not how tidy the smallest bin looks.

Having split once, it applies the identical logic to each resulting subset, then to their subsets, recursing until a stop rule fires.

### 2 · When it stops

CART stops recursing when any one of these is true:

- it hits `max_depth`;
- no further split would reduce impurity at all;
- one of several other stopping hyperparameters kicks in — `min_samples_split`, `min_samples_leaf`, `min_weight_fraction_leaf`, `max_leaf_nodes`.

Those are the same knobs the regularization lesson later turns up and down. Here they are only stop signs.

### 3 · Greedy, and why that is unavoidable

Crucially, this is a **greedy** search: it optimizes the split immediately in front of it and never looks ahead to ask whether a worse split now might enable a better tree several levels down. *Greedy* means take the best-looking option at each step and never revisit it.

That is not a shortcut CART's authors were lazy about — finding the genuinely optimal tree is **NP-complete**, meaning the only known way to guarantee optimality takes time that grows exponentially with the number of training rows. A "good enough, found quickly" tree is the realistic target, not the best possible tree.

If you have ever watched a query planner choose a join order, this is the same bargain: the truly optimal plan is unaffordable to search for, so the planner commits to locally sensible choices and ships something that runs.

### 4 · What it costs to predict, and to train

The payoff of that tradeoff shows up at prediction time.

| | Roughly costs | Grows with |
|---|---|---|
| one prediction | log₂(m) node visits | training rows only, very slowly |
| training | n times m times log₂(m) | features and rows together |

Because a CART tree is roughly balanced, classifying one instance means walking through about log₂(m) nodes — a number that grows only very slowly as the training set m grows, and does not depend on how many features exist at all, so predictions stay fast even on huge datasets. **Balanced** here means the leaves sit at roughly the same depth, so no walk is much longer than any other; log₂(m) is the binary logarithm, the number of halvings it takes to get from m rows down to one.

Training is pricier: comparing every feature against every row at every node makes training scale as roughly n features times m rows times log₂(m).

**One-liner for your notes:** CART greedily picks the (feature, threshold) pair with the lowest size-weighted impurity, recurses until a stop rule fires, and buys log₂(m) predictions at the price of n × m × log₂(m) training.

blocks.title: Equation 6-2
blocks.caption: CART cost function for classification
blocks.explain:
**Why the equation looks like this**

A split produces two groups, and you need to compare candidate splits with one number. Simply
averaging the two groups' impurities would be unfair: a 2-row perfectly pure sliver would outvote a
998-row mess. So each side's impurity is multiplied by that side's share of the rows first. The
result is a **weighted average impurity** — the impurity you would expect for a row picked at random
after the split. CART tries every (feature, threshold) pair and keeps whichever makes this number
smallest.

**Is this standard?** Yes. This is the canonical CART cost function for classification, not a
simplification for this chapter.

**The general form.** The shape never changes; only the impurity measure plugged in does:

| Plug in | And you get |
|---|---|
| Gini impurity G | this equation, the default |
| entropy H | the criterion="entropy" variant, next lesson |
| mean squared error | Equation 6-4, the regression tree |

There are exactly two terms because Scikit-Learn's CART only ever builds binary trees.

**One term to pin down:** **impurity** is any number that is 0 when a group is all one class and
grows as the group gets mixed. Gini impurity, from Equation 6-1, is one such number.

### Piece by piece

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| J(k, tₖ) | J of k and t-k | the cost of splitting on feature k at threshold tₖ |
| k | k | which feature the split tests |
| tₖ | t sub k | the threshold value that feature is compared against |
| m | m | how many rows are at this node before the split |
| m_left | m left | how many rows went left |
| m_right | m right | how many rows went right |
| m_left ÷ m | m left over m | the left side's share of the rows, its weight |
| G_left | G left | the left group's Gini impurity |
| G_right | G right | the right group's Gini impurity |

### In plain words

cost = (left's share of the rows × left's impurity) + (right's share × right's impurity).

### With real numbers

Take the iris tree's second split, the one at petal width 1.75 cm. Before it, 100 rows sit at that
node. It sends 54 rows left and the other 46 right.

1. left: 54 rows, impurity 0.168 (worked out under Equation 6-1)
2. right: 46 rows, holding 0 setosa, 1 versicolor and 45 virginica, so its impurity is
1 − 0² − (1÷46)² − (45÷46)² ≈ 0.043
3. weights: 54 ÷ 100 = 0.54 and 46 ÷ 100 = 0.46
4. weighted parts: 0.54 × 0.168 ≈ 0.091 and 0.46 × 0.043 ≈ 0.020
5. add them: J ≈ **0.111**

Compare that with the node before the split, whose own impurity was 0.5: the split cut the expected
impurity from 0.5 to about 0.111, which is why CART kept it.

items.term: Greedy is a cost decision, not a modelling one
items.text: Nothing about trees requires greediness — the greedy search is there purely because the optimal one is intractable. That is a useful category to recognise: an algorithm whose shape is dictated by compute budget rather than by the problem. Query planners, scheduling and compression all have the same structure, and they all share the same failure mode of committing early to a locally sensible choice.

items.term: Where the greedy choice actually goes wrong
items.text: A dataset whose real rule is 'A and B together' can defeat a greedy tree, because neither A nor B alone reduces impurity much, so the first split may be spent on an unrelated feature. The tree will usually still find the pattern eventually, just with more splits and fewer rows per leaf — which is to say, greediness often shows up as extra overfitting rather than as an obvious miss.

items.term: Why training and prediction costs diverge so sharply
items.text: Prediction touches one path through the tree, so it scales with depth. Training touches every feature of every row at every level, so it scales with the whole dataset repeatedly. That asymmetry is why trees stay usable at serving time on hardware that could never retrain them, and it is the same build-once, query-many economics as a precomputed table.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: A tree took one hour to train on one million rows. Using the training complexity given here, roughly how long should ten million rows take, all else equal?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The greedy search is a compromise forced by NP-completeness. Has anything changed — are there now solvers that find provably optimal trees for small problems, and what size can they handle?
Look up: footnote 1 of this chapter for what NP-complete means precisely, then the "Complexity" subsection of the Decision Trees page in the Scikit-Learn user guide.

items.term: Gini Impurity or Entropy?

blocks.content:
Gini impurity is the measure a tree minimizes by default; entropy is the alternative you can switch on, and in practice the choice almost never changes the result.

**The question this lesson answers:** CART needs a number saying how mixed a node is. Gini impurity is one such number — what is the other one, where did it come from, and does picking between them matter?

### The big picture

| | Gini impurity | Entropy |
|---|---|---|
| How to select | the default | criterion="entropy" |
| Hits zero when | the node is all one class | the node is all one class |
| Cost to compute | cheaper | more work per node |
| When they differ | isolates the most common class | slightly more balanced tree |

### 1 · Two measures, one job

Gini impurity is the default measure `DecisionTreeClassifier` minimizes, but setting `criterion="entropy"` swaps in a second option. Both answer the same question — how mixed are the classes at this node — and CART plugs whichever one you chose into the same size-weighted split search from the previous lesson.

### 2 · Where entropy came from

Entropy did not originate in machine learning at all. It started in thermodynamics as a way to measure how disordered a system of molecules is, sitting at zero when everything is still and ordered, and later resurfaced in Shannon's **information theory** as a measure of how much information an average message carries, hitting zero exactly when every message is identical.

The thread running through all three uses is the same: entropy is high when outcomes are spread out and unpredictable, and zero when there is only ever one outcome. A column with one distinct value tells you nothing new per row; a column with many equally likely values tells you a lot.

### 3 · Entropy inside a tree

Carried into a decision tree, a node's entropy is zero under the same condition Gini impurity hits zero under: every row at that node belongs to one class.

Mechanically it is computed as the negative sum, over each class present, of that class's share of the node times the base-2 logarithm of that share. Equation 6-3 below is that sentence in symbols, with the walkthrough underneath it, and the card below works it out for the same depth-2 left node the Gini card used, so you can compare the two numbers on identical data.

Two details that trip people up. The sum skips any class whose share is zero, because the logarithm of zero is undefined — a class that is simply absent contributes nothing. And the minus sign at the front exists because the share is always between 0 and 1, so its base-2 logarithm is always negative; flipping the sign makes the final entropy come out positive.

### 4 · Which one to use

In practice the choice rarely matters — the two measures tend to grow very similar trees, and Gini is cheaper to compute, which is reason enough to leave it as the default.

Where they do diverge, there is a consistent pattern: Gini impurity tends to carve the single most common class off into its own branch by itself, while entropy tends to spread the splits out into a somewhat more balanced tree shape.

Neither pattern is a correctness claim. If two settings give you similar accuracy and one is cheaper, the cheaper one wins until you have a measured reason to prefer the other — which is the same rule you would apply to any job configuration.

**One-liner for your notes:** Gini and entropy both hit zero on a pure node and usually grow near-identical trees, so keep the cheaper Gini default unless you have measured a reason not to.

blocks.title: Worked out: entropy of the depth-2 left node
blocks.content:
The depth-2 left node of the iris tree holds 54 training instances: 0 setosa, 49 versicolor and 5 virginica. The entropy formula only sums over classes whose share is not zero, so setosa (0/54) is skipped. For each remaining class, multiply its share by the base-2 logarithm of that share, add the results, and flip the sign:

H = −(49/54) log₂(49/54) − (5/54) log₂(5/54)

Here log₂(49/54) ≈ −0.140 and log₂(5/54) ≈ −3.433, so the two products are about −0.127 and −0.318. Their sum is about −0.445, and flipping the sign gives an entropy of about 0.445. The entropy is above 0 because the node mixes two classes.

blocks.title: Equation 6-3
blocks.caption: Entropy
blocks.explain:
**Why the equation looks like this**

Entropy asks a different question from Gini impurity: not "how likely are two random rows to
disagree" but "how surprising is the class of an average row here". The base-2 logarithm of a share
is the standard way to turn a probability into an amount of surprise, measured in **bits** — one bit
is the information in a single yes/no answer. A share of 1 (certain) gives log₂(1) = 0 surprise; a
rare class gives a large one. Multiplying each class's surprise by how often that class occurs and
adding gives the average surprise per row.

The leading minus sign is not decoration. Every share sits between 0 and 1, so every log₂ of it is
negative; the minus flips the total back to a positive number. And the sum deliberately skips any
class whose share is 0, because log₂(0) is undefined — a class that simply is not present
contributes nothing.

**Is this standard?** Yes. This is Shannon's entropy, unchanged from information theory, applied to
the class shares at a node. Base 2 is the usual convention; another base only rescales the number.

**The general form** is already general: the sum runs over every class present, for any number of
classes.

### Piece by piece

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| Hᵢ | H sub i | the entropy of node number i |
| − in front | minus | flips a negative total to a positive one |
| Σ with pᵢ,ₖ ≠ 0 | sum over classes with a non-zero share | add one term per class present |
| pᵢ,ₖ | p sub i k | class k's share of node i's rows |
| log₂(pᵢ,ₖ) | log base 2 of p | how many bits of surprise that share is worth |

### In plain words

entropy = minus the sum of (each class's share × the base-2 log of that share), skipping absent
classes.

### With real numbers

The same depth-2 left node: 54 rows, 0 setosa, 49 versicolor, 5 virginica.

1. setosa is 0 ÷ 54 = 0, so it is skipped entirely
2. versicolor: share 49 ÷ 54 ≈ 0.907, log₂ of that ≈ −0.140, product ≈ −0.127
3. virginica: share 5 ÷ 54 ≈ 0.093, log₂ of that ≈ −3.433, product ≈ −0.318
4. add the two products: about −0.445
5. flip the sign: entropy ≈ **0.445**

Sanity check with the same steps: a node split evenly between two classes has both shares at 0.5,
and log₂(0.5) = −1 exactly, so the two products are −0.5 each, summing to −1, and flipping the sign
gives an entropy of exactly **1** — one bit, one yes/no question's worth of uncertainty.

items.term: Why two measures survive when one usually wins
items.text: Gini and entropy agree on the only thing that must be true — zero for a pure node, larger for a mixed one — and differ only in how steeply they penalise middling mixtures. Since the split search compares candidates rather than reading absolute values, two measures with the same ordering mostly produce the same tree. The disagreements are confined to near-ties.

items.term: The difference is a shape preference, not an accuracy claim
items.text: Gini isolating the most frequent class and entropy balancing the tree are statements about tree shape. Neither is defended here as producing better predictions, and the chapter does not claim one does. If you ever choose between them, choose on measured accuracy for your data, not on the aesthetic of the resulting tree.

items.term: What 'cheaper to compute' is actually buying
items.text: The impurity is recomputed for every candidate threshold on every feature at every node, so a per-node cost difference is multiplied by an enormous count. A logarithm per class per candidate is genuinely more expensive than a multiplication. This is the same reason cheap operations inside a hot loop matter far more than their unit cost suggests.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: You need the fastest-to-train tree and don't especially care about the exact shape of the splits. Which impurity criterion do you pick, and why?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The chapter says the two criteria rarely differ. Where exactly do they disagree, and is the difference ever big enough to matter on real data?
Look up: Sebastian Raschka's analysis of Gini impurity versus entropy, which this chapter cites in its footnote 2.

items.term: Regularization Hyperparameters

blocks.content:
Left alone, a tree keeps splitting until it hugs the training rows as closely as it can, so regularizing a tree means capping how far it is allowed to grow.

**The question this lesson answers:** the iris tree was capped at depth 2 by hand. What happens if you do not cap a tree at all, which settings hold it back, and does holding it back actually pay off on data it has never seen?

### The big picture

```
free growth ─────────────────> tightly constrained
 max_depth=None                 max_depth small
 min_samples_leaf=1             min_samples_leaf=5
 fits training rows exactly     generalizes better
```

### 1 · Why a tree overfits so easily

A decision tree makes almost no assumptions about the shape of the data it is given, unlike a linear model, which assumes the relationship is a straight line. That freedom is the whole appeal, and it is also the problem: left alone, a tree will keep splitting until it hugs the training rows as closely as it can — which usually means overfitting them.

### 2 · What "nonparametric" actually means

It gets called a **nonparametric model**, and the label is a bit misleading: it is not that the tree has no parameters, it often has plenty, it is that the count of parameters is not fixed before training starts, so the structure is free to grow however far the data pulls it.

A **parametric** model such as linear regression fixes its parameter count in advance, which caps how far it can bend toward the training data — less overfitting risk, but more underfitting risk if the true pattern needed more flexibility. **Underfitting** is the opposite failure: the model is too rigid to capture the real pattern, so it is wrong on training and new data alike.

| | Parametric (linear model) | Nonparametric (tree) |
|---|---|---|
| Parameter count | fixed before training | grows with the data |
| Main risk | underfitting | overfitting |
| Freedom | capped by the model family | capped only by your settings |

The picture from your world: a fixed-width schema versus a structure that adds a column every time it meets a new value. One cannot express everything; the other will express your noise.

### 3 · The knobs

Reining a tree in during training is **regularization**, and `max_depth` is the blunt instrument for it — `None` by default (unlimited), and shrinking it trades fit for generalization.

Alongside it sit `max_features` (how many features get considered per split), `max_leaf_nodes`, `min_samples_split`, `min_samples_leaf`, and `min_weight_fraction_leaf` (`min_samples_leaf` expressed as a fraction of total weighted rows instead of a raw count).

The rule that saves you memorising six names: **raising any `min_*` or lowering any `max_*` tightens the constraint.** Every one of them is a different way of saying "stop splitting sooner".

### 4 · Pruning: the other route

A different family of algorithms takes the opposite route entirely: grow the tree with no restrictions at all, then prune back any node whose children are all leaves if a statistical test (a chi-squared test is the standard one) says its purity gain could plausibly be chance.

So one family stops early and the other cleans up afterwards. The second has more information to work with — it has already seen what the full tree looks like — at the cost of building something it will partly throw away.

### 5 · Does it pay off? The moons numbers

The moons dataset makes the payoff concrete. One tree trained with no constraints and a second with `min_samples_leaf=5` both fit their training rows, but the second scores better on a held-out test set generated from a different random seed, with an accuracy of 0.92 against 0.898 for the unconstrained tree.

Read that carefully, because it is the whole argument for regularization in one pair of numbers: on the training rows there was nothing to choose between them. The difference only appeared on data neither tree had seen. Figure 6-3 below shows the two decision boundaries side by side — the unconstrained one is visibly carved around individual points.

**One-liner for your notes:** a tree is nonparametric, so its structure grows until you stop it; raise any `min_*` or lower any `max_*` to regularize, and the payoff shows up only on held-out data (0.92 against 0.898).

blocks.caption: Decision boundaries of an unregularized tree (left) and a regularized tree (right)
blocks.alt: Figure 6-3: Decision boundaries of an unregularized tree (left) and a regularized tree (right)

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
>>> X_moons_test, y_moons_test = make_moons(n_samples=1000, noise=0.2,
...                                         random_state=43)
...
>>> tree_clf1.score(X_moons_test, y_moons_test)
0.898
>>> tree_clf2.score(X_moons_test, y_moons_test)
0.92
```

items.term: Nonparametric is about capacity, not parameter count
items.text: The useful reading of the word is: does the model's capacity to fit grow with the data it is given? A linear model's capacity is fixed the moment you choose it, so more rows make it more reliable. A tree's capacity grows with the rows, so more data does not automatically protect it — that protection has to come from the regularization settings instead.

items.term: Early stopping and pruning solve the same problem from opposite ends
items.text: Stopping early is cheap but blind: you refuse a split without knowing what it would have led to. Pruning is expensive but informed: it grows everything, then removes what a statistical test cannot justify. The general lesson is that a decision made with more information costs more to reach, and whether that is worth paying depends on how expensive the wasted work is.

items.term: Why 0.92 against 0.898 is the only honest evidence here
items.text: Both trees fit their training rows, so training accuracy could not separate them at all. The whole case for regularization rests on a score from rows generated with a different random seed. Any claim that a model 'fits well' that does not cite held-out data is not evidence — this pair of numbers is the smallest complete demonstration of why.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Between max_leaf_nodes and min_samples_leaf, which would you raise and which would you lower to make a tree LESS likely to overfit?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The pruning approach described here is an alternative algorithm, but Scikit-Learn does ship a pruning option of its own. What is it, and how does choosing its strength differ from tuning max_depth?
Look up: the "Minimal Cost-Complexity Pruning" subsection of the Decision Trees page in the Scikit-Learn user guide, and the ccp_alpha parameter on DecisionTreeClassifier.

items.term: Regression Trees

blocks.content:
Swap `DecisionTreeClassifier` for `DecisionTreeRegressor` and almost nothing changes: the same walk, the same growing procedure, and only one real difference — a leaf now holds a number instead of a class.

**The question this lesson answers:** a tree ends at a leaf that says "versicolor". What does it say instead when the thing you want predicted is a price, a count or a measurement?

### The big picture

| | Classification tree | Regression tree |
|---|---|---|
| A leaf holds | a class label | the mean target of its rows |
| A split minimizes | weighted Gini impurity | weighted MSE |
| The walk | root to leaf | identical |

### 1 · The only real change

Swap `DecisionTreeClassifier` for `DecisionTreeRegressor` and CART still grows the same kind of tree, walking the same way from root to leaf — the only real change is what sits at each leaf. Instead of a class label, a leaf now holds a plain numeric prediction: the average of the target values among the training rows that landed there.

The **target** is the column you are trying to predict, the answer column. In a classification tree it held a category; here it holds a number, and a leaf's prediction is simply its average.

### 2 · One walk, worked out

Fitted on a noisy quadratic dataset capped at `max_depth=2`, a new row with x1 = 0.2 might travel root (is x1 under 0.197? no) to a right child (is x1 under 0.772? yes) down to a leaf that predicts 0.111 — simply the mean target of the 110 training rows that ended up in that leaf, with a mean squared error of 0.015 across them.

Read the two tests slowly, because they are the whole mechanism: 0.2 is not under 0.197, so go right; 0.2 is under 0.772, so go left from there; done, and the answer is whatever that leaf averaged. Figure 6-4 below is this tree drawn out.

**Mean squared error (MSE)** is the average of the squared gaps between each row's real target and the value being predicted for it. Here, 0.015 is how far the leaf's 110 rows sit from 0.111 on average, in squared units — a measure of how tight the bucket is, not of how wrong the tree is.

Nothing here is smarter than a `GROUP BY` producing an `AVG`. What the tree contributes is choosing the grouping itself.

### 3 · The split rule changes to match

The split-choosing rule changes to match. Instead of minimizing weighted Gini impurity, CART now minimizes weighted MSE: for each candidate split it weighs the left and right subset's mean squared error by how many rows fall into each subset, and picks whichever split gets that combined number lowest. Equation 6-4 below is that sentence in symbols, with the walkthrough underneath it.

Practically, this pushes the algorithm to carve up the input space into regions where the rows are as close as possible to that region's own average target value. That is the same idea as impurity, restated for numbers: a "pure" region is no longer one where every row shares a class, but one where every row sits near the same value.

### 4 · Overfitting is just as real here

Overfitting is just as real a risk here as in classification — an unconstrained regression tree can produce a wildly jagged prediction curve that tracks noise rather than signal, and a modest constraint like `min_samples_leaf=10` is often enough to pull it back to something reasonable.

The jaggedness has a clear cause. Every leaf is a flat step, so with enough leaves a tree can put a step under almost every individual point, and the prediction curve turns into a staircase that follows the noise. Figure 6-5 below shows a depth-2 and a depth-3 version; Figure 6-6 shows unconstrained against `min_samples_leaf=10`.

**One-liner for your notes:** a regression tree is the same tree with numbers in its leaves — each leaf predicts its rows' mean target, and CART picks splits by minimizing size-weighted MSE instead of Gini impurity.

blocks.title: Equation 6-4
blocks.caption: CART cost function for regression
blocks.explain:
**Why the equation looks like this**

The top line is Equation 6-2 with one word swapped. The reasoning is identical: a split makes two
groups, each group's score is weighted by its share of the rows so a tiny group cannot outvote a
large one, and CART keeps whichever (feature, threshold) pair makes the total smallest. Only the
measure of "bad" changes, because the target is now a number, and "mixed classes" no longer means
anything.

The two definitions underneath it are the ones doing the real work:

- **ŷ_node** is the leaf's prediction, defined as the plain average of the target values of the rows
at that node.
- **MSE_node** is how far those rows sit from that average, squared and then averaged.

**Why the average, and not the median or anything else?** Because once you have decided to score by
squared error, the mean is the single constant that makes that score smallest — no other number you
could put in the leaf would give a lower MSE for those rows. The prediction rule and the cost
function are not two separate choices; the second one forces the first.

**Is this standard?** Yes. This is the canonical CART cost function for regression.

**The general form.** The weighted-average shape is shared with Equation 6-2 and does not change;
swapping the inner measure is what turns a classification tree into a regression tree.

### Piece by piece

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| J(k, tₖ) | J of k and t-k | the cost of splitting on feature k at threshold tₖ |
| m_left ÷ m | m left over m | the left group's share of the rows, its weight |
| MSE_left | M S E left | the left group's mean squared error |
| MSE_right | M S E right | the right group's mean squared error |
| ŷ_node | y hat node | the value this node predicts, its rows' average target |
| y⁽ⁱ⁾ | y superscript i | the real target value of training row i |
| Σ over i in node | sum over the rows in this node | add one term per row that landed here |
| m_node | m node | how many rows landed at this node |

### In plain words

- the leaf's prediction = add up the target values of its rows, divide by how many rows;
- the leaf's MSE = for each row, take (prediction − its real value), square it, then average those
squares;
- the split's cost = left's share × left's MSE + right's share × right's MSE.

### With real numbers

The regression tree's leaf reached by x1 = 0.2 holds 110 training rows.

1. add those 110 target values and divide by 110: the average is **0.111** — that is what the leaf
predicts for anything landing there
2. for each of the 110 rows take 0.111 minus its real target, square it, and average the 110 squares:
the result is a mean squared error of **0.015**

The split-level number J cannot be worked out here, because only this one leaf's count and MSE are
given — the sibling's are not. The shape is the same weighted sum as Equation 6-2 above: each side's
MSE multiplied by its share of the rows, added together.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

np.random.seed(42)
X_quad = np.random.rand(200, 1) - 0.5 # a single random input feature
y_quad = X_quad ** 2 + 0.025 * np.random.randn(200, 1)

tree_reg = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=2, random_state=42)
tree_reg.fit(X_quad, y_quad)
```

items.term: A regression tree is a step function, and that is a real limit
items.text: Because each leaf emits one constant, the prediction surface is flat slabs with jumps between them — it cannot slope, and it cannot extrapolate beyond the range of the training targets at all. Feed it an input far outside anything it was trained on and it will confidently return the average of whichever edge leaf it lands in. A linear model would at least keep sloping.

items.term: Why MSE and Gini impurity are the same idea
items.text: Both measure 'how much do the rows at this node disagree with the single answer we would give them'. For classes, disagreement means belonging to different classes; for numbers, it means sitting far from the mean. Recognising them as one idea is what makes the regression tree feel like the same algorithm rather than a second one to memorise.

items.term: Squared error is a choice with consequences
items.text: Squaring makes a leaf's prediction the mean, and the mean is pulled hard by extreme targets. A single wild target value can therefore move a whole leaf's prediction and change which split looked best. Scikit-Learn does offer absolute-error criteria for exactly this reason; the trade-off is the same one RMSE and MAE had back in Chapter 2.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: A regression tree leaf has 110 training rows with target values averaging 0.111. What value will this leaf predict for every new instance that lands there?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: A regression tree's leaf predicts a mean, which extreme target values pull hard. What does the tree do differently if you ask it to minimise absolute error instead, and when is that worth it?
Look up: the criterion parameter on sklearn.tree.DecisionTreeRegressor in the Scikit-Learn API reference, and compare it with this book's Chapter 2 discussion of RMSE versus MAE.

items.term: Sensitivity to Axis Orientation

blocks.content:
Every question a tree can ask is "is this one feature above or below a threshold", so every boundary it can draw is a straight cut square to one axis — and that makes the tree sensitive to how the data happens to be oriented.

**The question this lesson answers:** the iris classes separate neatly along petal length and width. What happens to the same tree when the same data is rotated 45 degrees, and what can you do about it?

### The big picture

```
boundary along an axis      boundary on a diagonal
   one clean cut              a staircase of steps
   generalizes well           fits, but fragile
```

### 1 · Why the boundary is always a staircase

A decision tree's splits are always perpendicular to one feature axis — every question is "is this one feature above or below some threshold" — which makes the tree's decision boundary look like a staircase of straight horizontal and vertical cuts.

That falls straight out of the question format. A single test names one column and one number, so the region it carves out has to be bounded by lines where that column equals that number. There is no way to express "petal length plus petal width is above 4" as one test.

### 2 · Rotate the data and the job gets harder

That is fine when the classes really do separate along the feature axes, but rotate a perfectly linearly-separable dataset by 45 degrees and the same tree, given the rotated version, has to approximate that single diagonal line with a large number of small orthogonal steps. **Linearly separable** means a single straight line can put every class on the correct side of it.

Both the original tree and the rotated one can still fit their own training rows exactly, but the rotated tree's jagged approximation is far less likely to generalize well to new points near that diagonal. Figure 6-7 below is the two side by side.

That gap is the point worth carrying away: "fits the training set perfectly" was true for both, and it told you nothing about which one to ship.

### 3 · The countermeasure

One practical countermeasure is to scale the features and then rotate the whole dataset with a **principal component analysis** transform (covered properly in Chapter 8) before handing it to the tree. PCA is a procedure that finds new axes lined up with the directions the data actually varies in, and re-expresses every row against those axes.

PCA's rotation reduces the correlation between features, and a tree often finds that easier to carve up with its axis-aligned splits, precisely because the rotation can line up the real separating direction with one of the transformed axes. Two features are **correlated** when knowing one tells you something about the other; a diagonal cloud of points is exactly what correlation looks like on a plot.

### 4 · The iris demonstration

Running the iris features through a `StandardScaler`-then-PCA pipeline before fitting a `DecisionTreeClassifier` demonstrates exactly this: the resulting tree manages to separate the classes well using essentially one derived feature, itself just a linear combination of the original petal length and width, where a comparable un-rotated tree needed both features and multiple splits to do the same job. Figure 6-8 below shows that tree's boundaries.

A **derived feature** here is a new column computed from the old ones — in your terms, a `SELECT` expression rather than a stored column. The tree never sees petal length and width again; it sees one blended column that happens to point along the direction the classes actually separate in.

**One-liner for your notes:** every tree split is perpendicular to one axis, so a diagonal boundary becomes a fragile staircase — scaling then rotating with PCA can line the real separating direction up with an axis and fix it.
