items.term: Histogram-Based Gradient Boosting

blocks.content:
Histogram-based gradient boosting bins every feature into at most 255 integers first, which makes training on large data hundreds of times faster.

**The question this lesson answers:** ordinary gradient boosting has to find the best split threshold for every feature at every node. On a large table that is unaffordable — what does scikit-learn change to make it affordable?

### The big picture

| | Regular GBRT | Histogram-based (HGB) |
|---|---|---|
| Feature values | raw floats, re-sorted | binned integers, up to 255 |
| Cost grows with | features x rows x log rows | bins x rows |
| Categorical and missing | need preprocessing | supported natively |

### 1 · Why the plain version does not scale

Regular GBRT scales poorly to very large datasets because finding the best split threshold for every feature at every node is expensive, with cost growing roughly with the number of features times the number of instances times the log of the number of instances.

That log factor is the sort. To find the best threshold on a column you have to put its values in order, and a tree does this again and again at every node.

### 2 · What binning changes

Scikit-Learn's histogram-based gradient boosting (HGB) sidesteps this by binning every input feature into integers up front — the max_bins hyperparameter caps this at 255 bins by default and cannot go higher.

**Binning** replaces each value with the number of the bucket it falls in, so a continuous column of prices becomes an integer from 0 to 254. This is the same move as bucketing a column before a join or an aggregation: you give up exact values and get a small, fixed set of possibilities instead.

Binned integer features remove the need to re-sort by feature value at every split, and integer-based data structures are both faster and more memory-efficient than working with raw floats, bringing the overall cost down to roughly the number of bins times the number of instances.

Notice what disappeared from the cost: the number of features no longer multiplies in through a sort, and the log is gone. In practice HGB can train hundreds of times faster than standard GBRT on large data.

### 3 · What binning costs

The trade-off is a bit of precision loss from binning, which acts like a mild regularizer — sometimes reducing overfitting, sometimes nudging the model toward underfitting depending on the dataset.

**Underfitting** is the opposite failure to overfitting: the model is too blunt to capture the real pattern, so it is mediocre on training and test data alike. Binning can push either way, and which one you get is a property of the dataset, not something you can reason out in advance.

### 4 · How the HGB classes differ

HistGradientBoostingRegressor and HistGradientBoostingClassifier mirror the ordinary GBRT classes with a handful of differences:

| Difference | Detail |
|---|---|
| early stopping | automatic above 10,000 instances |
| subsampling | not supported |
| n_estimators | renamed max_iter |
| tree knobs | only max_leaf_nodes, min_samples_leaf, max_depth |

Early stopping switches on automatically once you have more than 10,000 instances (though you can force it on or off), subsampling isn't supported, n_estimators is renamed max_iter, and only three tree hyperparameters remain tunable (max_leaf_nodes, min_samples_leaf, max_depth).

### 5 · The preprocessing it lets you delete

HGB also natively supports categorical features and missing values, provided categorical columns are pre-encoded as integers below max_bins (an OrdinalEncoder handles this) and their column indices are passed via categorical_features — which means an entire preprocessing pipeline for a mixed numeric/categorical dataset can skip imputers, scalers, and one-hot encoding altogether.

An **imputer** fills in missing values, a **scaler** puts numeric columns on a comparable range, and **one-hot encoding** turns one categorical column into one binary column per category. HGB needs none of the three. The pipeline in the code card below is the whole preprocessing step for the California housing data, and the book reports it reaching an RMSE of about 47,600 with no hyperparameter tuning at all.

**One-liner for your notes:** HGB bins every feature into at most 255 integers so splits stop needing a sort, trading a little precision for hundreds-of-times faster training on large data, plus native categorical and missing-value support that deletes most of the preprocessing pipeline.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.compose import make_column_transformer
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.preprocessing import OrdinalEncoder

hgb_reg = make_pipeline(
    make_column_transformer((OrdinalEncoder(), ["ocean_proximity"]),
                            remainder="passthrough"),
    HistGradientBoostingRegressor(categorical_features=[0], random_state=42)
)
hgb_reg.fit(housing, housing_labels)
```

items.term: Why binning is a regulariser and not only a speed trick
items.text: Collapsing values into at most 255 buckets removes the model's ability to split between two nearly identical values, and splits that fine are usually fitting noise. The same change therefore buys speed and often generalisation — but where small differences are real, it costs accuracy. One mechanism, opposite outcomes.

items.term: Why native categorical support matters beyond convenience
items.text: One-hot encoding a high-cardinality column hands a tree many nearly-empty binary columns, each a weak split candidate, which fragments the data and hurts the model as well as the runtime. Treating the column as integer categories lets a single node consider groupings directly.

items.term: Why the complexity change is the whole story
items.text: Going from a cost that grows with features times rows times log rows to one that grows with bins times rows removes both the sort and the per-feature multiplier. That is the difference between a method that stalls as a table grows and one that scales roughly in line with it; the large speedup is a consequence, not a separate optimisation.

items.term: Stacking: Learning the Aggregation Itself

blocks.content:
Every ensemble so far combined its members with a rule you chose in advance; stacking trains a model to learn that combination instead.

**The question this lesson answers:** why should a majority vote — or an average of probabilities — be the right way to merge three models? Could you not just train something to work out the merge?

### The big picture

```
base 1 ─> 3.1 ─┐
base 2 ─> 2.7 ─┼─> blender (a trained model) ─> 3.0
base 3 ─> 2.9 ─┘
```

Figure 7-11 below is that picture with the book's own numbers.

### 1 · Replace the rule with a model

Every ensemble method covered so far combines predictions with a fixed, hand-picked rule — majority vote, averaged probability, or a weighted vote.

Stacking (short for stacked generalization) replaces that fixed rule with a trained model: instead of deciding in advance how to aggregate, you train a final model — called a blender or meta learner — whose job is to take the base predictors' outputs as its own input features and learn the best way to combine them into a final prediction.

The blender is an ordinary model. What is unusual is only its input table: one column per base predictor, holding that predictor's output, with the original target as the answer column.

### 2 · Building the blender's training set

Building the blender's training set takes a specific two-step shape.

First, use cross_val_predict() to get out-of-sample predictions from every base predictor for every instance in the original training set — this matters because feeding the blender predictions a base model already saw during its own training would let it cheat.

**Out-of-sample** means the prediction for a row came from a copy of the model that was fitted without that row. A model recites rows it has seen, so its training-set predictions look far better than its real ones; a blender trained on those would learn to trust an accuracy that does not exist. Figure 7-12 below is this construction step.

Those out-of-sample predictions become the blender's input features (one column per base predictor, regardless of how many features the original data had), paired with the original targets.

| The blender's training set | |
|---|---|
| rows | one per original training instance |
| columns | one per base predictor |
| answer column | the original target, copied across |

So three base predictors on data with twenty original features still gives the blender a three-column table.

### 3 · Finishing the job

Once the blender itself is trained on this constructed dataset, every base predictor is retrained one final time, now on the full original training set.

The retraining is easy to miss and worth holding onto: the copies used to build the blender's inputs were each fitted on part of the data only, so the shipped base predictors are fresh ones fitted on everything.

It's possible to stack several blenders into layers — one trained via linear regression, another via random forest regression, then a further blender combining those — squeezing out a little more accuracy at a real cost in training time and complexity. Figure 7-13 below shows that multilayer shape.

### 4 · What it scores

Scikit-Learn provides StackingClassifier and StackingRegressor for this directly; applied to the same moons-dataset ensemble used for voting, a StackingClassifier reaches 92.8% test accuracy, edging out the 92% that soft voting achieved with the same three base predictors.

| Combination method | Test accuracy |
|---|---|
| hard voting | 91.2% |
| soft voting | 92% |
| stacking | 92.8% |

Each step up the table replaces a cruder combination rule with a better-informed one, and each costs more to train. That is the whole chapter in three rows.

**One-liner for your notes:** stacking trains a blender on the base predictors' out-of-sample predictions — one input column per base predictor — then retrains the bases on all the data, and on the book's moons example it reaches 92.8% against soft voting's 92%.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.ensemble import StackingClassifier

stacking_clf = StackingClassifier(
    estimators=[
        ('lr', LogisticRegression(random_state=42)),
        ('rf', RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42)),
        ('svc', SVC(probability=True, random_state=42))
    ],
    final_estimator=RandomForestClassifier(random_state=43),
    cv=5 # number of cross-validation folds
)
stacking_clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
```

items.term: Why a learned combination can beat a fixed one
items.text: A vote assumes every member is equally worth listening to, everywhere. A blender can learn that one member is reliable in one region of the input space and another elsewhere, and can even use disagreement between members as a signal. That is strictly more expressive than any rule fixed in advance.

items.term: Why leakage is the entire difficulty of stacking
items.text: A model's predictions on rows it trained on look unrealistically good, so a blender trained on those learns a level of trust that will not hold in production, and the finished ensemble is confidently worse than the honest version. The whole cross-validated construction exists to prevent that one failure.

items.term: Why extra layers rarely pay
items.text: Each further blender layer trains on the outputs of the layer below, so the information it sees is already a compressed summary: gains shrink quickly while training cost and the number of ways to leak both grow. The chapter's own numbers make the argument — 92% to 92.8% for a substantially more complicated system.

blocks.title: 9 book exercises
items: Exercise 1: If you have trained five different models on the exact same training data, and they all achieve 95% precision, is there any chance that you can combine these models to get better results? If so, how? If not, why?
Exercise 2: What is the difference between hard and soft voting classifiers?

Exercise 3: Is it possible to speed up training of a bagging ensemble by distributing it across multiple servers? What about pasting ensembles, boosting ensembles, random forests, or stacking ensembles?
Exercise 4: What is the benefit of out-of-bag evaluation?
Exercise 5: What makes extra-trees ensembles more random than regular random forests? How can this extra randomness help? Are extra-trees classifiers slower or faster than regular random forests?
Exercise 6: If your AdaBoost ensemble underfits the training data, which hyperparameters should you tweak, and how?
Exercise 7: If your gradient boosting ensemble overfits the training set, should you increase or decrease the learning rate?

Exercise 8: Load the MNIST dataset (introduced in Chapter 3), and split it into a training set, a validation set, and a test set (e.g., use 50,000 instances for training, 10,000 for validation, and 10,000 for testing). Then train various classifiers, such as a random forest classifier, an extra-trees classifier, and an SVM classifier. Next, try to combine them into an ensemble that outperforms each individual classifier on the validation set, using soft or hard voting. Once you have found one, try it on the test set. How much better does it perform compared to the individual classifiers?

Exercise 9: Run the individual classifiers from the previous exercise to make predictions on the validation set, and create a new training set with the resulting predictions: each training instance is a vector containing the set of predictions from all your classifiers for an image, and the target is the image's class. Train a classifier on this new training set. Congratulations—you have just trained a blender, and together with the classifiers it forms a stacking ensemble! Now evaluate the ensemble on the test set. For each image in the test set, make predictions with all your classifiers, then feed the predictions to the blender to get the ensemble's predictions. How does it compare to the voting classifier you trained earlier? Now try again using a StackingClassifier instead. Do you get better performance? If so, why?

items.term: The Curse of Dimensionality

blocks.content:
More features is not automatically more information: past a point, extra columns make training slower, make a good solution harder to find, and push every instance far away from every other one.

**The question this lesson answers:** a dataset arrives with hundreds or thousands of features per instance. What exactly goes wrong at that scale, and when is it worth throwing some of those features away?

### The big picture

```
more dimensions
 -> more empty room
 -> points end up far apart (sparse)
 -> a new point is far from every training row
 -> predictions become large extrapolations
 -> overfitting risk goes up
```

### 1 · Two problems wearing one name

Many machine learning datasets carry hundreds or thousands of features per instance, and that scale creates two separate problems the book calls the **curse of dimensionality**: training gets much slower, and it becomes genuinely harder for an algorithm to find a good solution at all. Keep them apart in your head — the first is a compute bill, the second is a quality problem, and only the second is interesting.

A **feature** is one input column; an **instance** is one row. So "1,000 dimensions" just means a table 1,000 columns wide, one row per record.

The saving grace is that real datasets rarely use their dimensions fully. In MNIST, the pixels near the image border are almost always blank and carry almost no signal, and neighboring pixels are so correlated that averaging pairs of them loses very little — both are candidates for dropping or merging. **Correlated** means two columns move together, so knowing one already tells you most of the other.

If you have ever looked at a 200-column table and found that forty columns are constant and another forty are near-copies of each other, you have already met this. The lake is wide; the information in it is not.

### 2 · Cutting dimensions is not free

Cutting dimensions is not free. It behaves like compressing a photo to JPEG: you save space and speed, but you throw away some information, and the resulting model can occasionally perform a touch worse.

So the book's advice is to try the full, unreduced data first and only reach for dimensionality reduction if training speed or storage genuinely demands it — reduction sometimes filters out noise and *helps* accuracy, but that is the exception rather than the rule.

A second, independent payoff is visualization: squeezing a dataset down to two or three dimensions lets you plot it and spot clusters or patterns by eye, which matters for communicating results to people who are not data scientists.

### 3 · The numbers that break your intuition

Human intuition, tuned for three dimensions, breaks down badly at scale. In a unit square, a random point has under a 1% chance of landing within 0.001 of an edge — the book's exact figure is about 0.4%; in a 10,000-dimensional unit hypercube, that same near-edge probability exceeds 99.999999%, so almost everything ends up near a border.

A **unit hypercube** is just the box where every coordinate runs from 0 to 1, in however many dimensions you like. Figure 8-1 below shows the first few: point, segment, square, cube, tesseract.

Distances get stranger too. Two random points in a unit square sit about 0.52 apart on average, in a 3D unit cube about 0.66, but in a million-dimensional unit hypercube the average jumps to roughly 408.

| Space | Measured | Value |
|---|---|---|
| unit square | chance of being within 0.001 of a border | about 0.4% |
| 10,000-D cube | same chance | over 99.999999% |
| unit square | average gap between two random points | about 0.52 |
| 3D unit cube | same | about 0.66 |
| 1,000,000-D | same | roughly 408 |

The card below works the 408 out: it is the square root of 1,000,000 divided by 6.

### 4 · Why that makes models worse

The practical fallout is that high-dimensional data is extremely **sparse** — instances sit far from each other and from any new point you want to predict on, forcing predictions to rely on large extrapolations and pushing up the risk of overfitting. **Extrapolation** means answering about a region where you have no nearby examples, as opposed to interpolating between two you do have.

Throwing more data at the problem does not scale either: the number of instances needed to hold a fixed density grows exponentially with the dimension count, to the point that even a mere 100 features could demand more training examples than there are atoms in the observable universe.

That last sentence is the one to remember. "Just collect more rows" is the standard data-engineering answer to a thin table, and here it is arithmetically unavailable.

**One-liner for your notes:** in high dimensions everything is near a border and far from everything else, so models extrapolate and overfit — and you cannot buy your way out with more rows, because the requirement grows exponentially.

blocks.title: Worked out: the high-dimension numbers
blocks.content: The book gives the figures behind these claims. In a unit square, a random point has only about a 0.4% chance of lying less than 0.001 from a border; in a 10,000-dimensional unit hypercube, that chance is greater than 99.999999%. For two random points, the average distance is roughly 0.52 in a unit square and roughly 0.66 in a 3D unit cube. For a 1,000,000-dimensional unit hypercube, the book approximates the average distance as √(1,000,000 / 6). Dividing 1,000,000 by 6 gives about 166,666.7, and the square root of that is about 408.25, which is the lesson's "roughly 408". The atoms-in-the-universe claim assumes 100 features that range from 0 to 1, spread out uniformly, with training instances within 0.1 of each other on average.

items.term: Two costs, two different fixes
items.text: Slow training and "hard to find a good solution" get bundled under one name, but they answer to different remedies. Slow training is a compute bill: more cores, fewer rows, a cheaper model all help. The second is about the data being too thin for its own width, and no hardware touches it at all — only fewer dimensions or more rows do, and the lesson shows that more rows is priced out of reach. Worth separating before you propose a fix, because one of them has a purchasing solution and the other does not.

items.term: Why sparsity hurts some models more than others
items.text: Anything that reasons from "what did similar rows do" — nearest neighbours, distance-based clustering, anything with a radius in it — leans directly on distances, and the lesson's numbers say distances stop being informative once everything is roughly equally far from everything. Models that split one feature at a time, or fit one global rule, degrade differently and often more gently. The book does not rank algorithms here; the point to carry is that the curse is not one uniform penalty applied equally to every method.

items.term: The exponential wall is not a budget problem
items.text: A requirement that grows exponentially does not yield to a bigger cluster or another year of collection: each added dimension multiplies what you need rather than adding to it. That is why the book reaches for "more atoms than the observable universe" instead of quoting a large number — the point is that no quantity is reachable. When a cost curve looks like this, the signal is to change the shape of the problem, not to scale the attempt.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The lesson says MNIST's border pixels carry almost no signal. How was that actually measured rather than assumed, and could you run the same measurement on one of your own wide tables?
Look up: Figure 7-6 in chapter 7 of this book — MNIST pixel importance according to a random forest classifier — which is the measurement that claim rests on.

items.term: Two Approaches to Dimensionality Reduction: Projection and Manifold Learning

blocks.content:
There are two ways to cut dimensions: flatten the data onto a lower-dimensional surface it already sits near (projection), or model the curved surface it actually sits on and unroll it (manifold learning).

**The question this lesson answers:** real data does not fill its columns evenly, so it lives inside a smaller space than its column count suggests. How do you get it down into that smaller space — and what do you do when the smaller space is bent rather than flat?

### The big picture

| Approach | Assumes the data sits | Swiss roll result |
|---|---|---|
| Projection | near a flat subspace | layers squashed together |
| Manifold learning | near a bent surface | unrolled |

### 1 · Projection: drop a perpendicular

Real datasets almost never spread their instances evenly across every dimension. Many features barely vary at all, and others move together, so the actual data tends to sit inside — or very near — a much smaller **subspace** of the full feature space. A subspace here means a flat slice: a line inside a plane, a plane inside a 3D space.

**Projection** exploits this directly: given a 3D dataset whose points cluster close to a tilted plane, you can drop a perpendicular line from each point onto that plane and read off two new coordinates, effectively turning a 3D dataset into a 2D one while keeping almost all of the structure.

Figures 8-2 and 8-3 below are the before and after. Note what the two new columns are: not two of the original three, but two *new* coordinates measured on the plane. Reduction almost never means "keep some columns and delete the rest" — it means deriving fewer, better columns out of all of them.

### 2 · Where projection breaks

Projection breaks down, though, when the low-dimensional subspace isn't flat — when it twists through the higher-dimensional space instead. The classic case is the Swiss roll (Figure 8-4 below): it genuinely lives on a 2D surface, but that surface is rolled up in 3D.

Flattening it by simply dropping one coordinate crushes different rolled-up layers on top of each other, destroying the very structure you wanted to keep. Figure 8-5 below puts the two side by side: squashed on the left, unrolled on the right. What you actually want is to unroll it.

### 3 · Manifold learning

This is where **manifold learning** comes in. A d-dimensional manifold is a region of an n-dimensional space (d smaller than n) that, zoomed in closely enough, looks like an ordinary flat d-dimensional surface — the Swiss roll is a 2D manifold bent into 3D.

Manifold-learning algorithms work by modeling that underlying surface directly rather than projecting onto a flat hyperplane. A **hyperplane** is the flat thing one step down from the space you are in: a line in 2D, a plane in 3D, and so on.

The whole approach rests on the **manifold assumption**: that most real high-dimensional datasets really do live near a much lower-dimensional manifold. It holds up surprisingly often in practice — think of MNIST digits, which are all connected strokes, roughly centered, with pale borders, so the space of *actual* handwritten digits is a tiny, structured sliver of the space of all possible images.

### 4 · The second assumption, which is not automatic

A second, weaker assumption usually rides along with the first: that a task like classification gets *simpler* once expressed in that lower-dimensional manifold space.

Sometimes it does — a curved decision boundary in the original space can become a straight line after unrolling. A **decision boundary** is the dividing surface a classifier draws between two classes.

But the book is careful to show this isn't automatic: a boundary that is a simple flat plane in the original space can turn into a scattered, jagged set of segments once the manifold is unrolled — four independent line segments, in the bottom row of Figure 8-6 below.

So the honest summary is asymmetric. Reducing dimensions reliably speeds up training; it does not reliably make the problem easier.

**One-liner for your notes:** projection flattens data onto a subspace it already lies near and fails on twisted data; manifold learning models the twist and unrolls it — and either way you reliably get speed, not necessarily an easier problem.

items.term: Why "the data lies near a subspace" is usually true
items.text: It restates something you already see in wide tables: columns that barely vary, and columns that are near-copies of one another. Every constant column is a dimension the data does not actually use, and every pair of tightly correlated columns is roughly one dimension pretending to be two. The manifold assumption is that same observation extended to curved relationships instead of straight ones.

items.term: New columns, not surviving columns
items.text: Projection does not select a subset of the original features — it builds new coordinates measured along new directions. That is the difference between feature selection (keep some columns) and feature extraction (derive fewer columns out of all of them). It matters downstream: after projection nobody can point at a column and say what it means, so interpretability is part of the price, alongside the variance you gave up.

items.term: When the second assumption fails, and why that is not a paradox
items.text: The bottom row of Figure 8-6 is the honest case: a boundary that was a single flat plane becomes four disconnected segments after unrolling. Unrolling rearranges which points are near which, so a rule that was simple in the old coordinates need not be simple in the new ones. Nothing contradicts anything — "simpler for the classifier" was never a property the reduction was optimising for, which is exactly why it cannot be relied on.

Look up: the scikit-learn user guide section on manifold learning (the `sklearn.manifold` module), which runs several methods over the same toy manifolds side by side.

items.term: PCA: Preserving Variance and Principal Components

blocks.content:
PCA picks the axis that keeps the most spread in the data, then keeps picking more axes at right angles to the ones already chosen, until it has as many as the dataset had dimensions.

**The question this lesson answers:** if reduction means projecting onto a lower-dimensional surface, which surface? Out of infinitely many candidate axes, what rule does PCA use to choose?

### The big picture

```
try candidate axes
 -> keep the one preserving the MOST variance
 -> which is also the one with the SMALLEST gaps
 -> repeat at right angles on what variance is left
```

### 1 · Two steps, one hard part

PCA is the dimensionality-reduction algorithm you reach for first. Its overall recipe is two steps: find the hyperplane that sits closest to the data, then project every point onto it. The hard part is choosing *which* hyperplane.

### 2 · The rule: keep the most variance

Picture a simple 2D dataset and three candidate 1D axes to project it onto, as in Figure 8-7 in the next lesson. Each candidate keeps a different amount of the data's spread: one keeps almost all of it, another keeps very little, and a third sits in between.

**Variance** is just how spread out the values are — the same idea as the spread you would eyeball with a `MIN`, `MAX` and a few percentiles, written as one number.

PCA's rule is to always pick the axis that keeps the most variance, on the reasoning that the axis losing the least spread is also the axis losing the least information. That reasoning is worth pausing on: a column where every row has nearly the same value tells you almost nothing about which row is which. Spread is what distinguishes rows, so spread is the proxy for information.

### 3 · The same rule, stated as a distance

There's an equivalent, more geometric way to state the same rule: that maximum-variance axis is exactly the one that minimizes the average squared gap between each original point and its projection.

| Way of saying it | You are maximising | You are minimising |
|---|---|---|
| variance version | spread kept after projecting | nothing explicitly |
| distance version | nothing explicitly | how far points move |

Both descriptions point at the same axis — that equivalence is the whole idea behind PCA.

### 4 · Components two, three, and onward

Once the first axis (the **first principal component**) is chosen, PCA looks for a second axis, at right angles to the first, that captures as much as possible of whatever variance is left over — and so on, one more orthogonal axis at a time, until it has as many axes as the dataset has dimensions.

**Orthogonal** means at right angles. Insisting on it is what stops component two from re-describing what component one already covered: each new axis can only account for spread the earlier ones did not. Each of these is called the *i*th principal component.

### 5 · The signs are not stable

For every one of them, PCA hands back a unit vector centered at the origin and pointing along that axis. A **unit vector** is an arrow of length exactly 1 that says only "this direction".

That vector's exact sign isn't reliable — a slightly different training sample can flip it — but the vector generally still lies on the same axis. In the rare case where two components carry nearly identical variance, their pair of vectors may even rotate or trade places, yet the plane the two of them define generally stays the same.

The practical consequence: do not build anything that depends on the sign of a component or on which of two near-equal components came first. The axis is meaningful; the arrowhead is not.

**One-liner for your notes:** PCA keeps the axis with the most variance — equivalently, the one points move least to reach — then repeats at right angles, and only the axes are stable, not the direction the vectors point.

items.term: Why variance is used as a stand-in for information
items.text: A column where every row has nearly the same value cannot help you tell rows apart, so it carries little information about which row is which; a column that spreads rows out can. That is the whole justification, and it is a heuristic rather than a theorem. It also quietly assumes the features are on comparable scales — the same measurement in metres and in millimetres has wildly different variance — which makes scaling before PCA a real decision. This chapter does not raise scaling; it is flagged here because it is the first thing the variance rule assumes.

items.term: The equivalence is worth more than either half
items.text: "Keeps the most variance" and "moves the points the least" describe one and the same axis. So PCA can be argued for from either direction: as preserving the most signal, or as distorting the data the least. Keep both in mind — when you later meet a method that optimises one of these without the other, the gap between them is exactly where its behaviour will part company with PCA's.

items.term: Why unstable signs are an operational hazard, not a curiosity
items.text: Because the axis is stable but the arrowhead is not, two PCA runs on slightly different samples can produce reduced datasets whose columns are sign-flipped copies of each other. Anything that stores component vectors, compares them across runs, or caches a fitted transform has to treat the sign as meaningless. The working rule: fit once, persist the fitted transform, apply it everywhere — never refit per batch and assume the outputs are comparable.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Why must the second principal component be orthogonal to the first? What would go wrong if it weren't?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: "Keep the most variance" is a choice, not a law. What would a reduction that maximised something else — separation between known classes, say — look like instead?

Look up: Karl Pearson, "On Lines and Planes of Closest Fit to Systems of Points in Space", Philosophical Magazine 2, no. 11 (1901): 559-572, which this book cites as PCA's origin — then this chapter's later lesson on LDA.

items.term: Finding Principal Components via SVD

blocks.content:
The principal components are not hunted for by trial and error: they fall straight out of one standard matrix factorisation, SVD, applied to the centred data.

**The question this lesson answers:** PCA wants the maximum-variance axes. What actually computes them, and what is the one preparation step that silently ruins the answer if you skip it?

### The big picture

```
X (centred) --SVD--> U   sigma   V transpose
                             columns of V = the
                             components, best first
```

### 1 · One standard factorisation

Once you know PCA wants the maximum-variance axes, the remaining question is mechanical: how do you actually compute them? The answer is a standard piece of linear algebra called **singular value decomposition (SVD)**.

A **factorisation** is the matrix version of writing 12 as 3 × 4: one object rewritten as a product of simpler ones. Feed SVD your (centered) training matrix X, and it factors X into three matrices, U, Σ and V transpose. **Transpose** means flipped over its diagonal, so rows become columns.

The columns of V are exactly the unit vectors that define every principal component, ordered from most to least variance explained — so the first column of V is the first principal component, the second column is the second, and so on. Equation 8-1 below is nothing more than a picture of that: V with the component vectors standing side by side as columns.

### 2 · The NumPy version

In NumPy this is one function call: `np.linalg.svd()` on the centered data returns `U`, `s`, and `Vt` (V already transposed), and the first two rows of `Vt` are the first two principal components.

Watch the flip. The maths says *columns of V*; the function hands you `Vt`, which is V already transposed, so the same vectors arrive as *rows*. That is why the code card below reads `c1 = Vt[0]` and not `V[:, 0]`.

Nothing about this computation is specific to Scikit-Learn — it's plain linear algebra that any library implementing SVD can do.

### 3 · The trap: centre the data first

There is one easy trap here, and the book flags it explicitly: **PCA only works correctly on data that is centered at the origin**, meaning every feature has had its mean subtracted off.

Centring is one pass: for each column, compute its average and subtract it, so the column's new average is 0. In the code card below that is the single line `X_centered = X - X.mean(axis=0)`.

Scikit-Learn's PCA class does this centering for you automatically behind the scenes, so it's easy to forget the step exists — but if you ever implement PCA yourself from raw SVD, or reach for a different library that doesn't center automatically, skipping this step silently produces the wrong axes.

Note the failure mode, because it is the dangerous kind: no exception, no warning, no obviously broken output. Just wrong axes, and everything downstream quietly built on them.

**One-liner for your notes:** SVD on the centred matrix hands back every principal component as a column of V, best first — and forgetting to centre gives you wrong axes with no error raised.

blocks.title: Equation 8-1
blocks.caption: Principal components matrix
blocks.explain:
**Why the equation looks like this**

Equation 8-1 is not a calculation — it is a container. Each principal component is one
direction, written as a unit vector (an arrow of length exactly 1 that says only "this
way"). There are n of them for n features, and they have to live somewhere, in a
definite order. V is that somewhere: the component vectors stood side by side as
columns, best first. The vertical bars drawn above and below each vector are only
scaffolding — they say "this is a whole column, not a single number".

**Is this standard?** Yes, and not only for PCA. SVD is a general matrix factorisation
used right across linear algebra, and writing X as U times Σ times V transpose is its
canonical form. PCA is one application of it. Nothing here was simplified for this
book or for this example.

**The general form.** The full factorisation is X = U Σ V transpose, where X is your
centred data. Each part carries something different:

| Part | Size, for n features | Carries |
|---|---|---|
| U | one row per instance | where each row sits on the new axes |
| Σ | a list of sizes | how much spread each axis carries |
| V | n by n | the axes themselves, the components |

PCA only ever reads V. The other two come out of the factorisation anyway, because
SVD produces all three at once.

**Terms this introduces:** a **matrix** is a grid of numbers, rows by columns; a
**column** of it is one vertical strip; **transpose** flips rows and columns, so the
first column of V becomes the first row of V transpose; a **factorisation** rewrites
one object as a product of simpler ones, the way 12 can be written as 3 times 4.

**Every piece of Equation 8-1**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| V | vee | the matrix holding every component |
| c₁ | c one | the first principal component |
| c₂ | c two | the second principal component |
| cₙ | c n | the last one, n-th of n features |
| ⋯ | and so on | the components between 2 and n |
| the bars | (nothing) | a reminder each c is a full column |
| n | n | how many features the data has |

**The formula in plain words**

V = every principal-component direction, one per column, sorted so the direction
keeping the most variance is first and the one keeping the least is last.

**Real shapes plugged in**

- The small 3D dataset in the code card below: n = 3, so V is 3 by 3 and holds three
component columns. `Vt[0]` and `Vt[1]` are c₁ and c₂.
- MNIST: n = 784, so V is 784 by 784 and holds 784 components. Keeping 154 of them
means using the first 154 and ignoring the remaining 630.

**How the ordering is produced — you never sort it yourself**

1. Centre X: for each column, subtract that column's average.
2. Run SVD once. It returns U, s and Vt together, in one call.
3. Σ comes back with its sizes already largest-first, and V's columns are arranged to
match — so the ranking is a by-product, not a second step.
4. Read components off the top: `Vt[0]` is the best axis, `Vt[1]` the next. Stop at
whatever d you want. There is no re-ranking and no search.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import numpy as np

X = [...] # create a small 3D dataset
X_centered = X - X.mean(axis=0)
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(X_centered)
c1 = Vt[0]
c2 = Vt[1]
```

items.term: Why centring is not optional, in one picture
items.text: Variance is measured around the mean. If the cloud of points sits far away from the origin, then the biggest direction of spread as seen from the origin is simply the direction pointing at the cloud — so the first component comes back describing where the data *is* rather than how it varies. Centring moves the origin into the middle of the data so the axes describe shape instead of position.

items.term: A failure with no error message is the expensive kind
items.text: Uncentred SVD raises nothing. You get vectors of the right shape, in a plausible order, and every downstream step runs happily. This is the same class of defect as a join on the wrong key that still returns rows: the pipeline is green and the numbers are wrong. Checks on shapes and exit codes cannot catch it; only a check on the result can.

items.term: Why a general-purpose factorisation rather than a PCA-specific algorithm
items.text: PCA's definition is geometric — the maximum-variance axes — and SVD is a general tool that happens to produce exactly those. The payoff is that decades of numerical work on SVD, including the randomized and incremental variants in a later lesson, transfer to PCA for free. It is the same argument as building on a standard file format instead of a bespoke one.

items: If you forgot to center your data before running SVD by hand, what would you expect to see go wrong in the resulting principal components?
