items.term: Projecting Down to d Dimensions and Using Scikit-Learn's PCA

blocks.content:
Reducing to d dimensions is one matrix multiply — the data times the first d component vectors — and Scikit-Learn wraps the whole pipeline in two lines.

**The question this lesson answers:** you have every principal component ranked by variance. How do you actually turn that into a dataset with fewer columns, and what does Scikit-Learn do for you?

### The big picture

```
   X          x    Wd        =   Xd-proj
 all rows,        first d        same rows,
 all columns      components     d columns
```

### 1 · Why the first d axes, and not some other d

Finding the principal components is only half the job — the other half is actually using them to shrink the dataset.

Once you have every axis ranked by how much variance it captures, reducing to *d* dimensions means projecting the data onto just the hyperplane spanned by the *first d* of those axes, since that choice is guaranteed to keep as much variance as any other choice of d axes could. **Spanned by** means the flat surface those d directions sweep out.

That guarantee is why nobody searches over combinations of axes. The components are already sorted best-first, so "keep the top d" is provably the best d-axis answer available — no tuning, no search.

### 2 · The multiply

Mechanically, you build a matrix Wd out of the first d columns of V, and the reduced dataset is simply the original data matrix multiplied by Wd. Equation 8-2 below is that one line, with its explanation underneath.

### 3 · The Scikit-Learn version

Scikit-Learn packages this whole pipeline — center the data, run SVD, keep the first *d* components, project — behind one class. `PCA(n_components=2)` followed by `fit_transform(X)` returns the training set reduced to two dimensions in a single call, with the centering handled automatically so you don't have to do it yourself. The code card below is the whole thing.

Two verbs worth separating, because every Scikit-Learn transformer has them:

| Call | Reads the data to | Gives back |
|---|---|---|
| `fit` | work out Wd | nothing useful |
| `transform` | apply Wd | the reduced data |
| `fit_transform` | both, in one pass | the reduced data |

### 4 · What components_ holds

After fitting, the object exposes a `components_` attribute holding the same information as Wd (transposed) — one row per component kept, which is a convenient way to inspect exactly which directions PCA decided mattered most.

Reading a row tells you what the new column actually *is*: a weighted mix of the original features, with the big weights naming the ones that dominate it. That is the closest thing PCA gives you to a column description.

The practical upshot is that everything from the raw math in the previous block collapses, in Scikit-Learn, into two or three lines: pick how many dimensions you want to keep, call fit_transform, and get back a dataset with that many columns instead of the original count.

**One-liner for your notes:** project by multiplying the data by the first d component vectors, and in Scikit-Learn that is `PCA(n_components=d).fit_transform(X)`, with `components_` telling you which directions it kept.

blocks.title: Equation 8-2
blocks.caption: Projecting the training set down to d dimensions
blocks.explain:
**Why the equation looks like this**

Measuring one row along one direction is a single arithmetic recipe: multiply each of
the row's values by that direction's weight for the same feature, and add the results
up. That one number is the row's new coordinate on that axis. You need to do it for
every row and every kept direction, and a matrix multiplication is exactly the
notation for "do that arithmetic for all pairs at once". So Equation 8-2 is not a new
idea on top of the previous lesson — it is the same projection, written once instead
of row by row.

**Is this standard?** Yes. Every linear transformation of a table is written as the
table multiplied by a matrix; this is the canonical form and it is not specific to
PCA. What makes it PCA is only *which* columns Wd holds — the top principal
components. Swap in a random matrix and the same equation is random projection, two
lessons later.

**The general form.** Xd-proj = X Wd covers every d from 1 up to n. At d = n nothing
is dropped and the multiply is a pure change of axes with no loss at all; every d
below that trades some variance for fewer columns. There is no separate formula for
the "keep everything" case.

**Terms this introduces:** a **hyperplane** is the flat surface the kept directions
sweep out — a line for d = 1, a plane for d = 2; **spanned by** means swept out by;
**matrix multiplication** here means the row-by-direction arithmetic described above.

**Every piece of Equation 8-2**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| Xd-proj | X d-proj | the reduced dataset, the output |
| X | capital X | the input data, one row per instance |
| Wd | W d | the first d component directions |
| d | d | how many dimensions you are keeping |
| the two side by side | X times W d | multiply the data by the directions |

**The formula in plain words**

reduced data = each row, measured along each of the d directions you kept.

**Real shapes plugged in**

| Case | X | Wd | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| Figure 8-2 dataset, d = 2 | m by 3 | 3 by 2 | m by 2 |
| MNIST, d = 154 | 60,000 by 784 | 784 by 154 | 60,000 by 154 |
| MNIST, d = 2 | 60,000 by 784 | 784 by 2 | 60,000 by 2 |

The row count never changes. Only the column count does — same instances, described
with fewer numbers each.

**How one output number is computed**

Take MNIST and the very first kept direction, and ask for one row's new first column:

1. Take that image's 784 centred pixel values.
2. Take the 784 weights in the first component (that is `components_[0]`).
3. Multiply pixel 1 by weight 1, pixel 2 by weight 2, and so on for all 784 pairs.
4. Add those 784 products together. That single number is the row's coordinate on
component one.
5. Repeat steps 2 to 4 with component two, then three, up to component 154. You now
have the 154 numbers that replace the original 784.

The book writes the same thing in two lines using the raw SVD output:
`W2 = Vt[:2].T` picks the first two directions, and `X2D = X_centered @ W2` is the
multiply.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

pca = PCA(n_components=2)
X2D = pca.fit_transform(X)
```

items.term: Why "the top d" is provably optimal, and where that guarantee stops
items.text: The guarantee is exact and narrow: among all possible choices of d axes, the first d principal components keep the most variance. It says nothing about keeping the most *useful* information for a particular downstream task — a direction carrying little variance can still be the one that separates two classes. That is precisely why a later lesson tunes d against the model that consumes the output instead of trusting the variance ranking alone.

items.term: Reduction is a fitted object, not a formula
items.text: Wd is learned from the training set. The test set, and every future row, must pass through that same fitted transform — never one refitted on them — or the two datasets end up described in different coordinate systems that only look compatible because the column counts match. Same discipline as reusing a lookup built from training data rather than rebuilding it per batch.

items.term: What the new columns actually are
items.text: Every output column is a weighted blend of all the original ones, with the weights sitting in a row of `components_`. A reduced dataset therefore has no surviving features and no missing features — it has d blends. If somebody downstream has to explain why a prediction happened, that blend is the wall they hit, and it is a cost worth naming out loud before you reduce.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Explain in your own words why Xd-proj = X · Wd captures 'as much variance as possible' among all choices of d axes.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The transform is fitted on the training set. What exactly goes wrong if you fit PCA on the training and test data together, and how would you detect that it happened?
Look up: the scikit-learn user guide section on pipelines and composite estimators, which exists largely to make that mistake hard to commit.

items.term: Explained Variance Ratio and Choosing the Right Number of Dimensions

blocks.content:
Each kept axis reports what share of the data's total spread it accounts for, and that one number per axis is how you decide how many axes to keep.

**The question this lesson answers:** PCA will happily reduce to any d you name. How do you choose d on evidence instead of by guessing?

### The big picture

| Way to choose d | What you do |
|---|---|
| variance target | smallest count reaching, say, 95% |
| float n_components | pass 0.95 and let PCA count |
| the elbow | plot the running total, find the bend |
| hyperparameter | tune jointly with the model that follows |
| visualization | 2 or 3, whatever the variance says |

### 1 · What the ratio is, and what it is not

Once a PCA object is fitted, it exposes `explained_variance_ratio_` — one number per kept component, giving the **share of the dataset's total variance that lies along that specific axis**.

This is worth being precise about, because it's easy to misread: it is not a count of instances, not an accuracy score, and not a measure of any single feature — it is purely how much of the *overall spread of the data* that one axis accounts for.

If the first two ratios for a 3D dataset come out to roughly 76% and 15%, that means those two axes together already explain 91% of the variance, leaving only about 9% unaccounted for — a strong signal that the third axis is carrying very little useful information.

### 2 · Choosing d from a variance target

That observation suggests a much better way to choose how many dimensions to keep than picking an arbitrary number: instead, pick the *smallest* number of components whose ratios add up to some target, commonly 95%. Visualization is the exception — there you pick 2 or 3 regardless of variance captured.

In code, this means fitting PCA with no cap, taking a running **cumulative sum** of the ratios — each entry being the total so far, exactly like a running total in a window function — and finding the first index where that sum crosses your threshold. The code card below does that for MNIST and lands on 154.

Scikit-Learn also lets you skip the arithmetic: pass a *float* between 0 and 1 as `n_components` and PCA works out the exact integer count itself, storing it afterward in `n_components_`.

### 3 · The elbow

A third option is purely visual — plot the cumulative sum against the number of components and look for the **elbow**, the point where the curve stops rising steeply. Figure 8-8 below is that plot for MNIST.

The elbow is a judgement call, not a computation: before it, each extra component buys real variance; after it, each one buys almost nothing.

### 4 · When a model consumes the output

When PCA is a preprocessing step ahead of a supervised model, the number of components kept is best treated as just another hyperparameter to search over jointly with the downstream model's own hyperparameters, rather than fixed in advance. A **hyperparameter** is a setting you choose before training, the way you pass a `--conf` flag when submitting a job.

Doing this search for MNIST turned up a striking result: a random forest classifier did best keeping only 23 of the original 784 dimensions, while a linear SGDClassifier needed roughly 70 — a reminder that the 'right' number of dimensions isn't a property of the dataset alone, it depends on what model consumes the reduced data.

The card below shows exactly how small that search was — 10 random combinations, 3-fold, on the first 1,000 instances — which is worth knowing before quoting 23 as a fact about MNIST.

**One-liner for your notes:** `explained_variance_ratio_` is share-of-spread per axis; keep the smallest count reaching your target (or pass the target as a float), but when a model eats the output, tune d alongside that model's own settings.

blocks.title: Worked out: the search that found 23 components
blocks.content: The 23 comes from a deliberately quick search. The book builds a two-step pipeline, `PCA(random_state=42)` followed by `RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42)`, and runs `RandomizedSearchCV` over two hyperparameters: `pca__n_components` drawn from `np.arange(10, 80)`, which is 10 to 79 components, and the forest's `n_estimators` drawn from `np.arange(50, 500)`. The search tries only 10 random combinations (`n_iter=10`) with `cv=3`, and it trains on just the first 1,000 MNIST training instances. The best combination it reports is 465 trees with 23 components, so a 784-dimensional dataset shrinks to 23 dimensions. The book ties this low number to the random forest being a pretty powerful model, and it says a linear model such as `SGDClassifier` would need to preserve more dimensions, about 70.

blocks.title: Figure 8-8
blocks.caption: Explained variance as a function of the number of dimensions
blocks.alt: Figure 8-8: Explained variance as a function of the number of dimensions

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
pca = PCA()
pca.fit(X_train)
cumsum = np.cumsum(pca.explained_variance_ratio_)
d = np.argmax(cumsum >= 0.95) + 1 # d equals 154
```

items.term: A 95% target is a convention, not a result
items.text: Nothing derives 95%. It is a round number that usually works, and this chapter itself shows how weak it is as a default: the MNIST search kept 23 dimensions for a random forest, far fewer than the 154 a 95% target produces. Treat the variance target as a fast first guess for when nothing downstream is measurable yet — not as the answer.

items.term: Why the right d depends on the model that follows
items.text: Variance ratios describe the data alone. A powerful model can rebuild structure from fewer, coarser inputs, while a linear model needs that structure handed to it more explicitly — which is exactly the lesson's result: 23 for a random forest, about 70 for a linear SGDClassifier, on the same dataset. The general lesson is bigger than PCA: any preprocessing setting tuned in isolation from its consumer is being tuned against the wrong objective.

items.term: Read the search before quoting the number
items.text: The 23 came from 10 random combinations, 3-fold, trained on the first 1,000 of 60,000 instances. That is enough to make the qualitative point and nowhere near enough to pin a number. Carrying "23" forward as a property of MNIST is exactly how a number written down once hardens into a fact — the card below is there so you can see the size of the evidence.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: You fit PCA and see explained_variance_ratio_ = [0.5, 0.3, 0.1, 0.1]. How many components would you keep for a 90% variance target, and why?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The elbow is judged by eye. Are there defined rules for choosing the number of components, and what do they assume that the variance-target rule does not?
Look up: the scikit-learn user guide page for `sklearn.decomposition.PCA`, in particular its `n_components='mle'` option and the paper that option references.

items.term: PCA for Compression and Reconstruction Error

blocks.content:
PCA doubles as a compressor: 154 columns instead of 784 for 95% of the variance, and because it is a linear projection you can run it backwards to get an approximation of the original back.

**The question this lesson answers:** once PCA has shrunk MNIST, how much smaller is it really, can you get the original back, and how do you measure what was lost?

### The big picture

```
784 cols --fit_transform--->  154 cols  (under 20%)
154 cols --inverse_transform--> 784 cols (close)
gap between original and recovered
     = reconstruction error
```

### 1 · The size win

Reduced dimensionality means a genuinely smaller dataset to store and process. Compressing MNIST down to the 154 dimensions needed for 95% of its variance shrinks it to under a fifth of its original footprint, for the cost of only 5% of the variance — a favorable trade that also makes any classifier trained on it substantially faster.

Two percentages, two different things, and they get confused constantly: 154 out of 784 is the **size** (about 19.6%, under a fifth), while 5% is the share of **variance** given up. The card below does that division.

### 2 · Running the projection backwards

Because PCA is a linear projection, it can be run in reverse: applying the inverse transformation maps the reduced data back up to the original 784 dimensions. Equation 8-3 below is that reverse step, explained underneath.

In Scikit-Learn the decompression step is one call, `inverse_transform()`, applied to the already-reduced data (the compression step was the earlier `fit_transform()`).

| Call | In | Out |
|---|---|---|
| `fit_transform` | 784 columns | 154 columns |
| `inverse_transform` | 154 columns | 784 columns |

Note what the second row does *not* say: it does not say "the original data". The column count comes back; the values only come close.

### 3 · What you cannot get back

This does not recover the original values exactly — the 5% of variance that was discarded during compression is genuinely gone — but the recovered data is usually a close approximation of the original, with only mild degradation visible if you compare recovered digit images side by side with the originals. Figure 8-9 below is exactly that comparison.

### 4 · Measuring the loss

The standard way to quantify how much was lost is the **reconstruction error**: the mean squared distance between each original point and its compressed-then-decompressed counterpart.

Read it as the same recipe you already know from regression error: take the gap per row, square it, average. Comparing the recovered output with the original data is a useful sanity check whenever you want concrete evidence of how much information a given number of kept components is actually preserving.

That is the honest answer to "is 154 enough?" — not an opinion, a measured number on your own data.

**One-liner for your notes:** PCA compresses MNIST to under a fifth of its size for 5% of its variance, `inverse_transform()` brings the shape back but not the lost detail, and reconstruction error is the number that says how much detail that was.

blocks.title: Worked out: why 154 features is under 20%
blocks.content: The size claim is a simple ratio of feature counts. MNIST starts with 784 features, and keeping 95% of the variance leaves 154 features. Dividing 154 by 784 gives about 0.196, so the compressed dataset holds roughly 19.6% as many values as the original, which is less than 20%, or under a fifth. The price is the variance that was dropped: 100% − 95% = 5%. Keep the two percentages apart: the 20% describes the size of the data, while the 5% describes the share of variance that was lost.

blocks.title: Figure 8-9
blocks.caption: MNIST compression that preserves 95% of the variance
blocks.alt: Figure 8-9: MNIST compression that preserves 95% of the variance

blocks.title: Equation 8-3
blocks.caption: PCA inverse transformation, back to the original number of dimensions
blocks.explain:
**Why the equation looks like this**

Going down, you multiplied by Wd. Going back up, you multiply by Wd transpose — the
same directions, turned on their side. That works for a specific reason: the kept
directions are unit vectors at right angles to each other, so reversing the
measurement is just re-assembling the row out of those directions, each one scaled by
the coordinate you recorded. Nothing has to be solved or inverted.

What cannot come back is anything that pointed *away* from the kept directions. That
part was not shrunk or approximated during the projection; it was never recorded at
all. Hence the recovered data is close, and never exact.

**Is this standard?** Yes. This is the canonical PCA inverse transformation, and it is
exactly what `inverse_transform()` computes. Nothing was simplified for the MNIST
example.

**The general form.** The pair Xd-proj = X Wd and Xrecovered = Xd-proj Wd transpose
holds for any d. At d = n the round trip returns the original data exactly, because
nothing was discarded. For every d below n the round trip is approximate, and the size
of the approximation is precisely the variance you chose not to keep.

**Terms this introduces:** **transpose** flips a matrix's rows and columns;
**at right angles** (orthogonal) means the kept directions do not overlap, so none of
them re-describes what another already covered; **reconstruction error** is the
measured gap after a full round trip, defined in the prose above.

**Every piece of Equation 8-3**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| Xrecovered | X recovered | the decompressed data, the output |
| Xd-proj | X d-proj | the reduced data, the input |
| Wd | W d | the d component directions that were kept |
| the raised T | transpose | Wd turned on its side |

**The formula in plain words**

recovered row = add up the kept directions, each one scaled by this row's coordinate
along it.

**Real shapes plugged in**

| Step | In | Matrix | Out |
|---|---|---|---|
| compress | 60,000 by 784 | 784 by 154 | 60,000 by 154 |
| decompress | 60,000 by 154 | 154 by 784 | 60,000 by 784 |

**The two percentages, computed**

1. Size: 154 divided by 784 is about 0.196, so the compressed data holds roughly
19.6% as many values — under a fifth.
2. Variance kept: 95%, by construction, because 154 was chosen as the smallest count
reaching that target.
3. Variance lost: 100% minus 95% = 5%. That 5% is what the round trip cannot return.

Keep the two apart. The 20% is about the size of the data; the 5% is about how much of
its spread was given up.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
X_recovered = pca.inverse_transform(X_reduced)
```

items.term: Lossy by construction, and why that is acceptable here
items.text: PCA discards the directions with the least spread and cannot get them back. That is not an implementation shortcoming, it is what the reduction *is*. The JPEG comparison from the first lesson is exact: both keep what a consumer is expected to notice and drop the rest. The thing to watch is that "what the consumer notices" was decided by variance, which need not match what your downstream task notices.

items.term: Reconstruction error is the one honest number
items.text: Explained variance is a claim about the data's own spread, computed at fit time. Reconstruction error is a measured gap on real rows after a full round trip. When you need evidence rather than a percentage — for a reviewer, or for your own confidence — the round trip is the thing to run, and it costs exactly one extra call.

items.term: Compression here is not the same as a file compressor
items.text: Zip and gzip are exact: the bytes come back. PCA is not, and its output is a smaller *table of numbers*, not a smaller encoding of the same table. The practical difference is that models train directly on the PCA output, whereas a zipped file has to be decompressed before anything can read it — which is why the size win here also buys a speed win.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Why can't inverse_transform() ever fully recover the original dataset once dimensionality has been reduced?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Reconstruction error is one number averaged over every row. How would you find out whether the loss is spread evenly or concentrated on a few unusual instances, and would that change your d?
Look up: the scikit-learn user guide page for `sklearn.decomposition.PCA`, specifically `inverse_transform` — and Figure 8-9 in this chapter, which shows the loss digit by digit rather than averaged.

items.term: Randomized PCA and Incremental PCA

blocks.content:
Two variants fix two different limits of plain PCA: randomized PCA when full SVD is too slow, incremental PCA when the data does not fit in memory.

**The question this lesson answers:** plain PCA runs a full SVD over the whole training set in RAM. What do you use when the feature count makes that too slow, or when the dataset is bigger than memory, or when it arrives as a stream?

### The big picture

| Variant | Fixes | How |
|---|---|---|
| full SVD | the baseline | exact; cost grows with n |
| randomized | too slow when n is big | approximate; cost grows with d |
| incremental | data bigger than RAM | one mini-batch at a time |
| random projection | even randomized too slow | the next lesson |

Here n is the original feature count and d is how many components you keep.

### 1 · Randomized PCA

Full SVD gets expensive as the original number of features n grows, since its cost scales with roughly n squared and n cubed terms.

**Randomized PCA**, selected by setting `svd_solver="randomized"`, trades a small amount of precision for a large speedup: it's a stochastic algorithm that only approximates the first *d* components, with a cost that scales with d instead of n — a huge win whenever you're keeping far fewer dimensions than you started with. **Stochastic** means it uses randomness internally, so it approximates rather than computes exactly.

The trade is the useful part: you were going to throw away all but d directions anyway, so paying to compute the other 630 exactly is wasted work.

### 2 · The auto rule

Scikit-Learn's default, `svd_solver="auto"`, actually switches to this randomized algorithm on its own whenever the data is reasonably large and the requested component count is well under the original feature count, falling back to exact full SVD otherwise; you can force the exact method with `svd_solver="full"` if you need the more precise result.

The card below gives the exact thresholds, and works through why `PCA(n_components=154)` on MNIST already uses the randomized path even if you never ask for it.

### 3 · Incremental PCA

A separate limitation of ordinary PCA is that it needs the *entire* training set sitting in memory at once.

**Incremental PCA (IPCA)** removes that requirement by processing the data in mini-batches: instead of calling `fit()` once on everything, you call `partial_fit()` once per batch, and the algorithm updates its estimate of the components incrementally.

This is the full-refresh versus incremental-load distinction you already know, moved inside the algorithm. It matters for two overlapping situations — datasets too large to fit in RAM, and streaming setups where PCA needs to be updated as new data arrives over time. The code card below splits MNIST into 100 mini-batches and feeds them one at a time.

### 4 · The memmap trick

A related trick uses NumPy's `memmap`, which lets you address a huge array stored on disk as though it were an ordinary in-memory array, loading only the small pieces actually being touched at any moment — convenient because it lets you call ordinary `fit()` and let IncrementalPCA manage memory internally instead of you hand-writing the batch loop.

It is the same idea as reading a file larger than RAM a chunk at a time, except the chunking is handled by the array object rather than by your loop.

### 5 · Where even randomized PCA runs out

Even randomized PCA has limits: for datasets with tens of thousands of features, the target dimensionality still has to stay fairly small for it to be fast, and beyond that point random projection becomes the better tool.

**One-liner for your notes:** randomized PCA buys speed by approximating only the d components you asked for, incremental PCA buys memory by taking mini-batches through `partial_fit()`, and past tens of thousands of features you switch tools entirely.

blocks.title: Worked out: the costs and the "auto" rule
blocks.content: The book states the costs and the switching rule exactly. Here m is the number of instances, n the number of features, and d the number of components kept. Full SVD costs O(m × n²) + O(n³), while randomized PCA costs O(m × d²) + O(d³), so randomized PCA is dramatically faster when d is much smaller than n, but d still must not be too large. With `svd_solver="auto"`, Scikit-Learn uses randomized PCA if max(m, n) > 500 and `n_components` is an integer smaller than 80% of min(m, n); otherwise it uses full SVD. For MNIST, m = 60,000 and n = 784, so max(m, n) = 60,000 is above 500, and 80% of min(m, n) is 0.8 × 784 = 627.2. Since 154 < 627.2, `PCA(n_components=154)` uses randomized PCA even without `svd_solver="randomized"`.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.decomposition import IncrementalPCA

n_batches = 100
inc_pca = IncrementalPCA(n_components=154)
for X_batch in np.array_split(X_train, n_batches):
    inc_pca.partial_fit(X_batch)

X_reduced = inc_pca.transform(X_train)
```

items.term: Approximate on purpose, and why that is the right trade
items.text: You asked for d directions and intend to throw the rest away, so computing all n of them exactly is work that goes straight in the bin. Randomized PCA spends effort in proportion to what you keep. The generalisable rule: when an exact intermediate result is about to be truncated, an approximation that is accurate on the kept part is not a compromise — it is the correct algorithm.

items.term: A default that silently changes algorithm is worth knowing about
items.text: Under `svd_solver="auto"` the identical call can run two different algorithms depending on the shape of your data, so behaviour can shift when the dataset crosses a threshold rather than when your code changes. That is fine once you know it, and a genuine mystery when you are chasing a small numerical difference between two runs of "the same" pipeline.

items.term: Mini-batches change what the algorithm can promise
items.text: Full SVD sees everything at once and gives the exact answer for that data. Incremental PCA maintains a running estimate updated batch by batch, so what it settles on can depend on batch size, and on order when the data is streamed. It is the same trade as an incremental load against a full refresh: cheaper and always current, at the cost of an answer that is maintained rather than recomputed.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: You have a dataset that doesn't fit in memory and arrives continuously as a stream. Which PCA variant fits, and why?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Incremental PCA updates its components as new data arrives. What happens when the incoming data's distribution shifts — does it adapt, and how quickly?

Look up: David A. Ross et al., "Incremental Learning for Robust Visual Tracking", International Journal of Computer Vision 77, no. 1-3 (2008): 125-141 — the algorithm this book says Scikit-Learn's IncrementalPCA implements.

items.term: Random Projection

blocks.content:
Random projection multiplies the data by a matrix of random numbers and calls that the reduction — no training at all — and a theorem says the distances between instances mostly survive it.

**The question this lesson answers:** when a dataset has tens of thousands of features and even randomized PCA is too slow, how do you cut dimensions without learning anything from the data first — and how do you know the result is not garbage?

### The big picture

```
pick target d from m and tolerance  (n never used)
build a random matrix, d rows x n columns
multiply the data by it. done. nothing fitted.
```

Here m is the number of instances (rows), n the number of features (columns), and d the target number of dimensions.

### 1 · Why a random map is not madness

Random projection sounds almost too simple to work: pick a random linear map down to a lower-dimensional space and use it, with no training at all.

What makes it viable is the **Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma**, a mathematical result showing that a sufficiently well-chosen random projection preserves pairwise distances with high probability — two instances that were close before projection stay close afterward, and two that were far apart stay far apart.

That property is the one most downstream work actually needs. Clustering, nearest-neighbour lookups and most similarity search care about *relative* distances, not about what the columns mean — so a transform that scrambles the meaning of every column but keeps the distances is still usable.

### 2 · The formula that ignores n

Dropping more dimensions naturally distorts more distances, so the lemma also supplies a formula for the *minimum* number of dimensions needed to keep that distortion under a chosen tolerance, written with the Greek letter epsilon and usually read as "how much squared distance you are willing to let change".

What's notable about that formula is what it does **not** depend on: it's a function of the number of instances m and the tolerance only — the original feature count n never appears in it.

A dataset with 5,000 instances and 20,000 features, tolerating a 10% change in squared distances, still needs a computed target of 7,300 dimensions, regardless of how large n actually was; Scikit-Learn exposes this exact calculation as `johnson_lindenstrauss_min_dim()`. The card below walks the arithmetic that turns 5,000 and 10% into 7,300.

Read that once more, because it is genuinely surprising: adding more columns to your table does not change the answer at all. Adding more *rows* does.

### 3 · Building the matrix

Given the target dimension *d*, the projection itself is just a random matrix drawn from a Gaussian distribution with mean zero and variance 1/d, multiplied against the data — no fitting step beyond knowing the data's shape. A **Gaussian distribution** is the familiar bell curve; drawing from it with mean zero means values scattered around 0.

Scikit-Learn's `GaussianRandomProjection` wraps exactly this recipe, as in the code card below. The only thing the algorithm needs is the dataset's shape, which is why there is nothing to fit.

### 4 · The sparse variant, which is the default advice

A second variant, `SparseRandomProjection`, produces a random matrix that is mostly zeros (its fraction of nonzero entries, the *density*, defaults to 1 over the square root of n) — this saves a large amount of memory and runs noticeably faster while preserving distances about as well, which is why the book recommends reaching for the sparse version by default, especially on large or already-sparse data.

The numbers behind "a large amount" in the book's own example: about 25 MB of matrix instead of almost 1.2 GB, and roughly 50% faster, with only about 1 cell in 141 nonzero at 20,000 features.

| | Gaussian | Sparse |
|---|---|---|
| Matrix | dense | mostly zeros |
| Memory, book example | almost 1.2 GB | about 25 MB |
| Distances | preserved | preserved about as well |

### 5 · Going back is the expensive direction

Reversing either transform requires computing a pseudo-inverse of the random projection matrix, which can itself be slow on a large matrix. A **pseudo-inverse** is the best available stand-in for an inverse when a matrix is not square and so has no true one.

**One-liner for your notes:** random projection needs no training — just a random matrix whose size comes from the row count and your distortion tolerance, never from the column count — and the sparse version is the one to reach for.

blocks.title: Worked out: where the 7,300 dimensions come from
blocks.content: The book's bound is d ≥ 4 log(m) / (½ ε² − ⅓ ε³), where m is the number of instances and ε is the tolerance. Take m = 5,000 and ε = 0.1. The log here is the natural logarithm, which is what yields 7,300: log(5,000) ≈ 8.517, so the numerator is 4 × 8.517 ≈ 34.07. In the denominator, ½ × 0.1² = 0.005 and ⅓ × 0.1³ ≈ 0.000333, so the denominator is 0.005 − 0.000333 ≈ 0.004667. Dividing 34.07 by 0.004667 gives about 7,300, the book's answer, and `johnson_lindenstrauss_min_dim(m, eps=ε)` with those values returns 7300. The feature count n = 20,000 appears nowhere in these steps, so the result does not depend on it.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.random_projection import GaussianRandomProjection

gaussian_rnd_proj = GaussianRandomProjection(eps=ε, random_state=42)
X_reduced = gaussian_rnd_proj.fit_transform(X) # same result as above
```

items.term: Why "no training at all" is not a trick
items.text: PCA reads the data to find the directions worth keeping. Random projection does not read it — the only input is the shape. That sounds strictly worse, and for variance kept it is; the lemma just says it is good enough for the property most downstream work actually leans on, which is relative distance. The general point is worth keeping: an algorithm that ignores the data can still be correct when what you need from it does not depend on the data.

items.term: Why the bound grows with rows and not with columns
items.text: The guarantee has to hold for every pair of instances at once, and the number of pairs grows with the row count. Adding columns creates no new pairs to protect, so the column count never enters the formula. That is exactly why the method scales so well on very wide data — the case where PCA's cost behaves worst.

items.term: Sparse matrices are an engineering win with no accuracy cost here
items.text: The sparse variant preserves distances about as well while using a fraction of the memory, because the guarantee never demanded a dense matrix — only a well-chosen one. Whenever a default carries a large cost for a property that nothing actually requires, that is the place to look for a cheaper construction satisfying the same theorem.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Explain why the Johnson-Lindenstrauss bound depends on the number of instances m but not on the original number of features n.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Random projection turns out to describe something biological as well as a preprocessing step. What was that result, and what does it suggest about when a random map is a sound design?
Look up: Sanjoy Dasgupta et al., "A neural algorithm for a fundamental computing problem", Science 358, no. 6364 (2017): 793-796, which this book cites for the fruit fly's olfactory system.

items.term: LLE (Locally Linear Embedding)

blocks.content:
LLE does not project anything: it learns how each point is built out of its nearest neighbours, then finds new low-dimensional positions where those same local relationships still hold.

**The question this lesson answers:** the Swiss roll has to be unrolled, not flattened. What does an algorithm actually optimise to unroll it, and what does that cost?

### The big picture

```
stage 1: points fixed   -> find weights (local shape)
stage 2: weights fixed  -> find new positions
                           in fewer dimensions
```

### 1 · A different route entirely

Locally linear embedding (LLE) takes a fundamentally different route from PCA and random projection: it does not project onto anything.

It's a **manifold learning** technique, and it earns its keep specifically on twisted manifolds — like the Swiss roll — where a flat projection would squash the structure, provided there isn't too much noise in the data.

### 2 · Stage one: local weights

LLE works in two stages. First, for every training instance, it looks at that instance's k nearest neighbors and solves for the set of weights that best reconstructs the instance as a weighted combination of just those neighbors.

Two constraints do all the work here: any instance that isn't one of the k nearest gets a weight of exactly zero, and the weights for each instance are normalized to sum to one. The first is what makes the method *local* — each row is described only by its own neighbourhood, never by the dataset as a whole. The second keeps each reconstruction a weighted average of those neighbours rather than a scaled-up version of them.

Solving this for every instance produces a weight matrix that captures the *local* linear structure of the data — how each point relates to its immediate surroundings, without reference to anything more global. Equation 8-4 below states that stage exactly, with its explanation underneath.

### 3 · Stage two: keep the weights, move the points

The second stage keeps those weights fixed and instead searches for a set of low-dimensional coordinates for every instance such that each point can still be reconstructed from its neighbors using those same weights, this time in the new, smaller space. Equation 8-5 below is that stage.

In other words, stage one learns local geometry in the original space; stage two finds new positions that preserve that same local geometry using far fewer coordinates.

| Stage | Held fixed | Searched for |
|---|---|---|
| one | the points | the weights |
| two | the weights | new, smaller coordinates |

Notice that the two stages optimise the *same shape of quantity* and simply swap which side is unknown. That symmetry is the whole design.

### 4 · What it gets right, and what it does not

Because both stages only ever consider a handful of nearest neighbors per instance, LLE is very good at faithfully unrolling a twisted surface locally — the Swiss roll comes out flattened with genuinely well-preserved local distances, as in Figure 8-10 below — but it makes no attempt to preserve distances across the whole dataset, so the unrolled result can come out visibly stretched or warped at a larger scale.

This follows directly from what it optimises. Nothing in either stage ever mentions two far-apart points, so nothing protects the distance between them.

### 5 · The cost

The catch is cost: the final stage of the algorithm scales with the square of the number of instances, which makes LLE a poor fit for very large datasets even though it can produce excellent embeddings for moderately sized ones.

Squared growth in rows is the kind of scaling you already distrust in a join: ten times the data is a hundred times the work.

**One-liner for your notes:** LLE learns each point as a weighted mix of its k nearest neighbours, then repositions every point in fewer dimensions keeping those weights — excellent locally, warped globally, and quadratic in the row count.

blocks.title: Figure 8-10
blocks.caption: Unrolled Swiss roll using LLE
blocks.alt: Figure 8-10: Unrolled Swiss roll using LLE

blocks.title: Equation 8-4
blocks.caption: LLE step 1: linearly modeling local relationships
blocks.latex: \begin{aligned} & \widehat{\mathbf{W}} = \underset{\mathbf{W}}{\operatorname{argmin}} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( \mathbf{x}^{(i)} - \sum_{j=1}^{m} w_{i,j} \mathbf{x}^{(j)} \right)^2 \\ & \text{subject to } \begin{cases} w_{i,j} = 0 & \text{if } \mathbf{x}^{(j)} \text{ is not one of the } k \text{ n.n. of } \mathbf{x}^{(i)} \\ \sum_{j=1}^{m} w_{i,j} = 1 & \text{for } i = 1, 2, \cdots, m \end{cases} \end{aligned}
blocks.explain:
**Why the equations look like this**

Both are the same sentence written twice: "find the thing that makes the total
reconstruction gap as small as possible". `argmin` is read as "the value of the thing
underneath that makes what follows smallest" — so Equation 8-4 says "the weight matrix
that minimises this total", and Equation 8-5 says "the set of new positions that
minimises this total". The bracket in each one is the same shape: an instance, minus
the reconstruction of that instance from its neighbours. Square it so an overshoot and
an undershoot cannot cancel out, and add over every instance.

The only real difference is which side is unknown. Stage one holds the points still
and solves for weights. Stage two holds those weights still and solves for points.
That is why the two equations look almost identical and mean opposite things.

**Why the two constraints, and why only on stage one.** The first — a weight of zero
for anything that is not one of the k nearest neighbours — is what makes the method
*local*: without it, a point could be described using rows on the other side of the
roll, and the method would lose the very thing it exists to capture. The second — the
weights for one instance summing to one — normalises each reconstruction into a
weighted average of those neighbours rather than a scaled-up or scaled-down version of
them. Stage two needs no constraints at all, because the weights it must respect are
already fixed.

**Is this standard?** Yes. This is the canonical two-stage formulation of LLE, from
the paper the book cites (Roweis and Saul, 2000). It is not a simplification written
for this chapter.

**The general form.** k (how many neighbours) and d (the target dimension) are the two
settings you choose; in the code card below they are 10 and 2. The equations do not
change shape when you change either one — only the size of the weight matrix and the
number of coordinates per point change.

**Terms these introduce:** a **weight** is how much one neighbour contributes to
rebuilding a point; the **weight matrix** is all of those together, one row per
instance; an **embedding** is the set of new low-dimensional positions; **argmin**
means "whichever value makes this smallest"; a **constraint** is a condition the
answer must satisfy while being minimised.

**Every piece of both equations**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| W with a hat | W hat | the best weight matrix, the answer to stage 1 |
| Z with a hat | Z hat | the best new positions, the answer to stage 2 |
| argmin | arg min over W | the W making what follows smallest |
| m | m | how many training instances there are |
| i | i | which instance we are rebuilding |
| j | j | which other instance is contributing |
| x with a raised i | x superscript i | instance i, in the original space |
| z with a raised i | z superscript i | instance i, in the new smaller space |
| w sub i j | w i j | how much instance j contributes to instance i |
| the sum sign | sum over j | add the contributions of every other instance |
| the outer sum | sum over i | add the gaps over every instance |
| the squared bracket | squared | multiply the gap by itself |
| k n.n. | k nearest neighbours | the k closest instances to this one |

**The formulas in plain words**

- Equation 8-4: choose the weights so that every point is as close as possible to a
weighted average of its k nearest neighbours — with non-neighbours contributing
nothing, and each point's weights adding up to one.
- Equation 8-5: keeping those weights, choose new positions in d dimensions so that
every point is still as close as possible to the same weighted average of the same
neighbours.

**Real numbers plugged in**

From the code card below: 1,000 Swiss roll samples with noise 0.2, k = 10 neighbours,
d = 2 output dimensions.

1. Stage one solves 1,000 small problems, one per instance. Each one has 10 unknown
weights, because the other 990 are forced to zero.
2. The weight matrix is therefore 1,000 by 1,000 with only 10 nonzero entries per row.
3. Stage two searches for 1,000 positions of 2 numbers each — 2,000 unknowns — and
changes none of the weights.

**Where the cost comes from**

The book gives three cost terms: finding the neighbours, optimising the weights, and
building the low-dimensional positions — and only the last one grows with the square
of the instance count. That is the term the lesson warns about. As a ratio: ten times
the rows is a hundred times that work, and a thousand times the rows is a million
times that work. It is the growth curve of a join with no key, and it is why the
answer for large data is a different algorithm rather than a tuned LLE.

blocks.title: Equation 8-5
blocks.caption: LLE step 2: reducing dimensionality while preserving relationships

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.datasets import make_swiss_roll
from sklearn.manifold import LocallyLinearEmbedding

X_swiss, t = make_swiss_roll(n_samples=1000, noise=0.2, random_state=42)
lle = LocallyLinearEmbedding(n_components=2, n_neighbors=10, random_state=42)
X_unrolled = lle.fit_transform(X_swiss)
```

items.term: Why "local" is the whole design and the whole limitation
items.text: Every constraint in stage one points inward: zero weight for non-neighbours, weights summing to one. That is what lets LLE follow a bend, because a rolled surface is locally flat everywhere even though it is globally curved. It is also exactly why the large-scale shape comes out warped — nothing in either stage ever writes down a relationship between two far-apart points, so nothing defends it. The strength and the weakness are the same sentence.

items.term: Fix one side, solve for the other — a pattern worth recognising
items.text: Stage one fixes the points and solves for weights; stage two fixes those weights and solves for points. Alternating which half is unknown is a standard way to attack a problem that is hard when both halves move at once. The same shape turns up again in clustering and in matrix factorisation, and recognising it makes several later algorithms read as variations rather than as new material.

items.term: Quadratic cost is a ceiling, not a warning
items.text: A term growing with the square of the row count means ten times the data is a hundred times the work, and a thousand times the data is a million times the work. That is not something you tune your way out of, which is why the book's answer for larger datasets is a different algorithm rather than a faster LLE. Knowing which cost term dominates is what tells you whether a method is worth optimising or worth replacing.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Why does LLE preserve local structure well but not global structure? Tie your answer back to what the algorithm actually optimizes.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The code uses k = 10 neighbours. What happens to the unrolled result when k is much smaller or much larger, and is there a principled way to choose it?
Look up: Sam T. Roweis and Lawrence K. Saul, "Nonlinear Dimensionality Reduction by Locally Linear Embedding", Science 290, no. 5500 (2000): 2323-2326 — the paper this book cites for LLE.

items.term: Other Dimensionality Reduction Techniques

blocks.content:
Four more reducers worth knowing by name, each optimising for something different: MDS keeps straight-line distances, Isomap keeps shortest-path distances, t-SNE keeps clusters visible, LDA keeps classes apart.

**The question this lesson answers:** beyond PCA, random projection and LLE, what else does Scikit-Learn ship — and which one do you pick for which job?

### The big picture

| Technique | Tries to preserve | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| MDS | straight-line distance, every pair | already low-dim data |
| Isomap | shortest-path distance on a graph | structure that curves |
| t-SNE | similar close, dissimilar apart | seeing clusters |
| LDA | separation between classes | feeding a classifier |

### 1 · MDS

**MDS (multidimensional scaling)** tries to preserve the straight-line distance between every pair of instances as it reduces dimensions — a strategy that works well on data that is already fairly low-dimensional, where random projection tends to struggle.

Note the division of labour with the previous lesson: both MDS and random projection are in the distance-preserving business, and each covers the end of the range the other is weak at.

### 2 · Isomap

**Isomap** instead builds a graph connecting each instance to its nearby neighbors and preserves geodesic distance — the number of nodes on the shortest path between the two instances in that graph — rather than straight-line distance, which lets it capture structure that curves through the original space.

**Geodesic** means distance measured along the surface rather than through the air. On a rolled-up Swiss roll, two points can be nearly touching in 3D while sitting on opposite ends of the unrolled sheet; straight-line distance says they are close, shortest-path-through-the-graph says they are not. It is the difference between two nodes being physically near each other and being many hops apart in a graph traversal.

### 3 · t-SNE

**t-SNE** takes yet another goal: keep instances that are already similar close together and push dissimilar ones apart, which makes it especially good for visually inspecting clusters in high-dimensional data, though it is mostly a visualization tool rather than a general-purpose preprocessing step.

Read that caveat as a warning, not a footnote. A method that deliberately exaggerates separation produces a picture that is easy to over-read, and a picture is not a feature table.

### 4 · LDA

Finally, **LDA (linear discriminant analysis)** is really a classification algorithm at heart, but during training it learns the axes that separate classes most cleanly — those axes can then be reused to project data onto a hyperplane that keeps classes as far apart as possible, making it a strong dimensionality-reduction step specifically when a classifier will run afterward.

This is the one technique here that looks at the labels. PCA, random projection, LLE, MDS, Isomap and t-SNE all reduce using the inputs alone; LDA uses the answer column as well, which is exactly why it can aim at class separation rather than at spread or distance.

### 5 · The Swiss roll test

Run against the Swiss roll, MDS keeps its overall curve, Isomap discards that curvature entirely, and t-SNE flattens it while also exaggerating cluster separation — each a different, deliberate trade-off. Figure 8-11 below puts the three side by side.

Whether keeping the large-scale curve is good or bad is not a property of the algorithm; it depends on what runs next.

**One-liner for your notes:** pick the reducer by what you need preserved — pairwise distance (MDS), distance along the surface (Isomap), visible clusters (t-SNE), or class separation (LDA, the only one here that reads the labels).

blocks.title: Figure 8-11
blocks.caption: Using various techniques to reduce the Swiss roll to 2D
blocks.alt: Figure 8-11: Using various techniques to reduce the Swiss roll to 2D

items.term: Reducers differ by what they refuse to lose
items.text: Every method here throws something away; they differ only in what they protect. PCA protects variance, random projection and MDS protect pairwise distance, Isomap protects distance measured along the surface, t-SNE protects who-is-near-whom, LDA protects separation between classes. Choosing a reducer is therefore not a quality ranking — it is naming which property the step after it depends on.

items.term: Supervised reduction is a different category
items.text: LDA reads the labels; none of the others do. That makes it strictly better informed when labels exist and unusable when they do not — and it also makes it capable of leaking the answer into the features if it is fitted on data that later gets scored. Any reduction that consumes the target has to be fitted under the same discipline as the model itself, not treated as neutral preprocessing.

items.term: A visualisation method is not a preprocessing method
items.text: t-SNE deliberately amplifies separation. That is a feature when a person is looking at the picture and a defect when a model consumes the output, because the distances in the result no longer mean what distances usually mean. The rule generalises: a transform tuned to make something legible to people is not automatically a transform that preserves what an algorithm needs.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: You need to reduce dimensionality specifically to help a downstream classifier separate its classes. Which of MDS, Isomap, t-SNE or LDA would you pick, and why?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: MDS keeps the Swiss roll's curve and Isomap discards it. For a real task rather than a picture, how would you decide whether keeping large-scale structure helps or hurts?
Look up: the scikit-learn user guide section on manifold learning (the `sklearn.manifold` module), which compares these methods on the same data and discusses the trade-offs.

Train a random forest classifier on the dataset and time how long it takes, then evaluate the resulting model on the test set. You should get a nice visualization with well-separated clusters of digits. Try using other dimensionality reduction algorithms, such as PCA, LLE, or MDS, and compare the resulting visualizations.

items.term: Why Machine Learning Needs Unsupervised Techniques

blocks.content:
Almost all the data in the world arrives with no answer column attached, and unsupervised learning is the set of techniques that work anyway.

**The question this lesson answers:** a factory line can photograph thousands of parts a day for almost nothing, but nobody has written "good" or "defective" beside any of those photos. What can you still learn from data that has no labels?

### The big picture

| Family | The question it answers |
|---|---|
| Clustering | which instances belong together? |
| Anomaly detection | which instances are not normal? |
| Density estimation | where is the data thick, and where thin? |

A **label** is the answer column — the value a supervised model is trained to reproduce. An **instance** is one row. Everything in this chapter runs with the rows and none of the answers.

### 1 · Labels are the scarce thing, not data

Most industry effort in machine learning goes toward supervised learning, but this chapter opens by pointing out an irony: almost all the data actually available in the world has no labels attached.

A concrete example makes the imbalance real: a factory line can generate thousands of photos of manufactured parts every day almost for free, but turning those photos into a usable defect classifier requires a human expert to sit down and label each one as good or bad. That labeling step is slow, expensive, and has to be redone every time the product changes, so the labeled subset stays small and the resulting classifier disappoints.

If you run ingestion pipelines this shape is familiar. The rows land cheaply and continuously; the column that says what each row *means* is the one a person fills in by hand, one row at a time. And a product change does not just add work — it invalidates the work already done, so the whole labeling process starts over from scratch.

### 2 · LeCun's cake

Yann LeCun's cake metaphor captures why that matters — unsupervised learning is the bulk of the cake, supervised learning is only the icing, and reinforcement learning is the cherry on top.

The ranking is by how much of the world's data each paradigm can use, not by how much attention each one gets. Supervised learning gets the investment; unsupervised learning has the data.

### 3 · Three families, three jobs

The chapter groups the unsupervised tasks it will cover into three families.

**Clustering** groups similar instances together without being told in advance what the groups are, and it turns out to be useful for far more than just grouping — customer segmentation, search, image segmentation, and even helping a supervised model when labels are scarce. In SQL terms it is a `GROUP BY` where the algorithm invents the grouping column instead of you naming it.

**Anomaly detection** (also called **outlier detection**) works the opposite direction: it learns what normal data looks like and then flags instances that don't fit that pattern. The normal instances are called **inliers**; the odd ones are **anomalies** or **outliers**.

**Density estimation** underlies both — it estimates the probability distribution that generated the data, and low-density regions are exactly where anomalies tend to live. **Density** here just means how crowded a region of the data is: many instances packed close together is high density, a lonely instance out on its own is low density.

That last sentence is the hinge of the whole chapter: once you can say how crowded any point in the data is, "this one is weird" becomes "this one sits where almost nothing else sits".

**One-liner for your notes:** labels are expensive and data is cheap, so this chapter learns structure from unlabeled rows in three ways — clustering (who groups with whom), anomaly detection (who does not fit), and density estimation (how crowded each region is), which is what the other two rest on.

items.term: Why “no labels” is an economic fact, not a technical one
items.text: The data lacks labels not because a sensor failed to record them but because the label is a human judgement that costs human time. That reframes the whole chapter: every technique in it is a way of making a fixed budget of human attention go further. The methods that win here are the ones that spend a person's hour better, not the ones with the cleverest mathematics.

items.term: Density is the primitive the other two rest on
items.text: Clustering asks which dense region a point belongs to; anomaly detection asks whether it belongs to any. Both are readings of the same estimated density, which is why the chapter ends on Gaussian mixtures — a density model that happens to cluster and to detect anomalies as well. If you keep one idea from this lesson, keep that the three tasks are three questions asked of one estimate.

items.term: Where the analogy to a derived column breaks
items.text: A label is not a derived column. A derived column can always be recomputed from the row; a label cannot, because the information was never in the row to begin with. That is why you cannot backfill labels the way you backfill a computed field, and why a product change invalidates existing labels rather than merely requiring a re-run.

items: Using your own example (not the factory one from the book), name a task where labeled data is scarce but unlabeled data is abundant.

items.term: What Clustering Is and Why It Matters

blocks.content:
Clustering is assigning every instance to a group of similar instances when nobody has told you what the groups are — and it turns out to be useful for far more than grouping.

**The question this lesson answers:** the iris dataset has three real species in it. If you delete the species column, can an algorithm find those three groups again from the raw measurements alone — and what else is that ability good for?

### The big picture

| | Classification | Clustering |
|---|---|---|
| Is given | the categories, from labeled examples | nothing but the rows |
| Must produce | the right category per instance | groups it invents itself |
| Learning type | supervised | unsupervised |

Both assign every instance to a category. That is the whole family resemblance, and the difference is one word: **told**.

### 1 · There is no single definition of a cluster

Clustering has no single textbook definition — what counts as a cluster depends entirely on the algorithm and the shape of the data. Some algorithms look for instances gathered tightly around a **centroid**, which is the mean point of a group, its centre of gravity. Others trace out continuous regions of high density regardless of shape. Some build a hierarchy of clusters nested inside clusters.

What ties them together is the goal: assign each instance to a group of similar instances, without anyone supplying the group labels in advance. That is the key contrast with classification — both assign every instance to a category, but classification is told the categories up front from labeled examples, while clustering has to discover them.

This is genuinely different from anything in SQL. A `GROUP BY country` needs a `country` column to exist. Clustering is a `GROUP BY` where the algorithm has to invent the grouping column first, from the other columns, and then group on it.

### 2 · The iris example

The iris dataset makes the contrast concrete: with species labels visible, a classifier separates the three species easily; strip the labels away and clustering has to rediscover roughly the same three groups from the raw measurements alone, and it does a surprisingly good job when it can see all four features rather than just two.

Figure 9-1 below shows both sides. The two-feature picture is the honest one for your eye: the lower-left group is obvious, and it is genuinely not obvious that the upper-right blob is two groups rather than one. The algorithm does better than your eye here only because it can use all four measurements at once, while the figure can only draw two of them.

A **feature** is one input column — here, petal length, petal width, sepal length, sepal width.

### 3 · What clustering is actually used for

Beyond the obvious "group similar things" use case, clustering is a workhorse behind several other techniques:

- **customer segmentation** — group customers by behaviour so marketing can target each segment
- **data analysis** — run it as a first pass over any new dataset to understand its structure
- **dimensionality reduction** — replace a raw feature vector with a shorter vector of distances-to-each-cluster-centre
- **feature engineering** — feed cluster membership in as an extra feature for a downstream supervised model
- **anomaly detection** — flag instances that don't fit well into any cluster
- **semi-supervised learning** — spread a handful of labels across an entire cluster
- **search engines** — power reverse-image search, by returning everything in the query image's cluster
- **image segmentation** — reduce an image's colour palette

The dimensionality-reduction trick deserves a second read, because it is not obvious. If you have 100 feature columns and 5 clusters, you can throw away the 100 columns and keep 5 numbers per row: how far that row is from each cluster centre. Five columns instead of a hundred, and often enough information left to carry on with.

The anomaly use is the mirror image of the same measurement: an instance that is far from *every* cluster centre — low affinity to all of them — is the one you flag.

**One-liner for your notes:** clustering invents the grouping column instead of being handed it, which is why it doubles as a dimensionality reducer, a feature generator, an anomaly detector and a label-spreader.

blocks.title: Figure 9-1
blocks.caption: Classification (left) versus clustering (right)
blocks.alt: Figure 9-1: Classification (left) versus clustering (right)

items.term: Why “no universal definition” is a design freedom, not sloppiness
items.text: Each algorithm's definition of a cluster is a hypothesis about what structure the data has: centroid-based says round blobs, density-based says connected dense regions, hierarchical says nested groups. Choosing an algorithm is therefore choosing a hypothesis. When two algorithms disagree badly on the same data, that is usually the data telling you neither hypothesis fits, not one of them being buggy.

items.term: Distances-to-reference-points generalises far past clustering
items.text: Replacing raw features with distances to k learned reference points is a pattern that reappears throughout machine learning — radial basis functions, prototype methods, vector quantisation. What makes it work is that the reference points are learned from the data rather than chosen by hand, so the new coordinates describe where a row sits relative to structure the data actually has.

items.term: The catch nobody states: cluster indices are not stable
items.text: Because the grouping column is invented, nothing guarantees that cluster 3 means the same thing after a refit, a different random seed, or new data. Anything you persist downstream must key off the cluster's content — its centroid, its members — rather than its number, or a harmless retraining silently scrambles every join built on it.

items.term: Fitting k-means and Reading Its Output

blocks.content:
Training k-means looks like any other Scikit-Learn estimator, with one difference that cannot be avoided: you must tell it how many clusters to find.

**The question this lesson answers:** given a dataset of five visible blobs and no labels at all, what do you actually type, and what does the fitted object hand back to you afterwards?

### The big picture

```
KMeans(n_clusters=k) ──fit_predict(X)──> y_pred
   fitted object then exposes:
     labels_          one cluster index per training row
     cluster_centers_ the k centroid coordinates
     predict(X_new)   nearest centroid wins
     transform(X)     distance to EVERY centroid
```

### 1 · The one hyperparameter you cannot skip

Training a k-means clusterer in Scikit-Learn takes exactly the shape you'd expect from any other estimator: instantiate it with the number of clusters you want, then call `fit` (or, since there's no separate labels to fit against, `fit_predict`, which trains and returns cluster assignments in one call).

The one hyperparameter you cannot skip is **k**, the number of clusters — the algorithm has no way to infer it from the data on its own, and picking it well is a real design decision, not a formality. A **hyperparameter** is a setting you choose before training and that stays fixed during it, like a `--conf` flag on a Spark submit rather than something the job works out for itself.

In the code card below, `k = 5` because Figure 9-2 shows five obvious blobs. Real data rarely offers that courtesy, which is why two later lessons are entirely about choosing k.

### 2 · What "label" means here — read this twice

Once trained, the fitted object exposes several useful attributes. `labels_` holds the cluster index assigned to each training instance — and it's worth being careful with vocabulary here: this "label" is just an arbitrary cluster index the algorithm invented, not a real-world class name the way a label means in classification.

Cluster 3 does not mean anything. It is a bucket number. Re-run with a different random seed and the same rows may land in a bucket called 1 instead, with no error anywhere, because nothing ever promised the numbering was stable.

`cluster_centers_` holds the coordinates of each cluster's centroid, and `predict()` assigns brand-new instances to whichever centroid is nearest, producing a **Voronoi-tessellation**-shaped decision boundary where every point in space belongs to its nearest centroid's region. Figure 9-3 below draws those regions: straight-edged tiles, one per centroid, covering the whole plane.

### 3 · Hard clustering versus soft clustering

Beyond **hard assignment** (one instance, one cluster), `transform()` gives you **soft clustering**: instead of a single label, it returns the distance from an instance to every centroid at once.

| | Hard clustering | Soft clustering |
|---|---|---|
| Method | predict() | transform() |
| Returns per row | one cluster index | k distances |
| Throws away | how close the runner-up was | nothing |

That second row is the interesting one. Feeding a high-dimensional dataset through `transform()` turns it into a k-dimensional dataset of distances, which is itself a legitimate nonlinear **dimensionality-reduction** technique, and those distances can also be handed to a downstream model as extra engineered features.

Concretely: 100 columns in, k columns out, where each output column is "distance to centroid j". You have replaced the raw measurements with a description of where each row sits relative to the structure the data itself revealed.

**One-liner for your notes:** you must supply k; afterwards `labels_` gives the invented cluster index per row, `predict()` sends new rows to the nearest centroid, and `transform()` returns all k distances, which doubles as a dimensionality reducer.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs

X, y = make_blobs([...]) # make the blobs: y contains the cluster IDs, but we
                          # will not use them; that's what we want to predict
k = 5
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=42)
y_pred = kmeans.fit_predict(X)
```

items.term: Why k must be supplied, and what that admission costs
items.text: k-means optimises a score that improves monotonically as k grows, so it has nothing internal that could tell it to stop. The requirement is not an interface wart; it is the algorithm admitting that “how many groups are there” is a question about the world, not about the data. Every method later in this chapter for choosing k is an external criterion smuggled in from outside the objective.

items.term: Soft clustering is where clustering stops being clustering
items.text: Once transform() hands back k distances, nothing has been partitioned — each row has simply been re-described in new coordinates. That is why the same fitted object is simultaneously a clusterer, a dimensionality reducer and a feature generator. The hard label is a lossy summary of the distances, not the other way round.

items.term: The vocabulary collision is worth defending against
items.text: labels_ meaning “cluster index” while label elsewhere means “ground-truth answer” causes real bugs when clustering output feeds a supervised pipeline. Renaming the column to cluster_id the moment it leaves the model costs nothing and removes an entire class of confusion, including the tempting mistake of scoring cluster indices against true classes.

items.term: How k-means Actually Finds Its Clusters

blocks.content:
k-means breaks a chicken-and-egg problem by guessing, then alternating between two steps that are each easy once the other is known.

**The question this lesson answers:** you need centroids to label the instances, and you need labels to compute the centroids, and you start with neither. How does the algorithm get off the ground, and why does it ever stop?

### The big picture

```
place k centroids at random
  ├─> label: each instance -> nearest centroid
  └─> re-centre: each centroid -> mean of its instances
repeat until the centroids stop moving
```

### 1 · The deadlock, and the way out

The k-means procedure is a neat chicken-and-egg trick.

- If you already knew where the centroids were, labeling every instance would be trivial — just assign it to the nearest one.
- If you already knew every instance's label, finding the centroids would be trivial too — just average the instances in each group.
- The problem is you start knowing neither.

k-means breaks the deadlock by guessing: it places k centroids at random starting positions (typically by picking k real instances from the dataset and using their locations), then alternates between the two easy steps — label every instance using the current centroids, then recompute each centroid as the mean of the instances now assigned to it — repeating until the centroids stop moving.

Note the initialisation detail, because it is easy to skim past: the starting centroids are usually *real rows lifted out of the dataset*, not arbitrary points in space. That guarantees every starting centroid sits somewhere the data actually lives.

Figure 9-4 below draws the loop, one panel per half-step.

### 2 · Why it always terminates

This is guaranteed to finish in a finite number of rounds, and usually a small one.

The argument is worth following because it is the only guarantee k-means offers:

1. Define the total squared distance between instances and their assigned centroid — this is a single number describing the whole clustering.
2. The labeling half-step can only lower it or leave it flat: moving an instance to a *nearer* centroid cannot increase its distance.
3. The re-centring half-step can only lower it or leave it flat either: the mean of a group is exactly the point that minimises squared distance to that group.
4. So the number keeps shrinking but can never go negative — and a quantity that keeps shrinking but can never go negative has to bottom out eventually.

### 3 · Terminating is not the same as being right

What convergence does not guarantee is optimality: the algorithm can settle into a **local optimum** that looks nothing like the best possible clustering, purely because of where the random centroids happened to start.

A local optimum is a solution that cannot be improved by any of the small moves the algorithm knows how to make, even though a completely different arrangement would be far better. The loop stops because nothing is moving, not because the answer is good. Figure 9-5 below shows two such dead ends on the same five blobs.

### 4 · How fast it actually is

In the worst theoretical case the running time can blow up exponentially with the number of instances, though in practice, on data that has real cluster structure, k-means runs close to linear time and is one of the fastest clustering methods available.

Read the condition, not just the claim: "on data that has real cluster structure". The reassuring speed is contingent on the data having the shape k-means is looking for.

**One-liner for your notes:** guess k centroids, then alternate label and re-centre; the total squared distance can only shrink so it must stop, but where it stops depends on where it started.

items.term: The standard way to prove an iterative algorithm halts
items.text: “It decreases at every step and cannot go below zero, so it must stop” is the template behind almost every convergence argument you will meet, including EM later in this chapter. Notice what it never gives you: no bound on where it stops, and no bound on how long it takes. Those need separate arguments, and k-means has a satisfying answer to neither.

items.term: A local optimum is a property of the search, not of the data
items.text: The five-blob dataset has one obviously best clustering, and k-means can still miss it, because the only moves available are “reassign to the nearest centroid” and “recompute the mean”. From a bad start, no sequence of those moves reaches the good answer. When you meet a local optimum, suspect the move set before you suspect the data.

items.term: Why the starting centroids are real rows
items.text: Seeding centroids at actual data locations guarantees that no centroid begins in empty space with zero members, which would otherwise produce an empty cluster and an undefined mean on the very first re-centring step. It is a small detail, and it is the difference between an algorithm that simply runs and one that needs a special case for degenerate input.
