items: Why does the k-means loop (label, then re-center, then repeat) always terminate instead of running forever?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: k-means was invented at Bell Labs for pulse-code modulation, not for data analysis. What was the original problem, and does it explain why the algorithm minimises squared distance rather than plain distance?
Look up: Stuart P. Lloyd, “Least Squares Quantization in PCM”, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 28, no. 2 (1982): 129-137 — footnote 1 of this chapter.

items.term: Fixing Bad Luck: Centroid Initialization and k-means++

blocks.content:
Because a random start can strand k-means in a bad solution, Scikit-Learn runs it several times and keeps the best — and starts it more cleverly than pure chance.

**The question this lesson answers:** the previous lesson showed k-means settling into visibly wrong clusterings depending on where its centroids happened to land. What does the library do about that, and how does it decide which of several runs was "best"?

### The big picture

| Escape route | What it does |
|---|---|
| init= plus n_init=1 | you supply the starting centroids yourself |
| n_init=10 (default) | 10 random restarts, keep the lowest inertia |
| k-means++ (default) | spread the starting centroids out on purpose |

### 1 · The manual route

The manual escape applies when you already have a good guess for where the centroids should sit — perhaps from an earlier clustering run — in which case you can hand `KMeans` an explicit array of starting points through the `init` parameter and set `n_init` to 1, since there's no point running multiple random restarts when you already know roughly where to start.

`n_init` is the number of independent restarts. Leaving it at 10 while also pinning `init` would run the same deterministic start ten times and throw nine of them away.

### 2 · The automatic route, and what "best" means

The automatic route is what actually runs by default: fit the whole algorithm `n_init` separate times, each with a different random start, and keep whichever run scored best.

"Best" is measured by **inertia** — the sum of squared distances from every instance to its assigned centroid — and lower inertia means a tighter, better clustering. This is the same quantity the previous lesson used to prove the loop terminates; here it is reused as a scoreboard between whole runs.

The book's numbers make the scoreboard concrete. On the five-blob dataset, the two unlucky solutions in Figure 9-5 score about 219.4 and 258.6, while the good clustering in Figure 9-3 scores 211.6 — so picking the lowest of several runs genuinely picks the picture you would have picked by eye.

Scikit-Learn defaults `n_init` to 10, so a single call to `fit()` is secretly ten full runs of the algorithm competing against each other. Worth knowing before you benchmark: your "one run" is ten.

### 3 · k-means++, the smarter start

The smarter fix, and the one that actually reduces how many restarts you need, is the **k-means++** initialization scheme.

Instead of placing all k centroids uniformly at random, it places them one at a time: the first is picked uniformly at random from the data, and every subsequent one is picked with a probability proportional to its squared distance from the nearest centroid already chosen.

Read that rule slowly, because the word "probability" is doing real work. It is not "pick the farthest point" — that would be deterministic and would chase outliers. It is a weighted lottery in which far-away points hold more tickets, and the weight is the *squared* distance, so twice as far means four times the tickets.

That weighting deliberately favors points far from existing centroids, which spreads the initial centroids out and makes a bad, clustered-together starting configuration far less likely. Two centroids landing inside the same real blob — the failure mode behind Figure 9-5 — becomes improbable rather than merely unlucky.

Scikit-Learn's `KMeans` uses k-means++ by default.

**One-liner for your notes:** inertia (total squared distance to the assigned centroid) is the scoreboard; `n_init=10` runs ten starts and keeps the lowest, and k-means++ makes each start better by drawing new centroids with probability proportional to squared distance from the nearest one already picked.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
good_init = np.array([[-3, 3], [-3, 2], [-3, 1], [-1, 2], [0, 2]])
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=5, init=good_init, n_init=1, random_state=42)
kmeans.fit(X)
```

items.term: Restarts are a confession about the loss surface
items.text: Running the same algorithm ten times and keeping the best only makes sense when the objective has many local minima and each run is cheap. That combination is common enough that the pattern recurs across machine learning, but it is a workaround rather than a solution: it lowers the probability of a bad answer without ever ruling one out.

items.term: Why the smarter initialisation is random rather than greedy
items.text: Always taking the point farthest from the existing centroids would be deterministic and would pick outliers every single time, since an outlier is by definition far from everything. Sampling with probability proportional to squared distance keeps the spreading effect while giving a lone extreme point only a modest chance of being chosen. The randomness here is a robustness device, not a shortcut.

items.term: The same number can be a valid criterion and an invalid one
items.text: Inertia is legitimate for choosing between runs at a fixed k, because every run was trying to minimise exactly that. It becomes illegitimate the moment k varies, because models with different k are no longer comparable on that scale. Knowing which comparison you are in matters more than knowing the formula.

items: Why does k-means++ make it less likely you'll need many random restarts, compared to plain uniform random initialization?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The k-means++ paper argues the smarter initialisation pays for itself. What does it actually prove about the quality of the final clustering — a worst-case guarantee, or an expectation?

Look up: David Arthur and Sergei Vassilvitskii, “k-Means++: The Advantages of Careful Seeding”, Proceedings of the 18th Annual ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms (2007): 1027-1035 — footnote 2 of this chapter.

items.term: Making k-means Faster: Elkan's Algorithm and Mini-Batch k-means

blocks.content:
Two separate improvements make k-means faster without trying to make it more accurate — one skips arithmetic, the other looks at less data.

**The question this lesson answers:** k-means is already fast. When it still is not fast enough, or the dataset does not fit in memory, what are the two levers, and what does each one cost you?

### The big picture

| | Elkan | Mini-batch |
|---|---|---|
| Changes | how distances are computed | how much data each round sees |
| Saves | unnecessary distance calculations | time and memory |
| Costs | bookkeeping overhead; can be slower | slightly worse final inertia |
| How to get it | algorithm="elkan" | MiniBatchKMeans |

Neither one changes what a good clustering is. They change how you get there.

### 1 · Elkan: skip the arithmetic you can prove is pointless

The first, due to Charles Elkan, skips distance calculations that the **triangle inequality** proves are unnecessary.

The triangle inequality is the ordinary fact that going straight from A to C is never longer than going A to B to C. If you already know a point's distance to two centroids and how far apart those centroids are, you can sometimes rule out one of them as the nearest without measuring anything new — the numbers you already hold bound the one you were about to compute.

This is the same instinct as a query planner pruning a partition: you are not computing a cheaper answer, you are proving you never needed the answer at all.

The catch is that keeping track of all those upper and lower distance bounds has its own overhead, so this acceleration helps a lot on some datasets and actually slows others down; it is opt-in via `algorithm="elkan"` rather than a default. A default that is sometimes a pessimisation cannot be a default.

### 2 · Mini-batch: look at a sample each round

The second improvement changes what data each iteration looks at rather than how it computes distances.

Ordinary k-means recomputes every centroid using the entire dataset on every iteration. **Mini-batch k-means** instead uses only a small random subset each time, nudging the centroids a little rather than recalculating them fully — the same mini-batch pattern used elsewhere in the book for online-style training.

If full-batch k-means is a nightly full refresh that rescans the whole table, mini-batch is a stream of micro-batches, each moving the answer a little. The analogy holds as far as "small increments instead of one big rescan"; it stops there, because every mini-batch here is a random sample of the same fixed dataset, not new arriving data.

### 3 · What you gain and what you give up

It typically runs three to four times faster than full-batch k-means — the book measures roughly 3.5 times on its own dataset — and, critically, it can process datasets too large to fit in memory at once.

That second property is the one that changes what is possible rather than just what is quick. The full-batch algorithm needs the whole dataset available to recompute a centroid; the mini-batch algorithm never needs more than one subset in RAM.

The tradeoff is a slightly worse final inertia than regular k-means would find — a small but visible gap in the book's benchmark, while the speed advantage of mini-batch k-means is greatest as k increases. Figure 9-6 below plots both facts side by side: quality on the left, time on the right.

Higher inertia means a slightly looser clustering. You are paying a little accuracy for a lot of speed, and knowing it is *higher* not lower is the point — an exam question will ask you that exact thing.

**One-liner for your notes:** Elkan trades bookkeeping for skipped distance calculations and is opt-in because it sometimes loses; mini-batch trades a slightly higher inertia for roughly 3.5x speed and the ability to cluster data that does not fit in memory.

blocks.caption: Mini-batch k-means has a higher inertia than k-means (left) but it is much faster (right),

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.cluster import MiniBatchKMeans

minibatch_kmeans = MiniBatchKMeans(n_clusters=5, random_state=42)
minibatch_kmeans.fit(X)
```

items.term: An optimisation that is sometimes a pessimisation
items.text: Elkan's bounds cost memory and bookkeeping for every instance against every centroid. When that overhead exceeds the distance computations it saves, the acceleration loses. This is the general shape of pruning: it pays only when the work being pruned is expensive relative to the test that prunes it — which is exactly why it ships opt-in rather than on.

items.term: Why an approximate method can beat an exact one
items.text: Mini-batch k-means deliberately accepts a worse answer. That is rational because the quality gap is small and roughly fixed while the speed gain grows with data size, so beyond some scale the approximate method finds a better clustering than the exact one finds within the time you actually have. Judging an algorithm on answer quality alone, ignoring the time budget, is the mistake this contrast exists to prevent.

items.term: Out-of-core is a different capability, not a faster version
items.text: Being able to cluster data that never fits in memory changes which problems are solvable at all, not merely how long they take. Speed is a gradient; the memory ceiling is a wall. When you compare these two improvements, notice that only one of them moves a wall — and that is usually the one worth reaching for first.

items.term: Choosing k: Why Inertia Alone Is a Trap

blocks.content:
You cannot choose k by picking the lowest inertia, because inertia always falls as k rises — so you read the shape of the curve instead of its minimum.

**The question this lesson answers:** k-means demands a number of clusters and gives you inertia as a quality score. Why can you not simply try every k and keep the best score, and what do you do instead?

### The big picture

```
inertia
  |*
  |  *
  |    *__ elbow at k=4
  |        *___
  |             *____
  +------------------------ k
  always falling -> minimum is useless
```

### 1 · Getting k wrong is visible

Picking the wrong k produces visibly bad clusterings — too few merges genuinely separate groups together, too many slices a single real cluster into arbitrary fragments — so getting k right matters. Figure 9-7 below shows both failures on the same five blobs, k too small on the left and too large on the right.

Note that the two failures are not symmetric in how they look. Too small looks like a clustering that is confidently wrong; too large looks like a clustering that is fussily right. Neither is what you want.

### 2 · Why the obvious method is broken

The tempting shortcut is to try several values of k and keep whichever one has the lowest inertia, since inertia is the metric k-means already optimizes internally.

That shortcut is broken by construction: inertia can only go down as k increases, because packing in more centroids always gives every instance a nearer center to attach to, all the way down to the degenerate case of one centroid per instance, where inertia hits zero.

Follow the degenerate case to the end, because it is the proof. Put a centroid on every single row. Every instance now sits at distance 0 from its own centroid, so the inertia of that clustering is exactly zero. Perfect score, zero information — you have described the data with a copy of the data.

A number that trends toward its best possible value at the most extreme (and clearly wrong) setting is not a stopping criterion. Anyone who has watched a model's training error fall to zero on the training set has met this shape before.

The book's example makes the trend concrete: inertia is roughly 653 at k=3, drops to about 212 at k=5, and keeps falling to about 119 at k=8 — monotonic, exactly as expected, and useless for choosing between them on its own.

### 3 · The elbow

The salvage is to plot inertia against k and look at the shape of the curve rather than its lowest point.

Early increases in k buy a large drop in inertia; past some point the curve flattens and further increases in k barely help. The bend where the steep part meets the flat part is called the **elbow**, and it's a reasonable (if coarse) candidate for k — in this dataset, that elbow sits around k=4, even though inertia keeps technically improving well beyond it.

The reasoning behind the bend: while k is below the number of real groups, each new centroid gets to split a genuinely mixed cluster, which buys a lot. Once every real group has its own centroid, each new one can only subdivide a group that was already coherent, which buys little. The elbow is where that changes.

Figure 9-8 below is that plot. Read it as a shape, not as a table of values.

**One-liner for your notes:** inertia falls monotonically with k and hits zero at one centroid per instance, so it cannot pick k; plot it against k and take the elbow, the bend where big gains turn into small ones.

blocks.caption: Bad choices for the number of clusters: when k is too small, separate clusters get merged
blocks.alt: Figure 9-7: Bad choices for the number of clusters: when k is too small, separate clusters get merged

blocks.caption: Plotting the inertia as a function of the number of clusters k

items.term: A metric a model optimises cannot select that model
items.text: Inertia is k-means's own objective, so “the model with the lowest inertia” only means “the model given the most freedom”. This generalises well past clustering: training loss cannot choose between model sizes either. Every technique in this chapter for choosing k is some way of importing information the objective does not contain.

items.term: Why the elbow works at all, and why it stays coarse
items.text: The bend exists because there is a real number of groups. Below it, each new centroid resolves a genuine mixture and buys a lot; above it, each new centroid only subdivides something already coherent and buys little. That is a real signal — but “where a curve bends” has no definition, so two readers of the same plot can pick different k. It is a heuristic with a reason behind it, which is the strongest claim available.

items.term: Push a setting to its extreme as a habit
items.text: Asking what a metric says at the most absurd possible setting is a cheap, general test of whether it can be trusted to choose anything. One centroid per instance drives inertia to zero, so the metric awards a perfect score to a model that has learned nothing. Run that check on any score before you let it pick a hyperparameter for you.

items.term: The Silhouette Score: A Sharper Tool for Choosing k

blocks.content:
The silhouette score asks a sharper question than inertia — for each instance, is it closer to its own cluster than to the next best one?

**The question this lesson answers:** the elbow said k=4 looked reasonable, but it could not tell you whether k=5 is just as good. What measurement can, and what does it cost?

### The big picture

| Coefficient near | Means |
|---|---|
| +1 | deep inside its own cluster, far from any rival |
| 0 | sitting right on a boundary between two clusters |
| −1 | probably assigned to the wrong cluster entirely |

### 1 · Why the elbow is not enough

The elbow method is quick but blunt — it only tells you roughly where a bend is, and it can't distinguish between two values of k that both look reasonable. The **silhouette score** is more expensive to compute but much more discriminating.

Expensive is literal. Inertia needs each instance's distance to one centroid. The silhouette needs each instance's distance to the *other instances*, which grows with the square of the dataset size.

### 2 · The coefficient, piece by piece

For a single instance, its silhouette coefficient is $(b - a) / \max(a, b)$, where $a$ is the average distance to other instances in its own cluster and $b$ is the average distance to instances in the nearest other cluster (the one that would be the best alternative home for it).

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| a | "a" | mean distance to its own cluster-mates |
| b | "b" | mean distance to the nearest OTHER cluster |
| b − a | "b minus a" | how much better its own cluster is |
| max(a, b) | "max of a and b" | the larger of the two, used to rescale |
| the whole | "b minus a over max a b" | one instance's silhouette coefficient |

**In plain words:** how much closer am I to my own group than to the next group, expressed as a fraction of the bigger of those two distances.

**With real numbers**, using the case from the cards below: an instance whose mean distance to its own cluster-mates is 2 and to the nearest other cluster is 6.

1. b − a = 6 − 2 = 4
2. max(a, b) = max(2, 6) = 6
3. 4 / 6 = 0.67

So 0.67 — comfortably inside its own cluster, though not at the extreme.

Dividing by `max(a, b)` is what pins the result between −1 and +1 whatever the units of your features are, which is what makes the three readings in the table above meaningful for any dataset.

The coefficient ranges from −1 to +1: near +1 means the instance sits comfortably deep inside its own cluster and far from any rival; near 0 means it's sitting right on a boundary between two clusters; near −1 means it may well have been assigned to the wrong cluster entirely.

### 3 · From one instance to one number

The silhouette score itself is just this coefficient averaged over every instance in the dataset, and Scikit-Learn computes it in one call given the data and the fitted labels. The code card below shows that call returning 0.655517642572828 for the five-blob model.

### 4 · What the extra resolution buys

Where this pays off over the elbow method is resolution: plotting the silhouette score against k in the book's example confirms k=4 is strong, but it also reveals that k=5 is nearly as good and clearly beats k=6 or k=7 — a distinction the inertia curve couldn't make at all. Figure 9-9 below is that plot.

Going one level deeper, a **silhouette diagram** plots every instance's individual coefficient, sorted by cluster, which exposes cluster-size imbalance that the single averaged score hides. An average of 0.66 can come from four balanced clusters or from one huge one and three slivers; the diagram shows which. The card below explains how to read the shapes, and Figure 9-10 shows them for several values of k.

**One-liner for your notes:** each instance scores (b − a) / max(a, b) — own-cluster distance against nearest-other-cluster distance, rescaled to −1..+1 — and averaging it over the dataset separates values of k that inertia cannot.

blocks.title: Reading a silhouette diagram
blocks.content:
A silhouette diagram draws one knife shape per cluster. The height of a knife shows how many instances the cluster holds, and its width shows the silhouette coefficients of those instances, sorted (wider is better). A vertical dashed line marks the mean silhouette score for that value of k. When many instances in a cluster stop short of the dashed line, the cluster is rather bad, because those instances are too close to other clusters.

In the book's diagrams, k = 3 and k = 6 give bad clusters, while k = 4 and k = 5 look good. With k = 4, the cluster at index 1 is rather big; with k = 5, all the clusters have similar sizes. So even though the overall silhouette score for k = 4 is slightly higher, the book prefers k = 5 to get clusters of similar sizes.

blocks.caption: Selecting the number of clusters k using the silhouette score
blocks.alt: Figure 9-9: Selecting the number of clusters k using the silhouette score

blocks.title: Figure 9-10
blocks.caption: Analyzing the silhouette diagrams for various values of k
blocks.alt: Figure 9-10: Analyzing the silhouette diagrams for various values of k

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
>>> from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score
>>> silhouette_score(X, kmeans.labels_)
0.655517642572828
```

items.term: Why the coefficient is rescaled, and what that buys
items.text: Dividing by the larger of the two distances makes the score dimensionless and bounded, so 0.65 means the same thing on pixel distances as on scaled financial features. A raw “b minus a” would be informative within one dataset and meaningless across datasets — and comparing k=4 against k=5 is exactly a comparison across differently-shaped clusterings.

items.term: Averaging hides shape, and shape is what you needed
items.text: One silhouette score compresses thousands of per-instance judgements into a single number, and the compression discards exactly the thing you were trying to see: whether the clusters are balanced. The diagram is the uncompressed view. This is the same argument as looking at a residual plot rather than only an error metric — and it is why the book prefers k=5 on shape after k=4 won on average.

items.term: Cost is why the blunt tool survives
items.text: Inertia needs one distance per instance; the silhouette needs distances between instances, which grows with the square of the dataset. The elbow is not kept for sentimental reasons — it is what stays affordable when the silhouette does not. Knowing which constraint binds is part of choosing the method.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: An instance has a silhouette coefficient of -0.4. What does that suggest about its cluster assignment?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: silhouette_score takes a metric argument. If you switch it from Euclidean to cosine distance, what changes about what a high score is claiming — and would that ever flip which k wins?
Look up: the scikit-learn user guide, “Clustering performance evaluation” — the “Silhouette Coefficient” subsection, plus the API reference for sklearn.metrics.silhouette_score.

items.term: Where k-means Breaks Down

blocks.content:
k-means judges everything by distance to a centre, so it quietly assumes clusters are round and similar in size — and on data that is not, it fails confidently.

**The question this lesson answers:** the algorithm is fast, scalable and simple. So where does it actually break, and is that something you can tune away?

### The big picture

```
k-means sees:          the data may be:
   O  O  O               (--)  ((( )))   /\
   round, same size      elliptical, different sizes,
                         different densities, tilted
```

### 1 · The assumption is in the mechanism, not in a setting

k-means earns its popularity by being fast, scalable, and simple to reason about, but it has real structural blind spots.

Because every decision it makes is based purely on distance to a centroid, it implicitly assumes clusters are roughly spherical and similar in size — a bias baked into the algorithm rather than a tunable setting.

That phrase is the whole lesson. There is no `cluster_shape="elliptical"` parameter to set. A centroid is a single point, and "nearest centroid wins" carves space into straight-edged tiles around points; a rule made only of points and distances cannot express *orientation* or *elongation*, because it has nowhere to put that information.

### 2 · What it looks like when it fails

Feed it three genuinely elliptical clusters of different sizes, densities, and orientations, and it produces solutions that look actively wrong to the eye: one otherwise-reasonable solution still misassigns a full quarter of one cluster to its neighbor, and a second local optimum is worse still, even though its inertia score is technically lower.

Sit with that last clause. The uglier picture wins on the score.

That is a reminder that inertia measures fit to a spherical assumption, not correctness. Inertia is the sum of squared distances to centroids — so it rewards exactly the arrangement that the centroid model prefers. Using it to judge a clustering the centroid model cannot represent is grading the answer with the same wrong ruler that produced it.

Figure 9-11 below shows both solutions.

The practical consequence for you: a metric that the model optimises internally is never an independent check on that model. This is why the next lessons reach for a different family rather than a different number.

### 3 · The fix is a different model

**Gaussian mixture models**, covered later in this chapter, handle exactly this elliptical-cluster case far better, because they explicitly model each cluster's own shape and orientation instead of just its center.

Where k-means stores one point per cluster, a Gaussian mixture stores a point *and* a description of the ellipse around it — so elongation and tilt have somewhere to live.

### 4 · The cheap mitigation you should do anyway

One practical mitigation that costs almost nothing: scale the input features before running k-means.

**Scaling** means putting every feature on a comparable range, so that a column measured in thousands does not automatically dominate a column measured in units. Unscaled features effectively stretch the distance metric along whichever axis has the largest raw range, distorting what "nearby" means and degrading the clustering.

Scaling doesn't guarantee round clusters, but it removes one easily avoidable source of bad results. It is the clustering equivalent of fixing units before you compare two columns: not clever, just necessary.

**One-liner for your notes:** k-means is structurally committed to round, similar-sized clusters because a centroid cannot encode shape or orientation, inertia rewards that same assumption so it cannot detect the failure, and the real fix is a Gaussian mixture — but scale your features first regardless.

blocks.title: Figure 9-11
blocks.caption: k-means fails to cluster these ellipsoidal blobs properly
blocks.alt: Figure 9-11: k-means fails to cluster these ellipsoidal blobs properly

items.term: Model bias is whatever the representation cannot express
items.text: A centroid is a point, and points plus a distance can only carve straight-edged, equal-in-all-directions regions. Elongation and tilt are not difficult for k-means, they are inexpressible — there is nowhere in the parameters to store them. Whenever a model fails in a consistent, characteristic way, ask what its parameters have no room to record; that is usually the answer.

items.term: A model's own objective is never an audit of that model
items.text: Here the visibly worse clustering scores better, because inertia and k-means share one assumption. It is the same failure as judging a straight-line model by how well a straight line fits curved data. An honest check has to come from outside the model family — your eyes, a differently-motivated metric, or a different model altogether.

items.term: Scaling is a hygiene step, not a fix
items.text: Scaling removes an accidental distortion of the distance metric; it does not make elliptical clusters round. Calling it a fix would hide a structural limitation behind a preprocessing step, and the next dataset would fail the same way. Do it always, and expect nothing from it beyond the removal of a known artefact.

items: Why does forgetting to scale your features before running k-means often hurt the result?

items: GaussianMixture has a covariance_type option whose “spherical” setting forces round clusters. Is a spherical Gaussian mixture then just k-means with extra steps, or does something still differ?

items.term: Clustering for Image Segmentation

blocks.content:
Clustering an image's pixels by colour is a real, useful application of k-means, and it works by throwing away the picture and keeping only a table of colours.

**The question this lesson answers:** an image is a grid of pixels, not a table of rows. How do you turn "split this photo into regions" into the ordinary clustering problem k-means already solves?

### The big picture

| Variant | Groups pixels that are |
|---|---|
| Colour segmentation | a similar colour |
| Semantic segmentation | part of the same TYPE of object |
| Instance segmentation | part of the same INDIVIDUAL object |

Only the first one is a k-means job. The other two need deep convolutional networks.

### 1 · Three levels of ambition

Image segmentation means splitting an image into meaningful regions, and the book distinguishes three levels of ambition.

**Colour segmentation** just groups pixels of similar colour. **Semantic segmentation** groups every pixel belonging to the same type of object — all pedestrians land in one segment, regardless of which specific person. **Instance segmentation** goes further still and separates each individual object into its own segment, so two pedestrians are two segments.

State-of-the-art semantic and instance segmentation both rely on deep convolutional networks, but plain colour segmentation is a perfect showcase for k-means precisely because it needs nothing fancier.

### 2 · Flattening the picture into a table

An RGB image loads as a 3D array — height, width, and three colour channels — where every pixel is really just a 3-number vector of red, green, and blue intensity. The book's ladybug photo loads with shape (533, 800, 3): 533 rows of pixels, 800 columns, 3 channels.

Reshape that array so every pixel becomes one row of a table (dropping the spatial height/width structure entirely, since colour segmentation doesn't need it), and you've turned image segmentation into an ordinary clustering problem over a colour point cloud.

That is what `image.reshape(-1, 3)` does in the code card below. The `-1` means "work out this dimension for me", so the 533 × 800 grid collapses into 426,400 rows of 3 columns. The result is exactly the shape every Scikit-Learn estimator wants: rows are samples, columns are features.

Three columns named `red`, `green`, `blue`, one row per pixel, and the fact that pixel 7 sat next to pixel 8 is simply not in the table any more. Colour segmentation does not need it, so it is not a loss.

### 3 · Cluster, then paint by numbers

Running k-means with, say, eight clusters groups similar colours together; replacing every pixel with its cluster's mean colour and reshaping back to the original image dimensions produces a colour-quantized image using only eight distinct colours total.

The one line worth decoding is `kmeans.cluster_centers_[kmeans.labels_]`. Read it right to left: `labels_` is one cluster index per pixel, and indexing the centre array by it swaps each index for that centre's actual colour. It is a lookup join — labels are the foreign key, `cluster_centers_` is the dimension table, and the output is one mean colour per pixel. Figure 9-12 below shows the result at several values of k.

### 4 · The failure that teaches you the most

The failure mode is instructive: a small, brightly coloured subject (the book's example is a ladybug) can lose its own dedicated cluster entirely and get absorbed into the surrounding colours, because k-means favors clusters of comparable size and a tiny bright region simply doesn't have enough pixels to outcompete the rest of the image for a cluster of its own. In the book's figure this happens once you use fewer than eight clusters.

Note what does *not* rescue it: being a vivid, unmistakable red. k-means is counting pixels, not noticing salience. A few thousand red pixels against hundreds of thousands of background pixels lose the vote, and the same-size bias from the previous lesson is exactly what is doing the losing.

**One-liner for your notes:** reshape the image to one row per pixel and three colour columns, cluster those rows, then swap each pixel for its cluster's mean colour — and expect small bright objects to be swallowed, because k-means prefers clusters of similar size.

blocks.title: Figure 9-12
blocks.caption: Image segmentation using k-means with various numbers of color clusters
blocks.alt: Figure 9-12: Image segmentation using k-means with various numbers of color clusters

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
X = image.reshape(-1, 3)
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=8, random_state=42).fit(X)
segmented_img = kmeans.cluster_centers_[kmeans.labels_]
segmented_img = segmented_img.reshape(image.shape)
```

items.term: Dropping structure on purpose
items.text: Reshaping the image throws away every spatial relationship, which sounds destructive until you notice that colour segmentation never uses spatial relationships. Deliberately discarding information the task does not need is a design move, not a compromise — and it is what lets one clustering algorithm serve a problem that looks nothing like clustering blobs.

items.term: Colour quantisation is vector quantisation
items.text: Replacing every pixel with its cluster's mean colour is the compression idea k-means was originally invented for: represent many values by a small codebook of representatives. Seen that way, cluster_centers_ is the codebook, labels_ is the compressed image, and the reconstruction error is the inertia you already know how to read.

items.term: The same-size bias, now in a photograph
items.text: The previous lesson's abstract limitation becomes visible here: the ladybug loses because it has few pixels, not because its colour is unremarkable. Hold onto that, because the same bias quietly decides outcomes in far less visual settings — a rare customer segment or a rare failure mode gets absorbed into its neighbours for exactly the same reason.

items: Why might a small, brightly colored object in a photo fail to get its own color cluster when k is small?

Look up: the scikit-learn examples gallery, “Color Quantization using K-Means”.

items.term: Clustering to Bootstrap Semi-Supervised Learning

blocks.content:
When you can only afford 50 labels, clustering tells you which 50 rows are worth labeling — and that choice alone is worth about ten accuracy points.

**The question this lesson answers:** you have 1,400 digit images and budget for a human to label exactly 50 of them. Which 50 should it be, and how much does the choice matter?

### The big picture

| Which 50 get labeled | Test accuracy |
|---|---|
| 50 random instances | about 74.8% |
| 50 representative instances | about 84.9% |
| (all 1,400, for reference) | about 90.7% |

Same budget. Same model. Different rows.

### 1 · The baseline, and why it is bad

**Semi-supervised learning** is exactly the situation where labeling is expensive: you have plenty of raw instances but can only afford to label a handful.

The book's demonstration uses the digits dataset with only 50 labels allowed out of a much larger training set, and the naive baseline — training logistic regression on 50 randomly chosen labeled instances — reaches only about 74.8% test accuracy, well below the roughly 90.7% you get with the full labeled set.

**Logistic regression** here is just the downstream classifier; nothing in this lesson depends on which one it is. The point is that the *same* classifier is used throughout, so any difference in accuracy comes from the data it was fed.

### 2 · Let clustering choose the rows

Clustering offers a smarter way to spend those same 50 labels.

Instead of labeling 50 random instances, cluster the entire training set into 50 clusters and, for each cluster, find the single training instance that sits closest to its centroid — the cluster's **representative instance**.

A representative instance is the most typical member of its group: the image that best embodies whatever that cluster is. Fifty clusters give fifty of them, one each.

Why that should help is worth saying out loud. Fifty random rows will over-sample whatever is common and may miss a whole digit entirely. Fifty cluster representatives are spread across the whole data by construction — one per region — so the human's effort is distributed rather than clumped.

### 3 · The two lines that find them

Scikit-Learn's `fit_transform()` conveniently returns the distance from every instance to every centroid in one call, so `np.argmin` with `axis=0`, which scans down each centroid's column of distances, picks out exactly those closest instances (one per centroid).

Picture the matrix, which the card below spells out: one row per training image, one column per centroid, and each cell holding one distance. With 1,400 training images and 50 clusters that is 1,400 rows and 50 columns.

- `axis=0` scans **down** a column: for centroid j, which image is nearest? That gives 50 image numbers, one per cluster — what we want.
- `axis=1` would scan **across** a row: for image i, which centroid is nearest? That gives 1,400 cluster indices, which is just `labels_` again.

Getting that axis backwards is the classic mistake, and it fails silently — you get an array of the wrong length and a confusing error much later.

A human then labels only those 50 representative images, one per cluster — the same labeling budget as before, but spent on instances that are far more informative than a random sample, because each one is a genuine best-case example of what its whole cluster looks like. Figure 9-13 below shows all fifty.

### 4 · What it bought

Training the same logistic regression on these 50 hand-picked representative images instead of 50 random ones jumps accuracy to about 84.9% — a large gain for the same amount of human labeling effort, and it comes entirely from choosing which 50 instances to label more wisely, not from labeling any more of them.

**One-liner for your notes:** cluster first, label the one instance nearest each centroid, and the same 50 human labels take the classifier from about 74.8% to about 84.9% — the gain is purely in which rows were chosen.

blocks.title: Worked out: finding the 50 representative digits
blocks.content:
The digits dataset has 1,797 grayscale 8 × 8 images, and the training set is the first 1,400 of them. k-means is fitted on that training set with 50 clusters. The call `kmeans.fit_transform(X_train)` returns `X_digits_dist`, a matrix with one row per training image and one column per centroid, so it has 1,400 rows and 50 columns. Each cell is the distance from one image to one centroid.

The call `np.argmin(X_digits_dist, axis=0)` works down each column: for every centroid, it returns the row number of the image with the smallest distance to that centroid. The result is 50 row numbers, one per cluster, and `X_train[representative_digit_idx]` picks out those 50 images for a human to label.

blocks.title: Figure 9-13
blocks.caption: Fifty representative digit images (one per cluster)
blocks.alt: Figure 9-13: Fifty representative digit images (one per cluster)

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
k = 50
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=42)
X_digits_dist = kmeans.fit_transform(X_train)
representative_digit_idx = np.argmin(X_digits_dist, axis=0)
X_representative_digits = X_train[representative_digit_idx]
```

items.term: The active ingredient is selection, not the algorithm
items.text: Both runs use the same classifier, the same budget and the same underlying data; only the choice of which rows a human looks at changes, and that alone is worth about ten accuracy points. It is the cheapest lever in the chapter and it requires no new model, which makes it the first thing to try whenever labels are the bottleneck.

items.term: Typicality and uncertainty are different selection rules
items.text: The instance closest to a centroid is the most typical member of its region, so its label is the one most likely to be right for everything nearby. Note what it is not: it is not the instance the model is least sure about, which is what active learning will chase later. Both are principled, and they win in different situations — typicality when you have no model yet, uncertainty once you do.

items.term: This works only if clusters line up with classes
items.text: The entire method assumes each cluster is dominated by a single digit. Nothing enforces that, and on data whose clusters cut across classes the representatives would be no better than a random sample. The measured gain is evidence that the assumption held here, not a guarantee that it holds anywhere else.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Why does labeling the 50 representative instances (one per cluster) beat labeling 50 random instances, given the exact same labeling budget?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Representative selection picks the most typical rows. SelfTrainingClassifier instead trusts the rows a model is most confident about. Which rule wins when the clusters do not line up with the classes?
Look up: SelfTrainingClassifier in the sklearn.semi_supervised package, and the scikit-learn user guide section “Semi-supervised learning”.

items.term: Label Propagation and Active Learning

blocks.content:
Once 50 representative instances are labeled, you can copy each label onto its whole cluster and end up with 1,400 labeled rows for no extra human effort.

**The question this lesson answers:** 50 hand-labeled representatives got the classifier to about 84.9%. Can those same 50 labels be stretched over the entire training set, and does the stretch hold?

### The big picture

```
50 human labels
  └─> copy onto each whole cluster -> 1,400 labeled rows
       └─> drop farthest 1% per cluster -> about 90.9%
```

### 1 · Propagate the label to the cluster

Having labeled just the 50 representative instances, the next idea is to go further: assume every other instance in a cluster shares its representative's label, and copy that label onto the whole cluster at once.

This is **label propagation**, and it turns 50 hand-labeled instances into a fully labeled training set of 1,400 instances, with almost no extra human effort. Training logistic regression on this propagated dataset lifts accuracy again, well past what the 50 representative-only labels achieved on their own — to about 89.4% in the book's run.

The assumption underneath is explicit and checkable: instances in the same cluster are the same digit. That is the whole bet. It is not a rule, it is a hypothesis about your clustering, and the last section of this lesson is what happens when you measure it.

### 2 · Trim the edges

The refinement worth knowing is that propagation is noisier at the edges of a cluster, where instances are less confidently similar to the representative.

Dropping roughly the farthest 1% of instances from their cluster's center — instances whose propagated label is least trustworthy — before training pushes accuracy up further still, to about 90.9%, using only 50 real human labels total, which actually edges out training on the fully labeled dataset.

Read that again, because it is genuinely surprising: 50 human labels beat 1,400 human labels. Two things are happening at once. The propagated labels are nearly as good as the real ones, and dropping the outer 1% also drops some genuinely awkward training rows that the fully labeled run kept.

Checking the propagated labels against their true values shows they're about 97.5% accurate, which is why this works so well. That number is the bet from section 1, measured — and it is the number that makes the whole trick legitimate rather than lucky. (The book notes the scale of what was saved: 50 labels is only about 5 examples per class on average.)

A caution that transfers: you could only compute that 97.5% because this is a teaching dataset where the true labels were available all along and were merely withheld. On a real project you do not get to check, so you must decide from the shape of your clusters how much you trust the copy.

### 3 · Active learning: spend the next labels where the model is confused

Active learning takes the idea one step further by putting a human back in the loop deliberately, but efficiently.

Under **uncertainty sampling**, the current model is used to predict on all unlabeled data, the instances it is least confident about are handed to a human expert for labeling, and the newly labeled instances are folded back into training — repeating until the accuracy gained per additional label no longer justifies the effort.

Rather than labeling instances at random, you spend the labeling budget exactly where the model is most confused.

| Strategy | Which rows a human labels |
|---|---|
| Baseline | 50 at random |
| Representatives | the one nearest each centroid |
| Uncertainty sampling | the ones the model is least sure about |

Note the difference in when the decision is made. Representatives are chosen *before* any classifier exists, using structure alone. Uncertainty sampling needs a trained model first, and then keeps asking it, so it is a loop rather than a step. Its stopping rule is economic rather than statistical: you stop once the accuracy gained per additional label no longer justifies the effort.

**One-liner for your notes:** copy each representative's label across its whole cluster (about 97.5% correct here), drop the farthest 1% of each cluster, and 50 human labels reach about 90.9% — then use uncertainty sampling to spend any further labels where the model is least confident.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
y_train_propagated = np.empty(len(X_train), dtype=np.int64)
for i in range(k):
    y_train_propagated[kmeans.labels_ == i] = y_representative_digits[i]
```

items.term: An assumption made cheap, then measured
items.text: Copying a label across a cluster is a bet that cluster membership implies class membership. What makes it good practice rather than wishful thinking is that the bet is checkable — here the propagated labels come out about 97.5% right. Make the assumption explicit, then measure it; a technique you cannot measure is a technique you cannot deploy.

items.term: Why trimming the edges helps twice
items.text: Instances far from their centroid are both the most likely to carry a wrong propagated label and, often, genuinely atypical examples. Dropping them removes label noise and awkward training rows in one move, which is how 50 labels can edge past 1,400. The general lesson: when label quality varies with a quantity you can measure, discarding the worst tail is usually cheaper than repairing it.

items.term: Two selection rules, opposite instincts, complementary
items.text: Representative selection picks the most typical rows and needs no model; uncertainty sampling picks the least confident rows and needs one. Structure gets you started when you have nothing, and model confidence takes over once you do. A labeling strategy that never switches from the first to the second leaves most of the budget's value unspent.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Why does dropping the farthest 1% of instances in each cluster before training tend to help, rather than just losing you data?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: LabelSpreading and LabelPropagation spread labels through a similarity graph rather than through k-means clusters. On a dataset like digits, does that beat the cluster-based propagation this lesson reached?
Look up: LabelSpreading and LabelPropagation in the sklearn.semi_supervised package — this chapter's own tip points at them.

items.term: DBSCAN: Clustering by Density

blocks.content:
DBSCAN never asks where the centres are — it asks where the data is crowded, which lets it find clusters of any shape at all.

**The question this lesson answers:** the "moons" dataset is two interlocking crescents. No centroid sits inside either of them, so k-means cannot win. What kind of algorithm can, and what do you have to tell it instead of k?

### The big picture

```
for each instance: count neighbours within eps
  >= min_samples  -> core instance (dense region)
  near a core one -> joins that core's cluster
  neither         -> anomaly, labels_ = -1
chains of core instances = one cluster, any shape
```

### 1 · A different definition of "cluster"

DBSCAN takes a completely different approach from k-means: instead of measuring distance to a centroid, it defines a cluster as a continuous region of high density, which lets it capture clusters of any shape — including the crescent-shaped "moons" dataset that would defeat a centroid-based method outright.

Nothing here is an average of anything. There is no centre to be far from, so an elongated, bent or branching cluster is no harder than a round one.

### 2 · The two hyperparameters, and the words they define

The mechanics rest on two hyperparameters, `eps` (ε) and `min_samples`. ε is the Greek letter epsilon, conventionally used for a small distance.

For every instance, DBSCAN counts how many other instances fall within distance ε of it — that neighborhood is the instance's **ε-neighborhood**. Any instance whose ε-neighborhood contains at least `min_samples` instances (counting itself) is a **core instance**, meaning it sits in a genuinely dense region.

So `eps` sets how far you look, and `min_samples` sets how many neighbours count as "crowded". Together they are a definition of dense, and the algorithm has no other one.

Every instance inside a core instance's neighborhood joins that core instance's cluster, and since that neighborhood can itself contain other core instances, clusters can chain together across long, winding sequences of core instances rather than staying compact.

The chaining is the mechanism behind "any shape". A cluster is whatever a chain of overlapping dense neighbourhoods can reach — so a crescent is just a long chain, and no step in it ever had to be near a centre.

Anything that is neither a core instance nor within reach of one is treated as an anomaly rather than forced into some cluster: its cluster index in `labels_` is set to **−1**. Unlike k-means, DBSCAN is allowed to say "this row belongs to nothing", and −1 is how it says so.

### 3 · eps is the setting that decides everything

The `eps` value matters enormously: too small and the algorithm fragments one real cluster into many small ones plus a pile of flagged anomalies; widened appropriately, the same data resolves into a clean, correct clustering.

The card below has the book's own before-and-after on the moons, and Figure 9-14 shows both. The logic is worth carrying: a bigger ε means more instances inside each neighbourhood, so more instances reach `min_samples` and become core instances, so the chains stop breaking.

### 4 · The missing predict()

A quirk worth remembering is that DBSCAN has no `predict()` method at all — only `fit_predict()` — because the authors deliberately left "which cluster does a brand-new instance belong to" as an open question for the user to answer with whatever classifier fits their task, commonly a `KNeighborsClassifier` trained on the core instances and their assigned cluster labels.

This is a design decision, not an oversight. There is no centroid to compare a new point against, and several reasonable answers exist — nearest core instance, nearest cluster, or "none of them" — so the library declines to pick one for you.

### 5 · What it costs

| Strength | Limit |
|---|---|
| any number of clusters, any shape | complexity roughly quadratic in dataset size |
| only two hyperparameters | struggles when cluster densities differ a lot |
| naturally robust to outliers | no predict() for new instances |

DBSCAN is simple, needs only two hyperparameters, and is naturally robust to outliers, but its complexity scales roughly quadratically with dataset size, so it doesn't scale to very large datasets, and it struggles when different clusters have very different densities.

The density limit follows straight from the mechanism: one ε and one `min_samples` define "dense" for the entire dataset, so a setting tight enough to separate a dense cluster will shatter a sparse one.

**One-liner for your notes:** DBSCAN grows clusters as chains of dense ε-neighborhoods, so it finds any shape and labels leftovers −1, at the cost of quadratic scaling, one global notion of density, and no predict() for new rows.

blocks.title: Worked out: eps = 0.05 versus eps = 0.2 on the moons
blocks.content: The book builds the moons dataset with `make_moons(n_samples=1000, noise=0.05)` and first fits `DBSCAN(eps=0.05, min_samples=5)`. With a neighborhood radius of only 0.05, the result has quite a lot of anomalies, which appear with the cluster index -1 in `labels_`, plus seven different clusters, although the data holds just two moons. Widening each instance's neighborhood by increasing eps to 0.2 gives a clustering that looks perfect. A larger ε-neighborhood contains more instances, so more instances reach min_samples and become core instances, and the chains of core instances no longer break each moon into pieces.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons

X, y = make_moons(n_samples=1000, noise=0.05)
dbscan = DBSCAN(eps=0.05, min_samples=5)
dbscan.fit(X)
```

items.term: Connectivity versus centrality as the definition of a cluster
items.text: k-means defines a cluster by a centre; DBSCAN defines it by reachability through dense neighbourhoods. That single change is what buys arbitrary shapes, and it is also why there is nothing to predict with afterwards — membership is a property of a chain, not a distance to a point. Almost every difference between the two algorithms falls out of this one choice.

items.term: One global notion of density is the real limitation
items.text: eps and min_samples define “dense” once, for the whole dataset. A dataset whose clusters genuinely differ in density has no single setting that works, and no amount of tuning fixes it — which is precisely the gap HDBSCAN was built to close. Recognising a limitation as structural rather than tunable saves a great deal of fruitless grid searching.

items.term: Declining to guess is a defensible API choice
items.text: The library could have shipped a predict() that assigns each new point to the nearest core instance. It deliberately does not, because several answers are reasonable and which one is right depends on the task — including whether “none of them” should be allowed. When a library leaves a decision to you, it is often flagging that the decision has real consequences.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Why can't you just call dbscan.predict(X_new) after fitting a DBSCAN model?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: DBSCAN fails when clusters have different densities. HDBSCAN is said to handle that — what does it let vary that DBSCAN holds fixed, and what does it ask you for in place of eps?
Look up: HDBSCAN, implemented in the scikit-learn-contrib project — this chapter's own tip recommends it.

items.term: Gaussian Mixture Models and the EM Algorithm

blocks.content:
A Gaussian mixture assumes each instance came from one of k bell-shaped distributions, and fitting it means recovering those distributions from the data alone.

**The question this lesson answers:** k-means could only place centres. How do you also learn each cluster's size, shape and orientation, when you never get to see which cluster generated any given row?

### The big picture

| k-means learns | A Gaussian mixture learns |
|---|---|
| a centre per cluster | a centre per cluster |
| — | a covariance: size, shape, orientation |
| — | a weight: how likely that cluster is |
| hard assignment: one cluster | soft assignment: a probability per cluster |

### 1 · What the model assumes

A **Gaussian mixture model** assumes every instance in the dataset was generated by one of k underlying **Gaussian distributions**, each with its own mean, its own **covariance** (which controls the ellipse's size, shape and orientation), and its own **weight** (the probability that any given instance came from it).

A Gaussian is the bell curve; in two or more dimensions it draws an ellipse of likely values around its mean. The mean is where the ellipse sits, the covariance is how it is stretched and tilted, the weight is what share of the data it produced.

You never observe which Gaussian generated a particular instance — that assignment is hidden — and you don't know the Gaussians' parameters going in either; fitting a `GaussianMixture` estimates both the mixture weights and every Gaussian's mean and covariance from the raw data alone.

Two unknowns and one observation. That is exactly the chicken-and-egg shape from the k-means lesson, one level harder.

Figure 9-16 below draws a fitted mixture: the means, the decision boundaries, and the density contours — the last of those being the thing k-means has no equivalent for.

### 2 · EM: the same alternating loop, made soft

Under the hood this runs on the **expectation-maximization (EM)** algorithm, and it should feel familiar because it mirrors k-means's alternating structure almost exactly: initialize the cluster parameters randomly, then alternate between an expectation step and a maximization step until nothing more changes.

The real difference is that EM works with **soft assignments** the whole way through.

In the **expectation step**, instead of assigning each instance to exactly one cluster, it computes a probability — called the **responsibility** — that the instance belongs to each of the k clusters given the current parameters. A row is not 100% cluster 2; it is 0.98 cluster 2 and 0.02 cluster 0.

In the **maximization step**, every cluster's mean, covariance and weight get recomputed using all the instances at once, but each instance is weighted by how responsible that cluster is for it, so a cluster is shaped mainly by the instances it's most confident belong to it.

| Step | k-means | EM |
|---|---|---|
| assign | nearest centroid wins, all or nothing | a probability per cluster |
| update | mean of the rows assigned to it | weighted over ALL rows, by responsibility |

The weighted update is what makes the extra parameters learnable. Because every row contributes a little to every cluster, a cluster sees enough of the data's spread to estimate not just a centre but a whole ellipse.

You can think of EM as k-means generalized to also learn each cluster's size, shape and orientation, not just its center — which is exactly why GMMs succeed on elliptical clusters where k-means fails. Figure 9-17 below shows what happens when you deliberately constrain those ellipses instead.

### 3 · The default that will bite you

Because EM, like k-means, can converge to a poor local solution, it's run multiple times (`n_init`) and the best result kept — and `n_init` defaults to just **1**, so setting it explicitly matters.

This is the opposite of `KMeans`, whose `n_init` defaults to 10. Same risk, different default, no warning. The code card below passes `n_init=10` for precisely this reason. (For scale: on the book's three-cluster example the fit converged in 4 iterations, so ten restarts is not an expensive habit.)

**One-liner for your notes:** a Gaussian mixture learns a mean, a covariance and a weight per cluster; EM alternates expectation (a responsibility per cluster per row) with maximization (every parameter recomputed over all rows, weighted by responsibility) — and its `n_init` defaults to 1, so set it.

blocks.caption: Gaussian mixtures for tied clusters (left) and spherical clusters (right)

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.mixture import GaussianMixture
gm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_init=10)
gm.fit(X)
```

items.term: Soft assignment is what makes the extra parameters learnable
items.text: Hard assignment gives each cluster only its own members, which is enough to estimate a mean and little more. Weighting every instance by responsibility lets each cluster see the whole dataset through its own lens, and that is what supplies enough information to fit a full covariance. The softness is not a refinement of k-means; it is the mechanism that makes shape and orientation estimable at all.

items.term: EM generalises far beyond mixtures
items.text: Guess the hidden variable, fit the parameters as if the guess were true, repeat. That pattern solves any problem with unobserved structure — missing data, hidden states in sequences, topics in documents. Recognising the shape is worth more than memorising the Gaussian case, because the Gaussian case is simply the friendliest instance of a general method.

items.term: The same risk, two different defaults
items.text: KMeans and GaussianMixture face the same local-optimum problem and ship n_init=10 and n_init=1 respectively, with no warning either way. The habit this should install: when two related estimators share a failure mode, check whether they also share the mitigation, because library defaults are historical accidents at least as often as they are recommendations.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: In one sentence, what does EM do differently from k-means during its 'assignment' step?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: EM is guaranteed to improve the likelihood at every step but not to reach the global maximum. What does n_init=10 actually buy you, and is there anything on the fitted object that would tell you the run was a bad one?
Look up: the scikit-learn user guide, section “Gaussian mixture models”, and its subsection on the expectation-maximization estimation algorithm.

items.term: Anomaly Detection and Choosing k with Gaussian Mixtures

blocks.content:
A fitted Gaussian mixture can tell you how dense the data is at any point, so flagging anomalies is just picking a density threshold — and choosing k needs a different tool entirely.

**The question this lesson answers:** a factory knows roughly 2% of its products are defective. How do you turn a fitted mixture into a detector that flags about that many, and how do you choose k when neither inertia nor the silhouette score is allowed?

### The big picture

```
score_samples(X)  ->  a density per instance
   pick a threshold ->  below it = anomaly
choosing k:  inertia NO   silhouette NO
             BIC / AIC YES  (lowest wins)
             BayesianGaussianMixture: k finds itself
```

### 1 · Density in, anomalies out

Because a fitted `GaussianMixture` can estimate the density of the data at any point via `score_samples()`, turning it into an anomaly detector is almost free: pick a density threshold, and flag any instance whose estimated density falls below it as an anomaly.

**Density** here means how much probability the fitted model puts at that location — high where the model thinks data belongs, low out in the empty parts. Figure 9-18 below marks the flagged instances as stars.

The threshold itself is usually set from domain knowledge — if a factory already knows roughly 2% of its products are defective, set the threshold so that about 2% of instances fall below it, then adjust up or down depending on whether you're seeing too many **false positives** (good products wrongly flagged) or too many **false negatives** (defects that slip through), the same precision/recall tradeoff from earlier chapters.

That is what `np.percentile(densities, 2)` does in the code card below: it returns the density value that 2% of the instances fall under, which becomes the cutoff. The **percentile** is a cut point in a sorted list — the 2nd percentile is the value below which 2% of the data sits.

Note that the business supplies the number. The model ranks every instance by how unusual it is; it cannot tell you where unusual becomes unacceptable, and nothing in the data can.

### 2 · Anomaly detection versus novelty detection

This differs from **novelty detection**, which additionally assumes the training data itself was clean and outlier-free — anomaly detection makes no such assumption, which is also why it's often used specifically to clean up a contaminated dataset in the first place.

| | Anomaly detection | Novelty detection |
|---|---|---|
| Training data | may already contain outliers | assumed clean |
| Typical use | find and remove the bad rows | flag genuinely new things |

The distinction is about what you promised the algorithm, not about what it outputs.

### 3 · Choosing k, when the usual tools are disqualified

Choosing k for a Gaussian mixture can't reuse inertia or the silhouette score, because both assume roughly spherical, evenly sized clusters — an assumption GMMs are specifically built to avoid.

Using either would grade an elliptical model with a ruler that only knows circles, which is the same mistake the k-means-limits lesson warned about, now pointing the other way.

Instead, the standard tools are **information criteria**: the **Bayesian information criterion (BIC)** and **Akaike information criterion (AIC)**, both of which reward a model that fits the data well but penalize it for having more parameters (more clusters means more parameters), so the best k is whichever **minimizes** BIC or AIC rather than whichever maximizes raw fit.

That built-in penalty is what makes them safe where inertia was not. Inertia could always be improved by adding clusters; here, adding a cluster adds parameters and therefore adds penalty, so the score can get worse. Equation 9-1 below is the exact form, with the explanation underneath it, and Figure 9-20 plots both criteria against k.

### 4 · Letting the model pick k for you

Rather than searching k by hand, `BayesianGaussianMixture` takes a generous upper-bound guess for the number of clusters and automatically drives the weights of unnecessary extra clusters down toward zero, effectively discovering the right k on its own.

A weight near zero means "this cluster explains essentially none of the data" — it is still in the model, but switched off. You give it a number you are confident is too big, and read off how many survive.

Though it still assumes the true clusters are roughly ellipsoidal, and struggles on data like the crescent-shaped moons dataset for the same reason plain k-means does. Figure 9-21 below shows that failure: no amount of automatic k-selection rescues a model whose shapes are wrong.

**One-liner for your notes:** threshold `score_samples()` at a business-chosen percentile to flag anomalies; pick k by the lowest BIC or AIC, because they penalise extra parameters where inertia and silhouette cannot be trusted on non-spherical clusters.

blocks.title: Reading Equation 9-1: BIC and AIC
blocks.content:
In Equation 9-1, m is the number of instances, p is the number of parameters the model learns, and $\hat{L}$ is the maximized value of the model's likelihood function, which you can think of as a measure of how well the model fits the data. The term $-2\log(\hat{L})$ gets smaller as the fit improves, while the penalty term ($\log(m)p$ for BIC, $2p$ for AIC) grows as the model learns more parameters, for example by adding clusters. A lower value is therefore better.

The two criteria often select the same model. When they differ, the model selected by BIC tends to be simpler (fewer parameters) but to fit the data slightly less well. In the book's example, `gm.bic(X)` and `gm.aic(X)` compute the scores, and both are lowest when k = 3.

blocks.title: Figure 9-18
blocks.caption: Anomaly detection using a Gaussian mixture model
blocks.alt: Figure 9-18: Anomaly detection using a Gaussian mixture model

blocks.title: Equation 9-1
blocks.caption: Bayesian information criterion (BIC) and Akaike information criterion (AIC)
blocks.explain:
**Why the equation has this shape**
Both lines say the same sentence in symbols: **how badly the model fits, plus a fine for every
number it had to learn.** Fit alone would always favour more clusters, because more clusters can
always trace the data more closely — the same runaway that made inertia useless for choosing k.
Adding a fine that grows with the number of learned parameters is what gives the score a real
minimum somewhere in the middle instead of at the extreme.

**Standard or ad hoc:** both are completely standard. BIC and AIC are general model-selection
criteria used far beyond Gaussian mixtures — any time you compare models with different numbers of
parameters that were fitted by maximising a likelihood.

**The general form:** every criterion in this family is `fine-per-parameter × p − 2 log(L̂)`. The two
here differ only in the fine: `log(m)` for BIC, a flat `2` for AIC. Because log(m) is bigger than 2
for any dataset above about seven rows, BIC charges more per parameter than AIC does — which is
exactly why BIC tends to pick the simpler model.

**Terms this introduces.** *Likelihood* is how plausible the fitted parameter values are given the
data you actually observed; it is the quantity EM was maximising all along. *Maximised likelihood*
is the best value it reached. A *parameter* is any number the model learned — and each extra
Gaussian brings a mean, a covariance and a weight, so k and p rise together.

### Every piece

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| BIC | "bee eye see" | Bayesian information criterion, lower is better |
| AIC | "ay eye see" | Akaike information criterion, lower is better |
| m | "em" | the number of instances in the dataset |
| p | "pee" | the number of parameters the model learned |
| log(m) | "log of em" | BIC's fine per parameter, grows with dataset size |
| 2 | "two" | AIC's fine per parameter, a flat charge |
| L̂ | "ell hat" | the maximised likelihood: how well the model fits |
| −2 log(L̂) | "minus two log ell hat" | the misfit term, smaller when the fit is better |
| − | "minus" | subtracts the fit reward from the complexity fine |

### In plain words

BIC = (fine per parameter × number of parameters) − (two times the log of how well it fits), where
the fine per parameter is log(m). AIC is the identical sentence with a flat fine of 2 instead.

### Real numbers from the book's run

For the three-cluster mixture in this chapter, `gm.bic(X)` returns 8189.747000497186 and
`gm.aic(X)` returns 8102.521720382148. Both are lowest at k = 3, so k = 3 is the model that wins.

### How those values are produced

L̂ is not chosen by you — it falls out of the fit. It is the likelihood at the parameter values EM
converged on, so the order is always: call `fit()` first, then `bic()` or `aic()`. You can read the
penalty difference straight off the two numbers:

1. BIC − AIC = 8189.747 − 8102.522 = 87.225
2. the misfit term is the same in both lines, so it cancels completely
3. what is left is only the difference between the two fines: log(m)p − 2p
4. so on this dataset BIC charges 87.225 more than AIC for exactly the same fitted model

That gap is the whole reason the two criteria can disagree, and the reason the one that disagrees
by charging more — BIC — is the one that ends up preferring fewer clusters.
