```python
densities = gm.score_samples(X)
density_threshold = np.percentile(densities, 2)
anomalies = X[densities < density_threshold]
```

items.term: Penalised fit is the general answer to “more is always better”
items.text: Any score that measures only fit will prefer the most flexible model. BIC and AIC fix that by charging for parameters, which is the same idea as regularisation and as an adjusted R-squared: make complexity cost something and the optimum moves back to the middle. Once you see the pattern, “inertia cannot choose k” stops looking like a special case.

items.term: The threshold is a business input, not a model output
items.text: score_samples ranks instances by how unusual they are; nothing in the data says where unusual becomes actionable. That boundary encodes the relative cost of a false positive against a false negative, which only the operation knows. A detector shipped without an explicit owner for that number ends up with the number chosen by accident.

items.term: Automating k does not relax a modelling assumption
items.text: BayesianGaussianMixture removes the search over k but keeps the ellipsoidal assumption, so on the moons it confidently settles on eight clusters where there are two. Automating a hyperparameter and fixing a wrong model family are different repairs, and it is worth being clear about which one your problem actually needs.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Why can't you use the silhouette score to pick the number of clusters for a Gaussian mixture model the way you would for k-means?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: This chapter varies only k when comparing BIC. Scikit-Learn's model-selection example also varies covariance_type. Does BIC ever prefer a constrained covariance over the unconstrained default, and what would that be telling you about the data?
Look up: the scikit-learn examples gallery, “Gaussian Mixture Model Selection”.

items.term: Beyond Gaussian Mixtures: Other Anomaly and Novelty Detectors

blocks.content:
Scikit-Learn ships four more detectors, and the only way to choose between them is to know which assumption each one makes about "normal".

**The question this lesson answers:** a Gaussian mixture is not always the right shape for your normal data. What else is available, what does each one assume, and which one is actually for novelty rather than anomalies?

### The big picture

| Algorithm | Assumes normal data is |
|---|---|
| Fast-MCD (EllipticEnvelope) | one single Gaussian, data contaminated |
| Isolation forest | anything, but anomalies sit far apart |
| Local outlier factor | anything, judged against local neighbours |
| One-class SVM | clean — this one is for NOVELTY detection |

### 1 · Fast-MCD: assume one ellipse, and be careful fitting it

**Fast-MCD**, exposed as `EllipticEnvelope`, assumes the normal instances come from a single Gaussian (not a mixture) and is designed to carefully ignore likely outliers while it estimates that Gaussian's shape — which makes it well suited to cleaning up a dataset before using it elsewhere.

The "carefully ignore" part is the whole trick. Outliers drag a naive mean and covariance toward themselves, which widens the ellipse, which makes the outliers look less extreme — the contamination hides itself. Fast-MCD estimates the ellipse from a subset it believes is clean, so the outliers never get a vote on the definition of normal.

### 2 · Isolation forest: how few cuts does it take to isolate you?

**Isolation forest** takes a completely different, tree-based approach: it grows random decision trees that split on random features and random thresholds until every instance sits alone.

Nothing is being learned in the usual sense — the splits are random. What varies is how many of them a given point survives.

Since an anomaly tends to sit far from everything else, it typically takes far fewer random splits to isolate it than to isolate a normal instance — an efficient trick that scales well even to high-dimensional data.

The intuition: a point out on its own gets cut off from the crowd by almost any early split, while a point in the middle of a dense mass needs many cuts before nothing else shares its region. Averaged over many random trees, "isolated early" is a robust signal.

### 3 · Local outlier factor: unusual compared to your neighbours

**Local outlier factor (LOF)** instead compares an instance's local density to its neighbors' local densities directly, flagging instances that are notably more isolated than their neighborhood suggests they should be.

The word doing the work is *local*. A point in a genuinely sparse region is not an outlier if everything around it is equally sparse. LOF asks a relative question — are you lonelier than your neighbours are? — which is why it copes with a dataset whose regions have different natural densities, the exact case DBSCAN struggles with.

### 4 · One-class SVM: the novelty specialist

**One-class SVM** is aimed specifically at novelty detection rather than plain anomaly detection: it maps instances into a high-dimensional space and finds a boundary separating them from the origin, which corresponds to carving out a compact region in the original space that should contain essentially all normal instances. Anything landing outside that boundary counts as **novel**.

This is the one that changes the contract. The previous three expect their training data to be dirty and are built to cope. One-class SVM is drawing a fence around *everything it was shown*, so an outlier in the training set ends up inside the fence, permanently redefined as normal. Feed it a clean dataset or do not use it.

It performs well, especially in high dimensions, but like every SVM variant it doesn't scale comfortably to large datasets.

**One-liner for your notes:** EllipticEnvelope assumes one Gaussian and ignores suspected outliers while fitting it, isolation forest counts how few random splits isolate a point, LOF compares a point's density to its neighbours', and one-class SVM fences in the training data — so only it requires clean training data, because it is a novelty detector.

items.term: Choose by assumption, not by reputation
items.text: Each of the four encodes a different claim about what normal looks like: one Gaussian, isolation under random splits, local density relative to neighbours, or a fence around clean training data. The right choice is whichever claim your data actually satisfies, which makes “what do I believe normal looks like here” the first question, ahead of any benchmark table.

items.term: Contaminated training data is the axis that splits the family
items.text: Anomaly detectors are built to survive dirty training data; a novelty detector is not, and will quietly certify any outlier it was trained on as normal. Because both produce the same kind of output, the mistake is invisible at the interface — it shows up only as anomalies that never fire, which is the hardest kind of bug to notice.

items.term: Randomness as a measuring instrument
items.text: Isolation forest learns nothing and still works, because the quantity it measures — how few random cuts separate a point from the rest — is itself informative about isolation. That is a useful counterexample to the instinct that a model must fit something to be useful. Sometimes the right move is to measure how easily a point falls out of the crowd.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Which of these four algorithms (EllipticEnvelope, isolation forest, LOF, one-class SVM) is specifically built for novelty detection rather than anomaly detection, and why does that distinction matter for how it's trained?

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The four algorithms make four different assumptions about normal data. Scikit-Learn plots all of them side by side on the same toy datasets — which dataset defeats each one, and is there a shape that defeats all four?
Look up: the scikit-learn user guide, section “Novelty and Outlier Detection”, and its comparison figure of outlier-detection algorithms on toy datasets.

Then compute the reconstruction error for each image. Next, take some of the modified images you built in the previous exercise and look at their reconstruction error: notice how much larger it is. If you plot a reconstructed image, you will see why: it tries to reconstruct a normal face.

sections.title: Chapter 10: Introduction to Artificial Neural Networks with Keras

items.term: Biological Foundations of Neural Networks

blocks.content:
Artificial neural networks were copied from a real one: researchers looked at the animal brain, where billions of very simple cells wired into layers produce complex behaviour, and built a software version of that idea.

**The question this lesson answers:** how does a single biological neuron take signals in, decide whether to pass anything on, and what changes once you stack billions of them into consecutive layers?

### The big picture

```
dendrites -> cell body -> axon -> telodendria -> synapses
 signals in    decide     out      branches      hand off
```

Read that left to right: everything arrives on one side, one decision happens in the middle, and one output leaves on the other side. That shape — many inputs, one decision, one output — is the whole thing that gets copied into software in the next lessons.

### 1 · The parts, in signal order

As Figure 10-1 below illustrates, a biological neuron consists of a central **cell body**, branching input structures called **dendrites**, and a long output extension called the **axon**. **Dendrites** are the branching extensions of the cell body that receive incoming chemical signals from neighbouring cells. In Figure 10-1 below, the **axon** is the long fibre that carries outgoing electrical signals away from the cell body toward other cells.

The axon splits into **telodendria** ending in **synaptic terminals**, which connect to the dendrites or cell bodies of neighboring neurons. Signals propagate through this system via electrical impulses known as **action potentials**. When an action potential reaches the end of an axon, it triggers the release of chemical signals called **neurotransmitters** across the synaptic gap.

Two words worth pinning down, because the rest of the chapter reuses the idea and not the chemistry:

| Term | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| action potential | AP, or just a signal | the electrical pulse travelling down the axon |
| neurotransmitter | neuro-transmitter | the chemical released at the far end |

### 2 · What makes one fire

Consider a biological neuron receiving incoming chemical signals from thousands of neighboring synapses within a few milliseconds. A neuron fires its own action potential by accumulating a sufficient threshold of neurotransmitters within a few milliseconds. If the net sum of these signals exceeds a specific activation threshold, the neuron fires its own electrical impulse down its axon to downstream neurons. Conversely, inhibitory neurotransmitters reduce the likelihood of firing.

Note the time window. It is not "enough signals ever", it is enough signals inside a few milliseconds — closer to a tumbling window in a stream than to a running total in a table.

### 3 · The power is in the layers, not the cell

When billions of these individually simple units are organized into consecutive layers — such as those in the human cerebral cortex shown in Figure 10-2 below — they form biological neural networks capable of massive computational power.

The key insight to remember is that complex intelligence in biological networks emerges from vast collections of simple, layered units passing signals through weighted connections.

### 4 · Why this idea kept being abandoned

The card below has the full history; the shape of it is two collapses and one revival. Interest in artificial neural networks went through repeated winters because early promises outpaced results in the 1960s, while competing methods like support vector machines initially offered stronger performance in the 1990s. Funding followed the results, both times.

What makes the current wave different is the availability of massive training datasets alongside modern GPU compute power. The card below adds two more reasons: the training algorithms improved, and a limitation everybody feared — getting stuck in a local optimum, meaning a solution that is the best in its own neighbourhood but not the best overall — turned out to be mild in practice.

**One-liner for your notes:** a neuron is many inputs, one threshold decision and one output, and the intelligence comes from stacking billions of them in layers — which is exactly the shape the rest of this chapter rebuilds in software.

blocks.title: Why ANN research stalled, then took off
blocks.content:
Artificial neural networks date back to 1943, when Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts presented the first ANN architecture. Early successes raised hopes of truly intelligent machines, but when it became clear in the 1960s that this promise would go unfulfilled, funding flew elsewhere and ANNs entered a long winter. Interest revived in the early 1980s, yet by the 1990s other techniques such as support vector machines seemed to offer better results and stronger theoretical foundations, so the study of neural networks was put on hold again.

The current wave is different for several reasons: there is now a huge quantity of data to train on, computing power has grown enormously (Moore's law, powerful GPU cards driven by the gaming industry, and cloud platforms), training algorithms have improved, and the feared local optima often perform almost as well as the global optimum.

items.term: How far the biological analogy is meant to go
items.text: The software version keeps three properties of the cell — many inputs, one threshold decision, one output — and throws away everything else: the chemistry, the timing, the geometry. That is a deliberate trade, not an oversight, and the book's own footnote shows the cost of forgetting it. Biological neurons appear to use a roughly S-shaped activation, so researchers stuck with S-shaped functions for a very long time, and it later turned out that ReLU generally works better in artificial networks. Copying biology bought the initial idea; continuing to copy it held the field back.

items.term: A winter is a funding story, not a mathematics story
items.text: Nothing about neural networks got worse in the 1960s or the 1990s. What changed was the comparison: expectations had been set too high, and later support vector machines seemed to offer better results and stronger theoretical foundations. Money followed the better-looking option both times. Worth knowing because it generalises — a technique being out of fashion is evidence about the state of its competitors and its funding, not proof that it is wrong.

items.term: Which of the modern reasons is actually load-bearing
items.text: Of the reasons in the card below, two are external to the method (more data, more compute) and two are about the method itself (better training algorithms, and local optima turning out to be benign). The second pair is the interesting one: a theoretical objection everybody believed — that training would get stuck in bad solutions — turned out to be mild in practice, especially for larger networks. A limitation that only shows up in theory is not the same thing as a limitation.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Biological neurons receive signals through dendrites and transmit output signals down a single long axon.
Communication between biological neurons occurs at synapses through chemical neurotransmitters triggered by electrical action potentials.
A biological neuron fires an electrical impulse only when it receives a sufficient quantity of excitatory signals within a brief timeframe.
Complex computations in brains emerge from organizing vast numbers of simple neurons into interconnected, consecutive layers.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: McCulloch and Pitts called their model a calculus of propositional logic, not a model of learning — their 1943 neuron has no weights to train at all. What did their paper actually claim it could do, and where does learning first enter the story?
Look up: Warren S. McCulloch and Walter Pitts, "A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity", The Bulletin of Mathematical Biology 5, no. 4 (1943), cited in this chapter.

items.term: Logical Computations with Neurons

blocks.content:
Strip a neuron down to "count the active inputs, fire if the count hits a threshold" and you have a logic gate — and gates wired together can compute any logical expression you like.

**The question this lesson answers:** what is the smallest possible mathematical model of a neuron, and what can you actually build out of it? McCulloch and Pitts answered both: a binary threshold unit, and out of those, any logical proposition.

### The big picture

```
A --\
     >-- [ count >= threshold ? ] --> C
B --/
```

Every network in Figure 10-3 below is that same picture with different wiring: how many lines run from each input, and whether a line excites or inhibits.

### 1 · The unit itself

Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts introduced the **artificial neuron**, a simplified model of a biological neuron that receives one or more binary inputs and produces a single binary output. **Binary** here just means on or off, 1 or 0 — no in-between values yet; numbers arrive in the next lesson.

The mechanism relies on a fixed activation **threshold**. A McCulloch-Pitts neuron activates when the number of active inputs meets or exceeds a set threshold; otherwise, it remains inactive with an output of zero. So it is not weighing anything or measuring strength — at this stage it is literally counting lines that are switched on.

Connections between neurons are typically **excitatory**, passing incoming signals forward to increase the total input count. However, connections can also be **inhibitory**, and an inhibitory connection prevents the receiving neuron from activating despite active excitatory inputs. Inhibition is not a minus one that you add up; it is an override.

### 2 · Reading Figure 10-3

All four networks in Figure 10-3 below use the same rule: a neuron activates when at least two of its input connections are active. The only thing that changes between them is the wiring.

| Network | Wiring | Computes |
|---|---|---|
| first | A sends two lines to C | identity |
| second | A sends one line, B sends one | logical AND |
| third | A sends two lines, B sends two | logical OR |
| fourth | A excites, B inhibits | A and not B |

The second network computes a logical AND because output neuron C receives two signals only when both input neurons A and B are active — one line each, and one line is not enough to reach a threshold of two.

The third network is the OR. Consider it with input neuron A active and input neuron B inactive: neuron C activates because neuron A alone sends two signals, reaching the threshold. If both input neurons A and B are active, neuron C receives four signals, which also exceeds the threshold. Neuron C stays off only when both inputs are inactive, receiving zero signals.

The card below walks through the first, second and fourth networks in the book's own words, including how the fourth becomes a logical NOT when A is held on permanently.

### 3 · Why this mattered

By combining excitatory connections, inhibitory connections, and specific thresholds, artificial neurons can be wired together to compute any logical expression. That is the conclusion McCulloch and Pitts demonstrated: networks of simple threshold neurons can be combined to compute any logical statement.

If you have ever built a gnarly filter out of nothing but `AND`, `OR` and `NOT`, this is the same claim one level lower down: a very small primitive, repeated, is enough to express the whole language. The key insight to remember is that even simple binary threshold units can serve as universal building blocks for complex computations.

**One-liner for your notes:** a McCulloch-Pitts neuron fires when at least a threshold number of its input lines are on, inhibition vetoes it outright, and that tiny rule wired up in different patterns covers all of boolean logic.

blocks.title: The other three networks in Figure 10-3
blocks.content: All four networks in Figure 10-3 use the rule that a neuron activates when at least two of its input connections are active. In the first network, the identity function, neuron A sends two connections to neuron C, so C is on exactly when A is on. In the second network, a logical AND, A and B each send one connection to C. A single input signal is not enough, so C activates only when both A and B are active. The fourth network adds an inhibitory connection from B: C is activated only if A is active and B is off. If A is active all the time, this network computes a logical NOT, since C is active when B is off, and vice versa.

blocks.title: Figure 10-3
blocks.caption: ANNs performing simple logical computations
blocks.alt: Figure 10-3: ANNs performing simple logical computations

items.term: Why 'can compute any logical proposition' is the whole point
items.text: A universality claim is what makes a primitive worth building on. It says you will never hit a logical expression this component cannot express, so any limitation you meet later is about training or efficiency, not about reach. The same style of claim comes back twice in this chapter — a large enough network with nonlinear activations can approximate any continuous function, and one hidden layer can in theory model any function. Each time, note what universality does not promise: nothing about how many units it takes, or how you would find the right wiring.

items.term: Counting lines is a weight in disguise
items.text: Running two connections from A to C instead of one is how this model says 'A matters twice as much'. That is a weight of 2, expressed by duplicating the wire because the model has no notion of a number on a connection yet. The perceptron in the next lesson makes it explicit, which is the single change that makes learning possible: you cannot smoothly adjust the number of wires, but you can smoothly adjust a weight.

items.term: Inhibition is a veto, not a negative number
items.text: In this model an inhibitory connection blocks the neuron outright, whatever the excitatory count is. That is different from adding −1 to a sum, where enough excitation would eventually outvote it. The distinction matters because later networks do it the other way round — a negative weight can always be outvoted — so 'inhibitory' in this lesson and 'negative weight' in the next are not the same mechanism.

blocks.title: Key points
items: McCulloch and Pitts introduced an artificial neuron model with binary inputs and a binary output.
A neuron activates its output when incoming active signals reach or exceed a predetermined threshold.
Connections can be excitatory to promote activation or inhibitory to prevent activation.
Networks of simple artificial neurons can be combined to compute any logical proposition.

items: These four networks are drawn by hand. Given a truth table you have never seen, is there a procedure that produces the wiring, and does it always terminate?
Look up: exercise 2 at the end of this chapter, which asks you to build an XOR network from threshold logic units using its canonical Boolean decomposition.

items.term: The Perceptron

blocks.content:
The perceptron replaces the on/off inputs of the previous lesson with real numbers and a weight on every connection, which finally makes the thing trainable — but it still draws only straight lines.

**The question this lesson answers:** if each input is now a number with an adjustable weight on it, how does one neuron turn those numbers into a decision, how are the weights learned, and what can this still not do?

### The big picture

```
inputs -> weighted sum + bias -> step function -> 0 or 1
   x            w·x + b            heaviside
```

### 1 · The unit: a threshold logic unit

The **perceptron**, invented in 1957 by Frank Rosenblatt, is one of the simplest artificial neural network (ANN) architectures. It uses artificial neurons called **threshold logic units (TLUs)**. A TLU computes a linear combination of numerical inputs, adds a bias term, and passes the result through a **step function** such as the Heaviside step function, as shown in Figure 10-4 below.

Three words, glossed once:

| Word | Say it as | What it means here |
|---|---|---|
| linear combination | — | multiply each input by its weight, add them up |
| bias | bias | one extra number added on, belonging to the neuron |
| step function | step | a rule that turns any number into a flat verdict |

The step function's whole job is the last arrow: it converts the weighted sum and bias into a threshold-based discrete output. Everything before it is continuous arithmetic; the step is where a number becomes a decision. Equation 10-1 below gives the two common step functions, with the explanation underneath it.

### 2 · A layer of them, and Equation 10-2

When multiple TLUs are arranged in a single fully connected layer (a **dense layer**), the network can perform multi-output linear binary classification. *Fully connected* means every input is wired to every neuron in the layer, with no gaps — Figure 10-5 below shows two inputs feeding three output neurons, so six connections.

Equation 10-2 expresses this vectorization concisely as $h_{\mathbf{W}, \mathbf{b}}(\mathbf{X}) = \phi(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W} + \mathbf{b})$, where $\mathbf{X}$ is the input matrix, $\mathbf{W}$ is the weight matrix, $\mathbf{b}$ is the bias vector, and $\phi$ represents the step function.

**Reading the formula, piece by piece:**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| X | capital X | the inputs, one row per instance, one column per feature |
| W | capital W | the connection weights, one row per input and one column per neuron |
| b | b | the bias terms, one per neuron |
| XW | X W | the matrix multiply: every instance against every neuron |
| + b | plus b | add each neuron's bias to its own column |
| φ | phi | the activation function, a step function here |

In plain words: multiply the input table by the weight table, add each neuron's bias, then apply the step function to every cell of the result. Matrix W contains all connection weights, with one row per input and one column per neuron — that is the collection of connection weights between inputs and neurons, and it is where everything the model has learned lives.

With real shapes, from Figure 10-5 below: two inputs and three output neurons means W has 2 rows and 3 columns, six weights in total, and b holds three bias terms. Feed in 100 instances and XW is 100 rows by 3 columns, one verdict per neuron per instance.

### 3 · Training it, and Equation 10-3

Consider training a perceptron using the rule in Equation 10-3 below: $w_{i,j}^{(\text{next step})} = w_{i,j} + \eta(y_j - \hat{y}_j)x_i$.

**Reading the formula, piece by piece:**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| wᵢⱼ | w i j | the weight from input i into neuron j |
| next step | next step | the value this weight will have after the update |
| η | eta | the learning rate, how big a correction to apply |
| yⱼ | y j | the target output: what neuron j should have said |
| ŷⱼ | y hat j | the prediction: what neuron j actually said |
| yⱼ − ŷⱼ | the error | how wrong this neuron was, as a signed number |
| xᵢ | x i | the value of input i for this training instance |

In plain words: new weight = old weight + learning rate × error × the input that fed it. Only weights on inputs that were actually switched on get moved, and they move in the direction that would have helped.

With the lesson's numbers: if learning rate η = 0.1, target output yⱼ = 1, prediction ŷⱼ = 0, and input value xᵢ = 2, the weight update will be 0.1 × (1 − 0) × 2 = 0.2. The connection weight is increased by 0.2 to reduce future prediction error.

Now read the same formula with a correct prediction. When the target output matches the predicted output, the error term is zero, the whole update term is zero, and the connection weight remains completely unchanged for that step. The rule only ever reacts to mistakes. This is the **perceptron learning rule**, and it updates connection weights based on prediction errors according to Hebbian principles — Donald Hebb's idea that a connection strengthens when the two cells it joins fire together.

### 4 · The wall it hits

The single-layer perceptron creates linear decision boundaries and cannot solve non-linear problems like exclusive OR (XOR). A **decision boundary** is the dividing line the model draws between the classes; a linear one is a straight line, and the XOR pattern on the left of Figure 10-6 below cannot be split by any straight line at all.

Stacking multiple perceptrons into a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) resolves this limitation: it enables the neural network to learn non-linear patterns such as XOR. The card below works through the MLP on the right of Figure 10-6 with real arithmetic, so you can watch it produce 1 for the inputs (0, 1) and 0 for the inputs (1, 1).

The python card below fits a Scikit-Learn `Perceptron` on two iris measurements, which is this whole lesson in eight lines.

**One-liner for your notes:** a TLU is a weighted sum plus a bias pushed through a step function, Equation 10-3 nudges a weight only when that neuron got the answer wrong, and one layer of them can only ever draw a straight boundary.

blocks.title: Worked out: the MLP of Figure 10-6 solves XOR
blocks.content:
In the MLP on the right of Figure 10-6, both hidden neurons give each input a weight of 1. The lower-left neuron then subtracts 3/2 and the lower-right neuron subtracts 1/2. The output neuron weights the lower-left output by –1 and the lower-right output by 1, then subtracts 1/2. A neuron outputs 1 when its result is positive and 0 when it is negative.

For inputs (0, 1), the book computes: lower-left $0 \times 1 + 1 \times 1 - 3/2 = -1/2$, negative, so 0; lower-right $0 \times 1 + 1 \times 1 - 1/2 = 1/2$, positive, so 1; output $0 \times (-1) + 1 \times 1 - 1/2 = 1/2$, positive, so the network outputs 1.

With the same weights, inputs (1, 1) give $1/2$ and $3/2$ in the hidden layer, so both output 1, and the output neuron gets $-1 + 1 - 1/2 = -1/2$, so the network outputs 0.

blocks.title: Figure 10-4
blocks.caption: TLU: an artificial neuron that computes a weighted sum of its inputs w x , plus a bias
blocks.alt: Figure 10-4: TLU: an artificial neuron that computes a weighted sum of its inputs w x , plus a bias

blocks.title: Equation 10-1
blocks.caption: Common step functions used in perceptrons (assuming threshold = 0)
blocks.explain:
**Why the equation looks like this**

A threshold logic unit has already done all its arithmetic by the time the step function runs: it has
multiplied each input by its weight, added them up and added the bias, producing one number called z.
The only job left is to turn that number into a verdict. That is why Equation 10-1 is not a curve or a
formula with parameters in it — it is a rule with two cases, and the only thing it looks at is which
side of zero z falls on.

**Is this standard?** The Heaviside step is the canonical choice for a perceptron, and the sign
function (sgn) is the common alternative — the book names both, and nothing here is simplified for
teaching. What *is* specific to this equation is the assumption printed in its own caption: threshold
= 0. The cut is at zero because the bias term has already absorbed any other threshold you might have
wanted, which is exactly what the bias is for.

**The general form.** A step function is the extreme member of the activation-function family. Every
activation takes the same z and returns one number; the step returns a flat verdict, while the sigmoid,
tanh and ReLU of the next lesson return something that still varies with z. That difference is not
cosmetic: a flat verdict has a slope of zero everywhere, which is precisely why the next lesson has to
replace it before gradient descent can work.

**Terms this introduces:** z is the weighted sum plus bias, the single number entering the step;
*threshold* is the value z is compared against, here zero; *Heaviside* and *sgn* are just the names of
these two particular rules.

**Reading Equation 10-1, piece by piece**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| heaviside(z) | heaviside of z | the first rule, output 0 or 1 |
| sgn(z) | sign of z | the second rule, output −1, 0 or +1 |
| z | z | the weighted sum plus the bias |
| the brace | if | a two-case or three-case rule, pick the matching line |
| z < 0 | z less than zero | the negative case |
| z ≥ 0 | z greater than or equal to zero | zero counts as the positive case here |

**The formula in plain words**

Heaviside: if the weighted sum plus bias is negative, output 0; otherwise output 1.
Sign: negative gives −1, exactly zero gives 0, positive gives +1.

**With real numbers**

Take a TLU with two inputs, weights 0.6 and −0.4, and a bias of −0.1, and feed it the inputs 2 and 1.

1. weighted sum: 0.6 × 2 = 1.2, and −0.4 × 1 = −0.4
2. add them: 1.2 + (−0.4) = 0.8
3. add the bias: 0.8 + (−0.1) = 0.7, and that is z
4. apply heaviside: 0.7 is not less than 0, so the output is 1

Change the bias to −0.9 and step 3 gives z = −0.1, so the same inputs now output 0. That is the bias
doing its job as a movable threshold.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.linear_model import Perceptron

iris = load_iris(as_frame=True)
X = iris.data[["petal length (cm)", "petal width (cm)"]].values
y = (iris.target == 0)

per_clf = Perceptron(random_state=42)
per_clf.fit(X, y)

X_new = [[2, 0.5], [3, 1]]
y_pred = per_clf.predict(X_new)
```

items.term: Why the update rule only fires on mistakes
items.text: Equation 10-3 multiplies by the error, so a correct prediction produces a zero update no matter how close the call was. That makes the rule cheap and stable, and it also explains the perceptron's weakest habit: training stops the moment there are no errors left on the training set, which is not the same as having found a good boundary. When the data is linearly separable there are infinitely many separating lines, and this rule returns whichever one it happened to stop on. Logistic regression, by contrast, keeps caring about how confident it was.

items.term: What 'linear decision boundary' rules out, exactly
items.text: The restriction is not about how many inputs there are or how complicated the data looks — it is that the boundary must be a single flat cut through the input space. XOR needs two regions that are diagonally opposite, and no single straight cut separates them. This is worth holding onto because it is the precise gap the next lesson fills: a hidden layer lets the network bend the space first and cut it straight afterwards.

items.term: Why the step function is both the point and the problem
items.text: The step is what turns a continuous sum into a decision, so it is the reason a TLU classifies at all. It is also flat everywhere it is defined, meaning a small change in a weight usually changes nothing about the output — which is fine for the error-driven rule in Equation 10-3, but fatal for gradient descent. The perceptron gets away with it because its learning rule never asks for a slope. Every method after this one does.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A threshold logic unit (TLU) computes a weighted sum of inputs plus bias and applies a step function.
Perceptrons are composed of one or more TLUs arranged in a fully connected dense layer.
The perceptron learning rule updates connection weights based on prediction errors according to Hebbian principles.
Single-layer perceptrons produce linear decision boundaries and cannot solve non-linear problems such as XOR.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Rosenblatt proved that this rule converges when the classes are linearly separable. What does the algorithm do when they are not — does it settle, oscillate, or drift?

Look up: the perceptron convergence theorem as stated in this chapter's "The Perceptron" section, alongside Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert's 1969 monograph Perceptrons, which the chapter cites for the limitations.

items.term: Multilayer Perceptrons and Backpropagation

blocks.content:
Stacking perceptron layers only becomes useful once you add two things: a curved activation function between the layers, and an efficient way to work out which weight caused how much of the error.

**The question this lesson answers:** why did simply stacking threshold logic units fail for decades, and what two changes — nonlinear activations and backpropagation — made deep stacks trainable?

### The big picture

```
forward -> measure loss -> reverse pass -> gradient step
 keep results   vs targets     chain rule     update all
```

That loop runs once per mini-batch, and a full sweep over the training set is one **epoch**.

### 1 · Two blockers, named

Early single-layer threshold logic units failed to learn complex nonlinear patterns. Simply stacking layers was insufficient for two separate reasons, and both had to be removed:

| Blocker | Why it stopped training |
|---|---|
| no efficient gradients | researchers lacked an efficient method to calculate error gradients across deep parameter networks |
| flat step functions | traditional step functions contained only flat segments, yielding zero derivatives that blocked gradient descent from updating network parameters |

A **gradient** is just the slope of the error with respect to one parameter: turn this weight up a little, does the error go up or down, and how fast. **Gradient descent** is the training loop that reads those slopes and steps every parameter downhill.

The second blocker is the one people find surprising. Step functions produce zero gradients on flat segments, preventing gradient descent updates: on a flat surface there is no downhill, so no step can be chosen. That is why researchers replaced the step function with differentiable activations.

### 2 · The architecture

To solve this, the **Multilayer Perceptron (MLP)** introduces nonlinear activation functions combined with **backpropagation**. As Figure 10-7 below shows, an MLP consists of an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer in a **feedforward** architecture — feedforward meaning the signal only ever travels one way, inputs to outputs, with no loops back.

Figure 10-7 below illustrates a Multilayer Perceptron with two input units, four hidden layer neurons, and three output layer neurons.

### 3 · What backpropagation actually does

Training begins with a forward pass: input data moves through the layers to compute prediction outputs while preserving all intermediate calculations. The algorithm evaluates network output against target labels using a loss function. A **loss function** is the single number saying how wrong the predictions were on this batch.

Next, during the reverse pass, reverse-mode automatic differentiation applies the calculus chain rule backward from output to input. So autodiff computes gradients analytically using the chain rule from output to input layer — analytically means it is computed exactly from the formulas, not estimated by trying small changes and watching what happens. This reverse pass efficiently computes error gradients for every connection weight and bias. Finally, gradient descent uses these gradients to update all parameters to reduce prediction error.

Consider an MLP processing a mini-batch of 32 instances. The forward pass computes intermediate activations across all neurons. The reverse pass tracks how much each weight contributed to output error, calculating specific gradients like $\frac{\partial L}{\partial w}$. Gradient descent then updates weights to minimize loss across epochs.

**Why this notation at all**

Backpropagation has to answer one question for every parameter in the network: if I nudge you, what
happens to the loss? A partial derivative is exactly that question written down, so it is the notation
the whole algorithm is built around. The curly ∂ rather than a straight d is the signal that everything
else is being held still while this one weight moves — which matters when there are 266,610 of them and
they all interact.

**Is this standard?** Yes, and it is not simplified. ∂L/∂w is the ordinary calculus notation for a
partial derivative, used unchanged across every deep learning framework. The reason the chapter shows
it rather than a formula for computing it is that there is no single formula: the value depends on
where in the network the weight sits, and the chain rule is what assembles it layer by layer.

**The general form.** The same expression exists for every parameter, so what the reverse pass really
produces is one of these per weight and per bias — a whole list, usually called the **gradient**.
Gradient descent then uses that list: every parameter moves a small step in the direction that lowers
L, and the size of the step is set by the learning rate.

**Terms this introduces:** the **loss** L is one number per mini-batch, not per instance; a
**derivative** is a slope, meaning a rate of change, not an amount; **the chain rule** is the calculus
rule for slopes of nested functions, which is what lets one weight deep in the network be blamed for an
error measured at the output.

**Reading the formula, piece by piece:**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| ∂ | partial | "the slope of, holding everything else still" |
| L | L | the loss, one number for this mini-batch |
| w | w | one single connection weight, out of many thousands |
| ∂L/∂w | partial L by partial w | how much the loss moves if this one weight moves |

In plain words: for every weight in the network, how much of the error is yours? One reverse pass answers that question for all of them at once, which is exactly why it is cheap enough to run on every mini-batch.

### 4 · The three replacement activations

Nonlinear activations like the **sigmoid function** $\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$, **hyperbolic tangent** $\text{tanh}(z) = 2\sigma(2z) - 1$, and **rectified linear unit** $\text{ReLU}(z) = \max(0, z)$ replace flat step functions. Figure 10-8 below plots all three next to their derivatives.

| Activation | Shape in words | Why it is used |
|---|---|---|
| sigmoid | S-curve squashed into 0 to 1 | well-defined nonzero derivative everywhere |
| tanh | the same S-curve, −1 to 1 | outputs centred near zero early in training |
| ReLU | flat at zero, then a 45-degree line | fast to compute, and the default |

The sigmoid has a well-defined nonzero derivative everywhere, so gradient descent can make progress at every step. ReLU is not differentiable at $z = 0$ and its derivative is 0 for $z < 0$, but it works very well in practice, is fast to compute, and has become the default.

Without nonlinear functions, stacked linear layers degenerate mathematically into a single linear function, failing to learn complex patterns — the network degenerates into an architecture equivalent to a single linear layer. The card below proves it in one line with two real functions.

### 5 · Start the weights at random, not at zero

Random weight initialization is critical to break symmetry; zero-initialized hidden weights learn identical features and fail to differentiate. If all connection weights in the hidden layers are initialized to zero, neurons in a layer remain identical because backpropagation updates them symmetry-wise identically, and the model acts as if it had only one neuron per layer no matter how wide you made it.

**One-liner for your notes:** an MLP is layers of neurons with a curved activation between them, and backpropagation is one forward pass that keeps its working, one reverse pass that blames each weight via the chain rule, and one gradient descent step.

blocks.title: Worked out: why stacked linear layers collapse
blocks.content:
The book shows why a network needs nonlinear activations using two linear functions, $f(x) = 2x + 3$ and $g(x) = 5x - 1$. Chaining them means putting $g(x)$ inside $f$: $f(g(x)) = 2(5x - 1) + 3 = 10x - 2 + 3 = 10x + 1$. The result is just another linear function, so a deep stack of layers with no nonlinearity between them is equivalent to a single layer and cannot solve very complex problems.

The network in Figure 10-7 is an MLP with two inputs, one hidden layer of four neurons, and three output neurons. If all its weights and biases started at zero, the neurons in a layer would stay identical, and the model would act as if it had only one neuron per layer.

items.term: Why two passes, and why that is the cheap part
items.text: The naive way to get a gradient is to nudge one weight, re-run the network, and see what the loss did — then repeat for every weight. On a network with 266,610 parameters that is 266,610 forward passes per step, which is why nobody could train an MLP for decades. Reverse-mode autodiff gets every one of those numbers from a single forward pass plus a single backward pass, because the chain rule lets a shared intermediate result be reused by everything downstream of it. The lesson is general: it is efficient precisely when there are many inputs and one output, which is the shape of every loss function.

items.term: Backpropagation is three things, and people mean different ones
items.text: The chapter is careful here and it is worth copying the care. Reverse-mode autodiff computes the gradients. Gradient descent uses them to move the parameters. Backpropagation is the whole procedure: forward pass, reverse pass, gradient step. So 'autodiff versus backprop' is not two algorithms competing — one is a component of the other, and the difference is the update step.

items.term: Why the symmetry argument kills zero initialisation but not zero biases
items.text: Identical starting weights make every neuron in a layer compute the same thing, receive the same gradient, and stay identical forever — width becomes decoration. Biases are different: two neurons with different incoming weights already differ, so starting their biases equal does not tie them together. That is why Keras randomises the weight matrix and sets the biases to zeros, and it is a good example of a rule being about the symmetry rather than about the number zero.

blocks.title: Key points
items: An MLP consists of an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer in a feedforward configuration.
Backpropagation combines reverse-mode automatic differentiation with gradient descent across forward and backward passes.
Nonlinear activation functions like sigmoid, tanh, and ReLU enable neural networks to learn complex non-linear functions.
Hidden layer weights must be initialized randomly to break symmetry during backpropagation updates.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The chapter says a large enough network with nonlinear activations can theoretically approximate any continuous function. What are the actual conditions on that claim, and what does it say about how many neurons you would need?

Look up: David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams, "Learning Internal Representations by Error Propagation" (Defense Technical Information Center technical report, September 1985), cited in this chapter, and Appendix B of this book for autodiff.

items.term: Building Regression Multi-Layer Perceptrons

blocks.content:
An MLP predicts a number instead of a class simply by choosing the right number of output neurons, the right output activation, and the right loss — the hidden layers do not change at all.

**The question this lesson answers:** given the California housing features, how do you wire an MLP so it outputs a house price, and which three decisions actually differ from the classification case?

### The big picture

| Decision | Driven by | Typical answer here |
|---|---|---|
| output neurons | how many numbers you predict | one per output dimension |
| output activation | the range the number may take | none, or one that bounds it |
| loss function | how you punish being wrong | MSE, or Huber with outliers |
| input scaling | gradient descent's patience | standardize before training |

### 1 · How many output neurons

Standard machine learning models often struggle to capture complex nonlinear relationships when predicting continuous numerical target values. A **Multi-Layer Perceptron** (MLP) configured for regression solves this problem by using stacked layers of artificial neurons to learn non-linear patterns.

The architecture requires choosing specific numbers of output neurons based on the dimensionality of the target. Predicting a single value like house price requires one output neuron, whereas predicting multiple continuous target values requires one neuron per output dimension.

Work the card's example: to locate the centre of an object in an image you predict 2D coordinates, so two output neurons. Add a bounding box and you need the width and the height as well. Predicting 2D coordinates takes 2 neurons and predicting width and height takes 2 more neurons, so four output neurons are required in total. One neuron, one number — the count is never a judgement call.

### 2 · Scale the inputs or the training stalls

To construct a regression MLP, input features are fed through one or more hidden layers equipped with non-linear activation functions such as the Rectified Linear Unit (**ReLU**). The output layer directly emits the final numerical predictions.

When feature scales differ drastically across input variables, gradient descent optimization stumbles and converges poorly. Preprocessing input features using scaling techniques such as **standardization** — rescaling each column so it has mean 0 and variance 1 — ensures stable training and fast convergence.

This is a real gotcha and not a formality: gradient descent optimization struggles to converge when input features possess varying scales, so a column of room counts and a column of incomes cannot be fed in raw. Put the scaler and the network in one pipeline and the scaling can never be forgotten at prediction time, the same way you would not hand-apply a transformation to some rows and not others.

### 3 · The worked example

Consider predicting house prices using the California housing dataset. The dataset contains continuous numerical features measured on different scales. A three-hidden-layer network with 50 neurons per layer is defined using the **MLPRegressor** class. A preprocessing pipeline standardizes the training features using a standard scaler before passing them to the neural network. The model minimizes the mean squared error (**MSE**) loss function using the Adam optimizer. Upon evaluating the trained pipeline on validation data, the model achieves a Root Mean Squared Error of approximately 0.505.

The python card below is the whole thing in about fifteen lines.

### 4 · Choosing the output activation

Choosing the output layer activation function dictates the valid range of network predictions; omitting an output activation permits unconstrained real number outputs, while functions like softplus guarantee strictly positive outputs.

| You need | Use in the output layer |
|---|---|
| any real number | no activation at all |
| strictly positive, no ceiling | ReLU or softplus |
| bounded 0 to 1 | sigmoid, targets scaled to match |
| bounded −1 to 1 | tanh, targets scaled to match |

So for a target that must be positive but has no upper limit, the answer is ReLU or softplus in the output layer. The card below defines softplus and gives the scaling rules for the bounded cases.

### 5 · The loss, and where this class runs out

The default loss is MSE. With many outliers, the Huber loss helps, and the reason is its shape: Huber loss is less sensitive to outliers due to its linear behavior for large errors. It is quadratic below a threshold δ (typically 1) and linear above it, so one wildly wrong district stops dominating the total.

That is also where this convenience class stops: MLPRegressor does not support custom activation functions in the output layer or alternative losses like Huber. Everything in section 4 is advice you cannot act on here, which is exactly why the chapter switches to Keras next.

**One-liner for your notes:** a regression MLP is one output neuron per predicted number, an output activation chosen from the target's range, MSE or Huber as the loss, and scaled inputs — and Scikit-Learn's MLPRegressor gives you only the last two.

blocks.title: Output neurons, output activations and the Huber loss
blocks.content:
To locate the center of an object in an image, an MLP predicts 2D coordinates, so it needs two output neurons. A bounding box adds two more numbers, the width and the height, for a total of four output neurons.

With no output activation, the MLP is free to output any value. To guarantee positive outputs, use ReLU or softplus in the output layer; softplus(z) = log(1 + exp(z)) is close to 0 when z is negative and close to z when z is positive. To keep predictions within a range, use the sigmoid (targets scaled to 0 to 1) or tanh (targets scaled to –1 to 1).

With many outliers, the Huber loss helps: it is quadratic when the error is smaller than a threshold δ (typically 1) but linear when the error is larger, so it is less sensitive to outliers than the MSE. The MLPRegressor class supports no output activation function and only supports the MSE.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.datasets import fetch_california_housing
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPRegressor
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

housing = fetch_california_housing()
X_train_full, X_test, y_train_full, y_test = train_test_split(
    housing.data, housing.target, random_state=42)
X_train, X_valid, y_train, y_valid = train_test_split(
    X_train_full, y_train_full, random_state=42)

mlp_reg = MLPRegressor(hidden_layer_sizes=[50, 50, 50], random_state=42)
pipeline = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), mlp_reg)
pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred = pipeline.predict(X_valid)
rmse = mean_squared_error(y_valid, y_pred, squared=False)
```

items.term: The output layer encodes a constraint you already know
items.text: Choosing softplus because prices cannot be negative is not a trick to improve accuracy — it is a way of telling the model something true that it would otherwise have to learn from data. Every constraint you build into the architecture is one the model cannot violate and does not have to spend capacity discovering. The cost is that a wrong constraint is unfixable by training, which is why the choice is driven by the meaning of the target and never by the validation score.

items.term: Why scaling is a convergence problem, not a correctness problem
items.text: Unscaled features do not make the model wrong in principle; a large weight could compensate for a small-numbered column. What they break is the search. Gradient descent takes one step size across all parameters, so a feature measured in tens of thousands and a feature measured in single digits need wildly different step sizes to move the same amount — and only one of them gets a sensible one. Standardizing puts every column on comparable footing so a single learning rate can serve them all.

items.term: What the Huber loss is really trading
items.text: MSE squares errors, so a single wild outlier can dominate the whole gradient and drag the model towards it. MAE does not, but its constant slope makes the final approach to a minimum less precise. Huber takes the quadratic behaviour near zero and the linear behaviour far away, so it converges cleanly on ordinary errors and refuses to be bullied by extreme ones. That is the general move — a loss is a statement about which mistakes you consider unacceptable, and it is a design decision, not a default.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Regression MLPs use one output neuron for single-value outputs and multiple output neurons for multivariate regression.
Input feature scaling via standardization is essential for efficient gradient descent optimization in neural networks.
Hidden layers typically use the ReLU activation function, whereas output activations depend on target value range constraints.
Mean squared error is the default loss function for regression MLPs, though alternative losses like Huber handle outliers better.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: MLPRegressor applies a little L2 regularization by default, controlled by its alpha hyperparameter, which this lesson does not discuss. What does alpha actually do to the weights, and how would you choose it?
Look up: the MLPRegressor page in the scikit-learn user guide (sklearn.neural_network), and Table 10-1 "Typical regression MLP architecture" in this chapter.

items.term: Classification Multilayer Perceptrons

blocks.content:
For classification the hidden layers stay exactly as they were; what changes is the number of output neurons and which activation sits on them — and that is decided entirely by whether the labels are exclusive.

**The question this lesson answers:** spam or ham, spam-and-urgent, or a handwritten digit from 0 to 9 — what output layer does each of those need, and which loss trains all three?

### The big picture

| Task | Output neurons | Output activation |
|---|---|---|
| binary | 1 | sigmoid |
| multilabel binary | 1 per binary label | sigmoid on each |
| multiclass | 1 per class | softmax across the layer |

One loss covers all three rows: **cross-entropy loss** serves as the standard objective function.

### 1 · One label, yes or no

Standard regression networks output continuous numerical values, which do not directly represent probability distributions over discrete categories. To perform classification tasks, a **Multilayer Perceptron** (MLP) must adapt its output layer architecture and activation functions according to the specific structure of the targets.

For binary classification, the network uses a single output neuron paired with the **sigmoid activation function**, producing an estimated probability between 0 and 1 for the positive class. One number is enough because the other probability is whatever is left over.

### 2 · Several independent yes/no labels

When predicting multiple independent binary attributes at once — known as multilabel binary classification — the network allocates one output neuron per binary label, with each output neuron using the sigmoid function independently. Because these predictions are independent, their output values do not need to sum to 1.

For example, an email system classifying messages as ham or spam and urgent or nonurgent uses multilabel binary classification with two sigmoid output neurons. A message might yield outputs of 0.90 for spam and 0.85 for urgent. Those add up to more than 1 and nothing is wrong: they are two separate questions, not two shares of the same answer.

This is the difference between two boolean columns and one enum column. Two booleans can both be true; an enum picks exactly one value. The output layer has to match which of those the label really is.

### 3 · Exactly one class out of many

For multiclass classification, where an instance belongs to exactly one class out of three or more possibilities, the architecture changes. As Figure 10-9 below shows, the output layer contains one neuron for every possible class, and the entire output layer uses the **softmax activation function**.

Softmax is not applied neuron by neuron like the sigmoid — it looks across the whole layer at once, which is what lets it enforce a shared budget. A multiclass MLP uses softmax because it ensures output values are probabilities between 0 and 1 that sum to exactly 1. The softmax function converts raw output scores into a valid probability distribution where each value lies between 0 and 1, and all output probabilities sum strictly to 1.

Classifying an image of a handwritten digit into one of ten mutually exclusive classes (0 through 9) requires ten output neurons controlled by a softmax activation layer, ensuring the probabilities across all ten classes sum to 1.0. So an MLP classifying handwritten digits into classes 0 through 9 needs 10 output neurons — one per class, always.

Reading Figure 10-9 below, the feature that identifies it as a multiclass model rather than a binary one is the presence of three distinct output neurons fed into a Softmax layer. A binary model would have a single neuron there.

### 4 · The loss is the same in all three cases

For training all these classification variants, **cross-entropy loss** serves as the standard objective function. It is the loss to reach for whenever the model outputs probabilities rather than raw numbers, which is every row of the table above.

**One-liner for your notes:** count the labels and ask whether they are mutually exclusive — exclusive means one softmax layer with a neuron per class, independent means one sigmoid neuron per label, and cross-entropy trains either.

blocks.caption: A modern MLP (including ReLU and softmax) for classification
blocks.alt: Figure 10-9: A modern MLP (including ReLU and softmax) for classification

items.term: Sigmoid versus softmax is a question about the labels, not the model
items.text: Both produce numbers between 0 and 1, so it is tempting to treat them as interchangeable. They are not: sigmoid scores each neuron on its own, softmax makes the neurons compete for a fixed total of 1. Use softmax on labels that are not actually exclusive and the model is forced to lower one probability to raise another, which is a claim about the world that is simply false. The architecture decision is downstream of a data-modelling question you should settle first: can two of these labels be true at once?

items.term: Why cross-entropy covers all three cases
items.text: Cross-entropy measures the distance between two probability distributions, and all three output layouts produce probabilities — that is the only property it needs. This is why the loss does not change across binary, multilabel and multiclass, while the output activation does. It also explains the pairing rule from the next lesson: the loss variant you name is about the shape of the labels, and the activation is about the shape of the predictions.

items.term: What a probability from a neural network is and is not
items.text: Softmax guarantees the outputs are between 0 and 1 and sum to 1, which makes them a valid distribution. It does not guarantee they are well calibrated — that a set of predictions at 0.9 turns out right about nine times in ten. Treat the numbers as a ranking with confidence attached unless something has checked the calibration, and be careful when they feed a threshold or a cost calculation downstream.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Binary classification uses one output neuron with a sigmoid activation function to output a single probability.
Multilabel binary classification uses one output neuron per label, each with a sigmoid activation function.
Multiclass classification uses one output neuron per class combined with a softmax output activation function.
The softmax activation function ensures output probabilities lie between 0 and 1 and sum to 1.
Cross-entropy loss is the standard loss function for training classification MLPs.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Softmax returns a confident-looking distribution even for an input unlike anything in the training set, because the probabilities are forced to sum to 1. How do practitioners detect that case?
Look up: the softmax function as introduced in Chapter 4 of this book, and Chapter 3 on multilabel and multiclass classification.

items.term: Loading and Preprocessing Datasets in Keras

blocks.content:
Before a single layer exists you load the images, carve a validation set out of the training set by hand, and divide every pixel by 255.0 — those three steps are the whole preprocessing story for Fashion MNIST.

**The question this lesson answers:** what shape and data type does Keras hand you, why must the pixels be rescaled before training, and where does the validation set come from when the loader only gives you two splits?

### The big picture

```
load_data() -> 60,000 train + 10,000 test
slice last 5,000 -> 55,000 train + 5,000 valid
divide by 255.0 -> floats from 0.0 to 1.0
```

### 1 · What the loader gives you

Raw image data often comes in large integer ranges and combined sets without a designated validation split, which can lead to inefficient gradient descent updates and improper model evaluation.

To address this problem, the **Keras** high-level API within TensorFlow provides built-in dataset utilities, such as `tf.keras.datasets.fashion_mnist`. Calling `load_data()` downloads and splits the dataset into initial training and testing sets. Fashion MNIST is a drop-in replacement for MNIST with 70,000 grayscale images across 10 classes.

The shape is where people trip. Keras loads images as 2D arrays of shape 28 × 28 instead of 1D vectors, which is the primary difference from how Scikit-Learn loads the same data — Scikit-Learn flattens each image into a 784-element row. They are stored as 8-bit unsigned integers (`uint8`) ranging from 0 to 255.

| | Keras | Scikit-Learn |
|---|---|---|
| shape per image | 28 × 28, still a grid | 784 values, one row |
| pixel type | uint8, 0 to 255 | floats |

Neither is wrong; they are two layouts of the same bytes. The grid layout matters later, in Chapter 14, where a layer needs to know which pixels are neighbours.

### 2 · Cutting a validation set by hand

In a typical scenario, out of the 60,000 default training samples, the last 5,000 samples are held out to create a dedicated validation set. This results in 55,000 training images, 5,000 validation images, and 10,000 test images.

If X_train_full contains 60,000 samples and you slice off the last 5,000 for validation, 55,000 samples remain in X_train. The slice `X_train_full[:-5000]` means "everything except the last 5,000", and `X_train_full[-5000:]` is the 5,000 you took. That is the only arithmetic here, and the python card below shows both slices.

### 3 · Why you divide by 255.0

To prepare the pixel intensities for neural network training, every image array is divided by 255.0, scaling the values to a floating-point range between 0.0 and 1.0. Pixel intensities are divided by 255.0 to scale pixel values into a 0.0 to 1.0 range for stable optimization.

It is the same reason the previous lesson standardized the housing columns: gradient descent behaves badly when the numbers it is stepping through are large or uneven. Dividing also converts the integers to floats, which is what the network wants anyway. The essential insight is that scaling inputs to a 0.0 to 1.0 floating-point range is vital for stable neural network training.

### 4 · Labels are indices, not names

Because the targets are numeric indices from 0 to 9, a list of class names like `["T-shirt/top", "Trouser", ...]` maps each target index to its human-readable category, as shown in Figure 10-10 below. This is a plain lookup list, the way a small dimension table maps a code to a label — position 9 is "Ankle boot". In Figure 10-10 below, the fashion item shown in the top-left corner is an ankle boot.

### 5 · One thing to know about Keras itself

The card below has the backend history. The short version: since version 2.4, TensorFlow is the backend framework strictly required to run Keras. Installing TensorFlow installs Keras too, and Keras will not work without it. PyTorch and JAX are separate deep learning libraries, not Keras backends.

**One-liner for your notes:** `load_data()` gives 60,000 training and 10,000 test images as 28 × 28 uint8 grids; you slice the last 5,000 off for validation and divide everything by 255.0 before a network ever sees it.

blocks.title: Keras and its TensorFlow backend
blocks.content: In the past, Keras could run on several backends: TensorFlow, PlaidML, Theano, and the Microsoft Cognitive Toolkit (CNTK), and the last two are now deprecated. Since version 2.4, however, Keras is TensorFlow-only. Installing TensorFlow automatically installs Keras as well, and Keras will not work without TensorFlow installed. When TensorFlow 2 came out, Keras was also chosen as the preferred high-level API of the framework. PyTorch, made by Facebook, and JAX, made by Google, are other popular deep learning libraries, not backends of Keras.

blocks.title: Figure 10-10
blocks.caption: Samples from Fashion MNIST
blocks.alt: Figure 10-10: Samples from Fashion MNIST

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

fashion_mnist = tf.keras.datasets.fashion_mnist.load_data()
(X_train_full, y_train_full), (X_test, y_test) = fashion_mnist

X_train, y_train = X_train_full[:-5000], y_train_full[:-5000]
X_valid, y_valid = X_train_full[-5000:], y_train_full[-5000:]

X_train, X_valid, X_test = X_train / 255.0, X_valid / 255.0, X_test / 255.0
class_names = ["T-shirt/top", "Trouser", "Pullover", "Dress", "Coat",
               "Sandal", "Shirt", "Sneaker", "Bag", "Ankle boot"]
```

items.term: Why the validation set is sliced off the training set and never the test set
items.text: Three splits exist because they answer three different questions: train fits the parameters, validation steers your choices, test estimates what happens on data nobody has looked at. The moment you tune anything against a set, that set stops being an honest estimate — it has leaked into your decisions. That is why the 5,000 come out of the 60,000 training images and the 10,000 test images are left untouched until the end.

items.term: Dividing by 255.0 is scaling, and it is not the same as standardizing
items.text: Both fix the same problem — gradient descent behaving badly on badly-ranged inputs — but they are different operations. Dividing by 255.0 maps a known, fixed range onto 0 to 1 and needs no statistics at all, which is why it is safe to apply to train, validation and test in one line. Standardizing subtracts a mean and divides by a standard deviation, and those must be measured on the training set only and then reused, or you have leaked information from the test set into preprocessing. Pixels have a known range; a housing column does not.

items.term: What the 28 by 28 shape is holding back for later
items.text: Flattening the grid immediately, which the next lesson does, throws away every fact about which pixels are next to each other. A dense layer cannot tell a neighbouring pixel from one on the far side of the image, so it has to learn spatial structure from scratch, one weight at a time. Keras keeps the grid shape in the loaded array for a reason: Chapter 14's convolutional layers consume it directly and exploit the neighbourhood that this chapter's model discards.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Keras is available as the primary high-level deep learning API within TensorFlow.
Fashion MNIST serves as a drop-in replacement for MNIST with 70,000 grayscale images across 10 classes.
Keras loads image datasets as 2D arrays of shape 28x28 with uint8 pixel values from 0 to 255.
Pixel values must be scaled to the 0.0 to 1.0 range by dividing by 255.0.
A custom validation split can be manually sliced from the loaded training data.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The chapter says a simple linear model reaches about 92% accuracy on MNIST but only about 83% on Fashion MNIST. What makes the clothing images harder for the same model?
Look up: the "Building an Image Classifier Using the Sequential API" section of this chapter, which reports both numbers, and Chapter 3 where MNIST is introduced.

items.term: Building Sequential Models with Keras

blocks.content:
The Sequential API builds a network by listing its layers in order, and for an image classifier that list is one Flatten layer followed by Dense layers.

**The question this lesson answers:** how do you turn a 28 × 28 image into a ten-class prediction with a plain stack of layers, and how many trainable numbers does that stack actually contain?

### The big picture

```
[28, 28] -> Flatten -> Dense 300 -> Dense 100 -> Dense 10
  image      784 vals    relu         relu       softmax
```

Each arrow is one layer in the list, in the order you wrote them. Nothing branches, nothing skips — that constraint is exactly what "sequential" means, and it is why this API is only four lines long.

### 1 · Flatten: a reshape, not a computation

When building deep learning classifiers for multidimensional inputs like images, models must flatten raw inputs into vectors and pass them through sequentially connected dense layers. Keras provides the **Sequential API** to stack layers in a single pipeline, solving the problem of manually chaining operations and tracking parameter shapes.

Inputs of shape [28, 28] are flattened into 784-dimensional vectors by a **Flatten** layer, which contains zero parameters and merely reshapes the data matrix. A Flatten layer reshapes multidimensional inputs into a 1D vector without adding trainable parameters — it is a free change of layout, like unpivoting a grid into one long row, and it learns nothing.

### 2 · Dense: where the parameters live

Next, **Dense** layers process the data using linear combinations and non-linear activation functions. *Dense* is the same idea as the fully connected layer from the perceptron lesson: every input is wired to every neuron.

As Equation 10-2 below shows, each dense layer computes $h_{\mathbf{W}, \mathbf{b}}(\mathbf{X}) = \phi(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W} + \mathbf{b})$, where $\mathbf{X}$ is the input matrix, $\mathbf{W}$ is the weight matrix, $\mathbf{b}$ is the vector of bias terms managed by the dense layer, one term per neuron, and $\phi$ is the activation function such as ReLU or Softmax. The explanation under Equation 10-2 below breaks every piece of it down with this network's real numbers.

### 3 · Counting the parameters

Consider a concrete example: a Dense layer with 300 neurons receiving 784 input features. The weight matrix $\mathbf{W}$ requires 784 × 300 = 235,200 parameters, while the bias vector $\mathbf{b}$ requires 300 parameters, totaling 235,500 trainable parameters for that single layer.

The recipe is always the same two terms — inputs × neurons, plus one bias per neuron:

| Layer | Weights | Biases | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dense 300 from 784 | 784 × 300 = 235,200 | 300 | 235,500 |
| Dense 100 from 300 | 300 × 100 = 30,000 | 100 | 30,100 |
| Dense 10 from 100 | 100 × 10 = 1,000 | 10 | 1,010 |

So a Dense layer with 100 neurons receiving input from 300 neurons holds 30,100 parameters in total. Dense layers often have a lot of parameters, which gives the model plenty of flexibility to fit the training data and also means it can overfit, especially without much training data.

### 4 · When the weight matrix gets created

The key insight to remember is that specifying the input shape upfront allows Keras to immediately build parameter matrices and calculate layer shapes before training starts. The shape of the weight matrix depends on the number of inputs, so Keras cannot allocate it until it knows that number.

If you create a Keras Sequential model without specifying an input shape, Keras delays building the parameter weights until data is fed or `build()` is called. Until then you cannot display the model summary or save the model — the parameters do not exist yet. It is a deferred plan, not an error.

### 5 · How the numbers start out

The card below shows `get_weights()` returning a (784, 300) weight array and a (300,) bias array for the first hidden layer. Look at what they contain: random weights break symmetry between neurons, whereas zero biases cause no issues. That is the rule from the backpropagation lesson applied here — identical starting weights would keep the neurons identical forever, but a shared bias of zero does no such harm.

**One-liner for your notes:** Sequential is a list of layers, Flatten is a free reshape with no parameters, and every Dense layer holds inputs × neurons weights plus one bias per neuron.

blocks.title: Inspecting and initializing a Dense layer
blocks.content:
Calling `get_weights()` on the first hidden layer returns its connection weights and biases: `weights.shape` is `(784, 300)` and `biases.shape` is `(300,)`. The Dense layer initialized the connection weights randomly, which is needed to break symmetry so that the neurons do not stay identical, and it initialized the biases to zeros, which is fine. A different method can be set with `kernel_initializer` (kernel is another name for the weight matrix) or `bias_initializer`.

If you do not specify the input shape, Keras simply waits until it knows the shape before it builds the model parameters. That happens when you feed it some data, for example during training, or when you call its `build()` method. Until then, you cannot display the model summary or save the model.
