blocks.caption: Visualizing learning curves with TensorBoard
blocks.alt: Figure 10-16: Visualizing learning curves with TensorBoard

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from pathlib import Path
from time import strftime
import tensorflow as tf

def get_run_logdir(root_logdir="my_logs"):
    return Path(root_logdir) / strftime("run_%Y_%m_%d_%H_%M_%S")

run_logdir = get_run_logdir()
tensorboard_cb = tf.keras.callbacks.TensorBoard(
    run_logdir, profile_batch=(100, 200)
)
history = model.fit(X_train, y_train, epochs=20, callbacks=[tensorboard_cb])
```

items.term: The filesystem is the whole protocol
items.text: Your training job writes event files; TensorBoard polls the directory and redraws. Nothing connects the two processes, which is exactly why this works from a notebook, from a remote box, from a finished run, or from a job that has since crashed. It also tells you where the failure modes are: a run that appears in the wrong chart or does not appear at all is almost always a path problem, not a tool problem.

items.term: Directory naming is the experiment log
items.text: A timestamped subdirectory per run is a naming convention doing the work of a tracking system: it guarantees uniqueness, it sorts chronologically, and it makes every run comparable without a database. The weakness is that a timestamp records when a run happened and nothing about what was in it, so a month later you cannot tell which directory held which learning rate. That is the gap the HPARAMS view in the tuner lesson fills, and it is why serious experiment tracking eventually stops being a folder name.

items.term: Profiling is sampled for the same reason any instrumentation is
items.text: Measuring costs resources and the first measurements are unrepresentative, so you sample a window after warm-up rather than instrumenting everything from the start. The chapter's window of batches 100 to 200 is a concrete instance of a habit worth generalising: exclude start-up, take a slice of steady state, and accept that observation is not free.

blocks.title: Key points
items: TensorBoard visualizes training statistics, graphs, learning curves, and performance profiles by reading binary event summary files.
Using unique, timestamped subdirectories under a shared root log folder prevents data overlap and enables cross-run comparisons.
The Keras TensorBoard callback automatically generates log subdirectories and records training and validation metrics during model execution.
Network profiling tracks execution speed to detect system bottlenecks and is configured using the profile_batch parameter.
Lower-level custom logging of custom data types such as text, images, and audio is supported through the tf.summary module.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: TensorBoard reads a binary event format, and tf.summary can write scalars, histograms, images, audio and text into it. What is actually in one of those records, and what makes the format append-friendly enough to be read while it is still being written?
Look up: the tf.summary module in the TensorFlow API documentation, which this chapter cites for low-level logging.

items.term: Hyperparameter Tuning with Keras Tuner

blocks.content:
Keras Tuner turns hyperparameter guessing into a declared search space plus a search algorithm: you write one model-building function with the choices left open, and the tuner fills them in trial after trial.

**The question this lesson answers:** how many layers, how many neurons, which learning rate, which optimizer? Instead of answering four questions by hand, how do you declare the ranges and let a search answer them?

### The big picture

```
build_model(hp) -> declares ranges
   tuner + oracle -> picks values, trains, scores
      repeat for max_trials -> best config
```

### 1 · Why automate this at all

Neural networks possess vast architectural flexibility, which makes selecting the optimal hyperparameter combination difficult. Choosing values manually for the number of layers, neuron counts, learning rates, and optimizer choices often leads to suboptimal model performance. The **Keras Tuner** library automates this search process by integrating directly with Keras models to evaluate multiple hyperparameter combinations systematically.

A **hyperparameter** is a setting you choose before training, which stays fixed while training runs — as opposed to weights and biases, which training itself computes. It is the same distinction as a job's submit-time configuration versus the data the job produces.

### 2 · Declaring the search space

To use Keras Tuner, you first define a model-building function that accepts a `kt.HyperParameters` object. Inside this function, hyperparameter ranges are registered using methods like `Int`, `Float`, or `Choice`. The `kt.HyperParameters` object defines parameter search spaces and retrieves specific values during search trials — those are its two jobs, and it does both through the same call: the first time it sees a name it registers the range, and on every trial it returns that trial's chosen value.

Consider a scenario where an MLP classifies Fashion MNIST images. The model builder defines `n_hidden` between 0 and 8 layers, `n_neurons` between 16 and 256, a logarithmic `learning_rate` scale between 0.0001 and 0.01, and an `optimizer` choice between SGD and Adam.

| Hyperparameter | Method | Range |
|---|---|---|
| n_hidden | hp.Int | 0 to 8 layers |
| n_neurons | hp.Int | 16 to 256 |
| learning_rate | hp.Float, log | 0.0001 to 0.01 |
| optimizer | hp.Choice | sgd or adam |

### 3 · Why the learning rate is sampled on a log scale

`sampling="log"` is utilized when registering a continuous learning rate hyperparameter because it ensures learning rate values are explored across different order-of-magnitude scales uniformly.

Sample that range evenly and almost every draw lands near the top of it, because 0.0001 to 0.01 is mostly made of the last stretch. On a log scale each decade — 0.0001 to 0.001, and 0.001 to 0.01 — gets the same share of the draws. For a setting whose sensible values span orders of magnitude, that is the only sampling that explores it fairly.

### 4 · Running the search

The tuner evaluates different parameter choices across multiple trials, tracking validation performance to select the best-performing model configuration. A `kt.RandomSearch` tuner executes 5 trials for 10 epochs each. Directed by its underlying oracle, the tuner logs validation accuracy for every trial and saves the resulting model configurations.

The **oracle** is the component inside a Keras Tuner instance that determines which hyperparameter values to try next. Splitting it out this way is what makes the tuners interchangeable: the same search space works with random search or with a smarter strategy, because only the oracle changes.

The card below covers resuming. If a tuner search is executed with `overwrite=False` and a higher `max_trials` limit, the tuner resumes execution from previous trials and runs only the remaining added trials — so a search does not have to run in one sitting, which matters when each trial is ten epochs of training.

### 5 · Reading the answer out

To retrieve the optimal hyperparameter configuration values after a search completes, call `get_best_hyperparameters()` on the tuner and access the `values` attribute of the top trial. `get_best_models()` returns the trained models themselves. The card below has the book's actual winner: `n_hidden` 5, `n_neurons` 70, a learning rate of 0.00041268008323824807, and the `adam` optimizer.

That learning rate is worth staring at. No human would have typed it, and no grid over round numbers would have contained it — which is a fair summary of why the search exists.

The essential insight is that Keras Tuner replaces manual trial-and-error by programmatically defining search spaces and using specialized algorithms to retrieve the best model weights and hyperparameter settings.

**One-liner for your notes:** write `build_model(hp)` with `hp.Int`, `hp.Float` and `hp.Choice` where the numbers would go, let a tuner and its oracle run the trials, then read the winner with `get_best_hyperparameters()`.

blocks.title: Resuming a search and reading the best values
blocks.content:
The `RandomSearch` tuner first calls `build_model()` once with an empty HyperParameters object, just to gather the hyperparameter specifications. It then runs the trials, training each model for 10 epochs and saving it in a subdirectory of `my_fashion_mnist/my_rnd_search`. Because `overwrite=True`, that directory is deleted before training starts. If you run the code a second time with `overwrite=False` and `max_trials=10`, the tuner continues where it left off and runs 5 more trials, so you do not have to run all the trials in one shot.

After the search, `get_best_hyperparameters(num_trials=3)` returns HyperParameters objects, and `top3_params[0].values` is a dictionary of the best values: `n_hidden` 5, `n_neurons` 70, a learning rate of 0.00041268008323824807, and the `adam` optimizer.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import keras_tuner as kt
import tensorflow as tf

def build_model(hp):
    n_hidden = hp.Int("n_hidden", min_value=0, max_value=8, default=2)
    n_neurons = hp.Int("n_neurons", min_value=16, max_value=256)
    learning_rate = hp.Float("learning_rate", min_value=1e-4, max_value=1e-2, sampling="log")
    optimizer = hp.Choice("optimizer", values=["sgd", "adam"])
    
    if optimizer == "sgd":
        opt = tf.keras.optimizers.SGD(learning_rate=learning_rate)
    else:
        opt = tf.keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=learning_rate)
        
    model = tf.keras.Sequential()
    model.add(tf.keras.layers.Flatten())
    for _ in range(n_hidden):
        model.add(tf.keras.layers.Dense(n_neurons, activation="relu"))
    model.add(tf.keras.layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax"))
    model.compile(loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", optimizer=opt, metrics=["accuracy"])
    return model
```

items.term: Declaring the space is the part that generalises
items.text: The build function does not choose values; it states what values are legal. That separation is what lets the same function be driven by random search, by Hyperband, or by Bayesian optimisation without a line changing — swap the oracle, keep the space. It is worth recognising as a pattern: describe the space of legal configurations once, and let different strategies explore it, rather than baking the search into the thing being searched.

items.term: Log sampling is about where the information is
items.text: Sampling 0.0001 to 0.01 uniformly puts about 90% of your draws in the top decade, so nine trials out of ten probe a region you already suspect is too large. Log sampling gives each decade equal attention because that is where the behaviour actually changes — the difference between 0.0001 and 0.001 matters as much as the difference between 0.001 and 0.01. The rule to carry: when a setting's sensible values span orders of magnitude, search it multiplicatively, not additively.

items.term: Random search is a stronger baseline than it looks
items.text: It sounds lazy against a grid, and it usually wins, because most hyperparameters barely matter and a grid spends its budget re-testing the ones that do not. Random search never repeats a value on the axis that matters, so with the same number of trials it covers the important dimension far better. The limitation is real though: it learns nothing from the trials it has already run, which is precisely the gap Hyperband and Bayesian optimisation close by spending the budget unevenly.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Keras Tuner automates hyperparameter optimization for Keras neural networks.
A model-builder function receives a HyperParameters object to define search spaces for model parameters.
The sampling argument allows log-scale parameter sampling to cover multiple magnitudes equally.
Tuners rely on an internal oracle component to decide the specific hyperparameter values for each trial.
The get_best_models and get_best_hyperparameters methods retrieve top-performing configurations.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Random search treats every trial as independent. Hyperband instead kills unpromising trials early and gives the survivors more epochs. How does it decide how much budget to hand out, and when does that go wrong?
Look up: Lisha Li et al., "Hyperband: A Novel Bandit-Based Approach to Hyperparameter Optimization", Journal of Machine Learning Research 18 (April 2018): 1-52, cited in this chapter.

items.term: Custom HyperModel Subclassing in Keras Tuner

blocks.content:
A plain model-building function can only tune what happens inside the model; subclassing `kt.HyperModel` gives you a `fit()` of your own, so preprocessing and training arguments become searchable too.

**The question this lesson answers:** "should I standardize the features?" and "what batch size?" are real hyperparameters — but neither lives inside the architecture, so where do you put them?

### The big picture

| Method | Owns | Tunable from here |
|---|---|---|
| `build(hp)` | the architecture | layers, neurons, learning rate |
| `fit(hp, model, X, y, **kwargs)` | the training call | preprocessing, batch size |

### 1 · The gap in the plain function

Standard hyperparameter tuning functions often limit search spaces to architecture parameters like layer counts or neuron units. When developers need to tune data preprocessing steps or custom training configuration options, standard model building functions become insufficient because they do not have direct access to data transformation logic or execution arguments.

The model-builder function returns a compiled model and then its job is over. Whatever happens between "here is a model" and "here is a trained model" is out of its reach — and that gap contains the scaling, the batch size, and anything else you do to the data on the way in.

### 2 · The subclass

To solve this issue, Keras Tuner provides the **kt.HyperModel** base class. By subclassing **kt.HyperModel**, developers can implement custom **build()** and **fit()** methods.

The **build()** method defines the network architecture using hyperparameter objects; it constructs and returns a compiled neural network architecture, doing the exact same job as a standalone model-building function. In the card below it simply calls the previous lesson's `build_model(hp)`, which is the honest way to show that nothing about section 2 of that lesson changes.

The **fit()** method receives the hyperparameter object, compiled model, training data, and fit keyword arguments. Spelled out, the `fit` method of a `kt.HyperModel` subclass accepts the hyperparameter object, compiled model, features, targets, and fit keyword arguments. Within **fit()**, hyperparameters can dynamically alter data preprocessing — such as toggling data normalization — or modify training parameters like batch sizes before invoking the model fitting procedure.

A developer subclasses `kt.HyperModel` instead of using a standard model building function to tune training options like batch size and preprocessing steps inside the fit method.

### 3 · The worked example

For instance, consider a classification task on the Fashion MNIST dataset. A developer creates a subclass called `MyClassificationHyperModel`. Inside its **fit()** method, the hyperparameter `hp.Boolean("normalize")` is evaluated. Conditional data preprocessing is handled during search trials by applying a Normalization layer inside `fit` when a Boolean hyperparameter evaluates to True: if the search algorithm selects `True` for this trial, a **tf.keras.layers.Normalization** layer standardizes the training features `X` before executing `model.fit(X, y, **kwargs)`. The tuner evaluates both normalized and raw feature pipelines seamlessly alongside architectural parameters.

`hp.Boolean` is the yes/no member of the same family as `hp.Int`, `hp.Float` and `hp.Choice` — the search space now has one more axis, and that axis is a preprocessing decision rather than a model one.

### 4 · One contract to respect

The `fit` method of a custom `kt.HyperModel` must return a history object produced by calling `model.fit` on the dataset. That is not a style preference: the tuner reads the metrics out of that History to score the trial, so a method that preprocesses beautifully and returns nothing scores nothing.

### 5 · Where the instance goes

Instances of HyperModel subclasses pass directly into tuners like `kt.Hyperband` or `kt.BayesianOptimization`, in the same argument position where the plain `build_model` function would have gone. Nothing else about running a search changes.

Defining search spaces within a dedicated class unifies model architecture design and data preprocessing optimization into a single search workflow. That is the real payoff: "normalize or not" stops being a decision you make once, outside the experiment, and becomes one more column in the trial table.

**One-liner for your notes:** subclass `kt.HyperModel` when the thing you want to tune is not inside the model — `build(hp)` returns the compiled model, `fit(hp, model, X, y, **kwargs)` owns preprocessing and training arguments and must return the History.

blocks.title: python example

items.term: Preprocessing is a hyperparameter and pretending otherwise biases the search
items.text: "Should I standardize?" is usually settled once, by hand, before any tuning starts — and then every architecture is searched under that one fixed assumption. But the best architecture with scaling and the best architecture without it need not be the same architecture. Pulling the preprocessing decision into the search space is what lets the two be chosen together, which matters whenever the decisions interact.

items.term: Why the hook is fit() and not a preprocessing argument
items.text: Keras Tuner could have offered a list of preprocessing options. Giving you the whole fit call instead is a deliberately open extension point: anything you can express in Python between receiving the data and calling model.fit is now searchable — scaling, augmentation, batch size, class weights, subsampling. The cost of that generality is the contract in the next paragraph: the tuner can only score your trial if you hand back what it expects.

items.term: Returning the History is the interface, and it is easy to break
items.text: The tuner reads the trial's metrics out of the History object your fit returns. Forget the return and nothing errors loudly — you have simply stopped reporting, and the search has no basis for comparison. That is the recurring shape of a framework hook: the framework supplies the arguments and you owe it a specific return value, and the failure mode of owing it and not paying is silence rather than an exception.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Subclassing kt.HyperModel allows hyperparameter tuning of data preprocessing and fit arguments.
The build method defines and returns the compiled Keras model architecture.
The fit method receives hyperparameters and handles dataset transformations prior to calling model fit.
Instances of HyperModel subclasses pass directly into tuners like kt.Hyperband or kt.BayesianOptimization.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: This subclass makes normalization a searchable Boolean. Batch size is mentioned as tunable in fit too, but the chapter does not show it. Where exactly would batch size be read and applied, given that the tuner also passes fit keyword arguments of its own?
Look up: the HyperModel class in the Keras Tuner documentation (keras.io/keras_tuner), which this chapter uses for the build and fit methods.

items.term: Choosing the Number of Hidden Layers in Neural Networks

blocks.content:
One hidden layer can in theory represent anything, but depth is what makes it affordable — a deep network reuses what the layer below it learned instead of rebuilding every pattern from scratch.

**The question this lesson answers:** if a single wide layer is already a universal tool, why does anyone stack layers at all, and how many should you start with?

### The big picture

```
layer 1: edges, line segments
layer 2: circles, polygons
layer 3: faces, objects
```

Each layer works with what the one below it produced. That is the whole argument for depth, and the reason a deep network needs far fewer neurons than a flat one.

### 1 · Shallow works, but it is expensive

When designing a neural network, a fundamental decision is determining how many **hidden layers** to include. While a shallow architecture with a single hidden layer can theoretically represent any complex function if given enough neurons, it is often wildly inefficient for complex real-world tasks. Flat networks require an exponentially larger number of neurons to model intricate relationships, which leads to slow training and excessive memory usage.

*Exponentially* is not a figure of speech here. It is the difference between a cost that grows steeply with complexity and one that grows gently — the same gap as between recomputing a result for every row and computing it once and reusing it.

### 2 · What depth actually buys

Deep architectures solve this efficiency problem by exploiting the **hierarchical structure** of real-world data. Deep neural networks are more parameter-efficient than shallow networks because they utilize hierarchical representations to model complex functions with exponentially fewer neurons.

Instead of learning complex patterns all at once, a deep network breaks the task into manageable levels of abstraction. The lowest hidden layers in a deep neural network typically extract low-level visual components such as line segments, edges, and simple orientations. Intermediate layers combine these low-level features to form intermediate shapes, like circles or polygons. Finally, the highest hidden layers assemble these shapes into complex high-level structures, such as human faces or objects. This multi-step process allows deep networks to reach much higher performance using far fewer parameters than shallow networks.

The book's picture for this is drawing a forest: leaf by leaf with no copy and paste takes forever, but draw one leaf, paste it into a branch, paste the branch into a tree, paste the tree into a forest, and you are done quickly. Real-world data is often structured that way, and depth is what lets a network exploit it.

### 3 · The measured example

Consider the **MNIST dataset**, which consists of handwritten digits. If you train a network with a single hidden layer containing a few hundred neurons, you can achieve roughly 97% accuracy. However, if you redistribute those same neurons across two hidden layers, the accuracy increases from around 97% to over 98% using roughly the same training time.

| Architecture | Neurons | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| 1 hidden layer | a few hundred | roughly 97% |
| 2 hidden layers | the same total | over 98% |

Same neuron budget, same training time, fewer errors. That is the cleanest evidence in the chapter that the arrangement matters and not only the size.

For even more complex tasks like speech recognition or large image classification, networks typically scale to dozens of layers.

### 4 · Reusing the bottom of somebody else's network

This hierarchical feature extraction also enables **transfer learning**. Because lower layers capture universal low-level features, you can reuse the trained bottom layers of an existing model for a new task — such as adapting a face recognition network to identify hairstyles — rather than training a new model from scratch. Transfer learning allows reuse of lower-layer weights from a trained model to avoid learning basic features from scratch.

Edges are edges in every photograph, so a network that has already learned them does not need to learn them again. Instead of randomly initialising the first few layers of the new network, you start them at the trained values, and the new model only has to learn the higher-level structures.

### 5 · What to actually do

The recommended strategy is to begin with one or two hidden layers and gradually increase layers until the model starts overfitting. **Overfitting** is the point where the model keeps getting better on the training data while getting worse on data it has not seen — the signal that you have added more capacity than the problem needs.

The card below adds the practical tail: very complex tasks need dozens of layers and a huge amount of training data, and you will rarely train those from scratch, because reusing a pretrained network is faster and needs far less data.

**One-liner for your notes:** depth beats width because each layer builds on the one below, so start with one or two hidden layers, add more until you overfit, and reuse a pretrained network's lower layers whenever the task is close enough.

blocks.title: How many hidden layers to start with
blocks.content: For many problems, you can start with just one or two hidden layers and the neural network will work just fine. For more complex problems, you can ramp up the number of hidden layers until you start overfitting the training set. Very complex tasks, such as large image classification or speech recognition, typically require networks with dozens of layers and a huge amount of training data. You will rarely have to train such networks from scratch: it is much more common to reuse parts of a pretrained state-of-the-art network that performs a similar task, which makes training a lot faster and needs much less data.

items.term: "Can represent" and "can be found" are different claims
items.text: One hidden layer can in theory model any function given enough neurons — and that guarantee is nearly useless on its own, because it says nothing about how many neurons, how much data, or whether gradient descent could ever find the right weights. Depth is not about extending what is representable; it is about making the good solutions reachable with a realistic number of parameters and examples. Any time you meet a universality result, ask what it costs and whether the search can get there.

items.term: Depth pays off because the data is hierarchical, not because deeper is better
items.text: The efficiency argument rests on a property of the data: edges compose into shapes, shapes into objects. Where that composition really exists, reusing a lower layer's output is like reusing a subquery instead of recomputing it, and the saving compounds with depth. Where it does not — genuinely flat, unstructured features — extra depth buys much less, which is why tabular problems often do fine with one or two hidden layers while images need dozens.

items.term: Transfer learning is the same argument, cashed in
items.text: If the lowest layers learn features that are universal rather than task-specific, then they are not really yours — they belong to the input domain. That is why you can take them from a face model and use them for hairstyles, and why the honest default for a hard vision task is to start from a pretrained network rather than from random weights. It also sets the limit: the further the new task is from the original domain, the less of the stack transfers.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A single hidden layer can theoretically model any function, but deep networks are much more parameter-efficient for complex problems.
Deep networks process data hierarchically, building complex concepts from low-level features like lines and edges.
Using multiple hidden layers allows models to achieve higher accuracy with fewer overall neurons and training samples.
Transfer learning reuses the lower layers of a pretrained network to kickstart training on a new, related task.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Transfer learning reuses the lower layers, but how much of the stack should you keep, and should those reused layers keep training or be frozen?
Look up: Chapter 11 of this book, "Training Deep Neural Networks", which this chapter defers the reuse-of-pretrained-layers discussion to.

items.term: Sizing Hidden Layers and Neurons in Neural Networks

blocks.content:
The input and output layer sizes are decided for you by the data; for the hidden layers, the modern advice is to make them all the same size, make them slightly too big, and let early stopping trim the excess.

**The question this lesson answers:** how wide should a hidden layer be, and what actually goes wrong if you make one too narrow?

### The big picture

```
input 784 (28 x 28)  -- fixed by the data
hidden ? ? ?         -- your only real choice
output 10 (classes)  -- fixed by the task
```

### 1 · Two of the three are not choices

When designing an artificial neural network, determining the number of neurons in the input and output layers is straightforward because the task requirements fix those dimensions. For instance, classifying image data like the MNIST dataset requires 784 input neurons for its 28 by 28 pixel grids and 10 output neurons for its target classes.

However, selecting the number of neurons in hidden layers requires a deliberate strategy to ensure the network has sufficient representational power without growing unnecessarily complex. **Representational power** is simply how much detail a layer is able to carry through to the next one.

### 2 · The pyramid, and why it was dropped

Historically, practitioners structured hidden layers like a pyramid, gradually reducing the number of neurons in subsequent layers — such as using 300, 200, and 100 neurons. The reasoning was that low-level features coalesce into fewer high-level concepts.

Modern deep learning has largely abandoned this pattern because using the same number of neurons across all hidden layers usually performs just as well or better, while simplifying hyperparameter tuning to a single value. Identical hidden layer sizes require tuning only one hyperparameter while yielding equal or superior performance.

| Shape | Hyperparameters to tune | Performance |
|---|---|---|
| pyramid 300, 200, 100 | one per layer | no better |
| flat 200, 200, 200 | one, total | as good or better |

The reason to care is search cost. The previous lesson's tuner had to explore `n_neurons` as a single number; a pyramid would have made it one axis per layer, and the search space grows with every axis you add.

### 3 · The failure mode: a bottleneck

A critical risk when sizing hidden layers is creating a **bottleneck layer**. The primary risk of a hidden layer with too few neurons is that the layer creates an information bottleneck that permanently discards vital data features.

The clearest illustration is dimensional: a hidden layer with 2 neurons attempts to process 3D data, forcing a permanent reduction in dimensions. If a hidden layer contains too few neurons, it loses essential information that subsequent layers cannot recover. Passing 3D input data into a hidden layer with only two neurons forces the data into two dimensions, permanently discarding critical details.

No matter how big and powerful the rest of the network is, that information will never be recovered. It is the same shape of mistake as dropping a column early in a pipeline: everything downstream inherits the loss, and no later stage can undo it.

### 4 · The stretch pants strategy

To avoid this, researchers often use the "stretch pants" strategy: build a network with slightly more neurons and layers than needed, and rely on **early stopping** or regularization to prevent overfitting. The stretch pants approach simplifies neural network architecture design because it selects a slightly oversized model and relies on regularization techniques to control model capacity.

The metaphor is the point: rather than spending time finding trousers that fit exactly, buy large stretchy ones that shrink to the right size. Oversizing costs some compute; undersizing costs information you cannot get back, so the two errors are not symmetric and the strategy leans towards the recoverable one.

Early stopping was the callback from an earlier lesson, and this is its second job: it is not only a time saver, it is the mechanism that makes deliberately oversizing a layer safe.

### 5 · Where to spend the next parameter

Ultimately, increasing the total number of layers provides more value than merely adding extra neurons per layer. Increasing the number of hidden layers provides more value than adding neurons to existing layers — the book's phrase is that you get more bang for your buck from depth. That follows directly from the previous lesson: an extra layer can build on everything below it, while an extra neuron in an existing layer only widens one step.

**One-liner for your notes:** input and output sizes come from the data, hidden layers should all be the same width, too narrow loses information forever, so oversize slightly and let early stopping handle it — and add depth before width.

items.term: The two errors are not symmetric, and that is the whole argument
items.text: Too many neurons costs compute and some overfitting risk, both of which you can manage afterwards with early stopping and regularization. Too few destroys information at that layer, and nothing downstream can rebuild it no matter how large the rest of the network is. When one mistake is recoverable and the other is not, the sensible default leans towards the recoverable one — which is exactly what the stretch pants advice encodes.

items.term: Equal layer widths is a search-cost decision as much as a modelling one
items.text: The evidence says equal widths perform as well or better, which is permission rather than a requirement. The stronger reason to adopt it is that a pyramid turns one hyperparameter into one per layer, and the tuner from the earlier lessons has to explore every one of them. Collapsing a whole family of shapes into a single number is a large saving for no measured loss, and recognising when a design choice can be collapsed that way is worth more than the specific rule.

items.term: Why a bottleneck is not always a defect
items.text: This lesson treats a narrow layer as damage, and for a classifier it is. But deliberately forcing data through a narrow layer is also a legitimate technique — it is how compression and representation-learning architectures work, where the point is to discover what can be thrown away. Same structure, opposite intent. The rule is not "narrow layers are bad", it is "a narrow layer destroys information, so only put one where losing information is what you want".

blocks.title: Key points
items: Input and output layer sizes are strictly determined by the dataset dimensions and target categories.
Using the same number of neurons across all hidden layers simplifies hyperparameter tuning while maintaining strong performance.
Hidden layers with too few neurons create bottleneck layers that irreversibly lose critical input information.
The stretch pants approach uses oversized layers paired with early stopping to auto-tune effective capacity.
Adding more layers generally improves neural network performance more effectively than adding more neurons per layer.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The chapter mentions that it can sometimes help to make the first hidden layer bigger than the others, which cuts against the equal-width rule. When does that exception apply?
Look up: the "Number of Neurons per Hidden Layer" section of this chapter, which states both the equal-size rule and the first-layer exception.

items.term: Tuning Learning Rate and Batch Size

blocks.content:
The learning rate is the one hyperparameter worth finding properly, and there is a cheap experiment that finds it: ramp it up during a short run and watch where the loss turns around.

**The question this lesson answers:** out of everything you could tune, which settings matter most, how do you find a good learning rate without training a dozen models, and what does changing the batch size oblige you to redo?

### The big picture

```
loss
 |  \___                /   <- loss shoots up here
 |      \______________/
 +---------------------------- learning rate (log scale)
        pick about 10x lower than the turning point
```

### 1 · Why the learning rate comes first

Training a neural network requires configuring several critical hyperparameters beyond the architecture itself. Setting these parameters incorrectly can cause training to diverge, proceed too slowly, or overfit the training data. The most essential hyperparameter to tune is the **learning rate**, which controls how aggressively the model updates its weights in response to estimated errors.

Too small and training crawls; too large and it diverges, meaning the loss grows instead of shrinking and the run is worthless. Everything else on this page is a smaller effect than getting this one roughly right.

### 2 · The ramp experiment

To find a suitable learning rate, you can train a model for a few hundred iterations while exponentially increasing the learning rate from a tiny value to a very large one. Plotting the loss against the learning rate on a logarithmic scale reveals a curve where the loss initially drops and eventually shoots up when the rate becomes unstable. The optimal learning rate is typically set about ten times lower than the point at which the loss begins to climb.

So the method is: increase the learning rate exponentially during a brief test run and pick a rate slightly below the point where loss rises. Read the three parts of that instruction separately.

| Part | Why it is that way |
|---|---|
| exponentially, not by equal steps | the useful range spans several orders of magnitude |
| a few hundred iterations | you need the shape of the curve, not a trained model |
| ten times lower than the turn | the turning point itself is already unstable |

The card below does the arithmetic for the ramp: going from 10⁻⁵ (0.00001) up to 10 in 500 iterations means multiplying by the same constant factor every iteration, roughly 1.028, which is about 2.8% per step.

### 3 · The worked reading

For example, suppose you test a network by increasing its learning rate from 10⁻⁵ to 10 over 500 iterations. If the loss reaches its minimum and starts climbing rapidly at a learning rate of 10⁻¹, you would select an optimal learning rate of 10⁻² to begin your actual model training.

In plain decimals: if a loss plot shows that the loss starts climbing at a learning rate of 0.1, the recommended optimal learning rate is 0.01. One decade lower than the turn — that is the whole rule.

### 4 · Batch size: a genuine trade-off

Another key hyperparameter is the **batch size**, which determines how many samples the model processes before updating weights. Large batch sizes utilize hardware accelerators like GPUs more efficiently by processing more samples per second. However, smaller batch sizes between 2 and 32 often help the model generalize better and avoid training instabilities, unless advanced techniques such as learning rate warmup are used.

The primary trade-off is therefore that large batch sizes improve GPU efficiency but may suffer from training instability and poor generalization. *Generalize* means doing well on data the model has not seen, which is the only performance that counts.

| Batch size | Gains | Costs |
|---|---|---|
| large | more samples per second on a GPU | instability early, may generalize worse |
| small, 2 to 32 | steadier training, better generalization | less efficient use of the hardware |

**Learning rate warmup** means starting with a small learning rate and ramping it up over the first part of training; it is what makes large batches workable, and it is covered in Chapter 11.

### 5 · The two settings you do not have to agonise over

Finally, the **activation function** for hidden layers defaults well to ReLU, while the number of training iterations is best managed automatically using early stopping. It is generally unnecessary to manually tune the exact number of training iterations because early stopping automatically terminates training when performance stops improving — the callback from the earlier lesson doing its third job.

### 6 · The catch that ties it all together

The single most important insight to remember is that hyperparameter values are interdependent: altering the batch size requires re-evaluating and updating the learning rate. So if you decide to change the batch size of your model, re-evaluate and update the learning rate, as the optimal rate depends on batch size.

Treat the pair as one setting measured together. Tuning them one at a time, and keeping the old learning rate after doubling the batch, is the most common way this advice gets wasted.

**One-liner for your notes:** ramp the learning rate exponentially over a few hundred iterations, take a value about ten times below where the loss turns up, prefer small batches unless you use warmup, leave activations at ReLU and iterations to early stopping — and re-tune the learning rate whenever the batch size moves.

blocks.title: Worked out: raising the learning rate from 1e-5 to 10
blocks.content:
The learning rate grows by multiplying it by the same constant factor at each iteration. To go from $10^{-5}$ to $10$ in 500 iterations, the book uses the factor $(10 / 10^{-5})^{1/500}$. Since $10 / 10^{-5} = 10^{6}$, the factor is $10^{6/500} = 10^{0.012} \approx 1.028$, so each iteration raises the learning rate by about 2.8%, and after 500 iterations it has been multiplied by $10^{6}$, reaching $10$.

Plot the loss against the learning rate on a log scale: the loss drops at first, then shoots back up once the rate is too large. The optimal learning rate is a bit lower than that turning point, typically about 10 times lower.

items.term: The ramp test measures the edge, not the optimum
items.text: Notice what the experiment actually finds: the point where training becomes unstable. It never trains a good model, and it does not need to — a few hundred iterations is enough to locate the cliff, and the working value is inferred by backing off a decade. That is a cheap-probe pattern worth stealing: when the quantity you want is hard to measure directly, find a nearby boundary that is easy to detect and derive from it.

items.term: Why the batch size argument has papers on both sides
items.text: The chapter cites a 2018 result concluding that small batches from 2 to 32 give better models in less time, and 2017 results showing batches up to 8,192 working fine with learning rate warmup. Both are right, because they are answering under different conditions: with a fixed recipe, large batches destabilise early training; with warmup and a retuned learning rate, they do not. The practical reading is the chapter's own — try large with warmup, fall back to small if training is unstable or the result disappoints — and the general reading is that a hyperparameter result is always conditional on the rest of the setup.

items.term: Interdependence is why one-at-a-time tuning stalls
items.text: The optimal learning rate depends on the batch size, so tuning one while holding the other fixed finds the best value only for the setting you happened to freeze. This is precisely what the tuner in the earlier lessons is for: it varies the axes jointly, and it is why a search can find a combination — 5 layers, 70 neurons, a learning rate of 0.00041268008323824807, Adam — that no sequence of individual adjustments would have reached.

blocks.title: Key points
items: The learning rate is the most critical hyperparameter to tune for stable model convergence.
Optimal learning rates are typically set about ten times lower than the point where training loss begins to climb.
Small batch sizes often provide better generalization, while large batch sizes maximize GPU processing efficiency.
Using early stopping removes the need to manually tune the exact number of training iterations.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The chapter's guidance is that the optimal learning rate is about half the maximum rate at which training diverges, and also about ten times below where the loss turns up on the ramp. How do those two rules of thumb sit together?

Look up: Leslie N. Smith, "A Disciplined Approach to Neural Network Hyper-Parameters: Part 1 - Learning Rate, Batch Size, Momentum, and Weight Decay", arXiv preprint arXiv:1803.09820 (2018), which this chapter recommends for hyperparameter best practices.

Exercise 2: In this exercise, you will design a diagram of an artificial neural network using traditional threshold logic units that implements the exclusive-OR (XOR) logical operation based on its canonical Boolean decomposition.

Exercise 6: In this exercise, you will analyze a fully connected multilayer perceptron with 10 input units, a single hidden layer of 50 ReLU neurons, and 3 ReLU output neurons to determine the matrix dimensions of its inputs, weights, biases, and outputs, as well as formulate its full matrix calculation equation.

Exercise 7: In this exercise, you will specify the required number of output neurons and appropriate activation functions for three distinct tasks: binary email classification, ten-class digit recognition on the MNIST dataset, and continuous housing price regression.

items.term: Solving Unstable Gradients with Proper Weight Initialization

blocks.content:
Deep networks often fail to train because the error signal shrinks to nothing on its way backward, and the first fix is choosing the right scale for the random numbers the weights start at.

**The question this lesson answers:** why does a deep network built from sigmoid activations and ordinary random weights stop learning in its lower layers, and what scale should the starting weights have instead?

### The big picture

```
forward   variance grows layer by layer, sigmoid saturates
backward  derivative near 0, gradient vanishes
result    lower layers barely move
fix       set starting variance from fan-in and fan-out
```

### 1 · What actually goes wrong

Training deep neural networks often fails because error gradients become unstable during **backpropagation**. Backpropagation is the pass that walks backward through the layers working out, for every weight, how much it contributed to the error; a **gradient** is that per-weight number, the slope telling gradient descent which way and how far to nudge the weight.

When training a deep network using standard normal weight initializations paired with logistic sigmoid activations, layer output variances grow progressively larger with each successive layer. **Variance** is just the spread of a set of numbers around their average. As a result, the sigmoid activations saturate in the top layers of the network, at either extreme of the curve. To **saturate** means the function has flattened out: pushing the input further barely changes the output.

The book's own picture for this is a chain of microphone amplifiers: if one is set too low nobody hears you, and if one is set too high your voice comes out saturated and unintelligible — and every amplifier in the chain has to pass the voice on at the same loudness it came in (book footnote 2, page index 516).

### 2 · Why a flat curve kills learning

When the inputs to a sigmoid function become very positive or negative, the function saturates near 1 or 0 where its derivative is virtually zero, and backpropagation then passes these near-zero derivatives backward, so the gradients vanish rapidly. A **derivative** here is the steepness of the curve at a point: flat curve, near-zero derivative, nothing to propagate.

Figure 11-1 below draws that curve, and the regions with a derivative near zero are at the extreme negative and positive values of z. The one steep region sits around z = 0. Because each layer multiplies the signal by its own near-zero derivative, the little that survives keeps getting diluted on the way down, leaving the lower layers' connection weights almost completely unupdated.

### 3 · Glorot's rule: keep the variance the same

Xavier Glorot and Yoshua Bengio proposed keeping the variance of layer outputs equal to the variance of their inputs, as well as keeping gradient variances equal before and after passing through a layer, so that network weight signals do not die out or explode during forward and backward passes.

Equal variance across directions requires setting connection weights randomly according to Equation 11-1 below, which defines **Glorot initialization** (also known as Xavier initialization). Weights are drawn from a zero-mean distribution with a variance of σ² = 1 / fan_avg, where fan_avg = (fan_in + fan_out) / 2. **fan-in** is how many inputs a layer has; **fan-out** is how many outputs it produces.

Worked through on the book's own numbers: consider a layer with 100 inputs (fan_in = 100) and 100 outputs (fan_out = 100). The average fan value is 100. Under Glorot initialization with a normal distribution, the target weight variance σ² is calculated as 1 / 100 = 0.01, resulting in a standard deviation of σ = 0.1. Initializing weights at this scaled variance keeps signals flowing stably without exploding or vanishing.

### 4 · One rule per activation function

Different activation functions require different variance scaling rules. For example, networks using ReLU activations require **He initialization**, which sets weight variance to 2 / fan_in to maintain stable signal flow across layers.

| Strategy | Variance | Use with |
|---|---|---|
| Glorot | 1 / fan_avg | none, tanh, sigmoid, softmax |
| He | 2 / fan_in | ReLU and its variants |
| LeCun | 1 / fan_in | SELU |

The full version of this is Table 11-1, in the card below, along with the Keras setting that switches a layer over.

**One-liner for your notes:** proper weight initialization preserves signal variance across network layers, preventing gradients from vanishing or exploding during training — Glorot at 1 / fan_avg for sigmoid-like activations, He at 2 / fan_in for ReLU.

blocks.title: Table 11-1: which initialization for which activation
blocks.content:
The book's **Table 11-1** gives the variance of the normal distribution each strategy uses:

- **Glorot**: $\sigma^2 = 1 / \text{fan}_{\text{avg}}$, for no activation, tanh, sigmoid and softmax.
- **He**: $\sigma^2 = 2 / \text{fan}_{\text{in}}$, for ReLU, leaky ReLU, ELU, GELU, Swish and Mish.
- **LeCun**: $\sigma^2 = 1 / \text{fan}_{\text{in}}$, for SELU.

LeCun initialization is simply Glorot initialization with $\text{fan}_{\text{avg}}$ replaced by $\text{fan}_{\text{in}}$. By default, Keras uses Glorot initialization with a uniform distribution; you switch a layer to He initialization with `kernel_initializer="he_normal"` or `"he_uniform"`.

blocks.title: Figure 11-1
blocks.caption: Sigmoid activation function saturation
blocks.alt: Figure 11-1: Sigmoid activation function saturation

blocks.title: Equation 11-1
blocks.caption: Glorot initialization (when using the sigmoid activation function)
blocks.explain:
**Why the equation looks like this**

The only thing you get to choose about the starting weights is how spread out they are. Too small and
the signal fades layer by layer; too large and it grows until the activation saturates. So the rule
has to be a spread, and it has to depend on how many connections meet at that layer — a neuron with
1,000 inputs adds up 1,000 little products, so each one must be smaller than in a neuron with 10.
That is why the layer's fan appears in the denominator, and why nothing else about the model does.

**Is this standard?** Yes, and it is still the default. Glorot initialization with a uniform
distribution is what Keras uses when you say nothing. Equation 11-1 is the canonical form, not a
simplification for this chapter. The uniform line underneath it is the same variance expressed as a
range instead of a spread.

**The general form.** All three strategies in Table 11-1 are the same equation with two knobs — the
number on top and which fan goes underneath:

| Strategy | Variance | Activation |
|---|---|---|
| Glorot | 1 / fan_avg | none, tanh, sigmoid, softmax |
| He | 2 / fan_in | ReLU and its variants |
| LeCun | 1 / fan_in | SELU |

LeCun initialization is simply Glorot initialization with fan_avg replaced by fan_in, so it coincides
with Glorot whenever a layer has as many outputs as inputs.

**Terms this introduces:** a **normal distribution** is the bell-shaped spread of random numbers,
described fully by its mean and its variance. **Variance** is the average squared distance from the
mean; the **standard deviation** σ is its square root, and it is in the same units as the numbers
themselves. **fan-in** is the count of inputs to the layer, **fan-out** the count of outputs.

**Every piece of Equation 11-1**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| mean 0 | mean zero | weights centre on zero, as many − as + |
| σ² | sigma squared | the variance you draw the weights with |
| fan_avg | fan average | (fan_in + fan_out) divided by 2 |
| 1 / fan_avg | one over fan average | the whole rule: more connections, smaller weights |
| r | r | the half-width of the uniform version |
| √(3 / fan_avg) | root three over fan average | the r that gives the same variance |

**The formula in plain words**

Draw each starting weight at random from a bell curve centred on zero, whose spread is one divided by
the average of the layer's input and output counts. Or draw it flat between −r and +r, with r chosen
so the spread comes out the same.

**Real numbers plugged in**

The lesson's layer has fan_in = 100 and fan_out = 100.

1. fan_avg = (100 + 100) / 2 = 100.
2. σ² = 1 / 100 = 0.01.
3. σ = the square root of 0.01 = 0.1.

So every weight in that layer starts as a random number from a bell curve centred on zero with a
standard deviation of 0.1 — in practice almost all of them land between −0.3 and +0.3. For the same
layer under He initialization the top number becomes 2 and the denominator becomes fan_in: σ² =
2 / 100 = 0.02, so σ = about 0.141 — wider, because ReLU throws away the negative half of the signal
and the surviving half has to carry it.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

# Dense layer using default Glorot uniform initialization
dense_glorot = tf.keras.layers.Dense(50, activation="tanh")

# Dense layer using He normal initialization for ReLU
dense_he = tf.keras.layers.Dense(50, activation="relu",
                                kernel_initializer="he_normal")

# Custom initialization using VarianceScaling
custom_init = tf.keras.initializers.VarianceScaling(
    scale=2.0, mode="fan_avg", distribution="uniform"
)
dense_custom = tf.keras.layers.Dense(50, activation="sigmoid",
                                  kernel_initializer=custom_init)
```

items.term: Why the fix is a variance and not a value
items.text: Nothing about a single starting weight is right or wrong; what matters is the spread of the whole layer's weights, because a neuron adds up hundreds of weight-times-input products and it is that sum whose size you are controlling. This is why the rule names a variance and leaves the individual draws to chance, and why two layers with different connection counts need different spreads even though they sit in the same network.

items.term: Why it is a compromise, not a guarantee
items.text: Glorot and Bengio wanted two things at once: outputs as spread out as inputs on the way forward, and gradients as spread out after a layer as before it on the way back. Those two demands only agree when the layer has the same number of inputs as outputs. Averaging fan-in and fan-out is the compromise when they disagree — which is most layers. Knowing it is a compromise tells you why He initialization can drop fan-out entirely and still work.

items.term: When this stops being enough
items.text: Initialization only fixes the first step. The weights then move, and after enough training they can drift back into a bad scale, which is the whole reason the batch normalization lesson exists. Treat good initialization as necessary and not sufficient: if gradients go unstable hours into a run, the initializer is not the thing to change.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Unstable gradients occur when backpropagated error signals vanish to near zero or explode to huge values.
Sigmoid activations saturate at extreme values, causing their derivatives to approach zero and stopping lower layers from learning.
Glorot initialization sets the initial weight variance to 1 divided by the average of the input and output connection counts, so the variance gets smaller as that average grows.
He initialization scales weight variance specifically to support non-linearities such as ReLU and its variants.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Glorot initialization assumes the layer's inputs are roughly independent and similarly scaled. What happens to the argument when they are strongly correlated, as raw pixels are — and does that change what the right starting variance is?

Look up: Xavier Glorot and Yoshua Bengio, "Understanding the Difficulty of Training Deep Feedforward Neural Networks", Proceedings of the 13th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (2010): 249-256 - the paper this equation comes from.

items.term: Modern Activation Functions in Deep Learning

blocks.content:
Plain ReLU can permanently switch a neuron off, so the chapter replaces it with activation functions that always leave a little slope — or a smooth curve — on the negative side.

**The question this lesson answers:** if a neuron's weighted sum goes negative and stays negative, ReLU outputs zero forever and gradient descent can never revive it. Which activation functions fix that, and which one should you reach for?

### The big picture

```
ReLU        flat 0 on the left  -> neuron can die
Leaky ReLU  small slope a       -> never fully dies
PReLU       that slope a learned during training
ELU / SELU  exponential curve, mean nearer 0
GELU/Swish/Mish  smooth, wiggly, best on hard tasks
```

### 1 · The dying ReLU problem

Standard activation functions like the Rectified Linear Unit suffer from the **dying ReLU** problem, where neurons stop outputting values other than zero when their weighted sum inputs become negative across all training instances. The **weighted sum** is the single number a neuron computes before its activation function: every input times its weight, added up.

Because the derivative of ReLU is zero for negative values, gradient descent cannot update these dead neurons. There is no slope to follow, so there is no update, so the weighted sum never changes, so the neuron stays dead. Modern activation functions resolve this issue by ensuring non-zero gradients or introducing smooth, non-monotonic curves.

### 2 · Leaky ReLU and PReLU: keep a little slope

To prevent dead neurons, variants such as **Leaky ReLU** introduce a small slope α for negative inputs, defined as LeakyReLU(z) = max(αz, z), as shown in Figure 11-2 below. Read the picture as: the right half is unchanged ReLU, and the left half applies a tiny non-zero slope α to inputs that are below zero, instead of flattening to zero.

When α is learned via backpropagation, it becomes a **Parametric ReLU (PReLU)** — the difference is exactly that: PReLU allows the slope parameter alpha to be learned during network training, rather than being fixed by you before the run.

Worked through with the lesson's numbers: consider a neuron with a negative input sum z = -2.0. Under a standard ReLU, the output is 0.0 and its gradient is 0.0, rendering the neuron dead. Under Leaky ReLU with a hyperparameter α = 0.2, the output is calculated as max(0.2 × (-2.0), -2.0) = -0.4, which yields a non-zero gradient of 0.2 during backpropagation and keeps the neuron active.

### 3 · ELU and SELU: a curve instead of a corner

Another alternative is the **Exponential Linear Unit (ELU)**, defined in Equation 11-2 below, which uses an exponential curve for negative inputs to keep the average output closer to zero.

A scaled version called **SELU** allows self-normalization in deep Multilayer Perceptrons if specific conditions like LeCun normal initialization are met. **Self-normalizing** means each layer's output keeps a mean near 0 and a spread near 1 by itself, with no normalization layer bolted on. A **Multilayer Perceptron (MLP)** is a plain stack of dense layers, nothing fancier. Figure 11-3 below plots ELU and SELU together; the full list of SELU's conditions is in the card below.

### 4 · The smooth family: GELU, Swish, Mish

More recent non-monotonic, smooth functions like **GELU**, **Swish**, and **Mish** (illustrated in Figure 11-4 below) generally outperform traditional ReLU variants on complex tasks by providing smooth curvatures that help gradient descent optimize complex patterns. **Non-monotonic** means the curve does not only rise: it dips before climbing again. **Smooth** means it has no sharp corner where the slope jumps, which is what ReLU has at zero.

| Family | Negative side | Reach for it when |
|---|---|---|
| ReLU | flat zero | simple task, speed matters |
| Leaky / PReLU | small slope | latency matters, avoid dead units |
| ELU / SELU | exponential curve | deep plain dense stacks |
| GELU / Swish / Mish | smooth dip | complex task, top accuracy |

The card below carries the book's cost side of this table, including why ReLU stays a good default.

**One-liner for your notes:** modern activation functions prevent zero-gradient dead zones and smooth out optimization landscapes to improve deep neural network training.

blocks.title: SELU's conditions, and the cost of GELU, Swish and Mish
blocks.content:
SELU makes a network self-normalize only when all of these conditions hold:

1. The input features are standardized: mean 0 and standard deviation 1.
2. Every hidden layer's weights use LeCun normal initialization (`kernel_initializer="lecun_normal"`).
3. The network is a plain MLP, a stack of dense layers. In recurrent networks or networks with skip connections, SELU will probably not outperform ELU.
4. You do not use ℓ1 or ℓ2 regularization, max-norm, batch norm, or regular dropout.

These smooth functions are not faster than ReLU. GELU is a bit more computationally intensive, Mish needs a bit more compute, and ReLU is very fast to compute. So the book calls ReLU a good default for simple tasks, Swish probably a better default for complex tasks, and leaky ReLU a good choice when runtime latency matters.

blocks.title: Figure 11-2
blocks.caption: Leaky ReLU: like ReLU, but with a small slope for negative values
blocks.alt: Figure 11-2: Leaky ReLU: like ReLU, but with a small slope for negative values

blocks.title: Equation 11-2
blocks.caption: ELU activation function
blocks.explain:
**Why these equations look like this**

Both shapes exist to fix one specific defect: ReLU is exactly flat to the left of zero, so a neuron
that lands there has no slope to follow and can never come back. Every fix in this lesson is a
different answer to "what should the left half do instead".

- **Leaky ReLU** keeps the cheapest possible answer: a straight line with a small slope α. Nothing
is curved, so it costs almost nothing to compute.
- **ELU (Equation 11-2)** curves instead, using an exponential so the left half flattens out
smoothly toward −α rather than running away downward. That gives a non-zero gradient AND an average
output nearer zero, which is what helps the vanishing-gradient problem.
- **GELU (Equation 11-3)** is not a patch at all: it multiplies the input by the probability that a
standard normal value is below it, so a very negative input gets scaled to nearly nothing and a very
positive one passes through nearly untouched. The dip near zero is a side effect of that shape, not
a design goal.

**Standard or ad hoc?** All three are canonical published forms, each from a named paper, and Keras
ships ELU, SELU and GELU by name. What is adjustable is α: 0.2 in the lesson's Leaky ReLU example,
usually 1 for ELU.

**The general form.** These are all "piecewise or smooth variants of ReLU", and they line up on one
spectrum by how much they bend:

| Function | Left of zero | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| ReLU | exactly 0 | cheapest |
| Leaky ReLU (α z) | straight, small slope | almost as cheap |
| ELU (α(exp z − 1)) | exponential curve | slower, exp is expensive |
| GELU (z Φ(z)) | smooth dip then flatten | most expensive |

**Terms these introduce:** **Φ** (phi) is the standard Gaussian cumulative distribution function —
Φ(z) is the probability that a random number drawn from a bell curve of mean 0 and variance 1 comes
out lower than z, so it runs from 0 up to 1. **exp(z)** is e raised to the power z, the curve that
grows fast on the right and flattens toward zero on the left. **Piecewise** means the function is
defined by cases: one rule for negative inputs, another for non-negative ones.

**Every piece of Equation 11-2 (ELU)**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| ELU_α(z) | E L U alpha of z | the output, for input z and setting α |
| z | z | the neuron's weighted sum coming in |
| α | alpha | how far down the left side is allowed to settle |
| exp(z) − 1 | exp z minus one | runs from −1 at very negative z up to 0 at z = 0 |
| if z < 0 | if z is below zero | the case that replaces ReLU's flat zero |
| if z ≥ 0 | if z is zero or above | unchanged: output equals input |

**The formulas in plain words**

ELU: if the input is negative, output alpha times (e-to-the-input minus one); otherwise output the
input unchanged. GELU: output the input multiplied by the chance a standard bell curve falls below it.

**Real numbers plugged in**

Take the lesson's dead-neuron case, z = −2.0.

1. **ReLU:** output 0.0, gradient 0.0 — nothing to learn from.
2. **Leaky ReLU, α = 0.2:** max(0.2 × (−2.0), −2.0) = max(−0.4, −2.0) = −0.4, and the gradient on that
side is the slope itself, 0.2.
3. **ELU, α = 1:** exp(−2.0) is about 0.135, so 1 × (0.135 − 1) = about −0.865 — negative, non-flat,
and already levelling off toward −1.

Same input, three different answers, and only the first one is dead.

blocks.caption: GELU activation function

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

# Dense layer using LeakyReLU with He initialization
leaky_relu = tf.keras.layers.LeakyReLU(alpha=0.2)
dense_leaky = tf.keras.layers.Dense(50, activation=leaky_relu,
                                    kernel_initializer="he_normal")

# Dense layer using standard ELU
dense_elu = tf.keras.layers.Dense(50, activation="elu",
                                  kernel_initializer="he_normal")

# Dense layer using self-normalizing SELU
dense_selu = tf.keras.layers.Dense(50, activation="selu",
                                   kernel_initializer="lecun_normal")
```

items.term: Why a dead neuron is worse than a bad one
items.text: A neuron with bad weights still receives gradient and can be corrected. A dead ReLU receives exactly zero gradient, so the mechanism that would fix it is the mechanism that is switched off. That is why the fixes all guarantee a non-zero slope somewhere rather than trying to choose better weights: they restore the feedback path rather than the answer.

items.term: The trade-off you are actually making
items.text: Every function past ReLU buys robustness with compute. ReLU is a comparison; Leaky ReLU is a comparison and a multiply; ELU needs an exponential; GELU and Mish need more still. For a model that will serve millions of predictions, that per-neuron cost is the deployment budget. This is why the book keeps ReLU as a default for simple tasks instead of always recommending the best-scoring function.

items.term: Why SELU's conditions are so restrictive
items.text: SELU does not add a normalizing step; it relies on the arithmetic of a plain dense stack working out so that mean and spread stay put layer after layer. Anything that changes that arithmetic — a skip connection, a recurrent loop, dropout zeroing values, a regularizer pulling weights — breaks the property. A guarantee that depends on the whole architecture is fragile in a way a layer you insert is not, and that is why SELU never took over.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Standard ReLU causes neurons to die when inputs are negative because its gradient becomes zero.
Leaky ReLU, PReLU, and ELU provide non-zero gradients for negative inputs to prevent neuron death.
SELU enables self-normalization in deep MLPs under specific constraints like LeCun initialization.
Smooth, non-monotonic functions like GELU, Swish, and Mish often achieve superior performance on complex tasks.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The book says Swish is probably a better default than ReLU for complex tasks, but ReLU is still what most production models ship. Find a benchmark that measures both accuracy and inference latency on the same model, and work out where the crossover actually sits.
Look up: Prajit Ramachandran et al., "Searching for Activation Functions", arXiv preprint arXiv:1710.05941 (2017) - the Swish paper, cited in this chapter's footnote 10.

items.term: Batch Normalization

blocks.content:
Batch normalization puts a small standardizing step inside the network, so every hidden layer receives inputs on a sane scale no matter what the layer below it has drifted to.

**The question this lesson answers:** good initialization fixes the gradients at the start of training, but they can go unstable again hours in. How do you keep each layer's inputs well behaved for the whole run — and how does that still work at test time, when you are predicting one row at a time?

### The big picture

```
mini-batch in
  1 mean       across the batch
  2 variance   across the batch
  3 standardize  (x - mean) / spread
  4 scale+shift  learnable gamma, beta
out
```

### 1 · Why another fix is needed

Even when proper weight initialization and non-saturating activations are used, vanishing or exploding gradients can reappear as deep neural networks train. Initialization only sets the starting point; the weights then move. **Batch normalization** resolves this instability by normalizing the inputs of intermediate layers throughout training.

A **mini-batch** is the small group of training rows processed together in one step — think of it as one micro-batch of rows rather than the whole table. Batch normalization gets its name because its statistics are computed over exactly that group.

### 2 · The four steps

Inserted right before or after an activation function, a batch normalization layer performs four steps on each mini-batch, as defined in Equation 11-4 below.

1. It computes the mean vector μ_B across the current mini-batch instances m_B.
2. It evaluates the batch variance σ_B².
3. It zero-centers and normalizes each instance x⁽ⁱ⁾ into x̂⁽ⁱ⁾ using a small constant ε to prevent division by zero.
4. It scales and shifts x̂⁽ⁱ⁾ using two learnable parameter vectors, γ and β.

The gamma and beta parameters allow the network to learn the optimal scale and shift for the normalized inputs, restoring the optimal scale and offset if plain zero-mean normalization restricts layer representation. Steps 1 to 3 are fixed arithmetic; step 4 is the part training gets a say in.

### 3 · One feature, one mini-batch, real numbers

Consider an input feature within a mini-batch of size m_B = 32. If the values across the batch yield a mean μ_B = 4.0 and a standard deviation σ_B = 2.0, an activation value x⁽ⁱ⁾ = 6.0 is transformed via step 3 into (6.0 − 4.0) / 2.0 = 1.0 (assuming ε is about 0). If backpropagation determines that the subsequent layer performs best when this feature is centered at 0.5 with a wider spread, gradient descent adjusts the parameters to γ = 1.5 and β = 0.5. The final output becomes z⁽ⁱ⁾ = 1.5 × 1.0 + 0.5 = 2.0.

### 4 · Test time: there is no batch

At test time, evaluating batch statistics is often impossible or unreliable for single instances — you may be scoring one row, and a mean over one row is meaningless. Therefore, during training, the layer maintains exponential moving averages of μ_B and σ_B as non-trainable parameters, to provide stable mean and standard deviation estimates for predictions at test time, using these frozen statistics during inference. An **exponential moving average** is a running average that keeps fading the old values, so it tracks the recent state without storing history.

In total, each batch-normalized input feature requires four parameters: two learned via backpropagation (γ, β) and two tracked through moving averages (final mean and standard deviation). So a layer feeding 200 features into batch normalization adds 4 × 200 = 800 parameters, half of them trainable.

### 5 · Two consequences worth knowing

| Consequence | Why |
|---|---|
| bias can be dropped | the beta parameter already acts as an offset vector |
| runtime cost removable | fuse scale and offset into the previous layer weights |

Because the batch normalization beta parameter already acts as an offset vector, the dense layer directly before it can be created with no bias of its own. And after training, the inference computational cost of batch normalization can be eliminated by fusing the scale and offset parameters directly into the previous layer weights — the card below works both through, with the book's real parameter counts.

**One-liner for your notes:** batch normalization standardizes each layer's inputs on the mini-batch and then re-scales them with two learned vectors, adding four parameters per feature and swapping in frozen moving averages at prediction time.

blocks.title: Parameter counts, dropping the bias, and fusing BN
blocks.content:
**Counting parameters.** In the book's model, the first BN layer follows the flattened 28 × 28 images, so it sees 784 inputs and adds 4 × 784 = 3,136 parameters. The next two see 300 and 100 inputs and add 1,200 and 400. Half of all these, the moving averages μ and σ, are non-trainable: (3,136 + 1,200 + 400) / 2 = 2,368.

**Dropping the bias.** A BN layer already has one offset parameter (β) per input, so the layer before it can use `use_bias=False`.

**Removing the runtime penalty.** BN makes predictions slower, but after training it can be fused into the previous layer. If that layer computes XW + b, BN computes γ ⊗ (XW + b − μ) / σ + β. Defining W′ = γ ⊗ W / σ and b′ = γ ⊗ (b − μ) / σ + β turns this into XW′ + b′, so the BN layer can be removed.
