```python
)
```

items.term: Why an equivalence can be true for one optimizer and false for another
items.text: The equivalence holds because, for SGD, a squared penalty in the loss differentiates into a term proportional to the weight, which is exactly a shrink. Adam then divides every gradient component by its own running scale — including that term. So the shrink each weight receives depends on its gradient history rather than being constant. The general warning is that a result proved for one update rule does not automatically survive a change of update rule.

items.term: Decoupling as a design pattern
items.text: AdamW's fix is not new maths, it is a reordering: stop routing the regularizer through the machinery that rescales things, and apply it directly afterwards. The same shape — take the operation that must not be distorted and move it outside the adaptive part — is worth recognising elsewhere.

items.term: Fast convergence is not good generalization
items.text: This lesson and its card make the point twice: adaptive optimizers reach a low training loss quickly and can still end up at a solution that tests worse than one plain Nesterov momentum found slowly. Those are two different measurements, and the chapter's optimizer table deliberately scores them in separate columns. Judge an optimizer on validation results, never on how fast the training loss fell.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Standard ℓ₂ regularization and weight decay are mathematically equivalent for SGD, but not for Adam.
AdamW correctly integrates weight decay by decoupling it from gradient-based adaptive updates.
Combining ℓ₂ regularization with traditional Adam often leads to inferior generalization performance.
Adaptive optimizers achieve fast convergence speed, but NAG may generalize better on certain datasets.
Tuning the weight_decay hyperparameter in AdamW helps control model regularization effectively.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: AdamW's weight decay is applied to the weights directly, so its effective strength no longer scales with the learning rate the way an L2 penalty's does. Work out what that means in practice when you change the learning rate or the schedule: does the decay need re-tuning too?
Look up: Ilya Loshchilov and Frank Hutter, "Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization", arXiv preprint arXiv:1711.05101 (2017) - the AdamW paper, footnote 22 in this chapter.

items.term: Learning Rate Scheduling

blocks.content:
A learning schedule changes the learning rate as training runs — big steps early to cover ground, small steps late to settle precisely.

**The question this lesson answers:** any single fixed learning rate is a compromise: high enough to make progress is too high to settle, low enough to settle is too low to get there. How do you get both, and which schedules are worth knowing?

### The big picture

```
too high        diverges
slightly high   fast at first, then stuck above the best
too low         gets there, takes forever
scheduled       high early, lower later -> fast AND precise
```

### 1 · Why one rate cannot do both jobs

Training deep neural networks requires choosing an appropriate learning rate. If the learning rate is fixed too high, optimization fluctuates near the minimum or diverges entirely. Conversely, choosing a rate that is too low results in extremely slow convergence.

Figure 11-9 below plots those cases as learning curves. Read it this way: when the learning rate η is set slightly too high, the loss drops quickly at first but plateaus at a suboptimal level — the optimizer is taking steps too big to fit inside the bottom of the valley, so it circles above it. As Figure 11-9 demonstrates, starting with a higher learning rate and systematically reducing it over time allows the model to make rapid early progress while still settling into a precise minimum.

### 2 · The named schedules

Techniques that adjust the learning rate during training are known as **learning schedules**.

| Schedule | What it does |
|---|---|
| exponential | divides the rate by a constant factor every s steps |
| performance | cuts the rate when validation stops improving |
| power | drops fast at first, then slower and slower |
| 1cycle | up for the first half, down for the second |

Common strategies include **exponential scheduling**, which scales the rate down by a constant factor over fixed intervals, and **performance scheduling**, which reduces the rate when validation metrics plateau. To **plateau** is to stop improving for several checks in a row. Another prominent approach is **1cycle scheduling**, where the learning rate increases linearly during the first half of training before dropping linearly in the second half.

Power scheduling is the fourth, and it drops the learning rate rapidly early on, then drops it progressively more slowly — the card below gives its formula and contrasts it with exponential scheduling, which instead keeps dividing by 10 at a fixed interval.

### 3 · What it is worth in practice

Consider training a model on the CIFAR-10 image dataset. Using a fixed standard optimization approach might require 800 epochs to reach a target validation accuracy of 90.3%. In contrast, applying a 1cycle learning rate schedule allows the same network architecture to achieve 91.9% validation accuracy in only 100 epochs, reaching convergence much faster.

| Approach | Epochs | Validation accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| standard, fixed | 800 | 90.3% |
| 1cycle | 100 | 91.9% |

Same architecture, same dataset — eight times fewer epochs and a better number.

### 4 · The resume trap

One practical detail, because it bites on the second run rather than the first. A custom epoch-based `LearningRateScheduler` function reads the epoch counter, and when you continue training on a loaded model the epoch counter resets to zero, potentially resetting the learning rate to a large value — which can wreck weights that were nearly finished.

Using `tf.keras.optimizers.schedules.ExponentialDecay` is often preferred when saving model checkpoints because it updates the rate at every step while automatically saving schedule state with the model. The state travels with the checkpoint, so a resume picks up where it stopped. The card below spells out both behaviours.

**One-liner for your notes:** the essential key to learning rate scheduling is dynamically decaying the step size to balance training speed with final model precision.

blocks.title: Power scheduling, and saving a schedule
blocks.content:
**How wrong rates behave.** A rate much too high can make training diverge. A rate slightly too high makes progress very quickly at first, then dances around the optimum and never settles.

**Power scheduling** sets $\eta(t) = \eta_0 / (1 + t/s)^c$, where c is usually 1. After s steps the rate is $\eta_0 / 2$, after s more steps $\eta_0 / 3$, then $\eta_0 / 4$, so it drops quickly at first and then more and more slowly. Exponential scheduling, $\eta(t) = \eta_0 \cdot 0.1^{t/s}$, instead keeps dividing the rate by 10 every s steps.

**Resuming training.** A `LearningRateScheduler` function that uses the `epoch` argument has a trap: the epoch is not saved and resets to 0 at each `fit()` call, which can bring back a very large learning rate unless you set `initial_epoch`. A `tf.keras.optimizers.schedules` object such as `ExponentialDecay` updates the rate at every step, and its state is saved with the model.

blocks.title: Figure 11-9
blocks.caption: Learning curves for various learning rates η
blocks.alt: Figure 11-9: Learning curves for various learning rates η

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

def exponential_decay(lr0, s):
    def exponential_decay_fn(epoch):
        return lr0 * 0.1 ** (epoch / s)
    return exponential_decay_fn

exponential_decay_fn = exponential_decay(lr0=0.01, s=20)
lr_scheduler = tf.keras.callbacks.LearningRateScheduler(exponential_decay_fn)

reduce_lr_cb = tf.keras.callbacks.ReduceLROnPlateau(factor=0.5, patience=5)

history = model.fit(X_train, y_train, epochs=25, callbacks=[reduce_lr_cb])
```

items.term: Why any fixed rate is a compromise
items.text: The step size you want depends on how far you are from the answer, and that changes during the run. Early on you are far away and a large step is almost free; near the minimum the same step overshoots every time. One number cannot be right for both phases, which is why a schedule beats even a perfectly tuned constant — and why the failure of a slightly-too-high rate is a plateau above the best value rather than divergence.

items.term: Why 1cycle goes up first
items.text: Every other schedule only ever decreases, so the rise in 1cycle is the surprising part. The argument is that a large rate early acts as exploration, pushing the weights out of the region they were initialized into before the long decay commits them. The evidence offered is empirical — the CIFAR-10 result — not a proof, and that is the honest way to hold it.

items.term: A schedule is state, and state has to survive a restart
items.text: The resume trap in this lesson is a general one: anything that depends on how long training has been running is state, and state that is not saved with the checkpoint is silently reset. It is worth asking of any callback you add — if this run were interrupted and resumed, what would this component believe?

blocks.title: Key points
items: A constant learning rate often forces a tradeoff between fast early progress and settling into the global minimum.
Exponential scheduling scales down the learning rate by a constant factor at regular step or epoch intervals.
Performance scheduling uses a callback to reduce the learning rate whenever the validation loss stops improving.
1cycle scheduling linearly increases the learning rate to a peak before linearly decreasing it across training.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: 1cycle also schedules the momentum, moving it in the opposite direction to the learning rate. Find out why the two are varied together and what breaks if you schedule only the learning rate.
Look up: Leslie N. Smith, "A Disciplined Approach to Neural Network Hyper-Parameters: Part 1 - Learning Rate, Batch Size, Momentum, and Weight Decay", arXiv preprint arXiv:1803.09820 (2018).

items.term: L1 and L2 Regularization

blocks.content:
L1 and L2 regularization add a penalty on the size of the weights to the loss, so the network pays for complexity it does not need.

**The question this lesson answers:** a network with millions of parameters can fit anything, including the noise. How do you charge it for using that freedom, and what is the difference between the two standard penalties?

### The big picture

```
loss you train on = task error + penalty on the weights
L2 penalty = sum of squared weights  -> all weights small
L1 penalty = sum of absolute weights -> many weights zero
```

### 1 · Why capacity is a liability

Deep neural networks contain thousands or even millions of parameters. While this huge parameter count grants the model immense flexibility to learn intricate patterns, it also makes the network vulnerable to **overfitting**, where it memorizes training noise rather than discovering generalizable rules. Applying L1 or L2 regularization prevents the network from overfitting the training dataset.

### 2 · The two penalties

To prevent overfitting, you can constrain the network's connection weights using regularization penalties added directly to the loss function during training.

**L2 regularization** adds a penalty proportional to the sum of the squared weight values, which encourages the network to keep all weight values small. It adds a penalty proportional to squared weight values to total loss. Because the penalty is squared, a weight of 10 costs a hundred times what a weight of 1 costs, so the pressure falls hardest on the biggest weights — but the pressure on a weight already near zero is tiny, which is why L2 shrinks without eliminating.

In contrast, **L1 regularization** adds a penalty proportional to the sum of the absolute weight values, pushing unnecessary weights down to exactly zero and creating a **sparse model**. That is the characteristic that distinguishes them: L1 regularization drives unnecessary weights to zero, creating sparse models. A **sparse model** is one where most weights are exactly 0, so it is smaller and faster to run.

| | Penalty on | Effect on weights |
|---|---|---|
| L2 | squared values | all shrink, none vanish |
| L1 | absolute values | unneeded ones hit zero |

The figure below draws that contrast.

### 3 · Applying it without repeating yourself

In a practical Keras implementation, applying L2 regularization with a factor of 0.01 to a layer is as simple as passing `kernel_regularizer=tf.keras.regularizers.l2(0.01)` to `tf.keras.layers.Dense`.

Because repeating these parameters across many layers leads to tedious and error-prone code, you can use Python's `functools.partial()` wrapper to build a reusable layer configured with your chosen regularizer, activation, and kernel initializer. It avoids code duplication by defining layer configuration defaults once. `partial()` takes a function and pins some of its arguments, handing you back a new function with those defaults baked in — the same move as defining a template once and stamping it out, rather than retyping the settings per layer. The code card below builds a `RegularizedDense` that way.

### 4 · The one incompatibility

One crucial detail to remember is that standard L2 regularization works smoothly with Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) and momentum, but it fails to work properly with the Adam optimizer. When combining weight decay with Adam, you must use the **AdamW** optimizer instead — that is the optimizer to use instead of standard L2 regularization when applying weight decay with Adam, for the reasons the AdamW lesson set out.

**One-liner for your notes:** by penalizing large weight values, regularization constrains network flexibility so that the model relies on simpler patterns that generalize effectively to unseen data — squared for L2, absolute for L1 and a sparse model.

blocks.caption: L1 regularization forces unnecessary weights to exact zero to produce a sparse model, while L2 regularization uniformly shrinks all weight values toward zero without eliminating them completely.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from functools import partial
import tensorflow as tf

RegularizedDense = partial(
    tf.keras.layers.Dense,
    activation="relu",
    kernel_initializer="he_normal",
    kernel_regularizer=tf.keras.regularizers.l2(0.01)
)

model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.Flatten(input_shape=[28, 28]),
    RegularizedDense(100),
    RegularizedDense(100),
    RegularizedDense(10, activation="softmax")
])
```

items.term: Why squared and absolute penalties behave so differently at zero
items.text: Near zero, the squared penalty's pressure fades away — halving an already tiny weight barely reduces its square — so L2 shrinks weights toward zero without ever arriving. The absolute penalty's pressure does not fade: the last step to zero is worth as much as any other, so weights land exactly on it. Sparsity is a consequence of that one property, not an extra feature bolted on.

items.term: Regularization is a claim about the world
items.text: Adding a penalty says you believe the true relationship is simpler than the data alone suggests. When that is right, validation improves. When it is wrong, you have biased the model on purpose and underfitting is the result — which is why the regularization factor is tuned against validation rather than set once and trusted.

items.term: Sparse for size, or sparse for interpretation
items.text: L1 is reached for on two very different grounds: a smaller, faster model, or a shorter list of features that mattered. The first is measurable. The second is weaker than it looks — when two inputs carry similar information, L1 keeps one and zeroes the other, and which one survives can flip between runs. Do not read a zeroed weight as proof the feature is irrelevant.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Overfitting occurs when high-capacity neural networks memorize training noise instead of general patterns.
L2 regularization penalizes squared weight magnitudes to keep weight values small throughout training.
L1 regularization penalizes absolute weight magnitudes, driving unneeded weight values down to zero.
Python's functools.partial helper simplifies applying identical regularizers across multiple layers.
Adam requires the specialized AdamW optimizer when applying weight decay instead of standard L2 regularizers.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The regularization factor 0.01 in this lesson is just an example. Find out how the right factor scales with the number of training instances and the size of the layer - and whether a factor tuned on one dataset transfers to another at all.
Look up: this book's Chapter 4, sections "Ridge Regression" and "Lasso Regression", which derive why the two penalties behave differently at zero.

items.term: Dropout Regularization

blocks.content:
Dropout switches off a random set of neurons at every training step, so no neuron can depend on any particular neighbour being there.

**The question this lesson answers:** neurons next to each other learn to cover for one another and jointly memorize noise. How does randomly deleting some of them during training produce a model that generalizes better — and what has to be rescaled to make that honest?

### The big picture

```
training step 1   drop a random subset -> train what is left
training step 2   drop a different subset
...
test time         nothing dropped, full network
```

### 1 · Co-adaptation, and the cure

Deep neural networks with high capacity often suffer from overfitting, where neighboring neurons co-adapt and memorize specific noise patterns in the training set rather than learning generalizable features. To **co-adapt** is for two neurons to specialise on each other: one only makes sense given what the other happens to output. **Dropout** solves this problem by introducing randomness during training to force the network to learn redundant and robust feature representations.

### 2 · The mechanism

At every training iteration, each neuron (except those in the output layer) has a probability p of being temporarily dropped out. Output-layer neurons are never dropped out during any training iteration — those are the predictions themselves, so there is nothing to be robust about.

As Figure 11-10 below shows, dropped neurons output zero for that step and do not participate in forward or backward propagation. In that figure, the dashed arrows and red crosses mark the connections and neurons that are deactivated and outputting zero for this iteration.

Because neurons cannot rely on specific neighbors being present, they cannot co-adapt and must remain useful on their own. That is why training with dropout helps a network generalize better: it stops neighboring neurons from co-adapting and forces reliance on many inputs.

### 3 · Why it counts as an ensemble

Mathematically, a network with N droppable neurons can form 2 to the power N unique sub-network configurations. Dropout can be viewed as training an implicit ensemble of these smaller networks that share weights, effectively averaging their predictions. An **ensemble** is a group of models whose predictions are combined; the point here is that you get the effect of one without paying to train many.

### 4 · The rescaling detail

To keep output scales consistent between training and testing, surviving signals must be scaled up. If half the inputs to a neuron are missing during training, that neuron sees roughly half the total signal it will see at test time, and the network would be reading different data in the two phases.

For instance, if the dropout rate p = 0.75, only 25% of neurons remain active on average during training. To compensate for the missing inputs, modern frameworks like Keras scale up the active outputs by dividing them by the keep probability 1 − p = 0.25 (multiplying by 4) during training.

| Dropout rate p | Keep probability 1 − p | Divide active outputs by |
|---|---|---|
| 0.75 | 0.25 | 0.25, i.e. multiply by 4 |
| 0.2 | 0.8 | 0.8 |

So with a dropout rate of p = 0.2, Keras divides the remaining active outputs by 0.8 during the training steps. At test time, dropout is deactivated entirely, allowing signals to pass through unchanged.

### 5 · Turning the dial

The rate is a hyperparameter you tune against the symptom. If a neural network is underfitting the training dataset, decrease the dropout rate to allow the network to retain more capacity; if it is overfitting, increase it. The card below has the book's usual ranges by architecture and the trap about comparing training loss with validation loss while dropout is on.

**One-liner for your notes:** **dropout** prevents neuron co-adaptation by randomly deactivating neurons during training, forcing the network to learn robust, distributed representations.

blocks.title: Tuning the dropout rate
blocks.content: The dropout rate p is typically set between 10% and 50%: closer to 20–30% in recurrent neural nets and closer to 40–50% in convolutional neural networks. If the model is overfitting, increase the dropout rate; if it underfits the training set, decrease it. It can also help to use a higher rate for large layers and a lower one for small layers, or to apply dropout only after the last hidden layer if full dropout is too strong. Dropout tends to slow down convergence significantly, but when it is tuned properly it often gives a better model. Because dropout is active only during training, evaluate the training loss without dropout before you compare it with the validation loss.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.Flatten(input_shape=[28, 28]),
    tf.keras.layers.Dropout(rate=0.2),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(100, activation="relu", kernel_initializer="he_normal"),
    tf.keras.layers.Dropout(rate=0.2),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(100, activation="relu", kernel_initializer="he_normal"),
    tf.keras.layers.Dropout(rate=0.2),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")
])
```

items.term: Why deliberately damaging the network helps
items.text: Dropout does not make the network better at training; it makes the training problem harder in a specific way. Every neuron must be useful without being able to count on any particular partner, so the network is pushed toward several partial explanations rather than one brittle joint one. The same idea underlies ensembles: several imperfect answers averaged beat one answer that was tuned until it fit.

items.term: The rescaling is about consistency, not about accuracy
items.text: Dividing by the keep probability exists so that a neuron sees the same total incoming signal during training as it will at test time. Skip it and the network is effectively trained on differently scaled data than it is evaluated on — a mismatch that shows up as poor test performance with nothing obviously wrong in the training curve. Any technique that changes behaviour between training and inference owes you this kind of correction.

items.term: Reading the training loss while dropout is on
items.text: Because dropout is active only during training, the training loss is measured on a deliberately handicapped network and the validation loss is not. The two numbers are therefore not comparable, and a model can be overfitting while they look similar. This is a measurement artefact, not a property of the model, and the fix is to re-evaluate the training loss with dropout off before drawing any conclusion.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Dropout randomly deactivates neurons with probability p at each training step.
Neurons in the output layer are never dropped out.
During training, remaining active outputs are scaled up by dividing by 1 - p.
Dropout prevents neuron co-adaptation and simulates an ensemble of sub-networks.
Dropout is completely turned off during inference.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Dropout is far less common in modern transformer training than it was in 2014, and batch normalization partly displaced it. Find out what replaced it and why - and whether the co-adaptation argument still holds for very large models.
Look up: Nitish Srivastava et al., "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting", Journal of Machine Learning Research 15 (2014): 1929-1958.

items.term: Monte Carlo Dropout

blocks.content:
Monte Carlo Dropout leaves dropout switched on at prediction time, runs the same input many times, and reads the spread of the answers as the model's uncertainty.

**The question this lesson answers:** a single forward pass gives you one probability and no idea how much to trust it. How do you turn an already-trained dropout model into one that reports its own uncertainty, without retraining it?

### The big picture

```
normal inference   dropout OFF, 1 pass  -> one number
MC dropout         dropout ON, 100 passes
   mean over passes -> calibrated probability
   std  over passes -> uncertainty
```

### 1 · The problem: confident and wrong

Standard neural networks often produce overconfident predictions without reflecting uncertainty accurately. This lack of reliability can lead to dangerous errors in risk-sensitive applications like autonomous driving or medical diagnosis. It is the unreliable probability estimates and hidden uncertainty in standard forward passes that **Monte Carlo Dropout** (MC Dropout) addresses, by providing better probability estimates and quantifying prediction variance without requiring model retraining.

**Monte Carlo** is the general name for estimating something by sampling it many times at random and averaging.

### 2 · The mechanism

The technique works by keeping **dropout** active during inference time. Instead of making a single forward pass with dropout disabled, the model evaluates the same input multiple times while forcing dropout on. It generates multiple distinct predictions for a single input instance by keeping dropout active during prediction so random units drop each pass.

Because different neurons are randomly deactivated during each pass, every run yields a slightly different output. Averaging these predictions produces a Monte Carlo estimate of the true output probability, while the standard deviation of predictions across the sample runs measures model uncertainty. **Standard deviation** is the ordinary measure of spread: small means the passes agreed, large means they did not.

Nothing is retrained. The weights are the ones the model already had.

### 3 · The book's own numbers

For example, consider a trained image classification model evaluating a single test image from Fashion MNIST. With standard dropout turned off during prediction, the model outputs a probability of 84.4% for class 9 (ankle boot).

Using MC Dropout with 100 sample predictions (`training=True`), the averaged prediction for class 9 decreases to 72.3%, while probabilities for class 5 (sandal) and class 7 (sneaker) rise to 6.7% and 20.9% respectively.

| Class | Dropout off | MC dropout, 100 passes |
|---|---|---|
| 9 ankle boot | 84.4% | 72.3% |
| 7 sneaker | — | 20.9% |
| 5 sandal | — | 6.7% |

Computing the standard deviation across the 100 runs reveals a high variance of 0.183 for class 9, signaling high prediction uncertainty that standard inference hid. Compare 0.183 against the 0.723 it is the spread of: that is not a confident answer, and the single pass never said so. The card below carries the array shapes and the small accuracy change.

### 4 · The two costs

First, latency. Increasing the sample count improves uncertainty estimates but increases inference time linearly — 100 passes cost 100 times one pass, so the sample count is a trade-off you set per application.

Second, a correctness trap. Setting global training mode enables unwanted training behavior in layers like BatchNormalization, so on a model that has such layers you do not force training mode on the whole model; you subclass `Dropout` instead, as the code card below does with `MCDropout`.

**One-liner for your notes:** keeping dropout active at inference time converts a single deterministic neural network into an ensemble of sampled networks, yielding better calibrated probabilities and explicit uncertainty measurements.

blocks.title: MC dropout array shapes and the MCDropout layer
blocks.content:
Each call `model(X_test, training=True)` returns one row per test instance and one column per class, so 10,000 instances and 10 classes give a matrix of shape [10000, 10]. Stacking 100 such calls makes `y_probas` a 3D array of shape [100, 10000, 10], and the mean over axis 0 gives `y_proba` of shape [10000, 10] again. For the first test image, the probability moved from 84.4% to 72.3% for class 9, from 2.4% to 6.7% for class 5, and from 13.2% to 20.9% for class 7. Accuracy rose slightly, from 87.0% to 87.2%.

Calling the whole model with `training=True` also puts layers such as `BatchNormalization` in training mode. For such models, do not force training mode: replace each `Dropout` layer with an `MCDropout` subclass whose `call()` always passes `training=True`.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf

class MCDropout(tf.keras.layers.Dropout):
    def call(self, inputs, training=False):
        return super().call(inputs, training=True)

# Perform 100 forward passes with active dropout
y_probas = np.stack([model(X_test, training=True)
                     for sample in range(100)])

# Mean probability across all samples
y_proba = y_probas.mean(axis=0)

# Standard deviation representing model uncertainty
y_std = y_probas.std(axis=0)
```

items.term: What the spread actually measures
items.text: The standard deviation across MC passes says how much the answer depended on which sub-network happened to be sampled. That is a measure of the model's own instability on this input, and it is genuinely useful — but it is not the whole of uncertainty. It says nothing about an input unlike anything in training, or about the labels being wrong. Treat a low spread as one piece of evidence, not as a guarantee.

items.term: Confidence and correctness are different things
items.text: The single pass reported 84.4% and the hundred passes reported 72.3% with a spread of 0.183. The prediction did not change; what changed is how much you should stake on it. A model that is right less often but honest about when it is unsure can be far more useful than a more accurate model that is confidently wrong, which is exactly the argument for risk-sensitive systems.

items.term: Getting it for free is the unusual part
items.text: MC dropout needs no retraining, no architecture change and no extra parameters — the randomness was already in the trained model and inference simply stops suppressing it. That is why it is worth knowing even when uncertainty is not your goal: the only cost is inference time, and you can choose how much by choosing the number of passes.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Monte Carlo Dropout keeps dropout active during inference to sample multiple predictions.
Averaging multiple prediction samples produces more reliable, well-calibrated class probabilities.
The standard deviation across prediction samples explicitly measures model uncertainty.
MC Dropout improves existing dropout models without needing model retraining.
Increasing the sample count improves precision but increases inference latency linearly.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: MC dropout measures the variation caused by sampling sub-networks. Find out what a deep ensemble - several independently trained models - measures instead, and which of the two is a better warning that an input is unlike anything in training.

Look up: Yarin Gal and Zoubin Ghahramani, "Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation: Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep Learning", Proceedings of the 33rd International Conference on Machine Learning (2016): 1050-1059.

items.term: Max-Norm Regularization

blocks.content:
Max-norm regularization does not touch the loss function at all: after every training step it measures each neuron's incoming weight vector and shrinks it back if it has grown past a set limit.

**The question this lesson answers:** L1 and L2 charge the model for large weights and hope it responds. What if you want a hard ceiling instead of a price — and what does enforcing one after each step buy you?

### The big picture

```
after each training step, for every neuron:
   measure the L2 norm of its incoming weights
   if norm <= r   leave it alone
   if norm >  r   multiply the vector by r / norm
```

### 1 · A different kind of regularizer

Deep neural networks with many parameters often suffer from overfitting and unstable gradients during training. Standard regularization techniques, such as L1 or L2 regularization, address overfitting by adding a penalty term directly to the loss function. However, **max-norm regularization** takes a different approach by directly constraining the magnitude of incoming weights for each neuron.

A neuron's **incoming weight vector** is the list of weights on the connections feeding into it — one number per input. The **L2 norm** of that list is its straight-line length: square each weight, add them, take the square root.

### 2 · The rule, step by step

Instead of modifying the loss function, max-norm regularization enforces a strict upper limit on the weight vector of every neuron. Specifically, it constrains the weight vector **w** of incoming connections such that its L2 norm does not exceed a designated hyperparameter *r*.

After each training step, the network measures the L2 norm of each weight vector. If the norm exceeds *r*, the network rescales the weight vector by multiplying it by *r* divided by its norm. If the norm is already less than or equal to *r*, the weights remain unchanged. So it enforces its constraint by rescaling weights after each training step if their norm exceeds r — a clamp applied after the fact, not a term in the objective.

| Situation | Action |
|---|---|
| norm at or below r | nothing |
| norm above r | multiply by r divided by the norm |

### 3 · On real numbers

For example, suppose a hyperparameter *r* is set to 1.0. If a neuron's incoming weight vector has an L2 norm of 2.0 after a gradient descent step, the constraint clips the vector. The weights are scaled down by a factor of 1.0 divided by 2.0, which is 0.5. As a result, the new L2 norm of the weight vector becomes exactly 1.0.

The same arithmetic with a different limit: if a neuron's weight vector has an L2 norm of 3.0 when r is 1.5, the weight vector is scaled down by a factor of 0.5 so its norm becomes 1.5. The direction the vector points is untouched; only its length changes.

### 4 · The dial and the switch

Reducing the value of *r* increases the strength of the regularization, which effectively prevents any single neuron from growing disproportionately large weights. Decreasing r increases regularization strength and helps reduce overfitting — a tighter ceiling means less room.

In Keras, max-norm regularization is specified for a layer by setting the kernel_constraint argument to tf.keras.constraints.max_norm(), as the code card below shows. That function defaults to applying the limit independently to each individual neuron's weights, which is what axis=0 means for a Dense layer; the card below explains why, and what to set for convolutional layers.

**One-liner for your notes:** **max-norm regularization** does not add a penalty to the loss function; instead, it enforces an explicit ceiling on weight vector norms after every step, which helps prevent overfitting and stabilizes gradients.

blocks.title: The axis argument of max_norm()
blocks.content: The `max_norm()` function has an `axis` argument that defaults to 0. A `Dense` layer's weights usually have the shape [number of inputs, number of neurons], so each column holds one neuron's incoming weights, and `axis=0` applies the max-norm limit to each neuron's weight vector independently. For convolutional layers you set the axis to match their weights, usually `axis=[0, 1, 2]`. The `kernel_constraint` covers only the connection weights; to constrain the bias terms as well, you set the separate `bias_constraint` argument.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

dense_layer = tf.keras.layers.Dense(
    100,
    activation="relu",
    kernel_initializer="he_normal",
    kernel_constraint=tf.keras.constraints.max_norm(1.0)
)
```

items.term: A constraint versus a penalty
items.text: L1 and L2 put a price on large weights and let the optimizer decide whether to pay it; max-norm forbids them outright. That is a real difference in guarantee: with a penalty the weights may still grow if the task rewards it enough, with a constraint they cannot. The trade is that a hard limit has no way to express 'slightly too big', so it does nothing at all until the limit is crossed.

items.term: Why per-neuron rather than per-layer
items.text: The constraint is applied to each neuron's own incoming weight vector, so a layer cannot satisfy it by having most neurons small and one enormous. The unit that overfits is the individual neuron, so that is the unit the ceiling is applied to — which is also why the axis setting matters and why it changes for convolutional layers.

items.term: Rescaling keeps direction and drops magnitude
items.text: Multiplying the whole vector by r divided by its norm changes only its length; the relative sizes of the weights are untouched. So the neuron keeps the pattern it had learned and only loses the confidence with which it asserts it. That is why max-norm can rein in a runaway neuron without discarding what it learned.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Max-norm regularization constrains incoming weight vectors so their L2 norm does not exceed a hyperparameter limit r.
This technique rescales weights after each training step rather than adding a penalty term to the loss function.
Lowering the value of hyperparameter r increases regularization strength to reduce overfitting.
Max-norm regularization can also help stabilize exploding or unstable gradients during network training.
In Keras, max-norm regularization is applied by setting the kernel_constraint argument of a layer.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Max-norm is applied after the optimizer step, so the optimizer's own state - momentum, or Adam's running averages - is not told that the weights were changed. Find out whether that causes a mismatch in practice, and how Keras orders the constraint against the update.
Look up: the Keras documentation page for tf.keras.constraints, which specifies max_norm, its axis argument and the other built-in constraints.

items.term: Default Configurations for Training Deep Neural Networks

blocks.content:
There are two default recipes for a deep network — one for ordinary architectures and one for a plain stack of dense layers — and a short list of exceptions that override them.

**The question this lesson answers:** after eleven chapters of initializers, activations, optimizers and regularizers, what do you actually type when you start a new model, before you have tuned anything?

### The big picture

| | Standard deep net | Self-normalizing stack |
|---|---|---|
| Initializer | He | LeCun |
| Activation | ReLU shallow, Swish deep | SELU |
| Normalization | batch norm if deep | none, self-normalizes |
| Optimizer | AdamW or NAG | NAG |
| Schedule | 1cycle | 1cycle |
| Dropout | standard | Alpha dropout |

### 1 · Why a default is worth having

Selecting the right combination of hyperparameter values when building a deep neural network can be overwhelming because there are dozens of initializers, activation functions, optimizers, and regularization methods to choose from. Setting up a reliable baseline configuration solves this problem by providing a strong starting point that works well across most standard tasks without requiring extensive hyperparameter tuning.

A baseline is not a claim about what is best. It is the configuration you start from so that anything you change afterwards has something to be measured against.

### 2 · The standard recipe

For a general deep neural network, practical defaults depend on the network depth. Standard networks benefit from using **He initialization** paired with the **ReLU activation function** for shallow architectures, or the **Swish activation function** for deeper models. When training deep networks, adding **Batch Normalization** helps stabilize training, while **AdamW** or **Nesterov accelerated gradients** serve as effective optimizers alongside a learning rate scheduler like **1cycle**.

For a standard deep network that does not self-normalize, that means He initialization with Swish activation and Batch Normalization.

### 3 · The self-normalizing recipe

However, if the architecture consists purely of a simple stack of dense layers, the model can achieve self-normalization. In this scenario, you should instead select **LeCun initialization** combined with the **SELU activation function**, which maintains stable mean and variance across layers without explicit normalization layers.

The requirement is strict: the architecture must consist of a simple stack of dense layers using SELU and LeCun initialization. Break that shape — add a recurrent layer, a skip connection — and self-normalization is no longer what you have.

Consider a scenario where a developer is building a standard multi-layer perceptron with ten dense layers. Instead of manually testing different combinations, they configure the model using LeCun normal initialization and SELU activations. If regularization becomes necessary to prevent overfitting, they apply **Alpha dropout** to preserve the self-normalizing property of the network. Alpha Dropout preserves the mean and variance of inputs to maintain self-normalization, which regular dropout would destroy. The card below lists the other choices that break it.

### 4 · The exceptions

Special application requirements modify these standard guidelines. For instance, low-latency deployment requires fast activations like ReLU, folding batch normalization into preceding layers, and using float16 precision — so if inference low-latency is the highest priority, fold Batch Normalization layers into previous layers and reduce float precision. **float16** means storing each number in 16 bits instead of 32: half the memory and usually faster arithmetic, at the cost of precision.

At the other end, when building a risk-sensitive application where uncertainty estimation is critical, use Monte Carlo dropout to obtain reliable probability estimates, as the MC dropout lesson showed.

**One-liner for your notes:** default configurations offer a high-performing starting baseline, but constraints such as network depth, prediction latency, and model sparsity ultimately dictate necessary architectural adjustments.

blocks.title: Alpha dropout, and what breaks self-normalization
blocks.content: Alpha dropout is a variant of dropout that preserves the mean and standard deviation of its inputs. It was introduced in the same paper as SELU, because regular dropout would break self-normalization. Other choices break it too: if you need a sparse model and use ℓ1 regularization, self-normalization no longer holds, so the book tells you to use the default configuration (He initialization, ReLU or Swish, batch norm if deep) instead of SELU. Whatever configuration you pick, do not forget to normalize the input features.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

# Standard self-normalizing deep neural network configuration
model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.Input(shape=(784,)),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(100, kernel_initializer="lecun_normal", activation="selu"),
    tf.keras.layers.AlphaDropout(rate=0.1),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(100, kernel_initializer="lecun_normal", activation="selu"),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")
])

optimizer = tf.keras.optimizers.SGD(learning_rate=0.01, momentum=0.9, nesterov=True)
model.compile(loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", optimizer=optimizer, metrics=["accuracy"])
```

items.term: What a default table is and is not
items.text: These two tables encode choices that were each argued for earlier in the chapter, collected so you do not have to re-derive them. They are a starting point measured against nothing yet — the book says outright not to treat them as hard rules. Their value is that any later change now has a baseline to be compared with, which is the only way a tuning result means anything.

items.term: Two recipes because there are two mechanisms
items.text: The standard recipe imports stability from a layer you insert; the self-normalizing recipe gets it from the arithmetic of the architecture itself. That is why they differ in more than one row: the initializer, the activation and the dropout variant all have to agree with the mechanism you chose. Mixing halves of the two tables is the common mistake.

items.term: The exceptions are constraints, not preferences
items.text: Low latency, sparsity and uncertainty are not opinions about what performs best — they are requirements from outside the model, and they outrank the defaults. That is the right way to read the exception list: work out what the deployment forbids first, then pick the best configuration inside what is left.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Standard deep networks typically perform best with He initialization combined with ReLU or Swish activations.
Networks built purely of sequential dense layers can self-normalize when using LeCun initialization and SELU.
Alpha Dropout must be used instead of standard dropout to preserve the self-normalizing properties of SELU networks.
Low-latency applications require faster activation functions, network pruning, and precision reduction.
Monte Carlo dropout provides reliable probability and uncertainty estimates for risk-sensitive applications.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The chapter's low-latency advice includes reducing float precision to 16 or even 8 bits. Find out what quantization-aware training is and why it exists - that is, what goes wrong if you simply reduce precision after training instead.
Look up: the TensorFlow Model Optimization Toolkit (TF-MOT) documentation, which this chapter names for both pruning and precision reduction.

items.term: End-of-chapter exercises

blocks.title: 8 book exercises
items: Exercise 1: Explain the specific technical problem that Glorot initialization and He initialization are designed to solve when training deep neural networks.
Exercise 2: Evaluate whether it is acceptable to initialize all weights in a network to the exact same value if that single value is selected randomly using He initialization.
Exercise 3: Determine if it is acceptable to initialize all bias terms in a neural network layer to zero.
Exercise 4: Describe the specific use cases and scenarios where you should choose each of the activation functions discussed in this chapter.
Exercise 5: Analyze what happens to model training if you set the momentum hyperparameter extremely close to 1, such as 0.99999, when using a Stochastic Gradient Descent optimizer.
Exercise 6: List and describe three distinct techniques used to produce a sparse neural network model.
Exercise 7: Compare how standard dropout and Monte Carlo dropout impact training time and inference speed when making predictions on new data instances.

Exercise 8: Practice building and training a deep neural network on the CIFAR-10 image dataset by executing the following detailed sub-tasks:
a. Construct a deep neural network featuring 20 hidden layers with 100 neurons each, applying He initialization and the Swish activation function throughout.
b. Train your model on the CIFAR-10 dataset using Nadam optimization along with early stopping, using a 10-neuron softmax output layer and tuning the learning rate appropriately.
c. Add batch normalization layers after the hidden layers, then compare the resulting learning curves and overall training speed to your initial model.
d. Modify the architecture by replacing batch normalization with SELU activation layers, ensuring the network meets all requirements for self-normalization.
e. Apply regularizing techniques using alpha dropout, and evaluate whether applying Monte Carlo dropout at inference time improves accuracy without retraining.
f. Retrain the neural network using a 1cycle learning rate schedule to measure its effect on final model accuracy and training efficiency.

sections.title: Chapter 12: Custom Models and Training with TensorFlow

items.term: TensorFlow Architecture and Lower-Level APIs

blocks.content:
TensorFlow is a stack, not a single library: Keras sits on top and covers almost everything, and a lower-level Python API sits underneath for the few cases where you need to drive tensors and gradients by hand.

**The question this lesson answers:** what do you do when Keras's standard layers, losses and training loop cannot express what you need — for example a dual-path network where one subnetwork updates via the RMSProp optimizer while another branch minimizes a custom loss using Nadam?

### The big picture

```
your Python code
  |- 95%  Keras + tf.data       (high level)
  |-  5%  low-level Python API  (tensors, tape)
              |
            ops -> kernels (CPU / GPU / TPU)
              |
         C++ execution engine
```

Figure 12-1 below maps the Python API; Figure 12-2 below is this same stack drawn as the book draws it.

### 1 · The 95/5 split

High-level APIs like **Keras** cover roughly 95% of machine learning use cases, providing standard layers, losses, and training loops. Keras is the part you have used so far; **tf.data** is the Data API for feeding it.

The other roughly 5% is the low-level Python API, and that is what this chapter is about. Researchers and engineers encounter situations requiring custom behavior, such as non-standard loss penalties, customized gradient updates across multiple optimizers, or direct tensor manipulations. To solve this limitation, TensorFlow exposes a multi-layered structure with a lower-level Python API.

At its foundation, TensorFlow behaves like an accelerated NumPy library capable of running operations across distributed environments, GPUs, and custom ASIC chips called **TPUs**. An **ASIC** is a chip built for one job only; a TPU is Google's, built for deep learning arithmetic.

### 2 · Ops, kernels, and the engine

As shown in Figure 12-2, high-level user code calls down into lower-level operations, or **ops**, which route into an underlying C++ execution engine.

| Layer | What it is |
|---|---|
| op | one operation, such as add or matmul |
| kernel | that op's code for ONE device type |
| engine | C++ runtime that schedules the ops |

Each operation contains dedicated hardware-specific implementations called **kernels**, tailored for CPUs, GPUs, or TPUs. One op, several kernels: the op says *what*, the kernel says *how, on this hardware*. You never pick a kernel yourself — the engine picks it from the device the tensor is on.

### 3 · The graph is a query plan

When executing code, TensorFlow can construct an optimized **computation graph** via a just-in-time compiler. A **just-in-time compiler** turns code into an optimised form at run time rather than ahead of time.

This graph prunes redundant calculations and schedules independent operations across hardware threads. If you have read a Trino or Spark query plan, this is the same idea in the same order: the planner throws away work nothing consumes, then runs the branches that do not depend on each other at the same time. You write the intent; the plan decides the execution.

### 4 · The example that forces you down a level

For example, consider an engineer who needs a dual-path network where one subnetwork updates via the RMSProp optimizer while another branch minimizes a custom loss using Nadam. Keras standard training loops cannot easily bifurcate these parameter updates in a single pass — *bifurcate* just means split into two paths.

The engineer drops down to the lower-level API using `tf.GradientTape` (shown in Figure 12-1 under autodiff), directly records the forward pass, computes explicit gradients, applies custom constraints, and assigns updates to hardware kernels using the execution engine. A **gradient** is the set of numbers saying how much each parameter should move to reduce the loss; recording the forward pass is what makes computing them possible, and lesson ch12-b10 is that mechanism on its own.

### 5 · The ecosystem around the library

**TensorFlow Hub** gives you a way to easily download and reuse pretrained neural networks — that is the piece to reach for when you want someone else's trained model rather than your own. Around it sit **TensorBoard** for visualization, **TensorFlow Extended (TFX)** for productionizing projects, the **model garden**, **TensorFlow Lite** for mobile and **TensorFlow.js** for the browser. The card below has the full list; models trained in Python can be exported to run on any of those platforms.

The core insight is that TensorFlow separates API convenience from hardware execution: high-level abstractions provide fast prototyping, while lower-level ops and device-specific kernels give complete control over computation without sacrificing cross-platform acceleration.

**One-liner for your notes:** Keras handles ~95% of the work; the remaining ~5% drops to the low-level Python API, where ops pick hardware-specific kernels and a just-in-time compiler prunes and parallelises the computation graph like a query planner.

blocks.title: The TensorFlow ecosystem and the 95% rule
blocks.content:
Géron says that 95% of the use cases you will meet need nothing other than Keras and tf.data (the Data API). The lower-level Python API is for the remaining few cases, roughly 5%, that need extra control.

Around the library itself sits a whole ecosystem:

- **TensorBoard** is the tool for visualization.
- **TensorFlow Extended (TFX)** is a set of libraries built by Google to productionize TensorFlow projects, with tools for data validation, preprocessing, model analysis and serving (TF Serving).
- **TensorFlow Hub** gives you a way to easily download and reuse pretrained neural networks.
- The **model garden** offers many neural network architectures, some of them pretrained.
- **TensorFlow Lite** runs models on mobile devices, including iOS and Android, and **TensorFlow.js** runs a model directly in the browser.

items.term: Why a stack instead of one API
items.text: The thing that varies most between machine learning projects is not what you compute but how much control you need over how it is computed. One API sized for the hard case makes the easy case verbose; one sized for the easy case makes the hard case impossible. Splitting them keeps almost all work short while leaving a door open underneath. The price you pay is that reading someone else's code now starts with working out which floor it is standing on.

items.term: Why a graph is worth the indirection
items.text: Running Python line by line is easy to debug and slow. A graph is a description of the work rather than the work itself, which is what makes it optimisable, parallelisable and shippable to another device or language. The trade is exact: once there is a graph, what you wrote is no longer literally what runs. Almost every surprise in the last lesson of this chapter comes from that one sentence.

items.term: One op, many kernels, is the portability trick
items.text: Keeping the operation separate from its per-device implementation is why the same model file runs on a laptop CPU, a server GPU and a phone. Adding hardware means adding kernels, not rewriting models. It breaks down where an op has no kernel for your device, which is the usual cause of a model that trains fine and refuses to run somewhere else.

blocks.title: Key points
items: High-level APIs handle most standard tasks, while lower-level APIs allow custom loss functions, layers, and training loops.
TensorFlow operations are written in efficient C++ with hardware-specific implementations called kernels for CPUs, GPUs, and TPUs.
Computation graphs allow optimizations such as node pruning and parallel execution across distributed systems.
Models trained using Python can be exported to execute across diverse platforms such as mobile devices or web browsers.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Kernels exist separately for CPUs, GPUs and TPUs. What does a TPU actually do differently from a GPU that makes it faster for these operations, and what kinds of model does that advantage not help?
Look up: Chapter 19, "Training and Deploying TensorFlow Models at Scale", in this book - the chapter this lesson points to for GPUs and TPUs.

items.term: Using TensorFlow Tensors and Variables

blocks.content:
A tensor is TensorFlow's array type: `tf.constant` makes one you cannot change, `tf.Variable` makes one you can, and TensorFlow will never quietly convert a type for you.

**The question this lesson answers:** neural network weights have to be updated on every training step, but tensors are immutable. So which data structure holds them, and what else does TensorFlow do differently from NumPy?

### The big picture

| | `tf.constant` | `tf.Variable` |
|---|---|---|
| Changeable | no, immutable | yes, in place |
| An op gives you | a NEW tensor | the same object, updated |
| Change it with | nothing | assign, assign_add |
| Used for | data, inputs | model parameters |

The figure below is that table drawn as two paths.

### 1 · Why a tensor at all

Numerical computation libraries must handle massive arrays efficiently across hardware like GPUs and CPUs. Python native lists are too slow for large-scale machine learning work, so machine learning frameworks rely on specialized array structures.

TensorFlow solves this problem by using a data structure called a **tensor**, which represents multidimensional arrays of a single data type. *Multidimensional* means it can be a single number, a list, a table, or a stack of tables; *a single data type* means one column type for the whole thing, the way a typed array is one type, not a row with mixed columns.

You can create immutable tensors using the `tf.constant()` function, which behaves similarly to NumPy ndarrays. An **ndarray** is NumPy's own array type — the thing pandas is built on. TensorFlow provides familiar math operators such as `+`, `-`, and `*`, as well as matrix multiplication via the `@` operator.

### 2 · Immutable means every op returns a new tensor

To see how tensors operate in practice, consider creating a matrix constant with values `[[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]]`. If you apply `tf.square()` to this tensor, TensorFlow returns a new tensor containing `[[1.0, 4.0], [9.0, 16.0]]` — each cell squared, and the original left untouched.

That is the same contract as an immutable file in a lakehouse: a transformation writes a new object rather than editing the old one in place.

A second difference of the same kind: in TensorFlow you must write `tf.transpose(t)`, because TensorFlow creates a new tensor with its own copy of the transposed data, while NumPy's `t.T` is just a transposed view on the same data. Copy versus view — that is the primary difference, and it is why `t.T` is not offered.

### 3 · Variables, for anything that must change

If you want to modify values dynamically during neural network training, standard tensors will fail because they are immutable. To solve this, TensorFlow offers the **tf.Variable** class, which supports in-place modifications using dedicated methods such as `assign()` or `assign_add()`. Model parameters live here.

You change a single cell the same way, through the cell's own `assign()`:

```
v.assign(v * 2)        # whole variable
v[0, 1].assign(42.)    # one cell, in place
```

Direct assignment such as `v[1] = [7., 8., 9.]` does not work: it raises a `TypeError`. The rule is easy to remember — always a method, never an equals sign.

### 4 · Strict types, on purpose

Strict type safety is a critical design feature of TensorFlow operations. Unlike NumPy, TensorFlow never performs automatic type conversions because hidden casting can degrade performance. If you try to add a 32-bit float tensor to a 64-bit float tensor, TensorFlow will raise an error unless you explicitly convert them using `tf.cast()`.

This is the Trino habit, not the MySQL habit: a strict engine refuses the mixed-type expression and makes you write the cast, because a cast you cannot see is a cost you cannot budget for.

One more default worth memorising: NumPy uses 64-bit precision by default, while TensorFlow uses 32-bit, because 32-bit precision uses less RAM and runs faster while remaining accurate enough for neural networks. So when you create a tensor from a NumPy array, set `dtype=tf.float32`. Going the other way is easy — the `numpy()` method hands a tensor back as a NumPy array.

**One-liner for your notes:** `tf.constant` is immutable so every op returns a new tensor, `tf.Variable` is the mutable one you update with `assign`, and TensorFlow never casts types for you — 32-bit is its default because it is fast, small and accurate enough.

blocks.title: Transpose copies, direct assignment fails, 32-bit is the default
blocks.content:
Some TensorFlow functions differ from NumPy on purpose. In TensorFlow you must write `tf.transpose(t)`, because `t.T` does not work, and the two do not do the same thing: TensorFlow creates a new tensor with its own copy of the transposed data, while NumPy's `t.T` is just a transposed view on the same data.

A `tf.Variable` is changed through its methods, such as `assign()`, or a cell's `assign()` like `v[0, 1].assign(42)`. Direct assignment such as `v[1] = [7., 8., 9.]` does not work: it raises a `TypeError`.

NumPy uses 64-bit precision by default, while TensorFlow uses 32-bit, because 32-bit precision is generally more than enough for neural networks, plus it runs faster and uses less RAM. So when you create a tensor from a NumPy array, set `dtype=tf.float32`.

blocks.caption: Immutable tensors generate a new tensor object when operations are performed, whereas variables update their existing state in place using specialized assignment methods.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

# Create an immutable tensor
t = tf.constant([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]])  # float32 tensor
print(tf.square(t))

# Type conversion must be explicit
t_64 = tf.constant(10., dtype=tf.float64)
t_cast = tf.cast(t_64, tf.float32)
print(t + t_cast)

# Mutable variable for trainable weights
v = tf.Variable([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]])
v.assign(v * 2)
v[0, 1].assign(42.)
```

items.term: Why immutability is the default
items.text: An immutable value can be shared across threads and devices with no locking, cached, reordered and recomputed freely, because nobody can change it underneath the engine. Mutable state forces the runtime to reason about who might write to it and when. So the framework makes mutation opt-in and confines it to the one place it is genuinely required: parameters that training must move.

items.term: Refusing an implicit cast is a design choice with a cost
items.text: Automatic conversion is convenient exactly in proportion to how invisible it is, and invisible work is both a performance cost you cannot budget for and a correctness risk you cannot review. Strictness moves that cost to the moment you write the code. The bill arrives when porting NumPy code, where the first hour is spent adding casts that were previously happening silently.

items.term: 32-bit is a trade, not a truth
items.text: Gradient descent is noisy and tolerant, so half the precision buys speed and memory at no practical accuracy cost. That argument is about neural network training specifically, not about arithmetic in general. Where it stops holding is numerically delicate work, such as large exponentials or square roots near zero, which is precisely where the autodiff lesson runs into infinities.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A standard TensorFlow tensor created with tf.constant is immutable.
TensorFlow requires explicit type conversions using tf.cast to avoid performance issues.
Neural network parameters use tf.Variable to allow in-place value updates via methods like assign.
NumPy arrays and TensorFlow tensors can be interchanged easily using the numpy method.
NumPy defaults to 64-bit precision, whereas TensorFlow defaults to 32-bit precision for better performance.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Beyond ordinary tensors, TensorFlow ships sparse tensors, ragged tensors, string tensors, sets and queues. Which of these would a text or a recommender pipeline actually hit, and why can an ordinary tensor not hold that data?
Look up: Appendix C, "Special Data Structures", in this book.

items.term: Implementing Custom Loss Functions in TensorFlow

blocks.content:
A custom loss in TensorFlow is just a Python function taking `(y_true, y_pred)` and returning one loss per sample using TensorFlow operations — and Huber loss is the worked example, because it fixes what MSE and MAE each get wrong on noisy data.

**The question this lesson answers:** your training set is noisy and full of outliers. MSE over-reacts to them and MAE trains slowly, so how do you write a loss that behaves like MSE near zero and like MAE far out, and hand it to Keras?

### The big picture

```
error = y_true - y_pred
        |
   |error| < 1.0 ?
    /            \
  yes             no
0.5 * error^2   |error| - 0.5
    \            /
      tf.where picks per sample
```

The figure below is the same routing; the code card below is those six lines in Python.

### 1 · What is wrong with the two standard choices

An **outlier** is a data point that sits far from the rest — here, a sample whose true value is odd because the data is noisy, not because the world is.

| | MSE | MAE |
|---|---|---|
| Does | squares each error | takes each error's size |
| Big errors | punished enormously | punished in proportion |
| Near zero | gradient shrinks smoothly | gradient stays constant |
| Cost | outliers drag the model | slow, less precise |

Mean Squared Error heavily penalizes large errors because it squares them, which causes the model to distort its predictions to accommodate outliers. Conversely, Mean Absolute Error treats all errors linearly, which makes it robust to outliers, but its constant gradient near zero can slow down training convergence and reduce final model precision.

The **gradient** is the slope the optimizer follows downhill. MAE's slope is the same size whether you are miles away or almost exactly right, so the last part of training is a series of equal steps that keep stepping past the answer.

### 2 · Huber takes one half of each

To strike a balance between these two approaches, developers can use the **Huber loss**. Huber loss behaves like MSE when errors are small, offering fast convergence and high accuracy, but transitions to MAE when errors are large, limiting the disruptive influence of outliers.

That is the whole advantage over plain MAE: it accelerates convergence and improves precision near zero error by behaving quadratically there. *Quadratic* means squared — a curve, so the slope shrinks as the error shrinks and the optimizer can settle.

### 3 · The signature Keras expects

When a specific mathematical loss formulation is required, TensorFlow allows developers to define a **custom loss function**.

A custom loss function in TensorFlow is defined as a standard Python function that accepts two arguments: the ground truth labels (`y_true`) and the model predictions (`y_pred`). **Ground truth** is simply the real answer from the data. Those two arguments, in that order, are the entire contract; Keras calls the function once per batch and passes them positionally.

Inside the function, all vector operations must be performed using TensorFlow operations to preserve automatic differentiation capability. **Automatic differentiation** is how TensorFlow works out the gradients: it can only do that for operations it recorded, so a NumPy or plain-Python calculation in the middle breaks the chain and there is nothing to differentiate.

### 4 · Building it, step by step

For example, to implement a manual Huber loss function, first calculate the residual vector by subtracting predictions from true labels. A **residual** is one sample's error.

Next, determine which samples have an absolute error less than `1.0`. For these small errors, compute half of the squared error. For larger errors, calculate the absolute error minus `0.5`. Finally, apply `tf.where` to select between the quadratic and linear loss terms based on the condition.

`tf.where(condition, a, b)` is a row-wise `CASE WHEN condition THEN a ELSE b END`: every sample is scored both ways, and `tf.where` keeps the right one for each. TensorFlow uses the resulting tensor of individual sample losses to compute gradients during training — one number per sample, not one number for the batch, which is what lets Keras weight samples later.

**One-liner for your notes:** write the loss as a function of `(y_true, y_pred)` built only from TensorFlow ops, return one loss per sample, and use `tf.where` as a per-row CASE WHEN to make Huber quadratic below the threshold and linear above it.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
def huber_fn(y_true, y_pred):
    error = y_true - y_pred
    is_small_error = tf.abs(error) < 1
    squared_loss = tf.square(error) / 2
    linear_loss  = tf.abs(error) - 0.5
    return tf.where(is_small_error, squared_loss, linear_loss)
```

items.term: Why the whole API is two vectors in, one vector out
items.text: Gradient descent needs only a differentiable function of the predictions, so that is the entire contract the framework can demand. Anything expressible in that form is interchangeable with anything else, which is why a loss, a metric and a regularizer can all be plain functions and why swapping one loss for another needs no other change in the program.

items.term: Returning per-sample losses, not the mean
items.text: It is possible to return the batch mean instead, and it is not recommended: once the loss has collapsed to one number, class weights and sample weights can no longer be applied, because there is nothing left to weight. Aggregation belongs to the framework, which knows about weighting; the loss function's job is to score each sample and stop.

items.term: Huber is an instance of a general move
items.text: The pattern is: pick the penalty by regime, and join the two so the result is smooth where it matters. It generalises anywhere one behaviour is right near the target and another is right far from it. What does not generalise is the threshold: it is measured in the units of your target, so a model whose target is in millions and one whose target is in fractions need very different values.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Mean Squared Error heavily penalizes outliers, whereas Mean Absolute Error can slow down model convergence.
Huber loss combines quadratic penalization for small errors with linear penalization for large errors.
A custom loss function in TensorFlow must take `y_true` and `y_pred` as its parameters.
TensorFlow tensor operations must be used inside custom loss functions to support automatic differentiation.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The threshold here is 1.0, which only makes sense if a typical error is around 1. How do you choose it for a target measured in millions, and what does Keras's own Huber implementation default to?
Look up: the `tf.keras.losses.Huber` entry in the Keras API documentation, alongside this book's Chapter 10, where the Huber loss and its threshold are introduced.

items.term: Loading Models with Custom Components

blocks.content:
A saved Keras model stores the names of your custom pieces, not their code, so loading it needs you to hand the names back to the real Python objects — or to subclass, so the settings travel inside the file.

**The question this lesson answers:** you trained with `create_huber(2.0)`, saved the model, and reloading it fails. What exactly did the file keep, what did it lose, and what are the two ways to fix it?

### The big picture

```
save  -> architecture + weights + the NAME "huber_fn"
      -> the Python code is NOT in the file
      -> the threshold 2.0 is NOT in the file

load  -> option A: custom_objects={"huber_fn": ...}
      -> option B: subclass Loss + get_config()
```

The figure below shows option A end to end; the code card below is option B.

### 1 · What the file actually contains

When you save a Keras model containing custom functions or classes, TensorFlow saves the architecture and weights, but it does not save the Python source code of your custom components. Consequently, attempting to reload the saved model without additional context causes TensorFlow to fail because it cannot recognize the custom object names in the saved configuration.

If you have ever restored a database catalog and found a view that references a user-defined function nobody registered, this is the same failure: the definition survived, the implementation it points at did not. **Deserialize** is the word for the reverse trip — turning the stored description back into a live object.

### 2 · Option A: hand Keras the map

To solve this issue, you must inform Keras how to deserialize your custom components when calling the loading function. One basic approach passes a dictionary mapping the saved object's name string to the actual Python object.

Consider a scenario where a model uses a custom Huber loss function named `create_huber(2.0)` configured with a threshold of `2.0`. Saving the model records the function name `huber_fn`, but omits the hyperparameter threshold value. A **hyperparameter** is a setting you choose before training rather than something training learns — here, where the curve stops being quadratic.

When calling `tf.keras.models.load_model()`, you supply the argument `custom_objects={"huber_fn": create_huber(2.0)}`. This maps the serialized name back to a freshly constructed function instance using the required threshold. Note which name is the key: `huber_fn`, the inner function Keras saw, not `create_huber`, the factory that built it.

So the limitation of a wrapper function factory is precise and worth stating plainly: the configured hyperparameter value is not preserved within the saved model configuration, so you must re-specify it by hand every time you load.

Alternatively, decorating a custom function makes it globally available to the loading mechanism automatically: decorate it with `@keras.utils.register_keras_serializable()` and there is no need to include it in the `custom_objects` dictionary at all.

### 3 · Option B: subclass, so the setting travels with the file

To avoid manually specifying hyperparameters during loading, the standard solution subclassing `tf.keras.losses.Loss` implements a `get_config()` method. This method serializes hyperparameter state alongside the parent class settings, allowing Keras to restore both the object and its state when provided with the class reference.

`get_config()` returns a plain dictionary of hyperparameter names and values. It begins with `super().get_config()`, which retrieves the base configurations the parent class owns — the name of the loss and the reduction setting — and then adds `"threshold"` to that dictionary. Skipping the `super()` call would silently drop those framework settings.

| | Function + custom_objects | Loss subclass + get_config |
|---|---|---|
| Threshold saved | no, retype it on load | yes, inside the file |
| On load you pass | the rebuilt function | the class itself |
| Write | one function | a small class |

You still map a name to an object on load either way — but with the subclass you map the class name to the class, and the threshold comes back on its own.

**One-liner for your notes:** saving records names, not code or hyperparameters, so either pass `custom_objects` (or register the function) on every load, or subclass `Loss` with a `get_config()` that starts from `super().get_config()` and let the settings ride inside the file.

blocks.title: What the parent Loss class takes care of
blocks.content:
In `HuberLoss`, the constructor passes `**kwargs` to the parent constructor, which handles the standard hyperparameters: the name of the loss and the reduction algorithm used to aggregate the individual instance losses. The default reduction is `"AUTO"`, which equals `"SUM_OVER_BATCH_SIZE"`: the sum of the instance losses, weighted by the sample weights if any, divided by the batch size. The other values are `"SUM"` and `"NONE"`.

The `get_config()` method returns a dictionary that maps each hyperparameter name to its value. It first calls `super().get_config()` to get the parent's settings, such as the name and the reduction, then adds `"threshold"`. When you save the model, Keras calls `get_config()`. When you load it, Keras calls the `from_config()` class method, which passes the config to the constructor. You still map the class name to the class: `custom_objects={"HuberLoss": HuberLoss}`.
