blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

dataset = tf.data.Dataset.range(10).repeat(2)
dataset = dataset.shuffle(buffer_size=4, seed=42).batch(7)

for item in dataset:
    print(item)
```

items.term: Why a buffer instead of a real shuffle
items.text: A true uniform shuffle needs every row available at once, because any row must be able to land in any position. On a stream that is impossible, so the buffer trades exactness for a fixed memory cost: a row can only move as far as the buffer is wide. The cost is bounded and predictable, which is the property that matters when the alternative is not running at all.

items.term: What 'independent and identically distributed' is actually protecting
items.text: Gradient descent updates the model from one batch at a time and assumes each batch is a fair sample of the whole. A batch drawn from one sorted region is not: the model gets pulled hard toward that region, then pulled back by the next one. It is the same reason you would not judge a table's distribution from its first thousand rows when the export was sorted.

items.term: The trap that survives a correct buffer
items.text: Shuffling fixes the order of rows; it does nothing about which rows exist. A training set that is 90% one class, or that covers only one month, is equally skewed shuffled or not. Shuffling is a protection against an ordering artefact, never against a sampling one, and the two get confused because both are described as 'the data was biased'.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Gradient descent optimization requires independent and identically distributed instances to avoid model bias.
The shuffle method maintains an in-memory buffer from which it randomly pulls items and adds new ones.
Buffer size must be chosen carefully to ensure sufficient randomness without exceeding available system memory.
Using a random seed enables deterministic and reproducible shuffling across program executions.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The chapter says a buffer that is small relative to the dataset shuffles poorly, but never says how large is large enough. How would you measure whether your buffer is actually big enough for your data, rather than guessing?

Look up: the "Randomly shuffling data" section of the TensorFlow guide "Better performance with the tf.data API" (tensorflow.org/guide/data_performance), which discusses the interaction of shuffle buffer size with repeat and memory.

items.term: Interleaving Data from Multiple CSV Files

blocks.content:
`interleave()` reads several files at once and takes one line from each in rotation, so the rows arriving at your model are mixed across files instead of arriving one whole file at a time.

**The question this lesson answers:** the training data is split across many CSV files. Read them one after another and every mini-batch comes from a single file — and one sequential reader leaves the CPU idle. How do you read many at once and blend the lines?

### The big picture

```
file_01 --\
file_02 ---> interleave(cycle_length=5) --> mixed lines
file_03 --/     one line from each, in turn
```

### 1 · Two problems, one method

If training data is grouped by file, reading one file at a time prevents instances from being effectively shuffled across the entire dataset. Furthermore, reading a single file sequentially creates an I/O bottleneck that leaves CPU resources idle.

Both are familiar from a partitioned folder in a lake. One reader walking `part-00000` to `part-00199` in order gives you a batch that is entirely one partition, and it also uses one disk stream when you have many cores waiting.

### 2 · The two steps

The process begins by creating a dataset of file paths using **`tf.data.Dataset.list_files()`**, which shuffles the file paths by default. So the file *order* is already random before any line is read.

Calling **`interleave()`** on this dataset opens a set number of files simultaneously and cycles through them, pulling one line from each file in turn to mix the data streams. The lambda you hand it says how to turn one path into a dataset — here, a **`tf.data.TextLineDataset`**, which yields the file's lines one by one, with `.skip(1)` to strip out CSV header rows.

### 3 · `cycle_length`, and what it costs

The number of concurrently opened files is controlled by the **`cycle_length`** parameter. For example, setting `cycle_length` to `5` opens five file paths at once.

As you iterate through the interleave dataset, it takes the first line from file one, the first line from file two, up through file five, and then repeats the cycle line by line.

The book recommends files of identical length: all five files then run out of lines together, and `interleave()` fetches the next five file paths from the source dataset and interleaves them the same way, until it runs out of file paths. If the files differ in length, the end of the longest file will not be interleaved — the short files finish early, and the tail of the long one is read without anything to blend it with.

That is the same argument for even part-file sizes you already make when writing a partitioned table: a skewed part-file is the one that ruins the read.

### 4 · Counting the datasets in the pipeline

This surprises people, and it is worth being able to count. With `cycle_length=5` there are **seven** dataset objects alive: one filepath dataset, one interleave dataset, and the five `TextLineDataset`s the interleave dataset creates internally — 1 + 1 + 5 = 7. The card below walks through it.

### 5 · Making the reads actually parallel

By default `interleave()` is sequential: it rotates through the files but reads them on one thread. To maximize performance, setting **`num_parallel_calls`** to **`tf.data.AUTOTUNE`** enables multithreaded reading, allowing TensorFlow to dynamically choose the optimal number of background threads based on CPU availability. Interleaving without it gives you mixing but no extra throughput.

**One-liner for your notes:** `list_files()` shuffles the paths, `interleave(cycle_length=n)` reads n files in rotation to mix their lines, and `num_parallel_calls=AUTOTUNE` is what makes those reads concurrent.

blocks.title: Worked out: seven datasets in the pipeline
blocks.content: When `interleave()` is called with `cycle_length=5`, count the dataset objects in the pipeline. There is 1 filepath dataset made by `list_files()`, 1 interleave dataset, and 5 `TextLineDataset`s that the interleave dataset creates internally, one for each file path it pulls. That makes 1 + 1 + 5 = 7 datasets in all. Iterating over the interleave dataset reads one line at a time from each of the five `TextLineDataset`s in turn. By default `interleave()` does this sequentially, with no parallelism; the files are only read in parallel when you set `num_parallel_calls` to a number of threads or to `tf.data.AUTOTUNE`.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
filepath_dataset = tf.data.Dataset.list_files(train_filepaths, seed=42)

n_readers = 5
dataset = filepath_dataset.interleave(
    lambda filepath: tf.data.TextLineDataset(filepath).skip(1),
    cycle_length=n_readers,
    num_parallel_calls=tf.data.AUTOTUNE
)

for line in dataset.take(5):
    print(line)
```

items.term: Two kinds of randomness, and why you need both
items.text: `list_files()` randomises which files are read; `interleave()` blends lines from several of them; `shuffle()` randomises within a window. They attack different scales, and none of them substitutes for another. Interleaving five files without a shuffle buffer still gives you a strictly rotating pattern — file 1, file 2, file 3 — which is a different order, not a random one.

items.term: Why file layout is a modelling decision, not just storage
items.text: The advice to keep files the same length is really advice about how you wrote the data. If your export wrote one file per day and the days differ in size, the long day's tail arrives unmixed. The same instinct applies as for part-file skew in a lake: how the data was partitioned on write constrains what the reader can do, and no amount of reader tuning recovers it.

items.term: What cycle_length costs
items.text: Every concurrently open file is an open handle, a read buffer and, with parallel calls, a thread. Raising cycle_length improves mixing and throughput up to the point where the storage device or the core count saturates, after which it only adds memory and contention. This is why AUTOTUNE exists for the thread count — but note that it tunes num_parallel_calls, not cycle_length, which stays your decision.

blocks.title: Key points
items: The tf.data.Dataset.list_files() function produces a dataset of file path strings shuffled by default.
The interleave() method opens multiple files concurrently and cycles through them to read lines.
The cycle_length parameter determines how many source files are read at the same time.
Using skip(1) inside the interleave mapping function easily removes CSV header rows.
Setting num_parallel_calls to tf.data.AUTOTUNE enables parallel I/O for higher pipeline throughput.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The book says interleaving works best with files of identical length. If your source data genuinely cannot be split evenly, what options exist — and what does `tf.data.Dataset.sample_from_datasets` do differently from `interleave`?
Look up: the TensorFlow guide "tf.data: Build TensorFlow input pipelines" (tensorflow.org/guide/data), sections on consuming sets of files and on `interleave`.

items.term: Preprocessing CSV Data with TensorFlow

blocks.content:
A CSV line arrives at the pipeline as one raw byte string; `tf.io.decode_csv` turns it into typed scalars, `tf.stack` assembles them into a feature vector, and a scaling step puts the numbers on a comparable scale.

**The question this lesson answers:** `TextLineDataset` handed you `b'4.20,44.0,5.32,0.91,846.0,2.33,37.47,-122.2,2.78'`. How do you get from that byte string to a pair of tensors a model can train on?

### The big picture

```
raw line -> decode_csv -> 9 scalars
         -> stack -> (x, y) -> scale
```

The figure below draws the same four stages.

### 1 · Why parsing and scaling both have to happen

Raw data loaded from files like CSVs typically enters an input pipeline as simple byte string tensors. A machine learning model cannot directly process unparsed text strings or unscaled numerical values. To train efficiently and achieve stable convergence, input pipelines must parse these raw strings into structured numerical tensors and apply feature scaling before feeding the data into the model.

**Convergence** is the training run settling onto good parameter values instead of bouncing around. Features on wildly different scales — a count in the thousands next to a ratio near 1 — make that harder, which is why scaling is not cosmetic.

### 2 · `record_defaults` is your schema

TensorFlow provides the `tf.io.decode_csv` function to convert raw string lines into a list of scalar tensors. This function accepts the line to parse alongside a list of **record defaults**. These defaults serve two critical purposes: they specify the expected data type for each column and define fallback values if a field is missing.

Three jobs, in one list:

| What it declares | How |
|---|---|
| the type of each column | by the type of the default value |
| the fallback for a missing field | by the value itself |
| that a column is required | by an empty tensor of that type |

Passing an empty tensor of a given type as a record default enforces that the column is required, causing TensorFlow to raise an error if a missing value occurs.

If you write DDL, this is the familiar pair: a column type plus `NOT NULL`. The list length also tells TensorFlow how many columns to expect, so a malformed row fails loudly rather than silently shifting values one column left.

### 3 · Nine scalars in, two tensors out

Consider a dataset with eight numerical features and one target column. Build a record defaults list containing eight zeros of floating-point type for the features and an empty `tf.float32` tensor for the target — zero is a reasonable fallback for a feature, but a missing **target** (the answer column the model is trained to predict) must never be quietly replaced by a guess.

When `tf.io.decode_csv` parses a byte string such as `b'4.20,44.0,5.32,0.91,846.0,2.33,37.47,-122.2,2.78'`, it outputs nine individual scalar tensors. Calling `tf.stack` on the first eight tensors combines them into a single one-dimensional tensor representing the input features. The final target value is stacked separately into its own single-element tensor.

`tf.stack` matters because the model wants one row-shaped vector, not nine loose numbers.

### 4 · Scaling, then mapping it over everything

After parsing, feature scaling is applied using precomputed statistical parameters. By subtracting the feature vector of mean values and dividing by the standard deviation vector, the features are normalized to standard scale. The **mean** is the average of a column across the training set and the **standard deviation** is its typical spread; both are computed once, in advance, on the training set only.

The single **preprocess** function combines parsing and standard scaling, allowing it to be mapped directly across every raw record in a TensorFlow dataset — one call to the dataset's `map()` method and every line in the stream goes through it.

**One-liner for your notes:** `record_defaults` is the CSV's schema (types, fallbacks, required columns), `tf.stack` builds the feature vector, and one `preprocess` function mapped over the dataset does both plus the scaling.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
n_inputs = 8
X_mean, X_std = [...]  # Precomputed mean and std vectors

def parse_csv_line(line):
    defs = [0.] * n_inputs + [tf.constant([], dtype=tf.float32)]
    fields = tf.io.decode_csv(line, record_defaults=defs)
    return tf.stack(fields[:-1]), tf.stack(fields[-1:])

def preprocess(line):
    x, y = parse_csv_line(line)
    return (x - X_mean) / X_std, y
```

items.term: Why a missing feature and a missing label are not the same problem
items.text: Defaulting a feature to zero is a modelling choice with a cost you can reason about: the model sees a plausible value and learns around it. Defaulting a label is different in kind — it invents an answer and trains the model to reproduce it. That is why the target column gets an empty tensor and the run fails instead. The general rule: it is acceptable to guess an input, never acceptable to guess the thing you are trying to predict.

items.term: Where the scaling statistics must come from
items.text: The means and standard deviations are computed on the training set only, and then reused unchanged on validation, test and production data. Computing them over everything would let information about the evaluation rows influence the transformation applied to the training rows — the model would be scored on data it had already, indirectly, seen. It is the same discipline as never joining a future fact into a snapshot you are about to evaluate against.

items.term: Parsing in the pipeline versus parsing once on write
items.text: Doing this inside `map()` means it runs for every row of every epoch. Doing it once and writing the parsed result to disk pays the cost a single time, and is the argument for the TFRecord half of this chapter. The trade is flexibility: a parsed and scaled file is frozen against the statistics that were current when you wrote it, so changing a feature means rewriting the dataset.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Raw CSV lines are parsed into individual tensors using the tf.io.decode_csv function.
The record_defaults argument specifies column types, default fallback values, and required fields.
The tf.stack function combines separate scalar tensors into structured one-dimensional feature arrays.
Standard feature scaling normalizes inputs by subtracting feature means and dividing by standard deviations.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: `record_defaults` fixes the number and type of columns at parse time. What happens to this pipeline when the upstream CSV gains a column, and what would you have to build for the change to fail loudly rather than shift every field?
Look up: the API documentation for `tf.io.decode_csv` (tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/io/decode_csv), particularly the `field_delim`, `select_cols` and `na_value` arguments.

items.term: Optimizing Data Pipelines with Prefetching

blocks.content:
`prefetch()` puts a one-batch queue between the CPU that prepares data and the GPU that trains on it, so the two stop taking turns and start running at the same time.

**The question this lesson answers:** your GPU is the expensive part of the machine and it is idle half of every step, waiting for the next batch. How do you overlap data preparation with training instead of alternating them?

### The big picture

```
no prefetch:  prep1 | train1 | prep2 | train2   (turns)
prefetch:     prep1 | prep2  | prep3            (overlap)
                     | train1 | train2
```

Figure 13-3 below is the book's version of this picture.

### 1 · The bottleneck

When training deep learning models, the GPU often spends substantial time sitting idle while waiting for the CPU to read data from disk, preprocess it, and form batches. This resource bottleneck slows down training because data preparation and model computations occur sequentially instead of concurrently.

This is a producer–consumer stall, the same shape as a single-threaded extract feeding a fast load: neither side is slow on its own, they are just never busy at the same time.

### 2 · What `prefetch()` does

TensorFlow provides the **prefetching** mechanism via the `prefetch()` method. Prefetching decouples the producer (CPU data pipeline) from the consumer (GPU training loop). By adding `.prefetch(1)` at the end of an input pipeline, the CPU prepares the next batch of data in parallel while the GPU processes the current batch.

The argument is a number of batches to keep ready. `prefetch(1)` keeps the dataset one batch ahead, which is generally fine; you can prefetch a few more, or pass `tf.data.AUTOTUNE` and let TensorFlow decide.

### 3 · The arithmetic

Consider a training setup where the CPU takes 50 milliseconds to load and parse a batch of 32 instances, while the GPU takes 50 milliseconds to execute forward and backward passes.

| | Per step |
|---|---|
| without prefetching | 50 ms prepare, then 50 ms train = 100 ms |
| with prefetching | prepare and train overlap = 50 ms |

With prefetching enabled, CPU preparation of batch n+1 happens simultaneously with GPU computation on batch n, reducing step time to 50 milliseconds total — half the wall clock for the same work.

When combined with multithreaded loading via `interleave()` and preprocessing via `map()`, CPU data preparation time can be reduced to less than GPU execution time, keeping GPU hardware utilization near 100%. *Near*, not at: as the card below records, the GPU still waits for the data transfer from the CPU to the GPU.

### 4 · The full pipeline, in order

As Figure 13-2 shows, a complete efficient pipeline chains several transformations together: file discovery using `list_files()`, parallel reading via `interleave()`, row-level transformations through `map()`, shuffling, batching, and finally prefetching.

The order is not arbitrary — shuffle before batch, and prefetch last, because prefetch has to sit at the consumer end of the chain.

The multithreading in that chain is one argument in two places: `num_parallel_calls` is the parameter on both `interleave()` and `map()` that spreads reading and preprocessing across CPU threads. Prefetching overlaps the CPU with the GPU; `num_parallel_calls` overlaps the CPU with itself.

### 5 · Where `cache()` goes

For small datasets fitting entirely in RAM, calling the `cache()` method right after loading and preprocessing ensures that expensive disk reads and parsing execute only once across all training epochs while preserving epoch-level shuffling.

That position is the whole trick: after the expensive work so it is not repeated, before the shuffle so each epoch still gets a fresh order. Cache after shuffling and you would freeze one order for the whole run.

**One-liner for your notes:** `prefetch()` overlaps CPU batch preparation with GPU training and roughly halves step time; `cache()` goes after loading and preprocessing but before shuffling, batching and prefetching.

blocks.title: Where cache() goes, and the GPU's short wait
blocks.content: The book gives an exact place for `cache()`: after loading and preprocessing the data, but before shuffling, repeating, batching and prefetching. Each instance is then read and preprocessed only once instead of once per epoch, while the data is still shuffled differently at each epoch and the next batch is still prepared in advance. With multithreaded loading and preprocessing plus prefetching, the GPU can be almost 100% utilized, but not fully: it still waits for the data transfer from the CPU to the GPU. A call to `prefetch(1)` keeps the dataset one batch ahead, which is generally fine; you can prefetch a few more batches, or pass `tf.data.AUTOTUNE` to let TensorFlow decide.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
def csv_reader_dataset(filepaths, n_readers=5, n_read_threads=None,
                       n_parse_threads=5, shuffle_buffer_size=10_000, seed=42,
                       batch_size=32):
    dataset = tf.data.Dataset.list_files(filepaths, seed=seed)
    dataset = dataset.interleave(
        lambda filepath: tf.data.TextLineDataset(filepath).skip(1),
        cycle_length=n_readers, num_parallel_calls=n_read_threads)
    dataset = dataset.map(preprocess, num_parallel_calls=n_parse_threads)
    dataset = dataset.shuffle(shuffle_buffer_size, seed=seed)
    return dataset.batch(batch_size).prefetch(1)
```

items.term: Prefetching is a queue, and queues have a depth
items.text: `prefetch(n)` is a bounded buffer between producer and consumer. Depth 1 is enough when preparation time is steady, because one spare batch covers the handover. It is not enough when preparation time is variable — one slow batch drains the queue and the GPU stalls anyway. Deeper queues absorb variance at the price of memory, which is the same calculation you would make sizing any buffer between a slow producer and a fast consumer.

items.term: The pipeline is only as fast as its slowest stage
items.text: Prefetching hides CPU time behind GPU time; it does not reduce it. If preparing a batch takes longer than a training step, the GPU still waits — just for the difference instead of the whole thing. That is why the chapter pairs prefetching with parallel reads and parallel parsing: you overlap first, then you shorten the stage that is still on the critical path. Measuring which stage that is comes before tuning either.

items.term: Why cache() has exactly one correct position
items.text: Its placement encodes a decision about what is expensive and what must stay fresh. Everything before the cache happens once for the whole run; everything after happens every epoch. Reading and parsing are expensive and identical each epoch, so they go before. Shuffling must differ each epoch, so it goes after. Get the order wrong in either direction and you either lose the per-epoch reshuffle or keep paying for the parse.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Prefetching allows the CPU to prepare upcoming data batches in parallel while the GPU processes the current batch.
Using multithreaded reading and parsing with prefetching maximizes GPU utilization.
A typical pipeline sequences file listing, interleaving, mapping, shuffling, batching, and prefetching.
The cache method stores preprocessed data in memory to avoid repeating disk reads and transformations every epoch.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The chapter says to tell whether the input pipeline is your bottleneck, but not how to measure it. What does the TensorFlow Profiler's input-pipeline analysis actually show, and what does an idle GPU look like in it?
Look up: the TensorFlow guide "Optimize TensorFlow performance using the Profiler" (tensorflow.org/guide/profiler), specifically its trace viewer and input-pipeline bottleneck analysis.

items.term: Using tf.data Datasets with Keras

blocks.content:
Keras takes a `tf.data.Dataset` anywhere it takes NumPy arrays, so once your pipeline exists you hand it to `fit()` and nothing else about the model changes.

**The question this lesson answers:** you have built `csv_reader_dataset()` and it streams batches from disk. What has to change in the model code to train on it instead of on arrays held in memory?

### The big picture

| Instead of | You write |
|---|---|
| `fit(X_train, y_train)` | `fit(train_set)` |
| `validation_data=(X_valid, y_valid)` | `validation_data=valid_set` |
| `evaluate(X_test, y_test)` | `evaluate(test_set)` |

Nothing else moves. The model architecture, the loss, the optimizer are untouched.

### 1 · Why you would bother

When working with large datasets, loading all data into memory as NumPy arrays is often impossible. The **tf.data API** solves this issue by streaming data directly from disk in batches during training. Once you construct pipeline functions that load and preprocess your data, you can pass these dataset objects directly into standard Keras model methods without modifying model architectures.

A **NumPy array** is Python's in-memory numeric array — fast, but it has to fit in RAM, all of it, at once. The dataset is the streaming alternative: a cursor over the data rather than a materialized copy.

### 2 · What `fit()` does for you

To train a Keras model using data pipelines, you pass a dataset object to the `fit()` method instead of passing separate feature and target arrays. The `fit()` method iterates over the batches that the pipeline (here `csv_reader_dataset()`) has already created, and it takes care of repeating the training dataset once per epoch, using a different random order at each epoch.

So you do not call `repeat()` yourself, and you do not rebuild the pipeline between epochs. The shuffle buffer inside the pipeline is what supplies the different order each time.

### 3 · The same for validation, evaluation and prediction

You can similarly pass validation and test datasets to the `fit()`, `evaluate()`, and `predict()` methods. If a dataset passed to `predict()` contains labels, Keras simply ignores them during inference.

That last point saves a step: you do not have to strip the answer column out of a test pipeline before predicting with it.

Concretely, with three pipelines `train_set`, `valid_set` and `test_set`: instead of writing `model.fit(X_train, y_train, validation_data=(X_valid, y_valid))`, you simply write `model.fit(train_set, validation_data=valid_set, epochs=5)`. Executing `model.evaluate(test_set)` returns the test loss across all batches streamed from the pipeline. To predict on three sample batches, extract them with `test_set.take(3)` and pass that subset directly to `model.predict()`.

### 4 · One knob worth knowing: `steps_per_execution`

`compile()` has a `steps_per_execution` argument. It sets how many batches `fit()` processes during each call to the `tf.function` it uses for training, and the default is 1. Setting it to 50 often gives a significant performance improvement, because the Python-side overhead is paid once per 50 batches instead of once per batch.

The trade-off is real: the `on_batch_*()` methods of Keras callbacks are then only called every 50 batches. If a callback of yours is meant to react per batch, it will not.

### 5 · Custom loops still work

Nothing about a dataset ties you to `fit()`. A dataset is iterable, so a custom training loop reads it with an ordinary Python `for` loop, one `(X_batch, y_batch)` pair at a time.

**One-liner for your notes:** Keras accepts `tf.data.Dataset` objects wherever it accepts arrays — `fit()` handles epoch repetition and ordering, `predict()` ignores any labels it finds, and training on data larger than RAM costs you no code changes.

blocks.title: Speeding up fit() with steps_per_execution
blocks.content: The `compile()` method has a `steps_per_execution` argument. It sets how many batches the `fit()` method processes during each call to the `tf.function` that it uses for training. The default is 1. Setting it to 50 often gives a significant performance improvement. The trade-off is that the `on_batch_*()` methods of Keras callbacks are then only called every 50 batches, instead of after every batch.

```python
train_set = csv_reader_dataset(train_filepaths)
valid_set = csv_reader_dataset(valid_filepaths)

model.fit(train_set, validation_data=valid_set, epochs=5)

test_mse = model.evaluate(test_set)
new_set = test_set.take(3)
y_pred = model.predict(new_set)
```

items.term: What the dataset boundary buys you
items.text: Because Keras accepts any object that yields batches, the data-loading decision and the modelling decision become independent. You can change the source from CSV to TFRecord, add caching, or move the scaling in or out of the pipeline, and the model code is untouched. That separation is the reason to build a `csv_reader_dataset()`-style function at all rather than inlining the chain.

items.term: Where the shuffling actually lives now
items.text: Passing a dataset means `fit()` no longer controls shuffling — its `shuffle` argument applies to arrays, not to a pipeline that already has its own buffer. So the randomness per epoch comes from the `shuffle()` you put in the chain, and if you left it out, every epoch sees the identical order and nothing warns you. The control moved; it did not disappear.

items.term: What steps_per_execution is really trading
items.text: Larger values amortise Python and graph-launch overhead across more batches, so the gain is largest when each batch is small and fast — exactly when per-step overhead dominates. What you give up is granularity: callbacks that fire per batch, such as a custom learning-rate schedule or a per-batch logger, now see one call per group. Throughput bought with observability is a trade worth making knowingly.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Keras methods like fit(), evaluate(), and predict() accept tf.data.Dataset objects directly.
Passing a dataset to fit() automatically handles epoch repetition and batch iteration.
Labels present in datasets passed to the predict() method are automatically ignored by Keras.
Custom training loops can naturally iterate over dataset objects batch by batch using a standard Python for loop.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: `fit()` repeats the dataset once per epoch — but what is an 'epoch' when the dataset is infinite, for example after calling `repeat()` with no argument? What does `steps_per_epoch` do in that case?
Look up: the Keras API documentation for `Model.fit` (keras.io), specifically the `steps_per_epoch` and `validation_steps` arguments and their notes on dataset inputs.

items.term: The TFRecord Data Format and Compression

blocks.content:
TFRecord is TensorFlow's own binary container format: a flat sequence of variable-length records, each wrapped in checksums, read fast and sequentially.

**The question this lesson answers:** CSV works, but parsing text costs CPU and the files are large. What does TensorFlow offer instead, and what is actually inside one of its files?

### The big picture

```
| length | CRC | data payload | CRC |   repeated, record
                                       after record
```

### 1 · The problem with text files

When training machine learning models on large datasets, reading data efficiently from disk or network storage is critical to avoid stalling the training pipeline. Plain text formats like CSV are slow to parse and consume significant disk space.

The **TFRecord** format solves this problem by providing a simple, binary container designed specifically for high-throughput data loading in TensorFlow.

If you have moved a table from CSV to a binary format, the motivation is the same one. One honest difference worth holding onto: a columnar format stores a schema and lets you read a subset of columns, while TFRecord does neither — it is a plain sequence of opaque byte strings, read front to back. The structure comes from what you put *inside* each record, which is the next few lessons.

### 2 · What one record contains

A **TFRecord** file consists of a sequential series of binary records of varying lengths. Each individual record contains the record length, a Cyclic Redundancy Check (**CRC checksum**) to verify that the length byte was not corrupted, the actual data payload, and a final **CRC checksum** to ensure data integrity.

A **CRC checksum** is a short number computed from some bytes; recompute it on read and compare, and a mismatch means the bytes changed. Two of them per record is deliberate: the length is checked separately because a corrupted length would make the reader mis-split every record after it, not just this one.

"Varying lengths" is the feature. Rows do not have to be the same size, so an image, a sentence and a numeric row all fit the same container.

### 3 · Writing and reading

| Direction | Class |
|---|---|
| write | `tf.io.TFRecordWriter` |
| read | `tf.data.TFRecordDataset` |

`TFRecordDataset` yields each payload as a string tensor and drops straight into a `tf.data` pipeline like any other source. Reading multiple TFRecord files simultaneously in parallel is a constructor argument: set `num_parallel_reads` to a number above one and the dataset reads that many files at once and interleaves their records.

### 4 · Compression

To optimize network bandwidth or save storage space, files can also be compressed using algorithms such as GZIP by passing a `tf.io.TFRecordOptions` object during writing and specifying the `compression_type` parameter during reading.

Both halves are required, and forgetting the reading half is the classic mistake — the file is not self-describing, so nothing tells the reader it is compressed.

For a concrete example: instantiate `tf.io.TFRecordOptions(compression_type="GZIP")`, pass it to `tf.io.TFRecordWriter("my_compressed.tfrecord", options)`, and write byte strings such as `b"Compress, compress, compress!"`. To read this data back as a tensor stream, instantiate `tf.data.TFRecordDataset(["my_compressed.tfrecord"], compression_type="GZIP")`, which decompresses and yields each binary payload as a string tensor.

**One-liner for your notes:** a TFRecord file is a sequence of variable-length binary records, each guarded by a length CRC and a data CRC, written with `TFRecordWriter` and read with `TFRecordDataset` — with GZIP set on both sides or not at all.

blocks.caption: A TFRecord file stores individual binary records enclosed with CRC checksums to ensure integrity. Optional GZIP compression reduces file size during storage and network transit.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

options = tf.io.TFRecordOptions(compression_type="GZIP")
with tf.io.TFRecordWriter("my_compressed.tfrecord", options) as f:
    f.write(b"This is the first record")
    f.write(b"This is the second record")

filepaths = ["my_compressed.tfrecord"]
dataset = tf.data.TFRecordDataset(filepaths, compression_type="GZIP")
for item in dataset:
    print(item)
```

items.term: Why two checksums and not one
items.text: The length and the payload fail differently. A corrupted payload spoils one record; a corrupted length spoils the reader's idea of where the next record starts, and therefore every record after it. Checking the length separately turns an unbounded failure into a bounded one. Any format that delimits records by a stored size has this problem, and this is the standard answer to it.

items.term: What TFRecord deliberately does not give you
items.text: No schema, no column pruning, no predicate pushdown, no footer of statistics. Every read is the whole record, front to back. That is a real loss compared with a columnar format, and it is accepted because training reads all the features of every row anyway — the access pattern is a full sequential scan, which is precisely the case where columnar layout earns least.

items.term: Compression is not free, and not always a win
items.text: GZIP shrinks bytes on disk and on the wire at the cost of CPU on every read. When the bottleneck is network or storage, that trade is good. When the bottleneck is already the CPU preparing batches — which is the situation the whole prefetching discussion is about — compression makes training slower. The right answer depends on which resource you are short of, which is why it is a flag and not a default.

blocks.title: Key points
items: The TFRecord format is TensorFlow's preferred binary format for efficient data storage and retrieval.
Each record in a TFRecord file contains length information and CRC checksums to ensure data integrity.
You write TFRecord files using tf.io.TFRecordWriter and read them using tf.data.TFRecordDataset.
Parallel reading across multiple TFRecord files is enabled by setting num_parallel_reads.
Files can be compressed using GZIP by setting compression options in both the writer and the dataset reader.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The chapter notes TFRecord is worth it when loading and parsing is the bottleneck. How much does it actually save over CSV for a given dataset, and how would you measure that rather than assume it?
Look up: the TensorFlow tutorial "TFRecord and tf.train.Example" (tensorflow.org/tutorials/load_data/tfrecord), then measure with the TensorFlow Profiler's input-pipeline analysis.

items.term: Introduction to Protocol Buffers

blocks.content:
A protocol buffer is a schema you write once, compile into classes for whatever language you use, and then serialize to a compact binary string that any other language can read back exactly.

**The question this lesson answers:** TFRecord records are just opaque bytes. What do you actually put inside them so that a Python writer and a C++ reader agree on what a record means?

### The big picture

```
schema.proto --protoc--> access classes (Python)
object --SerializeToString--> bytes
       --ParseFromString--> object
```

### 1 · Why not JSON

When working with large-scale data storage and network transmission, transferring raw complex objects efficiently across different programming languages presents a significant challenge. Plain text formats like JSON or XML can be verbose, slow to parse, and inefficient in memory usage.

**Protocol buffers**, also known as protobufs, solve this problem by offering a language-neutral, platform-neutral, and efficient binary format for serializing structured data.

If you have worked with Avro or Thrift, this is the same bargain: declare the shape up front, get a small binary payload and a fast parser, give up human readability.

### 2 · Schema, then compiler, then classes

To use protocol buffers, developers define data structures in a simple schema file using a syntax such as `proto3`. Each field within a schema message is assigned a specific data type, a field name, and a unique numeric tag used in the binary format.

That numeric tag is the part worth pausing on. The wire format stores the **tag**, not the field name, which is why the payload is small — and it is also what makes schema evolution work: rename a field and old data still reads, because the reader matches on the number.

The compiler tool `protoc` reads these definitions and automatically generates access classes in target languages such as Python. Those generated classes are what your code actually touches; you never hand-write a parser.

### 3 · The two methods you use

| Method | Direction |
|---|---|
| `SerializeToString()` | object to compact binary byte string |
| `ParseFromString()` | binary byte string back to object |

Consider a compiled `Person` class defined with a string `name`, an integer `id`, and a repeated string `email`. In Python, an object can be instantiated as `Person(name="Al", id=123, email=["a@b.com"])`. The code then changes the name to "Alice" and appends a second email, "c@d.com".

Calling `person.SerializeToString()` now outputs the byte string `b'\n\x05Alice\x10{\x1a\x07a@b.com\x1a\x07c@d.com'`, which is 27 bytes long. Reconstructing this binary payload via `person2.ParseFromString(serialized)` restores all initial attributes perfectly, making `person == person2` evaluate to true.

Twenty-seven bytes for a name, an id and two email addresses. The same record as JSON would be roughly twice that, and would need a text parser to read.

A **repeated** field is protobuf's word for a list. In the generated Python class it behaves like one: index it as `person.email[0]`, extend it with `append()`.

### 4 · The catch inside `tf.data`

Although Python access classes easily serialize and parse binary data, native TensorFlow pipelines require special TensorFlow operations such as `tf.io.decode_proto()` to parse protocol buffers performantly within dataset preprocessing pipelines.

The reason is mechanical: `ParseFromString()` is a plain Python method, not a TensorFlow operation, so it cannot live inside a `tf.data` preprocessing function unless you wrap it in `tf.py_function()` — which makes the code slower and less portable. The card below has the detail, including why in practice you use the protobufs TensorFlow already ships parsing operations for.

**One-liner for your notes:** protobufs are a compiled schema plus a compact tagged binary format — `SerializeToString()` out, `ParseFromString()` back, and inside a `tf.data` pipeline you need a real TensorFlow parsing op instead.

blocks.title: Why ParseFromString() does not fit in tf.data
blocks.content: Repeated fields such as `email` can be accessed like arrays, for example `person.email[0]`, and extended with `append()`. You could save a serialized `Person` to a TFRecord file, then load it and parse it with `ParseFromString()`, and it would work. However, `ParseFromString()` is not a TensorFlow operation, so it cannot be used in a preprocessing function inside a `tf.data` pipeline, unless you wrap it in a `tf.py_function()` operation, which makes the code slower and less portable. The `tf.io.decode_proto()` function can parse any protobuf, provided you give it the protobuf definition. In practice, though, you will generally use the predefined protobufs for which TensorFlow provides dedicated parsing operations.

blocks.caption: Protocol buffers compile a schema file into native language classes. Objects are converted to compact binary strings via SerializeToString and reconstructed using ParseFromString.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from person_pb2 import Person

# Create and modify a protobuf object
person = Person(name="Al", id=123, email=["a@b.com"])
person.name = "Alice"
person.email.append("c@d.com")

# Serialize to a compact byte string
serialized_bytes = person.SerializeToString()

# Reconstruct object from binary data
person2 = Person()
person2.ParseFromString(serialized_bytes)
assert person == person2
```

items.term: Why the field number is the real identity
items.text: Protobuf stores tags, not names, and that single decision produces most of its properties. The payload is small because a one-byte tag replaces a field name. Renaming a field is free because no reader ever saw the name. Adding a field is safe because old readers skip tags they do not know. And reusing a retired tag number is catastrophic for exactly the same reason — old data would be read as the new field. Schema evolution rules in Avro and Thrift exist for the same reason.

items.term: What 'language-neutral' actually removes
items.text: The schema is the contract, and every language generates its own access classes from it. So a Python trainer and a C++ serving binary agree by construction rather than by two teams keeping two parsers in step. Compare that with a pickled Python object, which is fast to produce and readable by exactly one runtime and often only one version of it.

items.term: Why a Python method cannot go inside a tf.data pipeline
items.text: The pipeline is compiled into a graph of TensorFlow operations that can run on multiple threads and without the Python interpreter. A plain Python method is none of those things, so it has to be called back into Python one element at a time, serialised by the interpreter. That is what `tf.py_function` does, and why it is slow — the same reason a Python UDF costs more than a built-in function in a query engine.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Protocol buffers are a language-neutral and highly efficient binary serialization format.
Data structures are defined in protobuf schema files and compiled into access classes using protoc.
Objects are converted to binary format using SerializeToString() and restored using ParseFromString().
TensorFlow includes pre-compiled protobuf classes and dedicated parsing operations for dataset pipelines.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Protobuf's compatibility rules are what make a schema safe to evolve. Which changes to a `.proto` file are backward compatible and which quietly corrupt old data?

Look up: the official "Protocol Buffers Language Guide (proto3)" at protobuf.dev, specifically its section on updating a message type. The book links the same material from https://homl.info/protobuf.

items.term: Representing Data with TensorFlow Example Protobufs

blocks.content:
`tf.train.Example` is the standard protobuf for one row of a dataset: a dictionary of named features, where every feature is a list of bytes, a list of floats, or a list of integers.

**The question this lesson answers:** you are about to write records into a TFRecord file. What shape should one record have so that TensorFlow can parse it without you writing a custom schema?

### The big picture

```
Example
 └ Features           (a dict: name -> Feature)
    └ Feature         (exactly one of the three)
       ├ BytesList    strings / raw bytes
       ├ FloatList    floats
       └ Int64List    integers
```

### 1 · Why a standard row format

When storing datasets in TFRecord files, machine learning pipelines require a standardized and efficient serialization format. TensorFlow solves this problem by using Protocol Buffers, specifically the **`tf.train.Example`** protobuf structure. An `Example` message represents a single data instance in a dataset, such as one row or record.

You could define your own protobuf. The reason almost nobody does is that TensorFlow already ships `Example` compiled, plus native operations that parse it inside a pipeline — a custom schema means running `protoc` yourself and then parsing with a general-purpose op.

### 2 · Three types, and only three

Inside an `Example` protobuf, data is organized as a dictionary of named features wrapped in a **`Features`** message. Each feature value in the dictionary is represented by a **`Feature`** object.

A `Feature` can hold exactly one of three distinct data types: a **`BytesList`** for raw byte strings, a **`FloatList`** for floating-point numbers, or an **`Int64List`** for integer values.

| Type | Holds |
|---|---|
| `BytesList` | raw byte strings |
| `FloatList` | floating-point numbers |
| `Int64List` | integer values |

"Exactly one of" is the protobuf idea of a choice field — a `Feature` is one of the three, never two. And every one of them is a *list*, so a scalar is simply a list of length one.

Numerical lists utilize **packed encoding** to maximize binary storage efficiency: the repeated numbers are stored as one contiguous run rather than each carrying its own tag. The card below covers this and the reason `Example` exists as a wrapper at all.

### 3 · Building one

To illustrate this structure, consider storing a user contact record. The person's name `"Alice"` is converted into a `BytesList`, their user identifier `123` is stored in an `Int64List`, and a list of email addresses is stored in another `BytesList`.

These individual `Feature` objects are grouped into a dictionary mapping keys to features, which is then assigned to a `Features` object inside the `Example`. Finally, calling the `SerializeToString()` method on the `Example` object converts the structured data into a binary byte string that can be written directly to a file using a `TFRecordWriter`.

Reading the code card below from the inside out helps: value, then list type, then `Feature`, then the dictionary, then `Features`, then `Example`. It is verbose, and the book says so — wrapping it in a small helper function is normal.

### 4 · Why the extra wrapper

An `Example` contains only a `Features` object, which looks like a pointless layer. It is not: it is a **version-compatibility hinge**. TensorFlow's developers may one day add more fields to `Example`, and as long as the new definition keeps the `features` field with the same ID, every record written today still parses. That is the same reason you add a column to a table rather than replacing the table.

**One-liner for your notes:** one dataset row equals one `Example`, holding a named dictionary of `Feature`s that are each a `BytesList`, `FloatList` or `Int64List`, serialized with `SerializeToString()` into a TFRecord.

blocks.title: Why Example wraps a Features object
blocks.content: An `Example` contains only a `Features` object, so why define `Example` at all? The reason is extensibility. TensorFlow's developers may one day decide to add more fields to `Example`. As long as the new `Example` definition still contains the `features` field with the same ID, it will be backward compatible. This extensibility is one of the great features of protobufs. In the same definition, the `FloatList` and `Int64List` fields are marked `[packed = true]`, which gives these repeated numerical fields a more efficient encoding.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from tensorflow.train import BytesList, FloatList, Int64List
from tensorflow.train import Feature, Features, Example

person_example = Example(
    features=Features(
        feature={
            "name": Feature(bytes_list=BytesList(value=[b"Alice"])),
            "id": Feature(int64_list=Int64List(value=[123])),
            "emails": Feature(bytes_list=BytesList(value=[b"a@b.com", b"c@d.com"]))
        }
    )
)
serialized_bytes = person_example.SerializeToString()
```

items.term: Why only three types, and why everything is a list
items.text: Bytes, floats and integers are enough because everything else can be encoded into one of them: an image becomes bytes, a timestamp becomes an integer, a category becomes bytes or an integer. A narrow type system is what keeps the parsing operations simple and fast. Making every field a list removes the second special case — there is no separate scalar type, only a list of length one — so a column that is single-valued today can hold several values tomorrow without a format change.

items.term: The cost of a self-describing row
items.text: Every record carries its own feature names, so a million records carry the string "name" a million times. That is the price of a format with no central schema, and it is why `Example` is a poor fit for wide numeric tables: hundreds of named scalar features per row means the keys can outweigh the data. Packing those features into one `FloatList` under a single key is the usual answer.

items.term: Extensibility as a design habit, not a protobuf trick
items.text: The reason `Example` wraps `Features` instead of being it is that a wrapper leaves room to add fields later without breaking readers. It costs one level of nesting today for the freedom to extend tomorrow. This is the same reason you add a column rather than replace a table, and the same reason an API returns an object rather than a bare array — the shape that can grow is worth a small amount of verbosity now.

blocks.title: Key points
items: An Example protobuf represents a single record consisting of a dictionary of named features.
A Feature object contains either a BytesList, a FloatList, or an Int64List.
Numerical lists in protobuf definitions use packed encoding to minimize file size.
Calling SerializeToString translates an Example object into binary format for TFRecord storage.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: A `BytesList` can hold any binary data, including a serialized image or a serialized tensor. What are the trade-offs of storing an image as raw bytes, as `tf.io.serialize_tensor` output, or as encoded JPEG inside a TFRecord?
Look up: the TensorFlow tutorial "TFRecord and tf.train.Example" (tensorflow.org/tutorials/load_data/tfrecord), which walks through writing image data into an Example.

items.term: Loading and Parsing Example Protobufs in TensorFlow

blocks.content:
Reading an `Example` back means supplying a description of what you expect: a dictionary saying, per feature, what type it is and whether its length is fixed.

**The question this lesson answers:** the TFRecord file gives you a serialized byte string. TensorFlow cannot guess what was inside it. How do you tell the parser, and what comes out?

### The big picture

| Descriptor | Declares | You get back |
|---|---|---|
| `FixedLenFeature` | shape, type, default value | a dense tensor |
| `VarLenFeature` | type only | a sparse tensor |

### 1 · Why a description is required at all

When storing data efficiently in TensorFlow, datasets are frequently saved as serialized binary records called **Example** protocol buffers. Because these records are stored as raw byte strings inside **TFRecord** files, TensorFlow cannot automatically decipher the data types or shapes of the original features. To train a model on this data, developers need a reliable method to parse these raw byte streams back into structured tensors.

The file carries no schema — that was the trade for the compact format. So the schema lives in your code, exactly like reading a headerless CSV with a schema you declare on the read side.

### 2 · The two descriptors

TensorFlow provides parsing functions such as `tf.io.parse_single_example()`. This function accepts a serialized string scalar tensor and a description dictionary that maps feature names to expected descriptors.

Fixed-length features use **FixedLenFeature** to define shape, data type, and default values, yielding regular **tensors**. Variable-length features use **VarLenFeature** to specify only the data type, yielding **sparse tensors** because different records may contain varying numbers of items.

A **dense tensor** is a full rectangular block of values. A **sparse tensor** stores only the positions that actually have values, which is what you need when row 1 has two emails and row 2 has five — there is no rectangle to fill.

### 3 · The worked example

Consider a contact list stored in `my_contacts.tfrecord`. A feature description dictionary defines `name` as a fixed-length string feature, `id` as a fixed-length integer feature, and `emails` as a variable-length string feature.

When parsing a contact record, `name` returns a standard tensor like `b"Alice"`, while `emails` returns a sparse tensor containing values like `[b"a@b.com", b"c@d.com"]`.

Two ways to get at the sparse one: developers can access sparse values directly using the `.values` attribute or convert them using `tf.sparse.to_dense()`. `.values` is the cheaper habit when you only want the contents.

### 4 · Parse in batches, not one at a time

A key insight to remember is that fixed-length features produce dense tensors, while variable-length features produce sparse tensors, and using `tf.io.parse_example()` on batches is much more efficient than parsing individual examples one by one.

The two functions take the same description dictionary; the difference is only whether you hand them one serialized string or a batch of them. So the pipeline reads `TFRecordDataset(...).batch(2).map(parse)` — batch first, then parse — and one parsing call covers the whole batch.

This is the same instinct as preferring a set-based operation over a row-by-row loop: the per-call overhead is paid once instead of once per record.

**One-liner for your notes:** you parse an `Example` by describing it — `FixedLenFeature` for fixed shapes (dense tensors), `VarLenFeature` for variable lists (sparse tensors) — and you batch before parsing so `parse_example()` does a whole batch at once.

blocks.title: Parsing serialized TFRecord features

blocks.title: python example

items.term: Schema-on-read, and who owns the risk
items.text: The file carries no schema, so the description dictionary in your code is the schema — and nothing checks it against what was written. Declare the wrong type and you get an error; declare the wrong default and you get plausible wrong values with no error at all. The writer and the reader are two programs that must agree by convention, which is exactly the class of bug the preprocessing-layer lessons later in this chapter are trying to eliminate elsewhere.

items.term: Why a variable-length feature cannot be dense
items.text: A dense tensor is a rectangle, and a rectangle needs every row the same width. Rows with two emails and rows with five have no rectangle, so the parser returns positions-and-values instead. Converting to dense with `tf.sparse.to_dense()` forces the rectangle by padding to the longest row, which is fine for a few emails and ruinous when one row has ten thousand — the padding, not the data, becomes the memory cost.

items.term: Why batching before parsing is the bigger win
items.text: Each parse call carries fixed overhead: dispatching the op, reading the description, allocating outputs. Parsing one record at a time pays it per row; parsing a batch pays it per batch and lets the work vectorise. This is the same reason a set-based statement beats a row-by-row cursor, and it generalises — wherever a pipeline offers a batched version of an operation, the batched version is the default and the single version is for debugging.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Serialized Example protocol buffers in TFRecord files must be explicitly parsed into structured tensors.
FixedLenFeature specifies shape, type, and default value to create standard dense tensors.
VarLenFeature specifies only data type and creates sparse tensors for features with varying lengths.
Sparse tensors can be converted to dense tensors or accessed directly using the values attribute.
Parsing datasets in batches using tf.io.parse_example() is more performant than parsing single examples.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: `FixedLenFeature` takes a shape, and every example so far uses the empty shape `[]`. When would you pass a non-empty shape, and what does `FixedLenSequenceFeature` add on top?
Look up: the API documentation for `tf.io.parse_example` (tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/io/parse_example), which lists all four feature descriptor types and shows the output shapes each produces.

items.term: SequenceExample Protobuf

blocks.content:
`SequenceExample` is the protobuf for rows that contain lists of lists: a flat `context` part for the metadata and a `feature_lists` part for the sequences.

**The question this lesson answers:** a document has one author but many sentences, and each sentence has a different number of words. `Example` stores flat named features. Where do the nested lists go?

### The big picture

```
SequenceExample
 ├ context        author: "Alice"        (flat metadata)
 └ feature_lists
     └ "content" = FeatureList
          ├ Feature: [3, 14, 9]   sentence 1
          └ Feature: [2, 7]       sentence 2
```

### 1 · What `Example` cannot do comfortably

Standard dataset structures often struggle to represent complex nested sequences efficiently. When training models on text documents or video frames, a single instance might contain top-level metadata alongside sequences of variable-length lists.

The standard **Example** protocol buffer handles flat features well, but it becomes cumbersome when representing lists of lists, such as a document containing multiple sentences of varying word lengths.

You have met this shape before: it is a parent row with a child table hanging off it. Flattening it into one wide row means either padding to the longest child or losing the boundaries between children.

### 2 · Two compartments

To solve this problem, TensorFlow provides the **SequenceExample** protocol buffer. This structure separates high-level metadata from sequential data. It contains two main components: a **context** field for top-level scalar or fixed-length features, and a **feature_lists** field that maps names to sequences of features.

| Part | Holds | Analogue |
|---|---|---|
| `context` | one value per instance | the parent row |
| `feature_lists` | named sequences | the child rows, grouped |

This separation allows you to structure sequential data cleanly without flattening complex nested relationships into arbitrary representations.

### 3 · The layering, named precisely

Consider a text classification dataset where each document has an author name and a list of sentences, with each sentence represented as an array of word IDs.

The document author goes into the **context** dictionary as a standard feature. The document text goes into the **feature_lists** dictionary under the key `content`, whose value is one **FeatureList**: a list of **Feature** objects in which each **Feature** represents one sentence, for example as a list of word identifiers.

Read that chain once more, because the names are nearly identical and the difference matters: `feature_lists` is the *map* of names to sequences; a `FeatureList` is *one* named sequence; a `Feature` is *one element* of it — here, one sentence. A **word ID** is just an integer standing for a word, assigned from a vocabulary.

### 4 · Parsing, and what varying lengths give you

When parsing a serialized record, you define feature descriptions for both the context and the sequence portions, then call `tf.io.parse_single_sequence_example`. It returns two dictionaries, one per compartment, matching the two descriptions you supplied.

If sentences have different lengths, the resulting sparse tensor can be converted into a **RaggedTensor** for efficient training, using `tf.RaggedTensor.from_sparse`. A **ragged tensor** is a tensor whose rows are allowed to have different lengths — an array column, essentially — which is the natural home for sentences that genuinely are not the same size.

The main insight to remember is that you should use **SequenceExample** instead of standard **Example** protobufs whenever your data instances contain variable-length sequential features or nested lists.

**One-liner for your notes:** `SequenceExample` splits a record into `context` (the flat parent fields) and `feature_lists` (named sequences of `Feature`s), parsed with `tf.io.parse_single_sequence_example` and usually turned into ragged tensors.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
context, feature_lists = tf.io.parse_single_sequence_example(
    serialized_sequence_example,
    context_features=context_descriptions,
    sequence_features=sequence_descriptions
)
content = tf.RaggedTensor.from_sparse(feature_lists["content"])
```

items.term: Why separating context from sequence is the whole design
items.text: Every alternative flattens something that should not be flattened. Repeat the author on every sentence and you have denormalised a one-to-many relation into duplication. Pad every document to the longest one and you store mostly padding. Keeping the parent fields in `context` and the children in `feature_lists` preserves the grain of both, which is the same reason you keep a header table and a line-item table rather than one wide one.

items.term: Ragged versus padded, and when each wins
items.text: A ragged tensor stores real lengths; a padded dense tensor stores a rectangle plus a mask. Ragged wins on memory when lengths vary a lot, because nothing is stored for the gaps. Padded wins on speed when lengths are similar, because dense operations are better optimised. The deciding number is the ratio of the longest row to the typical one — if it is small, pad; if one document is a hundred times the median, do not.

items.term: Nesting has a floor
items.text: `SequenceExample` gives you exactly one level of nesting: a record holds named sequences of features. It does not give you sequences of sequences of sequences. Deeper structure has to be encoded — flattened with explicit offsets, or serialized into a `BytesList` — which means the format has an opinion about how deep your data should be before you restructure it.

blocks.title: Key points
items: The SequenceExample protobuf is designed to handle nested lists and sequence data efficiently.
Data is divided into a context object for global metadata and a feature_lists object for sequential features.
Parsing functions like tf.io.parse_single_sequence_example return separate dictionaries for context and sequence data.
Variable-length sequences can be converted into RaggedTensor objects after parsing.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Ragged tensors are introduced here as a conversion target, but they are a full tensor type with their own operations. Which ordinary tensor operations work on a ragged tensor, and which force you back to dense first?
Look up: the TensorFlow guide "Ragged tensors" (tensorflow.org/guide/ragged_tensor), particularly its list of supported ops and its comparison with sparse tensors.

items.term: Keras Preprocessing and Normalization Layers

blocks.content:
Putting the preprocessing inside the model means the model itself does the scaling, so training and production can never drift apart — because there is only one copy of the logic.

**The question this lesson answers:** your training script scales the features and your serving code scales them again, somewhere else. How do you stop those two from silently disagreeing?

### The big picture

```
train:   raw -> [Normalization] -> Dense -> loss
serve:   raw -> [Normalization] -> Dense -> prediction
         ^ one layer object, shipped inside the model
```

### 1 · The bug this prevents

When deploying machine learning models, separate preprocessing pipelines often cause **preprocessing mismatch**, where production code transforms raw data differently than training code did. Including preprocessing layers directly inside Keras models solves this issue by standardizing feature transformations across both training and serving environments.

You already know this failure: the same business rule written twice, in two jobs, and only one of them gets the fix. Here it is worse than a wrong number in a report. As the card below puts it, if you are lucky you get a clear bug; if not, the model's accuracy just silently degrades — nothing errors, the predictions merely get worse.

### 2 · The `Normalization` layer and `adapt()`

The **`Normalization` layer** standardizes numerical inputs by shifting their mean to 0 and variance to 1. **Variance** is the squared spread of a column; putting every feature on mean 0 and variance 1 means no feature dominates simply because its numbers are bigger.

To use it, instantiate the layer and call its `adapt()` method on a representative sample of training data. The layer computes and stores the mean and variance statistics automatically — you never type them in, and they become part of the saved model.

`adapt()` is a *measuring* step, not a training step: it looks at data and stores statistics. The sample must be large enough to be representative, but a few hundred instances randomly sampled from the training set are generally enough. Details in the card below.

### 3 · Two placements, and why you want both

Directly placing the `Normalization` layer inside the training model, as shown in **Figure 13-4**, handles transformations automatically during training and inference. However, performing this transformation on the fly during every training epoch adds processing overhead — the same scaling, recomputed once per epoch, for every row.

To optimize performance, preprocess the dataset once using the adapted layer offline, train the core neural network on the scaled features, and then construct a final sequential model combining both the normalization layer and trained network prior to production deployment (see **Figure 13-5**).

| Stage | What runs | Why |
|---|---|---|
| before training | `adapt()`, then scale once | pay the cost one time |
| training | plain network on scaled data | no per-epoch scaling |
| deployment | layer wrapped around the network | raw data in, prediction out |

In production, raw new data passes through the preprocessing layers first and only then enters the neural network, all inside the one exported model — which is what Figure 13-5 below shows.

This is the materialize-once pattern: precompute the transform for the heavy repeated reads, and keep the transform itself attached for the live path.

### 4 · Writing your own

If a preprocessing layer you need does not exist, you write one. The book's own example of a custom feature-scaling layer computes:

$$\text{scaled\_input} = \frac{\text{inputs} - \mathbf{\mu}}{\mathbf{\sigma} + \epsilon}$$

where $\mathbf{\mu}$ and $\mathbf{\sigma}$ denote the feature means and standard deviations, and $\epsilon$ represents a small constant preventing division by zero. The why-layer under the formula walks through every piece of it, including why the epsilon is there at all.

**One-liner for your notes:** a preprocessing layer measured with `adapt()` and shipped inside the model removes preprocessing mismatch — scale once before training for speed, then wrap the layer around the trained network for deployment.

blocks.title: How much data adapt() needs, and why mismatch hurts
blocks.content: The sample you pass to `adapt()` must be large enough to be representative of your dataset, but it does not have to be the full training set. For the `Normalization` layer, a few hundred instances randomly sampled from the training set are generally enough to estimate the feature means and variances well. Keeping the layer inside the model removes preprocessing mismatch, which happens when people maintain different preprocessing code for training and production, then update one and forget the other. The production model then receives data preprocessed in a way it does not expect. If they are lucky, they get a clear bug. If not, the model's accuracy just silently degrades.

blocks.caption: Including preprocessing layers inside a model

blocks.title: Figure 13-5
blocks.caption: Preprocessing the data just once before training using preprocessing layers, then

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
norm_layer = tf.keras.layers.Normalization()
norm_layer.adapt(X_train)

X_train_scaled = norm_layer(X_train)
X_valid_scaled = norm_layer(X_valid)

model = tf.keras.models.Sequential([tf.keras.layers.Dense(1)])
model.compile(loss="mse", optimizer=tf.keras.optimizers.SGD(learning_rate=2e-3))
model.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train, epochs=5, validation_data=(X_valid_scaled, y_valid))

final_model = tf.keras.Sequential([norm_layer, model])
y_pred = final_model(X_test[:3])
```

items.term: Three places preprocessing can live, and what each costs
items.text: In the data files: fastest at training time, but the transformation must be reimplemented for production and the files are frozen against the choices you made. In the `tf.data` pipeline: flexible and parallel, but again a separate implementation for serving. Inside the model: one implementation, travels with the exported artifact, at the cost of running on every inference call and inside the training loop. The chapter's final answer takes two of the three at once — scale once offline, then wrap the same adapted layer into the model.

items.term: Why silent degradation is the worst failure mode
items.text: A mismatch that raises an exception is cheap: you see it, you fix it. A mismatch that merely shifts the inputs produces a model that still returns numbers, still passes health checks, and is just worse — and nothing in the serving stack can tell you, because the serving stack has no idea what the training distribution looked like. Monitoring the distribution of incoming features, not just uptime, is the only thing that catches it.

items.term: adapt() is a fitted parameter, so it belongs to the training set
items.text: The mean and variance the layer stores are learned from data, which makes them part of the model even though no gradient ever touched them. They must be measured on training data only, and they must be saved with the model — a layer re-adapted on production data is a different model from the one you evaluated. This is the same rule as fitting a scaler on the training split and only ever transforming with it afterwards.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Integrating preprocessing layers directly into models prevents preprocessing mismatch between training and production.
The adapt() method calculates statistics like mean and variance on a representative sample of training data.
Preprocessing features once prior to model fitting accelerates training while retaining export capability.
Wrapping an adapted preprocessing layer with a trained model preserves seamless production deployment.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The chapter puts the preprocessing layer inside the exported model. What does that cost at serving time, and how does it interact with running the model somewhere that is not Python — on a mobile device, or behind a serving binary?
Look up: the Keras guide "Working with preprocessing layers" (keras.io), particularly its section on preprocessing during training versus inference and on exporting an end-to-end model.

items.term: The Discretization Layer in TensorFlow

blocks.content:
The `Discretization` layer turns a continuous number into a bucket index — it is bucketing, exactly like a `CASE WHEN` over value ranges, done inside the model.

**The question this lesson answers:** age is a number, but its effect on the target is not a straight line — young and old behave differently from the middle. How do you hand the model ranges instead of raw values?

### The big picture

```
  -inf ......... 18 ......... 50 ......... +inf
      bin 0          bin 1         bin 2
```

Two boundaries produce three bins. N boundaries produce N + 1 bins.

### 1 · Why bucket a number at all

Numerical features in machine learning datasets often exhibit complex non-linear relationships with the target variable or possess **multimodal distributions**. A multimodal distribution is one with more than one cluster — two or three humps rather than a single peak.

In these scenarios, treating raw continuous values directly can make it difficult for a model to learn patterns effectively. The **Discretization layer** solves this problem by dividing a continuous numerical range into distinct sub-ranges called **bins** and mapping each bin to an integer category.

The trade is deliberate: you give up the fine detail inside a bin and gain the freedom for each bin to behave completely differently from its neighbours.

### 2 · Two ways to get the boundaries

This layer operates in one of two modes.

| Mode | You supply | Boundaries come from |
|---|---|---|
| explicit | `bin_boundaries` | your own domain knowledge |
| adapted | `num_bins` + `adapt()` | value percentiles in the data |

You can explicitly pass predefined continuous boundaries using the `bin_boundaries` argument. Alternatively, you can specify the total number of bins using `num_bins` and call the `adapt()` method on your dataset. When adapted, the layer computes boundaries automatically based on data **percentiles** so that each bin contains roughly an equal share of data points.

A percentile is the value below which a given share of the data falls, so this is quantile bucketing — the `NTILE` idea. Use explicit boundaries when 18 and 50 mean something real; use `num_bins` when you only want balanced buckets.

### 3 · The worked example

Consider a concrete example where we have a feature representing ages: 10, 93, 57, 18, 37, and 5.

If we instantiate a `Discretization` layer with `bin_boundaries=[18., 50.]`, TensorFlow creates three bins: values strictly below 18 map to index 0, values from 18 up to 50 map to index 1, and values of 50 or above map to index 2.

Passing our age data through this configured layer yields the integer category tensor `[[0], [2], [2], [1], [1], [0]]`. Check one: the fourth value is exactly 18.0, and it lands in bin 1, because the lower edge is included and the upper edge is not. Boundary behaviour is the thing to test first on any bucketing scheme, yours or a library's.

### 4 · The output is a label, not a number

The key insight to remember is that these discretized integer outputs represent unordered or non-proportionally scaled categories, meaning they should generally be encoded into representations like **one-hot vectors** before being passed deeper into a neural network.

A one-hot vector is a row of zeros with a single 1 marking which category applies. The reason you need it: bin 2 is not "twice" bin 1, and the gap from bin 0 to bin 1 is not the same size as the gap from bin 1 to bin 2. Feed the raw integers in and the model will assume an ordering and a spacing that the bins never had. Next lesson does the encoding.

**One-liner for your notes:** `Discretization` maps continuous values into bins — boundaries either given by you or found from percentiles by `adapt()` — and the resulting integers are category labels that must be encoded before the network sees them.
