blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

age = tf.constant([[10.], [93.], [57.], [18.], [37.], [5.]])

# Option 1: Manual bin boundaries
discretize_layer = tf.keras.layers.Discretization(bin_boundaries=[18., 50.])
age_categories = discretize_layer(age)

# Option 2: Automatic percentile boundaries
auto_layer = tf.keras.layers.Discretization(num_bins=3)
auto_layer.adapt(age)
auto_categories = auto_layer(age)
```

items.term: What you give up by bucketing
items.text: Inside a bin, every value becomes identical — a 19-year-old and a 49-year-old are the same input. You trade resolution for freedom: the model can now learn a completely different response per bin instead of being forced onto one smooth curve. That is a good trade when the relationship really has steps or humps in it, and a bad one when it was close to smooth, because you have thrown away information the model could have used.

items.term: Fixed boundaries versus percentile boundaries
items.text: Given boundaries encode domain meaning (18 is adulthood) and stay stable when the data shifts. Percentile boundaries balance the bin populations, which keeps every bin statistically useful, but they are measured from your sample — re-adapt on different data and the same input can land in a different bin. Stability against balance: pick the one whose failure you can live with, and never silently re-adapt in production.

items.term: Why the integers are not a scale
items.text: Bin 2 is not twice bin 1, and the distance from bin 0 to bin 1 is not the same quantity as from bin 1 to bin 2 — the bins may not even be the same width. Feeding the raw indices to a network asserts an order and an even spacing that do not exist, and the model will fit to that fiction. The same mistake is encoding country as 1, 2, 3 and letting a model average them.

blocks.title: Key points
items: The Discretization layer converts continuous numerical features into discrete categorical bin indices.
Bin boundaries can be manually set using bin_boundaries or computed automatically with num_bins and adapt().
Automatic adaptation places boundaries at specific value percentiles to balance data distribution across bins.
Output category integers should be further encoded, such as with one-hot vectors, before network input.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The layer can also learn boundaries from percentiles with `adapt()`. How does it compute those percentiles on a dataset too large to sort, and how exact is the answer?
Look up: the Keras API documentation for the `Discretization` layer (keras.io), which names the streaming quantile estimation it uses and its `epsilon` accuracy parameter.

items.term: The CategoryEncoding Layer

blocks.content:
`CategoryEncoding` turns category integers into indicator vectors — one-hot for a single feature, multi-hot when you pass several at once, and that default quietly loses which feature a category came from.

**The question this lesson answers:** you have bin indices 0, 1 and 2 from the last lesson. How do you present them to a network so it does not read them as ordered numbers — and what breaks when you encode two such features together?

### The big picture

| Input | `num_tokens=3`, default | `output_mode="count"` |
|---|---|---|
| `[1, 0]` | `[1., 1., 0.]` | `[1., 1., 0.]` |
| `[2, 2]` | `[0., 0., 1.]` | `[0., 0., 2.]` |

### 1 · Why encode at all

Machine learning models require numerical input representations rather than raw integer identifiers that imply false ordinal relationships. **Ordinal** means the values carry a real order and spacing; category IDs do not.

When dealing with categorical integer features containing only a few distinct values, **one-hot encoding** converts each categorical integer into a binary vector where a single element is set to 1 and all others are set to 0. The Keras **CategoryEncoding** layer performs this preprocessing step directly within a model pipeline.

If you have written a pivot that turns a status column into one indicator column per status, you have built this by hand. `num_tokens` is how many columns the pivot has.

### 2 · What happens with more than one feature

To encode a single feature, the layer takes integer categories and maps them to binary vectors determined by the `num_tokens` parameter.

When multiple categorical features using the same set of categories are passed together into a single **CategoryEncoding** layer, the layer performs **multi-hot encoding** by default. In multi-hot encoding, the resulting output vector contains a 1 for every category present across any of the input features.

Alternatively, setting `output_mode="count"` records the frequency of occurrence for each category rather than binary indicators.

### 3 · The information that gets lost

Consider an input array containing two categorical features for three samples, represented as `[[1, 0], [2, 2], [2, 0]]`.

If processed directly with `num_tokens=3`, multi-hot encoding loses feature identity because inputs `[1, 0]` and `[0, 1]` produce identical vectors of `[1., 1., 0.]`. Both say "category 0 is present somewhere and category 1 is present somewhere" — and that is all the vector can say.

Furthermore, the second sample `[2, 2]` produces `[0., 0., 1.]` under multi-hot encoding, but under `output_mode="count"`, it yields `[0., 0., 2.]`. Count mode recovers *how many*, but still not *which feature*.

This is the collision you get from a `UNION` of two keyspaces that share values: the rows merge and you can no longer tell which source a key came from.

### 4 · The fix: give each feature its own range

To preserve distinct feature identities, offset the second feature's indices by adding 3 (`two_age_categories + [0, 3]`) and set `num_tokens=6`. Processing this modified input produces 6-dimensional vectors like `[0., 1., 0., 1., 0., 0.]` for `[1, 0]`, keeping both features distinguishable.

Columns 0 to 2 now belong to the first feature and columns 3 to 5 to the second — you have namespaced the keys before merging them. The card below works the arithmetic through.

The key insight is that while multi-hot encoding reduces vector dimensionality, offsetting feature category identifiers prevents information loss by preserving which specific feature produced each category. The cost is more features fed to the model, and therefore more model parameters. Which one wins depends on the task, so it is worth testing both.

**One-liner for your notes:** `CategoryEncoding` one-hots a single feature and multi-hots several at once, which loses which feature each category came from — offset the second feature's IDs and widen `num_tokens` to keep them apart.

blocks.title: Worked out: offsetting the second feature
blocks.content: Take the samples `[[1, 0], [2, 2], [2, 0]]`, where both features use categories 0, 1 and 2. Adding `[0, 3]` leaves the first feature as it is and adds 3 to the second, giving `[[1, 3], [2, 5], [2, 3]]`. With `num_tokens=3 + 3`, columns 0 to 2 belong to the first feature and columns 3 to 5 to the second. The sample `[1, 0]` becomes `[1, 3]`, so a 1 goes in columns 1 and 3: `[0., 1., 0., 1., 0., 0.]`. By the same rule, `[0, 1]` becomes `[0, 4]` and is encoded as `[1., 0., 0., 0., 1., 0.]`, so the two samples no longer collide. The cost is that more features are fed to the model, which requires more model parameters.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf

two_age_categories = np.array([[1, 0], [2, 2], [2, 0]])
onehot_layer = tf.keras.layers.CategoryEncoding(num_tokens=6)
encoded = onehot_layer(two_age_categories + [0, 3])
```

items.term: Why a default that loses information is still a reasonable default
items.text: Multi-hot is compact: two features sharing three categories fit in three columns instead of six. When the features genuinely are interchangeable — a set of tags, a basket of products — the shared vector is the right representation and the 'lost' identity was never meaningful. The failure only appears when the features are distinct roles that happen to share a vocabulary, and only you know which case you are in.

items.term: Offsetting versus encoding separately
items.text: Encoding each feature on its own and concatenating the results gives exactly the same vector as offsetting the IDs and encoding once. Two routes, one destination — which is worth noticing, because it means the choice is about code clarity and not about the model. Offsetting is fewer layers; separate encoding is harder to get wrong when the features have different vocabularies.

items.term: Counting is a third representation, not a variant of the second
items.text: Multi-hot answers 'is this category present', count answers 'how many times'. They differ only when a category can repeat within one instance, which is precisely the case where the repetition carries information — three purchases of the same item is not the same event as one. Choosing between them is choosing whether multiplicity matters for your task, and no default can know that.

blocks.title: Key points
items: The CategoryEncoding layer converts integer categorical features into one-hot, multi-hot, or count representations.
Passing multiple features to the layer by default triggers multi-hot encoding, placing a 1 for any active category.
Setting output_mode="count" outputs the number of occurrences of each category in the input.
Multi-hot encoding loses information about which specific feature contained a given category value.
Adding index offsets to separate features avoids information loss at the cost of expanding the output dimensionality.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: One-hot is recommended when there are only a few categories — the chapter says less than a dozen or two. Where is the real crossover point to an embedding, and what determines it besides the raw count of categories?
Look up: the Keras API documentation for the `CategoryEncoding` layer (keras.io) for its output modes, then compare with the `Embedding` layer's guidance on vocabulary size and output dimension.

items.term: Categorical Encoding with StringLookup

blocks.content:
`StringLookup` builds a vocabulary from your training text and maps each string to an integer — a surrogate-key lookup, with a dedicated slot for anything it has never seen.

**The question this lesson answers:** the city column holds "Paris", "Auckland", "San Francisco". The model needs numbers. What number does each city get, and what happens the first time "Montreal" shows up in production?

### The big picture

| String | Index | Why |
|---|---|---|
| unknown | 0 | out-of-vocabulary slot |
| "Paris" | 1 | most frequent known category |
| "San Francisco" | 2 | next |
| "Auckland" | 3 | next |

### 1 · Adapting builds the dimension table

Machine learning models require numerical input, but real-world datasets often contain categorical features represented as text strings, such as names of cities or product categories. To make this text readable by a model, the Keras **StringLookup** layer converts text strings into integer indices or one-hot encoded vectors.

To use this layer, you first instantiate it and pass your training dataset to its `adapt()` method. During adaptation, the layer inspects the dataset to identify all unique string categories and ranks them by frequency.

This is a dimension table being built and surrogate keys handed out — except the key order is not arbitrary. By default, the most frequent known category receives integer index 1, the next receives index 2, and so on. Sorting by frequency is what lets you later truncate a vocabulary to the top N and know you kept the rows that matter.

### 2 · The unknown slot

Any unknown or **out-of-vocabulary** string encountered during inference is mapped to the index 0. Out-of-vocabulary, usually shortened to OOV, means simply: not in the vocabulary the layer learned.

This is the part a lookup table in a warehouse usually gets wrong — a join that silently drops the row. Here it cannot drop anything: an unrecognized string still gets an index, so the model always receives a value.

If you configure the layer with `output_mode="one_hot"`, it instead returns a binary vector representing the corresponding category index, saving you a separate encoding step.

### 3 · The worked example

Consider a training list of cities containing `["Auckland", "Paris", "Paris", "San Francisco"]`. When adapted, the layer identifies "Paris" as the most frequent category and assigns it index 1, while "Auckland" receives index 3.

If you pass `["Paris", "Auckland", "Montreal"]` into the layer, "Paris" becomes index 1, "Auckland" becomes index 3, and the unseen city "Montreal" is assigned the out-of-vocabulary index 0.

### 4 · More than one unknown bucket

When training on massive datasets, you might adapt the layer on a small subset, missing some rare categories. Every one of those then collapses into index 0, and the model cannot tell a missing rare city from any other missing rare city.

To prevent all unseen items from collapsing into a single index, you can increase `num_oov_indices`. This uses a **hashing trick** to distribute unknown strings pseudorandomly across multiple out-of-vocabulary buckets — a hash function on the string, taken modulo the number of buckets, so the same string always lands in the same bucket.

It is a partial fix, not a cure. Two unknown strings can still land in the same bucket — a **hashing collision** — and more buckets means more categories, more RAM and more model parameters once they are one-hot encoded. The card below works through the book's five-bucket run, where "Foo" and "Baz" collide.

**One-liner for your notes:** `StringLookup` adapts a frequency-ranked vocabulary (index 1 upwards) and sends anything unseen to the OOV index 0, with `num_oov_indices` buying extra unknown buckets at the price of more categories.

blocks.title: Worked out: five OOV buckets
blocks.content: Adapt `StringLookup(num_oov_indices=5)` to the same cities. The five out-of-vocabulary buckets take the IDs below 5, so the first known category's ID is now 5: "Paris" is encoded as 5 and "Auckland" as 7. The strings "Foo", "Bar" and "Baz" are all unknown, and they are encoded as 4, 3 and 4. "Bar" gets its own bucket (ID 3), but "Foo" and "Baz" land in the same bucket (ID 4), so the model cannot tell them apart. This is called a hashing collision. The only way to reduce the risk is to use more OOV buckets, but that also increases the total number of categories, which needs more RAM and extra model parameters once the categories are one-hot encoded.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

cities = ["Auckland", "Paris", "Paris", "San Francisco"]

str_lookup_layer = tf.keras.layers.StringLookup(output_mode="one_hot")
str_lookup_layer.adapt(cities)

input_cities = [["Paris"], ["Auckland"], ["Montreal"]]
output_tensor = str_lookup_layer(input_cities)
print(output_tensor)
```

items.term: Why frequency order is not an arbitrary choice
items.text: Ranking by frequency means the low indices are the common categories, so truncating the vocabulary to the first N keeps the ones that carry most of the data. It also makes the vocabulary stable under resampling: adapt on a different subset and the top entries almost certainly keep the same ranks, while the tail shuffles. Alphabetical order would give neither property.

items.term: The unknown bucket is a design decision about production, not training
items.text: During training there are no unknown categories — the vocabulary came from that data. Index 0 exists entirely for the day a value appears that nobody has seen, and it means the model produces something rather than failing. Whether 'something' is acceptable is a question about your task: a shrug is fine for a recommendation and not fine for a decision with consequences, in which case the unknown should be detected and routed, not silently encoded.

items.term: Hashing trades a known failure for an unknown one
items.text: More OOV buckets means fewer collisions, more categories, more parameters and more memory. But note what the failure looks like: with one bucket every rare category is confused with every other, which you can reason about; with several, two specific strings collide unpredictably and you will not know which. Hashing does not remove the collision risk, it only makes it rarer and harder to predict — the usual bargain whenever a hash replaces a lookup.

blocks.title: Key points
items: The StringLookup layer converts categorical text strings into numerical indices or one-hot vectors.
Known categories are assigned positive integers based on their frequency in the adapted dataset.
Unseen categories are assigned to out-of-vocabulary indices, which default to index 0.
Setting output_mode to one_hot transforms category indices directly into binary vector representations.
Increasing num_oov_indices uses hashing to split unknown categories across multiple out-of-vocabulary buckets.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The chapter mentions adapting on a subset of a very large training set. How do you decide how much of the vocabulary you are willing to miss, and what does `max_tokens` do to the tail you keep?
Look up: the Keras API documentation for the `StringLookup` layer (keras.io), particularly `max_tokens`, `num_oov_indices` and the `vocabulary` argument for supplying a vocabulary directly.

items.term: Encoding Categorical Features Using Embeddings

blocks.content:
An embedding is a small dense vector per category, stored in a trainable lookup table — so instead of 50,000 mostly-empty columns you get, say, two columns whose values the training run itself works out.

**The question this lesson answers:** one-hot encoding is fine for three cities. What do you do for 50,000 categories, and how does the model end up knowing that two of them are similar?

### The big picture

| Approach | Vector | Cost | Collisions |
|---|---|---|---|
| one-hot | 50,000 wide, mostly zeros | huge | none |
| hash buckets | small, fixed | low | yes |
| embedding | small and dense, learned | low | none |

### 1 · Why one-hot stops working

High-cardinality categorical features cause severe memory inefficiency when processed with one-hot encoding. For instance, a vocabulary of 50,000 categories creates massive, sparse vectors filled mostly with zeros. **Sparse** here just means almost every entry is 0.

Alternative methods like hash buckets avoid memory growth but introduce hash collisions, mapping distinct categories to identical integer IDs. That is the `Hashing` layer's bargain — and its own upside, recorded in the card below, is that it needs no `adapt()` step at all, which matters when the dataset is too big to fit in memory.

### 2 · The lookup table that learns

An **embedding** solves this problem by mapping each category to a low-dimensional, dense floating-point vector.

The `tf.keras.layers.Embedding` layer maintains a trainable **weight matrix** where each row represents a category ID and each column represents an embedding dimension. Look up the row for a category and that row *is* the encoding — nothing is computed, it is indexed.

Two things make it different from an ordinary dimension table:

1. Upon initialization, vector values are randomly assigned. The table starts as noise.
2. During backpropagation, gradient descent updates these weight vectors alongside the neural network parameters. The table is *edited by training*, like any other model parameter. **Backpropagation** is the pass that assigns blame for the error back through the model; **gradient descent** is the step that then nudges every value in the direction that reduces it.

### 3 · What training does to the vectors

As a result, the model performs **representation learning**, automatically placing semantically related categories near each other in vector space.

Consider an example using California housing ocean-proximity categories. Initially, "NEAR BAY" and "NEAR OCEAN" receive distinct random 2D vectors such as `[0.131, 0.890]` and `[0.631, 0.791]`.

As Figure 13-6 shows, training iteratively shifts these vectors closer together because both categories share similar impacts on housing prices, while moving them further away from the "INLAND" vector.

Nothing told the model that two of those categories are alike. It moved them together because doing so lowered the error — the similarity is a *consequence* of the prediction task, not an input to it. Figure 13-7 below shows the same effect for words.

### 4 · Wiring it up

To implement this in TensorFlow, categorical strings are first mapped to integer IDs using a `StringLookup` layer, and those IDs are subsequently passed to an `Embedding` layer within a `Sequential` pipeline. `StringLookup` does the text-to-ID step because `Embedding` indexes by integer and nothing else; `vocabulary_size()` gives the row count the embedding matrix needs.

One equivalence worth carrying: one-hot encoding followed by a `Dense` layer with no activation function and no biases is mathematically the same function as an `Embedding` layer, because a matrix multiplication against a one-hot vector *is* a row lookup. The `Embedding` layer simply avoids the multiplications by zero, and the card below gives the sizes.

The key insight is that an **Embedding** layer functions as a trainable lookup table that compresses sparse categorical data into dense vectors while capturing semantic relationships.

**One-liner for your notes:** an `Embedding` is a trainable lookup table of small dense vectors, chained after `StringLookup`, and gradient descent is what pulls similar categories together in that space.

blocks.title: Embedding versus one-hot plus Dense
blocks.content: One-hot encoding followed by a `Dense` layer with no activation function and no biases is equivalent to an `Embedding` layer: the `Dense` layer's weight matrix plays the role of the embedding matrix. For example, one-hot vectors of size 20 fed to a `Dense` layer with 10 units are equivalent to an `Embedding` layer with `input_dim=20` and `output_dim=10`. The `Embedding` layer uses far fewer computations, because it avoids many multiplications by zero, and the difference becomes clear as the embedding matrix grows. As for the `Hashing` layer, its benefit is that it needs no `adapt()` step at all, which is useful in an out-of-core setting, when the dataset is too large to fit in memory.

blocks.caption: Embeddings will gradually improve during training

blocks.title: Figure 13-7
blocks.caption: Word embeddings of similar words tend to be close, and some axes seem to encode
blocks.alt: Figure 13-7: Word embeddings of similar words tend to be close, and some axes seem to encode

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf
import numpy as np

ocean_prox = ["<1H OCEAN", "INLAND", "NEAR OCEAN", "NEAR BAY", "ISLAND"]
str_lookup_layer = tf.keras.layers.StringLookup()
str_lookup_layer.adapt(ocean_prox)

lookup_and_embed = tf.keras.Sequential([
    str_lookup_layer,
    tf.keras.layers.Embedding(input_dim=str_lookup_layer.vocabulary_size(),
                              output_dim=2)
])

lookup_and_embed(np.array([["<1H OCEAN"], ["ISLAND"]]))
```

items.term: Why the vectors move at all
items.text: Nothing in the setup says two categories are similar. The embedding rows are parameters like any other, and gradient descent moves each one in whatever direction reduces the error. If two categories need the same downstream behaviour, the cheapest way for training to get it is to give them similar vectors — so the similarity is an output of the prediction task, not an input to it. Change the target and the same categories can end up arranged completely differently.

items.term: Choosing the number of dimensions
items.text: Too few and unrelated categories are forced to share space they cannot both use; too many and each category gets enough room to be memorised, which is overfitting with extra steps. The book's own note draws one hard line: it is wasteful to use more embedding dimensions than the number of units in the layer that follows, because the following layer cannot pass on more than that anyway. Otherwise it is a hyperparameter you tune.

items.term: What an embedding cannot do that one-hot can
items.text: One-hot is exact and requires no training: every category is equidistant from every other, and nothing is ever confused. An embedding starts as noise and is only useful after training, which means it needs enough examples of each category to learn anything. A category seen three times ends up with an essentially random vector — worse than a one-hot column, not better. Embeddings pay off with many categories and plenty of data, which is exactly when one-hot stops being affordable.

blocks.title: Key points
items: One-hot encoding creates high-dimensional sparse vectors, whereas embeddings create dense, lower-dimensional representations.
The Keras Hashing layer hashes categories into fixed bins without adaptation, but it risks hash collisions.
Embedding layers wrap a weight matrix that gets updated via gradient descent during training.
Trainable embeddings group similar categories close together in the embedding space to improve prediction accuracy.
Chaining StringLookup and Embedding layers enables direct ingestion of raw categorical text features into neural networks.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The chapter says embeddings of similar categories end up near each other. How would you actually verify that on a trained model, rather than taking the figure on trust?

Look up: Tomáš Mikolov et al., "Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and Their Compositionality", Proceedings of the 26th International Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems 2 (2013): 3111–3119 — the paper the book cites for word embeddings.

items.term: Text Preprocessing with TextVectorization in Keras

blocks.content:
`TextVectorization` does the whole text-to-numbers job in one layer: clean the string, split it into words, learn a vocabulary, then emit either word IDs or weighted counts.

**The question this lesson answers:** a review arrives as the string "Question: be or be?". What sequence of numbers does the model actually see, and what does the choice of `output_mode` change about it?

### The big picture

```
"Question: be or be?"
  -> standardize   "question be or be"
  -> split         ["question","be","or","be"]
  -> vocabulary    integer IDs, or TF-IDF weights
```

### 1 · The four steps

Machine learning models cannot directly process raw text strings, so raw sentences must be converted into numerical representations before training. The `TextVectorization` layer in Keras solves this problem by standardizing text, splitting sentences into tokens, building a vocabulary, and converting words into integer indices or numerical vectors.

A **token** is one unit of text — here, one word. To prepare text, the layer standardizes inputs by default by converting text to lowercase and stripping punctuation. It then splits sentences on whitespace to extract individual words. So "Be", "be," and "be?" all become the same token.

Calling the `adapt()` method allows the layer to learn a vocabulary from training sentences, sorting words by frequency — the same frequency ranking `StringLookup` uses.

### 2 · The reserved indices

During transformation, index 0 is reserved for padding shorter sequences, index 1 represents out-of-vocabulary unknown words, and frequent words receive lower integer indices starting from 2.

| Index | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | padding |
| 1 | unknown word |
| 2 and up | known words, most frequent first |

**Padding** exists because a batch has to be one rectangular tensor: every row must be the same length, so short sentences are filled out with 0s until they match the longest one in the batch.

### 3 · TF-IDF: counting, but weighted

Counting words has an obvious flaw — "to" and "the" appear everywhere and tell you almost nothing. Setting the `output_mode` argument to `tf_idf` scales word occurrences using **term-frequency times inverse-document-frequency** weights, which reduces the influence of common words like 'to' while emphasizing informative rare words.

Read the name literally: term frequency is how often the word appears *in this sentence*; inverse document frequency is how rare it is *across the training sentences*. Multiply them.

Consider training on four sentences, so the total number of documents is d = 4, where a **document** is one training sentence. The word 'be' appears in f = 3 training sentences, where f counts how many training sentences contain the word.

The Keras formula is count × log(1 + d / (f + 1)). Converting the sentence 'Question: be or be?', the word 'be' appears twice, so it receives an encoding value of 2 × log(1 + 4 / (1 + 3)) ≈ 1.386. The rare word 'question' appears only once in training, so f = 1, and its single occurrence receives a weight of 1 × log(1 + 4 / (1 + 1)) ≈ 1.098.

Look at what that comparison shows: 'be' occurred **twice** in the sentence and 'question' only once, yet their weights are close — because 'question' is rare, its one appearance is worth nearly as much as two appearances of a common word. That is the whole point of the formula, and the why-layer below breaks down every piece of it.

### 4 · What it cannot do

The primary insight to remember is that `TextVectorization` provides a fast way to map raw text to numerical inputs, but **bag-of-words** outputs like TF-IDF lose word order entirely. Bag-of-words means exactly that: a bag, not a sequence. "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" produce the same vector.

The related limits are worth knowing now: it only works where words are separated by spaces, it cannot separate **homonyms** (the same spelling with different meanings, like "bear"), and it gives the model no hint that "evolution" and "evolutionary" are related.

**One-liner for your notes:** `TextVectorization` lowercases, strips punctuation, splits on whitespace and maps words to frequency-ranked IDs (0 padding, 1 unknown) — or to TF-IDF weights, which upweight rare words but throw word order away.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

train_data = ["To be", "!(to be)", "That's the question", "Be, be, be."]

# Instantiate and adapt layer for integer encoding
text_vec_layer = tf.keras.layers.TextVectorization()
text_vec_layer.adapt(train_data)

# Vectorize new input sentences
outputs = text_vec_layer(["Be good!", "Question: be or be?"])
print(outputs)
```

items.term: Standardization is a lossy decision made for you
items.text: Lowercasing and stripping punctuation are defaults, and both throw information away. Case distinguishes a proper noun from a common one; punctuation carries sentence boundaries and, in some tasks, sentiment. The defaults are right for topic classification and wrong for named-entity work, which is why `standardize=None` exists. The general point: any text pipeline's first step is a modelling decision wearing the costume of a cleanup step.

items.term: Why rarity is worth more than repetition
items.text: TF-IDF's whole claim is that a word appearing in every document cannot help you tell documents apart, no matter how often it occurs. That is an information argument, not a linguistic one, and it generalises well beyond text — the same reasoning says a column with one distinct value is useless as a feature, however many rows it has. The risk is the mirror image: a word appearing once, in one document, gets a high weight and may be a typo.

items.term: What losing word order actually costs
items.text: Bag-of-words models cannot represent negation, sequence or relation: 'not good' and 'good not' are the same input, and so are 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog'. For topic-level tasks that rarely matters, because topic lives in which words appear. For anything where meaning depends on arrangement, it is fatal, and no amount of weighting fixes it — you need a model that reads a sequence, which is what later chapters build.

blocks.title: Key points
items: The TextVectorization layer converts raw strings into integer sequences or numerical vectors for neural networks.
Calling adapt() learns vocabulary frequencies from training data while standardizing text to lowercase and removing punctuation.
Index 0 is used for sequence padding and index 1 is reserved for unknown out-of-vocabulary words.
Setting output_mode to 'tf_idf' downweights highly frequent words and upweights rare, informative terms.
Standard word-level vectorizations lose word order and cannot separate homonyms or subword relationships.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The chapter notes this approach cannot tell that 'evolution' and 'evolutionary' are related, and points at subword tokenizers as one answer. How does a subword vocabulary get built, and what does it do with a word it has never seen?
Look up: the TensorFlow Text guide "Subword tokenizers" (tensorflow.org/text/guide/subwords_tokenizer), which builds a WordPiece vocabulary from a dataset step by step.

items.term: Using Pretrained Language Models with TensorFlow Hub

blocks.content:
TensorFlow Hub lets you drop somebody else's already-trained text encoder into your model as a single Keras layer, and use it without training it.

**The question this lesson answers:** learning good representations of English takes a corpus and a compute budget you do not have. How do you get a sentence turned into a useful vector without training anything yourself?

### The big picture

```
raw text -> hub.KerasLayer (pretrained, frozen)
         -> 50-dim sentence vector
         -> your own Dense layers (these you train)
```

### 1 · Reuse instead of rebuild

Building natural language processing models from scratch requires massive computational resources and huge text datasets to learn meaningful representations of human language.

To solve this issue, developers can reuse **pretrained model components**, often called **modules**, that were previously trained on vast amounts of data by domain experts. The **TensorFlow Hub** library provides an online repository of these reusable components, enabling developers to easily download and integrate pretrained features directly into their neural networks.

This is dependency reuse, the ordinary kind: you would not write your own compression codec either. The difference is that the artifact here is learned weights rather than code, so you inherit the data it was trained on along with its behaviour.

### 2 · What the wrapper does

When you import a module using the `hub.KerasLayer` construct, TensorFlow Hub automatically downloads the pretrained assets and wraps them into a usable Keras layer. From that point it behaves like any other layer — it goes in a `Sequential` or a functional model with no special handling.

These modules typically bundle both text preprocessing logic and learned model weights. Consequently, the pretrained module itself generally requires no extra training, while the remaining custom layers of your model are trained normally on your specific target task.

That split is the practical shape of the technique:

| Part | Trained by | When |
|---|---|---|
| the module | its authors | already done |
| your layers on top | you | on your task |

### 3 · A concrete module

Consider the basic `nnlm-en-dim50/2` module hosted on TensorFlow Hub. This sentence encoder takes raw text strings as input and produces 50-dimensional **sentence embeddings** as output — one vector standing for a whole sentence, the same idea as the category embeddings two lessons back but one level up.

Internally, it parses each input string by splitting words on spaces, maps each word to an embedding vector using a matrix pretrained on the seven-billion-word Google News corpus, and averages those word vectors together.

Passing the batch `["To be", "Not to be"]` into this layer immediately yields a numerical array containing two 50-dimensional vectors, such as `[-0.25, 0.28, ...]` for the first phrase. No `adapt()`, no `fit()`, no vocabulary of your own.

The averaging step is worth noticing, because it inherits the limitation from the previous lesson: averaging word vectors discards word order, so "To be" and "be To" encode identically. The card below gives the book's precise rule, which is slightly more than a plain mean.

### 4 · What you actually get

The single most important insight to remember is that wrapping **pretrained modules** inside a `hub.KerasLayer` allows you to immediately convert raw text into high-quality semantic representations without needing to train the text encoder yourself.

"High-quality" is relative — this particular module is a fairly basic one, chosen because it is small. The heavyweight language models on Hub run to several gigabytes.

**One-liner for your notes:** `hub.KerasLayer` downloads a pretrained module and makes it an ordinary Keras layer — `nnlm-en-dim50/2` turns a raw sentence into a 50-dimensional vector by averaging Google-News-pretrained word embeddings, and needs no training from you.

blocks.title: The exact sentence embedding
blocks.content: The main text describes the sentence embedding of `nnlm-en-dim50` as the mean of the word embeddings, and a footnote in the book gives the precise rule. The sentence embedding is the mean word embedding multiplied by the square root of the number of words in the sentence. This compensates for the fact that the mean of n random vectors gets shorter as n grows.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf
import tensorflow_hub as hub

hub_layer = hub.KerasLayer("https://tfhub.dev/google/nnlm-en-dim50/2")
sentences = tf.constant(["To be", "Not to be"])
sentence_embeddings = hub_layer(sentences)
print(sentence_embeddings.numpy().round(2))
```

items.term: What you inherit along with the weights
items.text: A pretrained module brings its training corpus with it — its vocabulary, its register, its assumptions, and its biases. Google News is edited English from a particular period, so the module will do well on prose that resembles it and poorly on code, chat, dialect or another language. That is not a defect to be patched; it is the scope of the artifact, and the question to ask before reusing any pretrained component is which corpus produced it.

items.term: Frozen versus fine-tuned
items.text: The module requires no extra training, which is the fast path: its weights stay fixed and you train only the layers you added. Unfreezing it and letting training adjust it too can do better when your domain is far from the original corpus, at the cost of far more compute and the risk of destroying what made it useful with too large a learning rate. Frozen first is the sensible default, and the decision is measurable rather than a matter of taste.

items.term: An embedding of a sentence is a compression, and compression discards
items.text: One 50-dimensional vector has to stand for a whole sentence, so almost everything is thrown away by construction. Averaging word vectors discards order entirely — the same limitation as the bag-of-words encoding from the previous lesson, arrived at by a different route. It is enough for 'are these two sentences about the same thing', and nowhere near enough for anything that depends on who did what to whom.

blocks.title: Key points
items: TensorFlow Hub provides reusable pretrained model components called modules.
The `hub.KerasLayer` wrapper automatically downloads modules and integrates them into Keras models.
Pretrained modules combine preprocessing logic with trained weights, requiring no extra training.
The `nnlm-en-dim50` module converts raw sentences into 50-dimensional vectors by averaging word embeddings.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The book's footnote says this module's sentence embedding is the mean word embedding multiplied by the square root of the word count, to compensate for the mean of n random vectors getting shorter as n grows. Why does that shrinking happen, and what would go wrong in a model if it were not corrected?
Look up: the model page for `nnlm-en-dim50` on the TensorFlow Hub / Kaggle Models catalogue, which documents the module's architecture and preprocessing.

items.term: Keras Image Preprocessing Layers

blocks.content:
Keras ships layers that make images uniform — same height and width, pixel values on a sensible numeric range — plus augmentation layers that randomly vary the training images only.

**The question this lesson answers:** the image files are all different sizes and their pixels are integers from 0 to 255. What has to happen before a network can take them, and what can you add to squeeze more out of a small training set?

### The big picture

| Layer | Fixes |
|---|---|
| `Resizing` | height and width |
| `CenterCrop` | height and width, keeping the middle |
| `Rescaling` | the numeric range of the pixels |
| `RandomFlip`, `RandomRotation` | too little training variety |

### 1 · Two problems with a raw image

Deep learning models for computer vision require input images to have consistent spatial dimensions and normalized numerical values before training. Raw image files typically vary in size and store pixel intensity values as integers ranging from 0 to 255.

Passing raw, unstandardized inputs directly into a neural network causes shape mismatch errors and slow or unstable gradient descent convergence. Two separate failures: the shape one stops the run immediately, and the range one just makes training worse in ways you have to notice.

### 2 · The shape layers

To solve this, Keras provides specialized image preprocessing layers that transform tensors inside data pipelines or model architectures.

The **Resizing** layer alters image dimensions to a specified height and width. Setting the crop attribute to true ensures the target aspect ratio is maintained without stretching or distorting the content — resize a wide photo into a square and it squashes, unless you tell it to crop instead.

The **CenterCrop** layer trims the outer borders of an image to keep only a central rectangular patch. For example, passing full-sized sample color images of a temple and a flower, loaded using Scikit-Learn, into a Keras CenterCrop layer instantiated with a height of 100 pixels and a width of 100 pixels crops every image in the batch down to a uniform 100-by-100 central square.

Note what CenterCrop does *not* do: it discards the edges rather than shrinking them, so anything important near the border is gone.

### 3 · The range layer

The **Rescaling** layer applies a linear mathematical transformation to numerical pixel values: multiply by `scale`, then add `offset`.

For instance, applying a scale factor of two-divided-by-255 along with an offset of negative one rescales raw integer inputs from the zero-to-255 range into normalized floating-point numbers between negative one and positive one.

Check both ends and the rule is obvious — the card below does exactly that with the book's numbers. Pixel 0 maps to the bottom of the new range and pixel 255 maps to the top; everything in between rides along linearly.

### 4 · Augmentation, and when it is switched off

Additionally, Keras includes data augmentation layers such as **RandomFlip** and **RandomRotation**. These layers apply random geometric or color adjustments during training to expand dataset diversity and prevent overfitting, while remaining inactive during validation and testing.

**Overfitting** is the model memorizing the training images instead of learning what the object looks like; showing it the same photo flipped and rotated makes memorizing harder. The automatic switch-off matters just as much: a randomly rotated validation image would make your measured score noisy and not comparable between runs.

The key insight to remember is that Keras image preprocessing layers streamline input standardization and training-time data augmentation directly within TensorFlow graphics operations — underneath, they are the low-level `tf.image` package.

**One-liner for your notes:** `Resizing` and `CenterCrop` make the shape uniform, `Rescaling(scale, offset)` maps the pixel range linearly, and the `Random*` augmentation layers act during training only.

blocks.title: Worked out: Rescaling(scale=2/255, offset=-1)
blocks.content: The book's numbers follow one rule: each pixel value is multiplied by `scale`, and then `offset` is added. With `scale=2/255` and `offset=-1`, the smallest pixel value 0 becomes 0 × 2/255 − 1 = 0 − 1 = −1. The largest pixel value 255 becomes 255 × 2/255 − 1 = 2 − 1 = 1. So the range 0 to 255 is mapped to the range −1 to 1, which is the result the book gives.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.datasets import load_sample_images
import tensorflow as tf

images = load_sample_images()["images"]
crop_image_layer = tf.keras.layers.CenterCrop(height=100, width=100)
cropped_images = crop_image_layer(images)
```

items.term: Resize or crop is a choice about what you are willing to lose
items.text: Resizing to a fixed shape distorts geometry; cropping to the aspect ratio preserves it but discards pixels. Which is worse depends entirely on the task: a squashed face is still recognisably a face, while a crop that removes the object defeats the whole example. There is no default that is right for both, which is why the behaviour is a flag rather than a decision the library makes.

items.term: Why the pixel range matters more than it looks
items.text: Inputs in the hundreds produce large activations and large gradients in the first layer, which is what makes training unstable before anything has been learned. Rescaling to a small range centred near zero puts the first layer in the regime its initialisation assumed. Whether you choose 0 to 1 or −1 to 1 is usually dictated by the model you are reusing: a pretrained network expects the range it was trained on, and feeding it another one quietly degrades everything.

items.term: Augmentation only works while the result stays realistic
items.text: Random transformations help because they teach the model which variations are irrelevant. That argument holds only while the transformed image is something the real world could produce — flipping a photo of a cat is fine, flipping a photo of text is not, and rotating a digit far enough turns a 6 into a 9. Augmentation is not free variety; it is an assertion about which symmetries your problem actually has.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Resizing and CenterCrop layers adjust spatial dimensions of input images.
Rescaling alters numerical pixel intensity ranges to improve training stability.
Data augmentation layers apply random transformations exclusively during model training.
Preprocessing layers build upon low-level TensorFlow operations such as the tf.image package.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Augmentation layers are active during training and inactive at evaluation. Where exactly should they sit — inside the model, or in the `tf.data` pipeline — and what changes about performance and about the exported model in each case?
Look up: the Keras guide "Working with preprocessing layers" (keras.io), section "Image data augmentation", which contrasts the two placements directly.

items.term: Loading Data with TensorFlow Datasets

blocks.content:
TensorFlow Datasets is a catalogue: one `tfds.load()` call downloads a standard dataset, slices it into the splits you asked for, and hands back ready-to-use `tf.data` pipelines.

**The question this lesson answers:** you want MNIST, split 90/10 into train and validation with the test set kept whole. How much of that do you have to write yourself?

### The big picture

```
tfds.load(name, split=[...], as_supervised=True)
   -> train_set, valid_set, test_set
   -> .shuffle(...).batch(32).prefetch(1)
```

### 1 · What it takes off your hands

Machine learning workflows often require fetching, splitting, and preparing standard datasets for training. Downloading raw files manually, organizing directory structures, and writing custom parsing scripts can be tedious and prone to errors.

The **TensorFlow Datasets** library solves this problem by providing a centralized repository of popular datasets that can be downloaded and loaded into ready-to-use dataset objects with minimal effort.

This is a data catalogue with the ingestion already written: one identifier, and you get the parsed data rather than a folder of files and a parsing problem.

### 2 · Dictionaries by default, tuples on request

To load a dataset, you call the `tfds.load()` function. By default, TFDS returns dataset items as dictionary objects containing feature tensors and label tensors.

However, Keras models expect training data structured as simple tuples containing features and labels. Setting the argument `as_supervised=True` automatically transforms the default dictionary format into a tuple format consisting of `(features, labels)`.

| Argument | One item looks like |
|---|---|
| default | `{"image": ..., "label": ...}` |
| `as_supervised=True` | `(image, label)` |

You could do the conversion yourself with `map()`, and it is two lines. The argument just spares you the two lines — and only works for labelled datasets, since a tuple of features and labels needs labels to exist.

### 3 · Slicing the splits

Furthermore, the `split` argument allows flexible partitioning of datasets, enabling developers to slice datasets into custom proportions such as training, validation, and test subsets directly during the loading process.

Consider loading the MNIST dataset of handwritten digits. You can specify `split=["train[:90%]", "train[90%:]", "test"]` along with `as_supervised=True`. This command automatically splits the training data into a ninety percent training slice and a ten percent validation slice, while loading the complete test set separately.

The percentage syntax reads like a slice: `train[:90%]` is the first nine tenths of the train split, `train[90%:]` is the rest, and `test` is the whole test split. Three names in, three datasets out, in that order.

### 4 · It is still a `tf.data` pipeline

After loading, the training data is typically shuffled, batched into mini-batches of size thirty-two, and prefetched to optimize pipeline performance before being passed to a model — the same `shuffle` then `batch` then `prefetch` chain from earlier in this chapter. The validation and test sets are batched and cached; they are read identically every epoch, so caching them costs nothing and saves the re-read.

One extra option: `tfds.load()` can shuffle the files it downloads if you set `shuffle_files=True`. As the card below notes, that is file-level randomness and is usually not enough on its own, so the example still shuffles the rows with a buffer afterwards — the two-level shuffling argument from the lesson on `shuffle()`.

The key insight worth remembering is that setting `as_supervised=True` in `tfds.load()` seamlessly converts raw dataset dictionaries into feature-label tuples required by Keras models.

**One-liner for your notes:** `tfds.load()` downloads a catalogued dataset and slices it with `split=[...]` percentage syntax; `as_supervised=True` turns each item from a dictionary into the `(features, labels)` tuple Keras expects.

blocks.title: Shuffling the downloaded files
blocks.content: The `tfds.load()` function can shuffle the files it downloads: just set `shuffle_files=True`. However, shuffling the files may be insufficient on its own, so it is best to shuffle the training data some more, for example with `shuffle(buffer_size=10_000, seed=42)` before batching, as the book's MNIST example does.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf
import tensorflow_datasets as tfds

train_set, valid_set, test_set = tfds.load(
    name="mnist",
    split=["train[:90%]", "train[90%:]", "test"],
    as_supervised=True
)

train_set = train_set.shuffle(10_000, seed=42).batch(32).prefetch(1)
valid_set = valid_set.batch(32).cache()
test_set = test_set.batch(32).cache()
```

items.term: A catalogue is a reproducibility tool, not just a convenience
items.text: Because the dataset, its version and the split expression are all named in code, another person running the same line gets the same rows. Compare that with 'download the CSV from the link and split it 80/20', where two people almost never end up with the same training set. The value is less about saving the download and more about the comparison between two results meaning something.

items.term: Percentage splits are deterministic slices, not random samples
items.text: `train[:90%]` takes the first nine tenths in the dataset's stored order. If that order correlates with anything — collection date, class, source — the split is biased and no seed will save you, because nothing was random in the first place. Shuffling afterwards fixes the order the model sees, not which rows landed in which split. For benchmark datasets the stored order is usually already arbitrary; for your own data, do not assume it.

items.term: Why the validation and test sets get cache() and not shuffle()
items.text: They are read identically every epoch and never need reordering, so caching them is pure gain and shuffling them is pure waste. The asymmetry is worth internalising: the training set needs fresh randomness each epoch, while the evaluation sets need to be exactly the same every time, or your epoch-to-epoch comparison measures the sampling instead of the model.

blocks.title: Key points
items: TensorFlow Datasets (TFDS) provides convenient access to standard public datasets.
Setting as_supervised=True formats items as (features, labels) tuples required by Keras.
The split parameter allows custom slicing of training and test data using percentage syntax.
Loaded datasets integrate directly with pipeline methods like shuffle, batch, cache, and prefetch.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: TFDS datasets are versioned, and a version change can alter the splits. How does TFDS express versioning, and what does that imply for a result you want to reproduce in a year?
Look up: the TensorFlow Datasets documentation on dataset versioning and the split API (tensorflow.org/datasets/splits), plus the dataset catalogue at tensorflow.org/datasets/catalog/overview.

sections.title: Chapter 14: Deep Computer Vision Using Convolutional Neural Networks

items.term: Architecture of the Visual Cortex

blocks.content:
CNNs exist because a fully connected network cannot afford to look at every pixel, and because biology already solved that problem by letting each neuron watch only a small patch.

**The question this lesson answers:** if dense layers already work on small images, what breaks when the image gets bigger — and what did brain research suggest we do instead?

### The big picture

```
100x100 px -> 10,000 inputs
 x 1,000 neurons = 10,000,000 params  (one layer!)
fix: each neuron sees a small patch, weights reused
```

### 1 · Why the parameter count explodes

A **fully connected** layer is one where every neuron is wired to every input. Take a small image containing 100 × 100 pixels. That is 10,000 inputs. Put a modest layer of just 1,000 neurons on top and you need 10,000 × 1,000 = 10,000,000 parameters for that single layer.

A **parameter** here is one learned number — one weight the training has to find and store. Ten million of them for the first layer alone leads to severe overfitting and computational bottlenecks. **Overfitting** means the model memorises the training images instead of learning what a cat looks like, so it scores well on data it has seen and badly on data it has not.

If you think in tables: a dense layer is a join between every input column and every output column. Ten thousand columns joined to one thousand columns is ten million cells to maintain, and that is before the second layer.

### 2 · What the cortex does instead

Experiments by David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel revealed that neurons in the visual cortex do not monitor the entire visual field at once. Instead, individual neurons respond only to stimuli located within a limited region known as a **local receptive field** — the patch of the scene that one neuron is allowed to react to.

As Figure 14-1 below demonstrates, these small receptive fields overlap to tile the entire visual field. **Tile** means cover it completely with no gaps, like tiles on a floor; the overlap is what stops anything falling between two neurons.

### 3 · The hierarchy: simple parts, then combinations

Lower-level neurons detect simple features, such as horizontal or vertical lines, within their local field. Higher-level neurons receive input from neighboring lower-level neurons, allowing them to detect increasingly complex patterns over larger areas.

Consider a practical visual scenario: detecting a house in an image.

| Level | Looks at | Finds |
|---|---|---|
| first | tiny 3 × 3 regions | raw edges |
| next | the edge signals below it | triangles, rectangles |
| top | those shapes | a roof, a whole house |

Neurons in the initial layer scan tiny 3 × 3 regions to identify raw edges. Neurons in the next layer combine these edge signals to detect shapes like triangles or rectangles. Finally, top-level neurons combine these shapes to recognize complex objects like a roof or a complete house.

### 4 · From biology to the CNN

This hierarchical structure forms the foundation of modern **convolutional neural networks** (CNNs), which replace fully connected layers with local connectivity and weight sharing. **Weight sharing** means the same small set of weights is reused at every position instead of a fresh set per pixel — the same idea as writing one transformation and applying it to every row, rather than one rule per row.

The card below traces the line from the 1980 **neocognitron** through the 1998 **LeNet-5** paper by Yann LeCun et al., the architecture banks used to read handwritten digits on checks.

**One-liner for your notes:** dense layers cost one weight per pixel per neuron and blow up on real images, so CNNs copy the visual cortex — small overlapping receptive fields, reused weights, simple features combined into complex ones.

blocks.title: From the neocognitron to LeNet-5
blocks.content: Hubel and Wiesel's studies of the visual cortex inspired the **neocognitron**, a network introduced in 1980 that gradually evolved into what we now call convolutional neural networks. An important milestone came in 1998, when a paper by Yann LeCun et al. introduced the **LeNet-5** architecture, which banks widely used to recognize handwritten digits on checks. LeNet-5 kept familiar building blocks such as fully connected layers and sigmoid activation functions, and it added two new ones: convolutional layers and pooling layers. Deep Blue, by contrast, was the IBM chess supercomputer that beat the world champion Garry Kasparov in 1996; it was not a vision network.

blocks.alt: Figure 14-1: Biological neurons in the visual cortex respond to specific patterns in small regions of the visual field called receptive fields; as the visual signal makes its way through consecutive brain

items.term: Why local connectivity is a statement about images, not about brains
items.text: The cortex story is where the idea came from, but it is not why it works. It works because of a property of natural images: pixels close together are strongly related and pixels far apart usually are not, and the same pattern (an edge, a corner) can appear anywhere in the frame. A fully connected layer assumes neither of those and has to learn them from data, at the cost of one weight per pixel per neuron. Local receptive fields plus weight sharing build both assumptions into the architecture for free. The flip side: on data where those assumptions are false - shuffled columns in a table, say - a CNN has no advantage at all.

items.term: Weight sharing is a constraint, and constraints are what stop overfitting
items.text: Cutting ten million parameters to a few thousand is usually described as a saving in memory. The more important effect is statistical. Every extra free parameter is another way a model can fit noise it happened to see in training. Forcing every position to use the same filter means the filter's evidence comes from every position in every image at once, so it is far harder to fit an accident. This is the same reason a rule that must hold for all rows is more trustworthy than a per-row exception.

items.term: When the hierarchy assumption breaks
items.text: The layered story - edges, then shapes, then objects - assumes the thing you are looking for is built from small local parts in a consistent way. That is true for houses and faces. It is much weaker for tasks where the answer depends on a long-range relationship between two distant parts of the image, because the early layers physically cannot see both. Later architectures spend a lot of effort buying back that long-range view, through bigger strides, dilation, and eventually attention.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Fully connected networks require an unsustainable number of parameters when processing large image inputs.
Neurons in the visual cortex respond only to specific local areas called receptive fields.
Receptive fields overlap across biological neurons to cover the entire visual field.
Higher-level biological neurons build upon low-level neuron outputs to process complex visual features.
This local hierarchical organization directly inspired the design of convolutional neural networks.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Hubel and Wiesel found orientation-selective cells in the cat's visual cortex. Do the filters a modern CNN learns in its first layer actually resemble those biological receptive fields, or is the resemblance a story we tell after the fact?

Look up: Kunihiko Fukushima, "Neocognitron: A Self-Organizing Neural Network Model for a Mechanism of Pattern Recognition Unaffected by Shift in Position", Biological Cybernetics 36 (1980): 193-202 - cited in this chapter's footnote 4.

items.term: Convolutional Layers and Filters

blocks.content:
A convolutional layer keeps the image as a grid, wires each neuron to one small patch of that grid, and slides one shared set of weights — a filter — across the whole thing.

**The question this lesson answers:** what exactly is a convolutional layer made of, and which three knobs (receptive field, padding, stride) control the size of what comes out?

### The big picture

```
input grid ──(filter slides over it)──> feature map
   knobs: field size · zero padding · stride
```

### 1 · Keep the grid, drop the flattening

Standard fully connected neural networks require flattening images into one-dimensional vectors, which destroys spatial structure and creates excessive parameters. **Flattening** means laying the rows of the picture end to end into one long list, so "these two pixels were neighbours" stops being recorded anywhere.

A **convolutional layer** solves this problem by preserving two-dimensional spatial arrangements and connecting each neuron to only a local region of the previous layer. This small region of local connections is called a **receptive field**.

As shown in Figure 14-2 below, early layers focus on small low-level visual patterns, while higher layers assemble those patterns into complex representations.

### 2 · Zero padding: keep the output the same size

To control dimensions, networks use **zero padding**, which adds extra zero values around the input borders (as shown in Figure 14-3 below).

Without it, a neuron centred on a corner pixel would have half its receptive field hanging off the edge of the image, so the layer has to shrink. Padding the border with zeros gives those edge neurons something legal to look at, and the output keeps the height and width of the input.

### 3 · Stride: step further and the output shrinks

Networks can also downsample spatial dimensions by increasing the **stride**, which specifies the horizontal and vertical step distance between adjacent receptive fields. **Downsample** means deliberately produce a smaller grid than you started with.

| Stride | Fields are | Output |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | one cell apart | roughly the input size |
| 2 | two cells apart | about half the height and width |

As Figure 14-4 below illustrates, shifting receptive fields by a stride of 2 reduces a 5×7 padded input layer into a smaller 3×4 layer. The card below counts exactly why it lands on 3 and 4 rather than any other pair.

### 4 · Filters, and what one of them sees

Within a convolutional layer, neuron weights are structured into matrices called **filters** or kernels. A single filter sweeps across the input matrix using weight sharing — the same numbers are reused at every position, which is why the layer is cheap.

When a filter detects a specific visual feature — such as a vertical line or a horizontal edge — it activates strongly. The book's example filter for a vertical line is a 7 × 7 matrix full of zeros except for the central column, which is full of ones: every input is multiplied by zero except the ones lying on that central vertical line, so only a vertical line makes the neuron fire.

Passing a single filter across an entire layer produces a two-dimensional grid called a **feature map**. Figure 14-5 below shows two filters and the two feature maps they produce — in each one, the lines matching that filter come out enhanced while the rest is blurred.

### 5 · Nobody writes the filters by hand

Instead of requiring hand-crafted values, CNNs automatically learn optimal filter weights during model training. You choose how many filters and how big they are; training decides what each one looks for.

**One-liner for your notes:** a convolutional layer slides shared filters over a grid it never flattens — padding controls whether the output keeps its size, stride controls how much it shrinks, and each filter's sweep produces one feature map whose weights are learned, not written.

blocks.title: Worked out: why a stride of 2 gives a 3 × 4 layer
blocks.content:
In Figure 14-4 the input layer is 5 × 7, each receptive field is 3 × 3, and the stride is 2 in both directions. A neuron in row $i$ of the upper layer looks at input rows $i \times s_h$ to $i \times s_h + f_h - 1$, where $f_h$ is the field height and $s_h$ the vertical stride; columns work the same way with $f_w$ and $s_w$.

1. With $s_h = 2$, the fields start at rows 0, 2 and 4. A start at row 6 would lie past the 5 input rows (0 to 4), so the upper layer has **3 rows**.
2. With $s_w = 2$, the fields start at columns 0, 2, 4 and 6. A start at column 8 would lie past the 7 input columns (0 to 6), so it has **4 columns**.
3. The fields starting at row 4 or column 6 run past the edge, and zero padding fills the gap.
