items.term: Padding is a decision about the edges of your data, not a formality
items.text: With no padding, the pixels near the border take part in fewer receptive fields than the ones in the middle, so the network systematically sees less of them; stack thirty such layers and the outer band of the image has been quietly discounted. Zero padding restores their weight, but it does so by feeding the network invented zeros, which look to a filter like a dark region that is not really there. Neither is free. Classification networks usually accept the zeros; tasks that care about the edges of the frame have to think about it.

items.term: Stride versus pooling: two ways to shrink, with different costs
items.text: Stride 2 and a 2 by 2 pooling layer both halve the height and width, but not in the same way. A strided convolution shrinks while it is computing a learned feature, so the downsampling itself is trainable and it does less arithmetic. Pooling is a fixed rule applied after the full-resolution convolution has been computed, so it costs more and learns nothing, but it keeps the strongest response rather than whichever one happened to land on the sampled position. Which is better is a real architectural argument, not a settled fact.

items.term: Why learned filters beat hand-written ones
items.text: Classical computer vision spent decades hand-designing edge and corner detectors, and the book's vertical-line filter is exactly one of those. The reason training won is not that a learned filter is cleverer than a hand-written one at the first layer - early learned filters look remarkably like the hand-written ones. It is that nobody can hand-design the third layer, where the useful features are combinations with no name. Learning gets you the unnameable layers for the same price as the nameable ones.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Neurons in convolutional layers connect only to small local regions called receptive fields rather than every pixel.
Zero padding surrounds inputs with zeros to maintain layer dimensions across convolutions.
Stride defines the step size between adjacent receptive fields and reduces layer spatial dimensions.
Filters represent reusable weight matrices that activate when detecting specific local visual patterns.
Applying a single weight filter across an input produces a two-dimensional feature map.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The book's own footnote admits that what these layers compute is technically cross-correlation, not convolution. What is the difference, and why does it make no practical difference to a trained network?
Look up: footnote 6 of this chapter and the link it gives, https://homl.info/76, on convolution versus cross-correlation.

items.term: Stacking Multiple Feature Maps

blocks.content:
One filter finds one kind of thing, so a real convolutional layer runs many filters at once and stacks their outputs into a 3D block.

**The question this lesson answers:** a layer needs to spot edges *and* corners *and* colour blobs at the same time. How does it hold all of those, and how many weights does that actually cost?

### The big picture

```
       filter 1 ─> feature map 1  ┐
input  filter 2 ─> feature map 2  ├─ stacked = 3D output
       ...                        ┘
one neuron looks at ALL channels below it
```

### 1 · Many filters, one stack

A single two-dimensional filter can only detect one specific visual feature, such as a horizontal line or a sharp edge. To detect multiple visual characteristics simultaneously, a convolutional layer applies several distinct filters to its inputs, producing a three-dimensional output volume composed of stacked **feature maps**.

Each filter generates its own two-dimensional feature map, where every neuron represents the activation level of a specific feature at a given spatial location. **Activation level** just means how strongly that neuron fired — a big number where the feature is present, near zero where it is not.

Although individual feature maps operate in two dimensions, the overall layer output is three-dimensional because multiple feature maps are stacked together. Height and width are the picture; the third dimension, the **depth** or **channels**, is "which feature".

### 2 · Sharing inside a map, not across maps

Neurons within a single feature map share the exact same parameters, consisting of a kernel weight set and a **bias term**, which drastically reduces total parameter count and enables location-invariant feature detection. A **bias** is one extra number added to every weighted sum in that map — the book calls it a knob that tweaks the map's overall brightness. **Location-invariant** means once the layer has learned to spot the pattern in one place, it spots it everywhere, because it is literally the same weights being reapplied.

However, neurons across different feature maps utilize distinct sets of parameters. That is the whole point: map 3 is only different from map 7 because their weights differ.

| | Same feature map | Different feature maps |
|---|---|---|
| Weights and bias | identical, shared | different sets |
| Inputs at row i, col j | the same patch | the same patch |

### 3 · A neuron sees the full depth below it

As Figure 14-6 below shows, a neuron's receptive field spans across all feature maps or channels of the preceding layer. It is a small window in height and width, but it goes all the way down through the depth.

That is why the input position in Equation 14-1 depends only on the row and column — the card below spells this out: all neurons located in the same row and column but in different feature maps are connected to the outputs of exactly the same neurons in the previous layer.

### 4 · Counting the weights

For instance, consider an input RGB image with 3 color channels. If a convolutional layer applies a 3 × 3 kernel with a single filter, that filter contains 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 weights plus 1 bias term.

If the layer uses 32 independent filters instead, it produces 32 output feature maps, requiring 32 × 28 = 896 trainable parameters in total. Each filter costs the same 28 numbers; multiply by how many filters you asked for. Note what is *not* in that count: the height and width of the image. Because the weights are shared across positions, the picture's size never enters the parameter bill.

### 5 · The equation, and the one thing to carry away

Equation 14-1 below defines the mathematical output z at row i, column j, and feature map k for one neuron. It computes a weighted sum over the receptive field height f_h, width f_w, and all f_n' feature maps from the previous layer, then adds the filter bias b_k. The explanation underneath it walks every symbol.

The crucial insight to remember is that while parameter sharing within each feature map keeps parameter counts low, a neuron's receptive field always extends across the entire depth dimension of the previous layer.

**One-liner for your notes:** a conv layer is N filters producing N stacked feature maps; weights are shared across positions inside a map and never between maps, and each filter costs kernel height × kernel width × input channels + 1 bias — with the image size nowhere in that total.

blocks.title: Same position, same inputs
blocks.content: In Equation 14-1, the input position depends only on the neuron's row and column: $i' = i \times s_h + u$ and $j' = j \times s_w + v$, where $s_h$ and $s_w$ are the vertical and horizontal strides. The feature map index $k$ does not appear in these formulas. As a result, all neurons located in the same row $i$ and column $j$ but in different feature maps of a layer are connected to the outputs of exactly the same neurons in the previous layer, across all of its feature maps. What differs between those neurons is their parameters: each feature map $k$ has its own weights $w_{u,v,k',k}$ and its own bias $b_k$, which you can think of as a knob that tweaks the overall brightness of feature map $k$.

blocks.title: Figure 14-6
blocks.caption: Two convolutional layers with multiple filters each (kernels), processing a color image
blocks.alt: Figure 14-6: Two convolutional layers with multiple filters each (kernels), processing a color image

blocks.title: Equation 14-1
blocks.caption: Computing the output of a neuron in a convolutional layer
blocks.latex: z_{i,j,k} = b_k + \sum_{u=0}^{f_h - 1} \sum_{v=0}^{f_w - 1} \sum_{k'=0}^{f_{n'} - 1} x_{i',j',k'} \times w_{u,v,k',k} \quad \text{with } \begin{cases} i' = i \times s_h + u \\ j' = j \times s_w + v \end{cases}
blocks.explain:
**Why the equation looks like this**

The layer has to produce one number for every position in every feature map, and that number has to
depend on a small patch of the layer below, read across the whole of its depth. The operation itself
is therefore just a weighted sum plus a bias — the same thing a single ordinary neuron does. Every
symbol in Equation 14-1 beyond that is bookkeeping: *which* inputs and *which* weights. The three
nested sums are there only because the patch has a height, a width and a depth, so it takes three
counters to walk every input inside it.

**Is this standard, or simplified for the example?** Standard. This is the canonical definition of a
convolutional layer's output, with nothing dropped. The book says so in as many words: the equation
is "a bit ugly due to all the different indices", but all it does is calculate the weighted sum of
all the inputs, plus the bias term.

**The general form.** This *is* the general form, and the special cases fall out of it. Set the
receptive field to 1 by 1 and you have a 1 by 1 convolution, which mixes channels and ignores space.
Set the strides to 1 and the input row simplifies to i' = i. Make the receptive field as large as the
whole feature map and each filter fits in exactly one position — which is precisely the dense-layer
conversion used in the Fully Convolutional Networks lesson.

**Terms this introduces:** the **receptive field** is the small patch of the previous layer one
neuron is wired to; the **stride** is how far the patch moves between neighbouring neurons; a
**feature map** is the 2D grid produced by one filter; and the **bias** is a single number added to
every sum in a map, which the book describes as a knob that tweaks that map's overall brightness.

**Every piece of Equation 14-1**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| z at i, j, k | z sub i j k | the output of one neuron: row i, column j, feature map k |
| b sub k | b sub k | the bias for feature map k, one number shared by the whole map |
| u | u | which row inside the receptive field, 0 up to f sub h minus 1 |
| v | v | which column inside the receptive field, 0 up to f sub w minus 1 |
| k prime | k prime | which feature map of the PREVIOUS layer, 0 up to f sub n prime minus 1 |
| f sub h, f sub w | f sub h, f sub w | height and width of the receptive field |
| f sub n prime | f sub n prime | how many feature maps the previous layer has |
| s sub h, s sub w | s sub h, s sub w | the vertical and horizontal strides |
| x at i prime, j prime, k prime | x sub i prime j prime k prime | one input value from the previous layer |
| w at u, v, k prime, k | w sub u v k prime k | the weight this filter gives that position and input map |
| the three sum signs | sum over u, over v, over k prime | add up every input in the patch, full depth included |
| i prime = i times s sub h + u | — | which input ROW this is: patch start plus the offset |
| j prime = j times s sub w + v | — | which input COLUMN this is |
| the multiplication sign | times | each input value multiplied by its own weight |

**The formula in plain words**

output = bias + (add up, over every position in the patch and every input feature map: that input
value multiplied by its weight).

**Real numbers plugged in**

Take the lesson's own case — an RGB input, a 3 by 3 kernel, stride 1 — and ask for the neuron at row
4, column 6 of feature map 0.

1. f sub h = 3, f sub w = 3, f sub n prime = 3 (red, green, blue), and both strides are 1.
2. u runs 0, 1, 2; v runs 0, 1, 2; k prime runs 0, 1, 2. That is 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 products.
3. The input rows are i prime = 4 × 1 + u, so rows 4, 5 and 6. The input columns are
j prime = 6 × 1 + v, so columns 6, 7 and 8.
4. So this neuron multiplies 27 input values by its 27 weights, adds them up, and adds the one bias
b sub 0 — 28 numbers in total, which is exactly the per-filter parameter count the lesson gives.

**Why k never appears on the input side**

Look at the two side conditions: i prime and j prime are built from i, j, the strides and the
offsets, and nothing else. Change k and you change which weights and which bias are used — never
which inputs are read. That is the card's point, and it is why 32 filters can all share one reading
of the same patch.

items.term: The parameter count tells you where a design can and cannot afford to grow
items.text: Because a filter costs kernel height times kernel width times input channels plus one, the cost is linear in the kernel area and linear in the input depth - and the number of filters multiplies the whole thing. That single formula explains most of the architectural moves later in this chapter: shrink the input depth before an expensive kernel (the 1 by 1 bottleneck), shrink the kernel (two 3 by 3 instead of one 5 by 5), or stop mixing depth and space in one filter at all (separable convolutions). Every one of them is an attack on a different term in that product.

items.term: Location invariance is a design choice with a cost
items.text: Sharing one kernel across every position bakes in the assumption that a feature means the same thing wherever it appears. For photographs that is almost always right. It is wrong whenever position carries meaning - a fixed-layout form, a medical scan in a standard orientation, a game board - and in those cases a model that can learn position-specific weights may genuinely do better. The convolutional prior is a very good default, not a law.

items.term: Full-depth receptive fields are why channels stay expensive
items.text: A neuron's window is small in height and width but always spans the entire depth below it. So doubling the channel count of a layer doubles the reading cost of every neuron in the layer above, which is why architectures downsample space before they add channels: a quarter of the positions pays for twice the depth. Keep that trade in mind and the filter-doubling convention in the next few lessons stops looking arbitrary.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A convolutional layer uses multiple filters to produce a 3D output of stacked 2D feature maps.
Neurons within the same feature map share identical weights and bias parameters.
Neurons in different feature maps use different sets of parameters.
A neuron's receptive field extends across all feature maps or channels of the previous layer.
Equation 14-1 computes neuron outputs by summing weighted inputs across spatial dimensions and input channels.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: If each filter learns one feature, what do the learned filters in a trained network actually look like at layer 1, layer 3 and layer 5 - and how would you visualise them?

Look up: Matthew D. Zeiler and Rob Fergus, "Visualizing and Understanding Convolutional Networks", Proceedings of the European Conference on Computer Vision (2014): 818-833 - cited in this chapter's footnote 12.

items.term: Implementing Convolutional Layers with Keras

blocks.content:
In Keras a convolutional layer is one object, `Conv2D`, and the only things you must get right are the tensor shape going in and the padding option.

**The question this lesson answers:** you have two photographs in memory. What shape must they be in before `Conv2D` will accept them, and what shape comes back out?

### The big picture

```
[batch, height, width, channels]  ->  Conv2D  ->
[batch, height', width', filters]
   "valid" shrinks it · "same" keeps it (stride 1)
```

### 1 · Why this layer exists at all

Standard fully connected layers struggle with spatial image structures and scale poorly with high-resolution inputs. To process visual data efficiently, spatial features must be extracted locally using trainable filters.

Keras solves this problem using the `Conv2D` layer, which applies sliding convolutional kernels across 4D input tensors structured as `[batch_size, height, width, channels]`. A **tensor** is just an array with more than two dimensions; read that shape left to right as "how many images, how tall, how wide, how many colour planes".

### 2 · The two padding options

The layer operates by sliding local kernels of size `kernel_size` across the input image. The stride hyperparameter determines the step size of this movement, while padding options control border handling. A **hyperparameter** is a setting you choose before training and which training does not change.

| Option | Adds zeros? | Output size (strides=1) |
|---|---|---|
| valid (the default) | no | shrinks with kernel size |
| same | yes, around the border | matches the input |

Using default `padding="valid"` adds no extra zeros, causing feature maps to shrink based on kernel size. Using `padding="same"` pads the inputs with zeros so that output spatial dimensions match the input dimensions when `strides=1`.

Figure 14-7 below illustrates how `padding="valid"` reduces output spatial dimensions whereas `padding="same"` pads edges with zero values to preserve spatial dimensions. Figure 14-8 below shows the other case: once the stride is greater than 1, the output is much smaller even with `"same"` padding, because the stride is doing the shrinking, not the border.

Be warned that `"valid"` is a badly chosen name — it means *no padding at all*, not "the valid choice". Everyone uses this odd nomenclature, so learn it once.

### 3 · A worked shape

Consider an input batch containing 2 cropped images of size 70 × 120 pixels with 3 RGB color channels, yielding a tensor shape of `[2, 70, 120, 3]`.

Passing this tensor through a `Conv2D` layer configured with 32 filters, `kernel_size=7`, and `padding="valid"` produces an output tensor of shape `[2, 64, 114, 32]`:

1. batch stays 2 — one row in, one row out
2. height shrinks by 6 pixels: 70 − 7 + 1 = 64
3. width shrinks by 6 pixels: 120 − 7 + 1 = 114
4. the last dimension becomes 32, one plane per filter

Losing 6 comes from the kernel being 7 wide: it cannot start until 3 pixels in and must stop 3 pixels early, so 3 on each side disappear.

### 4 · What the layer actually stores

The card below reads the weights back with `get_weights()`. Two arrays come out: kernels shaped `(7, 7, 3, 32)` and biases shaped `(32,)`, meaning `[kernel_height, kernel_width, input_channels, output_channels]` and one bias per output channel. The kernels are initialized randomly and the biases start at zero.

Look at what is missing from those shapes: 70 and 120. The key insight to remember is that convolutional weights are shared across spatial dimensions, allowing `Conv2D` layers to process inputs of any height and width as long as the input color channels match the layer configuration. Height and width are free; channel count is a contract.

**One-liner for your notes:** `Conv2D` takes `[batch, height, width, channels]` and returns `[batch, height', width', filters]`; `"valid"` means no padding and a smaller output, `"same"` keeps the size at stride 1, and the kernel shape depends only on kernel size and channel counts — never on image size.

blocks.title: The shapes of the kernels and biases
blocks.content: After the book creates `Conv2D(filters=32, kernel_size=7)` and applies it to the RGB images, `conv_layer.get_weights()` returns a kernels array of shape `(7, 7, 3, 32)` and a biases array of shape `(32,)`. The kernels array is 4D, with shape `[kernel_height, kernel_width, input_channels, output_channels]`: 7 × 7 is the filter size, 3 is the number of input color channels, and 32 is the number of output feature maps, which equals the number of filters. The biases array is 1D, with one bias per output channel. The height and width of the input images appear in neither shape, because all the neurons in an output feature map share the same weights. The kernels are initialized randomly and the biases start at zero.

blocks.caption: The two padding options, when strides=1
blocks.alt: Figure 14-7: The two padding options, when strides=1

blocks.title: Figure 14-8
blocks.caption: With strides greater than 1, the output is much smaller even when using "same" padding

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf
from sklearn.datasets import load_sample_images

images = load_sample_images()["images"]
images = tf.keras.layers.CenterCrop(height=70, width=120)(images)
images = tf.keras.layers.Rescaling(scale=1 / 255)(images)

conv_layer = tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(filters=32, kernel_size=7, padding="same")
fmaps = conv_layer(images)

kernels, biases = conv_layer.get_weights()
print("Input shape:", images.shape)
print("Output shape:", fmaps.shape)
print("Kernels shape:", kernels.shape)
```

items.term: Why the kernel shape does not contain the image size, and what that enables
items.text: Nothing in a convolutional layer's weights records how big the picture was. That looks like a small implementation detail and is actually the property the last third of this chapter is built on: a trained network can be run on a larger image and will simply produce a larger output. That is what makes fully convolutional networks, sliding detection in one pass, and segmentation possible. A dense layer, whose weight count is tied to its input size, closes all of those doors.

items.term: The channel count is a contract; height and width are not
items.text: A layer will accept any height and width but insists on the exact number of input channels it was built for, because each kernel holds a separate set of weights per input channel. This asymmetry is worth internalising early, because the error it produces when you get it wrong - feeding a grayscale image to a layer expecting three channels - is about shapes and gives no hint about which of the four dimensions is the culprit.

items.term: Choosing padding is choosing how you want depth to shrink
items.text: With valid padding and a kernel of size k, every layer removes k - 1 pixels from each dimension, so a deep stack of 3 by 3 layers quietly eats its own borders and limits how deep you can go on a small input. Same padding removes that limit and lets depth be decided by what you want to learn rather than by arithmetic. That is why most modern architectures use same padding everywhere and do all their shrinking deliberately, with strides and pooling.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Input tensors to Keras Conv2D layers use a 4D shape formatted as batch size, height, width, and channels.
The default valid padding applies no zero-padding, shrinking spatial output dimensions based on filter size.
Setting padding to same adds zero-padding around borders to maintain input spatial dimensions when stride is 1.
Conv2D kernel weights depend only on filter size and channel counts, making them independent of input image dimensions.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Conv2D has an activation and a kernel_initializer argument this lesson never sets. What are their defaults, and what happens to a deep stack of convolutional layers if you leave the activation off?
Look up: the Keras API documentation for Conv2D, at https://keras.io/api/layers/convolution_layers/convolution2d/.

items.term: Memory Requirements in Convolutional Neural Networks

blocks.content:
The thing that fills your GPU is not the model's weights — it is the feature maps the forward pass has to keep around so backpropagation can use them.

**The question this lesson answers:** one convolutional layer holds only 15,200 weights, so why does training it on a batch of 100 images eat 1.2 gigabytes of RAM?

### The big picture

| | What is held | Freed when? |
|---|---|---|
| Inference | two consecutive layers | as soon as the next layer is computed |
| Training | every layer's activations | only after the backward pass |

### 1 · Parameters are small; activations are not

Training deep **convolutional neural networks** presents a significant hardware challenge because feature maps consume massive amounts of random-access memory. While convolutional layers generally contain far fewer parameters than fully connected layers, their intermediate activations require substantial storage.

An **activation** is one output number a neuron produced for one input image. The whole grid of them, for every filter, is the layer's output — and there are a lot of those numbers.

### 2 · Why training cannot throw them away

During the forward pass of model training, every layer produces intermediate outputs that must remain in memory until the backward pass completes, because the **backpropagation** algorithm relies on these preserved activations to compute parameter gradients.

**Backpropagation** is the algorithm that works out, for every weight, which direction to nudge it; to do that for a layer it needs to know what that layer received and produced. A **gradient** is that per-weight nudge direction and size.

During inference, memory can be freed immediately after computing the subsequent layer, requiring only enough RAM to hold two consecutive layers. However, during training, the network must retain the activations of all layers simultaneously.

This is the same shape as a pipeline that can stream a stage at a time versus one that must materialise every intermediate table before it can reconcile. This cumulative memory footprint scales directly with both the size of the intermediate feature maps and the mini-batch size used during training. A **mini-batch** is the group of images processed together in one training step.

### 3 · The numbers, on one layer

Consider a concrete example featuring a single convolutional layer with 200 filters of size 5 by 5, operating with a stride of 1 and same padding on a 150 by 100 RGB image.

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Trainable parameters | 15,200 |
| Output | 200 maps of 150 by 100 |
| Activations, one image | 12 megabytes |
| Activations, batch of 100 | 1.2 gigabytes |

The layer requires only 15,200 trainable parameters. However, its output consists of 200 feature maps of size 150 by 100. Using standard 32-bit floating-point numbers, one single image generates 12 megabytes of activation data. If training uses a mini-batch size of 100 images, this single layer consumes 1.2 gigabytes of RAM. Across a deep architecture with dozens of layers, total memory usage easily exceeds available GPU capacity.

The card below breaks all four of those numbers down step by step. For scale, the book notes in a footnote that a fully connected layer producing the same 200 × 150 × 100 outputs would need roughly 135 billion parameters — that is the comparison "far fewer parameters" is standing on.

### 4 · What to do when it crashes

The key insight to remember is that training memory is dominated by intermediate activations rather than model parameters, meaning that reducing batch size or using lower-precision float types is essential when facing **out-of-memory** errors.

The full list of levers, as the Key points below record it: reduce the mini-batch size, increase the stride so the feature maps come out smaller, switch from 32-bit to 16-bit floats, or remove a few layers. Every one of them attacks the activations, because that is where the memory actually went.

**One-liner for your notes:** training RAM is dominated by stored activations, not weights — inference needs only two consecutive layers, training needs them all, and the fixes are a smaller batch, a bigger stride, 16-bit floats, or fewer layers.

blocks.title: Worked out: 15,200 parameters, 12 MB and 1.2 GB
blocks.content:
The layer has 200 filters of size 5 × 5, with stride 1 and "same" padding, applied to a 150 × 100 RGB image with 3 channels.

1. **Parameters:** each filter has 5 × 5 × 3 = 75 weights plus 1 bias term, so the layer holds (5 × 5 × 3 + 1) × 200 = 15,200 parameters.
2. **Computation:** each of the 200 feature maps contains 150 × 100 neurons, and each neuron computes a weighted sum of its 75 inputs, which is a total of 225 million float multiplications.
3. **Memory for one image:** with 32-bit floats, the output occupies 200 × 150 × 100 × 32 = 96 million bits, which is 12 MB.
4. **Memory for a batch:** if a training batch contains 100 instances, this one layer uses 100 × 12 MB = 1.2 GB of RAM.

blocks.caption: Model parameters occupy a small, fixed amount of memory, whereas intermediate feature map activations consume massive amounts of memory during training because every layer must be retained for backpropagation.

items.term: The memory bill and the parameter count measure different things
items.text: Parameters scale with the architecture and are fixed; activations scale with the architecture times the batch size times the image size. So two models with identical parameter counts can have wildly different training footprints, and a model that fits in memory at batch size 16 may not at 64. When you plan hardware, count activations. When you plan download size or a mobile deployment, count parameters. Confusing the two is how people conclude a small model will train on a small GPU.

items.term: Every fix for out-of-memory trades away something different
items.text: A smaller batch means noisier gradient estimates and often a different effective learning rate. A bigger stride permanently discards spatial detail the later layers can never recover. Sixteen-bit floats reduce numerical precision and can destabilise training without care. Removing layers reduces capacity outright. None of these is a free win, which is why the right answer depends on which resource you are actually short of and what the task tolerates.

items.term: Why the forward pass must keep everything
items.text: The reason is structural, not an implementation quirk: computing how to change a layer's weights requires knowing what that layer received, and the backward pass visits the layers in reverse order, so the very first layer's inputs are needed last. That is what makes training memory proportional to depth while inference memory is proportional to the widest pair of adjacent layers. It is also the hook for a real technique - recomputing some activations instead of storing them, trading compute for memory.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Convolutional layers have relatively few parameters but generate large intermediate feature maps.
Training requires keeping all intermediate activations in RAM for backpropagation, whereas inference only requires holding two consecutive layers.
Activation memory footprint scales linearly with the mini-batch size.
Out-of-memory errors can be resolved by reducing mini-batch size, increasing stride, using 16-bit floats, or removing layers.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: 16-bit floats halve the activation memory. Which parts of a network can safely run in 16-bit and which must stay in 32-bit, and what goes wrong if you convert everything?
Look up: Chapter 19 of this book, which covers training across devices and the precision trade-offs involved.

items.term: Pooling Layers in Convolutional Neural Networks

blocks.content:
A pooling layer shrinks a feature map by keeping one number per small window and throwing the rest away — and it has nothing to learn.

**The question this lesson answers:** the feature maps are too big and too expensive. How do you make them smaller without adding a single parameter, and what do you lose by doing it?

### The big picture

```
 1  5        max over the 2x2 window
 3  2   ──>      5        (1, 3 and 2 are dropped)
 stride 2: half the height, half the width
```

### 1 · What pooling is for

Deep convolutional neural networks often struggle with extreme computational load, memory consumption, and overfitting when processing high-resolution feature maps. To solve this problem, **pooling layers** downsample input feature maps to shrink their spatial dimensions while preserving key features.

### 2 · A layer with no weights

Unlike standard convolutional layers, neurons in a pooling layer do not learn any weights or bias parameters. Instead, a pooling neuron slides across a receptive field defined by a kernel size, stride, and padding setting, aggregating values using a deterministic function such as maximum or mean calculation.

**Deterministic** means the rule is fixed in advance and never changes: the same window always gives the same answer, because there is nothing in there to train. It is closer to a `MAX()` over a group than to anything learned.

| | Convolutional layer | Pooling layer |
|---|---|---|
| Weights | learned filters plus bias | none at all |
| Operation | weighted sum | fixed max or mean |
| Depth | changes, one map per filter | unchanged |

Each input channel is processed independently, meaning the depth of the volume remains unchanged. Pooling makes the picture smaller; it never makes it shallower.

### 3 · Max pooling, one window at a time

As shown in **Figure 14-9** below, consider a lower-left 2 × 2 receptive field with input values 1, 5, 3, and 2. Applying a **max pooling** layer with a 2 × 2 kernel and a stride of 2 selects the maximum value, 5, and drops the remaining three values.

This downsampling step reduces both the height and width of the feature map by half, eliminating 75% of the spatial inputs. Half the height times half the width is a quarter of the area, so three of every four numbers are gone. Pooling is destructive on purpose.

### 4 · The prize: invariance to small shifts

Beyond reducing parameters and computation, max pooling offers small-scale **translation invariance**. **Translation** here means a shift in position, not a change of language; **invariance** means the output does not change when the input does.

Because the maximum value in a window is retained regardless of slight shifts, minor spatial shifts in the input image frequently produce identical output maps. The card below works through Figure 14-10 with three images, where the second and third are the first shifted one and two pixels right: the first two give identical outputs, and the third is off by one pixel, so there is still 50% invariance. The book adds that max pooling also buys a small amount of rotational invariance and a slight scale invariance.

### 5 · The price: you no longer know where things are

However, this loss of spatial resolution makes pooling unsuitable for dense prediction tasks like semantic segmentation, where exact spatial **equivariance** is required.

**Semantic segmentation** is classifying each pixel according to the object it belongs to. **Equivariance** is the opposite deal from invariance: shift the input one pixel right and the output should also shift one pixel right. Invariance is what you want when the answer is "there is a cat"; equivariance is what you want when the answer is "these exact pixels are cat".

**One-liner for your notes:** pooling is a fixed max or mean over a sliding window with zero parameters — it quarters the area and drops 75% of the values, buying small-shift invariance for classification and costing you the exact positions segmentation needs.

blocks.title: Invariance versus equivariance
blocks.content: Figure 14-10 sends three images A, B and C through a max pooling layer with a 2 × 2 kernel and stride 2; B and C are A shifted one and two pixels to the right. The outputs for A and B are identical, which is what **translation invariance** means. The output for C is shifted one pixel to the right, so there is still 50% invariance. Such invariance is useful in classification, where the prediction should not depend on these details. It is not always desirable, though. In **semantic segmentation**, the task of classifying each pixel according to the object it belongs to, an input translated one pixel to the right should give an output translated one pixel to the right. The goal there is **equivariance**: a small change to the inputs should lead to a corresponding small change in the output.

blocks.title: Figure 14-9
blocks.caption: Max pooling layer (2 × 2 pooling kernel, stride 2, no padding)
blocks.alt: Figure 14-9: Max pooling layer (2 × 2 pooling kernel, stride 2, no padding)

blocks.title: Figure 14-10
blocks.caption: Invariance to small translations
blocks.alt: Figure 14-10: Invariance to small translations

items.term: Invariance and equivariance are a choice, and the task decides
items.text: Both words describe how the output reacts when the input shifts. Invariance means it does not react; equivariance means it shifts with it. Classification wants the first, segmentation and detection want the second, and a single network cannot maximise both. This is the cleanest example in the chapter of an architectural component being good or bad only relative to a task - max pooling is not better or worse than the alternative, it is a commitment.

items.term: Dropping 75% of the values is cheaper than it sounds, and sometimes it is not
items.text: Discarding three of four numbers sounds catastrophic until you notice that neighbouring positions in a feature map are highly redundant - a strong edge response usually lights up several adjacent cells. Pooling exploits that redundancy. The assumption fails for small objects and fine textures, where a feature may occupy a single cell and the max in a coarser window is dominated by something else entirely, which is one reason detecting small objects remains hard.

items.term: Stateless by design, and why that matters
items.text: A pooling layer has no weights, so it cannot overfit, cannot be initialised badly, and behaves identically during training and inference. That makes it a very safe way to spend compute reduction. The price is that it cannot adapt: it applies the same rule to the first layer and the last, to textures and to faces. Architectures that replace pooling with strided convolutions are buying adaptability back and paying for it with parameters and the risk that comes with them.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Pooling layers downsample feature maps to reduce computational cost, memory usage, and overfitting.
Pooling neurons possess no trainable weights and aggregate inputs using functions like max or mean.
Pooling operates on each feature map channel independently, preserving the total channel depth.
Max pooling provides small-scale translation invariance, which benefits image classification tasks.
The spatial reduction from pooling can harm tasks like semantic segmentation that demand exact location details.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Some modern architectures drop pooling entirely and use strided convolutions for all downsampling. What is actually lost or gained, and which tasks show the difference?

Look up: Jonathan Long et al., "Fully Convolutional Networks for Semantic Segmentation", Proceedings of the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (2015): 3431-3440 - cited in this chapter's footnote 30, for what pooling costs a pixel-level task.

items.term: Implementing Pooling Layers with Keras

blocks.content:
Keras gives you three pooling moves: shrink the picture (`MaxPool2D`), pool across channels instead of space, or collapse each whole feature map to one number (`GlobalAvgPool2D`).

**The question this lesson answers:** which pooling layer do you reach for, what does each one default to, and what shape comes out the other side?

### The big picture

| Layer | Pools over | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| MaxPool2D | a small window in height and width | halves height and width |
| depthwise max | groups of feature maps | invariance to rotation etc. |
| GlobalAvgPool2D | the whole height and width | one number per map |

### 1 · Spatial max pooling and its defaults

Convolutional neural networks require a mechanism to reduce spatial dimensions, lower computational costs, and gain invariance to small translations or transformations. **Pooling layers** address this challenge by downsampling feature maps through spatial aggregation operations.

In Keras, spatial pooling is typically performed using **max pooling** or **average pooling**. The standard `MaxPool2D` layer slides a kernel across spatial dimensions and extracts the maximum value within each window. By default, setting a pool size of 2 uses a stride of 2 and valid padding, halving both the height and width of the input maps.

Two defaults worth memorising, because you will not be asked for them: the stride follows the pool size, and there is no padding.

### 2 · Why max and not average

Max pooling is preferred over average pooling because it suppresses noise by preserving only the strongest feature signals, providing cleaner data to downstream layers.

That sounds backwards at first — a mean keeps more information than a max. But a mean keeps the weak, meaningless responses too, and blends them into the strong one. The max hands the next layer only the evidence that the feature was really there. The book adds two smaller reasons: max pooling gives stronger translation invariance than average pooling, and it costs slightly less compute.

### 3 · Pooling along depth instead of space

Pooling can also operate along the depth (channel) axis rather than spatial axes. As shown in Figure 14-11 below, **depthwise max pooling** evaluates maximum values across groups of feature maps.

This allows a network to achieve invariance against variations such as object rotation, thickness, or brightness, by selecting the most active filter response among a set of rotated patterns. If six filters each learned the same digit at a different tilt, taking the max across those six says "one of them matched" without caring which — so the tilt stops mattering. Keras ships no such layer, which is why the code card below defines a small custom `DepthPool` class.

### 4 · Global average pooling, the extreme case

Finally, modern architectures often employ **global average pooling** near the network output. The `GlobalAvgPool2D` layer computes the mean across the entire height and width of each feature map.

For a concrete example, if a batch of 2 RGB images with spatial dimensions of 28 × 28 (shape `[2, 28, 28, 3]`) is passed to a `GlobalAvgPool2D` layer, it reduces each spatial 28 × 28 matrix to its overall mean. The layer outputs a tensor of shape `(2, 3)`, representing the average intensity of the red, green, and blue channels for each image instance.

Read that as a `GROUP BY image, channel` with an `AVG` — 784 values per channel become one. The card below shows the same layer written by hand as a `Lambda` wrapping a mean over axes 1 and 2, and applies it to the book's two 70 × 120 sample images, again giving shape `(2, 3)`. It also says the honest thing: the layer is extremely destructive, and useful anyway just before the output layer.

### 5 · The two jobs, side by side

The key insight to remember is that while spatial max pooling compresses local dimensions, global average pooling condenses full feature maps into single summary values prior to final classification. One is a resize; the other is a summary.

**One-liner for your notes:** `MaxPool2D(pool_size=2)` defaults to stride 2 with no padding and halves the map; max beats average because it forwards only the strong signals; and `GlobalAvgPool2D` collapses each entire map to one number, turning `[2, 28, 28, 3]` into `(2, 3)`.

blocks.title: Global average pooling as a Lambda layer
blocks.content:
A global average pooling layer computes the mean of each entire feature map, like an average pooling layer whose kernel has the same spatial size as the inputs, so it outputs a single number per feature map and per instance. `tf.keras.layers.GlobalAvgPool2D()` is equivalent to a `Lambda` layer that computes the mean over the spatial dimensions, height (axis 1) and width (axis 2):

```python
global_avg_pool = tf.keras.layers.Lambda(
    lambda X: tf.reduce_mean(X, axis=[1, 2]))
```

Applied to the book's two 70 × 120 RGB sample images, the layer returns a tensor of shape `(2, 3)`: the mean intensity of red, green and blue for each image. The layer is extremely destructive, but it can be useful just before the output layer.

blocks.caption: Depthwise max pooling can help the CNN learn to be invariant (to rotation in this
blocks.alt: Figure 14-11: Depthwise max pooling can help the CNN learn to be invariant (to rotation in this

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

# Spatial max pooling with a 2x2 kernel
max_pool = tf.keras.layers.MaxPool2D(pool_size=2)

# Global average pooling over spatial dimensions
global_avg_pool = tf.keras.layers.GlobalAvgPool2D()

# Custom depthwise max pooling layer
class DepthPool(tf.keras.layers.Layer):
    def __init__(self, pool_size=2, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.pool_size = pool_size
    def call(self, inputs):
        shape = tf.shape(inputs)
        groups = shape[-1] // self.pool_size
        new_shape = tf.concat([shape[:-1], [groups, self.pool_size]], axis=0)
        return tf.reduce_max(tf.reshape(inputs, new_shape), axis=-1)
```

items.term: Why the more informative operation is the worse default
items.text: Averaging preserves more of the numbers in a window than taking the max, and yet max pooling wins in practice. The reason is what the next layer needs: after a ReLU, a feature map is mostly zeros with a few strong responses, and averaging dilutes those responses with the zeros around them. The max forwards the evidence undiluted. This is a good general lesson - preserving information is not the goal, preserving the useful signal is.

items.term: Depthwise pooling buys invariance by spending filters
items.text: Pooling across a group of filters trained on rotated versions of a pattern makes the output rotation-invariant, but note the cost: you had to spend several filters learning the same pattern at different angles. Invariance is not free; it is purchased either with parameters (learn every variant, then pool) or with data (augment the training set so one filter learns to tolerate the variation). The next lesson on AlexNet takes the second route, which is why depthwise pooling stayed rare.

items.term: Global average pooling is destructive on purpose
items.text: Collapsing a whole feature map to one number throws away every trace of where the feature was, and that is precisely the point when the next layer is a classifier: it removes the need for a huge dense layer, and with it a large share of a network's parameters and overfitting risk. The same property makes it exactly wrong in the middle of a network or for any task that needs positions, which is why you see it only at the top.

blocks.title: Key points
items: MaxPool2D defaults to a stride equal to its pool size and uses valid padding.
Max pooling generally outperforms average pooling because it retains dominant features while filtering noise.
Depthwise max pooling enables invariance to transformations such as rotation by pooling across channel groups.
Global average pooling reduces each entire spatial feature map to a single mean value per channel.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Max pooling wins for classification. Is there any task or layer position where average pooling measurably beats it, and what would explain that?
Look up: the Keras API documentation for pooling layers, at https://keras.io/api/layers/pooling_layers/.

items.term: Typical CNN Architecture

blocks.content:
The standard CNN is one repeating recipe: a couple of convolutions, a pooling layer, repeat — the picture getting smaller and the stack of feature maps getting deeper — then flatten and finish with dense layers.

**The question this lesson answers:** given the building blocks from the last few lessons, what order do you actually put them in, and why do the filter counts keep doubling?

### The big picture

```
28x28x1 ─conv─pool─> 14x14x128 ─conv─pool─> 7x7x256
        ─Flatten─> dense ─> softmax (10 classes)
   space shrinks  ·  depth grows
```

### 1 · The repeating block

Standard dense networks struggle with image processing because raw pixel inputs contain massive numbers of parameters and discard spatial geometry. A **convolutional neural network (CNN)** solves this problem by structuring feature extraction hierarchically before applying fully connected classification layers.

As Figure 14-12 below shows, a typical CNN architecture alternates between convolutional blocks and pooling layers before finishing with a regular feedforward network. Each convolutional layer applies filters followed by a **rectified linear unit (ReLU)** activation function to detect visual patterns. ReLU is the simplest possible non-linearity: keep the number if it is positive, otherwise output zero. Without something like it, a stack of convolutions would collapse mathematically into one convolution and could learn nothing complex.

Next, a **pooling layer** reduces the spatial dimensions (height and width) of the representations. Stacking these operations shrinks spatial dimensions progressively while increasing channel depth.

### 2 · Two small kernels beat one big one

Stacking multiple small filters (such as two consecutive 3 × 3 kernels) is preferred over a single large filter (such as a 5 × 5) because it uses fewer parameters and computations while enabling greater non-linearity.

Two stacked 3 × 3 layers end up seeing the same 5 × 5 patch of the input, but they cost less and there is a ReLU in between them, so the pair can express something a single linear filter cannot.

The card below gives the one exception: the **first** convolutional layer can have a large kernel, usually with a stride of 2 or more, because the input image generally has only three channels so a large kernel is not too costly there.

### 3 · Walking the Fashion MNIST model

Consider classifying a 28 × 28 grayscale image from Fashion MNIST.

| Stage | Spatial size | Channels |
|---|---|---|
| after the 7 × 7 convolution | 28 × 28 | 64 |
| after the first max pooling | 14 × 14 | 64 |
| after two 3 × 3 convolutions | 14 × 14 | 128 |
| after the second pooling | 7 × 7 | 128 |
| next stage | 7 × 7 | 256 |

The network processes the input through a 7 × 7 convolution yielding 64 channels, then a max pooling layer with pool size 2 divides the spatial resolution to 14 × 14. Two subsequent 3 × 3 convolutions produce 128 channels, followed by another pooling step that halves the spatial dimensions to 7 × 7.

### 4 · Why doubling the filters is safe

Because pooling reduces the spatial footprint by a factor of 4 in area, the network safely doubles filter counts to 256 in the next stage without exploding computational cost.

Halving height and width quarters the number of positions. Doubling the channels only doubles the work per position. Quarter times double is still half — so the layer got cheaper, not more expensive, even though it is now richer. There is also a reason to want more channels up there: there are only so many low-level features (short edges, small arcs) but a great many ways to combine them into higher-level ones.

### 5 · Flatten, then classify

At the end of the feature extraction pipeline, a **Flatten layer** converts the multidimensional feature maps into a one-dimensional array, feeding regular dense layers capped by a **softmax** output layer. Dense layers accept one flat row of features per instance, so the 7 × 7 × 256 block has to be unrolled first. **Softmax** turns the final scores into probabilities that add up to 1.

The flattened outputs pass through dense layers with 50% dropout to produce 10 class probabilities. **Dropout** randomly ignores half the neurons on each training step, which stops the dense layers memorising the training set. The book reports this model reaching over 92% accuracy on the Fashion MNIST test set.

The core insight of standard CNN design is to trade spatial resolution for feature depth: as representations shrink in height and width, the network increases the number of feature channels to capture increasingly rich combinations of visual patterns.

**One-liner for your notes:** conv + ReLU, conv + ReLU, pool, repeat — halving the picture and doubling the filters each round because a quarter of the area pays for twice the channels — then Flatten into dense layers and a softmax.

blocks.title: When a large kernel is fine
blocks.content: A common mistake is to use convolution kernels that are too large. Instead of one convolutional layer with a 5 × 5 kernel, stack two layers with 3 × 3 kernels: the stack uses fewer parameters, requires fewer computations, and usually performs better. The one exception is the **first** convolutional layer. It can typically have a large kernel (e.g., 5 × 5), usually with a stride of 2 or more. This reduces the spatial dimension of the image without losing too much information, and since the input image generally has only three channels, the large kernel is not too costly. In the Fashion MNIST model, the first layer uses 64 fairly large 7 × 7 filters but keeps the default stride of 1, because the 28 × 28 input images are not very large.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    DefaultConv2D(filters=64, kernel_size=7, input_shape=[28, 28, 1]),
    tf.keras.layers.MaxPool2D(),
    DefaultConv2D(filters=128),
    DefaultConv2D(filters=128),
    tf.keras.layers.MaxPool2D(),
    DefaultConv2D(filters=256),
    DefaultConv2D(filters=256),
    tf.keras.layers.MaxPool2D(),
    tf.keras.layers.Flatten(),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(units=128, activation="relu"),
    tf.keras.layers.Dropout(0.5),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(units=10, activation="softmax")
])
```

items.term: Why two small kernels beat one big one, in numbers
items.text: Count the weights per input channel: one 5 by 5 filter needs 25, while two stacked 3 by 3 filters need 9 plus 9, which is 18 - and the pair sees the same 5 by 5 patch of the input. You get a smaller parameter count, less arithmetic, and a non-linearity in the middle that the single layer cannot express. Once you see that arithmetic, VGG's whole design becomes obvious, and so does the first-layer exception: at three input channels the saving is tiny and a big kernel buys real early downsampling.

items.term: The shrink-and-deepen pattern is a compute budget being rebalanced
items.text: Halving height and width quarters the positions; doubling channels doubles the work per position and quadruples the cost of the filters that read them. Architectures pair the two moves so the cost per stage stays roughly flat while the representation moves from many cheap positions to few rich ones. Read any CNN diagram with that in mind and the filter counts stop looking like magic numbers.

items.term: The dense head is where the parameters used to hide
items.text: Flattening a 7 by 7 by 256 block gives 12,544 numbers, and a dense layer on top of that carries a weight for every one of them per unit - which is why old architectures held most of their parameters in the last two layers and relied on heavy dropout to survive it. Knowing that makes the later move to global average pooling read as what it is: deleting the most overfitting-prone part of the network rather than a mere tidy-up.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Typical CNNs alternate between convolutional layers and pooling layers before finishing with dense layers.
Spatial dimensions decrease with depth while the number of feature channels increases.
Stacking two 3x3 convolutions requires fewer parameters and computations than using one 5x5 convolution.
Doubling feature maps after downsampling keeps compute and parameter footprints balanced.
Feature maps must be flattened into a 1D vector before entering fully connected dense layers.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Two 3 by 3 layers cover the same patch as one 5 by 5. How far does that argument go - is a stack of 3 by 3 layers always preferable to a 7 by 7 one, and what stops the logic at some point?
Look up: Karen Simonyan and Andrew Zisserman, "Very Deep Convolutional Networks for Large-Scale Image Recognition", arXiv preprint arXiv:1409.1556 (2014) - cited in this chapter's footnote 15.

items.term: Classic CNN Architectures: LeNet-5 and AlexNet

blocks.content:
LeNet-5 set the classic CNN layout in 1998; AlexNet kept that layout in 2012, made it much deeper, and added the regularization needed to stop a deep network memorising its training set.

**The question this lesson answers:** what actually changed between the first famous CNN and the one that won ImageNet fourteen years later — in structure, and in how overfitting was held back?

### The big picture

| | LeNet-5 (1998) | AlexNet (2012) |
|---|---|---|
| Layout | conv, pool, conv, pool, dense | same idea, far deeper |
| Stacking | one pooling after each conv | several convs stacked, then pool |
| Regularization | — | 50% dropout plus data augmentation |
| Extra | — | local response normalization |

### 1 · LeNet-5, the template

Early image recognition models struggled to extract complex spatial patterns without overfitting on small datasets. To solve this problem, Yann LeCun introduced **LeNet-5** in 1998, establishing the classic convolutional network layout: alternating convolutional layers and pooling layers followed by fully connected dense layers.

While LeNet-5 successfully recognized handwritten digits, deeper networks required more capacity and stronger regularization to prevent overfitting on large-scale datasets. **Capacity** is how much a model is able to represent — more layers and filters means more capacity. **Regularization** is anything you add deliberately to stop a model fitting its training data too closely.

### 2 · AlexNet's structural change

In 2012, the **AlexNet** architecture expanded upon LeNet-5 by introducing a significantly deeper structure. Unlike LeNet-5, AlexNet was the first network to stack multiple convolutional layers directly on top of one another before applying max pooling.

That one change is worth pausing on: LeNet-5 pooled after every convolution, so the picture shrank constantly and there was little room to get deep. Letting two or three convolutions run back to back at the same resolution before pooling is what made depth affordable. The book records the payoff — AlexNet, built by Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton, won the 2012 ImageNet challenge with a top-five error rate of 17% while the second-best entry managed only 26%.

### 3 · Regularization one: dropout

It achieved superior generalization through two primary regularization techniques. The first is applying a 50% dropout rate to its fully connected layers: on each training step half the neurons in those layers are ignored, so no single neuron can become indispensable.

### 4 · Regularization two: data augmentation

The second is utilizing **data augmentation**. As Figure 14-13 below shows, data augmentation artificially expands a dataset by creating realistic variations of images through random shifting, horizontal flipping, and contrast modifications. This forces the model to remain invariant to changes in orientation, brightness, and position.

The card below adds the rule that makes it work: the variations must be *learnable*. Shifting, rotating and resizing teach the model something real about position, orientation and size; contrast changes teach it about lighting; horizontal flips work except for text and other asymmetrical objects. Simply adding white noise will not help, because noise carries no pattern to learn. The ideal test is that a human should not be able to tell an augmented image from an original.

### 5 · Local response normalization: make the maps disagree

Additionally, AlexNet introduced a competitive normalization step called **local response normalization** (LRN). As Equation 14-2 below shows, LRN calculates a normalized output b_i by dividing a neuron's activation a_i by a factor derived from the squared activations of neighboring feature maps within a depth radius r.

"Neighboring" here means neighbouring in *depth*, not in space — the feature maps sitting directly above and below this one in the stack, at the very same pixel position. For example, setting the hyperparameter r = 5 causes a strongly activated neuron to laterally inhibit neighboring neurons at the same spatial coordinates across adjacent feature maps. **Inhibit** means damp down: the louder this map shouts at a location, the more the other maps' outputs at that location get divided down.

This biological inhibition encourages individual feature maps to specialize in distinct visual patterns. If two filters both learn "vertical edge", they fight, and one of them is pushed to find something else — so the layer explores a wider range of features. The explanation under Equation 14-2 below walks every symbol and plugs in AlexNet's own settings.

The essential insight to remember is that scaling up network depth requires combining stacked convolutional layers with strong regularization methods, such as data augmentation and competitive normalization, to prevent severe overfitting.

**One-liner for your notes:** AlexNet is LeNet-5 made deep — convolutions stacked back to back before pooling — held together by 50% dropout, realistic data augmentation, and LRN, which makes neighbouring feature maps compete so they specialise.

blocks.title: Data augmentation done right, and the LRN radius
blocks.content:
**Data augmentation** artificially enlarges the training set by generating many realistic variants of each training instance, which reduces overfitting. Ideally, a human should not be able to tell whether an image was augmented. Simply adding white noise will not help, because the modifications should be learnable and white noise is not. As Figure 14-13 shows, you can slightly shift, rotate and resize every picture, which makes the model more tolerant to variations in the position, orientation and size of objects. Images with various contrasts make it tolerant to lighting, and horizontal flips work except for text and other asymmetrical objects.

In Equation 14-2, $r$ is the depth radius. For example, with $r = 2$ a strongly activated neuron inhibits the neurons located in the feature maps immediately above and below its own. AlexNet uses $r = 5$, $\alpha = 0.0001$, $\beta = 0.75$ and $k = 2$.

blocks.title: Figure 14-13
blocks.caption: Generating new training instances from existing ones
blocks.alt: Figure 14-13: Generating new training instances from existing ones

blocks.title: Equation 14-2
blocks.caption: Local response normalization (LRN)
blocks.latex: b_i = a_i \left( k + \alpha \sum_{j=j_{\text{low}}}^{j_{\text{high}}} {a_j}^2 \right)^{-\beta} \quad \text{with} \quad \begin{cases} j_{\text{high}} = \min \left( i + \frac{r}{2}, f_n - 1 \right) \\ j_{\text{low}} = \max \left( 0, i - \frac{r}{2} \right) \end{cases}
blocks.explain:
**Why the equation looks like this**

Local response normalization is a divide-by-how-loud-your-neighbours-are step. The goal is that a
neuron's output should be damped when the *other* feature maps at the same pixel are also firing
hard, so that the maps are pushed to compete rather than all learning the same thing. That goal
fixes the shape: keep the neuron's own activation, and divide it by a number that grows with its
neighbours' activity.

Four details follow from that, and each one is a deliberate choice:

- The neighbours' activations are **squared** before being added, so size counts and sign does not,
and one very loud neighbour counts for far more than several mild ones.
- The sum runs only over feature maps within a depth radius r of map i. These are neighbours in
*depth*, at the very same row and column — not neighbours in space.
- The whole bracket is raised to the power minus beta, and a negative power means division: raising
to minus beta is "divide by the bracket raised to beta". Beta is 0.75, which makes that division
gentler than dividing by the bracket outright.
- k sits inside the bracket so it can never be zero. If no neighbour fires at all you divide by k to
the power beta, not by nothing.

**Is this standard, or simplified for the example?** It is AlexNet's own formula, given in full, not
a simplification. The book presents it as the competitive normalization step AlexNet applies right
after the ReLU in two of its layers, and gives the exact hyperparameter values that architecture
used.

**The general form.** There is none beyond this. r, alpha, beta and k are the four knobs, and
changing them is the only way the formula varies.

**Terms this introduces:** a **hyperparameter** is a value you choose before training and which
training never changes; the **depth radius** r is how far up and down the stack of feature maps the
competition reaches; **lateral inhibition** is the biological name for one active unit damping its
neighbours; and an **activation** here is the neuron's output after the ReLU and before this
normalization.

**Every piece of Equation 14-2**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| b sub i | b sub i | the normalized output for the neuron in feature map i, at one row and column |
| a sub i | a sub i | that same neuron's activation, after ReLU and before normalization |
| a sub j | a sub j | the activation at the SAME row and column in neighbouring feature map j |
| k | k | the bias: a constant inside the bracket so it is never zero |
| alpha | alpha | how strongly the neighbours' squared activations count |
| beta | beta | how hard the division bites |
| r | r | the depth radius: how many neighbouring maps take part |
| f sub n | f sub n | the total number of feature maps in the layer |
| the sum sign | sum of a sub j squared, from j low to j high | add up the neighbours' squared activations |
| j low = max of 0 and i minus r over 2 | — | the lowest neighbouring map, clipped so you cannot run off the bottom |
| j high = min of i plus r over 2 and f sub n minus 1 | — | the highest neighbouring map, clipped at the last one |
| the power minus beta | to the minus beta | divide by the bracket raised to beta |

**The formula in plain words**

normalized output = the neuron's own activation, divided by (a constant, plus a small multiple of the
summed squares of its depth-neighbours' activations), with that whole bracket raised to the power
beta first.

**Real numbers plugged in**

AlexNet uses r = 5, alpha = 0.0001, beta = 0.75 and k = 2, so the equation becomes:

b sub i = a sub i × (2 + 0.0001 × the sum of the neighbours' squared activations) to the power
minus 0.75.

Two cases are worth seeing:

1. **Quiet neighbours.** If the neighbouring activations are all near zero, the sum is near zero and
the bracket is 2 to the power minus 0.75, which is about 0.59. Every neuron is scaled by that same
constant, so nothing changes relative to anything else.
2. **A loud neighbourhood.** alpha is deliberately tiny at 0.0001, so it takes a large summed energy
before the bracket moves at all. That is the design: LRN only bites when the competition at that
pixel is genuinely strong.

And for the radius itself, the card below gives the small case: with r = 2, j low is i minus 1 and
j high is i plus 1, so a strongly activated neuron inhibits the neurons in the feature maps
immediately above and below its own.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow import keras

# Local Response Normalization implemented as a Keras layer
lrn_layer = keras.layers.Lambda(
    lambda x: tf.nn.local_response_normalization(
        x, depth_radius=5, bias=2.0, alpha=0.0001, beta=0.75
    )
)
```

items.term: Data augmentation is a way of stating what should not matter
items.text: Every augmentation is a claim about the task: flipping horizontally says left-right orientation is irrelevant, changing contrast says lighting is irrelevant. That is why white noise fails - it is not a claim about anything - and why horizontal flips are wrong for text, where orientation carries the meaning. Choose augmentations by asking which transformations genuinely leave the label unchanged in your domain, not by copying a list.

items.term: Competition between units is a recurring idea worth recognising
items.text: LRN makes feature maps at the same location suppress each other so they are pushed to specialise. The same instinct - force units to disagree rather than hoping they will - shows up in dropout, which stops neurons co-adapting, and later in the squeeze-and-excitation blocks that reweight channels against each other. Redundant units are the failure mode; competition is one family of answers to it.

items.term: Why this normalization step faded and what replaced its job
items.text: LRN normalizes across a handful of neighbouring feature maps at one spatial position, using four hand-chosen hyperparameters. Later architectures in this same chapter use batch normalization instead, which rescales a layer's outputs using statistics gathered over the batch and has no depth radius to tune. Notice what carried over and what did not: the goal of keeping activations well-behaved survived; the specific lateral-inhibition mechanism did not.

blocks.title: Key points
items: LeNet-5 established the foundational CNN design using stacked convolution, average pooling, and dense layers.
AlexNet increased model capacity by stacking multiple convolutional layers directly on top of each other.
Data augmentation reduces overfitting by generating realistic variants of training images.
Local response normalization encourages feature map specialization through competitive lateral inhibition.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: AlexNet stacked two of its five convolutional layers before pooling, not all of them. What decided which layers were stacked, and was that choice ever justified beyond trial and error?

Look up: Alex Krizhevsky et al., "ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks", Proceedings of the 25th International Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems 1 (2012): 1097-1105 - cited in this chapter's footnote 11.

items.term: GoogLeNet and Inception Modules

blocks.content:
GoogLeNet's trick is a sub-network, the inception module, that looks at the same input through several kernel sizes at once — and uses 1 × 1 convolutions to make that affordable.

**The question this lesson answers:** objects appear at different sizes, so which kernel size should a layer use? GoogLeNet's answer is "all of them, in parallel" — and the interesting part is how it pays for that.

### The big picture

```
        ┌─ 1x1 ─────────────┐
input ──┼─ 1x1 -> 3x3 ──────┼─> depth concat
        ├─ 1x1 -> 5x5 ──────┤
        └─ 3x3 pool -> 1x1 ─┘
 all stride 1, same padding -> same H and W
```

### 1 · Four branches, one output

Deep neural networks face heavy computational costs and overfitting risks when scaled up using traditional stacks of layers. To solve this efficiency problem, the **GoogLeNet** architecture introduces sub-networks called **inception modules**. These modules enable the network to capture multi-scale spatial patterns while keeping the parameter count low.

As Figure 14-14 below demonstrates, an inception module feeds its input signal into four parallel branches simultaneously. The layers inside these paths utilize different kernel sizes, specifically 1 × 1, 3 × 3, and 5 × 5, alongside a max pooling layer.

### 2 · Why the outputs can be glued together

Because all four paths use a stride of 1 and standard same padding, every output feature map retains the exact height and width of the input. Consequently, a final depth concatenation layer stacks all output feature maps along the channel dimension.

This is the whole reason the module is legal. Concatenating along depth is a `UNION` of columns, not of rows: the grids must line up exactly, or there is nothing to stack. Same padding and stride 1 on every branch is what guarantees they do.

### 3 · The 1 × 1 convolution, which sounds useless and is not

A key innovation inside the inception module is the use of 1 × 1 convolutional layers. A filter that sees one pixel cannot possibly find a shape — so what is it for?

While a single pixel filter cannot extract spatial structures, it captures relationships across channel dimensions. Remember that a neuron's receptive field always spans the full depth: a 1 × 1 filter still reads every channel at that one position. It is a learned mix of the channels, applied identically at every pixel.

Furthermore, when configured to output fewer feature maps than its input, a 1 × 1 convolution acts as a **bottleneck layer** that drastically reduces channel depth. **Bottleneck** means deliberately narrow: fewer channels come out than went in.

For example, before running a costly 5 × 5 convolution on a high-dimensional feature map, a 1 × 1 convolution reduces the channel depth first, cutting down both parameter counts and memory footprint. A 5 × 5 filter costs 25 weights for every input channel, so cutting the input channels first is where the saving lands.

### 4 · The full network, and where the parameters went

GoogLeNet combines nine of these inception modules into a single tall stack, as illustrated in Figure 14-15 below.

Near the top of the network, a **global average pooling layer** computes the spatial mean of each feature map. This removes remaining spatial location details and eliminates the need for massive fully connected layers, reducing parameters to roughly 6 million — ten times fewer than AlexNet, which held roughly 60 million.

Throwing away location is safe here precisely because the task is classification: you want to know *whether* there is a dog, not where. And it is the fully connected layers, not the convolutions, that were holding most of the weights — so deleting them is what the parameter count reflects. The book records the result: GoogLeNet won the 2014 ImageNet challenge, pushing the top-five error rate below 7%.

### 5 · The runner-up, for contrast

The card below describes **VGGNet**, the entry that came second that year. It is the opposite design philosophy: no parallel branches at all, just 2 or 3 convolutional layers and a pooling layer, then again 2 or 3 convolutional layers and a pooling layer, reaching 16 or 19 convolutional layers, all built from small 3 × 3 filters — but a great many of them.

The single most important insight to remember is that 1 × 1 bottleneck convolutions allow deep networks to process multi-scale spatial features efficiently without parameter explosion.

**One-liner for your notes:** an inception module runs 1 × 1, 3 × 3, 5 × 5 and pooling in parallel and concatenates them along depth — possible because every branch is stride 1 with same padding, and affordable because 1 × 1 bottlenecks cut the channel count first.

blocks.title: VGGNet, the runner-up of 2014
blocks.content: The runner-up in the ILSVRC 2014 challenge, which GoogLeNet won, was **VGGNet**, developed by Karen Simonyan and Andrew Zisserman of the Visual Geometry Group (VGG) research lab at Oxford University. Unlike GoogLeNet with its inception modules, VGGNet has a very simple and classical architecture: 2 or 3 convolutional layers and a pooling layer, then again 2 or 3 convolutional layers and a pooling layer, and so on, for a total of 16 or 19 convolutional layers depending on the variant. It ends with a final dense network made of 2 hidden layers and the output layer. It uses small 3 × 3 filters, but it has many of them.
