blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
base_model = tf.keras.applications.xception.Xception(
    weights="imagenet", include_top=False
)
avg = tf.keras.layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(base_model.output)
class_output = tf.keras.layers.Dense(n_classes, activation="softmax")(avg)
loc_output = tf.keras.layers.Dense(4)(avg)
model = tf.keras.Model(
    inputs=base_model.input, outputs=[class_output, loc_output]
)
model.compile(
    loss=["sparse_categorical_crossentropy", "mse"],
    loss_weights=[0.8, 0.2],
    optimizer=optimizer,
    metrics=["accuracy"],
)
```

items.term: Two heads on one trunk is the general pattern for multi-task learning
items.text: The tasks share a feature extractor and diverge only at the last layer, which is cheaper than two networks and often more accurate than either alone, because the localisation signal teaches the shared features something the class labels alone would not. It also creates a coupling: the two tasks now compete for the same representation, which is what the loss weights are there to arbitrate.

items.term: Training loss and evaluation metric are allowed to differ, and usually should
items.text: MSE is used to train because it is smooth and differentiable everywhere; IoU is used to report because it means something to a human. That split is normal across machine learning - the quantity you can optimise is rarely the quantity you care about. The thing to watch is that they stay correlated, because when they drift apart the model happily optimises the one you are not reading.

items.term: The square-root trick is a statement about relative error
items.text: Raw MSE on width and height treats a 10-pixel miss as equally bad on a tiny object and a huge one, which does not match how anyone judges a bounding box. Predicting square roots makes the penalty grow more slowly for large boxes, shifting the model's effort toward the small ones. This is the same reasoning behind taking logs of a skewed target - you are reshaping the loss to match what an error actually costs.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Object localization is framed as a regression task that predicts four continuous values for a bounding box.
A dual-output network architecture predicts object classes and bounding box coordinates simultaneously.
Bounding box coordinates and dimensions are normalized between 0 and 1 for consistent regression targets.
Mean Squared Error (MSE) is commonly used to train the regression output, while Intersection over Union (IoU) evaluates bounding box overlap accuracy.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Getting bounding box labels is described as one of the hardest and costliest parts of a vision project. What does a realistic annotation workflow look like, and how is label quality actually checked?
Look up: Adriana Kovashka et al., "Crowdsourcing in Computer Vision", Foundations and Trends in Computer Graphics and Vision 10, no. 3 (2014): 177-243 - cited in this chapter's footnote 29.

items.term: Sliding-CNN Object Detection

blocks.content:
The first approach to finding several objects was brute force: take a single-object CNN, slide it over every region of the image, then throw away the duplicate boxes.

**The question this lesson answers:** your network can classify and localise one centred object. How do you use it on a photograph containing three roses in different places — and what stops you getting nine boxes for three flowers?

### The big picture

```
5x7 grid, CNN reads every 3x3 region -> 15 predictions
each: class probabilities + box + objectness
then non-max suppression removes the duplicates
```

### 1 · Why one box is not enough

Standard image classification models assume a single target object is centered within an image. When an image contains multiple objects at arbitrary positions, standard classification networks fail to localize and identify every instance.

To solve this problem, early computer vision systems used the **sliding-CNN** approach to locate and categorize multiple targets systematically.

### 2 · Slide the window, predict at every stop

This technique divides an image into a regular grid and slides a bounding window across all possible regions. At each step, a trained Convolutional Neural Network evaluates the cropped sub-image to predict class probabilities, bounding box coordinates, and an **objectness score**.

The objectness score represents the estimated probability that an object is centered inside that local window, typically predicted using a single dense unit with a sigmoid activation function. It is a plain yes-or-no question — is anything here? — so it is one unit trained with binary cross-entropy, separate from the class probabilities. The book notes that adding a "no-object" class instead generally worked less well: "is an object present?" and "what type of object is it?" are best answered separately.

As shown in Figure 14-25 below, a window slides across 3 × 3 regions of a 5 × 7 grid, outputting predictions at each location.

| Window over | Objectness | What you do |
|---|---|---|
| a rose, centred | high | keep the box and the class |
| background | low | ignore the whole prediction |

A window centered over a rose produces a high objectness score and bounding box, whereas a window over background pixels yields a low objectness score, allowing the model to ignore invalid predictions.

The card below counts the stops exactly: 5 − 3 + 1 = 3 positions down, 7 − 3 + 1 = 5 across, so 15 predicted boxes. It also makes an important point about them — a predicted box may exceed the boundary of its own 3 × 3 region, and that is fine: even when the CNN cannot see the bottom of a rose, it can make a reasonable guess about where that part is.

### 3 · Non-max suppression, the cleanup pass

Because overlapping sliding windows frequently detect the same object multiple times, postprocessing is necessary.

Systems apply **non-max suppression** in a loop:

1. First discard boxes below a minimum objectness threshold — the network itself says there is nothing there.
2. Select the box with the highest objectness score and keep it.
3. Remove all remaining overlapping boxes that exceed a chosen Intersection over Union (IoU) threshold, such as 60% — heavy overlap with an already-kept box means it is the same object again.
4. Repeat from step 2 until only distinct bounding boxes remain.

The name says what it does: suppress everything that is not the local maximum. And note it is IoU, from the previous lesson, doing the "is this the same object" test — overlap divided by union, with a threshold you pick.

### 4 · The cost

The essential insight is that evaluating candidate regions across spatial grids enables multi-object detection, but redundant predictions must be filtered out using non-max suppression.

The practical problem is speed. Since objects vary in size you may also want to slide the CNN again across larger 4 × 4 regions, multiplying the work again. The approach works pretty well, but it requires running the CNN many times — 15 times in this small example — so it is quite slow. That cost is exactly what the next two lessons remove.

**One-liner for your notes:** slide a single-object CNN over every grid region, have it predict a class, a box and an objectness score at each stop, then keep the highest-objectness box and suppress every remaining box that overlaps it too much — correct, and far too slow.

blocks.title: Worked out: 15 predictions, and the cost
blocks.content:
In Figure 14-25 the image is chopped into a 5 × 7 grid, and the CNN looks at every 3 × 3 region.

1. Vertically, a window 3 cells tall fits in 5 − 3 + 1 = 3 positions.
2. Horizontally, a window 3 cells wide fits in 7 − 3 + 1 = 5 positions.
3. That gives a 3 × 5 grid of 15 predicted bounding boxes, each with its class probabilities and objectness score.

A predicted box may exceed the boundary of its 3 × 3 region: even when the CNN cannot see the bottom part of a rose, it can make a reasonable guess about where that part is. Since objects vary in size, you may slide the CNN again across larger 4 × 4 regions. The approach works pretty well, but it requires running the CNN many times (15 times in this example), so it is quite slow.

blocks.caption: Detecting multiple objects by sliding a CNN across the image
blocks.alt: Figure 14-25: Detecting multiple objects by sliding a CNN across the image

items.term: Objectness is separated from classification on purpose
items.text: The book notes that adding a 'no object' class to the classifier worked less well than a separate objectness output. The reason is that 'is anything here' and 'what is it' are different questions with different evidence, and forcing them into one softmax makes them compete for the same probability mass. Splitting a decision into independent questions when they really are independent is a recurring design move worth keeping.

items.term: Non-max suppression is a heuristic with hyperparameters you own
items.text: Two numbers decide what the detector reports: the objectness threshold and the IoU threshold. Raise the first and you lose faint true detections; lower it and you flood the output. Raise the second and two genuinely overlapping objects get merged into one; lower it and duplicates survive. These are tuned per application, and a detector's reported accuracy is always accuracy at some particular setting of them.

items.term: Redundant computation, not the CNN, is what makes this slow
items.text: Adjacent sliding windows overlap heavily, so the same convolutions are recomputed dozens of times over the same pixels. That observation is the whole content of the next two lessons: if the network were fully convolutional, the shared work would be done once and every window position would come out of a single pass. Recognising redundant recomputation is usually more valuable than making the redundant step faster.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Object detection requires both localizing and classifying multiple objects within an image.
The sliding-CNN approach shifts a classification window across spatial grid regions to generate candidate bounding boxes.
An objectness score estimates whether an object is centered in the current window and allows filtering out empty regions.
Non-max suppression removes redundant, highly overlapping bounding boxes based on objectness scores and IoU thresholds.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Instead of sliding a window everywhere, two-stage detectors first propose a few likely regions. How are those proposals generated, and what does that buy over an exhaustive slide?

Look up: Shaoqing Ren et al., "Faster R-CNN: Towards Real-Time Object Detection with Region Proposal Networks", Proceedings of the 28th International Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems 1 (2015): 91-99 - cited in this chapter's footnote 36.

items.term: Fully Convolutional Networks

blocks.content:
A dense layer can be rewritten as a convolutional layer that computes exactly the same numbers — and once you do that, the network accepts images of any size and returns a whole grid of predictions in one pass.

**The question this lesson answers:** why is a CNN locked to one input size, and what does removing that lock buy you for object detection?

### The big picture

```
dense: N units over an HxW map  ==  conv: N filters
                                   of size HxW, valid
 224 image -> 7x7 bottleneck -> 1x1 grid of N numbers
 448 image -> 14x14         -> 8x8 grid of N numbers
```

### 1 · Where the fixed size comes from

Standard convolutional neural networks (CNNs) rely on dense layers at their output. These dense layers impose a strict constraint: the network can only accept input images of a fixed spatial resolution because each dense neuron requires a fixed number of weights matching the exact spatial size of the input features.

That is the whole reason, and it is mechanical rather than deep. A dense neuron holds one weight per input value. Change the image size, the feature map size changes, the number of input values changes — and the neuron now has the wrong number of weights. This fixed-size restriction prevents traditional CNNs from processing images of arbitrary sizes in a single pass.

Convolutional and pooling layers never had this problem: their weights depend on kernel size and channel count, not on how big the picture is.

### 2 · The conversion

To solve this limitation, **fully convolutional networks** (FCNs) replace the traditional dense output layers with equivalent convolutional layers.

A dense layer with N neurons sitting above a spatial feature map of size H × W can be directly converted into a convolutional layer. This converted layer uses N filters, each of size H × W, with valid padding.

| Dense layer | Equivalent conv layer |
|---|---|
| N units | N filters |
| reads the whole H × W map | filter size H × W |
| — | valid padding |

Because a spatial convolution computes the exact same weighted sums over local regions, the mathematical output of this convolutional layer is identical to the output of the dense layer. Make the filter as big as the whole feature map and, with valid padding, it fits in exactly one position: it computes one weighted sum over every input, plus a bias — which is precisely what one dense neuron does. Nothing is approximated, and you can even copy the dense layer's weights straight across.

However, unlike dense layers, convolutional filters can slide over spatial inputs of any size. That is the entire prize.

### 3 · What happens when you feed it a bigger image

As Figure 14-26 below shows, feeding a larger image into an FCN scales up the spatial size of the feature maps throughout the network.

For example, consider a network trained on 224 × 224 images whose bottleneck feature map is 7 × 7. The **bottleneck** is the last convolutional layer before the output. Replacing its 10-unit dense layer with a convolutional layer using 10 filters of size 7 × 7 yields a single 1 × 1 spatial grid containing 10 predictions — same answer as before, just shaped differently.

If we instead feed this FCN a larger 448 × 448 image, the bottleneck feature map expands to 14 × 14. The final convolutional layer with valid padding then computes predictions across an 8 × 8 spatial grid (14 − 7 + 1 = 8). Each of these 64 grid positions contains the 10 prediction values for that spatial region.

In the book's detection network those 10 numbers are 5 class probabilities, 1 objectness score, and 4 bounding box coordinates — so each of the 64 positions is a full detection.

Once the swap is done there is no dense layer anywhere, which is where the name comes from: a fully convolutional network contains only convolutional layers and spatial pooling layers, and both of those accept any input size.

### 4 · This is the sliding window, done once

Compare it with the previous lesson. There, you ran the CNN 15 separate times. Here the same 8 × 8 = 64 window positions are computed by one forward pass, because the convolution is already a sliding operation and the shared work between overlapping windows is done once instead of 64 times.

The key insight to remember is that replacing dense layers with equivalent convolutional layers allows a neural network to process images of any spatial resolution in a single forward pass, efficiently sliding predictions across larger inputs.

**One-liner for your notes:** a dense layer of N units over an H × W map equals N filters of size H × W with valid padding — swap them and the network loses its fixed input size and starts returning a grid of predictions from one pass instead of one prediction per crop.

items.term: The equivalence is exact, which is why the weights transfer
items.text: This is not an approximation that trades a little accuracy for flexibility - a filter as large as the feature map under valid padding computes the identical weighted sum a dense neuron does. That is why a trained classifier can be converted after the fact by copying its weights, with no retraining. Exact reformulations like this are rare and worth spotting, because they give you a new capability for free.

items.term: Weight sharing is what makes 'any input size' possible
items.text: A dense layer is tied to its input size because it has a separate weight per input. A convolutional layer has weights per kernel position and per channel, quantities that do not depend on the picture at all, so there is simply nothing in it to break when the image grows. Every size-flexible property in this chapter traces back to that one asymmetry.

items.term: One pass over a big image versus many passes over crops
items.text: Both compute the same 64 predictions; the FCN does it once because overlapping windows share intermediate results and the convolution computes them a single time. Two caveats keep this honest: the arithmetic is identical only when the strides divide evenly and padding is consistent, and the whole large image's activations must fit in memory at once, which the crop-by-crop version never required.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Dense layers require fixed spatial input shapes because their weight matrices have a static size.
A dense layer converts to a convolutional layer by setting filter count to unit count and filter size to the feature map size with valid padding.
Fully convolutional networks consist entirely of convolutional and pooling layers, accepting arbitrary image dimensions.
Processing larger images in an FCN outputs spatial grids of predictions instead of single vector outputs.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The 448 by 448 example divides evenly down to 14 by 14. What happens to the output grid when the input size does not divide neatly, or when a layer uses a stride other than 1 or 2?
Look up: footnotes 31 and 32 of this chapter, which state the exceptions, and Jonathan Long et al., "Fully Convolutional Networks for Semantic Segmentation", CVPR (2015): 3431-3440.

items.term: The You Only Look Once Object Detection Model

blocks.content:
YOLO makes object detection one regression problem solved in one forward pass — hence the name, You Only Look Once — which is what makes real-time video detection possible.

**The question this lesson answers:** if every grid cell gets to predict boxes, how does the model decide which cell owns which object, and what does it do when two objects share a cell?

### The big picture

```
image -> grid of cells; each cell outputs:
   box 1 + objectness · box 2 + objectness
   ONE class probability distribution (shared)
 a cell owns an object if that object's CENTER is in it
```

### 1 · One pass instead of two stages

Standard object detection systems often rely on multi-step pipelines that propose candidate regions before running full classification networks. This two-stage approach causes significant processing delays and prevents real-time video analysis.

The **You Only Look Once** (YOLO) architecture, proposed by Joseph Redmon et al. in a 2015 paper, solves this efficiency problem by treating object detection as a single regression task, predicting bounding boxes and class probabilities directly from an image in one forward pass.

### 2 · Who owns an object: the centre rule

To accomplish this, YOLO divides an image into a grid of cells. Each grid cell is responsible for detecting any object whose bounding box center falls within that specific cell.

This rule is doing real work. An object usually overlaps many cells, so without a tie-breaker every one of them would claim it and you would be back to deduplicating dozens of boxes. Keying ownership to the single cell holding the centre means exactly one cell is responsible, by construction.

### 3 · Coordinates are local, sizes are not

The coordinates of the bounding box are defined relative to the cell, ranging from (0, 0) at the top-left to (1, 1) at the bottom-right, although the overall width and height of the bounding box can extend across surrounding grid cells.

| Quantity | Measured against | Range |
|---|---|---|
| centre x and y | the owning cell | 0 to 1 |
| width and height | the image | may exceed the cell |

The centre must be inside the cell — that is what ownership means — so a 0-to-1 coordinate is exactly right for it and easy for a sigmoid to produce. The size has no such limit: a car is far bigger than one cell.

### 4 · Two boxes, one class distribution

To handle multiple objects with nearby centers, each grid cell predicts two distinct bounding boxes alongside their corresponding confidence scores, known as **objectness scores**.

For example, imagine a single grid cell containing the center points for both a tall person and a wide car. The grid cell generates two bounding boxes: a narrow vertical box for the person and a wide horizontal box for the car.

But the model outputs a single class probability distribution per grid cell, such as predicting high probabilities for both person and car classes. Note the asymmetry — two boxes, one shared set of class scores. In the original YOLO that distribution covers 20 classes, because it was trained on the PASCAL VOC dataset.

### 5 · Matching boxes to classes afterwards

That asymmetry leaves a puzzle: which of the two boxes is the person and which is the car?

During postprocessing, the system evaluates how well the geometry of each predicted bounding box matches the spatial regions of the class probability map, correctly matching the vertical box to the person class and the horizontal box to the car class. Across the whole image, the class probability map has a large region where "car" dominates and a smaller region inside it where "person" dominates; each box is assigned the class whose region it lines up with.

The card below places YOLO among its relatives: SSD and EfficientDet are also "look once" models, while **Faster R-CNN** is the two-stage kind — a CNN, then a region proposal network that suggests likely boxes, then a classifier run for each proposed box.

The key insight behind YOLO is that framing detection as a single spatial grid evaluation yields exceptional processing speed, enabling real-time detection on video streams without sacrificing overall accuracy.

**One-liner for your notes:** YOLO splits the image into cells, gives each cell two boxes with objectness scores and one shared class distribution, assigns an object to the cell holding its centre with cell-relative coordinates, and gets all of it from a single forward pass.

blocks.title: Look-once models versus Faster R-CNN
blocks.content: YOLO is so fast that it can run in real time on a video. Like a fully convolutional network, it processes the whole image only once instead of running a CNN on many separate regions, and SSD and EfficientDet are also "look once" detection models. **Faster R-CNN** is more complex. The image first goes through a CNN, then the output is passed to a region proposal network (RPN) that proposes the bounding boxes most likely to contain an object, and finally a classifier is run for each proposed bounding box, based on the cropped output of the CNN. A look-once model skips those separate proposal and per-box classification stages and makes all of its predictions in a single pass.

items.term: Assigning responsibility by centre is how the duplicate problem is designed away
items.text: The sliding-CNN approach produced duplicates and then removed them afterwards with non-max suppression. YOLO instead makes duplicates structurally unlikely: exactly one cell owns each object, by a rule that needs no postprocessing to enforce. Preventing a class of error in the representation is almost always better than detecting and repairing it later - though note YOLO still runs non-max suppression, because two cells can still both fire.

items.term: One class distribution per cell is a real limitation, not just a detail
items.text: Sharing one distribution between two boxes is what forces the awkward postprocessing step that matches box geometry to regions of the class map, and it fails when two different classes have centres in the same cell. Later versions of YOLO give each box its own class scores. Seeing why the original design needed that fix-up is a good way to understand what later versions were buying.

items.term: Cell-relative coordinates make the regression easy to learn
items.text: Predicting an absolute pixel coordinate means the target range depends on the image size and most of the range is wrong for any given cell. Predicting an offset within the owning cell means every target lies in 0 to 1 and a sigmoid produces exactly that range. Reframing a target so its natural range matches the output activation is a small change that makes a large difference to how easily a network learns it.

blocks.title: Key points
items: YOLO processes an entire image in a single pass by dividing it into a spatial grid.
A grid cell predicts objects only if the center of their bounding box falls inside that cell.
Each grid cell outputs two bounding boxes with objectness scores and one class probability distribution.
Bounding box coordinates are normalized relative to the cell, but box dimensions can extend beyond cell boundaries.
Postprocessing matches individual bounding boxes to class probability map regions to resolve final object labels.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Later YOLO versions introduced anchor priors - predefined box shapes the model adjusts rather than predicting sizes from scratch. Why does starting from a prior shape help, and how are the priors chosen?

Look up: Joseph Redmon et al., "You Only Look Once: Unified, Real-Time Object Detection", Proceedings of the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (2016): 779-788 - cited in this chapter's footnote 33.

items.term: Object Tracking with DeepSORT

blocks.content:
Tracking is not detection repeated — it is the problem of deciding which box in this frame is the same object as which box in the last one, and DeepSORT answers it with motion *plus* appearance.

**The question this lesson answers:** two balls collide and bounce apart. Why does a position-only tracker swap their identities, and what extra signal fixes it?

### The big picture

```
new detections ─> deep embedder (what it looks like) ─┐
existing tracks ─> Kalman filter (where it should be) ─┤
                     Hungarian algorithm  <────────────┘
                     -> updated tracks
```

### 1 · Why tracking is hard

Object tracking in video streams is challenging because objects move, change orientation, alter appearance under different lighting, and become temporarily occluded. **Occluded** means hidden behind something else.

Simple detection models treat each frame independently, which makes maintaining consistent identity labels across consecutive frames difficult. A detector gives you three boxes this frame and three boxes next frame; nothing in it says which is which. That matching step is the **association problem**.

The **DeepSORT** algorithm solves this association problem by combining classical state estimation algorithms with modern deep learning representations. **State estimation** means guessing where something is now from where it has been.

### 2 · The three components

DeepSORT operates using three main components working together.

| Component | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| Kalman filter | where should this track be now? |
| deep learning model | how similar do these two look? |
| Hungarian algorithm | which detection goes with which track? |

First, it uses a **Kalman filter** to predict the expected position of an existing target in the current frame, relying on the assumption that objects generally maintain constant velocities. **Constant velocity** means same speed, same direction — a straight-line guess.

Next, a **deep learning model** generates appearance feature embeddings for newly detected objects, allowing the system to measure visual similarity between existing targets and new bounding boxes. An **embedding** is a short list of numbers standing for what something looks like; two crops of the same object give two nearby lists.

Finally, the **Hungarian algorithm** computes an optimal assignment that maps new detections to tracked objects by simultaneously minimizing positional distance and visual discrepancy. It is a classical method for the assignment problem: given a cost for every possible pairing, find the set of pairings with the lowest total cost. Crucially it optimises the assignment as a whole rather than greedily taking the best match one at a time.

### 3 · The bouncing balls, step by step

To understand this interaction, consider a scenario where a red ball and a blue ball collide and bounce off each other in opposite directions.

1. Based strictly on prior motion vectors, the Kalman filter predicts that both balls will continue straight, effectively passing through each other. It has no model of collisions — constant velocity is the only assumption it makes.
2. If the system evaluated only bounding box positions, the matching algorithm would incorrectly swap their identities after the bounce, because each ball's new position sits closest to the *other* ball's prediction.
3. However, because DeepSORT incorporates the appearance resemblance score from its deep learning model, the matching step recognizes that the red object's visual appearance matches its original track rather than the blue one, correctly preserving their identities despite the abrupt trajectory change.

The two signals fail in different situations, which is exactly why using both works. Motion breaks when an object does something unexpected; appearance breaks when two objects look alike. Combined into one cost, each covers for the other — though note the honest limit: if the two balls were the same colour, appearance would have nothing to contribute.

### 4 · What the combination buys

The essential insight of DeepSORT is that combining motion estimation with visual feature embeddings prevents tracking errors during sudden directional changes or occlusions. An object that disappears behind a pillar and reappears has a broken motion history but an intact look.

**One-liner for your notes:** Kalman filter says where each track should be, a deep model says what each track looks like, and the Hungarian algorithm assigns detections to tracks on the combined cost — so a bounce or an occlusion no longer swaps identities.

items.term: Fusing two signals works because they fail independently
items.text: Motion prediction breaks when an object does something unexpected; appearance breaks when two objects look alike. Combining them into one assignment cost covers each failure with the other's strength - which also tells you exactly when DeepSORT still breaks: identical-looking objects that collide. Whenever you see two cues combined, ask what each one's failure mode is and whether they overlap.

items.term: Global assignment beats greedy matching
items.text: The Hungarian algorithm finds the set of pairings with the lowest total cost, rather than repeatedly taking the best available pair. Those differ: a greedy first choice can force two later pairings that are both terrible. Tracking is full of these situations, because the detections in a frame compete for the same tracks, and solving the whole frame at once is what keeps one ambiguous object from corrupting its neighbours.

items.term: The constant-velocity assumption is doing more work than it appears
items.text: The Kalman filter's whole prediction rests on objects continuing at the same speed and direction, which is wrong at every bounce, turn and stop - and it is still useful, because it is right between those moments and it degrades predictably. That is the useful shape of a good approximation: cheap, correct most of the time, and wrong in ways another signal can cover.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Object tracking maintains consistent identities across video frames despite motion, scale changes, and occlusions.
Kalman filters estimate future positions by assuming objects move at a constant velocity.
Deep learning models extract visual embeddings to evaluate resemblance between detections and tracked objects.
The Hungarian algorithm finds the optimal mapping by minimizing position distances and appearance differences.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: DeepSORT's appearance model must produce embeddings that stay stable as an object turns and changes lighting. How is such a model trained, given that its target is similarity rather than a class?
Look up: Nicolai Wojke et al., "Simple Online and Realtime Tracking with a Deep Association Metric", arXiv preprint arXiv:1703.07402 (2017) - cited in this chapter's footnote 38.

items.term: Semantic Segmentation with FCNs

blocks.content:
Labelling every pixel means you have to undo the shrinking a CNN spent its whole depth doing — with a trainable upsampling layer, plus skip connections that fetch back the detail from lower layers.

**The question this lesson answers:** the network knows there is a bicycle somewhere in the bottom left. How do you get from that to a label on every single pixel?

### The big picture

```
downsample x32 (strides + pooling)  ->  coarse but semantic
  upsample x2  +  add a lower, sharper layer
  upsample x16                         ->  full resolution
```

### 1 · What the CNN threw away

Standard convolutional neural networks downsample images through strided convolutions and pooling layers. While this helps identify global object presence, it destroys spatial resolution, making precise pixel-level localization impossible.

**Semantic segmentation** solves this problem by classifying every individual pixel into an object category, such as road, car, or sky. The card below draws the line to **instance segmentation**: in semantic segmentation different objects of the same class are not distinguished, so all the bicycles in Figure 14-27 below end up as one big lump of pixels, whereas instance segmentation identifies each individual bicycle — as Mask R-CNN does by adding a pixel mask to each bounding box.

The size of the problem is concrete: the book's network applies an overall stride of 32, meaning its last layer outputs feature maps 32 times smaller than the input image. Those maps know *what* is present and barely anything about *where*.

### 2 · Transposed convolutions: trainable upsampling

To restore lost spatial resolution, Fully Convolutional Networks (FCNs) use **transposed convolutional layers** for upsampling. **Upsampling** means producing a bigger grid than you were given.

As Figure 14-28 below shows, a transposed convolution stretches an input tensor by inserting zeros between elements before applying a standard convolution with learnable parameters. Spread the values out, fill the gaps with zeros, then convolve — and because that convolution has weights, the layer *learns* how to fill the gaps rather than following a fixed rule.

That is the advantage over plain **bilinear interpolation**, which averages neighbouring pixels by a fixed formula and, as the book notes, only works reasonably up to about a factor of 4 or 8.

Watch the stride here, because it behaves backwards from everything else in this chapter: in a transposed convolutional layer the stride defines how much the input is stretched, not the size of the filter steps, so the larger the stride, the larger the output.

| Layer | Larger stride means |
|---|---|
| Conv2D, pooling | smaller output |
| Conv2DTranspose | larger output |

### 3 · Why one big upsample is not enough

However, directly upsampling a heavily downsampled feature map (e.g., by a factor of 32) yields blurry predictions. There is simply no fine detail left in a map 32 times too small to invent the edge of a bicycle wheel from — the information is gone, not hidden.

### 4 · Skip connections fetch the detail back

To recover fine spatial details, architectures introduce **skip connections** from earlier, higher-resolution layers.

As shown in Figure 14-29 below, an FCN upsamples its bottleneck feature map by a factor of 2, adds the higher-resolution feature map from a lower layer, and then upsamples the combined result by a factor of 16 to recover the full input resolution. Two times sixteen is thirty-two, so the total scaling still undoes the network's overall stride — it is just done in two moves with a sharper ingredient mixed in between.

These skip connections have the same shape as ResNet's, but a different job. In ResNet they carried the gradient down; here they carry *resolution* forward. The lower layer knows exactly where the edges are and very little about what they belong to; the upsampled bottleneck knows what it is looking at and roughly where. Adding them gives a map with both.

### 5 · Dilated convolutions, the free receptive field

The card below adds one more tool. Setting `dilation_rate` to 2 or more on a convolutional layer inserts rows and columns of zeros into the filter: a 1 × 3 filter `[[1,2,3]]` with a dilation rate of 4 becomes `[[1, 0, 0, 0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 3]]`. The layer gets a larger receptive field at no computational price and with no extra parameters.

That matters here specifically because the usual way to see more of the image is to downsample — and downsampling is the thing segmentation cannot afford. Dilation widens the view without shrinking anything, and the zeros cost nothing because there are still only three weights to learn and three multiplications to do.

The essential insight is that combining deep semantic features from higher layers with fine spatial details from lower layers via skip connections enables accurate pixel-level classification.

**One-liner for your notes:** segmentation needs the resolution a CNN's strides destroyed, so an FCN upsamples with trainable transposed convolutions (bigger stride, bigger output) and adds in lower, sharper layers through skip connections — with dilated filters widening the view for free.

blocks.title: Instance segmentation, strides and dilation
blocks.content:
In semantic segmentation, different objects of the same class are not distinguished: all the bicycles in Figure 14-27 end up as one big lump of pixels. **Instance segmentation** is similar, but each object is distinguished from the others, so it identifies each individual bicycle. Mask R-CNN does this by extending Faster R-CNN with a pixel mask for each bounding box.

In a transposed convolutional layer (`Conv2DTranspose`), the stride defines how much the input is stretched, not the size of the filter steps, so the larger the stride, the larger the output. Setting `dilation_rate` to 2 or more on a convolutional layer inserts rows and columns of zeros into the filter: a 1 × 3 filter `[[1,2,3]]` with a dilation rate of 4 becomes `[[1, 0, 0, 0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 3]]`. The layer gets a larger receptive field at no computational price and with no extra parameters.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

# Transposed convolution to upsample spatial resolution by a factor of 2
upsample_layer = tf.keras.layers.Conv2DTranspose(
    filters=64,
    kernel_size=3,
    strides=2,
    padding="same",
    activation="relu"
)

# À-trous (dilated) convolution for expanded receptive field
dilated_layer = tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(
    filters=64,
    kernel_size=3,
    dilation_rate=2,
    padding="same",
    activation="relu"
)
```

items.term: Information that has been discarded cannot be upsampled back
items.text: A trainable upsampling layer can learn a better interpolation than a fixed rule, but it cannot recover detail that a stride-32 network already destroyed - which is exactly why one big upsample gives blurry masks. The skip connections are not a refinement, they are the only source of the missing information. Whenever a pipeline needs precision it threw away earlier, look for a path back to the stage that still had it.

items.term: The same wiring, two completely different purposes
items.text: ResNet's skip connections exist to carry gradients through depth; an FCN's exist to carry resolution forward to the output. Both add a lower layer's signal to a higher one, and the motivation is unrelated. This is worth noticing because architecture diagrams look alike while meaning different things - reading a skip connection always requires asking what it is rescuing.

items.term: Dilation attacks the trade-off rather than accepting it
items.text: The usual way to see more of an image is to downsample, which is the one thing segmentation cannot afford. Dilated filters widen the receptive field without shrinking anything and without extra weights, which makes them the natural tool for dense prediction. The catch is what dilation does not fix: with large rates the sampled positions are sparse, so fine local structure between the holes is simply not looked at.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Semantic segmentation classifies every pixel into a class without separating individual object instances.
Strided layers in traditional CNNs cause loss of fine spatial resolution.
Transposed convolutional layers perform trainable upsampling by stretching inputs with zeros.
Skip connections combine high-level semantic features with high-resolution lower-layer outputs.
Dilated convolutions increase the receptive field without adding extra parameters or downsampling.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Semantic segmentation merges every bicycle into one region. What has to be added to separate them, and where in the pipeline does that extra work happen?
Look up: Kaiming He et al., "Mask R-CNN", arXiv preprint arXiv:1703.06870 (2017) - cited in this chapter's footnote 40.

sections.title: Chapter 15: Processing Sequences Using RNNs and CNNs

items.term: Recurrent Neurons and Layers

blocks.content:
A recurrent neuron is an ordinary neuron with one extra wire: its own output from the previous time step comes back in as a second input.

**The question this lesson answers:** a feedforward network takes a fixed-size input and reads it once, in one direction. Sentences, audio and daily ridership arrive as **sequential data** of arbitrary length. How do you give a neuron a memory of what came before it?

### The big picture

```
 x(t) ───┐
         ├──> [ neuron ] ──> y(t) ──┬──> out
 y(t-1) ─┘         ^                │
                   └────────────────┘
                     one step later
```

That loop is the whole idea. Everything else in this lesson is bookkeeping about shapes.

### 1 · Why feedforward networks cannot do this

Standard feedforward neural networks accept a fixed-size input and process data strictly in one direction from input to output. They fail to capture **temporal dependencies** — patterns that depend on order and on how far apart two events are — because they lack a mechanism to retain past information.

In your world, that is a query with no `LAG()` and no window frame: every row is scored on its own columns and nothing else. If yesterday matters, a plain feedforward net has nowhere to put it.

**Recurrent neural networks** (RNNs) fix this by adding feedback loops that feed a neuron's past output back into itself as an input for the next step.

### 2 · Unrolling: the same neuron, drawn once per step

As **Figure 15-1** below shows, unrolling a recurrent neuron across the time axis reveals that at time step $t$, it processes both the current input $\mathbf{x}_{(t)}$ and its previous output $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{(t-1)}$.

*Unrolling* does not copy the neuron. It is the same neuron drawn once per time step, the way a recursive CTE is one query definition drawn as many passes. Since there is no previous output at the very first time step, it is generally set to 0 — that is the seed row of the recursion.

### 3 · One neuron becomes a layer: two weight matrices

When expanded to a layer of recurrent neurons (**Figure 15-2** below), each neuron has two weight vectors, $\mathbf{w}_x$ for current inputs and $\mathbf{w}_{\hat{y}}$ for outputs from the previous time step. The whole layer places all of them in two weight matrices, $\mathbf{W}_x$ and $\mathbf{W}_{\hat{y}}$.

As defined in **Equation 15-1** below, the single-instance output is $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{(t)} = \phi(\mathbf{W}_x^\top \mathbf{x}_{(t)} + \mathbf{W}_{\hat{y}}^\top \hat{\mathbf{y}}_{(t-1)} + \mathbf{b})$. The why-layer and the symbol table sit directly under that equation.

For a whole **mini-batch** — a small group of instances scored together — Equation 15-2 below does the same job for every instance at once. The two weight matrices are often concatenated vertically into a single combined weight matrix $\mathbf{W}$, and the inputs and previous outputs are concatenated horizontally, so one matrix multiply covers both halves. The card below gives the exact shapes.

### 4 · Watch it run: two steps with real numbers

Take a single recurrent neuron with input weight 1.0, recurrent weight 0.5, bias 0, and the identity activation $\phi(z) = z$ — meaning the activation does nothing, so you can see the arithmetic:

| Step | Input | Previous output | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| t = 0 | 2 | 0 (no history) | (1.0 x 2) + (0.5 x 0) = 2.0 |
| t = 1 | 3 | 2.0 | (1.0 x 3) + (0.5 x 2.0) = 4.0 |

The 2.0 carried into step 1 is the memory. Nothing else stores it.

### 5 · Memory cells

Because the recurrent output at step $t$ is recursively built on previous steps, the network acts as a **memory cell**: a part of a neural network that preserves some state across time steps, capable of preserving historical context over time.

### 6 · Four shapes an RNN can take

| Shape | Feeds in | Gives back | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| sequence-to-sequence | a sequence | a sequence | power use shifted one day ahead |
| sequence-to-vector | a sequence | one value | a sentiment score for a review |
| vector-to-sequence | one vector | a sequence | a caption for an image |
| encoder-decoder | a sequence | a sequence | translating a sentence |

An **encoder–decoder** is a sequence-to-vector encoder followed by a vector-to-sequence decoder, and it is the right pattern for translating a full sentence from one language into another, because the last words of a sentence can affect the first words of the translation. **Figure 15-4** below draws all four; the card below spells out the shapes.

**One-liner for your notes:** a recurrent neuron feeds its own previous output back in, so unrolled through time it carries a memory of every input since t = 0 — one extra weight matrix is the entire trick.

blocks.title: Mini-batch shapes and the four input/output shapes
blocks.content:
For a whole mini-batch (Equation 15-2), the inputs at time step $t$ form a matrix $\mathbf{X}_{(t)}$ of shape $m \times n_\text{inputs}$, where $m$ is the number of instances. $\mathbf{W}_x$ is $n_\text{inputs} \times n_\text{neurons}$, $\mathbf{W}_{\hat{y}}$ is $n_\text{neurons} \times n_\text{neurons}$, and the output $\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{(t)}$ is $m \times n_\text{neurons}$. The two weight matrices are often concatenated vertically into one matrix $\mathbf{W}$ of shape $(n_\text{inputs} + n_\text{neurons}) \times n_\text{neurons}$, and the inputs and previous outputs are concatenated horizontally.

An RNN can take four shapes. A sequence-to-sequence network outputs a sequence, such as power consumption shifted one day ahead. A sequence-to-vector network keeps only the last output, such as a sentiment score for a review. A vector-to-sequence network turns one input vector, such as an image, into a sequence like a caption. An encoder–decoder (a sequence-to-vector encoder followed by a vector-to-sequence decoder) translates much better than a single sequence-to-sequence RNN, because the last words of a sentence can affect the first words of the translation.

blocks.title: Equation 15-1
blocks.caption: Output of a recurrent layer for a single instance
blocks.explain:
**Why the equation looks like this**

A recurrent layer has to answer one question at every time step: given what is arriving now and what
I concluded a moment ago, what do I conclude now? So the formula is a sum of exactly two weighted
inputs plus a bias, run through an activation. The current input gets one weight matrix, the previous
output gets another, and the two contributions are simply added because nothing says one should
override the other - the weights themselves learn how much each matters.

**Is this standard?** Yes. This is the canonical definition of a simple recurrent layer, not a
simplification made for the example. Equation 15-2 is the same formula written for a whole mini-batch
at once, and the second line of it is a pure rewrite: stack the two weight matrices vertically into
one matrix and put the inputs and previous outputs side by side, and the two multiplications become
one. Same numbers, one matrix multiply instead of two.

**The general form.** Replace the single activation with a gated structure and you get the LSTM
(Equation 15-4) and GRU (Equation 15-5) cells later in this chapter. They keep this shape - weighted
current input, weighted previous state, bias, activation - and repeat it four times or three times
with different jobs.

**Terms this introduces:** an **activation function**, written phi, is the fixed non-linear curve
applied at the end of a neuron's arithmetic; the **bias** is a constant added before it, so a neuron
can output something other than zero on all-zero input; the **transpose** mark on a weight matrix
just says the matrix is laid on its side so the multiplication lines up; a **vector** is an ordered
list of numbers and a **matrix** is a grid of them.

**Every piece of Equation 15-1**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| y-hat with (t) | y hat at t | this layer's output at time step t |
| phi | phi | the activation function, e.g. ReLU |
| W with x | W sub x | weights for the current input |
| the transpose mark | transpose | the matrix laid on its side to multiply |
| x with (t) | x at t | the input vector at time step t |
| W with y-hat | W sub y hat | weights for the previous output |
| y-hat with (t-1) | y hat at t minus 1 | the layer's own output one step ago |
| b | b | the bias vector, one number per neuron |
| the plus signs | plus | add the three contributions together |

**Extra pieces in Equation 15-2 (the mini-batch version)**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| X with (t) | capital X at t | all instances' inputs at step t, m rows |
| Y-hat with (t) | capital Y hat at t | all instances' outputs at step t |
| m | m | how many instances in the mini-batch |
| n inputs | n inputs | how many input features per step |
| n neurons | n neurons | how many neurons in the layer |
| the square brackets | concatenated with | inputs and previous outputs side by side |
| W alone | capital W | the two weight matrices stacked vertically |

Shapes, since they are what break in practice: X at t is m by n-inputs, W sub x is n-inputs by
n-neurons, W sub y-hat is n-neurons by n-neurons, the output is m by n-neurons, and the stacked W is
(n-inputs + n-neurons) by n-neurons.

**The formula in plain words**

output now = activation of ( weights x input now + weights x output a moment ago + bias ).

**With real numbers**

Take this lesson's own neuron: input weight 1.0, recurrent weight 0.5, bias 0, and the identity
activation, which returns whatever it is given.

1. At t = 0 the input is 2 and there is no previous output, so the previous output is 0.
2. Weighted input: 1.0 x 2 = 2.0. Weighted history: 0.5 x 0 = 0. Bias: 0.
3. Add them: 2.0 + 0 + 0 = 2.0. The identity activation leaves it at 2.0, so the output is 2.0.
4. At t = 1 the input is 3 and the previous output is now that 2.0.
5. Weighted input: 1.0 x 3 = 3.0. Weighted history: 0.5 x 2.0 = 1.0.
6. Add them: 3.0 + 1.0 + 0 = 4.0, so the output is 4.0.

Notice what step 5 shows: the 2.0 from the first step is still contributing at the second step, at
half strength. Run it further and that contribution keeps halving but never quite disappears - which
is both how the memory works and, later in this chapter, why it fades.

---

items.term: Why one extra weight matrix is enough to make it a sequence model
items.text: The recurrence adds no new kind of arithmetic - it is still a weighted sum plus a bias plus an activation. What changes is that one of the inputs is the layer's own previous answer, which makes the output at step t depend on every input since t = 0. That is why the memory has no fixed length: it is not stored anywhere, it is carried. The cost is that the memory is also not addressable - you cannot ask the cell what it remembers about step 3, only observe what it currently holds.

items.term: Where the basic cell breaks
items.text: A single recurrent neuron or a plain layer of them is a very basic cell, and it learns only short patterns - typically about ten steps, depending on the task. It breaks quietly, not loudly: nothing errors, the model simply stops improving on anything that depends on older context. That limit is the reason LSTM and GRU cells exist later in this chapter, and roughly ten times longer is what they buy.

items.term: What the four shapes generalise to
items.text: The four shapes are not four architectures, they are four choices about which outputs the loss reads. Keep every output and it is sequence-to-sequence; keep only the last and it is sequence-to-vector; repeat one input and keep every output and it is vector-to-sequence. Once you see it that way, switching between them in Keras is one argument, and the encoder-decoder is simply two of them chained through a single vector bottleneck.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Recurrent neural networks contain backward connections that allow activations to flow across time steps.
Unrolling an RNN reveals how a recurrent layer processes inputs along a sequential time axis.
A recurrent neuron maintains two sets of weights: one for current inputs and another for outputs of the previous step.
At time step t = 0, the initial previous output vector is typically initialized to zeros.
RNN architectures can be configured for sequence-to-sequence, sequence-to-vector, vector-to-sequence, or encoder-decoder tasks.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: A recurrent cell carries state forward, but nothing in this lesson says how far back that state stays useful - the book says a basic cell learns only about 10 steps. How would you measure, for a given series, the point at which extra history stops changing the forecast?
Look up: Chapter 16 of this book, which implements the encoder-decoder sketched in Figure 15-4 and shows what the single-vector bottleneck between encoder and decoder costs.

items.term: Backpropagation Through Time

blocks.content:
To train an RNN you unroll it through time and then run ordinary backpropagation over the unrolled graph — that is the whole of BPTT.

**The question this lesson answers:** the network's connections form loops in time, and backpropagation needs a graph with no loops. How do you train a recurrent network at all, and which time steps actually receive a gradient?

### The big picture

```
 forward (dashed) ->  y0  y1  y2  y3  y4
                              \   |   /
 loss uses last three  ------>  LOSS
 backward (solid)    <--  gradients, y2..y4 only
```

### 1 · Why standard backpropagation cannot start

Standard backpropagation cannot directly train recurrent neural networks because connections form temporal loops. To overcome this obstacle, the network is unrolled across time steps, transforming sequential feedback into a feedforward graph structure. This technique is called **backpropagation through time** (BPTT).

*Backpropagation* is the standard way a neural network learns: run the data forward, measure the error, then push that error backward through the network to work out how much each weight should change.

Unrolling is the same move as turning a loop into a flat DAG of stages before a planner can schedule it. Once it is flat, nothing special is needed.

### 2 · The forward pass, then the loss

Training begins with a forward pass through the unrolled network, as Figure 15-5 below displays via dashed arrows. The model generates predictions $\hat{Y}_{(i)}$ for each time step $i$. A **loss function** $\mathcal{L}$ — the single number saying how wrong the predictions are — then evaluates the predictions against target outputs $Y_{(i)}$.

Depending on the task, the loss function may ignore specific time steps. For instance, a sequence-to-vector network ignores all outputs except the final one, so its gradients flow backward starting exclusively from the final time step.

### 3 · Gradients only flow where the loss looked

Consider an unrolled sequence spanning five time steps from index 0 to index 4. As Figure 15-5 shows, if the loss function relies only on the final three outputs ($\hat{Y}_{(2)}$, $\hat{Y}_{(3)}$, and $\hat{Y}_{(4)}$), gradients propagate backward strictly through those evaluated steps. The unmeasured predictions $\hat{Y}_{(0)}$ and $\hat{Y}_{(1)}$ do not generate gradient flows, because outputs zero and one are excluded from computing the network loss.

The rule is the one you already use when reading a query plan: a column nothing selects contributes nothing downstream. A prediction the loss never reads cannot tell any weight to move.

The card below explains the two arrow styles in the figure: the solid arrows are the backward propagation of gradients through the unrolled network.

### 4 · One update, many accumulated gradients

Because the weight matrix $\mathbf{W}$ and bias vector $\mathbf{b}$ are shared across all time steps, gradients calculated at each step accumulate to update these shared parameters during a single gradient descent step.

| | Feedforward net | Unrolled RNN |
|---|---|---|
| Weights per layer | used once per pass | reused at every time step |
| Gradient per weight | computed once | summed over every evaluated step |
| Update | one step | still one step, after the sum |

That accumulation is an aggregate, not a race: every step contributes a partial gradient and the sum is applied once, exactly like summing partial counts before a single write.

**One-liner for your notes:** BPTT = unroll the loop into a flat graph, run normal backprop, and let the shared weights collect one gradient per evaluated time step before a single update.

blocks.title: Reading the arrows in Figure 15-5
blocks.content: Figure 15-5 uses two kinds of arrows. The dashed arrows show the forward pass through the unrolled network. The solid arrows show the backward pass: the gradients of the loss function are propagated backward through the unrolled network, and they only flow through the outputs that the loss uses, here $\hat{Y}_{(2)}$, $\hat{Y}_{(3)}$ and $\hat{Y}_{(4)}$. Because the same parameters $\mathbf{W}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are used at every time step, their gradients are tweaked several times during backprop. Only when the backward phase is complete and all the gradients have been computed does BPTT perform a gradient descent step, exactly as regular backpropagation does.

blocks.title: Figure 15-5
blocks.caption: Backpropagation through time
blocks.alt: Figure 15-5: Backpropagation through time

items.term: Why sharing the weights is the point, not an optimisation
items.text: It would be possible to give each time step its own weights - but then a 56-step sequence would be a 56-layer network with no ability to generalise across positions, and a pattern learned at step 4 would be useless at step 40. Sharing forces the cell to learn a rule that is true at any position, which is exactly what makes a sequence model transferable to sequences of a different length.

items.term: The cost hidden in the same sharing
items.text: Because one weight is multiplied into the gradient once per time step, the gradient it receives is a product of many similar terms. Slightly greater than one, repeated fifty times, explodes; slightly less than one, repeated fifty times, vanishes. That is the unstable gradients problem, and it is a direct consequence of the sharing that made the model work at all - not a bug in the implementation.

items.term: What choosing which outputs to score actually decides
items.text: Ignoring early outputs in the loss is free in the forward pass but expensive in the backward one: those steps then receive gradient only indirectly, through the state they passed forward. A sequence-to-vector RNN is the extreme case, where the first time step is fifty-odd multiplications away from any error signal. That is a large part of why scoring at every step, later in this chapter, trains faster and steadier.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Unrolling an RNN through time allows standard backpropagation to process sequential data.
The loss function can evaluate all predictions or select a subset of temporal outputs.
Gradients flow backward only through time steps that directly contribute to the loss function.
Shared weights and biases accumulate gradients across all evaluated unrolled time steps.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Here the whole 56-step sequence is unrolled before any update. What do people do when a sequence is thousands of steps long and unrolling it does not fit in memory, and what does that truncation cost in terms of patterns the model can no longer learn?
Look up: Chapter 16 of this book, its stateful RNN section, which preserves the hidden state between training iterations instead of unrolling everything at once.

items.term: Time Series Forecasting and Seasonality

blocks.content:
Before any neural network appears, you look at the series, find the repeating pattern, and copy it — that copy is the baseline every model afterwards has to beat.

**The question this lesson answers:** given daily bus and rail ridership in Chicago, how good is "tomorrow looks like the same weekday last week", and how do you strip out the repeating pattern so a model can learn the rest?

### The big picture

| Term | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| forecasting | predicting future sequential values |
| multivariate | several values recorded at each time step |
| seasonality | a pattern that repeats at a fixed interval |
| naive forecast | just copy a past value |
| differencing | subtract the value from k steps ago |
| stationary | statistics stay constant over time |

### 1 · What the data is

Predicting future sequential values, known as **forecasting**, presents unique challenges because sequential data often contains complex repeating patterns and long-term directional shifts.

When multiple variables are tracked simultaneously over regular time intervals, such as daily bus and rail passenger counts, the dataset forms a **multivariate time series**. A multivariate time series contains multiple values recorded at each time step; one column alone would be univariate.

If you have ever built a daily fact table with one row per date and several measure columns, you have already stored a multivariate time series. The only new idea is that the order of the rows now carries information.

Standard machine learning models often struggle with raw temporal data due to underlying structural patterns like **seasonality**, which refers to regular patterns that repeat at fixed intervals such as days, weeks, or years.

### 2 · The naive baseline, and why 7 days

To establish a baseline, practitioners frequently use **naive forecasting**, which predicts future values by simply copying past observations. When strong weekly seasonality is present, shifting the series by a 7-day lag provides a remarkably effective baseline: transit ridership exhibits strong weekly seasonality that repeats regularly, so last Tuesday is a good guess for this Tuesday.

This is `LAG(value, 7) OVER (ORDER BY date)` and nothing more. It costs nothing, and it is often hard to beat.

### 3 · Scoring it: MAE against MAPE

We can evaluate forecast accuracy using metrics such as Mean Absolute Error (**MAE**) — the average size of the miss, in riders — and Mean Absolute Percentage Error (**MAPE**) — the average size of the miss expressed as a share of that day's actual value.

Analyzing Chicago transit ridership between March and May 2019 reveals a strong weekly cycle. Applying a 7-day naive forecast yields:

| Series | MAE | MAPE |
|---|---|---|
| bus | about 43,916 riders | about 8.3% |
| rail | about 42,143 riders | about 9.0% |

Although rail has a lower absolute error, calculating the MAPE reveals that bus forecasts are actually more accurate proportionally, because total bus ridership is significantly higher. That is the whole reason MAPE exists: it scales forecast errors relative to target values, allowing fair comparison across different volume scales — the same reason you report a percentage of rows rejected rather than a raw reject count when two feeds are different sizes.

Figure 15-7 below plots the 7-day difference, and it shows one large spike downward at the end of May. A holiday weekend occurred, causing actual ridership to be much lower than the previous week: the day types for May 25 to 27 are A, U, U, a long weekend whose Monday was the Memorial Day holiday. The card below works the arithmetic.

### 4 · Differencing, and what stationary buys you

Subtracting past lagged values from current values — a process called **differencing** — helps eliminate seasonality and long-term trends, transforming the data into a **stationary** time series whose statistical properties remain constant over time.

Figures 15-8 and 15-9 below show the same move on a yearly scale: a 12-month difference removes both the yearly season and the long-term trend.

The main benefit of applying differencing before modeling is that it removes trend and seasonality, producing a stationary series that is easier to model. Once the model forecasts the differenced series well, you add the subtracted past values back to get real numbers again — the same round trip as storing deltas and re-integrating them into a running total.

**One-liner for your notes:** copy last week as the baseline (MAE about 43,916 bus and 42,143 rail), compare with MAPE when the volumes differ, and difference the series to strip trend and seasonality before modelling.

blocks.title: Worked out: the naive forecast's MAE and MAPE
blocks.content: The naive forecast for day $t$ is the value from day $t-7$, so each forecast error is the 7-day difference $y_{(t)} - y_{(t-7)}$. Averaging the absolute differences over March, April and May 2019 gives the MAE: about 43,916 bus riders and 42,143 rail riders. For the MAPE, each difference is first divided by that day's actual value, and the absolute results are averaged: 0.082938 for bus (about 8.3%) and 0.089948 for rail (about 9.0%). Bus ridership is larger, so its raw errors are larger, but relative to the targets the bus forecasts are slightly better. The largest differences appear at the end of May: the day types for May 25 to 27 are A, U, U, a long weekend whose Monday was the Memorial Day holiday. When large errors hurt quadratically more than small ones, the MSE may be preferable, since it strongly penalizes large errors.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import pandas as pd

path = "datasets/ridership/CTA_-_Ridership_-_Daily_Boarding_Totals.csv"
df = pd.read_csv(path, parse_dates=["service_date"])
df.columns = ["date", "day_type", "bus", "rail", "total"]
df = df.sort_values("date").set_index("date").drop(columns=["total"]).drop_duplicates()

# Compute 7-day differencing and evaluation metrics
diff_7 = df[["bus", "rail"]].diff(7)["2019-03":"2019-05"]
mae = diff_7.abs().mean()
targets = df[["bus", "rail"]]["2019-03":"2019-05"]
mape = (diff_7 / targets).abs().mean()
```

items.term: Why a naive baseline is mandatory, not optional
items.text: The number that matters is never the model's error, it is the model's error against the cheapest thing that could have worked. A copy of last week costs nothing to build, nothing to serve and never breaks - so any model that does not clearly beat it is negative value once you count the training, the monitoring and the failure modes. The book keeps the naive number in view for the whole chapter for exactly this reason.

items.term: Choosing a metric is choosing what counts as a bad day
items.text: MAE treats a miss of 100,000 as ten times a miss of 10,000. MSE treats it as a hundred times. MAPE treats a miss as a share of the day, so a bad Sunday counts more than the same absolute miss on a Wednesday. None is neutral. The right question is what a large error costs downstream - if the project suffers quadratically more from large errors than from small ones, MSE may be preferable.

items.term: When differencing stops helping
items.text: Differencing removes trend and seasonality, but it also destroys level: a differenced series says how much things changed, never where they stand. You get the level back by adding the subtracted values, which means any error in the base value persists forever. It also amplifies noise, because you subtract two noisy numbers to get a smaller one. Difference when the trend is the problem, not as a reflex.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A multivariate time series records multiple changing features over regular temporal intervals.
Seasonality refers to periodic, repeating patterns in time series data over fixed durations like weeks or years.
Naive forecasting serves as a baseline by copying past values, such as using a 7-day lag for weekly patterns.
Differencing removes trends and seasonality to render a time series stationary for easier modeling.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The 7-day lag was chosen by eye from Figure 15-6. What is the principled way to discover which lags carry signal in a series you have never seen, before you pick a baseline?
Look up: the statsmodels time series analysis (tsa) user guide, specifically its autocorrelation and partial autocorrelation plotting functions, plot_acf and plot_pacf.

items.term: The ARMA Model Family and SARIMA

blocks.content:
ARMA forecasts tomorrow as a weighted sum of recent actual values plus a weighted sum of its own recent mistakes; ARIMA and SARIMA are that same model with differencing bolted on the front.

**The question this lesson answers:** before reaching for a neural network, what does the classical statistical family do with a time series, and what do its letters p, d, q, P, D, Q and s actually mean?

### The big picture

```
 SARIMA = differencing  +  ARMA  +  a seasonal copy
            d, D           p, q       P, D, Q at lag s
```

### 1 · Why plain regression drifts

Standard regression methods struggle with time series data because temporal trends and non-stationary behavior cause forecasts to drift over time. To solve this problem, classical time series analysis relies on the **ARMA model family** to capture lag relationships and seasonal patterns explicitly.

*Non-stationary* means the statistics move: the average of the series in 2016 is not the average in 2019, so a rule fitted on one stretch is wrong on the next.

### 2 · The two halves of ARMA

An **ARMA model** combines an autoregressive (AR) component and a moving average (MA) component.

| Half | Sums over | Reads | Hyperparameter |
|---|---|---|---|
| autoregressive | past observed values | the series itself | p |
| moving average | past forecast errors | its own misses | q |

Equation 15-3 below shows how the forecast $\hat{y}_{(t)}$ is calculated by taking a weighted sum of $p$ past observed values and adding a weighted sum of $q$ past forecast errors $\epsilon_{(t-i)}$ — so the second summation term computes a weighted sum over past forecast errors to adjust the prediction. The error term is defined as the difference between the true observed value and the forecasted value, $\epsilon_{(t)} = y_{(t)} - \hat{y}_{(t)}$.

The first half is a window function over the last p rows. The second half is the part with no SQL analogy worth stretching: the model looks at how wrong it has just been and corrects itself.

### 3 · Differencing: the I in ARIMA

When a time series exhibits a non-stationary trend, plain ARMA models fail. The **ARIMA model** introduces $d$ rounds of **differencing** to remove polynomial trends. The primary purpose of differencing in ARIMA models is that it transforms non-stationary time series into stationary ones. Subtracting consecutive terms once removes linear trends, whereas two rounds of differencing remove quadratic trends.

Consider the quadratic series 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36:

| Round | Series |
|---|---|
| start | 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36 |
| after 1 round | 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 |
| after 2 rounds | 2, 2, 2, 2 |

Two rounds of differencing turn that quadratic series into a constant one, which is exactly what ARMA wants. The figure below draws the same three stages.

### 4 · The seasonal copy: SARIMA

For periodic patterns, the **SARIMA model** adds seasonal components $P$, $D$, and $Q$ evaluated at steps equal to the period $s$. P, D and Q do the same jobs as p, d and q, but applied at lag s, 2s, 3s and so on. The hyperparameter s represents the period length of the main repeating seasonal pattern — 7 here, because the week is the cycle.

### 5 · Running it, and one API trap

The card below reads a real call. Two things are worth carrying:

- Data is passed at object instantiation rather than to `fit()`. That is how the statsmodels ARIMA API differs from the standard Scikit-Learn API during model setup, and it catches everyone once.
- On the measured run, SARIMA reaches an MAE of about 32,041 over March to May 2019, well below the naive 42,143 — but on the single day June 1, 2019 it forecast 427,759 against a real 379,044, worse than naive that day. One day proves nothing; the three-month average does.

**One-liner for your notes:** ARMA = weighted past values + weighted past errors; the I is d rounds of differencing to kill trends; SARIMA repeats the whole thing at lag s, and here s = 7 beats naive by about 10,000 riders of MAE.

blocks.title: Reading the statsmodels ARIMA call
blocks.content: In `ARIMA(rail_series, order=(1, 0, 0), seasonal_order=(0, 1, 1, 7))`, the order means $p = 1$, $d = 0$ and $q = 0$, and the seasonal order means $P = 0$, $D = 1$, $Q = 1$ and $s = 7$, a weekly season. The statsmodels API differs a bit from Scikit-Learn's: the data is passed to the model at construction time, instead of to the `fit()` method. The call `asfreq("D")` sets the frequency to daily, so the class does not have to guess it. Pretending today is May 31, 2019, the forecast for June 1 is 427,759 passengers, while the real count was 379,044, so the forecast is 12.9% off; naive forecasting (426,932) was 12.6% off. Retraining every day to forecast each day of March to May 2019 gives an MAE of about 32,041, well below the naive MAE of 42,143.
