blocks.title: Equation 15-3
blocks.caption: Forecasting using an ARMA model
blocks.explain:
**Why the equation looks like this**

The forecast is written as two sums added together because ARMA is two ideas bolted into one line.
The first sum says tomorrow resembles the recent past, so take the last p values and weight them. The
second sum says the model has been making mistakes with a pattern, so take the last q errors and
weight those too, as a correction. Both are plain weighted sums - straight lines, no curves - because
this is a linear model; that is the family's defining limitation and the source of its speed and its
interpretability.

**Is this standard?** Yes. This is the canonical ARMA formulation, developed by Herman Wold in the
1930s and unchanged since. It is not simplified for the ridership example.

**The general form.** ARIMA is this same equation applied after d rounds of differencing, with the
subtracted values added back at the end. SARIMA is ARIMA plus a second copy of the whole structure
evaluated at lag s, 2s, 3s and so on, controlled by P, D and Q - which is why the family has seven
hyperparameters in total.

**Terms this introduces:** a **lag** is how many steps back you look, so y at t minus i is the value
i steps ago; a **hyperparameter** is a setting you choose before training rather than something
training learns, like a `--conf` flag on a job submit; the **learned weights** alpha and theta are
what training does fit; a **forecast error** epsilon is the actual value minus what the model
predicted for that same step.

**Every piece of Equation 15-3**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| y-hat with (t) | y hat at t | the model's forecast for time step t |
| y with (t) | y at t | the real observed value at time step t |
| the first sum sign | sum from i equals 1 to p | add over the p most recent values |
| p | p | how many past values to look at |
| alpha with i | alpha sub i | learned weight on the value i steps back |
| y with (t-i) | y at t minus i | the actual value i steps back |
| the second sum sign | sum from i equals 1 to q | add over the q most recent errors |
| q | q | how many past errors to look at |
| theta with i | theta sub i | learned weight on the error i steps back |
| epsilon with (t-i) | epsilon at t minus i | the forecast error i steps back |
| the second line | with epsilon at t equals | the definition of the error term |

**The formula in plain words**

forecast for today = ( weighted sum of the last p actual values ) + ( weighted sum of the last q
forecast errors ), where an error means the actual value minus what was forecast for that day.

**With real numbers**

The book does not print the fitted alpha and theta values for the rail model, so the piece that can
be computed exactly here is the error term, which is the second line of the equation.

1. Pretending today is May 31, 2019, the SARIMA model forecasts 427,759 rail passengers for June 1.
2. The real count for that day was 379,044.
3. The error for that step is the actual minus the forecast: 379,044 - 427,759 = -48,715.
4. As a share of the actual value that is about 12.9% off, which is what the card below reports.
5. That signed error, -48,715, is exactly the kind of number the moving-average half would feed into
the next day's forecast as epsilon at t minus 1.

One day is not a verdict: repeated daily over March, April and May 2019 the same model reaches an MAE
of about 32,041 against naive forecasting's 42,143.

---

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from statsmodels.tsa.arima.model import ARIMA

rail_series = df.loc["2019-01-01":"2019-05-31"]["rail"].asfreq("D")
model = ARIMA(rail_series,
              order=(1, 0, 0),
              seasonal_order=(0, 1, 1, 7))
model = model.fit()
y_pred = model.forecast()
```

items.term: Why a model of its own errors is not circular
items.text: The moving-average half looks strange: the model uses its own past mistakes as inputs. It works because a forecast error is the part of yesterday the model could not explain, and if those leftovers are themselves correlated - a shock that takes a few days to fade - then they carry real information the autoregressive half missed. When the errors are genuinely random, the fitted weights go to zero and the component costs nothing.

items.term: The cost of the assumption ARMA makes
items.text: ARMA assumes the series is stationary, and everything the family adds is machinery for forcing that assumption to hold: d rounds of differencing for trend, P, D, Q at lag s for season. That is why it has seven hyperparameters. A neural network makes no such assumption, which is convenient, but it also means nothing warns you when the assumption is the thing that broke.

items.term: Why this baseline is worth the effort at all
items.text: SARIMA's roughly 32,041 MAE beat naive forecasting by a wide margin with no GPU, no training loop and a handful of integers to tune. That number is what tells you whether a neural network is earning its complexity. A classical baseline that is hard to beat is not a failure of the deep model - it is information about how much structure the data actually has.

blocks.title: Key points
items: The ARMA model combines past time series values and past forecast errors to generate predictions.
Differencing converts non-stationary time series into stationary ones by removing polynomial trends.
The ARIMA model extends ARMA by applying $d$ rounds of differencing before running ARMA.
The SARIMA model incorporates additional seasonal parameters $P$, $D$, $Q$, and seasonal period $s$.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: SARIMA has seven hyperparameters and this lesson sets them by hand. Beyond grid search, how do practitioners actually choose p, d, q, P, D, Q and s, and what does an information criterion such as AIC or BIC add over just picking the lowest MAE?
Look up: George Box and Gwilym Jenkins, Time Series Analysis (Wiley, 1970), the book that introduced the ARIMA model and the identification procedure named after them.

items.term: Preparing Time Series Data for Machine Learning

blocks.content:
A model cannot read a time series directly — you first cut it into fixed-length windows, each paired with the value that came next.

**The question this lesson answers:** you have one long column of daily numbers. How do you turn it into the rows-with-a-label shape that supervised training requires, and what does Keras give you for free?

### The big picture

```
 series:  0  1  2  3  4  5
 window   [0 1 2] -> target 3
 window   [1 2 3] -> target 4
 window   [2 3 4] -> target 5
```

### 1 · Windows are the rows

Standard machine learning models cannot directly process raw, continuous time series data without structured input-target pairs. Supervised learning algorithms require defined feature sequences paired with target values, which is why time series data must be converted into fixed-length windows before training.

To train a model for forecasting, we must transform a sequential time series into fixed-length feature windows and corresponding target values. For instance, to predict tomorrow's value from the past 56 days, each training instance must consist of a sequence of 56 consecutive observation steps matched with the single target value at step 57.

This is a rolling window, the same shape as `ROWS BETWEEN 55 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`. The difference is that you materialise every window as its own training row, so 56 days of history becomes 56 feature columns, and the next day becomes the label.

### 2 · The one-line way

The utility function **`tf.keras.utils.timeseries_dataset_from_array()`** converts a continuous sequence into a structured **`tf.data.Dataset`** of overlapping sliding windows and target values.

Consider a simple array containing six sequential numbers `[0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`. If we configure a sequence length of 3 and align targets shifted by 3 steps, the utility function produces sliding input windows of `[0, 1, 2]`, `[1, 2, 3]`, and `[2, 3, 4]`. The corresponding target scalar values for these inputs are `3`, `4`, and `5` respectively — so for the window `[1, 2, 3]` the scalar target value is 4.

Batching these with a batch size of 2 groups the first two window-target pairs into a batch tensor while leaving the remaining window in a final batch of size 1. That is the general rule: when the total number of extracted windows is not evenly divisible by `batch_size`, the final batch in the dataset contains fewer window instances than the specified batch size. A **batch** here is just a group of rows handed to the trainer together, like a micro-batch in a streaming job.

### 3 · The manual way, and why it exists

Alternatively, calling **`window()`** on a dataset creates nested window datasets, which must be flattened using **`flat_map()`** into numerical tensors before model training. The primary function of `flat_map()` is that it converts a nested dataset of window datasets into a flat dataset containing tensors.

| Step | What you hold |
|---|---|
| after window() | a dataset of datasets (a list of lists) |
| after flat_map() | a flat dataset of tensors |
| after map() | each tensor split into inputs and target |

A **tensor** is simply an array of numbers with a known shape — the thing the model can actually consume. The card below walks the exact calls, including why the short tail windows appear and which argument removes them.

### 4 · Shuffle the windows, not their contents

When training with gradient descent, the sliding training windows should be shuffled to approximate independent and identically distributed data, preventing temporal order bias during batching. Shuffling satisfies the assumption of independent and identically distributed training samples.

Note what is shuffled: the windows, as whole rows. The order *inside* a window is the signal and is never touched. It is the same distinction as shuffling partitions for load balance while the rows inside a partition keep their order.

**One-liner for your notes:** slice the series into fixed-length windows paired with the next value, let `timeseries_dataset_from_array()` do it, and shuffle the windows (never their contents) so gradient descent sees independent rows.

blocks.title: Worked out: window(), drop_remainder and flat_map()
blocks.content: Calling `tf.data.Dataset.range(6).window(4, shift=1)` produces six windows: [0 1 2 3], [1 2 3 4], [2 3 4 5], and then the shorter [3 4 5], [4 5] and [5], because the last windows reach the end of the series. The smaller windows are removed by passing `drop_remainder=True` to `window()`; `flat_map()` does not drop anything. Each window is still a dataset, so `flat_map(lambda window_ds: window_ds.batch(4))` turns each window dataset into a single tensor of size 4 and flattens the result into the tensors [0 1 2 3], [1 2 3 4] and [2 3 4 5]. Finally, `map(lambda window: (window[:-1], window[-1]))` splits each window into its inputs and its target, which, once batched, matches the output of `timeseries_dataset_from_array()`.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

my_series = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
my_dataset = tf.keras.utils.timeseries_dataset_from_array(
    my_series,
    targets=my_series[3:],
    sequence_length=3,
    batch_size=2
)
for inputs, targets in my_dataset:
    print(inputs.numpy(), targets.numpy())
```

items.term: Why windowing is where forecasting projects quietly go wrong
items.text: Every leak in a forecasting project is a windowing bug: a target that overlaps its own inputs, a validation window that starts inside the training period, a shuffle applied before the split. The model cannot detect any of these - it will happily report an excellent score. The window construction is the contract, and it deserves the same scrutiny you would give a join key.

items.term: Overlapping windows are correlated rows, and that has a price
items.text: Consecutive 56-day windows share 55 of their 56 values, so training rows are nearly duplicates of each other. Shuffling fixes the ordering assumption gradient descent needs, but it does not make the rows independent in any real sense. The practical consequence is that the effective number of training examples is far smaller than the row count suggests, which is one reason bigger models overfit this data so readily.

items.term: Why the split is across time and almost never random
items.text: A random split would put a Tuesday in training and the Wednesday next to it in validation, and the validation score would then measure interpolation rather than forecasting. Splitting by date is the only split that answers the question actually being asked. The book notes one exception: when you have many independent entities you may be able to split across them instead - but only if they are genuinely uncorrelated.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Machine learning models require time series data to be formatted into fixed input windows paired with future targets.
The utility function tf.keras.utils.timeseries_dataset_from_array() automates sliding window generation and batching.
Using the dataset window() method produces nested datasets that must be flattened with flat_map() into tensors.
Shuffling training windows ensures instances are independent and identically distributed for gradient descent training.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Overlapping windows mean consecutive training rows share almost all their values. How does that affect how much you can trust a validation score computed the same way, and what do people do about it?
Look up: the Keras API documentation for tf.keras.utils.timeseries_dataset_from_array, in particular its sequence_stride, sampling_rate and start_index arguments, none of which this lesson uses.

items.term: Forecasting Time Series with Simple RNNs

blocks.content:
The smallest possible RNN has three parameters and scores worse than naive forecasting; widening it to 32 neurons and adding one plain output layer makes it the best model in the chapter so far.

**The question this lesson answers:** what does a `SimpleRNN` layer actually compute, why does a one-neuron version fail badly on this data, and what two changes fix it?

### The big picture

| Model | Parameters | Validation MAE |
|---|---|---|
| linear, all 56 days at once | 57 | about 37,866 |
| SimpleRNN with 1 neuron | 3 | greater than 100,000 |
| SimpleRNN 32 + Dense 1 | many | 27,703 |

### 1 · What a recurrent layer adds over a linear model

Standard linear models forecast time series by looking at all past time steps simultaneously in a fixed window. However, linear models do not maintain an internal state that updates sequentially over time. A **SimpleRNN** layer addresses this problem by processing sequence data one step at a time, using an internal **state** — a running memory vector — to carry information from prior steps to future steps.

The linear model is a single wide `SELECT` over 56 lag columns. The RNN is a loop that walks the 56 days in order and keeps a running value, closer to an incremental load than to a full scan.

### 2 · The input shape, and the one step it repeats

In a single-neuron recurrent model, the network accepts a 3D tensor input of shape `[batch size, time steps, dimensionality]` — those are the standard input shape dimensions Keras recurrent layers expect for sequence data. For univariate series, dimensionality is one.

At the first time step, the recurrent neuron initializes its hidden state to zero and receives the first input. It calculates a weighted sum of the input and previous state, adds a bias term, and applies the default **hyperbolic tangent (tanh)** activation function — a squashing curve whose output can never leave the range −1 to +1. This calculated result becomes the output as well as the new state passed to the next step.

By default, Keras recurrent layers operate as a sequence-to-vector model: the default output behavior of a standard SimpleRNN layer is that it outputs only a vector containing the result of the final time step.

### 3 · Why the one-neuron model fails, twice over

Consider a basic network with one recurrent neuron processing a sequence of 56 time steps. This single-neuron model has only three trainable parameters: two input weights and one bias term.

Two separate things are wrong with it:

1. **Too little memory.** Three parameters, and the only history it carries is a single number. The linear model it is competing with had 57 parameters and could see all 56 previous values at once.
2. **The wrong output range.** Because its state memory is a single number constrained between -1 and +1 by the tanh activation, it cannot effectively predict larger target values. The scaled series runs from 0 to about 1.4, so the default hyperbolic tangent activation bounds output values between -1 and +1 and there is simply no way to reach 1.4.

That second point is a units bug, not a learning failure — the same class of problem as a column whose declared type cannot hold the values you are about to write.

### 4 · The fix: widen, then unclamp

To solve this limitation, we attach a **Dense** layer with a single linear output neuron on top of a larger layer containing 32 recurrent neurons. A *dense* layer is the ordinary fully connected layer: every input feeds every output.

The 32 recurrent neurons carry complex state information across time, and the Dense layer projects the final 32-dimensional recurrent state into a single output without value limits, significantly lowering the forecast error. With no activation function on that Dense layer, nothing squashes the result, so any value is reachable.

The card below has the parameter arithmetic and the measured scores: 27,703 validation MAE, which even beats SARIMA.

**One-liner for your notes:** a recurrent layer needs enough neurons to remember anything and an unconstrained Dense layer on top to leave tanh's −1 to +1 cage — 32 + Dense(1) took the MAE from over 100,000 down to 27,703.

blocks.title: Worked out: parameter counts and validation scores
blocks.content: The single-neuron model `SimpleRNN(1, input_shape=[None, 1])` receives two input values at each time step: the current input value and its own previous output. It has one weight for each of them plus a bias term, so the whole model has three parameters. The linear model trained before it, a `Dense(1)` layer that looks at all 56 previous values at once, had a total of 57 parameters (56 weights plus a bias) and a validation MAE of about 37,866. The single-neuron RNN scores a validation MAE greater than 100,000, partly because the scaled series runs from 0 to about 1.4 while tanh can only output values between –1 and +1. With 32 recurrent neurons and a `Dense(1)` output layer, the validation MAE drops to 27,703, which even beats SARIMA.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

univar_model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.SimpleRNN(32, input_shape=[None, 1]),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(1)
])

opt = tf.keras.optimizers.SGD(learning_rate=0.02, momentum=0.9)
univar_model.compile(
    loss=tf.keras.losses.Huber(),
    optimizer=opt,
    metrics=["mae"]
)
```

items.term: Two failures that look identical from the loss curve
items.text: The single-neuron model failed for two unrelated reasons - too little capacity, and an output range that cannot reach the targets. Both show up as a large MAE, and no metric distinguishes them. The range failure is the cheaper one to find and the easier to miss: check what your target values are and what your final layer can physically emit, before touching anything else.

items.term: Why the last layer usually has no activation
items.text: An activation function on the output layer is a claim about the range of the answer. For a bounded target such as a probability, that claim is useful. For a price or a passenger count it is simply false, and it caps the model at whatever the function's ceiling happens to be. Leaving the final Dense layer linear is the default for regression for exactly this reason.

items.term: What the 3 versus 57 parameter comparison really shows
items.text: The linear model with 57 parameters beat the recurrent model with 3, which is not an argument against recurrence - it is an argument about capacity. The recurrent structure is a constraint that says the same rule applies at every step; that constraint pays off only when the layer has enough width to hold something worth carrying. Structure without capacity loses to no structure with capacity.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Recurrent layers in Keras expect 3D input tensors representing batch size, time steps, and dimensionality.
A single recurrent neuron uses default tanh activation, restricting outputs between -1 and +1.
By default, Keras recurrent layers act as sequence-to-vector models returning only the final step output.
Combining a multi-neuron SimpleRNN layer with a unconstrained Dense output layer drastically improves forecasting performance.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The book keeps tanh because it saturates. What happens if you use ReLU in a recurrent layer anyway, and under what initialization does that become workable rather than unstable?
Look up: Quoc V. Le et al., "A Simple Way to Initialize Recurrent Networks of Rectified Linear Units" (2015), cited in this chapter's first footnote.

items.term: Forecasting Using a Deep RNN

blocks.content:
Stacking recurrent layers is one line each, but every layer that feeds another one must be told to hand over the whole sequence, not just its last output.

**The question this lesson answers:** how do you make an RNN deeper, what single argument makes stacking work, and does deeper actually win here?

### The big picture

```
 SimpleRNN 32  return_sequences=True   -> 3D out
 SimpleRNN 32  return_sequences=True   -> 3D out
 SimpleRNN 32  (default)               -> 2D out
 Dense 1                               -> forecast
```

### 1 · What a deep RNN is

Simple recurrent neural networks with a single recurrent layer often struggle to learn complex patterns in sequential time series data. To increase the representational capacity of a model, network architectures frequently stack multiple recurrent layers on top of one another, creating a **deep RNN**.

As **Figure 15-10** below illustrates, information flows horizontally across time steps and vertically across stacked recurrent layers. Two directions, one picture: sideways is memory, upwards is abstraction.

### 2 · The one argument that makes stacking legal

In a deep architecture, intermediate recurrent layers must pass sequence data to the layer above them. To implement this in Keras, every recurrent layer preceding another recurrent layer must have `return_sequences=True`.

| Setting | Output | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| return_sequences=True | 3D, one vector per time step | feeding another recurrent layer |
| default (False) | 2D, the last step only | the top of the stack |

A standard Keras recurrent layer expects as its input a 3D tensor representing batch size, time steps, and features. So if `return_sequences=True` is omitted on an intermediate layer in a stacked RNN, the layer outputs a 2D array, causing the next recurrent layer to raise an input format error. It is a shape contract between stages, and breaking it fails loudly rather than silently — which is the good case.

### 3 · The top of the stack

The final recurrent layer typically omits this setting, returning a single vector for each sequence that a **Dense layer** transforms into a final forecast. A Dense layer is typically placed at the very top of a deep RNN forecasting architecture to map the final recurrent vector output to the target output dimension for prediction: 32 numbers in, as many numbers out as you need forecasts.

### 4 · Does depth pay here?

Consider an example where we build a deep model using three consecutive `SimpleRNN` layers with 32 units each, followed by a final `Dense(1)` layer. The first two layers set `return_sequences=True` to provide 3D outputs to subsequent layers, while the third recurrent layer outputs a single 2D vector for the final step.

| Model | Validation MAE |
|---|---|
| naive, 7-day lag (rail) | about 42,143 |
| SARIMA | about 32,041 |
| deep RNN, three layers | about 31,211 |
| single 32-neuron RNN + Dense | 27,703 |

The three-layer deep RNN achieved an MAE of about 31,211, which was worse than the shallower RNN. It outperforms simple baseline models, but it demonstrates that adding layers can sometimes lead to overfitting when a model becomes too large for the dataset — more capacity than the data can pay for. The card below places the number against the others.

**One-liner for your notes:** stack recurrent layers freely, but set `return_sequences=True` on every layer that feeds another one — and here three layers (31,211) lost to one (27,703), so depth is a hypothesis, not an upgrade.

blocks.title: Worked out: where the deep RNN's 31,211 stands
blocks.content: The deep RNN's validation MAE of about 31,211 makes sense next to the earlier scores. Naive forecasting reached about 42,143 on rail and SARIMA about 32,041, so the deep model beats both baselines. The single-layer model with 32 recurrent neurons and a Dense output reached 27,703, so the three-layer model does not beat that shallower RNN; it looks a bit too large for the task. If you forget `return_sequences=True` on a recurrent layer that feeds another one, that layer outputs a 2D array holding only the output of the last time step instead of a 3D array of shape [batch size, time steps, dimensionality] with outputs for all time steps, and the next recurrent layer complains that it is not fed sequences in the expected 3D format.

blocks.caption: A deep RNN (left) unrolled through time (right)

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
deep_model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.SimpleRNN(32, return_sequences=True, input_shape=[None, 1]),
    tf.keras.layers.SimpleRNN(32, return_sequences=True),
    tf.keras.layers.SimpleRNN(32),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(1)
])
```

items.term: Depth is a hypothesis about the data, not a quality setting
items.text: Three layers lost to one here, on about three years of daily rows. More layers means more parameters fitted from the same small number of genuinely independent windows, so the extra capacity gets spent memorising rather than generalising. Depth pays when the task really does compose - short patterns into longer ones - and when there is enough data to identify both levels.

items.term: Why the shape error is the good kind of failure
items.text: Forgetting return_sequences=True raises an error rather than silently training on the last step. That is a well-designed contract: the failure is loud, immediate and local. Contrast it with the target-alignment mistakes later in this chapter, which produce a trained model and a plausible score while comparing forecasts against the wrong days.

items.term: What stacking changes about the state
items.text: Each recurrent layer keeps its own state, so a three-layer stack carries three independent memories updated at the same cadence. The layers are not looking further back in time than a single layer would - they are looking at more abstract versions of the same span. If the problem is that the window is too short, adding depth does not address it; lengthening the sequence or shortening it with a convolution does.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A deep RNN is created by stacking multiple recurrent layers on top of one another.
Intermediate recurrent layers require setting return_sequences=True to output 3D tensors.
The final recurrent layer usually outputs a 2D vector that feeds into a Dense layer for prediction.
Increasing RNN depth increases capacity but can lead to worse performance if the model becomes too large for the task.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Three layers overfit here on about three years of daily data. What signals, other than trying it, would tell you in advance how much capacity a given time series can support?
Look up: Chapter 11 of this book, its section "The Vanishing/Exploding Gradients Problems", plus its treatment of regularization for deep networks.

items.term: Forecasting Multivariate Time Series

blocks.content:
Feeding an RNN more columns per time step costs one number in the input shape and buys a large drop in error.

**The question this lesson answers:** rail ridership is not the only thing you know about tomorrow — you also have bus numbers and you already know whether tomorrow is a weekday, a weekend or a holiday. How do you hand all of that to the model?

### The big picture

```
 per time step, 5 numbers:
   bus | rail | dayW | dayA | dayU
                       \__ tomorrow's type, shifted back __/
```

### 1 · What one column leaves on the table

Standard univariate time series forecasting relies on a single sequence of historical observations to predict future values. The problem with relying on a single variable is that useful context from correlated events or known future events is completely ignored. **Multivariate time series** forecasting solves this issue by feeding multiple parallel data features into the model at each time step.

This is the same argument as joining a dimension onto a fact table: the measure alone is weaker than the measure plus its context.

### 2 · Two kinds of extra column

| Kind | Example | Why it helps |
|---|---|---|
| a correlated series | bus ridership beside rail | the two move together |
| a known future attribute | tomorrow is a holiday | you know it in advance |

The second kind is the interesting one. Known future events like whether tomorrow is a weekday, weekend, or holiday can be shifted by one day into the future and converted into **one-hot encoded** features — one yes/no column per category, exactly one of them set. The day type is shifted with `shift(-1)`: it aligns tomorrow's known day type with today's step so the model has future context. This is not leakage, because a calendar is genuinely known ahead of time — the same reason a date dimension is safe to join and a measured actual is not.

If there are two original series and three one-hot encoded day types, the model receives five total features per time step.

### 3 · What actually changes in the model

Neural networks handle multivariate inputs with exceptional flexibility, requiring minimal changes to their architecture. The primary architectural modification required to adapt a univariate RNN to process multivariate input is that the input shape feature dimension in the first layer must match the total input column count.

Consider a concrete scenario using historical transit data. A dataset is constructed with five columns: normalized bus ridership, normalized rail ridership, and three binary columns representing the shifted next-day type. In a scenario with bus data, rail data, and three one-hot day type columns, the RNN expects an input feature dimension of five, reflecting all continuous series and one-hot features. The target stays focused strictly on the rail series.

That is the whole edit: `input_shape=[None, 1]` becomes `input_shape=[None, 5]`. This simple architectural adjustment allows the model to leverage cross-series correlations and calendar context, significantly dropping the validation mean absolute error compared to single-variable models — 22,062 against 27,703 for the univariate RNN, per the card below.

### 4 · One model, several targets

Models can also be configured as **multitask learning** systems by outputting multiple target variables at once. To modify a single-output multivariate RNN model to perform multitask forecasting for two series, you set the targets to include both series and increase the final Dense layer units to two.

A major potential benefit of training a single model for multitask forecasting across related series is that shared feature representations can act as a regularizer and prevent overfitting across tasks: having to do well at two jobs stops the model memorising either one. It is not guaranteed, though — the card below records that here the multitask model reached 25,330 for rail and 26,369 for bus, not quite matching dedicated models.

**One-liner for your notes:** more columns per step costs one number in `input_shape`, calendar facts about tomorrow are legal inputs because you really know them, and multitask output is two Dense units — but it can still lose to two dedicated models.

blocks.title: Worked out: multivariate and multitask scores
blocks.content: The day type is shifted with `shift(-1)`, so each day's row holds tomorrow's day type, which is known in advance and is given to the model as an input. With five inputs per step (bus, rail and three one-hot day-type columns), the RNN reaches a validation MAE of 22,062 on rail, compared with 27,703 for the univariate RNN. To forecast both series, set the targets to `mulvar_train[["bus", "rail"]][seq_length:]` (and the same for validation) and give the output `Dense` layer two neurons. A single model for related tasks often performs better than separate models, because features learned for one task may help the others and because performing well across several tasks acts as a form of regularization against overfitting. It is not guaranteed: here the multitask RNN reaches 25,330 for rail and 26,369 for bus, not quite as good as dedicated models.

blocks.content:
```python
df_mulvar = df[["bus", "rail"]] / 1e6
df_mulvar["next_day_type"] = df["day_type"].shift(-1)
df_mulvar = pd.get_dummies(df_mulvar)

train_ds = tf.keras.utils.timeseries_dataset_from_array(
    mulvar_train.to_numpy(),
    targets=mulvar_train["rail"][seq_length:]

    tf.keras.layers.SimpleRNN(32, input_shape=[None, 5]),
```

items.term: The line between a legal future feature and leakage
items.text: Shifting tomorrow's day type back into today's row looks exactly like leakage and is not, because a calendar is knowable in advance and would be knowable in production too. The test is not whether the value belongs to a future timestamp; it is whether you would genuinely have it at prediction time. Shift tomorrow's measured ridership the same way and the model becomes excellent in validation and useless in production.

items.term: Why more columns helped so much more than more layers
items.text: Five inputs per step took the MAE from 27,703 to 22,062; a third recurrent layer took it from 27,703 to 31,211. That ordering is typical and worth internalising: information the model did not previously have beats capacity to reprocess information it already had. Feature work is usually the cheaper lever, and it is the one a data engineer is already equipped to pull.

items.term: Multitask learning is a regulariser that can cost you
items.text: Sharing one model across related targets often helps, because features learned for one task are useful for the others and having to perform well at several tasks resists overfitting. It is not free: the shared trunk must compromise between the tasks, which is why the multitask model here reached 25,330 for rail against 22,062 for the dedicated one. Try it, measure it, and keep whichever wins.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Multivariate time series forecasting incorporates multiple parallel feature columns at each time step to improve prediction accuracy.
Known future information, such as tomorrow's day type, can be shifted by one day so that the model is given tomorrow's value as an input at today's time step.
Adapting an RNN for multivariate input primarily requires updating the input shape dimension to match the number of input features.
Multitask forecasting allows a single model to predict multiple output series simultaneously by adjusting the target shape and output layer size.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Weather is an obvious extra input for transit ridership, but tomorrow's weather is a forecast, not a fact. How should a feature whose future value is itself predicted be handled differently from one that is genuinely known, such as the calendar?
Look up: Chapter 10 of this book, where multitask learning and models with multiple inputs and outputs are introduced.

items.term: Forecasting Several Time Steps Ahead

blocks.content:
To forecast 14 days you can either call a one-day model 14 times and watch its errors compound, or train one model whose output layer has 14 units.

**The question this lesson answers:** every model so far predicted exactly one step ahead. What do you do when the business wants the next two weeks?

### The big picture

```
 iterative : predict -> append -> predict -> append ...
             errors ride along and grow

 direct    : one pass -> Dense(14) -> 14 values at once
```

### 1 · Iterative forecasting

The first approach is **iterative forecasting**, where a model trained to predict a single step ahead is called repeatedly. In each step, the model predicts the next value, which is then concatenated to the input sequence as if it were an actual observation — it is appended to the input sequence as if it had occurred. The extended sequence is then fed back into the model to predict the subsequent step.

The primary drawback of using an iterative one-step-ahead model to forecast 14 steps into the future is **error accumulation**: early prediction errors accumulate and degrade future steps. Any small prediction mistake made early in the loop feeds into future inputs, causing errors to multiply over longer horizons, as illustrated in Figure 15-11 below.

You have seen this failure shape before: a derived value written back into the source it is derived from. The second run no longer knows which numbers were measured and which were guessed.

### 2 · Direct multi-step forecasting

The second approach is **direct multi-step forecasting**, where the network predicts all future steps simultaneously in one shot. Direct multi-step forecasting configures its output layer by setting the output layer to a Dense layer with 14 units — one output unit per day of the horizon, rather than one unit called 14 times.

### 3 · Building the dataset for it

To implement this using Keras, a dataset is constructed with sequences of length `seq_length + 14`. The total sequence length is set to `seq_length + 14` to provide enough data to split into inputs and 14 target steps: a mapping function splits each sequence into an input window of `seq_length` time steps and a target vector containing the next 14 values.

| Piece | Length | Role |
|---|---|---|
| the raw window | seq_length + 14 | what gets cut |
| the input part | seq_length (56) | history |
| the target part | 14 | the horizon |

Cutting one long slice and then splitting it is cheaper than reading the series twice, and it guarantees the two halves line up.

### 4 · The shapes at prediction time

For example, if our historical context is 56 days of data, the model processes the shape `[1, 56, 5]` and outputs a tensor of shape `[1, 14]`. So when passing a single batch of 56 historical days to a direct 14-step model, the shape of the output predictions `Y_pred` is `[1, 14]`: one sequence, fourteen forecasts.

This direct output prevents error accumulation across steps, though accuracy still naturally degrades for predictions further into the future — being wrong about day 14 is simply harder than being wrong about day 1, and that is honest degradation rather than compounding.

**One-liner for your notes:** never loop a one-step model when you can widen its output layer — `Dense(14)` predicts the whole horizon in one pass and cannot feed its own mistakes back into its inputs.

```python
ahead_model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.SimpleRNN(32, input_shape=[None, 5]),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(14)

# Input tensor with sequence length of 56 and 5 features
X = mulvar_valid.to_numpy()[np.newaxis, :56]

# Predict all 14 future days simultaneously
Y_pred = ahead_model.predict(X)  # Output shape: [1, 14]
```

items.term: Why iterative forecasting degrades faster than it looks
items.text: The error at step two is not the model's one-step error plus the error at step one - it is the model's error given an input it has never seen in training, because that input is now partly synthetic. The distribution of inputs drifts away from the training distribution with every iteration, so the degradation is compounding rather than additive. Small horizons hide this; long ones do not.

items.term: What the direct model gives up in exchange
items.text: One output unit per horizon step means the model never has to consume its own output, but it also means each of the fourteen outputs is learned separately and nothing enforces that they form a coherent trajectory. The forecast for day 7 and day 8 can disagree in ways a step-by-step model could not produce. For most forecasting work that is a price worth paying; for generation tasks it is not.

items.term: The horizon is a product decision, not a modelling one
items.text: Every extra step in the horizon costs output units, costs training signal per unit, and degrades naturally with distance. Fourteen here comes from the question asked - the next two weeks - not from anything in the data. Fixing the horizon before choosing the architecture keeps you from optimising a number nobody needs.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Iterative forecasting uses a one-step-ahead model recursively by appending predictions back into the input sequence.
The primary downside of iterative forecasting is that early errors accumulate and degrade later predictions.
Direct multi-step forecasting trains a model to output all future time steps simultaneously in a single vector.
Direct multi-step targets are created by slicing sequences into historical inputs and multi-value target vectors.
A final Dense layer with N units allows a sequence-to-vector model to forecast N steps at once.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Accuracy degrades with horizon - 25,519 at t + 1 and 34,322 at t + 14 on the sequence-to-sequence run. How would you decide where to cut the horizon, and how would you report that degradation to someone who has to act on day 14?
Look up: this chapter's notebook at https://homl.info/colab3, which contains the full training runs and the per-horizon evaluation code.

items.term: Sequence-to-Sequence Forecasting

blocks.content:
Instead of scoring the model only at the last time step, score it at every time step — the gradients get shorter paths, and training gets both faster and steadier.

**The question this lesson answers:** the direct 14-step model works, but its loss only looks at the final output of a 56-step sequence. What does that cost, and what does turning it into a sequence-to-sequence model buy?

### The big picture

```
 seq-to-vector : loss only at step 55  -> 1 gradient path
 seq-to-seq    : loss at every step    -> 56 gradient paths
```

### 1 · The long gradient path problem

When predicting future values in time series data using traditional sequence-to-vector models, error gradients only compute at the final step. This limitation forces gradients to flow backwards through long temporal chains, which destabilizes gradient calculations and slows training significantly.

Converting the architecture to a **sequence-to-sequence model** solves this issue by predicting future targets at every step of the sequence rather than only at the very end. The primary architectural advantage over a sequence-to-vector RNN is that gradient signals flow from every time step, stabilizing and accelerating the model training process.

Think of it as checking each stage of a pipeline instead of only the final table: when something is off, you learn where, immediately, instead of inferring it from one number at the end.

### 2 · What the targets look like now

In this approach, the model receives inputs at every single step and produces immediate multi-step forecasts for that point in time. At time step 0, it predicts values for steps 1 through 14; at step 1, it predicts steps 2 through 15.

Consider a short input sequence `[0, 1, 2, 3]` evaluated to predict the next two future values at each point:

| Step | Input | Target |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | 1, 2 |
| 1 | 1 | 2, 3 |
| 3 | 3 | 4, 5 |

For time step 0 with input `0`, the target sequence contains `[1, 2]`. For step 1 with input `1`, the target vector contains `[2, 3]`. At step 3 with input `3`, the target vector contains `[4, 5]`. The target is no longer one vector per sequence; it is a sequence of vectors, one per step.

### 3 · Why the overlap is not cheating

The targets obviously contain values that also appear later in the input window, which looks like leakage. It is not. Because recurrent neural networks operate as **causal models**, they only process present and past inputs, ensuring future values are never leaked during predictions. An RNN considered at step 1 has literally not been shown step 2 yet: it processes inputs sequentially without accessing future steps beyond the current point.

The guarantee is structural, the same way a window frame ending at `CURRENT ROW` cannot see the rows after it however the data is laid out.

### 4 · Building it, and reading it afterwards

To build this model in Keras, configure a `SimpleRNN` layer with `return_sequences=True` so it outputs predictions for all steps, followed by a `Dense` layer configured to output 14 units at each step. Setting `return_sequences=True` is the parameter configuration necessary in a Keras SimpleRNN layer to enable sequence-to-sequence output, and it lets the dense layer apply forecasts across all time steps.

Because the model computes losses at every time step, error gradients flow directly into each temporal layer without having to travel across the entire sequence history. Training becomes substantially faster and more stable as a result.

During post-training inference, predictions from early time steps are discarded in favor of the output at the final step: model predictions are extracted by selecting only the target output vector produced at the final time step. All those intermediate outputs exist to train the model, not to be read.

**One-liner for your notes:** `return_sequences=True` plus `Dense(14)` scores the model at every step, giving many short gradient paths instead of one long one — and at inference you keep only the last step's 14 numbers.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

seq2seq_model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.SimpleRNN(
        32, 
        return_sequences=True, 
        input_shape=[None, 5]
    ),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(14)
])

# Predict next 14 steps using only the last temporal output
X_val = mulvar_valid.to_numpy()[np.newaxis, :56]
y_pred_14 = seq2seq_model.predict(X_val)[0, -1]
```

items.term: Why more loss terms is the actual speed-up
items.text: The change is not architectural in any deep sense: the same layer, one argument different. What changes is that the loss now has one term per time step instead of one per sequence, so a 56-step window produces 56 sources of gradient rather than one. Training signal per training row went up by a large factor at no extra data cost, and that is where the stability and the speed come from.

items.term: Causality is structural here, and that is rarer than it sounds
items.text: An RNN cannot look ahead because it physically has not read ahead - it is not a rule someone enforced, it is the shape of the computation. Convolutions do not have that property and need causal padding to get it, as the WaveNet lesson shows. When a guarantee comes from structure rather than discipline, it cannot be forgotten in a refactor.

items.term: Why the intermediate outputs are discarded and that is fine
items.text: At inference only the last step's vector is used, so most of what the model computes is thrown away. That feels wasteful until you notice the discarded outputs were never for you - they were the training signal. Accuracy also degrades with horizon within that final vector: on the measured run t + 1 was 25,519 and t + 14 was 34,322.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Sequence-to-sequence models generate target forecasts at every single time step rather than only at the end.
Computing losses at every temporal step produces more gradient paths, speeding up and stabilizing training.
Recurrent models act as causal models because they strictly process current and historical data without looking ahead.
Setting `return_sequences=True` in recurrent layers allows dense layers to apply forecasts across all time steps.
During post-training inference, predictions from early time steps are discarded in favor of the output at the final step.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The Dense layer is applied at every time step here without any extra wrapper. When would you actually need Keras's TimeDistributed layer, and what does it do that a Dense layer applied to a sequence does not?
Look up: the Keras API documentation for the TimeDistributed layer, mentioned in this section of the book.

items.term: Fighting Unstable Gradients in Recurrent Neural Networks

blocks.content:
An unrolled RNN is a very deep network that reuses one set of weights at every level, so anything that grows slightly per step grows explosively over the sequence.

**The question this lesson answers:** RNNs over long sequences train slowly or blow up. Which of the usual deep-learning fixes still work here, which one actively makes things worse, and what replaces it?

### The big picture

| Technique | In an RNN |
|---|---|
| ReLU activation | often worse, outputs can grow unbounded |
| tanh activation | the default, and it saturates on purpose |
| gradient clipping | still useful |
| batch normalization | poor between time steps |
| layer normalization | the one that fits |

### 1 · Why the same weights make it fragile

Training recurrent neural networks over long sequences creates very deep computational graphs that frequently suffer from exploding or vanishing gradients. Because the exact same weights are reused across every single time step, small numerical updates can multiply repeatedly across the sequence.

*Exploding gradients* means the numbers pushed backward grow until training diverges; *vanishing* is the mirror case where they shrink to nothing and nothing learns.

Non-saturating activation functions like ReLU often aggravate this instability in recurrent models by allowing layer outputs to grow without bound over successive time steps: repeated weight reuse across time steps allows unbounded outputs to explode. A *saturating* function such as tanh flattens out at its limits, so a step can never hand the next step an arbitrarily large number — which is exactly why tanh is the default.

Consider a sequence of length 50 processed by an unrolled recurrent network. If an unnormalized update slightly increases the hidden state vector at step 1, that change compounds exponentially through step 50, causing gradient explosion.

### 2 · Why batch normalization is the wrong tool here

To stabilize training, recurrent networks typically rely on saturating activation functions such as the hyperbolic tangent, alongside techniques like gradient clipping and specialized normalization.

*Normalization* means rescaling a set of numbers to a common range so later layers see a stable scale. **Batch normalization** does that using statistics gathered across the batch. Standard batch normalization functions poorly when applied across time steps because feature statistics fluctuate rapidly across sequential inputs.

Instead, **layer normalization** stabilizes training by computing normalization statistics across the feature dimension independently for each sequence instance and time step. Layer normalization is preferred over batch normalization within recurrent layers because layer normalization operates across features per step without batch statistics.

| | Batch norm | Layer norm |
|---|---|---|
| Normalizes across | the batch | the features of one instance |
| Statistics from | the whole batch, over training | computed per step, on the fly |
| Train vs test | behaves differently | behaves the same |

The card below adds the detail, including that a 2015 paper found batch norm only slightly better than nothing even between recurrent layers.

### 3 · Where the normalization goes

Inserting a custom recurrent cell with **layer normalization** normalizes the combined hidden state and input vector at step 1 prior to applying the activation function. This keeps feature scaling consistent from step 1 to step 50 without needing moving averages across the training batch.

In the custom `LNSimpleRNNCell` implementation in the code below, layer normalization is applied after the linear operation but prior to applying the activation function. That ordering is the point of writing a custom cell at all: the stock cell applies its activation immediately, leaving no seam to normalize in.

Applying **layer normalization** along the feature dimension at each time step allows deep recurrent networks to maintain stable gradient flow across long sequences.

### 4 · Two dropout knobs, and error bars for free

*Dropout* randomly switches off a fraction of values during training so the model cannot lean on any one of them. Keras recurrent layers give you two rates, and the primary difference between them is that dropout applies to inputs, whereas recurrent_dropout applies to hidden states — that is, to what travels between time steps.

There is a bonus: Monte Carlo (MC) dropout can be used when forecasting time series with an RNN by running inference multiple times with `training=True` to estimate uncertainty. Train with `recurrent_dropout`, call the model several times with dropout still active, and the spread of the answers is your error bar. The card below has the recipe.

**One-liner for your notes:** keep tanh, clip gradients, skip batch norm, and normalize across the features of each instance at each step — layer normalization is the RNN-shaped answer, and `dropout` vs `recurrent_dropout` is inputs vs hidden states.

blocks.title: Normalization and dropout options for RNNs
blocks.content: Batch normalization cannot be used between time steps, only between recurrent layers, and a 2015 paper found it only slightly better than nothing there. Layer normalization, like BN, learns a scale and an offset parameter for each input, but it normalizes across the features dimension, computes its statistics on the fly at each time step for each instance, and behaves the same way during training and testing. For dropout, most Keras recurrent layers and cells have two hyperparameters: `dropout` sets the dropout rate applied to the inputs, and `recurrent_dropout` sets the rate for the hidden states, between time steps. To get error bars on a forecast, you can use MC dropout: train with `recurrent_dropout`, call the model several times with `model(X, training=True)` so that dropout stays active, and compute the mean and standard deviation of the predictions for each time step.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
class LNSimpleRNNCell(tf.keras.layers.Layer):
    def __init__(self, units, activation="tanh", **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.state_size = units
        self.output_size = units
        self.simple_rnn_cell = tf.keras.layers.SimpleRNNCell(units, activation=None)
        self.layer_norm = tf.keras.layers.LayerNormalization()
        self.activation = tf.keras.activations.get(activation)

    def call(self, inputs, states):
        outputs, new_states = self.simple_rnn_cell(inputs, states)
        norm_outputs = self.activation(self.layer_norm(outputs))
        return norm_outputs, [norm_outputs]
```

items.term: Why the RNN fix set differs from the deep-net fix set
items.text: Most deep-net remedies carry over, but two do not, and both fail for the same structural reason: the same weights and the same normalisation parameters are reused at every step. Batch norm cannot adapt its statistics per step, and a non-saturating activation has nothing stopping a small increase from compounding. Depth created by repetition is not the same as depth created by stacking, and it does not take the same medicine.

items.term: Saturation is a feature here, and a cost elsewhere
items.text: tanh flattening at its limits is exactly what stops outputs exploding across fifty steps - and the same flattening is what made the single-neuron model unable to predict 1.4, and what kills gradients in very deep feedforward nets. The same property is the fix in one place and the defect in another, which is why the range problem is solved with an unconstrained Dense layer on top rather than by changing the activation.

items.term: What MC dropout is really reporting
items.text: Running the model several times with dropout still active gives a spread, and that spread estimates the model's uncertainty about its own parameters. It does not estimate the uncertainty in the world - a pandemic, a new holiday, a route change - which is the kind that actually ruins forecasts. Useful error bars, honestly labelled: uncertainty given that the past still holds.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Recurrent networks reuse the same weights at every time step, which can cause outputs and gradients to explode.
Non-saturating activations like ReLU often increase instability in RNNs compared to saturating functions like tanh.
Batch normalization across recurrent time steps performs poorly due to shifting sequence scales.
Layer normalization stabilizes RNNs by normalizing across the feature dimension independently for each time step.
Keras recurrent layers support input dropout and recurrent dropout to regularize sequence models effectively.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Layer normalization is used here right after the linear combination. Where else in a recurrent cell could it go, and does the placement measurably matter?
Look up: Jimmy Lei Ba et al., "Layer Normalization", arXiv preprint arXiv:1607.06450 (2016), the paper this technique comes from.

items.term: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) Cells

blocks.content:
An LSTM cell keeps two memories instead of one — a long-term line that runs almost untouched from step to step, and three learned gates that decide what to erase from it, what to add, and what to read out.

**The question this lesson answers:** a simple recurrent cell forgets its early inputs by the end of a long sequence. What structure lets a network carry one fact across many steps and still update itself every step?

### The big picture

```
 c(t-1) ──[forget]──(+)─────────────────> c(t)
                     ^                     |
            [input]──┘                  [output]
                 ^                          |
               g(t)                      h(t) = y(t)
```

Two lanes: `c` is the long-term state, `h` is the short-term state and the cell's output.

### 1 · The problem: information fades

Standard recurrent neural networks struggle to process long sequences because information fades quickly across time steps, creating a short-term memory problem. By the end of a long input sequence, the network retains virtually no trace of its initial inputs — that rapid loss of early sequence information across multiple time steps is the problem that led to the LSTM cell.

Each step rewrites the whole state, so nothing survives unless it is rewritten correctly every single time. It is a pipeline where each stage fully overwrites the previous table: after fifty stages the original values are gone even though nobody deleted them.

**Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)** cells solve this challenge by introducing a dedicated long-term state that carries key information across many time steps with minimal transformation.

### 2 · Two states, four layers

An LSTM cell splits its hidden state into a long-term state $\mathbf{c}_{(t)}$ and a short-term state $\mathbf{h}_{(t)}$. As Figure 15-12 below shows, the cell uses four internal **fully connected layers** — layers where every input feeds every output — to manage these states.

| Layer | Symbol | Activation | Job |
|---|---|---|---|
| main | g(t) | tanh | propose new memories |
| forget gate | f(t) | logistic | what to erase from c |
| input gate | i(t) | logistic | what of g to add to c |
| output gate | o(t) | logistic | what of c to read out |

The main layer generates candidate memories $\mathbf{g}_{(t)}$ using a $\tanh$ activation. The remaining three layers act as **gate controllers** using logistic activation functions, which produce outputs between 0 and 1 to regulate element-wise multiplication operations.

A gate is therefore not a switch someone sets — it is a number the network learns, per element, per time step. Multiply by something near 0 and that element is closed; multiply by something near 1 and it passes through.

### 3 · What each gate does

- The **forget gate** vector $\mathbf{f}_{(t)}$ determines which values to erase from the previous long-term state $\mathbf{c}_{(t-1)}$.
- The **input gate** vector $\mathbf{i}_{(t)}$ controls which components of the new candidate state $\mathbf{g}_{(t)}$ to add into the long-term memory.
- The **output gate** vector $\mathbf{o}_{(t)}$ filters the updated long-term memory after it passes through a $\tanh$ function, producing the current short-term state $\mathbf{h}_{(t)}$ and cell output $\mathbf{y}_{(t)}$.

So the long-term state is updated by multiplying f(t) with c(t-1) element-wise, then adding the product of i(t) and g(t) — an erase followed by an insert, which is exactly a `MERGE`: delete the matched parts, insert the new ones, leave everything else alone.

That also answers how the short-term state h(t) differs from the candidate memory g(t): candidate g(t) comes from the main fully connected layer, whereas h(t) is the filtered long-term state exported as output.

### 4 · A worked case, and one default worth knowing

Consider a text-processing scenario where a model reads a subject early in a sentence. The input gate detects the subject and stores its attributes in $\mathbf{c}_{(t)}$. As subsequent words arrive, the forget gate maintains this value near 1 so the memory is preserved. When the sentence finishes, the output gate reads this stored subject memory to guide the final prediction.

One default matters in practice: TensorFlow initializes the forget gate bias vector (b with subscript f) to 1s instead of 0s by default, to prevent the network from forgetting critical information at the start of training. A forget gate starting near 0 would wipe the long-term state before learning ever began.

The central insight of the LSTM architecture is that splitting memory into dual states and controlling information flow via multiplicative gates allows networks to learn much longer patterns than basic cells, although LSTM cells still have a hard time learning long-term patterns in sequences of 100 time steps or more.

**One-liner for your notes:** LSTM = a long-term lane `c` that is only ever erased-then-added-to, plus three learned 0-to-1 gates (forget, input, output) that decide what to drop, store and read at each step.

blocks.title: Figure 15-12
blocks.caption: An LSTM cell
blocks.alt: Figure 15-12: An LSTM cell

blocks.title: Equation 15-4
blocks.caption: LSTM computations
blocks.explain:
**Why the equation looks like this**

Six lines look like a lot until you notice the first four are the same formula four times over. Each
of i, f, o and g is a weighted sum of the current input plus a weighted sum of the previous
short-term state plus a bias - exactly the shape of Equation 15-1 - and the only differences are
which weights are used and which curve is applied at the end. The last two lines are where the cell
actually differs from a simple one: line five updates the long-term memory, and line six reads it
out.

Line five is the important one, and it is written as an erase followed by an add on purpose. Multiply
the old long-term state by the forget gate to drop parts of it, then add the candidate filtered by
the input gate. Because the long-term state is never squashed by an activation on this path, a value
can travel many steps almost untouched - which is precisely the fading problem this cell exists to
fix.

**Is this standard?** Yes. This is the canonical LSTM as used everywhere, written for a single
instance; the mini-batch version is very similar. There are several variants of the cell, and the GRU
in the next lesson is the most popular of them.

**The general form.** Every one of the four inner layers has the form: weights times the input, plus
weights times the previous short-term state, plus a bias, through an activation. Only the activation
differs - a logistic curve for the three gates, because a gate must land between 0 and 1, and tanh
for the main layer, because a proposed memory may legitimately be negative.

**Terms this introduces:** the **logistic** function, written sigma, squashes any number into the
range 0 to 1, which is what makes a gate a gate; **tanh** squashes into -1 to +1; the **circled times
sign** means element-wise multiplication - multiply the first number by the first number, the second
by the second, with no mixing between positions; a **candidate** memory is a proposal that may or may
not be written.

**Every piece of Equation 15-4**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| i with (t) | i at t | the input gate, what of g to store |
| f with (t) | f at t | the forget gate, what of c to erase |
| o with (t) | o at t | the output gate, what of c to read out |
| g with (t) | g at t | the candidate memory from the main layer |
| c with (t) | c at t | the long-term state after this step |
| c with (t-1) | c at t minus 1 | the long-term state before this step |
| h with (t) | h at t | the short-term state, also the output |
| h with (t-1) | h at t minus 1 | the short-term state one step ago |
| y with (t) | y at t | the cell's output, equal to h at t |
| x with (t) | x at t | the input vector at this time step |
| sigma | sigma | the logistic curve, output between 0 and 1 |
| tanh | tan h | the curve with output between -1 and +1 |
| W with xi, xf, xo, xg | W sub x i and so on | each layer's weights for the input |
| W with hi, hf, ho, hg | W sub h i and so on | each layer's weights for the previous h |
| b with i, f, o, g | b sub i and so on | each layer's bias vector |
| the circled times | element-wise times | multiply position by position |

**The formula in plain words**

- Compute three gate vectors and one candidate vector, each from the current input and the previous
short-term state.
- New long-term memory = ( old long-term memory, with the forget gate applied ) + ( the candidate,
with the input gate applied ).
- New short-term memory and output = the new long-term memory, squashed by tanh, with the output gate
applied.

**With real numbers**

The book gives no trained weights, but it gives the two gate values that matter, 0 and 1, and the
whole design is readable from those. Take one single slot of the state - one element - and follow it
through the lesson's sentence example, where a subject is stored early and must survive.

1. Storing it. The input gate for that slot outputs 1 and the forget gate outputs 0, so the new
long-term value = (0 x old) + (1 x candidate) = the candidate. The slot has been overwritten.
2. Holding it. At every later word the forget gate for that slot stays near 1 and the input gate near
0, so the new value = (1 x old) + (0 x candidate) = old. The memory is passed through unchanged,
with no multiplication shrinking it.
3. Reading it. At the end of the sentence the output gate for that slot opens to 1, so the short-term
state for that slot = 1 x tanh(the stored value) and the cell finally exposes what it kept.
4. Ignoring it. With the output gate at 0 the same slot contributes nothing to the output while still
being preserved in c - which is the difference between remembering something and saying it.

Step 2 is the entire point: multiplying by 1 and adding 0 is the identity, so a fact can cross many
time steps without being degraded.

---

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.LSTM(32, return_sequences=True, input_shape=[None, 5]),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(14)
])
```

items.term: Why an additive path is what fixes forgetting
items.text: The long-term state is updated by multiply-then-add and is otherwise passed straight through untransformed. Because it is not squashed by an activation at every step, a value can survive many steps essentially intact, and the gradient flowing back along that path is not multiplied down at each one. Every architecture that handles long ranges has some version of this untouched path - it is the same idea as a residual connection, moved into the time axis.

items.term: Gates are learned, per element, per step - and that is the whole design
items.text: Nothing in the cell is a hand-written rule about what to keep. Each gate is a layer whose output is a vector of numbers between 0 and 1, recomputed from the current input and the previous short-term state at every step. So the cell can learn to hold one slot open for the whole sentence while overwriting another slot every word. When you read the equations, the interesting question is not the arithmetic, it is what a trained gate ends up keying on.

items.term: Where LSTM still fails
items.text: Even with the long-term lane, LSTM cells have a hard time learning long-term patterns in sequences of 100 time steps or more. The state is a fixed-size vector, so everything competes for the same slots - there is no way to add capacity for a longer context without widening the cell everywhere. That fixed-width bottleneck is what attention mechanisms remove, and it is why the field moved on.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Standard RNN cells suffer from short-term memory loss as signals fade over time steps.
LSTM cells split the internal state into a long-term state vector c and a short-term state vector h.
Three gate controllers (forget, input, and output gates) use sigmoid activations to regulate memory flow.
The main layer generates new candidate memories using a hyperbolic tangent (tanh) activation function.
TensorFlow initializes the forget gate bias vector to 1s by default to prevent early memory loss during training.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The gates are learned, so nobody decides what the forget gate keys on. What do people find when they inspect a trained LSTM's gate activations on real sequences - do individual state slots end up tracking interpretable things?
Look up: Sepp Hochreiter and Jurgen Schmidhuber, "Long Short-Term Memory", Neural Computation 9, no. 8 (1997): 1735-1780, the original LSTM paper.

items.term: Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) Cells

blocks.content:
A GRU is an LSTM with the parts merged: one state vector instead of two, one gate doing both forget and input, and no output gate at all.

**The question this lesson answers:** LSTM works but carries four internal layers and two states. How much of that can you remove before performance drops — and what does the simpler cell actually compute?

### The big picture

| | LSTM | GRU |
|---|---|---|
| State vectors | two, c and h | one, h |
| Forget and input | two separate gates | one update gate z |
| Output gate | yes | none, full state is output |
| Extra gate | none | reset gate r |

### 1 · Why simplify at all

Standard Recurrent Neural Networks often struggle to maintain long-term memory because some information is lost at each time step as the data is transformed. While Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks fix this issue by maintaining two distinct hidden state vectors and using three separate gates, their complex architecture requires significant computational parameters. The **gated recurrent unit (GRU)** cell solves this efficiency problem by streamlining the internal architecture of long-memory recurrent cells while maintaining comparable predictive performance.

### 2 · The three simplifications

As Figure 15-13 below illustrates, the GRU cell simplifies the traditional memory mechanism in three major ways.

1. **One state.** It combines the separate cell state and hidden state into a single state vector, $\mathbf{h}_{(t)}$.
2. **One gate for two jobs.** It combines the forget gate and the input gate into a single update gate controller, $\mathbf{z}_{(t)}$. When the update gate outputs a value close to 1, the cell retains the previous memory state $\mathbf{h}_{(t-1)}$ and ignores new input. Conversely, when $\mathbf{z}_{(t)}$ is close to 0, the cell erases old memory and overwrites it with candidate hidden vector $\mathbf{g}_{(t)}$.
3. **No output gate.** The GRU cell eliminates the dedicated output gate entirely, outputting its full state vector at every step — so compared with a standard LSTM cell, the component missing in a GRU cell is a dedicated output gate controlling what part of the state vector is output.

When the update gate z(t) outputs a value equal to 1 in a GRU cell, the forget gate opens completely while the input gate closes to keep old memory. The card below spells out that coupling: whenever a memory must be stored, the location where it will be stored is erased first. It is one slot, written or kept, never both.

### 3 · The reset gate, the one genuinely new piece

Equation 15-5 below details the complete mathematical operations inside the cell, with its why-layer and symbol table underneath.

A reset gate vector, $\mathbf{r}_{(t)}$, controls how much of the previous state $\mathbf{h}_{(t-1)}$ is passed to the main candidate layer $\mathbf{g}_{(t)}$ — it determines how much of the previous state is exposed to compute candidate g(t). For instance, if $\mathbf{r}_{(t)}$ is equal to 0, the candidate layer completely ignores past memory and relies solely on the current input vector $\mathbf{x}_{(t)}$.

Two gates, two different questions: the reset gate decides what the *proposal* is allowed to look at, and the update gate decides how much of that proposal is *kept*.

### 4 · The blend, with a number

Then, the state update equation mixes the old memory with the new candidate using $(1 - \mathbf{z}_{(t)})$. If $\mathbf{z}_{(t)} = 0.8$, the network keeps 80% of the old hidden state and incorporates 20% of the candidate memory.

That is a weighted blend of old and new per element — the same arithmetic as an exponential moving average, except the weight is learned and recomputed at every step instead of being a constant you set.

### 5 · Choosing one in practice

A practitioner might choose a GRU layer over an LSTM layer in a Keras model because GRUs have fewer parameters, making them faster to compute while performing similarly. In Keras it is a one-word edit: replace `SimpleRNN` or `LSTM` with `GRU`. The card below notes the limit both cells share — a fairly limited short-term memory, and a hard time learning long-term patterns in sequences of 100 time steps or more.

**One-liner for your notes:** GRU = one state vector, one update gate z doing forget and input together (keep z of the old, take 1 − z of the new), plus a reset gate that decides what the candidate may see — fewer parameters, similar results.

blocks.title: How z(t) works as both the forget and input gate
blocks.content: In a GRU, the single gate controller $\mathbf{z}_{(t)}$ drives both the forget gate and the input gate. If it outputs a 1, the forget gate is open (= 1), so the old state is kept, and the input gate is closed (1 – 1 = 0), so the candidate $\mathbf{g}_{(t)}$ is not added. If it outputs a 0, the opposite happens. In other words, whenever a memory must be stored, the location where it will be stored is erased first. In Keras, you use a GRU by replacing `SimpleRNN` or `LSTM` with `GRU`, and `tf.keras.layers.GRUCell` is available for custom cells. LSTM and GRU cells handle much longer sequences than simple RNNs, but they still have a fairly limited short-term memory and have a hard time learning long-term patterns in sequences of 100 time steps or more.
