blocks.title: Equation 15-5
blocks.caption: GRU computations
blocks.explain:
**Why the equation looks like this**

Four lines instead of the LSTM's six, and the savings come from two deliberate removals. There is no
separate line for the input gate, because the update gate z serves as both: what it keeps of the old
state is z, and what it admits of the new candidate is one minus z. And there is no output gate line
at all, because the full state is the output.

The last line is the shape worth recognising - a blend. z times the old plus one minus z times the
new is a weighted average whose weights always add to one, so the state cannot inflate simply by
being updated. That is a different safety property from the LSTM's erase-then-add, and it is the
reason the coupling is not merely a saving.

The third line is where the reset gate earns its place: it is applied to the previous state *before*
the candidate is computed, so it controls what the proposal is allowed to see - not what is kept.

**Is this standard?** Yes. This is the canonical GRU as proposed by Kyunghyun Cho and colleagues in
2014, written for a single instance, and it is what Keras's GRU layer implements.

**The general form.** The first three lines have the same shape as every recurrent layer in this
chapter: weights times the input, plus weights times the previous state, plus a bias, through an
activation - logistic for the gates, tanh for the candidate. The one structural difference from
Equation 15-4 is that the candidate line multiplies the previous state by r before weighting it.

**Terms this introduces:** the **candidate** g is a proposed new state that may or may not be
adopted; **sigma** is the logistic curve giving a number between 0 and 1; the **circled times sign**
is element-wise multiplication, position by position with no mixing; **one minus z** is taken element
by element, so each slot has its own blend ratio.

**Every piece of Equation 15-5**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| z with (t) | z at t | the update gate, how much old state to keep |
| r with (t) | r at t | the reset gate, how much old state g may see |
| g with (t) | g at t | the candidate new state |
| h with (t) | h at t | the state after this step, also the output |
| h with (t-1) | h at t minus 1 | the state before this step |
| x with (t) | x at t | the input vector at this time step |
| sigma | sigma | the logistic curve, output between 0 and 1 |
| tanh | tan h | the curve with output between -1 and +1 |
| W with xz, xr, xg | W sub x z and so on | each layer's weights for the input |
| W with hz, hr, hg | W sub h z and so on | each layer's weights for the previous h |
| b with z, r, g | b sub z and so on | each layer's bias vector |
| the circled times | element-wise times | multiply position by position |
| one minus z | one minus z | the share given to the candidate |

**The formula in plain words**

- Compute two gate vectors, z and r, from the current input and the previous state.
- Compute a candidate state from the current input and the previous state *after r has filtered it*.
- New state = z of the old state + (one minus z) of the candidate. That state is also the output.

**With real numbers**

The book gives two concrete gate values for this cell, and both are worth walking.

1. The reset gate at 0. The candidate line multiplies the previous state by r first, so r equal to 0
makes that whole term zero: the candidate layer completely ignores past memory and relies solely
on the current input. The cell can start fresh mid-sequence without erasing what it already holds.
2. The update gate at 0.8, for one slot. Keep 0.8 of the old state and take 0.2 of the candidate -
80% old, 20% new, exactly as this lesson states. The two shares always sum to 1.
3. The update gate at 1. Keep 1 x old and take (1 - 1) = 0 of the candidate: the forget gate is fully
open and the input gate fully closed, so the memory is held and nothing is written.
4. The update gate at 0. Keep 0 x old and take 1 x candidate: the old value is erased and replaced
in the same operation - which is what "whenever a memory must be stored, the location where it
will be stored is erased first" means arithmetically.

---

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

# Create a Sequential model using a GRU layer
model = tf.keras.models.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.GRU(64, return_sequences=True, input_shape=[None, 1]),
    tf.keras.layers.GRU(32),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(1)
])

# Alternative: custom recurrent step using GRUCell
gru_cell = tf.keras.layers.GRUCell(units=32)
rnn_layer = tf.keras.layers.RNN(gru_cell)
```

items.term: What coupling the two gates actually assumes
items.text: Tying the input gate to one minus the forget gate encodes a belief: a slot worth writing to is a slot worth clearing first. That is usually true and it halves the gate parameters, but it removes an option the LSTM has - holding an old memory while also adding to it. When a GRU underperforms an LSTM on a task, this constraint is often the reason worth checking.

items.term: Two gates, two different questions
items.text: It is easy to blur the reset gate and the update gate together. The reset gate decides what the candidate is allowed to look at when it is computed; the update gate decides how much of that candidate survives into the state. Reset controls the proposal, update controls the merge. They can and do pull in opposite directions - ignore the past when proposing, keep most of the past when merging.

items.term: Why simpler won on popularity rather than on accuracy
items.text: GRU spread because it performs about as well with fewer parameters and trains faster, not because it is more expressive - it is strictly less so. That is a common shape in engineering: when two designs score the same, the cheaper one wins on every axis that is not the score. The honest summary is that the choice between them is empirical and usually not where your gains are.

blocks.title: Key points
items: The GRU cell simplifies the LSTM architecture by merging the cell state and hidden state into a single vector.
A single update gate controls both memory retention and memory erasure simultaneously.
The reset gate determines how much past information is exposed when computing new memory candidates.
GRUs eliminate the output gate, outputting the entire state vector at each time step.
GRUs train faster than LSTMs due to having fewer parameters while achieving comparable performance.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: GRU and LSTM perform similarly here. Across many tasks, does the choice between them, or between any of the other LSTM variants, ever make a reliable difference?
Look up: Klaus Greff et al., "LSTM: A Search Space Odyssey", IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems 28, no. 10 (2017): 2222-2232, which compares LSTM variants systematically.

items.term: 1D Convolutional Layers for Sequence Processing

blocks.content:
Putting a 1D convolutional layer in front of a recurrent layer shortens the sequence before the RNN ever sees it, so the RNN can cover twice the history for the same work.

**The question this lesson answers:** LSTM and GRU still lose the plot on very long sequences. How do you feed a recurrent layer 112 days instead of 56 without doubling its cost — and what has to change about the targets when you do?

### The big picture

```
 112 days ─> Conv1D k=4 s=2 ─> 55 steps ─> GRU ─> Dense 14
             filters slide,       half as
             stride skips         many steps
```

### 1 · What a 1D convolution does to a sequence

Recurrent neural networks often struggle to process long input sequences efficiently, as step-by-step computation is slow and fails to condense local noise. A **1D convolutional layer** solves this by sliding small filters along the temporal dimension of a sequence. A 1D convolutional layer extracts features from sequence data because it slides 1D filters across the temporal dimension to detect short sequential patterns.

Each filter acts as a short pattern detector, producing a 1D **feature map** — one output series saying how strongly that pattern matched at each position. Applying multiple filters creates a multi-dimensional feature output at each temporal offset.

A filter of size 4 is a rolling window of 4 days with learned weights, evaluated at every offset. The difference from a window function is that the weights are learned rather than written by you, and there are 32 different ones.

### 2 · Stride, and why shortening helps

By setting a **stride** greater than 1 — the number of steps the filter jumps between evaluations — the convolutional layer downsamples the sequence, shortening its total temporal length while retaining essential information. The primary change when setting the stride of a 1D convolutional layer to 2 is that it reduces the output sequence length by half by stepping two units at a time.

This length reduction allows subsequent **recurrent layers** (such as GRUs) to process much longer historical time windows without exploding computational complexity. So adding a 1D convolutional layer before a GRU layer can improve performance on long sequences because it downsamples the sequence, making it easier for GRU layers to capture longer patterns.

It is the pre-aggregation move you already make: roll raw events up to a coarser grain first, then run the expensive job over fewer rows with the same signal in them.

### 3 · Two effects on length, two fixes to the targets

Consider an input sequence lengthened to 112 days. We pass this into a 1D convolutional layer configured with 32 filters, a kernel size of 4, and a stride of 2.

| Cause | Effect on output | Fix to the targets |
|---|---|---|
| kernel spans 4 steps | first prediction starts at step 4 | drop the first 3 targets |
| stride is 2 | output length is halved | keep every 2nd target |

Because the filter spans 4 time steps, the initial prediction offset starts at step 4. Because the stride is 2, the output length is halved. Consequently, target sequences must be cropped and downsampled using `Y[:, 3::2]` to match the shortened output dimension. In that target dataset transformation, the slice aligns targets with the receptive field offset and downsampled output sequence: the `3` is the crop, the `::2` is the downsample. The card below walks the arithmetic step by step.

Getting this wrong does not crash — it silently compares each forecast against the wrong day. That is the same class of bug as an off-by-one in a date join, and just as quiet.

### 4 · The general padding rule

More generally, the output sequence length when using a stride of 1 and 'same' padding on a 1D convolutional layer remains identical to the input sequence length. *Padding* means adding filler values at the edges so the filter has something to sit on; `"same"` adds enough to preserve the length, while `"valid"` padding or a stride greater than 1 makes the output shorter. Since here the kernel is larger than the stride, all inputs are still used, so nothing is thrown away — only condensed.

Combining 1D convolutions with recurrent layers reduces sequence length and filters local noise, enabling models to learn long-term temporal dependencies far more effectively.

**One-liner for your notes:** a `Conv1D` in front of a GRU is pre-aggregation for sequences — stride 2 halves the length so the RNN sees twice the history, and the targets must be cropped by the kernel offset and downsampled by the stride.

blocks.title: Worked out: why the targets become Y[:, 3::2]
blocks.content: The `Conv1D` layer uses a kernel of size 4 and a stride of 2, on input sequences doubled to 112 days. Because the kernel covers 4 steps, the first output of the convolutional layer is based on input time steps 0 to 3, so the first forecasts are for time steps 4 to 17 instead of 1 to 14. The first three time steps of the targets must therefore be cropped off, which is the `3` in `Y[:, 3::2]`. The stride of 2 halves the output length, so the targets are also downsampled by a factor of 2, which is the `::2`. Since the kernel is larger than the stride, all inputs are still used. In general, a stride of 1 with "same" padding keeps the output sequence as long as the input sequence, while "valid" padding or a stride greater than 1 makes it shorter.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
conv_rnn_model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.Conv1D(filters=32, kernel_size=4, strides=2,
                           activation="relu", input_shape=[None, 5]),
    tf.keras.layers.GRU(32, return_sequences=True),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(14)
])

downsampled_train = longer_train.map(lambda X, Y: (X, Y[:, 3::2]))
```

items.term: Why shortening the sequence helps a model that already handles sequences
items.text: A GRU can in principle read 112 steps; the problem is that useful signal and local noise arrive at the same rate, and the state has to survive every step. A strided convolution condenses groups of steps into learned summaries, so the recurrent layer sees fewer, denser steps covering the same span. The gain is not raw speed - it is a shorter path between the start of the window and the prediction.

items.term: What the layer can and cannot learn to preserve
items.text: Because the kernel is larger than the stride, every input contributes to some output, so the layer can learn to keep the useful information and drop only the unimportant detail. Make the stride larger than the kernel and inputs are skipped outright, with no chance of recovery. The kernel-versus-stride relationship is therefore a statement about whether downsampling is lossy by construction.

items.term: Target alignment is where this class of model silently lies
items.text: The crop and the downsample are not decoration; they are what makes forecast number k line up with day number k. Get them wrong and nothing errors - the model trains, the loss falls, and the reported score describes a comparison against the wrong days. Any time a layer changes sequence length, the alignment of the targets is a thing to derive and check, not to copy.

blocks.title: Key points
items: 1D convolutional layers slide filters along a sequence to extract local temporal patterns.
Setting a stride greater than 1 downsamples sequence length while extracting essential features.
Shortening sequences allows subsequent recurrent layers to detect longer-term dependencies.
Target datasets must be cropped and downsampled to match the convolutional layer output shape.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Here the convolution feeds a GRU. What happens if you also put 1D pooling layers in the stack, and how does pooling over a time axis differ in effect from a strided convolution?
Look up: Chapter 14 of this book, its treatment of 2D convolutional and pooling layers, padding modes and the output-size arithmetic that carries over to one dimension.

items.term: Understanding the WaveNet Architecture

blocks.content:
WaveNet drops recurrence entirely: it stacks 1D convolutional layers whose inputs are spaced further apart at every level, so the reach doubles per layer while the parameter count per filter never moves.

**The question this lesson answers:** if you want to cover thousands of time steps, recurrence is too slow and plain convolutions need huge kernels. What architecture covers a long history cheaply — and how does it avoid reading the future?

### The big picture

```
 layer 4  rate 8   sees 16 steps
 layer 3  rate 4   sees  8 steps
 layer 2  rate 2   sees  4 steps
 layer 1  rate 1   sees  2 steps
```

Kernel size stays 2 all the way up. Only the spacing changes.

### 1 · What both alternatives cost

Standard recurrent networks struggle to capture dependencies over thousands of time steps because backpropagation through time becomes computationally expensive and prone to unstable gradients. Standard one-dimensional convolutional networks cover long sequences only by stacking many deep layers or using large kernels, which drastically increases parameter counts.

WaveNet is what solves the problem of processing long sequences in recurrent neural networks: it processes thousands of time steps efficiently using dilated convolutions.

### 2 · Dilation: same filter, wider spacing

To solve this issue, the **WaveNet** architecture uses stacked 1D convolutional layers with exponentially increasing **dilation rates**. The dilation rate defines how far apart a neuron's inputs are spaced.

The lower layers use small dilation rates, such as 1 or 2, allowing them to capture short-term localized patterns. Higher layers double the dilation rate to values like 4, 8, and beyond, expanding the overall **receptive field** — the total span of original time steps one output neuron ultimately depends on — exponentially without increasing the number of parameters per filter. Doubling the dilation rate at each layer expands the receptive field exponentially without increasing parameter counts.

That is the trade every data engineer likes: reach grows geometrically, cost grows linearly. Compare the alternative of simply widening the window, where cost grows with reach.

For example, as Figure 15-14 below shows, stacking layers with kernel size 2 and dilation rates of 1, 2, 4, and 8 allows a output neuron at the top layer to cover a receptive field of 16 time steps using only four thin convolutional layers — so in a stack with kernel size 2 and dilation rates 1, 2, 4 and 8, a neuron in the fourth layer sees 16 time steps. The card below shows the doubling one layer at a time.

### 3 · Causal padding: never read the future

To prevent the network from violating temporal causality — that is, peeking into future time steps when generating predictions — WaveNet uses **causal padding**. Causal padding pads the sequence with zeros exclusively at the beginning, ensuring that every output step depends only on current and past inputs. This is why causal padding is essential when building a WaveNet model for time series forecasting: it ensures that predictions at step t only rely on step t and past steps.

A convolution is symmetric by default: centred on step t it would read t−1 and t+1 alike. On an image that is fine. On a forecast it is leakage, and the model would score beautifully in training and fail in production. Padding only the left-hand side removes the right-hand reach by construction.

A useful side effect: every layer then outputs a sequence the same length as its input, so unlike the strided model of the previous lesson, the full 112-day targets need no cropping or downsampling.

### 4 · The real thing, and the last layer

In the original paper, DeepMind researchers stacked groups of ten layers with dilation rates doubling from 1 up to 512. A single stack of ten such layers acts like a convolutional layer with a kernel of size 1,024, while being much faster and using far fewer parameters; the authors stacked three of these groups.

| Version | Rates | Groups |
|---|---|---|
| the paper | 1, 2, 4 … 512 | three stacks of ten layers |
| the code below | 1, 2, 4, 8 twice | one pass |

The model ends with a `Conv1D` of 14 filters and kernel size 1. The equivalent operation of using a 1D convolution layer with a kernel size of 1 is that it acts like a Dense layer applied independently to each time step: with no span, the filter has nothing to slide over and just remixes the channels at each position.

**One-liner for your notes:** WaveNet stacks small causal convolutions with doubling dilation rates, so the receptive field doubles per layer at flat parameter cost — ten layers reach like a kernel of 1,024, and causal padding is what keeps it from reading the future.

blocks.title: Worked out: WaveNet receptive fields
blocks.content: With a kernel size of 2, the dilation rate sets how far apart each neuron's two inputs are. The first layer (rate 1) sees 2 time steps, the second (rate 2) sees 4, the third (rate 4) sees 8, and the fourth (rate 8) sees 16: each doubling of the rate doubles the receptive field. In the paper, one stack of 10 layers with rates 1, 2, 4, …, 512 therefore acts like a single convolutional layer with a kernel of size 1,024, and the authors stacked three such groups. In the Keras version, `(1, 2, 4, 8) * 2` gives the rates 1, 2, 4, 8, 1, 2, 4, 8. Thanks to causal padding, every layer outputs a sequence of the same length as its input, so the full 112-day targets need no cropping or downsampling. The final `Conv1D` with 14 filters of size 1 is equivalent to a `Dense` layer with 14 units applied at each time step.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
wavenet_model = tf.keras.Sequential()
wavenet_model.add(tf.keras.layers.Input(shape=[None, 5]))
for rate in (1, 2, 4, 8) * 2:
    wavenet_model.add(tf.keras.layers.Conv1D(
        filters=32, kernel_size=2, padding="causal", activation="relu",
        dilation_rate=rate))
wavenet_model.add(tf.keras.layers.Conv1D(filters=14, kernel_size=1))
```

items.term: Why exponential dilation is the efficient way to buy reach
items.text: Reach can be bought three ways: more layers, bigger kernels, or wider spacing. The first two cost parameters in proportion to the reach; doubling the dilation doubles the reach for free, because the kernel stays size 2. Ten layers then cover 1,024 steps with the parameter budget of ten tiny layers. The trade-off is resolution - at high dilation a neuron samples the distant past sparsely rather than reading all of it.

items.term: Causal padding is a discipline convolutions do not have by default
items.text: A convolution centred on step t naturally reads both sides, which is correct for images and is leakage for forecasts. Padding only the left-hand side is what removes the future from the receptive field, and it is an easy thing to leave out - the model still trains, still scores well in validation, and is wrong in production. Compare an RNN, where causality cannot be forgotten because nothing has read ahead.

items.term: What it means that the recurrent layers can be dropped entirely
items.text: WaveNet handles very long sequences with no recurrence at all, which removes the sequential dependency and lets the whole sequence be processed in parallel. On this ridership task the models perform similarly, so the architecture is not the story - but the direction is. Removing the sequential bottleneck while keeping long-range reach is the same motivation that produced attention and the transformer in the next chapter.

blocks.title: Key points
items: WaveNet uses 1D convolutional layers with exponentially doubling dilation rates.
Exponential dilation rates allow the receptive field to expand dramatically while keeping parameter counts low.
Causal padding ensures that predictions depend only on past and present time steps.
Lower layers extract short-term patterns, while upper layers capture long-term context.

sections.title: Chapter 16: Natural Language Processing with RNNs and Attention

items.term: Preparing Datasets for Character RNNs

blocks.content:
Before a network can learn to write Shakespeare, the raw text has to become pairs of number sequences: an input window and the same window shifted one character forward.

**The question this lesson answers:** you have one long string of 1,115,394 characters. What exactly do you feed a network so that it learns to predict the next token in a sequence given the preceding context?

### The big picture

```
1,115,394 chars  ->  character IDs 0..38
   -> slice windows of 100 + 1 = 101
        -> input  = first 100 characters
        -> target = last  100 characters
```

The target is the input shifted one step into the future. That single design choice is what turns "a pile of text" into a supervised training set with no human labelling at all.

### 1 · Text to integers

Raw text cannot be processed directly by neural networks. First the text is converted to lowercase and split into individual characters using a **TextVectorization** layer — a Keras layer that scans the text once and assigns an integer identifier to each distinct character. (In the book it is switched to character mode and lowercasing at construction time; page index 750.)

That layer reserves two identifiers it does not need here: one for **padding** (filler used to make short sequences the same length) and one for **unknown** tokens (anything it never saw). By subtracting two from these identifiers, we drop the reserved padding and unknown tokens, yielding zero-indexed IDs for 39 unique characters across a dataset of 1,115,394 characters.

Think of it as a dimension table with 39 rows that the layer builds for you, then a `- 2` to shift the surrogate keys down so they start at zero.

### 2 · One long sequence to overlapping windows

Next, the continuous sequence of character IDs is sliced into overlapping windows of a chosen length, such as 100 characters. To construct target sequences for sequence-to-sequence training, windows are created with a total length of 100 + 1 = 101 characters.

Why the extra character: the pipeline then splits each 101-character slice into an input sequence of the first 100 characters and a target sequence of the last 100 characters, effectively shifting the target by one time step into the future. Without that one spare character the last input position would have no answer to learn from.

For example, given an input window encoding the text string "to be or not to b", the target sequence generated for training is the identical length string shifted by one character, representing "o be or not to be".

As Figure 16-1 below shows, these windows are extracted via `window()` and `flat_map()`, optionally shuffled, batched, and mapped into input-target pairs. In lakehouse terms: a sliding-window read over one ordered column, then a projection into two columns — `inputs` and `targets`.

### 3 · Window length is a dial, and it has a hard edge

The window length is a setting you can tune, and the book sets it to 100. The trade-off runs one way only:

| Window length | Training | What the model can learn |
|---|---|---|
| shorter | easier and faster | nothing longer than the window |
| longer | harder and slower | longer patterns become reachable |

So the window should not be made too small. With `length = 100`, the char-RNN cannot learn patterns longer than 100 characters. It is a hard ceiling, not a soft preference — the model never sees further back than one window, so a rhyme scheme spanning 200 characters is invisible to it.

### 4 · The three-way split

Splitting the primary dataset allocates 1,000,000 characters for training, 60,000 characters for validation, and the remaining characters for testing — roughly 90% training, 5% validation and 5% testing. Because the text is one continuous stream, the split is by position, not by random sampling: characters 0 to 1,000,000, then 1,000,000 to 1,060,000, then the rest.

**One-liner for your notes:** slice the character-ID stream into windows of length + 1, split each into the first `length` characters and the last `length` characters, and you have a next-character training set that needs no labels.

blocks.title: Choosing the window length
blocks.content:
The window length is a setting you can tune, and the book sets it to 100. Shorter windows make an RNN easier and faster to train, but they come with a hard limit: the RNN cannot learn any pattern that is longer than the window length, so the window should not be made too small. With `length = 100`, the char-RNN cannot learn patterns longer than 100 characters.

The split of the encoded text follows the same code: roughly 90% of the text goes to training (the first 1,000,000 characters), 5% to validation (characters 1,000,000 to 1,060,000) and 5% to testing (the rest).

items.term: Why the target is the input shifted by one, and not something cleverer
items.text: Shifting by one turns an unlabelled pile of text into a fully labelled training set, at zero annotation cost, because the answer for every position is already sitting one character to the right. This is the trick behind every language model in this chapter and the reason they can be trained on the whole internet. It generalises to anything with a natural order - the next event in a session, the next row in a time series. It breaks the moment the thing you want predicted is not already present in the data, which is when you are back to paying for labels.

items.term: The window length is a memory ceiling, not a speed knob
items.text: It is tempting to read 'shorter is faster' and pick a small window. But the window is also the furthest back the model can ever see: a pattern spanning 150 characters is not learned badly at length 100, it is not learned at all. So the choice is really 'what is the longest structure I need the model to notice', and cost is the constraint on that answer rather than the other way round.

items.term: Why the split is by position, not random
items.text: The dataset is one continuous stream, so a random row-level split would put windows overlapping the same passage on both sides of the boundary - the validation set would contain text the model trained on. Splitting at character 1,000,000 keeps them disjoint. The same hazard exists in any windowed or time-ordered dataset, and it is the standard way a validation score ends up flattering a model.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Character-level encoding maps text characters directly to integer identifiers using a TextVectorization layer.
Unused padding and unknown token IDs are subtracted to yield a clean vocabulary of distinct character IDs.
Training targets are created by shifting the input sequence window forward by exactly one time step.
The TensorFlow dataset pipeline processes continuous sequences using windowing, flattening, shuffling, and batching.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The windows here overlap by design (shift=1), so the same character appears in up to 100 different training windows. What does that do to the meaning of one epoch, and does it change how you should read the validation curve?
Look up: the TensorFlow `tf.data.Dataset` API documentation for `window()`, `flat_map()` and `shuffle()`, which are the three calls the lesson's pipeline is built from.

items.term: Building and Training a Char-RNN Model

blocks.content:
The Char-RNN is three layers deep: turn character IDs into vectors, run a recurrent layer over them, then output one probability per possible next character at every step.

**The question this lesson answers:** given windows of 100 character IDs and their shifted targets, what network shape actually learns "which character comes next", and why does each layer have to be there?

### The big picture

```
IDs  ->  Embedding 16  ->  GRU 128  ->  Dense 39 + softmax
[b,w]      [b,w,16]        [b,w,128]     [b,w,39]
```

`b` is the batch size and `w` the window length. Notice the first two dimensions never change: one row per sequence, one column per time step. Only the last dimension is rewritten by each layer.

### 1 · Why not an ordinary feedforward network

Modeling natural language at the character level requires an architecture that can process sequences of character IDs and output probabilities for every possible next character. A standard feedforward network cannot track sequence history efficiently, so we construct a specialized recurrent model called a **Char-RNN** to handle this task. *Recurrent* means the layer carries a running state from one time step to the next, so what it saw at character 7 still colours what it does at character 8.

### 2 · The three layers, one job each

To build this network, we first pass sequence inputs into an **Embedding layer**. This layer converts discrete character IDs into dense vector representations — a learned lookup table with one row per character ID and one column per embedding dimension. ID 12 is just a label; its embedding row is a set of numbers training is free to move around so that similar characters end up near each other.

Next, a recurrent layer such as a **GRU layer** processes these vector sequences across time steps, keeping track of sequential context. Finally, a **Dense layer** with a **softmax activation function** outputs a probability distribution over all distinct character tokens for each time step in the batch. **Softmax** turns a row of raw scores into positive numbers that sum to 1, so the row reads as probabilities.

| Layer | Turns | Into |
|---|---|---|
| Embedding | one character ID | a dense vector of 16 numbers |
| GRU | a vector plus past state | a 128-number state per step |
| Dense + softmax | that state | 39 probabilities summing to 1 |

### 3 · The example, dimension by dimension

For example, suppose our dataset contains 39 distinct characters. The model uses an input **Embedding layer** with 16 output dimensions, converting input tensors of shape `[batch_size, window_length]` into 3D output tensors of shape `[batch_size, window_length, 16]`. A GRU layer with 128 units processes this output while keeping sequence dimensions intact. The final Dense layer produces 39 probability outputs at each time step, summing to 1.

The Dense layer's width is not a tuning choice: it must have one unit per distinct character, so 39 characters means 39 units. The 16 and the 128 *are* tuning choices.

### 4 · Why `return_sequences=True` matters

The essential insight to remember is that returning full sequences from the GRU layer allows the Dense output layer to evaluate and train on next-character predictions at every individual time step across the context window.

Without it, the GRU would hand back only its final state and you would get one prediction per 100-character window instead of 100. Same data, one hundredth of the training signal.

The model is compiled with the `"sparse_categorical_crossentropy"` loss, which is the standard choice when the targets are plain integer class indices — here, character IDs — rather than one-hot rows.

### 5 · Wrapping it so it reads raw text

To streamline predictions on raw text, we can wrap the trained network inside a sequential pipeline that includes a **TextVectorization layer** to handle raw string processing automatically. The card below spells out the middle piece: a Lambda layer that subtracts 2, because the trained model expects IDs 0 to 38 while a raw string comes out of TextVectorization starting at 2.

When given the input sequence string `"To be or not to b"`, the wrapped model processes the text, extracts the final time step's probability array, and correctly predicts the character `'e'` using an argmax operation over the vocabulary index. **Argmax** simply means "the position of the largest value".

**One-liner for your notes:** Embedding to make IDs learnable, GRU to carry context, Dense-plus-softmax one unit per character — and `return_sequences=True` so every time step is a training example.

blocks.title: Wrapping the model so it reads raw text
blocks.content:
The model itself was trained on character IDs from 0 to 38, because 2 was subtracted from every ID to drop the padding token (ID 0) and the unknown token (ID 1), which are not used. A raw string, however, comes out of the TextVectorization layer with IDs that start at 2. So the final `shakespeare_model` stacks three parts: the TextVectorization layer, a Lambda layer that subtracts 2 from the character IDs, and the trained model.

To predict the next character of "To be or not to b", the wrapped model takes the probabilities at the last time step, `tf.argmax` picks the most probable ID, and adding 2 back gives the vocabulary index of that character, which is 'e'.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.Embedding(input_dim=n_tokens, output_dim=16),
    tf.keras.layers.GRU(128, return_sequences=True),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(n_tokens, activation="softmax")
])
model.compile(loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", optimizer="nadam")

shakespeare_model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    text_vec_layer,
    tf.keras.layers.Lambda(lambda X: X - 2),
    model
])
```

items.term: Why an Embedding layer instead of the raw ID
items.text: Feeding the integer 12 straight into a network implies that character 12 is 'bigger' than character 5 and 'between' 11 and 13, none of which is true - the IDs are arbitrary labels. A one-hot column per character removes the false ordering but gives every pair of characters the same distance, which is equally wrong. An embedding is the middle option: a short row of numbers per character that training is free to arrange, so vowels can end up near vowels if that helps. The same argument applies to any high-cardinality categorical column.

items.term: What `return_sequences=True` really buys
items.text: It is not a formatting choice, it is a hundredfold change in training signal. With it, a 100-character window produces 100 supervised predictions; without it, one. That is why the char-RNN trains on a modest dataset at all. The trade is that the loss now averages over every position, including the early ones where the model has almost no context to work with - which is why the first few characters of generated text are usually the weakest.

items.term: Why the output width is forced and the others are not
items.text: The 16 and the 128 are hyperparameters: make them bigger and the model has more capacity and costs more. The 39 is not negotiable - it is the size of the answer space, so it is determined by the data, not by you. A useful habit when reading any architecture: separate the numbers the problem fixes from the numbers you chose, because only the second kind are worth tuning.

blocks.title: Key points
items: The Embedding layer maps discrete character IDs to dense vector representations.
Setting return_sequences=True on the GRU layer ensures predictions are generated at every time step.
The output Dense layer uses a softmax activation function to output character probabilities.
Combining vectorization and token offset layers directly with the model simplifies raw text inference.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The embedding size here is 16 for 39 characters, but 128 for a 1,000-word vocabulary later in this chapter. Is there a principled way to pick that width, or is it purely empirical?
Look up: the Keras API documentation for `tf.keras.layers.Embedding`, particularly `input_dim`, `output_dim` and `mask_zero`.

items.term: Generating Text with Temperature Sampling

blocks.content:
Generating text means sampling the next character from the model's predicted probabilities, and **temperature** is the one dial that decides how adventurous that sampling is.

**The question this lesson answers:** the trained char-RNN gives you 39 probabilities for the next character. Which one do you actually pick, and what happens to the output when you change how you pick?

### The big picture

| Temperature | What it does to the odds | Output |
|---|---|---|
| near 0 | widens the gap, top char dominates | rigid, predictable |
| 1 | leaves the model's own odds alone | creative yet readable |
| 100 | flattens everything toward equal | chaotic gibberish |

### 1 · Greedy decoding, and why it disappoints

When generating new text with a character-level recurrent neural network, simply choosing the character with the highest predicted probability at every step is called **greedy decoding**. However, greedy decoding often fails in practice because it repeatedly generates the same words and phrases in a predictable loop.

The reason is that it is deterministic: the same context always produces the same next character, so once the text wanders into a phrase it has seen often, it loops there forever.

To produce more interesting and diverse text, the model can instead sample the next character randomly based on its predicted probability distribution using functions like `tf.random.categorical()`. Sampling means a character with 10% probability genuinely gets picked about one time in ten, instead of never.

### 2 · Temperature: dividing the logits

To control how creative or deterministic the generated output is, engineers introduce a parameter called **temperature**. Before sampling, the logarithm of the predicted probabilities, known as the **logits**, is divided by the temperature value.

A **logit** here is just the log of a probability — a score on a scale where the differences add rather than multiply. Dividing that whole row by one number is what stretches or squashes the gaps between characters:

| Divide by | Effect on the gaps | Result |
|---|---|---|
| a small number | gaps get bigger | the leader runs away with it |
| a large number | gaps get smaller | everything looks equally likely |

Dividing the logits by a temperature close to zero increases the gap between probabilities, favoring high-probability characters and producing rigid, predictable text suitable for precise tasks like mathematical equations. Conversely, dividing by a very high temperature flattens the probability distribution, making all characters nearly equally likely to be selected and creating chaotic, highly random output.

### 3 · The same prompt at three temperatures

Consider an example where the model evaluates a initial prompt such as "To be or not to be".

- When using a low temperature of 0.01, the model predictably selects top-ranked characters, generating coherent text like "To be or not to be the duke".
- Raising the temperature to 1 yields creative yet readable phrases like "To be or not to behold?".
- However, increasing the temperature to an extreme value of 100 flattens the probabilities so completely that the model outputs gibberish containing random punctuation and letters like "To be or not to bef ,mt'&o3fpadm!".

Nothing about the trained model changed between those three lines. Only the division changed. The same weights, read three different ways.

### 4 · Where the balance sits

The central insight to remember is that temperature scales log probabilities to strike a balance between repetitive predictability and random nonsense during text generation.

The card below shows the two helper functions: `next_char()` does one step — predict, rescale the logits, sample, map the ID back to a character — and `extend_text()` just calls it in a loop, appending each new character to the text it feeds back in.

**One-liner for your notes:** greedy decoding loops, pure sampling is livelier, and temperature is the single number that slides you between the two by dividing the logits before the draw.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
def next_char(text, temperature=1):
    y_proba = shakespeare_model.predict([text])[0, -1:]
    rescaled_logits = tf.math.log(y_proba) / temperature
    char_id = tf.random.categorical(rescaled_logits, num_samples=1)[0, 0]
    return text_vec_layer.get_vocabulary()[char_id + 2]

def extend_text(text, n_chars=50, temperature=1):
    for _ in range(n_chars):
        text += next_char(text, temperature)
    return text
```

items.term: Why the most likely character is not the most likely sentence
items.text: Greedy decoding maximises one step at a time, and a chain of individually-best choices is not the best chain - the second-best character now can open up a far better continuation. That gap is the whole reason both sampling and, later in this chapter, beam search exist. It is the same trap as any greedy algorithm: locally optimal, globally not.

items.term: Temperature is a decoding choice, not a model change
items.text: Nothing about the trained weights differs between temperature 0.01 and 100 - only how the same probabilities are read. That matters operationally: you can expose temperature as a per-request setting, tune it without retraining, and use different values for different jobs from one deployed model. It also means a bad temperature can make a good model look broken, which is worth checking before blaming training.

items.term: Where the low-temperature setting stops being safe
items.text: Pushing temperature toward zero makes output rigid and predictable, which is what you want for precise text. But it reintroduces exactly the repetition problem greedy decoding had, because near zero it *is* greedy decoding. So 'more accurate' and 'less repetitive' pull in opposite directions on this one dial, and there is no setting that gives you both.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Greedy decoding selects the most likely character at each step but leads to repetitive text.
Sampling next characters randomly using predicted probabilities increases text diversity.
Temperature scales the logits prior to sampling to control randomness.
Low temperatures favor high-probability characters, while high temperatures flatten probabilities toward uniform randomness.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Temperature reshapes the whole distribution. What is the alternative of simply cutting off the tail instead - sampling only from the top few characters, or from the smallest set whose probabilities add up to a threshold - and when would you prefer that to a temperature change?

Look up: this book's own remark a page after the temperature example, that a common technique is to sample only from the top k characters, or only from the smallest set of top characters whose total probability exceeds some threshold, which is called nucleus sampling (book page index 755).

items.term: Preserving Hidden States Across Batches with Stateful RNNs

blocks.content:
A stateful RNN keeps its hidden state from one batch to the next, so the model can learn patterns longer than a single training window.

**The question this lesson answers:** the char-RNN cannot learn any pattern longer than its 100-character window. How do you get long-range memory without backpropagating through a longer sequence?

### The big picture

```
stateless:  [batch 1] state->0   [batch 2] state->0
stateful :  [batch 1] state ---> [batch 2] carries on
```

The arrow is the whole idea. Everything else in this lesson — no shuffling, non-overlapping windows, a fixed batch size, a reset callback — exists only to keep that arrow honest.

### 1 · What resetting costs you

Standard stateless recurrent neural networks reset their hidden state to zeros at the start of every training batch. This resetting prevents the network from learning long-term dependencies that extend past the length of a single training sequence.

A **stateful RNN** solves this limitation by retaining its final hidden state at the end of a batch and using it as the initial state for the next batch. Consequently, the network learns extended text patterns despite only backpropagating over short window lengths — the gradient still only travels 100 steps, but the *state* has travelled much further.

| | Stateless | Stateful |
|---|---|---|
| State at batch start | zeros | last batch's final state |
| Windows | overlapping, shuffled | consecutive, in order |
| Can learn patterns | up to the window | beyond the window |

### 2 · The data has to arrive in order

To make statefulness effective, the dataset must feed continuous text sequences sequentially. As Figure 16-2 below shows, sequential sequence fragments are extracted using non-overlapping windows (`shift=length`) without shuffling.

Both halves matter and for the same reason. Shuffling would hand batch 2 a window from somewhere else entirely, so the carried state would be about the wrong passage. Overlapping windows would make batch 2 re-read text batch 1 had already consumed.

In a single-sequence batching approach, batch 1 receives sequence window 1, and batch 2 receives window 2, allowing the model to carry state continuously from window 1 directly into window 2.

This is the same discipline as an incremental load with a watermark: each run must start exactly where the previous run stopped, so you cannot shuffle the partitions and you cannot re-read overlapping ranges.

### 3 · Why the batch size is 1

The card below gives the reason plainly: batching is hard for a stateful RNN. With `batch(32)`, the first batch would hold windows 1 to 32 and the second batch windows 33 to 64, so window 33 would not continue where window 1 left off. The simplest fix is to use a batch size of 1.

That is also why the model must be told its batch size up front. Building a stateful RNN in Keras requires setting `stateful=True` on recurrent layers like `tf.keras.layers.GRU` and explicitly declaring `batch_input_shape=[1, None]` on the first layer so the model allocates internal state vectors per batch item. A stateful RNN keeps one state for each input sequence in the batch, so it has to know how many states to allocate before training starts. The `None` is the sequence length, which stays free.

### 4 · Resetting once per epoch

Because the state carries over continuously across batches, training requires a custom callback to invoke `model.reset_states()` at the start of each new epoch, preventing states from carrying over between unrelated text iterations.

An **epoch** is one full pass over the training data. At the end of one pass the reader is at the end of Shakespeare; at the start of the next it is back at the beginning, and a state carried across that seam would be memory of the wrong text.

### 5 · Predicting afterwards

The fixed batch size follows the trained model around. After training, the model can only make predictions for batches of the same size as the ones used during training, which is a batch size of 1 here. To remove this restriction, create an identical stateless model and copy the stateful model's weights into it. The weights are the learned part; statefulness is only a wiring choice, so the copy loses nothing.

**One-liner for your notes:** a stateful RNN carries its hidden state across batches, which buys long-range memory but costs you shuffling, overlapping windows, a free batch size, and one reset per epoch.

blocks.title: Predicting with a trained stateful model
blocks.content:
A stateful RNN keeps one state for each input sequence in the batch, so the batch size is fixed into the model through `batch_input_shape`. After training, the model can only make predictions for batches of the same size as the ones used during training, which is a batch size of 1 here. To remove this restriction, create an identical stateless model and copy the stateful model's weights into it.

The batch size is 1 in the first place because batching is hard for a stateful RNN. With `batch(32)`, the first batch would hold windows 1 to 32 and the second batch windows 33 to 64, so window 33 would not continue where window 1 left off.

blocks.title: Figure 16-2
blocks.caption: Preparing a dataset of consecutive sequence fragments for a stateful RNN
blocks.alt: Figure 16-2: Preparing a dataset of consecutive sequence fragments for a stateful RNN

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.Embedding(input_dim=n_tokens, output_dim=16,
                              batch_input_shape=[1, None]),
    tf.keras.layers.GRU(128, return_sequences=True, stateful=True),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(n_tokens, activation="softmax")
])

class ResetStatesCallback(tf.keras.callbacks.Callback):
    def on_epoch_begin(self, epoch, logs):
        self.model.reset_states()

model.compile(loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", optimizer="nadam")
model.fit(stateful_train_set, epochs=10, callbacks=[ResetStatesCallback()])
```

items.term: The state travels further than the gradient
items.text: This is the subtle part and it is easy to misread. Backpropagation still only reaches back through one window, so the model is never *credited* for something 500 characters ago. What crosses the batch boundary is the state - the summary the model has already built. So a stateful RNN can use long context, but it learns to build that context only from short-range signal. That is why it helps and why it is not a complete answer to long-range dependency, which is what attention eventually solves.

items.term: Statefulness costs you every convenience at once
items.text: No shuffling, no overlapping windows, a batch size frozen into the model, and a callback to reset each epoch. Each one exists to protect the same invariant: batch n+1 must continue exactly where batch n stopped. Whenever a design demands strict ordering across units of work, expect the same bill - no parallelism, no reshuffling, and recovery logic at the seams.

items.term: Why copying the weights into a stateless model is legitimate
items.text: The weights are what training learned; statefulness is only a decision about what to do with the hidden state between batches. Two models with identical layer shapes can therefore share weights and differ in that decision. The general lesson is worth carrying: training-time and serving-time architectures need only agree on the parameters, not on the plumbing around them.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A stateful RNN preserves its final hidden state after processing a batch and reuses it as the initial hidden state for the next batch.
Data for stateful RNNs must be prepared sequentially without overlapping windows or random shuffling.
Keras stateful layers require a defined batch input shape to allocate state buffers correctly.
Hidden states must be manually reset using `model.reset_states()` at the beginning of each epoch.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Batch size 1 is described as the simplest solution, not the only one. What does it actually cost in training throughput, and how would you build consecutive batches of 32 without breaking the continuity the state depends on?

items.term: Sentiment Analysis with RNNs and Masking

blocks.content:
Classifying a movie review as positive or negative with an RNN works — right up until the padding added to make batches rectangular destroys the model's memory.

**The question this lesson answers:** the IMDb reviews are all different lengths, and a batch has to be a rectangle. What does the padding do to a GRU, and why does the accuracy sit at 50%?

### The big picture

```
"Great movie" -> [86, 18, 0, 0, ... 0]
                  ^^^^^^  ^^^^^^^^^^^
                  2 real  padding the GRU still reads
```

The model does not know the zeros are filler. It processes them as real time steps, and by the end it has forgotten the two words that mattered.

### 1 · The task and the data

Natural language processing applications often require text classification to determine subjective tones, such as whether a movie review is positive or negative. The primary challenge arises from converting raw text strings into numerical representations while preserving sequence information across varying sentence lengths.

Consider the IMDb dataset consisting of 50,000 movie reviews labeled with binary targets: 0 for negative and 1 for positive. The split used here takes 25,000 training reviews into batches.

### 2 · Text to a rectangle

To process text data, raw strings are tokenized into sequences of word IDs using tools like **TextVectorization**. **Tokenize** means cut the string into units — here words, not characters as in the char-RNN.

Because sentences within a batch vary in length, shorter sequences are filled with padding tokens to ensure uniform matrix dimensions. A batch is a matrix, and a matrix has no ragged rows, so every row is stretched to the length of the longest review in it with token 0.

An **Embedding** layer converts these discrete word IDs into dense vector representations. A recurrent neural network, such as a **GRU** layer, then processes the sequence step by step, updating its internal hidden state before passing the final state to a dense output neuron with a sigmoid activation function for binary prediction. **Sigmoid** squashes one number into the range 0 to 1, so the output reads as "probability this review is positive".

### 3 · The failure, in one worked case

If a short review contains 10 actual words followed by 100 padding tokens, the GRU layer processes all 100 padding steps after the text. Consequently, the recurrent state degrades, causing the model to forget the meaningful content and perform no better than random guessing.

A GRU's memory is short by design. Ten useful steps followed by a hundred meaningless ones is a hundred chances to overwrite what it learned. The critical takeaway is that variable-length sequences produce heavy padding in recurrent networks, which destroys the internal state unless the padding tokens are explicitly ignored or masked. The next lesson is that fix.

### 4 · Why the vocabulary stops at 1,000

The vocabulary is limited to 1,000 tokens: the 998 most frequent words plus a padding token and a token for unknown words. Very rare words are unlikely to matter for this task, and a smaller vocabulary reduces the number of parameters the model needs to learn — the embedding table has one row per token, so the vocabulary size is a direct multiplier on model size.

### 5 · Where splitting on spaces breaks

TextVectorization uses spaces to find word boundaries, which does not work well in some languages:

| Language | Problem |
|---|---|
| Chinese | no spaces between words at all |
| Vietnamese | spaces appear even inside one word |
| German | several words joined with no space |

Put plainly: Chinese lacks space boundaries altogether, while German frequently combines multiple words into compound terms, so a splitter that trusts spaces produces the wrong units in both.

**Subword tokenization** addresses this: instead of whole words, the vocabulary holds word fragments. **Byte pair encoding (BPE)** splits the training set into individual characters, then repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pairs until the vocabulary reaches the desired size.

The payoff is that unseen words stop being unknown. A model that never saw "smartest" can still infer its meaning if it learned "smart" and the suffix "est", meaning "the most". For English IMDb reviews, spaces are good enough.

**One-liner for your notes:** IMDb is 50,000 reviews labelled 0 or 1, and a word-level GRU fails on it at 50% accuracy purely because the padding that makes batches rectangular is read as real input.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf
import tensorflow_datasets as tfds

raw_train, raw_valid, raw_test = tfds.load(
    name="imdb_reviews",
    split=["train[:90%]", "train[90%:]", "test"],
    as_supervised=True
)
train_set = raw_train.shuffle(5000, seed=42).batch(32).prefetch(1)

text_vec_layer = tf.keras.layers.TextVectorization(max_tokens=1000)
text_vec_layer.adapt(train_set.map(lambda reviews, labels: reviews))

model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    text_vec_layer,
    tf.keras.layers.Embedding(1000, 128),
    tf.keras.layers.GRU(128),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")
])
```

items.term: A 50% accuracy is a diagnosis, not a tuning problem
items.text: On a balanced two-class task, 50% is exactly what a coin gets - so the model has learned nothing, not merely learned badly. That distinction matters: 'learned badly' points at capacity, learning rate or data volume, while 'learned nothing' points at something structurally wrong between the input and the loss. Reading the number as a category rather than a score is what sends you looking at the padding instead of at the optimiser.

items.term: Why the vocabulary cut is cheap here and expensive elsewhere
items.text: Keeping the 998 most frequent words works for sentiment because the signal words - terrible, superb - are common. On a task where the rare words carry the meaning, such as product codes or named entities, the same cut would throw the task away. The rule is not 'small vocabularies are good', it is 'check whether the words you are dropping are the ones that decide the answer'.

items.term: Subword tokenization changes what 'unknown' means
items.text: With a word vocabulary, an unseen word becomes a single unknown token and all its information is gone. With subwords, it becomes a sequence of known fragments that still carry meaning, so coverage degrades gradually instead of falling off a cliff. That is why it matters most exactly where word tokenization is weakest: morphologically rich languages, compounds, and any domain that invents words faster than you retrain.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Sentiment analysis on the IMDb dataset serves as a benchmark text classification task for NLP.
TextVectorization converts raw string sequences into numerical token representations based on a fixed vocabulary size.
Embedding layers transform discrete token indices into continuous vector spaces suitable for neural networks.
Unmasked padding across variable-length sequence batches causes recurrent layers like GRUs to forget meaningful initial content.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Byte pair encoding merges the most frequent adjacent pairs until the vocabulary reaches a target size. Who picks that size, and what actually goes wrong at the two extremes - a vocabulary of a few hundred, or of a hundred thousand?

Look up: Rico Sennrich et al., "Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units", Proceedings of the 54th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics 1 (2016): 1715-1725 - the paper that introduced BPE for this purpose.

items.term: Masking in Sequential Models

blocks.content:
Masking is a boolean flag travelling alongside your data that says "this time step is filler — skip it", and in Keras you switch it on with one argument.

**The question this lesson answers:** padding tokens wrecked the sentiment model in the previous lesson. How do you make every layer downstream ignore them, and what happens at a masked time step?

### The big picture

```
token ids   [ 86 ,  18 ,  0   ,  0    ]
mask        [True, True, False, False ]
GRU         update  update  copy   copy
```

The mask is the same shape as the input. Where it is `False`, the recurrent layer does not update — it copies forward what it already had.

### 1 · What masking is for

Variable-length sequence processing requires padding shorter sequences with zero values to maintain consistent matrix shapes. However, standard neural network layers process these padding tokens as real data, which can degrade training loss and validation accuracy.

**Masking** solves this issue by identifying uninformative padding values and instructing downstream layers to ignore them completely during computation. It is the same instinct as a `WHERE col IS NOT NULL` that travels with the rows instead of being re-stated at every step.

### 2 · Turning it on, and how it spreads

When using Keras, setting `mask_zero=True` in an **Embedding** layer creates a boolean tensor that evaluates to `False` for any token index equal to zero and `True` elsewhere.

This mask automatically propagates through layers whose `supports_masking` attribute is enabled — each layer hands it to the next as long as the chain holds. Where the chain stops is a rule worth memorising:

| Layer setting | Mask behaviour |
|---|---|
| `return_sequences=True` | layer uses the mask and passes it on |
| `return_sequences=False` | layer uses the mask, propagation stops |

If sequence output is enabled via `return_sequences=True`, the layer continues propagating the mask to subsequent stages. If `return_sequences=False`, mask propagation stops at that layer. That is not a bug: a layer that returns one vector instead of a sequence has no time steps left for a downstream layer to mask.

### 3 · What a masked step actually does

When a recurrent layer encounters a time step marked as `False`, it ignores the input and copies the output state from the prior time step.

Consider a sequence of token identifiers like `[86, 18, 0, 0]`, where `0` represents padding. The **Embedding** layer computes a mask of `[True, True, False, False]`. A recurrent layer like a **GRU** processes the first two time steps normally. Upon reaching the third step, the mask reads `False`, prompting the GRU to ignore the zero token and duplicate its hidden state from step two.

So the state that leaves the sequence is the state as of the last real word. Exactly what you wanted.

### 4 · When you have to do it by hand

Automatic propagation only works while every layer in the path supports it. If manual control is needed due to unsupported architectures like 1D convolutions, developers can compute the mask using `tf.math.not_equal(inputs, 0)` and pass it directly via the layer's `call()` method. That expression reads "True wherever the input is not zero", which is precisely what `mask_zero=True` would have built for you.

A layer that needs to *change* the mask before handing it on implements `compute_mask()`, which takes the inputs and the previous mask and returns the updated mask; its default implementation just returns the previous mask unchanged. To write a custom layer with masking support, give its `call()` method a `mask` argument and make the method use the mask, and set `self.supports_masking = True` in the constructor if the mask must be propagated.

The essential insight is that masking prevents dummy padding values from distorting model memory and loss computations across temporal time steps.

**One-liner for your notes:** `mask_zero=True` builds a boolean "this is real" tensor that rides along with the data; a masked recurrent step copies the previous state instead of updating, and propagation stops at the first layer with `return_sequences=False`.

blocks.title: Updating a mask with compute_mask()
blocks.content:
Some layers need to change the mask before passing it to the next layer. Such a layer implements the `compute_mask()` method, which takes two arguments, the inputs and the previous mask, and returns the updated mask. The default implementation of `compute_mask()` just returns the previous mask unchanged.

To write a custom layer with masking support, give its `call()` method a `mask` argument and make the method use the mask. If the mask must be propagated to the next layers, set `self.supports_masking = True` in the constructor. If the mask must be updated before it is propagated, implement `compute_mask()`.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
inputs = tf.keras.layers.Input(shape=[], dtype=tf.string)
token_ids = text_vec_layer(inputs)
mask = tf.math.not_equal(token_ids, 0)
Z = tf.keras.layers.Embedding(vocab_size, embed_size)(token_ids)
Z = tf.keras.layers.GRU(128, dropout=0.2)(Z, mask=mask)
outputs = tf.keras.layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")(Z)
model = tf.keras.Model(inputs=[inputs], outputs=[outputs])
```

items.term: Why copying the state is the right thing to do at a masked step
items.text: The alternatives are worse. Zeroing the state would erase the review; running the layer normally would let padding overwrite it; skipping the step entirely would mean different rows in the batch finishing at different times, which is exactly the ragged shape padding existed to avoid. Copying keeps the matrix rectangular while making the extra steps a no-op. It is the same move as an idempotent write: the operation still runs, it just does not change anything.

items.term: Mask propagation stops for a reason, and the rule is mechanical
items.text: A layer with `return_sequences=False` emits one vector, not a sequence, so there are no time steps left downstream for a mask to describe. Propagation therefore ends there by necessity, not by convention. Knowing this saves a debugging session: if a layer three steps down 'ignores the mask', check whether something upstream collapsed the sequence.

items.term: Automatic masking is a convenience with a hard edge
items.text: It works while every layer in the path supports it. Mix in something that does not - a 1D convolution, a custom layer - and the mask silently stops travelling; nothing errors, the accuracy is just worse. That silence is the risk. When a model mixes layer families, computing the mask explicitly and passing it is the safer default even though it is more code.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Padding tokens distort sequence calculations unless explicitly ignored by network layers.
Setting mask_zero=True on an Embedding layer creates and passes a boolean mask downstream.
Recurrent layers handle masked time steps by copying the hidden output of the previous step.
Mask propagation stops automatically when return_sequences is set to False in recurrent layers.
Custom architectures can pass explicit boolean masks directly to supported layer call methods.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Masking is one of three ways to handle variable lengths here; the other two are bucketing sequences of similar length into the same batch, and ragged tensors. What does each cost in throughput and in code complexity?
Look up: the Keras guide "Understanding masking & padding", which covers `mask_zero`, `supports_masking` and `compute_mask()` together with worked examples.

items.term: Reusing Pretrained Embeddings and Language Models

blocks.content:
Rather than learning word meanings from your own small dataset, download meanings somebody else learned from a huge one — and prefer a model that reads the whole sentence over a fixed table of vectors.

**The question this lesson answers:** 25,000 movie reviews is not enough text to learn what English words mean. What can you reuse instead, and why did the field move from pretrained *embeddings* to pretrained *language models*?

### The big picture

| Approach | One word gets | Knows context |
|---|---|---|
| Static embeddings (Word2vec, GloVe) | one fixed vector, always | no |
| Contextualized embeddings (ELMo) | a vector per sentence it appears in | yes |
| Full pretrained model (ULMFiT) | the whole model is reused and fine-tuned | yes |

### 1 · Why reuse at all

Training word embeddings from scratch requires vast amounts of text data, which small domain-specific datasets often lack. Early natural language processing systems solved this problem by importing static **pretrained word embeddings**, such as Word2vec or GloVe, which were trained on massive text corpora. These static vectors grouped words with similar meanings together.

An **embedding** is a row of numbers standing in for a word; "grouped together" means similar words land near each other in that space, so a model that has learned something about one of them has partly learned it about the others.

### 2 · The flaw in a fixed vector

However, static embeddings suffer from a major flaw: they assign a single vector to every word regardless of context, failing to distinguish between different meanings of polysemous words like "right" in "left and right" versus "right and wrong". **Polysemous** just means one spelling, several meanings.

A static embedding table is a dimension table with one row per word. That is exactly its limitation: one row cannot hold two meanings.

### 3 · Contextual representations

To overcome this limitation, researchers developed **contextualized word embeddings** and full **pretrained language models**, such as ELMo and ULMFiT. Instead of mapping a token to a fixed vector, these methods process entire sentences through deep recurrent neural networks to generate dynamic representations based on surrounding context.

ELMo works differently from static embeddings: its contextualized word embeddings are learned from the internal states of a deep **bidirectional** language model — one that reads the sentence both forwards and backwards — so the representation of a word depends on the sentence around it.

Additionally, full language model fine-tuning allows a model trained on unlabeled text to transfer its learned language structures directly to downstream target tasks. **Fine-tuning** means continuing to train a pretrained model on your own, much smaller, labelled task.

### 4 · The number that made the case

Consider the performance impact demonstrated by ULMFiT: when fine-tuned on a target text classification task, a pretrained language model achieved the same accuracy using only 100 labeled examples as a non-pretrained model trained from scratch on 10,000 examples. That is a hundredfold reduction in the labelling you have to pay for.

The ULMFiT authors trained an LSTM language model on a huge text corpus with **self-supervised learning**, which means the labels are generated automatically from the data itself instead of being written by people. A language model can learn this way because its target is simply the next word of the text — the same trick the char-RNN used at character level. They then fine-tuned the model on various tasks, and it beat the state of the art on six text classification tasks, reducing the error rate by 18–24% in most cases.

### 5 · Doing it today

Developers can easily utilize this technique today using pre-built modules on platforms like TensorFlow Hub. For example, loading the Universal Sentence Encoder allows a sequential Keras model to accept raw string inputs directly, converting full sentences into rich vector representations for sentiment classification.

In the card below, `input_shape=[]` is what declares those inputs: an empty shape means each input is a single scalar string, not a sequence you have tokenized yourself. The module does the tokenizing.

The central insight of modern natural language processing is that reusing pretrained contextual language models drastically reduces the required volume of labeled training data while outperforming traditional static embeddings.

**One-liner for your notes:** static embeddings give one vector per word forever; contextual models give one per sentence, and reusing a whole pretrained language model let ULMFiT match on 100 labels what scratch training needed 10,000 for.

blocks.title: Self-supervised pretraining
blocks.content:
The ULMFiT authors trained an LSTM language model on a huge text corpus with **self-supervised learning**, which means the labels are generated automatically from the data itself instead of being written by people. A language model can learn this way because its target is simply the next word of the text. They then fine-tuned the model on various tasks, and it beat the state of the art on six text classification tasks, reducing the error rate by 18–24% in most cases.

ELMo works differently from static embeddings: its contextualized word embeddings are learned from the internal states of a deep bidirectional language model, so the representation of a word depends on the sentence around it.
