blocks.content:
```python
import os
import tensorflow as tf
import tensorflow_hub as hub

os.environ["TFHUB_CACHE_DIR"] = "my_tfhub_cache"

model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    hub.KerasLayer(
        "https://tfhub.dev/google/universal-sentence-encoder/4",
        trainable=True,
        dtype=tf.string,
        input_shape=[]
    ),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")
])
```

items.term: One row per word is a modelling decision, and it is the flaw
items.text: A static embedding table is a dimension table keyed on the spelling. That key is the problem: 'right' has one row, so it must hold one meaning. Contextual models drop the table and compute the representation from the sentence instead, which is why the same word can come back different every time. The general point is that the choice of key decides what you can and cannot distinguish, long before any training happens.

items.term: Self-supervision is what makes the scale possible
items.text: Predicting the next word needs no annotator, so the training set is 'all the text you can find' rather than 'all the text someone was paid to label'. That is the entire reason pretrained language models could be trained on corpora thousands of times larger than any labelled dataset. It generalises: whenever part of your data can be reconstructed from the rest, you have a free supervised task hiding in an unlabelled pile.

items.term: What the 100-versus-10,000 number is actually telling you
items.text: It is not that pretraining makes models better in general - it is that it moves where the learning happens. Everything about the language is learned once, expensively, from unlabelled text; your labels only have to teach the task. So the number to watch when deciding whether to fine-tune is not accuracy, it is how many labels you can afford, because that is the axis pretraining moves.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Static embeddings like Word2vec map each word to a single vector regardless of sentence context.
Contextualized embeddings generate word representations dynamically using deep language models.
Unsupervised pretraining allows models to learn language structure from unlabeled text before fine-tuning.
Pretrained language models dramatically reduce the number of labeled examples needed for high performance.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: ULMFiT matched on 100 labels what scratch training needed 10,000 for, on text classification. Does that ratio survive when the target domain is far from the pretraining corpus - clinical notes, legal contracts, log lines - and what does the literature say degrades first?

Look up: Jeremy Howard and Sebastian Ruder, "Universal Language Model Fine-Tuning for Text Classification", Proceedings of the 56th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics 1 (2018): 328-339.

items.term: Encoder-Decoder Networks for Translation

blocks.content:
Translation needs two networks, not one: an encoder that reads the whole source sentence into a state, and a decoder that writes the translation one word at a time.

**The question this lesson answers:** "I like soccer" is three English words and "me gusta el fútbol" is four Spanish ones. How does a network map a sequence of one length onto a sequence of another?

### The big picture

```
English  -> ENCODER -> state -> DECODER -> Spanish
                                  ^  |
                        training: |  |  ground-truth word
                        inference:|  +-- its own last output
```

That little loop is the whole lesson: what goes into the decoder's next step is a ground-truth word during training and the model's own prediction at inference.

### 1 · Why two networks

Machine translation requires mapping input sequences of variable length to output sequences of variable length, which standard fixed-input recurrent networks cannot achieve directly. An **Encoder-Decoder network** solves this problem by separating the translation task into two connected neural network components.

First, the **encoder** processes the source language tokens sequentially through an **Embedding** layer and recurrent layers to compress the full sentence context into a final hidden state. Next, the **decoder** accepts this state vector to initialize its own recurrent states and generate output tokens in the target language.

Splitting the job is what frees the lengths: the encoder stops when the English runs out, the decoder stops when it decides the Spanish is done. Neither has to match the other.

### 2 · Teacher forcing

As Figure 16-3 below shows, during training, the model uses a technique called **teacher forcing**, where target sentences are shifted by one step and fed directly into the decoder alongside a start-of-sequence token (`startofseq`).

Concretely: at each step the decoder is given the word it *should* have produced at the previous step, no matter what it actually produced. This prevents early step prediction errors from cascading down the sequence, speeding up training convergence significantly.

| | Decoder input at step t | Effect of an early mistake |
|---|---|---|
| Training (teacher forcing) | the true previous word | contained — later steps still see good input |
| Inference | its own previous output | cascades into everything after |

### 3 · Inference has no answer key

At inference time, as illustrated in Figure 16-4 below, target ground-truth sentences are unavailable; the decoder must instead feed its own previous step output into the next step input until it emits an end-of-sequence token (`endofseq`).

So the two special tokens are not decoration. `startofseq` gives the decoder something to condition on at step zero, when there is no previous word at all, and `endofseq` is the only way the loop knows to stop — the output length is not fixed anywhere else.

### 4 · The worked example

For example, translating the English phrase "I like soccer" into Spanish begins by converting the words into token IDs like `3`, `36`, and `854`. The encoder processes these tokens to build a context vector. The decoder is then initialized with this vector and given the start token `startofseq`.

Using **teacher forcing** during training, step zero receives `startofseq` and aims to predict "Me", while step one receives the ground-truth token "Me" (ID `14`) to predict "gusta".

### 5 · One classification per step

At each step, the decoder outputs a score for every word in the output vocabulary, which is Spanish here, and the softmax activation function turns these scores into probabilities. For example, at the first step the word "Me" may get a probability of 7%, "Yo" a probability of 1%, and so on, and the word with the highest probability is output.

In the Keras model this is a Dense output layer with one unit per vocabulary word and the softmax activation. Because each step is very much like a regular classification task, the model can be trained with the `"sparse_categorical_crossentropy"` loss, just like the char-RNN.

The crucial insight is that **teacher forcing** accelerates training by supplying ground-truth target tokens as inputs, whereas inference must sequentially feed predicted tokens back into the network.

**One-liner for your notes:** the encoder squeezes the source sentence into a state and the decoder unrolls it into the target, fed the true previous word during training and its own previous output at inference, stopping at `endofseq`.

blocks.content: At each step, the decoder outputs a score for every word in the output vocabulary, which is Spanish here, and the softmax activation function turns these scores into probabilities. For example, at the first step the word "Me" may get a probability of 7%, "Yo" a probability of 1%, and so on, and the word with the highest probability is output. In the Keras model this is a Dense output layer with one unit per vocabulary word and the softmax activation. Because each step is very much like a regular classification task, the model can be trained with the `"sparse_categorical_crossentropy"` loss, just like the char-RNN.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np

url = "https://storage.googleapis.com/download.tensorflow.org/data/spa-eng.zip"
path = tf.keras.utils.get_file("spa-eng.zip", origin=url, cache_dir="datasets", extract=True)
text = (Path(path).with_name("spa-eng") / "spa.txt").read_text()
text = text.replace("¡", "").replace("¿", "")
pairs = [line.split("\t") for line in text.splitlines()]
np.random.shuffle(pairs)
sentences_en, sentences_es = zip(*pairs)

vocab_size = 1000
max_length = 50
text_vec_layer_en = tf.keras.layers.TextVectorization(vocab_size, output_sequence_length=max_length)
text_vec_layer_es = tf.keras.layers.TextVectorization(vocab_size, output_sequence_length=max_length)
text_vec_layer_en.adapt(sentences_en)
text_vec_layer_es.adapt([f"startofseq {s} endofseq" for s in sentences_es])
```

items.term: Teacher forcing trades a training-time convenience for a serving-time mismatch
items.text: During training the decoder always receives a correct previous word; at inference it receives whatever it just produced, mistakes included. So the model is being evaluated under conditions it never trained on. That gap is why translations degrade as sentences get longer - the further in, the more likely the decoder is standing on its own earlier error. The speedup is real and so is the mismatch; both are true at once.

items.term: Special tokens are protocol, not vocabulary
items.text: `startofseq` and `endofseq` are not words anyone will translate. They exist to answer two questions the architecture cannot otherwise answer: what does the decoder condition on at step zero, and how does a variable-length output know it is finished. Any unused strings would do, which is the tell that they are framing rather than content - the same role a header and a terminator play in a message format.

items.term: Why every decoder step is an ordinary classification
items.text: Once you see that each step outputs one score per vocabulary word and softmaxes them, the whole seq2seq model stops being exotic: it is a chain of classifications over the vocabulary, which is why the same `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` loss works here as in the char-RNN. What makes translation hard is not the loss, it is that step t's input is step t-1's output.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Encoder-Decoder architectures enable sequence-to-sequence translation between variable lengths.
Teacher forcing feeds actual target words into the decoder during training to stabilize learning.
Special tokens like startofseq and endofseq mark sequence boundaries for decoder operations.
During inference, the decoder relies on its own prior predictions instead of target labels.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: If teacher forcing creates a gap between training and inference conditions, can you close it by gradually feeding the decoder its own predictions as training goes on - and does that actually help?
Look up: Samy Bengio et al., "Scheduled Sampling for Sequence Prediction with Recurrent Neural Networks", arXiv preprint arXiv:1506.03099 (2015), which proposes exactly that gradual switch.

items.term: Encoder–Decoder Networks for Machine Translation

blocks.content:
This is the same encoder–decoder idea as the previous lesson, now written as actual Keras: two inputs, an LSTM that hands over its states, and a second LSTM that starts from them.

**The question this lesson answers:** a Keras `Sequential` model is one chain of layers. Translation needs two inputs and a state handover between two branches. What does the code look like, and which argument does each piece of the handover?

### The big picture

```
en text -> vectorize -> embed -> LSTM(512, return_state) -.
                                                          v
es text -> vectorize -> embed -> LSTM(512, initial_state=..)
                                          |
                                          v
                       Dense(vocab, softmax) -> word probs
```

### 1 · Why not a plain sequential model

Translating sequences of varying lengths requires mapping an input sequence into a fixed-length vector before generating the target sequence. A standard sequential network cannot easily process two distinct inputs or transfer hidden memory states across separate network branches.

An **Encoder–Decoder network** resolves this issue by splitting the translation task into two specialized recurrent neural networks: an encoder that reads the source text and a decoder that generates the target language text. In Keras that means the functional API — separate `Input` layers wired by hand — rather than a single stack.

### 2 · `return_state=True`, and why an LSTM has two states

The encoder processes the source sequence through an **LSTM layer** configured with `return_state=True`. This setting captures the final short-term and long-term hidden states, which summarize the entire source sentence.

An **LSTM** (long short-term memory) cell carries two things forward rather than one: a short-term state, which is also its output at that step, and a long-term state, its internal memory line. `return_state=True` is what makes the layer hand both of them back to you instead of discarding them.

| Setting | Gives you |
|---|---|
| default | only the layer's output |
| `return_state=True` | output plus the final short-term and long-term states |
| `return_sequences=True` | one output per time step, not just the last |

### 3 · The handover

The decoder takes the target sentence shifted by one time step as its input and initializes its internal memory using the states extracted from the encoder. By feeding the decoder its own target context along with the encoder hidden states, the model learns to output probabilities for target vocabulary words via a final dense layer with softmax activation.

In the card below the handover is the single argument `initial_state=encoder_state` on the decoder LSTM. Everything the encoder understood about the English sentence reaches the decoder through that one argument.

Note also that both embedding layers are created with masking enabled, so padded positions are ignored correctly — the same `mask_zero=True` rule from the masking lesson, applied on both sides.

### 4 · Translating, step by step

Consider an example translating an English sentence into Spanish. The input layer receives the source text 'I like soccer'. The encoder processes these tokens and outputs its final two hidden states. Next, the decoder receives the target sequence starting with a special prefix token, such as 'startofseq', and uses the encoder hidden states as its `initial_state`. The decoder computes word probabilities step by step, predicting 'me', then 'gusta', then 'el', then 'fútbol', and finally stopping when encountering the 'endofseq' token.

Autoregressive translation — feeding each prediction back in — requires calling model predictions iteratively until encountering an end-of-sequence token. There is no single `predict()` that produces the whole sentence, because step t's input is step t-1's output.

### 5 · When the vocabulary gets big

Outputting a probability for every possible word gets slow when the vocabulary is large. With 50,000 Spanish words instead of 1,000, the decoder would output 50,000-dimensional vectors, and computing the softmax function over such a large vector would be very computationally intensive.

**Sampled softmax**, introduced in 2015 by Sébastien Jean et al., avoids this during training. It looks only at the logits for the correct word and for a random sample of incorrect words, then computes an approximation of the loss from those logits. In TensorFlow this is `tf.nn.sampled_softmax_loss()`.

At inference time the normal softmax is used instead, because sampled softmax requires knowing the target word, and the target is not known when you translate a new sentence. That is the whole restriction in one sentence: the shortcut needs the answer, and at inference there is no answer.

The primary insight to remember is that the encoder condenses the entire input context into final hidden states, which serve as the starting state for the decoder to generate predictions.

**One-liner for your notes:** `return_state=True` on the encoder LSTM plus `initial_state=` on the decoder LSTM is the entire handover; sampled softmax makes a 50,000-word vocabulary trainable but cannot be used at inference.

It looks only at the logits for the correct word and for a random sample of incorrect words, then computes an approximation of the loss from those logits. blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
encoder_inputs = tf.keras.layers.Input(shape=[], dtype=tf.string)
decoder_inputs = tf.keras.layers.Input(shape=[], dtype=tf.string)

encoder_embeddings = encoder_embedding_layer(text_vec_layer_en(encoder_inputs))
decoder_embeddings = decoder_embedding_layer(text_vec_layer_es(decoder_inputs))

encoder = tf.keras.layers.LSTM(512, return_state=True)
encoder_outputs, *encoder_state = encoder(encoder_embeddings)

decoder = tf.keras.layers.LSTM(512, return_sequences=True)
decoder_outputs = decoder(decoder_embeddings, initial_state=encoder_state)

output_layer = tf.keras.layers.Dense(vocab_size, activation="softmax")
Y_proba = output_layer(decoder_outputs)

model = tf.keras.Model(inputs=[encoder_inputs, decoder_inputs], outputs=[Y_proba])
```

items.term: The fixed-size handover is the design's ceiling
items.text: Everything the encoder understood must fit through `initial_state` - two vectors, the same size whether the sentence was three words or forty. That is a fixed-width channel carrying variable-width information, so it is the first thing to fail as sentences get longer. Recognising that bottleneck is what motivates attention later in this chapter, where the decoder gets to read all the encoder outputs instead of a summary.

items.term: Sampled softmax approximates the loss, not the model
items.text: It changes how the training signal is computed, not what the model is - which is exactly why it can be dropped at inference with no change to the architecture. The condition it needs is that you know the correct answer, so it can compare it against a random sample of wrong ones. That makes it a training-only optimisation by nature, not by choice, and the same logic rules out any similar shortcut at serving time.

items.term: Why the output layer, of all places, is the expensive one
items.text: The recurrent layers cost the same regardless of vocabulary size, but the output layer has one unit per word, so its cost scales with the vocabulary - the jump from 1,000 to 50,000 words is a fiftyfold increase in that layer alone, at every time step. When something is slow, the dimension that scales with your cardinality is usually where to look first.

blocks.title: Key points
items: An Encoder–Decoder architecture processes source and target sequences using separate inputs and recurrent layers.
The encoder LSTM uses return_state=True to extract its final hidden states representing the source text context.
The decoder LSTM uses the encoder final state as its initial state to generate target sequence predictions.
Masking must be enabled in embedding layers using mask_zero=True to ensure padded positions are ignored correctly.
Autoregressive translation requires calling model predictions iteratively until encountering an end-of-sequence token.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Sampled softmax approximates the loss over a random sample of wrong words. How many negative samples are enough, and does drawing them uniformly rather than by word frequency change the outcome?

Look up: Sébastien Jean et al., "On Using Very Large Target Vocabulary for Neural Machine Translation", Proceedings of the 53rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (2015): 1-10, the paper that introduced the technique.

items.term: Bidirectional Recurrent Neural Networks

blocks.content:
A bidirectional layer runs two copies of a recurrent layer over the same words — one forwards, one backwards — and glues their outputs together, so every word is encoded knowing what comes after it.

**The question this lesson answers:** to encode "right" correctly you need the words that follow it. A normal RNN only ever looks backwards. What do you change, and what breaks downstream when you do?

### The big picture

```
   the   right   arm
   ->    ->      ->     forward layer
   <-    <-      <-     backward layer
   |     |       |
   concatenate at each step
```

### 1 · Causal is right for forecasting, wrong for reading

Standard recurrent neural networks process sequences in a strictly forward direction. This **causal** approach — causal meaning it cannot look into the future — works well for time series forecasting, but it creates a limitation in natural language tasks where future context clarifies current meaning.

For example, understanding the word "right" in phrases like "the right arm" versus "the right to criticize" requires looking at subsequent words. At the moment the forward layer reaches "right" it has seen only "the", which settles nothing.

### 2 · Two directions, concatenated

To solve this, a **bidirectional recurrent layer** processes input sequences in two directions simultaneously. As Figure 16-5 below demonstrates, one recurrent layer reads the sequence from left to right, while a cloned layer reads the sequence from right to left. At each time step, the model combines the outputs from both directions, usually by concatenating their state values. Consequently, the representation for every token incorporates both past and future context.

Concatenating means the widths add. So the output width per time step is always double the wrapped layer's unit count:

| Wrapped layer | Forward | Backward | Output per step |
|---|---|---|---|
| LSTM 256 units | 256 | 256 | 512 |
| GRU 64 units | 64 | 64 | 128 |

Consider an encoder using a wrapped `tf.keras.layers.LSTM` with 256 units. The forward LSTM generates a 256-dimensional output vector, and the backward LSTM generates another 256-dimensional vector. Concatenating these vectors produces a total output vector size of 512 at each time step. (The book makes the same point at the smallest scale: a 10-unit layer wrapped bidirectionally outputs 20 values per time step — page index 770.)

### 3 · The state-count problem

However, an issue arises when passing hidden states to a unidirectional decoder. An LSTM bidirectional encoder outputs four final states: forward short-term, forward long-term, backward short-term, and backward long-term.

Because a standard decoder LSTM expects only two states, you must concatenate the two short-term states together and the two long-term states together before initializing the decoder. Note *which* pairs go together: short with short, long with long — you are widening each kind of state, not mixing kinds.

### 4 · Why the decoder stays one-directional

The essential insight to remember is that bidirectional layers provide complete contextual awareness by combining forward and backward sequences, making them ideal for encoders but unsuitable for causal decoders.

The decoder's job is to predict the next word. A backward pass over the target sentence would let it read the very words it is supposed to be predicting — it would score beautifully during training and be useless at inference, where those words do not exist yet. So bidirectional layers belong in text classification and in sequence-to-sequence encoders, never in a decoder that generates.

**One-liner for your notes:** wrap a recurrent layer in `Bidirectional` to read both ways and double the output width; an LSTM encoder then returns four states, which you concatenate short-with-short and long-with-long — and never do this in a decoder.
