blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, TFAutoModelForSequenceClassification
import tensorflow as tf

model_name = "huggingface/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-mnli"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
model = TFAutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(model_name)

sentences = [("I like soccer.", "We all love soccer!"), ("Joe lived a long time.", "Joe is old.")]
inputs = tokenizer(sentences, padding=True, return_tensors="tf").data

outputs = model(inputs)
probas = tf.keras.activations.softmax(outputs.logits)
predictions = tf.argmax(probas, axis=1)
```

items.term: Model and tokenizer are one artifact, not two
items.text: Every ID the model was trained on means a specific token in a specific vocabulary. Pair the model with a different tokenizer and nothing errors - the IDs are still valid integers - but they mean different words, and the predictions become quietly wrong. That is why the library downloads both together and why pinning a model version means pinning its tokenizer too. Silent schema drift, with the same failure mode you would get from a mismatched dimension table.

items.term: Logits versus probabilities is a contract, and it bites at fine-tuning time
items.text: A model that outputs logits and a loss that expects probabilities will still run and still produce a number - just the wrong one, because the softmax gets applied twice or not at all. `from_logits=True` is how you state which side of the contract your model is on. The general lesson is that 'it ran without error' says nothing when both sides accept the same shape.

items.term: An average score is not evidence of fairness
items.text: The biased sentiment example scores well on a benchmark and still labels a whole nationality negative. An aggregate hides exactly the failures that matter, because the affected subset is a small share of the rows. Evaluating by subset and running counterfactual tests - change one attribute, assert the prediction does not move - turns fairness into something you can check automatically, the same way an invariant check beats eyeballing a total.

blocks.title: Key points
items: The pipeline function provides a simple interface to run inference for common NLP tasks using default pretrained models.
AutoTokenizer and AutoModel classes enable detailed control over tokenization, padding, and model output manipulation.
Tokenizer outputs include input IDs and attention masks to distinguish content tokens from padding.
Fine-tuning Hugging Face TensorFlow models requires using SparseCategoricalCrossentropy with from_logits set to True.
Pretrained models can inherit biases from training data, requiring subset evaluation and counterfactual testing before deployment.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The book says adding a neutral class during fine-tuning makes most of the country bias disappear. That is a striking claim: the fix was in the label design, not the data. What else is known to reduce bias without touching the training corpus?

Look up: the Hugging Face documentation at https://huggingface.co/docs and the model list at https://huggingface.co/models, both of which the book points to, for model cards that record intended use and known limitations.

sections.title: Chapter 17: Autoencoders, GANs, and Diffusion Models

items.term: Overview of Generative Unsupervised Models

blocks.content:
Autoencoders, GANs and diffusion models are three ways to learn from data that carries no answer column, and all three can also generate brand-new data that looks like the data they were trained on.

**The question this lesson answers:** you have a large pile of data and nobody has labelled any of it. Which neural-network architectures can still learn something useful from it, and what stops each one from simply memorising what it was shown?

### The big picture

| Family | Learns by | Makes new data by |
|---|---|---|
| Autoencoder | copying input to output | decoding a coding |
| GAN | two networks competing | generator reads noise |
| Diffusion | removing a little noise | denoising, many steps |

### 1 · Why "no labels" is the problem worth solving

In traditional machine learning, models often require extensive labeled datasets, which can be expensive and difficult to gather. A **label** is the answer column — the value you want the model to fill in for rows it has never seen. Collecting the inputs is usually cheap; getting a person to write the answer next to each row is not.

Unsupervised models solve this problem by discovering patterns directly from unlabeled data. **Unsupervised** simply means there is no answer column at all. Three key architectures for unsupervised learning and data generation are autoencoders, generative adversarial networks, and diffusion models.

### 2 · Autoencoders: copy your input, but through a narrow pipe

**Autoencoders** operate by learning to copy their inputs to their outputs through restricted internal pathways. An autoencoder compresses input data into a lower-dimensional representation called a **coding** or **latent representation**, and then attempts to reconstruct the original input.

A **latent representation** is just a short internal description of a row — think of a wide table squeezed into a handful of derived columns, where the columns were invented by training rather than chosen by you.

Copying looks like a pointless task until you notice the catch. By placing constraints on this process—such as limiting the latent layer size or adding noise to the input—the network cannot simply memorize the data. Instead, it is forced to learn efficient feature representations, making it useful for dimensionality reduction and data generation.

### 3 · GANs: two networks with opposite jobs

**Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)** employ two neural networks that compete against each other: a **generator** that creates synthetic data and a **discriminator** that attempts to distinguish real training samples from fake ones. For instance, when generating face images, the generator acts like a counterfeit artist creating synthetic portraits, while the discriminator acts like an investigator detecting fakes. Through this competitive training, the generator learns to produce extremely realistic images.

Nobody writes down what a realistic face looks like. The scoring rule is the other network, and it keeps getting harder.

### 4 · Diffusion models: learn to undo noise, one small step at a time

**Diffusion models** take a different approach by learning to iteratively remove small amounts of noise from data. To generate a new image, a diffusion model takes an image of pure Gaussian noise and repeatedly applies its learned denoising steps until a clear, detailed image emerges.

**Gaussian noise** is random values drawn from the familiar bell curve. Pure Gaussian noise is a picture of nothing but static.

### 5 · Same goal, three different bargains

| | Trained by | The cost |
|---|---|---|
| Autoencoder | constrained reconstruction | codings are a byproduct |
| GAN | adversarial competition | training is unstable |
| Diffusion | denoising, easy to train | generation is slow |

The key insight to remember is that while all three architectures learn latent representations without labels, they balance trade-offs differently: autoencoders rely on constrained reconstruction, GANs leverage competitive adversarial training for realistic details, and diffusion models offer high sample quality and easy training at the cost of slower generation speeds.

The figure below lays the three pipelines side by side; the rest of the chapter walks each one in turn.

**One-liner for your notes:** three unlabelled-data architectures, three bargains — autoencoders squeeze, GANs compete, diffusion denoises slowly but well.

items.term: Why 'no labels' pushed people toward generation in the first place
items.text: The three families here were not invented to make pictures; they were invented to learn structure without an answer column, and generation fell out of that. An autoencoder's codings are, in the book's own phrasing, a byproduct of learning the identity function under a constraint. That is worth holding on to, because it tells you what to expect when the generated output disappoints: the model was never optimising for beauty, it was optimising for a constraint you chose.

items.term: The trade-offs are not a ranking
items.text: Easy training, high sample quality and fast generation are three different axes and no architecture here wins all three. A GAN generates in one forward pass but is unstable to train. A diffusion model trains stably and samples well but needs many sequential passes. An autoencoder trains most easily of all and gives you a usable compressed representation, but a plain one generates nothing worth looking at. Which one is right depends on whether your cost is engineer-hours, inference latency or output quality.

items.term: Where the generality ends
items.text: Everything in this chapter is demonstrated on images, but nothing in the three mechanisms is image-specific: an autoencoder bottleneck, an adversarial critic and a denoising chain all apply to tabular rows, audio and time series. What is image-specific is the architecture inside them — convolutions, transpose convolutions, U-Nets. Swap those for layers that suit your data and the surrounding idea is unchanged.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Autoencoders, GANs, and diffusion models are unsupervised neural network architectures capable of learning latent representations.
Autoencoders compress inputs into low-dimensional codings under architectural constraints to discover efficient features.
Generative Adversarial Networks pit a data generator against a real-versus-fake discriminator in a competitive training setup.
Diffusion models generate clear data samples by repeatedly removing noise from an initial image of Gaussian noise.
Each generative architecture offers distinct trade-offs regarding training stability, generation speed, and output quality.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The chapter says diffusion models are slower to generate than GANs. How much slower, in practice, for a given image size and quality target — and which of the two would you actually deploy behind a latency budget?
Look up: this chapter's own notebook, linked from the book at https://homl.info/colab3, which runs all three architectures end to end.

items.term: Efficient Data Representations in Autoencoders

blocks.content:
An autoencoder is a network trained to reproduce its own input, with a deliberate bottleneck in the middle so that the only way to succeed is to find the patterns in the data.

**The question this lesson answers:** if you train a network to output exactly what you fed it, what could it possibly learn? The answer is: nothing at all, unless you make the middle of the network too small to hold a copy.

### The big picture

```
x (3 vals) -> encoder -> latent (2) -> decoder -> x̂ (3)
                            ^                        ^
                       bottleneck          reconstruction loss
```

### 1 · The setup

High-dimensional data often contains redundant information. Storing or memorizing raw data without discovering underlying structure requires excessive capacity. To solve this problem, neural networks can be forced to learn compressed representations that capture essential patterns rather than memorizing raw noise.

**High-dimensional** just means many columns per row. **Capacity** is how much a network is able to remember — more layers and more neurons mean more capacity.

### 2 · Two halves and a loss

An **autoencoder** addresses this challenge by attempting to copy its input to its output through a restricted internal bottleneck. As Figure 17-1 illustrates, the network architecture consists of two primary components: an **encoder** (or recognition network) that maps the high-dimensional input $x$ to a low-dimensional **latent representation**, and a **decoder** (or generative network) that maps this internal representation back to a reconstructed output $\hat{x}$. The network is trained using a **reconstruction loss**, which penalizes differences between the original inputs and their outputs.

| Part | Other name | Turns | Into |
|---|---|---|---|
| encoder | recognition network | the input | a short coding |
| decoder | generative network | the coding | a reconstruction |

The hat in x̂ (say "x hat") is the usual notation for "the model's version of x", as opposed to the real x. The outputs are often called the **reconstructions**, because the autoencoder is trying to rebuild what it was given.

Because the decoder has to rebuild every input value, the output layer of an autoencoder has exactly as many units as the input layer. Figure 17-1 below shows that plainly: three inputs on the left, three outputs on the right.

### 3 · Why the bottleneck is the whole trick

Consider a concrete scenario where an autoencoder receives a three-dimensional vector containing coordinates from a 3D space, such as $(x_1, x_2, x_3)$. If the hidden layer of the encoder contains only two neurons, the network must squeeze the 3D input into a 2D bottleneck space. To successfully reconstruct the original 3D points, the network cannot simply copy every coordinate. Instead, it must discover lower-dimensional mathematical patterns or surfaces within the data to preserve maximum information in two dimensions.

In data-engineering terms: you are told to rebuild a three-column table from a two-column staging table you get to design yourself. The only way to win is to find a relationship between the three columns and store the part that cannot be derived.

### 4 · The chess players

The card below tells the Chase and Simon story, and it is the clearest picture of why compression and understanding are the same thing here. Expert chess players memorised realistic boards in five seconds and random boards no better than anyone else. They were not remembering 32 pieces; they were remembering a handful of familiar patterns. Experts recognized structured game patterns to store information efficiently, and that is exactly what a bottleneck forces a network to do.

The essential insight is that restricting internal capacity forces the network to discover efficient, low-dimensional patterns in data rather than memorizing individual inputs.

**One-liner for your notes:** encoder squeezes, decoder rebuilds, reconstruction loss scores the rebuild — and the bottleneck is what turns copying into learning.

blocks.title: The chess memory experiment
blocks.content: In the early 1970s, William Chase and Herbert Simon studied how memory, perception and pattern matching relate. Expert chess players could memorize the positions of all the pieces after looking at the board for just five seconds, but only when the pieces were in realistic positions taken from actual games, not when they were placed randomly. The experts do not have a much better memory than other people. They simply see chess patterns more easily thanks to their experience, and noticing patterns helps them store information efficiently. An autoencoder works in the same way: it looks at the inputs, converts them to an efficient latent representation, and then outputs something that looks very close to the inputs.

blocks.title: Figure 17-1
blocks.caption: The chess memory experiment (left) and a simple autoencoder (right)
blocks.alt: Figure 17-1: The chess memory experiment (left) and a simple autoencoder (right)

items.term: Why compression and understanding are the same thing here
items.text: The chess result is not a decoration on the lesson; it is the argument. The experts did not have more storage, they had better patterns, and patterns are exactly what lets a fixed amount of storage hold more. The same reasoning explains why the bottleneck works: if the coding layer cannot hold a copy, the only remaining way to reconstruct the input is to hold the rule that generated it. Compression is forced abstraction.

items.term: What the constraint does NOT guarantee
items.text: A bottleneck forces the network to drop something; it does not force it to drop the right thing. A capacity limit is a pressure, not a specification — if the dropped information happens to be what your downstream task needed, reconstruction loss will still look fine, because reconstruction loss measures the average pixel, not the feature you cared about. This is why a low reconstruction loss is never on its own evidence that the codings are useful.

items.term: Where the idea generalises
items.text: Any time you force a wide thing through a narrow thing and demand the wide thing back, you get the same effect. That covers PCA, hashing schemes, lossy compression codecs, and embedding layers. What is new here is only that the narrow representation is learned from the data rather than designed by a person — which is also why it is harder to explain afterwards.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Autoencoders compress high-dimensional inputs into low-dimensional latent representations.
An autoencoder consists of an encoder network and a decoder network.
The output layer of an autoencoder has the same number of units as the input layer.
Reconstruction loss measures the discrepancy between the network inputs and outputs.
Bottleneck constraints force the model to learn meaningful patterns instead of memorizing data.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: How do you actually tell whether an autoencoder's codings are good, given that reconstruction loss can look fine while the codings are useless for anything downstream?
Look up: William G. Chase and Herbert A. Simon, 'Perception in Chess', Cognitive Psychology 4, no. 1 (1973): 55-81 — the study this lesson's card describes.

items.term: PCA with an Undercomplete Linear Autoencoder

blocks.content:
Make the autoencoder's hidden layer smaller than its input, use straight-line activations and mean squared error, and the network ends up doing principal component analysis.

**The question this lesson answers:** what is the simplest possible autoencoder, and what does it turn out to be equivalent to? A 3D dataset squeezed to 2D by two linear neurons lands on the same plane PCA would have chosen.

### The big picture

```
3D points -> 2 linear neurons -> 2D codings -> 3 outputs
             (encoder)                         (decoder)
   loss = mean squared error against the input itself
```

### 1 · Undercomplete: the layer that is too small on purpose

High-dimensional data can be difficult to visualize and computationally expensive to process. To reduce dimensionality without losing essential information, models must extract the most significant features while discarding minor noise. An **undercomplete autoencoder** addresses this challenge by limiting the hidden layer to fewer units than the input layer, preventing the network from simply copying the input.

That is the entire definition: the hidden coding layer has fewer neurons than the input layer. "Undercomplete" is the book's word for a pipe that is too narrow to pass a copy through.

### 2 · Linear plus MSE equals PCA

When an undercomplete autoencoder uses strictly linear activation functions and is trained using the **mean squared error** (MSE) loss function, it mathematically performs **principal component analysis** (PCA). The network learns a lower-dimensional linear subspace that captures the maximum variance of the original data. The **encoder** maps the inputs down to this smaller latent dimension (the **codings**), and the **decoder** attempts to reconstruct the original inputs from those codings.

Three terms, glossed once:

| Term | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| activation function | the bend applied after each neuron |
| linear activation | no bend at all, just a weighted sum |
| variance | how spread out the values are |

**PCA** (chapter 8) finds the flat surface that the data sits closest to and projects everything onto it. The reason linear plus MSE lands there is that PCA is itself a linear transformation — so if you forbid the network any bends, the best it can do is the best flat projection, which is what PCA already computes. Figure 17-2's caption calls the result *approximate* PCA, which is the honest word: the network is fitted by gradient descent, not solved in closed form.

### 3 · The example, end to end

For example, consider a dataset containing points in three-dimensional space ($x_1, x_2, x_3$). An encoder with two linear neurons compresses this data into a two-dimensional vector ($z_1, z_2$). As Figure 17-2 shows, training the model using the input data as its own target forces the autoencoder to find the optimal 2D plane onto which the 3D data points are projected, successfully retaining maximum data variance just as standard PCA would.

Figure 17-2 has two panels. The left panel is the original 3D dataset; the right panel is the output of the coding layer, so every point there is a 2D coding. The code card below trains for 500 epochs and then calls the encoder to read those codings out.

### 4 · Self-supervised: the labels write themselves

The target data fed to the model is the exact same input data. `autoencoder.fit(X_train, X_train, ...)` passes `X_train` twice — once as the inputs and once as the answers.

That is why this counts as **self-supervised learning**: it is ordinary supervised training, but the labels are generated automatically directly from the input data rather than typed in by a person. The machinery is the same; only where the answer column comes from has changed.

The essential insight to remember is that a linear undercomplete autoencoder optimized with MSE loss is functionally equivalent to classical PCA.

**One-liner for your notes:** narrow hidden layer + linear activations + MSE = PCA, trained self-supervised by handing the model its own inputs as the answers.

blocks.title: Reading Figure 17-2
blocks.content: The code trains the autoencoder for 500 epochs with `X_train` as both the inputs and the targets, then calls `encoder.predict(X_train)` to get the codings. Figure 17-2 has two panels. The left panel shows the original 3D dataset. The right panel shows the output of the autoencoder's hidden layer, which is the coding layer, so every point there is a 2D coding. The autoencoder found the best 2D plane to project the data onto, preserving as much variance as it could, just like PCA. Because the labels are generated automatically (they are simply equal to the inputs), this is a form of self-supervised learning.

blocks.title: Figure 17-2
blocks.caption: Approximate PCA performed by an undercomplete linear autoencoder
blocks.alt: Figure 17-2: Approximate PCA performed by an undercomplete linear autoencoder

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

encoder = tf.keras.Sequential([tf.keras.layers.Dense(2)])
decoder = tf.keras.Sequential([tf.keras.layers.Dense(3)])
autoencoder = tf.keras.Sequential([encoder, decoder])

optimizer = tf.keras.optimizers.SGD(learning_rate=0.5)
autoencoder.compile(loss="mse", optimizer=optimizer)

history = autoencoder.fit(X_train, X_train, epochs=500, verbose=False)
codings = encoder.predict(X_train)
```

items.term: Why linear plus MSE lands exactly on PCA
items.text: PCA asks for the flat subspace that keeps the most variance. A linear encoder followed by a linear decoder can only ever produce a flat subspace, because a chain of linear maps is itself a linear map — no bend is available anywhere. MSE is the same thing PCA minimises. So the network is being asked for the best member of exactly the family PCA searches, judged by exactly PCA's criterion. It cannot land anywhere else.

items.term: So why use the autoencoder at all
items.text: If you only want PCA, use PCA: it is solved in closed form, it is faster, and it is deterministic. The autoencoder version earns its keep the moment you remove a restriction — switch the activations to something nonlinear and you get a curved surface PCA cannot express, which is the whole rest of this chapter. The linear case is a sanity check that the machinery is sound, not a recommendation.

items.term: When this equivalence breaks
items.text: It is 'approximate PCA', as Figure 17-2's caption says, and the gap matters. Gradient descent may stop short of the optimum, so the plane can be slightly off. The autoencoder's two coding axes are also not guaranteed to be the principal components themselves, ordered and orthogonal — any rotation within the same plane reconstructs equally well and so costs the same. The subspace matches; the coordinates on it need not.

blocks.title: Key points
items: An undercomplete autoencoder has a hidden coding layer smaller than its input layer.
Using linear activations and mean squared error loss causes an autoencoder to perform principal component analysis.
Autoencoders perform self-supervised learning by using input data as training targets.
The encoder extracts compressed representations while the decoder reconstructs original inputs.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: PCA is solved exactly and instantly for a 3D dataset. At what data size or shape does training a linear autoencoder start to beat running PCA directly, and which PCA variant would you compare against?
Look up: the scikit-learn user guide, 'Decomposing signals in components (matrix factorization problems)', particularly its PCA and IncrementalPCA sections.

items.term: Stacked Autoencoders

blocks.content:
A stacked autoencoder is just an autoencoder with more than one hidden layer on each side, which lets it learn richer codings than a single squeeze can.

**The question this lesson answers:** one hidden layer found a flat plane. What do you get by adding layers, and what do the extra layers cost you?

### The big picture

```
784 -> 100 -> 30 -> 100 -> 784      (Fashion MNIST)
        encoder  ^  decoder
              the codings
```

The shape is a sandwich: sizes fall, hit the middle, then rise back in mirror image.

### 1 · Why depth at all

Shallow networks often struggle to extract complex abstract representations from high-dimensional data. **Stacked autoencoders** solve this problem by incorporating multiple hidden layers, allowing the network to learn rich, hierarchical data representations. Adding extra hidden layers enables the autoencoder to learn more complex data codings.

**Hierarchical** means each layer builds on the one before it: early layers pick up edges and strokes, later layers pick up whole shapes. One layer can only manage one such step.

A stacked autoencoder consists of two main parts arranged symmetrically around a bottleneck coding layer. The **encoder** compresses high-dimensional inputs through hidden layers of decreasing neuron counts. The central coding layer forms the tightest bottleneck, holding the compressed representation. The **decoder** mirrors this structure, using layers of increasing sizes to reconstruct the original input vector from the codings.

### 2 · The Fashion MNIST numbers

Consider an autoencoder designed for 28 × 28 Fashion MNIST grayscale images, as shown in Figure 17-3. The network flattens each image into a 784-dimensional input vector. The encoder passes this input to a dense layer with 100 neurons, followed by a coding layer with 30 neurons. The decoder receives this 30-dimensional coding, passes it to a dense layer of 100 neurons, and outputs a 784-dimensional reconstruction reshaped back into a 28 × 28 image.

| Layer | Size | Role |
|---|---|---|
| input | 784 | one flattened 28 by 28 image |
| hidden 1 | 100 | first squeeze |
| coding | 30 | the central bottleneck |
| hidden 2 | 100 | first expansion |
| output | 784 | the reconstruction |

**Flatten** means laying the 28 rows of 28 pixels end to end into one row of 784 numbers, the way you would unpivot a grid into a single wide record. Training uses identical target data as input data ($X_{train}$ paired with $X_{train}$) under mean squared error loss — the same self-supervised trick as before, so the exact same input images are the targets.

Figure 17-4 below puts originals on top and reconstructions underneath. They are recognisable but a bit lossy.

### 3 · What a trained encoder is good for

Two uses, both shown in the figures below.

**Visualisation.** 30 dimensions is still too many to plot, so Figure 17-5 runs the encoder first and then t-SNE, a separate dimensionality-reduction method, to get down to 2 for a scatterplot.

**Pretraining.** Pretrained autoencoder encoder layers can be extracted to initialize supervised classifiers when labeled training data is scarce, as Figure 17-6 shows. Train the autoencoder on everything you have, unlabelled included; then the encoder layers can be reused as the lower layers for a classifier and you only spend your few labels on the top. Figure 17-7 shows the older variant where you train one shallow autoencoder at a time and stack them afterwards.

### 4 · Tying weights: half the parameters, same job

To prevent overfitting and reduce parameter counts, modern implementations often perform weight tying. By forcing decoder weight matrices to equal the transpose of their corresponding encoder weight matrices ($W_{decoder} = W_{encoder}^T$), the model reduces its parameter count by roughly half while retaining reconstruction quality.

The **transpose** of a matrix is that matrix flipped over its diagonal, so rows become columns. An encoder layer's weights map 784 values down to 100; flipped, exactly the same numbers map 100 values back up to 784. So instead of learning a second, independent set of decoder weights, the decoder borrows the encoder's and reads them the other way round. It halves the number of weights to reduce overfitting, and it speeds up training.

**One-liner for your notes:** stack layers symmetrically around the coding layer for richer codings, reuse the encoder when labels are scarce, and tie the decoder's weights to the encoder's transpose to halve the parameters.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
stacked_encoder = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.Flatten(),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(100, activation="relu"),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(30, activation="relu"),
])
stacked_decoder = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(100, activation="relu"),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(28 * 28),
    tf.keras.layers.Reshape([28, 28])
])
stacked_ae = tf.keras.Sequential([stacked_encoder, stacked_decoder])
stacked_ae.compile(loss="mse", optimizer="nadam")
history = stacked_ae.fit(X_train, X_train, epochs=20,
                         validation_data=(X_valid, X_valid))
```

items.term: Depth buys expressiveness, and expressiveness is a risk
items.text: More layers let the autoencoder learn more complex codings, but the book is blunt about the other edge: an encoder powerful enough could map each input to a single arbitrary number and the decoder learn the reverse. That reconstructs the training set perfectly and has learned nothing. The bottleneck is a capacity limit, and capacity is a budget you can accidentally over-fund. More depth is not free improvement.

items.term: Why tying weights is more than a parameter saving
items.text: Halving the parameters is the advertised benefit, but the constraint also says something about the model: it asserts that decoding is the mirror of encoding. That is a real assumption, and it is a form of regularisation in its own right — the decoder is no longer free to learn a transformation unrelated to the encoder's. The book reports roughly the same reconstruction error with almost half the parameters, which says the assumption costs little here.

items.term: Why pretraining works when labels are scarce
items.text: The encoder learns what the data looks like, and that question does not need labels. Only the last step — what to call each thing — does. So spend all your unlabelled data on the hard, general part and your few labels on the cheap, specific part. The book notes you may want to freeze the pretrained layers when labels are very scarce, which is the same instinct: the fewer labels you have, the less you should let them reshape.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Stacked autoencoders use multiple hidden layers to learn complex codings.
The network architecture is symmetrical around the central coding layer.
Tying decoder weights to the transpose of encoder weights reduces the overall parameter count by half.
Pretrained encoder layers can be reused for supervised downstream tasks with limited labels.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Unsupervised pretraining with autoencoders was once the only way to train deep nets, and the book says the techniques of chapter 11 largely replaced it. Where is it still the better choice today?
Look up: Yoshua Bengio et al., 'Greedy Layer-Wise Training of Deep Networks' — this chapter's footnote 2, and the origin of the one-autoencoder-at-a-time method in Figure 17-7.

items.term: Convolutional Autoencoders

blocks.content:
For images, swap the dense layers for convolutional ones: the encoder shrinks the picture with convolutions and pooling, and the decoder grows it back with transpose convolutions.

**The question this lesson answers:** a dense autoencoder flattens a 28 by 28 image into 784 unrelated numbers. What do you use instead when the input is a picture, and how does the decoder get the picture's shape back?

### The big picture

```
28x28x1 -> conv + pool -> 3x3x64 -> transpose conv -> 28x28x1
           shrink space           grow space back
           grow depth            shrink depth back
```

### 1 · Why dense layers are the wrong tool here

Standard dense neural networks struggle with image data because flattening full-resolution images creates an excessively large number of trainable parameters. Additionally, fully connected networks do not natively preserve the two-dimensional spatial structures present in visual data. A **convolutional autoencoder** solves this problem by utilizing convolutional architectures specifically suited for image processing.

**Spatial structure** is the fact that two pixels next to each other are related. Flattening throws that away: after the flatten, pixel 1 and pixel 2 are no more related than pixel 1 and pixel 700. A **convolution** is a small window that slides over the image and looks at each neighbourhood, so neighbourhood information survives.

### 2 · The encoder shrinks space and grows depth

The model consists of two main components: an encoder and a decoder. The **encoder** acts as a standard convolutional neural network, employing convolutional layers and pooling layers to gradually decrease spatial dimensions (height and width) while increasing the feature depth (number of channels). This process compresses the image into a compact latent representation.

Two axes move in opposite directions, and that is the pattern worth memorising:

| Axis | What it is | In the encoder |
|---|---|---|
| spatial (height, width) | how big the picture is | shrinks |
| depth (channels) | how many features per spot | grows |

A **channel** or **feature map** is one layer of the stack: one detector's answer at every position. **Pooling** shrinks height and width by keeping one value per small block.

### 3 · The decoder runs it backwards

To reconstruct the original image, the **decoder** performs the inverse operation. It utilizes **transpose convolutional layers** (or upsampling layers combined with standard convolutions) to upscale spatial dimensions and reduce channel depth back to the input format.

Note the alternative in that sentence: you do not strictly need transpose convolutions. Combining spatial upsampling layers with standard convolutional layers gets you the same upscaling — upsampling raises the resolution and the convolution then cleans up the features.

### 4 · The Fashion MNIST walk-through

Consider an input image from the Fashion MNIST dataset with dimensions of 28 by 28 pixels and 1 channel. The encoder passes the image through successive convolution and max-pooling layers, reducing the spatial resolution down to 3 by 3 with 64 feature maps before outputting a compact representation vector. The decoder receives this compressed representation, reshapes it to 3 by 3 spatial dimensions with 16 feature maps, and applies transpose convolutions with stride 2 to iteratively upscale the representations back to a 28 by 28 single-channel image.

The comments in the code card below mark each step: 28 by 28 to 14 by 14 to 7 by 7 to 3 by 3, with depth going 16, 32, 64. A **stride** of 2 means the window moves two pixels at a time, which is what halves the size going down and doubles it going up.

Whichever layer type you use, the bottleneck rule from earlier still applies: an undercomplete autoencoder contains fewer dimensions than the input data to enforce feature compression.

The crucial insight to remember is that transpose convolutional layers allow autoencoders to invert spatial downsampling, enabling exact restoration of image dimensions while retaining structural spatial patterns.

**One-liner for your notes:** convolutions keep neighbouring pixels neighbours — encoder shrinks space and grows depth, decoder does the reverse with transpose convolutions.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
conv_encoder = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.Reshape([28, 28, 1]),
    tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(16, 3, padding="same", activation="relu"),
    tf.keras.layers.MaxPool2D(pool_size=2),  # output: 14 × 14 x 16
    tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(32, 3, padding="same", activation="relu"),
    tf.keras.layers.MaxPool2D(pool_size=2),  # output: 7 × 7 x 32
    tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(64, 3, padding="same", activation="relu"),
    tf.keras.layers.MaxPool2D(pool_size=2),  # output: 3 × 3 x 64
    tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(30, 3, padding="same", activation="relu"),
    tf.keras.layers.GlobalAvgPool2D()  # output: 30
])
conv_decoder = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(3 * 3 * 16),
    tf.keras.layers.Reshape((3, 3, 16)),
    tf.keras.layers.Conv2DTranspose(32, 3, strides=2, activation="relu"),
    tf.keras.layers.Conv2DTranspose(16, 3, strides=2, padding="same",
                                    activation="relu"),
    tf.keras.layers.Conv2DTranspose(1, 3, strides=2, padding="same"),
    tf.keras.layers.Reshape([28, 28])
])
conv_ae = tf.keras.Sequential([conv_encoder, conv_decoder])
```

items.term: Why the depth axis grows while the space axis shrinks
items.text: It looks like a contradiction — you are compressing, so why is anything getting bigger? Because the two axes carry different things. Height and width carry where; channels carry what. Early layers need many positions and few kinds of answer (is there an edge here?); later layers need few positions and many kinds of answer (is this a sleeve, a heel, a collar?). Shrinking space while growing depth is trading location detail for description detail.

items.term: Transpose convolution is not an inverse
items.text: The name suggests undoing the convolution, and it does not: it restores the shape, not the information. Anything the encoder discarded is gone, and the decoder is inventing a plausible filling. That is why reconstructions come back recognisable but soft. Knowing this stops you from expecting a convolutional autoencoder to work as lossless compression — the dimensions are exactly restored, the pixels are not.

items.term: Where the choice between the two upscaling routes matters
items.text: Transpose convolutions learn how to upscale, which is more expressive but can leave regular checkerboard patterns when the stride and kernel size interact badly. Upsampling followed by an ordinary convolution splits the job — a fixed, dumb enlargement, then a learned clean-up — and is often steadier for that reason. The book presents them as alternatives; in practice this is a knob worth trying both ways when your outputs look patterned.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Dense autoencoders perform poorly on images because they fail to capture spatial structure efficienty.
The encoder reduces spatial height and width while expanding channel depth using convolutions and pooling.
The decoder expands spatial dimensions back to original input sizes using transpose convolutional layers.
Undercomplete autoencoders restrict coding layer size to force models to learn meaningful features.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The book offers transpose convolutions or upsampling-plus-convolution as equal alternatives for the decoder. What actually makes practitioners pick one over the other, and what artifacts does each tend to leave behind?
Look up: Jonathan Masci et al., 'Stacked Convolutional Auto-Encoders for Hierarchical Feature Extraction', ICANN 2011: 52-59 — this chapter's footnote 3.

items.term: Denoising Autoencoders

blocks.content:
A denoising autoencoder is fed a damaged copy of the input and scored against the clean original, so the only way to lower its loss is to learn what the data usually looks like.

**The question this lesson answers:** a bottleneck stops a network copying its input. What do you do when the hidden layers are roomy enough to memorise anyway? You break the input on the way in.

### The big picture

```
clean x -> [add noise] -> encoder -> decoder -> x̂
    |                                            |
    +----------- loss compares these -------------+
```

The noise sits between the input and the encoder. The loss still points at the clean original.

### 1 · The problem with a roomy autoencoder

Standard autoencoders risk memorizing inputs without learning meaningful representations if the hidden layers have too much capacity. To force the network to extract useful underlying patterns, we corrupt the input data with noise during training while forcing the model to reconstruct the original, uncorrupted target.

This is the second way to stop trivial copying. The first was making the middle too small; this one leaves the middle alone and damages the input instead.

### 2 · Two ways to corrupt, one place to put them

A **denoising autoencoder** receives corrupted inputs through either continuous additive noise, like **Gaussian noise**, or complete pixel dropping, using a **dropout layer**.

| Method | What it does to a pixel |
|---|---|
| Gaussian noise | adds a small random amount to it |
| dropout | sets it to zero outright |

As Figure 17-8 shows, this corrupting layer is placed directly between the initial input layer and the first hidden layer of the encoder. Figure 17-8 below draws both options side by side: Gaussian noise on the left, dropout on the right.

### 3 · Training only — and why that matters

The noise generation process occurs exclusively during model training; during testing or inference, the noise layer is deactivated so the model can process clean or real-world corrupted inputs directly.

**Inference** is simply using the trained model on new data. Keras handles this for you: `GaussianNoise` and `Dropout` layers are automatically disabled so the model processes inputs without adding noise at evaluation time. You do not switch anything off by hand, and you should not be surprised that predictions are deterministic afterwards.

The targets never change either. The loss is always computed against the uncorrupted, original input values before noise was applied — that is the whole objective: recover the clean original.

### 4 · The 50-percent example

Consider an image processing pipeline handling 28 × 28 grayscale images from the Fashion MNIST dataset. During training, a dropout layer randomly sets 50% of the input pixels to zero. Half of the input values are randomly set to zero during each training step, and a different half is chosen every step.

The corrupted input passes through the encoder and decoder to produce a clean reconstruction. Figure 17-9 demonstrates how the trained network receives incomplete inputs with half of their pixels missing and successfully restores missing structures. Look closely at the bottom row: the autoencoder guesses details that are not actually in the input, such as the top of the white shirt. It is not recovering that detail — it is inventing a plausible one, because it has learned what shirts look like.

Beyond cleaning images, these models can be used for unsupervised pretraining and feature extraction, exactly like the stacked autoencoders in the previous lesson.

The essential insight is that by learning to remove artificial noise, the autoencoder learns the underlying structure of the underlying data distribution rather than a simple identity mapping.

**One-liner for your notes:** damage the input, score against the clean original, and the network has to learn the data's structure — noise on during training, off at inference.
