blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
dropout_encoder = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.Flatten(),
    tf.keras.layers.Dropout(0.5),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(100, activation="relu"),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(30, activation="relu")
])
dropout_decoder = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(100, activation="relu"),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(28 * 28),
    tf.keras.layers.Reshape([28, 28])
])
dropout_ae = tf.keras.Sequential([dropout_encoder, dropout_decoder])
```

items.term: Two different constraints, one shared goal
items.text: The bottleneck and the noise are attacking the same failure from opposite sides. The bottleneck removes the network's capacity to memorise. The noise removes the input's reliability, so memorising a specific input is not even useful. You can use either, or both, and a denoising autoencoder with a roomy middle is a perfectly normal design — which is the point, since it buys back the capacity the bottleneck had to spend.

items.term: Why the reconstruction is allowed to be a guess
items.text: The network fills in the top of the white shirt even though those pixels were never in its input. That is not a bug in the evaluation; it is the objective working. The loss compares against the clean original, so producing detail that was destroyed is exactly what earns a low loss. Note the consequence for real denoising work: the output is the model's best guess at what was probably there, not a recovery of what was there. On an image that is charming. On a measurement, it is fabrication.

items.term: What the noise rate actually controls
items.text: A dropout rate of 0.5 is a strong corruption, and the rate is a dial on how hard the task is. Too little noise and the network can nearly copy again; too much and there is not enough signal left to reconstruct from, so it learns the dataset average instead of anything specific. The right setting depends on how redundant your data is — images are extremely redundant, which is why half the pixels can vanish and the garment is still identifiable.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Denoising autoencoders receive corrupted inputs but are trained to reconstruct clean targets.
Noise can be added using Gaussian noise or dropout layers placed right after the input.
The corrupting noise layer is active only during training and is automatically turned off during inference.
These models can be used for image denoising, unsupervised pretraining, and feature extraction.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Denoising autoencoders learn to remove the noise you trained them on. What happens when the real-world corruption has a different character — compression artifacts, say, rather than dropped pixels — and how do people handle that mismatch?
Look up: Pascal Vincent et al., 'Extracting and Composing Robust Features with Denoising Autoencoders', ICML 2008: 1096-1103 — this chapter's footnote 4.

items.term: Sparse Autoencoders

blocks.content:
A sparse autoencoder is allowed a big coding layer but is punished for switching too many of those neurons on at once, so each neuron has to earn its place by learning one distinct feature.

**The question this lesson answers:** you want a large coding layer, because rich features need room — but a large layer can just copy the input. How do you keep the room and still force the network to be selective?

### The big picture

```
coding layer: 300 sigmoid units, but only ~10% active
   penalty = how far actual activation q is from target p
   p = 0.1 (the target)     q = measured over the batch
```

### 1 · Sparsity as the constraint

Standard autoencoders often copy inputs through hidden layers without extracting meaningful features, especially when the coding layer has high capacity. **Sparse autoencoders** solve this issue by adding a constraint to the cost function that penalizes active neurons, forcing the network to represent each input using only a small subset of coding units.

**Sparse** here means most values are zero or near zero — the same word you would use for a mostly-empty column. The constraint forces the network to represent inputs using a small combination of active neurons, so each neuron in the coding layer typically ends up representing one useful feature. If you could speak only a few words per month, you would make them count.

To implement sparsity, the network typically uses a sigmoid activation function in a large coding layer (such as 300 units) so that activations stay between 0 and 1. The **sigmoid** is the S-shaped squashing function that maps any number into the range 0 to 1, which is what lets an activation be read as "how on is this neuron".

### 2 · Route one: ℓ1 on the activations

One approach applies $\ell_1$ regularization directly to these activations, pushing most codings toward zero while preserving essential non-zero values required for accurate reconstruction.

**ℓ1 regularization** adds the sum of absolute values to the loss. Applied to activations rather than weights, it adds the sum of absolute values of codings to the training loss. Keras spells this `ActivityRegularization(l1=1e-4)`: as the card below explains, the layer returns its inputs unchanged and the penalty is a side effect, active during training only.

Why ℓ1 and not ℓ2 (squares)? ℓ1 pushes the unneeded codings all the way to zero while leaving the important ones alone; ℓ2 would just shrink everything a bit. The network still has to reconstruct the input, so it is forced to keep at least a few nonzero values.

### 3 · Route two: measure the actual sparsity, then penalise the gap

Alternatively, one can measure the actual mean activation $q$ across a training batch for each neuron and penalize deviations from a target sparsity $p$ (e.g., $p = 0.1$).

| Symbol | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| p | p | the target activation rate, e.g. 0.1 |
| q | q | the measured mean activation of one neuron |

The mean is taken over the whole training batch, which is why the batch size must not be too small — with too few rows the mean is not a reliable estimate, exactly as a small sample is not a reliable `AVG`.

### 4 · Why KL divergence rather than squared error

While mean squared error can measure the gap between $p$ and $q$, using **Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence** provides much stronger gradients as actual sparsity diverges from the target, as shown in Figure 17-10. Equation 17-1 below defines general KL divergence between two discrete probability distributions, and Equation 17-2 below is the simplified version for the target sparsity $p$ and the actual mean activation $q$, with the full walk-through underneath it.

Figure 17-10 below is the argument in one picture: KL divergence rises significantly steeper than both MAE and MSE as sparsity deviates from the target of 0.1. A **gradient** is how hard the loss pushes back; a flat curve barely pushes, a steep one pushes hard.

For example, if a neuron has a mean batch activation of $q = 0.3$ against a target of $p = 0.1$, Equation 17-2 calculates a high penalty.

### 5 · The one knob you have to tune

Adding this penalty weighted by a hyperparameter forces the model to maintain roughly 10% average activation per neuron while retaining high-quality reconstruction. The **sparsity weight** is that hyperparameter — a number you set before training, as you would pass a `--conf` value when submitting a job.

If the weight is too high, the model sticks closely to the target sparsity but the autoencoder fails to reconstruct inputs properly, which makes it useless. If it is too low, the model mostly ignores the sparsity objective and learns no interesting features.

| Weight | What happens |
|---|---|
| too high | sparsity dominates, reconstructions break |
| too low | sparsity ignored, no interesting features |
| right | roughly 10% sparsity, good reconstructions |

Sparsity constraints force autoencoders to discover distinct, highly specialized features by limiting how many neurons can activate simultaneously.

**One-liner for your notes:** big sigmoid coding layer, penalty on how many neurons fire — ℓ1 for the simple version, KL divergence against a target rate of 0.1 for the better one.

blocks.title: How the two sparsity penalties behave
blocks.content: The `ActivityRegularization(l1=1e-4)` layer returns its inputs unchanged, but as a side effect it adds a training loss equal to the sum of the absolute values of its inputs. This only affects training. For the KL approach, the mean activation of each neuron is computed over the whole training batch, so the batch size must not be too small, or the mean will not be accurate. In the book's example, a neuron with an average activation of 0.3 and a target of 0.1 must be penalized to activate less. Adding the squared error $(0.3 - 0.1)^2$ would work, but the KL divergence has much stronger gradients. The summed sparsity loss is multiplied by a sparsity weight. If the weight is too high, the model sticks to the target sparsity but may not reconstruct the inputs properly. If it is too low, the model mostly ignores sparsity and learns no interesting features.

blocks.title: Figure 17-10
blocks.caption: Sparsity loss
blocks.alt: Figure 17-10: Sparsity loss

blocks.title: Equation 17-1
blocks.caption: Kullback–Leibler divergence
blocks.explain:
**Why the equation looks like this**

The penalty has one job: the neuron fires on average q of the time, you asked for p, so how bad is
that? Squared error would answer it, and the book says so outright — adding the squared error of
(0.3 minus 0.1) would work. It is not used because it is not *strong* enough. Squared error is nearly
flat near the target and grows only mildly far from it, so a neuron sitting at q of 0.5 barely feels a
push. KL divergence grows without limit as q approaches 0 or 1, which is exactly where the push needs
to be hardest. Figure 17-10 is that difference drawn.

**Is this standard?** Yes, both. Equation 17-1 is the textbook definition of Kullback–Leibler
divergence between two discrete probability distributions, used across statistics and machine
learning — nothing was simplified for this example. Equation 17-2 is not a second formula: it is
Equation 17-1 with the distributions filled in for the case here.

**The general form.** Equation 17-1 is the general form and Equation 17-2 is its special case. The
step between them is short:

- a neuron either fires or it does not, so each distribution has exactly two outcomes;
- the target distribution is (p, 1 − p) and the measured one is (q, 1 − q);
- so the sum over i in Equation 17-1 has just two terms — and writing those two terms out *is*
Equation 17-2.

A two-outcome distribution like this is called a **Bernoulli** distribution: one coin flip with a
fixed bias.

**Terms this introduces.** A **discrete probability distribution** is a list of outcomes with a
probability against each, adding up to 1. A **divergence** is a one-way measure of difference:
D of P from Q need not equal D of Q from P, so despite behaving like a distance it is not one. The
**natural logarithm** written log here is the usual one — it turns a ratio into a signed amount, zero
when the ratio is 1, negative below and positive above.

**Every piece of Equation 17-2**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| D with subscript KL | D K L | the score this returns |
| p ‖ q | p against q | which two rates are compared |
| p | p | target activation rate, here 0.1 |
| q | q | measured mean activation, here 0.3 |
| log of p over q | log of p over q | how far off the firing rate is |
| 1 − p | one minus p | target rate of staying quiet |
| 1 − q | one minus q | measured rate of staying quiet |
| the plus in the middle | plus | add the firing and quiet halves |

**The formula in plain words**

penalty = (how often you asked it to fire) × log(asked ÷ measured)
+ (how often you asked it to stay quiet) × log(asked quiet ÷ measured quiet)

Both halves are counted, which is why a neuron that fires too *rarely* is penalised as well as one
that fires too often. The target is a rate to hit, not a ceiling to stay under.

**With the book's real numbers**

The book's example is a neuron measured at q of 0.3 against a target p of 0.1.

1. Firing half: 0.1 × log(0.1 ÷ 0.3) = 0.1 × log(0.3333) = 0.1 × (−1.0986) = **−0.1099**
2. Quiet half: 0.9 × log(0.9 ÷ 0.7) = 0.9 × log(1.2857) = 0.9 × 0.2513 = **0.2262**
3. Add them: −0.1099 + 0.2262 = **0.1163**

The squared error the book compares it against is (0.3 − 0.1) squared = **0.04**. So at this gap the
KL penalty is already about 2.9 times larger.

The gap that matters most is at the extremes, and it is not a matter of degree. Squared error against
a target of 0.1 can never exceed (1 − 0.1) squared = 0.81, no matter how wrong the neuron gets. KL
keeps climbing: at q of 0.95 it is 2.376, at q of 0.99 it is 3.821, and it has no ceiling at all. A
loss with a ceiling stops pushing once you are far enough away; that is the failure Figure 17-10 is
warning about.

**Then what happens to the number**

Each neuron's penalty is computed this way, all of them are summed, and the total is multiplied by
the sparsity weight before being added to the reconstruction loss. That multiplication is the only
knob you tune.

blocks.title: Equation 17-2
blocks.caption: KL divergence between the target sparsity p and the actual sparsity q
blocks.latex: D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(p \parallel q\right) = p \log \frac{p}{q} + (1 - p) \log \frac{1 - p}{1 - q}

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
class KLDivergenceRegularizer(tf.keras.regularizers.Regularizer):
    def __init__(self, weight, target):
        self.weight = weight
        self.target = target

    def __call__(self, inputs):
        mean_activities = tf.reduce_mean(inputs, axis=0)
        return self.weight * (
            kl_divergence(self.target, mean_activities) +
            kl_divergence(1. - self.target, 1. - mean_activities))

kld_reg = KLDivergenceRegularizer(weight=5e-3, target=0.1)
sparse_kl_encoder = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.Flatten(),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(100, activation="relu"),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(300, activation="sigmoid", activity_regularizer=kld_reg)
])
```

items.term: Sparsity is a different kind of constraint from a bottleneck
items.text: A bottleneck limits how many numbers exist. Sparsity limits how many of them are non-zero at any one time, while leaving 300 of them available. That distinction is worth holding: the first gives every input the same small vocabulary to describe itself with; the second gives every input a large vocabulary but forbids long sentences. The second tends to produce features that are individually interpretable, because a neuron that only fires for a few inputs is a neuron that means something specific.

items.term: Why the penalty is measured over a batch, not per example
items.text: The target is an average firing rate, so it can only be measured across many examples — a single input either fires a neuron or it does not, and asking one input to be 10 percent on is meaningless. That is why the batch size matters here in a way it does not for ordinary losses: the penalty is estimated from a sample, and a small sample gives a noisy estimate, so the model gets pushed around by sampling noise rather than by real over-activity.

items.term: Both directions are penalised, and that is deliberate
items.text: KL divergence against a target of 0.1 punishes a neuron that fires 30 percent of the time and also one that fires 2 percent of the time. The second may look harmless — surely sparser is better? — but a neuron that almost never fires is capacity you paid for and are not using, and it contributes nothing to reconstruction. The target is a rate to hit, not a ceiling to stay under.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Sparsity constraints limit the number of active neurons in the coding layer, forcing useful feature extraction.
Activations in the coding layer are usually constrained between 0 and 1 using the sigmoid activation function.
Simple sparsity uses L1 activity regularization to push coding values toward zero.
Target sparsity penalizes the KL divergence between target activation probability p and batch mean activation q.
KL divergence provides steeper gradients than mean squared error when actual sparsity deviates from target values.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The sparsity weight has no principled setting in the book — too high breaks reconstruction, too low does nothing. How do practitioners actually choose it, and is there a way to watch the measured sparsity during training rather than guessing?
Look up: the Keras API documentation for tf.keras.layers.ActivityRegularization and the tf.keras.regularizers module, which is where the l1 and custom-regularizer machinery in this lesson lives.

items.term: Variational Autoencoders

blocks.content:
A variational autoencoder makes the encoder output a *distribution* instead of a point, samples the coding from it, and adds a second loss that pulls all those distributions toward one standard bell curve — which turns the autoencoder into a generator.

**The question this lesson answers:** feed a random vector into an ordinary trained decoder and you get garbage, because the latent space has holes. How do you train a latent space with no holes, so that any random vector decodes into something valid?

### The big picture

| | Ordinary autoencoder | Variational autoencoder |
|---|---|---|
| Encoder gives | one fixed coding | a mean μ and a spread σ |
| Coding is | that vector | sampled from that bell curve |
| Loss is | reconstruction | reconstruction + latent loss |
| Random input | garbage out | a new, valid instance |

### 1 · The hole problem

Standard autoencoders map inputs directly to deterministic vectors in a latent space, which often leaves gaps where decoding yields meaningless garbage. This structural limitation prevents them from easily generating novel instances that resemble the original training data.

**Deterministic** means the same input always gives exactly the same coding. Nothing in ordinary training says the space *between* two training codings has to mean anything, so mostly it does not.

### 2 · Output a distribution, not a point

**Variational autoencoders** (VAEs) solve this problem by converting deterministic autoencoders into probabilistic generative models. Instead of mapping an input directly to a single fixed coding, the encoder outputs two statistical parameters: a mean vector $\mu$ and a standard deviation vector $\sigma$. The model then randomly samples a coding from a Gaussian distribution parameterized by $\mu$ and $\sigma$ before passing it to the decoder.

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| μ | mu | the centre of the bell curve |
| σ | sigma | how wide the bell curve is |
| the coding | z | one random draw from that curve |

As [fig-17-11] shows, this stochastic step forces the codings to form a smooth, continuous Gaussian cloud in the latent space. **Stochastic** means involving chance — run the same input through twice and you get two slightly different codings. The right-hand side of Figure 17-11 below traces one training instance through: the encoder produces μ and σ, a coding is sampled (notice it does not sit exactly on μ), and the decoder decodes that.

### 3 · Two losses, pulling in different directions

To balance reconstruction quality with continuous latent properties, VAEs use a two-part cost function. The first component is a standard reconstruction loss, such as mean squared error, which encourages the model to accurately reconstruct the input. The second component is the latent loss, calculated using the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. As defined in [eq-17-3], this loss pushes the distribution of the codings toward a standard normal Gaussian distribution, which is another way of saying it encourages the distribution of latent codings to match a standard normal Gaussian distribution.

A **standard normal Gaussian** is the bell curve with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Equation 17-3 below is the latent loss, with the full symbol-by-symbol walk-through underneath it.

The two losses genuinely fight each other. Reconstruction wants every input to get its own far-apart, unambiguous coding. The latent loss wants every coding to look like a draw from one shared bell curve centred on zero. The compromise is a latent space that is packed, overlapping and smooth — which is exactly what makes random sampling work.

### 4 · The gamma trick

For numerical stability and faster training, implementation routines typically parameterize the standard deviation as $\gamma = \log(\sigma^2)$, rewriting the latent loss as shown in [eq-17-4]. Predicting log variance gamma instead of sigma speeds up network training and improves mathematical stability during gradient calculations.

The reason is that σ must never be negative, and a plain `Dense` layer can output anything. γ (gamma) is a logarithm, so it is free to be any number at all — negative γ simply means a small σ — and the exponential that converts it back is applied later, where it cannot produce an impossible value. Equation 17-4 below is Equation 17-3 rewritten in terms of γ.

### 5 · One image through the machine

Consider an instance processing a 28 × 28 image through a VAE. The encoder calculates mean $\mu$ and log-variance $\gamma$ vectors. A layer samples a standard random normal noise vector $\epsilon$, scales it by $\exp(\gamma / 2)$, and adds $\mu$. The decoder processes this sampled vector to output the reconstructed 28 × 28 image.

That scaling is not arbitrary: since γ is log(σ²), exp(γ/2) is σ. So the layer draws a standard bell-curve sample, stretches it to the width the encoder asked for, and shifts it to the centre the encoder asked for. The `Sampling` layer in the code card below is those three lines.

### 6 · Why the loss is divided by 784

The card below covers this in full, and it is worth reading once because the number looks magic. Keras computes the `"mse"` loss as the mean over all 784 pixels, but the VAE's reconstruction loss is supposed to be the *sum* of the pixel errors. So the reconstruction loss arrives 784 times smaller than intended. Dividing the latent loss by 784 too puts the two back on the same footing — it offsets Keras computing mean reconstruction loss across pixels instead of the total sum.

Because the overall latent space follows a standard normal Gaussian distribution, new samples can be synthesized post-training simply by feeding standard random normal noise into the trained decoder.

The core insight of a VAE is that parameterizing latent representations as probability distributions forces the latent space to remain smooth and continuous, transforming the autoencoder into a generative model.

**One-liner for your notes:** the encoder emits μ and γ, the coding is a random draw from that bell curve, and a KL latent loss pulls the whole cloud toward standard normal — which is what makes random vectors decode into real-looking things.

blocks.title: Scaling the latent loss by 784
blocks.content: The book adds the latent loss with `variational_ae.add_loss(tf.reduce_mean(latent_loss) / 784.)`. First, Equation 17-4 gives the latent loss of each instance, summed over the last axis. Next, the mean over all instances in the batch is taken. Finally, the result is divided by 784, the number of pixels in a 28 × 28 image. The reason is that the VAE's reconstruction loss should be the sum of the pixel reconstruction errors, but the Keras `"mse"` loss computes the mean over all 784 pixels, so the reconstruction loss is 784 times smaller than needed. Dividing the latent loss by 784 gives it the appropriate scale compared to the reconstruction loss. The final loss is then 784 times smaller than it should be, which just means a larger learning rate should be used. In the sampling layer, multiplying by $\exp(\gamma/2)$ gives $\sigma$, because $\gamma = \log(\sigma^2)$.

blocks.title: Figure 17-11
blocks.caption: A variational autoencoder (left) and an instance going through it (right)
blocks.alt: Figure 17-11: A variational autoencoder (left) and an instance going through it (right)

blocks.title: Equation 17-3
blocks.caption: Variational autoencoder’s latent loss
blocks.explain:
**Why the equation looks like this**

You want every input's little Gaussian cloud to end up looking like the *one* standard bell curve —
centred on 0, width 1. So the penalty has to be zero exactly when mu is 0 and sigma is 1, and grow
whenever the encoder drifts from either. That is what the bracket does: it measures, per dimension,
"how far is this Gaussian from the standard one", and the sum adds that up over all n coding
dimensions.

The minus one-half in front is not decoration. Without it the bracket is largest when the match is
perfect; the minus flips it so that a perfect match gives zero and any drift gives a positive
penalty, and the half is what falls out of the Gaussian algebra when the general KL formula is
simplified for this case.

**Is this standard?** Yes. Equation 17-3 is the canonical closed-form KL divergence between a
Gaussian with mean mu and standard deviation sigma and the standard normal, and it is what every VAE
implementation uses. It is not an approximation invented for Fashion MNIST. Equation 17-4 is the same
equation with one substitution — nothing new is being claimed, only rewritten.

**The general form.** This *is* a special case of Equation 17-1 from the previous lesson, the general
KL divergence, worked out for two Gaussians instead of two firing rates. The book notes the maths is
more involved than the sparse-autoencoder version because of the Gaussian noise, but that the
equations simplify — Equation 17-3 is the result of that simplification, which is why it contains
only logs, squares and an exponential rather than a sum over outcomes.

**Terms this introduces.** **Variance** is the square of the standard deviation, so log-variance
gamma equals log of sigma squared. **exp** is the exponential function, the inverse of log; it turns
any number, negative included, into a positive one — which is why gamma is safe to predict and sigma
is not. **Per dimension** matters: the codings have n dimensions and each one gets its own mu and
sigma, so the bracket is evaluated n times and summed.

**Every piece of Equation 17-4**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| script L | L | the latent loss for one instance |
| minus one-half | minus a half | flips the sign, from the algebra |
| the sum sign | sum from i equals 1 to n | add over every coding dimension |
| n | n | how many numbers are in a coding |
| i | i | which dimension, 1 up to n |
| the 1 in the bracket | one | the constant that makes a perfect match score zero |
| gamma with subscript i | gamma i | log-variance for dimension i |
| exp of gamma i | e to the gamma i | the variance itself, always positive |
| mu with subscript i squared | mu i squared | how far this dimension's centre is from 0 |

Equation 17-3 is the identical bracket with log of sigma squared written out in place of gamma, and
sigma squared in place of exp of gamma. Same quantity, different spelling.

**The formula in plain words**

latent loss = a half × the sum over dimensions of
(the variance − 1 − log of the variance) + (the centre squared)

Read it as two complaints per dimension: *your spread is not 1* and *your centre is not 0*.

**With real numbers, one dimension at a time**

Plugging the book's own Equation 17-4 into three cases makes the shape obvious:

| mu | sigma | gamma | Loss for that dimension |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1 | 0 | 0.000 — a perfect match, no penalty |
| 2 | 1 | 0 | 2.000 — right width, centre far off |
| 0 | 0.5 | −1.386 | 0.318 — right centre, too narrow |

Check the first row by hand, because it is the one that proves the shape is right: minus a half times
(1 + 0 − 1 − 0) = minus a half times 0 = 0. An encoder that has already landed on standard normal is
charged nothing, and every other answer costs something.

**And then the division by 784**

The per-instance losses are averaged over the batch and the result divided by 784, the number of
pixels in a 28 by 28 image. This is not part of the equation — it is a correction for how Keras
computes the reconstruction loss. Keras averages the squared error over 784 pixels where the VAE
wants the sum, so reconstruction arrives 784 times too small; dividing the latent loss by 784 too
restores the ratio between them. The final loss is 784 times smaller than it should be, which is
harmless: use a larger learning rate.

blocks.title: Equation 17-4
blocks.caption: Variational autoencoder’s latent loss, rewritten using γ = log(σ²)

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
class Sampling(tf.keras.layers.Layer):
    def call(self, inputs):
        mean, log_var = inputs
        epsilon = tf.random.normal(tf.shape(log_var))
        return epsilon * tf.exp(log_var / 2) + mean

codings_size = 10
inputs = tf.keras.layers.Input(shape=[28, 28])
z = tf.keras.layers.Flatten()(inputs)
z = tf.keras.layers.Dense(150, activation="relu")(z)
codings_mean = tf.keras.layers.Dense(codings_size)(z)
codings_log_var = tf.keras.layers.Dense(codings_size)(z)
codings = Sampling()([codings_mean, codings_log_var])
encoder = tf.keras.Model(inputs=[inputs], outputs=[codings])
```

items.term: Why randomness is what fills the holes
items.text: The sampling step is the mechanism, not a detail. Because the coding is drawn at random near mu, one input maps to a small cloud of codings rather than a point, and the decoder is forced to produce something sensible for every point in that cloud. Repeat over the whole training set and the clouds overlap, which is what leaves no gaps between them. A deterministic encoder never has to make the space between two training points mean anything; a noisy one has no choice.

items.term: The two losses are a genuine tension, and the ratio is a design decision
items.text: Reconstruction wants codings spread far apart and unambiguous; the latent loss wants them all piled onto one standard bell curve. Whichever you weight more, you get: weight reconstruction too heavily and the latent space develops holes again and generation degrades; weight the latent loss too heavily and every input collapses toward the same coding and reconstructions turn to mush. The divide-by-784 is not bookkeeping pedantry — it is what sets that ratio, and it is why the book can then say 'just use a larger learning rate'.

items.term: Why VAE samples are blurry, structurally
items.text: Averaging is baked in. The decoder must produce an acceptable output for every coding in an input's cloud, and the loss that scores it is pixel-wise squared error, which is minimised by predicting the average of the plausible answers. An average of several plausible sharp edges is a soft edge. This is not a tuning failure and no amount of training removes it — it is the direct consequence of the objective, and it is exactly the weakness adversarial training attacks by replacing the pixel-wise loss with a critic.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Variational autoencoders are probabilistic models that output mean and variance parameters rather than fixed codings.
The total loss combines a reconstruction loss with a KL divergence latent loss that shapes the latent space into a Gaussian distribution.
Parameterizing log variance gamma instead of standard deviation improves numerical stability during network training.
Generating new synthetic samples requires only sampling random vectors from a Gaussian prior and feeding them to the decoder.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The latent loss here is the KL divergence against a standard normal prior. What changes if you choose a different prior, and what problem are people trying to solve when they do?
Look up: Diederik Kingma and Max Welling, 'Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes', arXiv:1312.6114 (2013) — this chapter's footnote 6, the paper that introduced VAEs.

items.term: Generating Images and Semantic Interpolation with VAEs

blocks.content:
Once a VAE is trained, you can throw away the encoder: feed random Gaussian vectors straight into the decoder and it produces new clothing images, and moving along a line in that space morphs one garment smoothly into another.

**The question this lesson answers:** the latent space is now a smooth Gaussian cloud. What can you actually do with that? Two things: generate items that were never in the training set, and travel between two items in a way that stays meaningful the whole way.

### The big picture

```
random Gaussian vector -> variational decoder -> new image
walk a straight line in that space -> pants become a sweater
```

### 1 · Why random vectors work here and not before

Standard autoencoders compress inputs into low-dimensional latent vectors, but their latent spaces often contain gaps. Passing random vectors into a standard decoder usually results in nonsensical noise rather than valid images. A **variational autoencoder** (VAE) solves this problem by enforcing a structured latent space where codings follow a standard normal distribution. This continuity makes image generation and smooth transitions possible.

The VAE training forces its latent space to be continuous and organized around a normal distribution, so a fresh random draw from that same normal distribution lands somewhere the decoder has already learned to handle. That is the whole reason the trick works.

### 2 · Generating new items

To generate brand new images using a trained VAE, you can sample random codings directly from a Gaussian distribution and pass them into the **variational decoder**. As shown in Figure 17-12, decoding these random Gaussian codings produces entirely new synthetic items of clothing, such as shoes, pants, and shirts.

The first two lines of the code card below are the entire generation step: draw a batch of normal noise of the coding size, call the decoder on it. There is no input image anywhere.

While the generated output images can appear somewhat blurry, they successfully capture the overall structural shapes of the underlying data distribution. Blurriness is the characteristic flaw of a basic VAE: the generated images tend to appear somewhat blurry, because averaging over a distribution smooths away sharp edges. Hold on to that — it is the exact weakness GANs are about to fix.

### 3 · Two kinds of "in between"

Because the latent space of a VAE is continuous and smooth, you can also perform **semantic interpolation**. **Interpolation** means producing the steps between two things; **semantic** means the steps are meaningful rather than cosmetic.

| | Pixel-level | Latent-space (semantic) |
|---|---|---|
| Works on | the two pictures | the two codings |
| Halfway looks like | both, overlaid faintly | one plausible garment |
| Result | ghosting artifacts | a real transition |

Pixel-level interpolation between two images simply overlays them with varying transparency, which creates unnatural artifacts. In contrast, latent-space interpolation modifies codings along a line in the latent space before decoding them. Pixel interpolation overlays pixels, while semantic interpolation transforms underlying visual features.

### 4 · Walking one axis

As illustrated in Figure 17-13, linearly altering a single dimension of the coding array gradually transforms the decoded image from one meaningful class into another, smoothly shifting a pair of pants into a sweater.

The recipe in the code card below is two lines: create a zero matrix of seven codings, then assign a linear sequence of values to one chosen column — `np.linspace(-0.8, 0.8, 7)` on axis 3. Every other dimension stays at zero, so only one thing varies, and Figure 17-13 below shows that single axis carrying the image from pants to sweater.

The key insight to remember is that variational autoencoders structure their latent space continuously around a Gaussian distribution, enabling both random image generation and smooth semantic transitions between different object categories.

**One-liner for your notes:** a trained VAE decoder turns random normal noise into new garments, and a straight line in latent space turns pants into a sweater without ever passing through a ghostly overlay.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf

# Generate novel images from random Gaussian codings
codings = tf.random.normal(shape=[3 * 7, codings_size])
images = variational_decoder(codings).numpy()

# Perform semantic interpolation along latent axis 3
codings = np.zeros([7, codings_size])
codings[:, 3] = np.linspace(-0.8, 0.8, 7)
images = variational_decoder(codings).numpy()
```

items.term: Why a straight line in latent space is a meaningful path
items.text: It is only meaningful because the latent loss made it so. Training pulled every coding onto one shared Gaussian cloud, so the points along a line between two codings are themselves plausible codings — the decoder has effectively seen that neighbourhood. In an ordinary autoencoder the same line passes through regions no training example ever occupied, and the decoder has no obligation to do anything sensible there. The interpolation is a test of the space, not a feature of the decoder.

items.term: What 'axis 3 looks best' tells you
items.text: The book's own comment on that line is honest and worth reading twice: the useful axis was found by looking, not derived. Nothing in the training makes dimension 3 mean 'pants-ness'. The latent loss encourages the dimensions to be independent, but it never labels them, so which axis carries which trait is an accident of initialisation. This is the practical limit of the disentanglement you get for free — and it is exactly the gap StyleGAN later attacks deliberately.

items.term: Blurriness is a property of the objective, not of effort
items.text: The book's reconstruction loss is pixel-wise MSE, which is minimised by predicting the average of every plausible answer. Where the model is uncertain about an edge, the average of several sharp edges in slightly different places is one soft edge. Training longer does not fix this, because the soft edge genuinely has the lower loss. Only changing what scores the output — an adversarial critic, for instance — changes the outcome.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Variational autoencoders generate new images by feeding random Gaussian codings into the trained decoder.
Generated VAE images tend to look realistic in structure but can often suffer from blurriness.
Pixel-level interpolation simply overlays two images, whereas latent-space interpolation transforms semantic features.
Linear changes along dimensions of the latent space produce smooth category transitions, such as turning pants into sweaters.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Semantic interpolation worked along one hand-picked axis. What techniques exist for finding which latent directions carry which meaning, rather than eyeballing them one at a time?
Look up: Carl Doersch, 'Tutorial on Variational Autoencoders' (2016) — the tutorial the book recommends in footnote 8 for the mathematical detail behind this lesson.

items.term: Generative Adversarial Networks

blocks.content:
A GAN trains two networks against each other: a generator that turns noise into fake images, and a discriminator that tries to spot the fakes — and each training step trains one of them, then the other.

**The question this lesson answers:** there is no answer column telling you how realistic a generated image is. So where does the training signal come from? From a second network whose only job is to catch you.

### The big picture

```
noise -> generator -> fake image --+
                                   +-> discriminator
real training image ---------------+     real? fake?
```

### 1 · The two players

Standard supervised models require explicit target labels for training data. Generative modeling aims to generate synthetic samples without relying on explicit target outputs. A **Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)** framing resolves this by structuring training as a zero-sum game between two competing neural networks: a **generator** and a **discriminator**. **Zero-sum** means one side's gain is exactly the other side's loss.

As Figure 17-14 shows, the **generator** receives a vector of Gaussian noise (latent codings) as input and outputs a synthetic data sample, such as an image. The **discriminator** is a binary classifier that takes an image as input—either real from the dataset or fake from the generator—and outputs a probability score classifying it as real (1) or fake (0). Its job is to classify whether an input image is a real sample or a generated fake.

The generator is doing the same job as a VAE decoder — noise in, image out. What has changed is entirely how it is trained.

### 2 · Phase 1: train the discriminator

Training operates in two alternating phases per step.

**Phase 1 (Train Discriminator):** The generator creates a batch of fake images. These are combined with real training images. Labels are assigned (0 for fake, 1 for real). The discriminator updates its weights using **binary cross-entropy loss** while generator weights remain unfrozen but unused.

**Binary cross-entropy** is the standard loss for a yes/no classifier: it punishes confident wrong answers hardest. This phase is completely ordinary supervised learning — you have a labelled batch and a binary classifier, nothing exotic.

### 3 · Phase 2: train the generator, and lie about the labels

**Phase 2 (Train Generator):** A batch of random Gaussian noise is fed into the full combined model (generator followed by discriminator). All target labels are set to 1. The discriminator's weights are frozen so backpropagation only updates generator weights, optimizing the generator to produce outputs that trick the discriminator.

Every image in this batch is fake, and every label says "real". That deliberate lie is the point: the loss now measures how far the discriminator is from being fooled, and the gradient that reduces it flows back through the frozen discriminator into the generator.

Freezing matters. Freezing discriminator weights so phase two backpropagation only updates generator parameters is what keeps the discriminator from simply learning to call everything real. The card below explains the Keras detail that makes this work: `discriminator.trainable = False` is read only when a model is compiled, so the discriminator still trains under its own `train_on_batch()` and stays frozen under the combined model's.

| | Phase 1 | Phase 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Batch holds | fakes and real images | fakes only |
| Labels | 0 for fake, 1 for real | all 1 |
| Weights updated | discriminator | generator |

### 4 · The shapes, concretely

For example, training a GAN on Fashion MNIST with a batch size of 32 uses a noise input of shape [32, 30]. In phase one, the discriminator evaluates 32 fake images labeled 0 and 32 real images labeled 1. In phase two, the generator processes 32 new noise vectors, aiming to make the discriminator evaluate all 32 outputs as 1.

So a coding here is 30 numbers, and each training step touches 64 images in phase one and 32 fresh noise vectors in phase two.

### 5 · The strangest part

The core insight of a GAN is that the generator never sees real images directly; it improves entirely via gradients backpropagated through the discriminator. It receives gradients backpropagated through the discriminator during phase two, and nothing else. Everything it learns about real clothing arrives secondhand, through another network's opinion — and the better the discriminator gets, the more information those secondhand gradients carry.

**One-liner for your notes:** phase one teaches the critic with honest labels, phase two teaches the forger with dishonest ones, and the forger never once looks at a real image.

blocks.title: Worked out: the batch shapes and freezing the discriminator
blocks.content: In the book's Fashion MNIST GAN, `codings_size = 30` and `batch_size = 32`, so each noise batch has shape [32, 30]. In phase one, the generator turns that noise into 32 fake images, which are concatenated with 32 real images, and the targets `y1` are 32 zeros followed by 32 ones. In phase two, a fresh [32, 30] noise batch is fed to `gan` with 32 targets of 1. The discriminator and the `gan` model are both compiled with binary cross-entropy and RMSProp. The generator is never compiled on its own, because it is only trained through `gan`. Before compiling `gan`, the code sets `discriminator.trainable = False`. Keras reads this attribute only when a model is compiled, so the discriminator still trains when its own `train_on_batch()` is called, but it stays frozen when `gan.train_on_batch()` is called.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
def train_gan(gan, dataset, batch_size, codings_size, n_epochs):
    generator, discriminator = gan.layers
    for epoch in range(n_epochs):
        for X_batch in dataset:
            # phase 1 - training the discriminator
            noise = tf.random.normal(shape=[batch_size, codings_size])
            generated_images = generator(noise)
            X_fake_and_real = tf.concat([generated_images, X_batch], axis=0)
            y1 = tf.constant([[0.]] * batch_size + [[1.]] * batch_size)
            discriminator.train_on_batch(X_fake_and_real, y1)
            # phase 2 - training the generator
            noise = tf.random.normal(shape=[batch_size, codings_size])
            y2 = tf.constant([[1.]] * batch_size)
            gan.train_on_batch(noise, y2)
```

items.term: The loss function is a moving target, and that changes everything you know about training
items.text: In every earlier chapter, a falling loss meant the model was getting better, because the thing being measured stood still. Here the discriminator's loss falls when the generator gets worse, and the generator's loss falls when the discriminator gets worse. Neither curve tells you whether the pair is improving. This single fact is why GANs need different monitoring, different stopping criteria and, as the next lesson shows, a great deal more patience.

items.term: Why lying about the labels in phase two is the correct implementation
items.text: Labelling fake images as real looks like a bug. It is the cleanest way to express 'make the discriminator wrong' using ordinary supervised machinery: the loss becomes large exactly when the discriminator is not fooled, and the gradient that shrinks it is the gradient that improves the forgery. The alternative — flipping the sign on the discriminator's loss — is mathematically related but behaves worse early in training, when the discriminator is winning easily and that gradient nearly vanishes.

items.term: What the freezing actually protects
items.text: Without freezing, phase two would find the much easier solution: leave the generator alone and teach the discriminator to call everything real. The loss would drop beautifully and nothing would be learned. Freezing removes that escape route, which is a general lesson about adversarial setups — if both players can move during one optimisation step, the optimiser will always take the cheaper move, and the cheaper move is usually the one that destroys the game.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A GAN consists of a generator that outputs synthetic data and a discriminator that classifies samples as real or fake.
Discriminator training uses binary cross-entropy loss on a combined batch of labeled fake and real images.
Generator training passes noise through the full model with targets set to 1 while freezing discriminator weights.
The generator never receives real training images directly and relies strictly on backpropagated gradients from the discriminator.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: If neither loss curve tells you whether a GAN is improving, what do people actually watch to decide when to stop training and which checkpoint to keep?
Look up: Ian Goodfellow et al., 'Generative Adversarial Nets', NeurIPS 2014: 2672-2680 — this chapter's footnote 9, the paper that introduced the two-phase game.

items.term: Understanding Difficulties in GAN Training

blocks.content:
GANs are hard to train because two networks chasing each other need not settle anywhere — the usual failure is mode collapse, where the generator gives up on variety and produces one kind of image.

**The question this lesson answers:** the theory says a GAN has a perfect resting point. Why does training so often never get there, and what do people actually do about it?

### The big picture

```
ideal:  generator perfect  ->  discriminator guesses 50/50
real:   shoes -> shoes -> shoes -> shirts -> shirts -> ...
        (the generator cycles through classes, mastering none)
```

### 1 · The resting point that theory promises

Generative Adversarial Networks train two models simultaneously in a zero-sum game, which creates unique optimization challenges. In theory, training converges to a **Nash equilibrium**, a state where neither the generator nor the discriminator can improve its strategy given the other model's current state.

A **Nash equilibrium** is named after the mathematician John Nash: it is a situation where no player would be better off changing their own strategy, assuming the others do not change theirs. Everybody driving on the left is a Nash equilibrium; so is everybody driving on the right.

At this ideal equilibrium, the generator produces perfectly realistic images, and the discriminator can only guess randomly with a fifty percent accuracy rate. However, standard optimization methods do not guarantee that a Generative Adversarial Network will ever reach this target state. The equilibrium exists; nothing makes training walk to it.

### 2 · Mode collapse, step by step

In practice, training often fails due to a problem known as **mode collapse**. A **mode** is one bump in the data distribution — here, one class of clothing.

1. Consider a scenario where a generator happens to produce fake images of shoes slightly better than images of shirts.
2. Because shoe images fool the discriminator more effectively, the generator receives stronger positive rewards for making shoes.
3. The generator responds by producing shoes exclusively, completely forgetting how to generate shirts or other classes.
4. Concurrently, the discriminator adapts to only evaluate shoes.
5. Once the discriminator learns to detect fake shoes, the generator shifts entirely to a different class like shirts, forgetting shoes entirely.

The training process then cycles continuously between single classes without learning a full, diverse distribution. The generator output diversity degrades as it focuses on generating a limited subset of classes — and because neither side ever holds still, neither ever gets good.

### 3 · Oscillation and hyperparameter sensitivity

Furthermore, the competing objectives can cause model parameters to oscillate unpredictably, making training unstable and highly sensitive to hyperparameters. The dual competing networks create complex dynamic interactions that easily oscillate or diverge, so training may begin properly and then suddenly diverge for no apparent reason.

The card below records a real instance of this from the book's own code: the GAN was compiled with RMSProp rather than Nadam, because training with Nadam ran into a severe mode collapse. Same architecture, same data — a different optimizer was the difference between working and not.

This is unlike anything in a normal supervised pipeline. There the loss is a fixed target and going down is going well. Here the target moves every step, so a falling loss can mean your opponent got worse rather than you got better.

### 4 · Two standard counter-measures

To address these instability issues and maintain output diversity, researchers utilize strategies such as **experience replay**, which trains the discriminator on a historical buffer of generated images, and **mini-batch discrimination**, which explicitly penalizes batches that lack diversity.

| Technique | What it does | Which problem |
|---|---|---|
| experience replay | keeps old fakes in a buffer | discriminator overfits |
| mini-batch discrimination | scores variety within a batch | mode collapse |

Experience replay stores historical generated images in a buffer to prevent overfitting to current generator outputs, so the discriminator sees a wider mix of fakes than just whatever the generator made this second. Mini-batch discrimination measures sample diversity within a batch, penalizing low diversity to prevent mode collapse: it hands the discriminator a similarity statistic, which lets it reject a whole batch of near-identical fakes at once and pushes the generator back toward variety.

**One-liner for your notes:** two moving targets need not converge — mode collapse is the generator cycling through one class at a time, and replay buffers plus batch-diversity statistics are the standard patches.

blocks.title: How the fixes work, and why the optimizer mattered
blocks.content: Because many factors affect these unstable dynamics, GANs are very sensitive to hyperparameters, and tuning them can take a lot of effort. For example, the book's GAN was compiled with RMSProp rather than Nadam, because training with Nadam ran into a severe mode collapse. Experience replay stores the images produced by the generator at each iteration in a replay buffer, gradually dropping older ones, and trains the discriminator on real images plus fake images drawn from this buffer. This reduces the chance that the discriminator overfits the latest generator's outputs. Mini-batch discrimination measures how similar the images are across a batch and gives this statistic to the discriminator, which can then easily reject a whole batch of fake images that lack diversity. This pushes the generator toward a greater variety of images.

items.term: Why a guaranteed equilibrium guarantees nothing
items.text: The GAN paper proves a Nash equilibrium exists where the generator is perfect and the discriminator guesses. Existence and reachability are different claims, and only the first was proved. Gradient descent is a local, greedy procedure following two gradients that point at each other; nothing in it is a search for an equilibrium. This gap between 'the solution exists' and 'this algorithm finds it' shows up all over optimisation, and mistaking one for the other is a reliable way to waste a week.

items.term: Mode collapse is a rational response, not a malfunction
items.text: The generator is doing exactly what it was asked: maximise the chance of fooling the discriminator right now. Nothing in the objective rewards covering the whole data distribution — diversity is something we want, never something we told it to want. That is why the fixes are all about putting diversity into the signal: mini-batch discrimination makes low variety visible to the critic, and experience replay stops the critic forgetting what it already caught.

items.term: The optimizer story is the useful warning
items.text: The book's GAN uses RMSProp rather than Nadam because Nadam caused a severe mode collapse. Same architecture, same data, same code — one hyperparameter apart from working. In ordinary supervised training a different optimizer changes how fast you converge; here it changes whether you converge at all. Treat a GAN result as conditional on its full hyperparameter set, and be suspicious of any comparison that varies the architecture without holding the rest fixed.

blocks.title: Key points
items: GANs aim for a Nash equilibrium where generated images are perfectly realistic and the discriminator guesses randomly.
Mode collapse occurs when the generator learns to produce only a limited variety of outputs, repeatedly forgetting other classes.
Training dynamics in GANs are unstable and frequently suffer from parameter oscillation and sudden divergence.
Experience replay stores past generated images in a buffer to prevent the discriminator from overfitting to recent outputs.
Mini-batch discrimination measures diversity across a batch to discourage the generator from collapsing into a single mode.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Many papers propose new GAN loss functions to fix these instabilities. How much of the reported improvement survives when everything is tuned equally, and what does that suggest about reading GAN results?

Look up: Mario Lucic et al., 'Are GANs Created Equal? A Large-Scale Study', NeurIPS 2018: 698-707 — this chapter's footnote 11, which the book cites as questioning the efficiency of those new cost functions.

items.term: Deep Convolutional GANs (DCGANs)

blocks.content:
DCGAN is a short list of architecture rules — no pooling, batch norm almost everywhere, ReLU and tanh in the generator, leaky ReLU in the discriminator — that made deep convolutional GANs trainable.

**The question this lesson answers:** convolutions are obviously the right layer for images, so why did deep convolutional GANs not work until 2015? Because the details matter, and these are the details that were found to work.

### The big picture

```
noise 100 -> dense -> 7x7x128
   -> tconv stride 2 -> 14x14x64
   -> tconv stride 2 -> 28x28x1   (tanh)
```

### 1 · The problem

Standard generative adversarial networks often suffer from extreme instability during training, especially when scaling up to generate realistic spatial images. Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Networks, or **DCGANs**, solve this issue by establishing specific architectural guidelines that stabilize deep convolutional networks for image generation.

These guidelines were not derived from theory. They came out of experimenting with many different architectures and hyperparameters until something trained reliably, which is worth knowing: they are empirical rules of thumb, and the book is explicit that they work in many cases but not always.

### 2 · The guidelines, as a table

To build a stable DCGAN, researchers replace pooling layers with spatial strides. The discriminator uses **strided convolutions** to downsample images, while the generator uses **transposed convolutions** to upsample low-dimensional latent vectors into full-resolution images. Batch normalization is applied throughout both networks to stabilize gradient flow, excluding the generator's output layer and the discriminator's input layer. Additionally, fully connected hidden layers are removed. For activation functions, the generator utilizes **ReLU** activations for hidden layers and **tanh** for its final output, whereas the discriminator relies on **leaky ReLU** activations across its layers.

| Choice | Generator | Discriminator |
|---|---|---|
| resizing | transposed convolutions | strided convolutions |
| batch norm | yes, except output layer | yes, except input layer |
| hidden activation | ReLU | leaky ReLU |
| final activation | tanh | — |

Four terms, glossed once:

- **Strided convolution** — a convolution whose window jumps 2 pixels at a time, so the output is half the size. It replaces pooling because the network gets to *learn* how to downsample instead of being told.
- **Batch normalization** — rescales each layer's outputs to a steady mean and spread, which keeps gradients from exploding or vanishing as they travel.
- **ReLU** — keep positives, zero out negatives. **Leaky ReLU** lets a small slice of the negatives through instead of zeroing them, so a neuron that goes negative still receives a gradient rather than going permanently silent.
- **tanh** — an S-shaped squash like sigmoid, but into the range −1 to 1 instead of 0 to 1.

### 3 · The generator, shape by shape

Consider an example designed for generating 28 × 28 grayscale images. The generator starts with a random noise vector of size 100, projects it to a 7 × 7 × 128 tensor using a dense layer, and reshapes it. A transposed convolutional layer with a stride of 2 upsamples this spatial dimension to 14 × 14 × 64. A second transposed convolutional layer with a stride of 2 further expands it to a 28 × 28 × 1 image output.

| Step | Shape | Depth goes |
|---|---|---|
| dense then reshape | 7 by 7 by 128 | — |
| transposed conv, stride 2 | 14 by 14 by 64 | 128 to 64 |
| transposed conv, stride 2 | 28 by 28 by 1 | 64 to 1 |

The dense layer projects 100 numbers to 6,272 of them, which is 7 × 7 × 128, before the reshape. Each transposed convolution doubles the picture and halves the feature depth, so the tensor becomes wider on screen and thinner in features as it approaches being an image.

### 4 · Why the training images get rescaled

That last layer uses tanh, which produces values between −1 and 1. Because the generator output layer uses tanh, the real training images must be rescaled to that same interval — otherwise the discriminator could tell real from fake by checking the value range alone, which teaches it nothing useful. The card below shows the one-line reshape-and-rescale that does it.

That card also records a deviation worth noticing: in the book's discriminator, the BatchNormalization layers were replaced with Dropout layers, because training was otherwise unstable. The guidelines are guidelines.

### 5 · What you get

As Figure 17-16 demonstrates, after 50 epochs of training the generator produces images that are still not perfect, although many of them are pretty convincing.

Furthermore, Figure 17-17 shows that DCGANs construct a structured latent space, allowing mathematical operations like adding or subtracting feature vectors directly in latent space to perform semantic arithmetic on faces. Averaged codings for "men with glasses", minus "men without glasses", plus "women without glasses", decode into a woman with glasses. Done at the pixel level that would just give three overlapping faces; done in latent space it gives a face. This is semantic manipulation of visual features in latent space, the same idea as the VAE's semantic interpolation, now doing arithmetic rather than a walk.

The essential insight to remember is that DCGANs achieve training stability by swapping pooling for strided or transposed convolutions and enforcing strict activation and normalization choices across both networks.

**One-liner for your notes:** DCGAN is a recipe, not a theory — strides instead of pooling, batch norm everywhere but the two boundary layers, ReLU plus tanh generating and leaky ReLU judging.

blocks.content: The generator takes codings of size 100, and a Dense layer projects them to 6,272 dimensions (7 × 7 × 128), which are reshaped into a 7 × 7 × 128 tensor. The first transposed convolution, with a stride of 2, upsamples 7 × 7 to 14 × 14 and reduces the depth from 128 to 64. The second one upsamples 14 × 14 to 28 × 28 and reduces the depth from 64 to 1. This last layer uses tanh, so its outputs range from −1 to 1, and the training set must be rescaled to that same range: `X_train.reshape(-1, 28, 28, 1) * 2. - 1.` adds the channel axis and maps pixel values from 0–1 to −1–1. In the book's discriminator, the BatchNormalization layers were replaced with Dropout layers, because training was otherwise unstable.

blocks.content:
```python
codings_size = 100

generator = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(7 * 7 * 128),
    tf.keras.layers.Reshape([7, 7, 128]),
    tf.keras.layers.BatchNormalization(),
    tf.keras.layers.Conv2DTranspose(64, kernel_size=5, strides=2,
                                    padding="same", activation="relu"),
    tf.keras.layers.BatchNormalization(),

                                    padding="same", activation="tanh"),
])
```

items.term: Why the two exception layers are exceptions
items.text: Batch normalization everywhere except the generator's output and the discriminator's input is the oddest-looking rule in the list, and it has a reason. Normalising the generator's output would fight the tanh that has to put pixels in the minus-one-to-one range. Normalising the discriminator's input would erase real differences in brightness and contrast between real and fake batches, which is information the critic legitimately needs. Both exceptions sit exactly where the network touches the outside world.

items.term: Why leaky ReLU on the judging side
items.text: A plain ReLU zeroes every negative, and a unit stuck in the negative region receives no gradient and never recovers. In a normal classifier that is survivable. In a discriminator it is not, because the discriminator is the generator's only source of learning signal — every dead unit is a permanent hole in the feedback the generator ever receives. Leaky ReLU keeps a trickle of gradient flowing so units can come back.

items.term: Strided convolutions instead of pooling, as a general principle
items.text: Pooling is a fixed rule for throwing information away: keep the maximum of each block, always. A strided convolution learns which combination to keep. Where a network's whole job is the fine detail of an image, letting it choose what to discard beats a hard-coded rule. The same substitution appears well outside GANs — modern classifiers often drop pooling for the same reason.

blocks.title: Key points
items: DCGANs replace pooling layers with strided convolutions in the discriminator and transposed convolutions in the generator.
Batch normalization stabilizes training across network layers, except at the generator output and discriminator input.
The generator uses ReLU activations for hidden layers and tanh for the final image output layer.
The discriminator relies on leaky ReLU activation functions for its hidden convolutional layers.
DCGANs structure latent space representations so semantic concepts can be manipulated using vector arithmetic.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The book's tip mentions conditional GANs: feed the class as an extra input to both networks and you can choose what gets generated. What does that change about the training loop, and what does it cost you?
Look up: Mehdi Mirza and Simon Osindero, 'Conditional Generative Adversarial Nets', arXiv:1411.1784 (2014) — this chapter's footnote 14.

items.term: Progressive Growing of GANs

blocks.content:
Progressive growing trains a GAN on tiny images first, then adds a pair of layers to both networks to double the resolution, over and over — and fades each new pair in gradually so nothing already learned gets wrecked.

**The question this lesson answers:** GANs at high resolution fail because the networks must learn face shape and skin texture at the same time. How do you let them learn the coarse structure first and the fine detail later?

### The big picture

```
4x4 -> 8x8 -> 16x16 -> ... -> 1024x1024
 |      |       |
 train, then add layers and double again
```

### 1 · One problem, one idea

Training Generative Adversarial Networks to produce high-resolution images is notoriously unstable. Direct generation of large images forces networks to learn coarse structures and fine details simultaneously, leading to training failure or poor image quality.

To solve this issue, progressive growing starts training with low-resolution images, such as 4 × 4 pixels. Once training stabilizes at a lower resolution, new convolutional layers are added to both the generator and the discriminator to double the image resolution step-by-step (8 × 8, 16 × 16, up to 1024 × 1024). Previously trained layers remain active and trainable throughout the process.

This resembles the greedy layer-wise training of stacked autoencoders from earlier in the chapter: build a small thing, get it working, then extend it — rather than launching the full-size job and hoping.

### 2 · Fading a new layer in

As Figure 17-18 shows, when expanding the generator from 4 × 4 to 8 × 8, an upsampling layer scales up the feature maps. To prevent abrupt changes from shocking the network, new layers fade in gradually.

The final image is a weighted sum using parameter $\alpha$ (alpha): the upsampled legacy output is weighted by 1 − α, while the new branch output receives weight $\alpha$. Training transitions $\alpha$ smoothly from 0 to 1 over time.

| α is | Output is | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | all legacy branch | new layers contribute nothing |
| 0.5 | half and half | the crossfade, mid-way |
| 1 | all new branch | the new layers have taken over |

If you have ever cut a pipeline over from an old table to a new one by routing a rising share of traffic to the new one instead of flipping a switch, that is exactly this. Dropping the new layers in at full strength would hand the already-trained layers inputs they have never seen.

### 3 · Three more stability tricks

Additional stability mechanisms include mini-batch standard deviation layers to prevent mode collapse, equalized learning rate to scale weights dynamically at runtime, and pixelwise normalization after generator convolutional layers.

| Mechanism | Where | What it fixes |
|---|---|---|
| mini-batch std dev | end of discriminator | mode collapse |
| equalized learning rate | every layer, at runtime | uneven learning speeds |
| pixelwise normalization | after each generator conv | activation explosions |

The **mini-batch standard deviation layer** feeds batch diversity statistics to the discriminator to avert mode collapse. It computes the spread of values across the whole batch and hands that one number to the discriminator as an extra feature map, so a batch of near-identical fakes is easy to reject — the discriminator can see the low variety directly rather than having to infer it image by image.

**Pixelwise normalization** is applied after every convolutional layer within the architecture of the generator network. It divides each activation by the root-mean-square of the activations at the same spot across all channels, which stops values exploding when the two networks push hard against each other.

### 4 · Equalized learning rate, and why it is not what its name suggests

The name sounds like a learning-rate schedule; it is not. It rescales parameter weights at runtime during every execution step.

Equalized learning rate does not use He initialization — the usual scheme that sizes the starting weights by how many inputs a layer has. Instead it initializes all weights from a plain bell curve with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, then divides them by that same He factor *every time the layer runs*, rather than once at the start.

The card below has the reasoning in full, and it is worth reading because it is genuinely non-obvious. Adaptive optimizers such as RMSProp and Adam divide each update by the parameter's own recent spread. A parameter whose values range widely therefore takes longer to move; one with a narrow range may lurch. Putting the rescaling inside the model keeps that range identical for every parameter, so they all learn at the same speed.

The key insight to remember is that **gradually increasing image resolution during training stabilizes GAN optimization and produces superior high-definition images**.

**One-liner for your notes:** grow the picture in doublings, crossfade each new layer in with α from 0 to 1, and stabilise the rest with batch-diversity statistics, runtime weight rescaling and per-pixel normalisation.

blocks.title: Equalized learning rate, step by step
blocks.content: Equalized learning rate does not use He initialization. Instead, it initializes all weights from a Gaussian distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. The weights are then scaled down at runtime, every time the layer is executed, by the same factor as in He initialization, which is based on $\sqrt{2/n_\text{inputs}}$, where $n_\text{inputs}$ is the number of inputs to the layer. Why it helps: adaptive optimizers such as RMSProp and Adam normalize each gradient update by its estimated standard deviation, so parameters with a large dynamic range take longer to train, while parameters with a small range may be updated too quickly. Rescaling inside the model keeps the dynamic range the same for all parameters, so they learn at the same speed. The paper showed that this significantly improved the GAN's performance with these optimizers.
