blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

def pixelwise_normalization(inputs):
    # Normalize across channels at each pixel location
    mean_sq = tf.reduce_mean(tf.square(inputs), axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    return inputs / tf.sqrt(mean_sq + 1e-8)

def minibatch_std_dev(inputs):
    # Calculate batch diversity statistic
    batch_size, height, width, _ = tf.shape(inputs)
    s = tf.math.reduce_std(inputs, axis=[0, -1])
    v = tf.reduce_mean(s)
    stat_map = tf.fill([batch_size, height, width, 1], v)
    return tf.concat([inputs, stat_map], axis=-1)
```

items.term: Why curriculum beats brute force here
items.text: Asking a GAN for 1024 by 1024 from scratch means the generator must get face geometry and pore texture right at the same time, while a discriminator that is also learning both judges it. Starting at 4 by 4 removes the fine detail from the problem entirely until the coarse structure is settled, then adds it back one doubling at a time. Each stage is a small, already-solved-looking problem. This is the same instinct as the greedy layer-wise autoencoder training earlier in the chapter, and the same instinct behind any staged migration.

items.term: The crossfade is about not invalidating what already works
items.text: Dropping a randomly initialised layer into a trained network at full strength hands every downstream layer inputs it has never seen, and the damage flows back through weights that were fine a moment ago. Ramping alpha from 0 to 1 means the new branch's contribution starts at nothing and grows only as fast as the older layers can adapt. Any time you extend a trained system, this is the shape of the safe answer: run the new path in parallel, shift traffic gradually, never flip.

items.term: Equalized learning rate is a fix for the optimizer, not for the network
items.text: This one is genuinely unusual. He initialization scales the weights once, at the start, and then adaptive optimizers like Adam and RMSProp divide each update by the parameter's own recent spread — which quietly means parameters with different scales learn at different speeds, and that difference persists for the whole run. Moving the scaling inside the forward pass makes every parameter's range identical, so the optimizer's normalisation treats them all alike. The lesson generalises: when an optimizer's behaviour depends on parameter scale, controlling that scale is a real design lever.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Progressive growing begins training at low resolutions and incrementally adds layers to reach high resolutions.
New layers fade in smoothly using a weighted sum parameter $\alpha$ that scales from 0 to 1.
Mini-batch standard deviation layers feed batch diversity statistics directly into the discriminator to prevent mode collapse.
Equalized learning rate rescales weights at runtime to balance dynamic range across parameters.
Pixelwise normalization prevents activation explosions within the generator.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Progressive growing was state of the art and is now largely superseded. What replaced it for high-resolution GAN training, and which of its four tricks survived into later architectures?
Look up: Tero Karras et al., 'Progressive Growing of GANs for Improved Quality, Stability, and Variation', ICLR 2018 — this chapter's footnote 15, the paper this lesson describes.

items.term: StyleGAN Generator Architecture

blocks.content:
StyleGAN rebuilds only the generator: a mapping network turns the latent vector into a style vector, and a synthesis network starts from a fixed learned tensor and has that style injected at every resolution, with separate noise for the random details.

**The question this lesson answers:** in an ordinary GAN one latent vector has to carry the face shape, the skin tone and the exact position of every stray hair. How do you split those apart so you can control each independently?

### The big picture

```
z -> mapping net (8-layer MLP) -> w -> "A" -> styles
const 4x4x512 -> [+noise -> AdaIN -> conv] x many -> image
```

### 1 · What is being solved

Traditional GAN generators struggle to control visual features at specific scales without creating artifacts. They force a single latent vector to encode high-level semantics, low-level textures, and microscopic random noise all at once. This coupling limits image quality and feature disentanglement.

**Disentanglement** means being able to change one property without dragging others along with it. **High-level semantics** are things like age or face shape; **low-level textures** are things like skin tone; **microscopic random noise** is the placement of individual freckles and hairs. One vector carrying all three is why changing one thing changed everything.

### 2 · Two networks inside the generator

**StyleGAN** solves this problem by completely redesigning the generator network while keeping the discriminator unchanged. The loss function is unchanged too. The generator splits into two distinct components: a **mapping network** and a **synthesis network**, as Figure 17-19 shows.

| Network | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| mapping | latent vector z | style vector w |
| synthesis | a learned constant | the image |

The mapping network consists of an eight-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP) that transforms an initial latent vector $\mathbf{z}$ into an intermediate style vector $\mathbf{w}$. An **MLP** is a plain stack of fully-connected layers. Affine transformations (labeled "A" in Figure 17-19) convert $\mathbf{w}$ into specific style vectors for different scales of the synthesis network — an **affine transformation** here is just a dense layer with no activation function, so the "A" boxes are scale-and-shift adapters, one per resolution level.

### 3 · The synthesis network starts from a constant

The synthesis network does not take $\mathbf{z}$ as its input. Instead, it starts from a constant learned input array of shape 4 × 4 × 512. It processes this tensor through upsampling and convolutional layers.

"Constant" and "learned" together sound contradictory. They are not: backpropagation tweaks this tensor during training like any other weight, and then it is frozen for every image the finished model ever makes. Every generated face begins from the identical starting block; all the variety arrives later, through the styles and the noise.

### 4 · The two things injected at every level

At each scale, two key operations occur.

First, explicit Gaussian noise (scaled via learned parameters, labeled "B") is added directly to every layer — to the input and to the outputs of the convolutional layers, before the activation function — to control fine stochastic details like hair placement or freckles. Each noise input is a single feature map of Gaussian noise, broadcast to all feature maps of that level and scaled by learned per-feature factors.

Second, an **adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN)** layer standardizes each feature map and applies scale and shift factors derived from the style vector $\mathbf{w}$. Standardising means subtracting the feature map's mean and dividing by its standard deviation, so every feature map arrives at a common baseline; the style vector then supplies one scale and one bias term per feature map, which is what makes "style" a concrete, per-map pair of numbers rather than a vague idea.

For example, during a generation pass, a 4 × 4 resolution block receives a high-level style from $\mathbf{w}$ that controls general face shape or age. Later, an 8 × 8 or higher block receives fine-scale styles controlling color tones, alongside independent noise inputs that alter exact hair placement without altering structural features.

Why give noise its own door? Because otherwise the randomness has to come out of the codings, which means spending the latent vector's limited capacity storing static — and that static then has to survive the whole journey through the network. Direct noise inputs handle fine stochastic details like hair or freckles without wasting latent space.

### 5 · Mixing regularization

The card below covers **mixing regularization**, or style mixing: two codings are pushed through the mapping network, and the synthesis network uses the first style vector for the early levels and the second for the rest, with the cutoff picked at random. This prevents adjacent scale levels from assuming their styles are strictly correlated, which encourages locality — each style vector ends up affecting only a limited number of traits.

The key insight is that separating noise input and controlling layer-wise features via intermediate style vectors disentangles visual attributes across scale levels.

**One-liner for your notes:** mapping network makes the style, synthesis network starts from a constant and gets that style injected per resolution through AdaIN, and stray-hair randomness comes in through its own noise inputs.

blocks.title: Mixing regularization (style mixing)
blocks.content: StyleGAN also uses a technique called mixing regularization, or style mixing. For a percentage of the generated images, two different codings, $c_1$ and $c_2$, are sent through the mapping network, giving two style vectors $w_1$ and $w_2$. The synthesis network then uses the styles $w_1$ for the first levels and the styles $w_2$ for the remaining levels, and the cutoff level is picked randomly. This prevents the network from assuming that styles at adjacent levels are correlated, which encourages locality: each style vector only affects a limited number of traits in the generated image. The added noise also differs per level: each noise input is a single feature map of Gaussian noise, broadcast to all feature maps of that level and scaled by learned per-feature factors (the "B" boxes) before it is added.

items.term: Why an extra network before the generator improves anything
items.text: It seems wasteful: z goes through eight dense layers before generating begins. The point is that z is forced to be a plain Gaussian — that is what you sample from — and a plain Gaussian has a fixed, round shape, while the real distribution of faces does not. Forcing the generator to read a round distribution directly means entangling traits that should be separate. The mapping network's output w is under no such constraint, so it is free to take whatever shape lets traits separate cleanly.

items.term: Giving randomness its own channel is the reusable idea
items.text: Every image has content that matters and content that is genuinely arbitrary — the exact scatter of freckles, the exact fall of individual hairs. Making one vector carry both means spending representational capacity on noise and dragging the noise through the whole network. Separating them costs almost nothing and buys two things at once: the latent vector gets its full capacity back for things that matter, and the noise can be resampled to get a different hair scatter on the same face. Any generative system with a 'which parts are arbitrary?' answer can use this.

items.term: Why style is injected repeatedly rather than once at the input
items.text: A single input vector has to travel the whole network to influence the last layer, so late layers get a weakened, entangled version of it. AdaIN injects at every resolution instead, which means the style controlling the 4 by 4 block and the style controlling the 64 by 64 block are separate vectors that can be set independently — which is precisely what makes coarse and fine control separable. Mixing regularization then hardens that separation by training the model on images whose early and late styles come from different codings.

blocks.title: Key points
items: StyleGAN modifies only the generator architecture, leaving the discriminator unchanged.
An eight-layer MLP mapping network maps latent vector z to intermediate vector w.
The synthesis network begins with a learned constant input rather than the latent code.
AdaIN layers inject style factors at each spatial resolution to scale and shift normalized feature maps.
Explicit broadcasted Gaussian noise provides stochastic variation independently from the high-level style codes.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: StyleGAN separates style from noise so traits can be controlled independently. How well does that separation actually hold up — can you change one attribute of a generated face without changing others, and how is that measured?
Look up: Tero Karras et al., 'A Style-Based Generator Architecture for Generative Adversarial Networks', arXiv:1812.04948 (2018) — this chapter's footnote 17.

items.term: Diffusion Models and the Forward Process

blocks.content:
A diffusion model is built on a process you define yourself: add a little Gaussian noise to an image over and over until nothing is left, then train a network to undo one step of it.

**The question this lesson answers:** GAN training is a fight between two networks that need not converge. What if instead you defined a destruction process with known mathematics, and only asked the network to reverse it one small step at a time?

### The big picture

```
x0 -> x1 -> x2 -> ... -> xT    forward: add noise (defined)
x0 <- x1 <- x2 <- ... <- xT    reverse: remove it (learned)
```

Only the bottom row is learned. The top row is arithmetic you wrote down.

### 1 · Why this is a different bargain

Generative models like GANs often suffer from unstable training dynamics. **Diffusion models** solve this problem by modeling image generation as an iterative process inspired by thermodynamics. Instead of generating an image in a single step, the system learns to reverse a gradual degradation process.

The thermodynamics image is a drop of milk spreading through tea. Spreading is easy and needs no model. Un-spreading is the hard part, and it is the only part a network is asked to learn — and it is asked to learn it one tiny step at a time, which is a far easier target than "produce a convincing image from nothing".

### 2 · The forward process

The mechanism relies on two complementary paths: a **forward process** and a **reverse process**. In the forward process, independent Gaussian noise is added to a clean starting image $\mathbf{x}_0$ across a series of discrete time steps $t = 1, 2, \dots, T$.

**Independent** per pixel is also called **isotropic**: each pixel gets its own draw, nothing is correlated across the picture. $\mathbf{x}_0$ is the clean image, $\mathbf{x}_T$ is the fully destroyed one, and $t$ is where you are between them.

At each step $t$, the image pixel values are scaled by $\sqrt{1 - \beta_t}$ while isotropic Gaussian noise with variance $\beta_t$ is added. As Figure 17-20 illustrates, the original signal gradually fades until the final image $\mathbf{x}_T$ becomes pure standard Gaussian noise.

That scaling factor is doing real work, and it is not cosmetic. The card below spells it out: $\sqrt{1 - \beta_t}$ is slightly smaller than 1, so repeating it drives the mean of the pixel values toward 0, and it shrinks the variance by exactly the amount the added noise puts back. Scaling by $\sqrt{1 - \beta_t}$ ensures pixel values maintain zero mean and unit variance as $t$ approaches $T$ — the distribution can only converge to standard normal, which is precisely the distribution you will sample from later.

### 3 · Two equations for the same process

Figure 17-20 below labels both directions: $q$ runs along the top arrows for the forward process, and $p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{t-1} \mid \mathbf{x}_t)$ runs along the bottom arrows — it represents the parameterized reverse process learned by a neural network to remove noise, and the θ subscript is just shorthand for "this one has weights in it".

Equation 17-5 below defines the step-by-step transition probability $q(\mathbf{x}_t \mid \mathbf{x}_{t-1})$: given the previous image, what does the next one look like?

Because compounding Gaussian distributions yields another Gaussian, Equation 17-6 below provides a closed-form shortcut: any noisy image $\mathbf{x}_t$ can be directly sampled from $\mathbf{x}_0$ using the cumulative signal factor $\bar{\alpha}_t = \prod_{i=1}^t (1 - \beta_i)$.

| | Equation 17-5 | Equation 17-6 |
|---|---|---|
| Goes from | one step before | the clean image |
| To get step t | run it t times | one calculation |
| Used for | defining the process | actually training |

This shortcut is why training is affordable at all: it allows direct sampling of a noisy state from the clean state in one step, so you never have to walk 2,000 steps to build one training example. Both equations have their symbols broken down underneath them.

### 4 · A concrete step

For a concrete scenario, consider an initial cat image $\mathbf{x}_0$ processed over $T = 4000$ steps using a cosine variance schedule. At step $t = 2000$, the cumulative factor $\bar{\alpha}_t$ drops to approximately 0.5. The noisy image is directly generated as $\mathbf{x}_{2000} = \sqrt{0.5}\mathbf{x}_0 + \sqrt{1 - 0.5}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$, blending equal parts scaled signal and standard Gaussian noise $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$.

So at the halfway point the cat is still exactly half there, by variance. That is what a schedule is for.

### 5 · The schedule

Equation 17-7 below is the cosine variance schedule that produces that behaviour, with its own walk-through underneath. Two knobs appear in it, and the card below names both: $s$ is a tiny value which prevents $\beta_t$ from being too small near $t = 0$, and the authors used $s = 0.008$; $\beta_t$ is also clipped to be no larger than 0.999, to avoid instabilities near $t = T$. Figure 17-21 below plots the two curves — the noise variance β rising, the remaining signal variance α̅ falling from 1 to 0.

The central insight of diffusion models is that by systematically defining a forward process that converts complex data into pure Gaussian noise, a neural network can be trained to reverse each step and construct high-quality images from random noise.

The card below also states the bargain plainly: DDPMs are much easier to train than GANs and give more diverse, higher-quality images, but they take a very long time to generate images compared to GANs or VAEs.

**One-liner for your notes:** you define the destruction (scale by √(1−β), add noise with variance β), a shortcut equation jumps straight to any step, and the network only ever learns to undo one step.

blocks.title: Worked out: why the noise ends at mean 0 and variance 1
blocks.content:
**The scaling factor.** $\sqrt{1-\beta_t}$ is a bit smaller than 1, so applying it at every step (like repeatedly multiplying a number by 0.99) pushes the mean of the pixel values toward 0. The standard deviation is also scaled by $\sqrt{1-\beta_t}$, so the variance is multiplied by $1-\beta_t$, the square of the factor. Noise with variance $\beta_t$ is then added, and variances add up, so the variance can only converge to $1-\beta_t+\beta_t = 1$.

**The schedule knobs.** $s$ is a tiny value that prevents $\beta_t$ from being too small near $t = 0$; the authors used $s = 0.008$. $\beta_t$ is also clipped to be no larger than 0.999, to avoid instabilities near $t = T$.

**The trade-off.** DDPMs are much easier to train than GANs and give more diverse, higher-quality images, but they take a very long time to generate images compared to GANs or VAEs.

blocks.title: Equation 17-5
blocks.caption: Probability distribution q of the forward diffusion process
blocks.explain:
**Why these equations look like this**

All three say the same thing at different zoom levels, so read them as one story rather than three
formulas.

Equation 17-5 is one step of the destruction. It has exactly two moving parts because the step has
exactly two jobs: shrink what is already there, and add a fixed amount of fresh randomness. Shrinking
alone would fade the image to grey; adding alone would let the values grow without limit. Doing both,
with the shrink factor tied to the amount added, is what makes the whole sequence land on a known
distribution — mean 0, variance 1 — no matter what image you started from. The card above works the
arithmetic through: the variance is multiplied by (1 − beta) and then beta is added back, so it can
only converge to 1.

Equation 17-6 is the same process after t steps, collapsed into one. It exists because adding many
Gaussians gives another Gaussian, so the whole chain has a closed form and you never have to walk it.

Equation 17-7 is not part of the process at all — it is the *schedule*, the choice of how fast to
destroy. The process would work with any beta values; this equation is one particular good choice.

**Are they standard?** Equations 17-5 and 17-6 are the canonical formulation of the forward diffusion
process and appear in this form in every DDPM paper — nothing is simplified. Equation 17-7 is
specifically the **cosine** schedule from the improved DDPM paper, and it is a deliberate replacement
for the original paper's linear schedule, which used T of 1,000 and faded the signal at a steady rate.
So the first two are the standard; the third is a tuned choice, and the book is explicit that it was
changed because the linear one behaved badly at the ends.

**Terms these introduce.** A **variance** is how spread out random values are; here it is the knob for
how much noise is added. **Isotropic** means the noise is drawn independently for each pixel, with the
same variance everywhere — that is what the identity matrix I in Equation 17-5 encodes. **N of a mean
and a variance** is read as "the Gaussian distribution with this centre and this spread", so the
equations are describing a distribution to draw from, not a single value. The **capital pi** in the
definition of alpha-bar means multiply the terms together, the way a capital sigma means add them.

**Every piece of Equations 17-5 and 17-6**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| q of x t given x t−1 | q of x t given x t minus 1 | the distribution of the next image |
| script N | N | "a Gaussian with this centre and spread" |
| x with subscript 0 | x nought | the clean starting image |
| x with subscript t | x t | the image after t noising steps |
| x with subscript T | x T | the fully destroyed image, pure static |
| beta with subscript t | beta t | variance of the noise added at step t |
| root of 1 minus beta t | root of one minus beta t | the shrink factor on the signal |
| bold I | I | identity matrix — same noise everywhere |
| alpha-bar with subscript t | alpha bar t | how much signal survives after t steps |
| root of alpha-bar t | root alpha bar t | the shrink factor from 0 straight to t |
| 1 minus alpha-bar t | one minus alpha bar t | the noise variance from 0 straight to t |

**The formulas in plain words**

Equation 17-5: next image = (this image, shrunk a little) + (a little fresh noise), where the shrink
and the noise are sized to keep the total spread at 1.

Equation 17-6: image at step t = (the clean image, shrunk by root of alpha-bar t) + (noise, scaled by
root of one minus alpha-bar t). Signal and noise, mixed by a ratio that the schedule fixes.

Equation 17-7: beta at step t is set so that alpha-bar follows a cosine curve from 1 down to 0.

**With real numbers**

Running the book's own schedule function with T of 4,000 and s of 0.008 gives the alpha-bar values
below, and these are what Figure 17-21 plots:

| t | alpha-bar | root alpha-bar | root of 1 − alpha-bar |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 0.000 |
| 1,000 | 0.847 | 0.920 | 0.391 |
| 2,000 | 0.494 | 0.703 | 0.711 |
| 3,000 | 0.144 | 0.380 | 0.925 |
| 4,000 | 0.000 | 0.000 | 1.000 |

The t of 2,000 row is the lesson's own example. Alpha-bar is 0.494, which rounds to the approximately
0.5 the text quotes, so Equation 17-6 mixes the cat and the static in almost exactly equal parts:
0.703 of the image plus 0.711 of pure noise. Halfway through the clock is also halfway through the
destruction — which is the entire purpose of choosing a schedule.

**How one noisy training image is actually built**

Take one clean Fashion MNIST image, rescaled so its pixels run from −1 to 1.

1. Draw a random step, say t of 2,000.
2. Look up alpha-bar at 2,000: **0.494**.
3. Multiply every pixel by the square root of that: **0.703**.
4. Draw a fresh standard-normal value for every pixel, and multiply it by the square root of
(1 − 0.494): **0.711**.
5. Add the two together. That is x at step 2,000, and the noise you drew in step 4 is the answer the
network will be trained to predict.

Note what did *not* happen: no loop over 2,000 steps. That is Equation 17-6 earning its place.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf

def variance_schedule(T, s=0.008, max_beta=0.999):
    t = np.arange(T + 1)
    f = np.cos((t / T + s) / (1 + s) * np.pi / 2) ** 2
    alpha = np.clip(f[1:] / f[:-1], 1 - max_beta, 1)
    alpha = np.append(1, alpha).astype(np.float32)
    beta = 1 - alpha
    alpha_cumprod = np.cumprod(alpha)
    return alpha, alpha_cumprod, beta

T = 4000
alpha, alpha_cumprod, beta = variance_schedule(T)
```

items.term: Why defining the hard direction yourself is the whole trick
items.text: A GAN has to learn what an image is from nothing, judged by a critic that is also learning. A diffusion model is handed a destruction process with known mathematics and asked only to undo one small step of it. That is a supervised problem with a free, exact answer column — you generated the noise, so you know it — which is why training is stable. The insight generalises beyond images: if you can define a reversible corruption of your data, you have manufactured a supervised task out of unlabelled data.

items.term: Why a thousand small steps rather than one big one
items.text: Undoing a tiny bit of noise is nearly a local, almost-linear problem, and a network can learn it well. Undoing all the noise at once is the original impossible problem. Splitting a hard mapping into many easy ones is what buys the sample quality — and it is also exactly what makes generation slow, since the steps must run in order. The quality and the slowness are the same design decision seen from two sides.

items.term: What the schedule is actually choosing
items.text: The variance schedule decides how the signal budget is spent across the time steps, and the shape matters. A linear schedule destroys the image too fast at the start, so many early steps carry almost no information worth learning from. The cosine schedule changes slowly at both ends and quickly in the middle, which spreads the useful, ambiguous region — where reversing is neither trivial nor hopeless — across more of the range. Moving from linear at T equals 1,000 to cosine at T equals 4,000 was one of the changes that let DDPMs overtake GANs.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Diffusion models formulate generation as the reverse of a stochastic noise addition process.
The forward process gradually adds Gaussian noise over discrete time steps until the original image becomes random noise.
Equation 17-6 provides a shortcut to sample noisy images at any arbitrary step without computing intermediate states.
A cosine variance schedule ensures smooth decay of signal variance across all time steps.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The book uses a cosine schedule with T of 4,000, replacing the original linear schedule with T of 1,000. How much of the quality gain came from the schedule shape rather than simply from more steps?
Look up: Alex Nichol and Prafulla Dhariwal, 'Improved Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models' (2021) — this chapter's footnote 21, the paper that introduced the cosine schedule in Equation 17-7.

items.term: Training and Sampling in Diffusion Models

blocks.content:
Train the network to predict the noise that was added — not the clean image — then generate by starting from pure static and subtracting a little predicted noise T times.

**The question this lesson answers:** the forward process is defined and the shortcut lets you make a noisy image at any step for free. What exactly does the network predict, and what does the generation loop look like?

### The big picture

```
TRAIN:  pick random t -> make x_t from x0 -> predict the noise
MAKE:   x_T = static -> subtract a bit, 4000 times -> x_0
```

### 1 · Predict the noise, not the picture

Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (**DDPM**) solve the problem of generating realistic images by learning to reverse a gradual noise-addition process. During training, a model is trained to predict the specific Gaussian noise added to an image at a given time step $t$, rather than predicting the clean image directly, because noise prediction yields superior training stability and image quality.

This is the single most surprising design choice in the chapter, and the honest justification is empirical: the authors tried predicting the original image directly and it simply does not work as well. One intuition for why: at high t the clean image is almost unknowable, but the noise is exactly what you generated a moment ago, so the target is always well defined and always the same size.

### 2 · Building a training batch

To construct training batches, a random time step $t$ between 1 and $T$ is sampled for each clean image $\mathbf{x}_0$. Cumulative variance scaling factors are gathered to directly calculate the corrupted image $\mathbf{x}_t$ in one step using Gaussian noise $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$.

| Piece of the batch | Is |
|---|---|
| input 1 | the noisy image x at step t |
| input 2 | the time step t itself |
| target | the exact noise ε that was used |

Every image in the batch gets its own random t, so one pass over the data teaches the network about noise levels all across the range rather than one at a time. The target is free: you generated ε yourself to make the noisy image, so you already have the answer column.

### 3 · Why the time step is an input

The neural network takes both the noisy image $\mathbf{x}_t$ and the time step $t$ (encoded via positional encodings) as inputs, predicting the target noise $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$. Loss functions such as Mean Absolute Error (**MAE**) or **Huber loss** are used to update the network weights.

The time step has to be an input because the same picture means different things at different t. Barely-fuzzy static at t = 100 hides almost nothing; the same picture at t = 3900 hides almost everything. Passing t in allows the network to adjust its noise prediction based on the specific noise level it is looking at.

**Positional encodings** are the transformer trick from chapter 16 for turning an integer position into a vector of sine and cosine values, so the network can read "how far along" as a smooth signal rather than a bare number. The card below notes that the DDPM authors used a modified U-Net, and fed these time encodings in through dense layers at every level of it.

**Huber loss** behaves like squared error for small errors and like absolute error for large ones, so a few wild misses cannot dominate the update.

### 4 · The generation loop

During image generation, sampling starts with pure Gaussian noise $\mathbf{x}_T$. The algorithm iteratively removes small amounts of predicted noise over $T$ sequential steps. Equation 17-8 below shows how the intermediate representation $\mathbf{x}_{t-1}$ is computed from $\mathbf{x}_t$ using the model's noise prediction $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_t, t)$ combined with a scaled random noise term $\mathbf{z}$, and the full breakdown sits underneath it.

The addition of a scaled random Gaussian noise term z at each step is what makes the reverse process stochastic: run the loop twice from different starting static and you get two different images. Repeating this reverse step $T$ times yields a clear, highly detailed output image, as demonstrated by the synthesized Fashion MNIST samples in Figure 17-22 below. The code card below is that loop in eight lines — note it counts `for t in range(T, 0, -1)`, backwards.

### 5 · The price, and one way around it

The critical trade-off to remember is that while diffusion models produce exceptionally diverse, high-quality images, sampling requires hundreds or thousands of sequential forward passes through the network, making image generation computationally slow.

Sequential is the painful word. A GAN generator is one forward pass; 4,000 steps cannot be run in parallel, because each one needs the output of the last. This is the same distinction as a set-based query versus a row-by-row cursor, and it is why generation takes minutes rather than milliseconds.

| | GAN or VAE | DDPM |
|---|---|---|
| Passes to make one image | 1 | up to T |
| Training | unstable, fiddly | much easier |
| Sample quality and variety | good | higher, more diverse |

Latent diffusion models execute the diffusion process in a compressed latent space using an autoencoder, which is the main way this cost is reduced — the card below describes it: a powerful autoencoder compresses each image into a much smaller latent space, the whole diffusion process happens there, and the autoencoder decompresses the result at the end. Fewer numbers per step means faster steps, and the image quality stays outstanding.

**One-liner for your notes:** the target is the noise, the time step is an input, and generation is T sequential subtractions — slow, but stable to train and high quality.

blocks.title: The DDPM network and latent diffusion
blocks.content: The DDPM authors used a modified U-Net: a convolutional network that gradually downsamples the input images and then upsamples them again, with skip connections from each downsampling level to the matching upsampling level. The time steps are encoded with the same technique as the positional encodings in transformers, and at every level of the U-Net these encodings pass through Dense layers and are fed in. A latent diffusion model adds a powerful autoencoder. The autoencoder compresses each training image into a much smaller latent space, the diffusion process takes place there, and then the autoencoder decompresses the final latent representation to produce the output image. This considerably speeds up image generation and dramatically reduces training time and cost, while the quality of the images stays outstanding.

blocks.title: Equation 17-8
blocks.caption: Going one step in reverse in the diffusion process
blocks.explain:
**Why the equation looks like this**

Generation is Equation 17-6 run backwards, and it has three jobs, which is why it has three parts.

Take the noisy image. Subtract the noise the network predicts — but only the fraction of it that
belongs to *this one step*, which is what the beta over root term scales it down to. Then undo the
shrink that the forward step applied, by dividing by the root of alpha. Then add a small amount of
fresh random noise back in.

The last part is the one that looks wrong. You are trying to remove noise; why put some back? Because
the network's prediction is a best guess, an average over everything the noisy image could have come
from. Landing exactly on that average every step walks you down the middle of the distribution and
out to a blurry, averaged image. The injected z keeps the walk random, so the run commits to one
specific plausible image rather than the mean of all of them — and it is why two runs from different
starting static give two different pictures.

**Is this standard?** Yes. This is the DDPM sampling step exactly as published, and it is what the
book's own `generate()` function implements line for line. Nothing was simplified. What *is* a
simplification is elsewhere in the design: the standard deviation of the injected noise is taken as
the root of beta, which is one of two reasonable choices in the original paper.

**The general form.** Repeat this step for t from T down to 1, feeding each output into the next. On
the very last step the fresh noise is left out — the book's code uses `tf.zeros` when t is 1 — because
the result is the finished image and there is nothing left to keep random.

**Terms this introduces.** **Theta** is the standard symbol for "the model's learned weights", so
epsilon-theta means "the noise as predicted by the trained network" rather than the real noise, which
you do not know at generation time. **z** is a fresh draw of standard-normal noise, a different one at
every step. Alpha, beta and alpha-bar are the schedule values from the previous lesson, looked up for
this t.

**Every piece of Equation 17-8**

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| x with subscript t−1 | x t minus 1 | the slightly cleaner image you are computing |
| x with subscript t | x t | the image you have now |
| 1 over root alpha t | one over root alpha t | undoes this step's shrink |
| beta with subscript t | beta t | noise variance the schedule used at t |
| root of 1 minus alpha-bar t | root of one minus alpha bar t | total noise scale at step t |
| epsilon-theta of x t and t | epsilon theta of x t and t | the noise the network predicts |
| the big bracket | — | the image with this step's noise removed |
| root beta t | root beta t | how much fresh randomness to add back |
| z | z | a fresh standard-normal draw |

**The formula in plain words**

cleaner image = (noisy image − this step's share of the predicted noise) ÷ this step's shrink factor,
then + a little fresh randomness.

**With real numbers, for one step**

Take t of 2,000 on the book's schedule (T of 4,000, s of 0.008). The three coefficients are:

| Quantity | Value | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| alpha at 2,000 | 0.999212 | the step's shrink, squared |
| beta at 2,000 | 0.000788 | the step's noise variance |
| alpha-bar at 2,000 | 0.49384 | total signal left at this point |
| 1 over root alpha | 1.000394 | scales the image back up |
| beta over root of 1 − alpha-bar | 0.001108 | how much predicted noise to subtract |
| root beta | 0.02808 | how much fresh noise to add |

So one reverse step at the halfway point does this to every pixel: subtract about **0.0011** of the
predicted noise, multiply by about **1.0004**, then add about **0.028** of a fresh random value.

Those numbers are tiny, and that is the point — and also the cost. A single step barely changes the
picture, so no one step can go badly wrong; but you need four thousand of them, one after another,
and they cannot be run in parallel. The stability and the slowness are the same number seen twice.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
def generate(model, batch_size=32):
    X = tf.random.normal([batch_size, 28, 28, 1])
    for t in range(T, 0, -1):
        noise = (tf.random.normal if t > 1 else tf.zeros)(tf.shape(X))
        X_noise = model({"X_noisy": X, "time": tf.constant([t] * batch_size)})
        X = (
            1 / alpha[t] ** 0.5
            * (X - beta[t] / (1 - alpha_cumprod[t]) ** 0.5 * X_noise)
            + (1 - alpha[t]) ** 0.5 * noise
        )
    return X
```

items.term: Why predicting the noise beats predicting the image
items.text: The honest answer in the book is that the authors tried both and this one works better. A usable intuition: the noise target has the same scale and the same difficulty at every time step, whereas the clean-image target is nearly free at t of 1 and nearly impossible at t of 4,000. One network, one set of weights, has to serve all time steps — so a target whose difficulty is roughly constant across them is a far kinder thing to fit. The pattern recurs elsewhere: predicting the residual is often easier than predicting the value.

items.term: Why the time step must be an input, and what that costs
items.text: The same noisy image means different things at different t, so without t the network cannot know how much to remove and will average over all the possibilities. Feeding t in makes the network effectively thousands of denoisers sharing one set of weights. That sharing is the reason one model suffices — but it also means the model must generalise across noise levels, which is why the encoding of t is not an afterthought and why the DDPM authors reached for transformer-style positional encodings rather than a raw integer.

items.term: Latent diffusion is the same cost argument applied one level down
items.text: The cost of diffusion is steps times work-per-step, and the number of steps is hard to cut without hurting quality. So attack the other factor: run the whole process on a compressed representation instead of on pixels. The autoencoder does the compressing and decompressing, the diffusion model never sees a pixel, and the per-step work drops by whatever the compression ratio is. It is worth noticing that this makes the autoencoder from the start of this chapter a load-bearing component of the current state of the art rather than a historical stepping stone.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Diffusion models are trained to predict the noise added to an image rather than predicting the clean image directly.
Time steps are embedded into the neural network using positional encodings similar to those used in Transformers.
Sampling requires starting from pure Gaussian noise and applying an iterative reverse step process over many time steps.
Latent diffusion models perform the noise addition and removal process in a compressed latent space to speed up training and generation.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Generation needs T sequential passes, and the book notes you can use a smaller T or reuse a prediction across several steps at the cost of quality. What do the faster samplers actually do differently, and how much quality do they give up?
Look up: Jonathan Ho et al., 'Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models' (2020) — this chapter's footnote 20, the paper Equation 17-8 comes from.

Exercise 3: Explain whether an autoencoder that achieves perfect reconstruction of its inputs is necessarily a good model, and describe how you can evaluate the overall performance of an autoencoder.
Exercise 4: Define undercomplete and overcomplete autoencoders, and discuss the main risks associated with excessively undercomplete architectures as well as overcomplete architectures.
Exercise 5: Describe the mechanism of tying weights in a stacked autoencoder, and explain the main benefits of using this architectural constraint.

Exercise 8: Identify and explain the main technical difficulties and instability issues encountered when training Generative Adversarial Networks.

Exercise 10: Detail a step-by-step procedure for using a deep denoising autoencoder to pretrain an image classifier, including evaluating reconstruction performance, visualizing neuron activations in the coding layer, and comparing classification results with and without pretraining on a limited set of labeled images.

items.term: Foundations of Reinforcement Learning

blocks.content:
Reinforcement learning trains an agent by letting it act, watching what happens, and paying it a reward, instead of showing it the right answer for every step.

**The question this lesson answers:** nobody can write down the correct action for a thermostat at every minute of every day. So how do you train a system when you have no answer column to learn from?

### The big picture

```
        +------ observation, reward ------+
        |                                 |
        v                                 |
     AGENT  ------------ action ------> ENVIRONMENT
```

That loop is the whole framework. Everything else in this chapter is a different way of deciding what the arrow labelled `action` should contain.

### 1 · Why the usual ML setup does not fit

Standard machine learning algorithms rely on explicit labels or static target values, which makes them unsuitable for complex control tasks where sequential decision-making is required. A **label** is the answer column — the value training learns to fill in for rows it has never seen. In many real-world settings, explicit instructions on what action to take at every single moment are unavailable.

Reinforcement learning solves this fundamental challenge by framing learning as an interactive trial-and-error process between an **agent** (the software making the decisions) and an **environment** (everything the agent acts on and observes).

If the best action at each step were known, the agent could be trained with regular supervised learning. In reinforcement learning, the only guidance comes through rewards.

### 2 · The four words in the loop

| Word | What it is |
|---|---|
| observation | what the agent can see of the current state |
| action | what the agent does in response |
| reward | one number saying how that turned out |
| environment | the thing that emits observations and rewards |

The software agent receives observations about the current state of the environment and selects actions based on those observations. In response, the environment returns updated observations and signals known as **rewards**.

The primary goal of the agent is to learn a strategy that maximizes its total expected cumulative rewards over time. Rewards can be positive, serving as an encouragement for beneficial actions, or negative, acting as a penalty for undesirable outcomes or unnecessary delays.

### 3 · The thermostat, read off Figure 18-1

Consider a smart thermostat attempting to optimize home energy usage. As shown in **Figure 18-1** below, reinforcement learning applies to physical systems as well as virtual settings.

The thermostat acts as the agent, observing room temperatures and user presence. It performs actions by toggling heating or cooling cycles. The system receives positive rewards for keeping the temperature near the preferred setting while consuming minimal electricity, and negative rewards whenever occupants manually override the temperature settings. Over time, the thermostat learns to anticipate human daily routines without explicit human programming.

### 4 · Rewards do not have to be positive

Rewards do not have to include any positive values at all. In a maze, the agent can get a negative reward at every time step, so it had better find the exit as quickly as possible. In a board game such as Go, the agent may only get a reward when it wins.

Both are legal reward designs, and they pull the agent in completely different directions — one towards speed, one towards a single outcome at the very end. The card below adds the 2013 result where deep learning was first applied to this loop.

### 5 · Long-term, not immediate

The essential core of reinforcement learning lies in evaluating the long-term consequences of actions rather than seeking immediate gratification, ensuring optimal decisions across sequential steps.

That single sentence is why the next several lessons exist: turning "this whole episode went badly" into "this particular action was the mistake" is the hard part, and it has its own name — the credit assignment problem.

**One-liner for your notes:** an agent acts on an environment, gets observations and rewards back, and learns a strategy that maximises total reward over time rather than the reward of the next step.

blocks.title: Negative rewards, and deep learning meets RL
blocks.content:
Rewards do not have to include any positive values at all. In a maze, for example, the agent can get a negative reward at every time step, so it had better find the exit as quickly as possible. In a board game such as Go, the agent may only get a reward when it wins.

If the best action at each step were known, the agent could be trained with regular supervised learning. In reinforcement learning, the only guidance comes through rewards. In 2013, DeepMind showed a system that learned to play just about any Atari game from scratch, using only raw pixels as inputs and without any prior knowledge of the rules. The trick was to apply the power of deep learning (neural networks) to reinforcement learning.

items.term: Why a reward is not a label
items.text: A label tells you what the correct action was; a reward only tells you how well things went, and usually much later. That single difference is what forces everything else in this chapter to exist - returns, advantages, Q-values. If you ever find yourself with the right action written down for each step, stop: supervised learning is cheaper, more stable and will beat RL at that job.

items.term: Reward design is the real specification
items.text: The two designs in this lesson pull an agent in opposite directions. A negative reward at every step optimises for speed; a reward only on a win optimises for the final outcome and says nothing about how. The agent will maximise whatever you actually wrote, not what you meant - so the reward function, not the algorithm, is where most real RL projects go wrong.

items.term: Where the thermostat example stops being cosy
items.text: The thermostat learns by being wrong in a real house with real occupants. Every RL system that acts on the physical world has that property: its training data is generated by its own mistakes. That is the whole reason the next lesson but one reaches for a simulator.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Reinforcement learning trains software agents to make optimal sequential decisions by interacting directly with an environment.
The core interaction loop relies on observing the environment state, executing an action, and receiving a reward signal.
The primary objective of a reinforcement learning agent is to maximize its total expected rewards over time.
Reward signals can be positive to reward desirable outcomes or negative to penalize undesirable events or wasted time.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The 2013 Atari agent learned from raw pixels with no knowledge of the rules. What was it actually given as a reward signal, and was one network trained per game or one across all of them?
Look up: Volodymyr Mnih et al., “Playing Atari with Deep Reinforcement Learning”, arXiv:1312.5602 (2013) — the paper behind the result in the card above.

items.term: Policy Search in Reinforcement Learning

blocks.content:
A policy is the thing that turns an observation into an action, and policy search is any method for hunting through the possible policies for one that collects more reward.

**The question this lesson answers:** a robotic vacuum cleaner moves forward with probability p and randomly rotates within an angle range r. Which pair of numbers picks up the most dust in 30 minutes, and how would you find it?

### The big picture

```
observation -> POLICY -> action
              (a few parameters: p, r)

search the parameter space three ways:
  brute force  |  genetic algorithms  |  policy gradients
```

### 1 · What a policy is

In reinforcement learning, an agent must decide which action to take based on environment inputs. The algorithm that maps observations to actions is called a **policy**. The goal of an agent is to find a policy that maximizes its cumulative reward over time.

A policy can be any algorithm at all. As Figure 18-2 below illustrates, a neural network can act as a policy by accepting environment observations as inputs and outputting actions.

**Policy parameters** are the handful of numbers that define which policy you have. They are the thing being searched for — the same role that model parameters play in ordinary training.

### 2 · Deterministic and stochastic

Policies can also be non-deterministic, known as a **stochastic policy**, where actions are chosen probabilistically rather than deterministically. *Stochastic* just means "with randomness in it".

Consider a robotic vacuum cleaner operating in a room. The robot uses a simple stochastic policy defined by two parameters: the probability $p$ of moving forward each second, and the angle range $r$ for random left or right rotations.

The randomness is not sloppiness. It gives the robot an erratic trajectory, which guarantees that it will eventually get to any place it can reach and pick up all the dust.

### 3 · Reading Figure 18-3

As Figure 18-3 below shows, different parameter pairs $(p, r)$ yield completely different trajectories. The left half of the figure is the **policy space** — every possible combination of the parameters — and each plotted point in it is one specific combination of the policy parameters, the probability $p$ and the angle range $r$. The right half shows how the robot actually behaves at that point.

### 4 · Three ways to search the space

| Method | How it searches | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| brute force | try many pairs, keep the best | dies when the space is large |
| genetic algorithm | breed the winners, mutate | only needs a score per policy |
| policy gradients | nudge parameters uphill | needs a usable gradient |

A brute-force policy search evaluates many distinct pairs of $(p, r)$ to find which combination collects the most dust in 30 minutes. However, finding an optimal policy is challenging when the set of possible strategy parameters is large. When the policy space is too large — which is generally the case — finding a good set of parameters this way is like searching for a needle in a gigantic haystack.

Alternatively, genetic algorithms maintain a population of candidate policies, evaluate their performance, and generate offspring from the top performers with random mutations. The book's concrete version: create 100 random policies, kill the 80 worst, and let each of the 20 survivors produce 4 offspring, each a copy of its parent plus some random variation.

Another advanced approach uses **policy gradients**, which estimate how changes in policy parameters alter the expected reward and tweak those parameters directly in the direction of higher performance. Concretely: slightly increase $p$, check whether the robot picks up more dust, and if it does, increase $p$ some more, otherwise reduce it.

The fundamental takeaway is that policy search methods optimize an agent's strategy by exploring the policy parameter space through brute force, evolutionary algorithms, or gradient-based methods.

**One-liner for your notes:** the policy is the observation-to-action rule, its parameters are what you are searching for, and brute force, genetic algorithms and policy gradients are three ways to run that search.

items.term: Why randomness in a policy is not sloppiness
items.text: A deterministic vacuum policy can get permanently stuck against a wall or in a loop. The random rotation is what guarantees the robot eventually reaches anywhere it can reach. Randomness here is coverage insurance, not a lack of confidence - and the same reasoning returns in the next lesson, where a neural network deliberately samples its action instead of taking the best one.

items.term: Genetic search versus gradient search
items.text: A genetic algorithm only needs a score per policy, so it works when the reward is a black box with no usable gradient. Policy gradients need that gradient but then move in a straight line towards better parameters instead of guessing. Rule of thumb: gradients when you can differentiate the path from parameters to reward, evolution when you cannot.

items.term: Policy parameters are not model parameters
items.text: In this lesson p and r are the entire policy - two numbers, no network. That is worth noticing because it separates the concept from the implementation: policy search is a way of searching a parameter space, and it does not care whether that space has 2 dimensions or 2 million.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A policy defines how a reinforcement learning agent chooses actions based on observations.
Stochastic policies introduce randomness into action selection.
Policy search finds optimal parameters via brute-force, genetic algorithms, or policy gradients.
Genetic algorithms refine policies across generations by selecting high-performing candidates and mutating them.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: When does an evolutionary policy search actually beat a gradient-based one in practice, and can evolution change the shape of the network rather than only its numbers?
Look up: the NEAT algorithm (NeuroEvolution of Augmenting Topologies), which this chapter names as an example of a genetic algorithm used for reinforcement learning.

items.term: Simulating Environments with OpenAI Gym

blocks.content:
OpenAI Gym is a library of simulated environments plus one standard interface — `reset` and `step` — so an agent can practise millions of times without touching real hardware.

**The question this lesson answers:** you need an environment before you can train an agent. What exactly does a Gym environment hand back when you reset it and when you step it, and what do those numbers mean for CartPole?

### The big picture

| Call | Gives you back |
|---|---|
| gym.make("CartPole-v1") | the simulation object |
| env.reset(seed=42) | obs, info |
| env.step(action) | obs, reward, done, truncated, info |

Three calls is the entire contract. Every Gym environment — Atari, board games, 3D physics — answers the same three, which is why agent code written once runs against all of them.

### 1 · Why simulate at all

Training reinforcement learning agents in the physical world is slow, dangerous, and expensive. Real hardware cannot be sped up, and physical damage cannot be undone. If the robot falls off a cliff, you cannot click Undo, and it is generally too expensive to train 1,000 robots in parallel.

To solve this problem, **OpenAI Gym** provides simulated environments that allow agents to learn rapidly inside software without physical risks. It establishes a standard interface between agents and environment simulators.

### 2 · Resetting: starting an episode

An environment is initialized using `gym.make()`, which returns a simulation object. Calling `env.reset()` starts a new episode and returns an initial **observation** vector along with an auxiliary information dictionary. The observation vector contains the current physical state of the environment.

An **episode** is one complete run — from reset until the pole falls or the step limit is hit. Passing a seed makes the episode reproducible, which is why the book scores its policy with `seed=episode`.

### 3 · CartPole's four numbers

As Figure 18-4 below illustrates, the classic **CartPole** environment (`CartPole-v1`) models a cart moving horizontally to keep a balanced pole upright. Its observation array consists of four floating-point values:

| Index | Measurement |
|---|---|
| obs[0] | cart position |
| obs[1] | cart velocity |
| obs[2] | pole angle |
| obs[3] | pole angular velocity |

The third value, `obs[2]`, is the current angle of the balanced pole, and it is the one the hardcoded policy below reads.

### 4 · Acting: the action space and the five returns

To interact with the environment, an agent sends an action via `env.step(action)`. For CartPole, the **action space** is `Discrete(2)`, accepting integer `0` for left acceleration or `1` for right acceleration. An **action space** is simply the environment's declaration of which inputs are legal.

Executing `env.step(action)` updates the simulation state and returns five key variables: the new observation, a float **reward** signal, a boolean `done` flag indicating natural termination, a boolean `truncated` flag indicating early truncation, and an `info` dictionary.

`done` means the episode really ended — the pole fell. `truncated` means it was cut short by a limit rather than by failure. They are separate booleans because they mean different things, and the deep Q-learning code later in the chapter treats both as "stop bootstrapping here".

### 5 · Scoring a hardcoded policy

In a concrete trial using a basic policy that pushes right whenever the pole tilts right (`obs[2] > 0`), evaluating the strategy across 500 episodes produces an average reward of roughly 41.7 steps, with a maximum of only 63 steps. The card below shows the exact run and the full set of statistics.

That average of 41.7 is not a failure — it is the baseline. Every learned policy in the rest of the chapter has to beat it to be worth anything.

The key insight to remember is that standard simulation loops decouple the agent's policy logic from physical execution through unified state step returns.

**One-liner for your notes:** `reset` gives you obs and info, `step` gives you obs, reward, done, truncated and info, and CartPole's four observation numbers are cart position, cart velocity, pole angle and pole angular velocity.

blocks.title: Worked out: scoring the basic CartPole policy
blocks.content:
In CartPole, the reward is 1.0 at every step, no matter what the agent does, so an episode's total reward equals the number of steps the pole stayed up. An episode ends (`done` is True) when the pole tilts too much or goes off the screen, or after 200 steps, which counts as a win.

To score the basic policy (accelerate left if `obs[2] < 0`, otherwise right), the book plays 500 episodes. Each episode is reset with `seed=episode`, runs for at most 200 steps, and adds up its rewards; each sum is appended to a list called `totals`. Then `np.mean(totals), np.std(totals), min(totals), max(totals)` returns (41.698, 8.389445512070509, 24.0, 63.0). So the policy survives about 41.7 steps on average and never more than 63.

blocks.title: Figure 18-4
blocks.caption: The CartPole environment
blocks.alt: Figure 18-4: The CartPole environment

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import gym

env = gym.make("CartPole-v1", render_mode="rgb_array")
obs, info = env.reset(seed=42)

def basic_policy(obs):
    angle = obs[2]
    return 0 if angle < 0 else 1

for step in range(200):
    action = basic_policy(obs)
    obs, reward, done, truncated, info = env.step(action)
    if done or truncated:
        break

env.close()
```

items.term: Why the interface matters more than the simulator
items.text: Gym's value is not the physics; it is that every environment answers reset and step with the same shapes. That is what lets one agent implementation be pointed at CartPole, then at an Atari game, with no change to the learning code. It is the same reason a storage layer is worth defining once: the contract, not the contents.

items.term: done and truncated mean different things on purpose
items.text: done means the episode genuinely failed - the pole fell. truncated means it was cut off by a step limit while the pole was still up. Collapsing the two loses information: a run that was stopped by the clock was not a failure, and later in this chapter the training code has to know which it was before it decides whether there is a future worth looking ahead to.

items.term: 41.7 is a baseline, not a result
items.text: The hardcoded policy is deliberately stupid, and it is the number every later method has to beat. Keeping a cheap baseline is how you tell whether a complicated method is actually earning its complexity - here the learned policy reaches roughly 200, the environment's own maximum.

blocks.title: Key points
items: OpenAI Gym provides standardized simulated environments to safely and rapidly train reinforcement learning agents.
The reset method starts a new episode and returns the initial observation and extra environment info.
The step method executes an action and returns five values: observation, reward, done, truncated, and info.
CartPole observations include cart position, cart velocity, pole angle, and pole angular velocity.
Environments expose their valid inputs through their action space property, such as Discrete(2).

blocks.title: Look it up
items: CartPole episodes can end by failure or by hitting a step limit. What limit does CartPole-v1 set, and which of the five step() return values tells you which of the two happened?
Look up: the CartPole-v1 page in the Gym classic-control environment documentation.

items.term: Neural Network Policies

blocks.content:
A neural network policy takes the observation as input and outputs a probability for each action, and the agent then rolls a dice weighted by those probabilities instead of always taking the best one.

**The question this lesson answers:** the hardcoded CartPole rule averaged 41.7 steps. If a network replaces that rule, what should it output — the action, or something else — and why deliberately not always take the action it rates highest?

### The big picture

```
obs (4 numbers) -> hidden layer -> sigmoid -> p
   sample:  action 0 (left)  with probability p
            action 1 (right) with probability 1 - p
```

### 1 · Why a network replaces the rule

In reinforcement learning, standard hardcoded rules fail when environments become complex. A **neural network policy** solves this problem by using a neural network to map environment observations directly to action probabilities, allowing the agent to learn optimal behavior from experience.

The network accepts the current observation vector as input.

### 2 · The output is a probability, not a decision

Instead of deterministically choosing the action with the highest estimated score, the network outputs a probability distribution over all possible actions. The agent then samples an action randomly based on these estimated probabilities.

As Figure 18-5 below shows, in a two-action system like the CartPole environment, the network takes a four-dimensional state observation as input, processes it through a hidden layer, and ends at a single output neuron that uses a **sigmoid activation function** to produce a scalar $p$, representing the probability of selecting action 0 (moving left). Consequently, the probability of selecting action 1 (moving right) is whatever is left over, 1 minus p.

A **sigmoid** is an activation function that squashes any number into the range 0 to 1, which is exactly what a probability needs.

For example, if the model outputs $p = 0.7$, the agent has a 70% chance of choosing to move left and a 30% chance of choosing to move right. Read the output the same way every time: the neuron's value is the chance of action 0, and whatever is left over is the chance of action 1.

### 3 · Why sample instead of taking the best

This stochastic sampling mechanism directly addresses the fundamental **exploration/exploitation dilemma**: by sampling probabilistically rather than acting deterministically, the agent balances exploiting actions known to yield high rewards with exploring alternative actions that might yield even higher rewards later.

The book's picture for it: you go to a restaurant for the first time and every dish looks equally appealing, so you pick one at random. If it turns out to be good you can raise the chance you order it next time — but not to 100%, or you will never try the others, some of which may be better.

Sampling actions according to the network's output probabilities is what balances exploration and exploitation.

### 4 · Two actions or many

| Actions | Output layer |
|---|---|
| 2 | one neuron, sigmoid, gives p and 1 minus p |
| 4 or more | one neuron per action, softmax |

If an environment has more than two possible actions, there would be one output neuron per action, using the **softmax** activation function instead — softmax being the multi-way version of sigmoid, producing one probability per action that together add up to 1.

### 5 · When the current observation is enough

In fully observable, noise-free environments like CartPole, the current observation captures the complete state. Therefore, past observations and historical actions can be safely ignored without losing critical information.

That is a property of this environment, not a general licence. If the environment revealed the cart's position but not its velocity, you would need the previous observation too, just to work the velocity out.

The key insight worth remembering is that sampling actions probabilistically from network outputs prevents premature convergence on sub-optimal strategies by continuously balancing exploration and exploitation.

**One-liner for your notes:** the policy network outputs action probabilities, the agent samples from them so it keeps exploring, and one sigmoid neuron covers two actions while softmax covers more.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(5, activation="relu"),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid"),
])
```

items.term: Why not just take the highest-rated action
items.text: A greedy policy can only ever exploit what it already believes. If its first estimate of an action is too low by chance, it will never pick that action again and never find out. Sampling keeps a small door open for every action, which is the only reason the estimates can ever be corrected.

items.term: What hidden state would cost you
items.text: CartPole hands the agent velocity directly, so one observation is the whole state. Remove velocity and a single frame becomes ambiguous - the same position could be moving either way - and the policy would need the previous observation too. Noisy observations cause the same problem. This is a property of the environment you must check, not an assumption you may make.

items.term: One sigmoid neuron and two softmax neurons are the same thing
items.text: For two actions, outputting p and letting the other be the remainder is exactly what a two-way softmax does, with half the parameters. Softmax is simply the version that still works at four actions or forty, which is why it is the general answer.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A neural network policy takes environment observations as input and outputs action probabilities.
Sampling actions according to network output probabilities balances exploration and exploitation.
Binary action environments require a single output neuron with a sigmoid activation function.
Multi-action environments require one output neuron per action using a softmax activation function.
Noise-free environments containing full state information do not require tracking past observations.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: A sigmoid or a softmax gives you a probability per action, which only works when the actions are a short list. What does a policy network output when the action is continuous, such as a steering angle?
Look up: Tuomas Haarnoja et al., “Soft Actor-Critic: Off-Policy Maximum Entropy Deep Reinforcement Learning with a Stochastic Actor”, ICML (2018): 1856–1865.

items.term: The Credit Assignment Problem and Action Advantage

blocks.content:
When an episode ends badly, the agent has to decide which of its many actions deserves the blame — and it does that by scoring each action with its discounted future rewards, then asking whether that score beat the average.

**The question this lesson answers:** the pole fell after 100 steps. The last push was not solely responsible, so how do you hand out credit and blame across all 100 actions using only the rewards?

### The big picture

```
one action -> return    = reward now + discounted later
many episodes -> advantage = (return - mean) / std
```

Two numbers, two different jobs. The **return** says what an action earned. The **advantage** says whether that was better or worse than usual.

### 1 · The problem has a name

In supervised learning, an algorithm receives a direct target label for every training instance. Reinforcement learning agents do not have explicit labels for each step; instead, they receive feedback through delayed and sparse rewards. *Sparse* means most steps pay nothing at all; *delayed* means the payment arrives long after the action that caused it.

When a failure occurs after a long sequence of decisions, the agent must figure out which specific decisions caused the eventual failure and which ones contributed to earlier success. This difficulty in assigning credit or blame across a sequence of actions is known as the **credit assignment problem**. The book's picture: a dog rewarded hours after it behaved well has no way to know what the reward is for.

### 2 · The return, and the arithmetic behind it

To address this challenge, agents evaluate each decision by calculating its **return**, which is the sum of all future rewards following that action. Because immediate outcomes are usually more reliable and direct than distant outcomes, future rewards are multiplied by a **discount factor** γ (gamma) raised to the power of the time delay.

| Piece | Say it as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| γ | gamma | the discount factor, between 0 and 1 |
| γ to the power 1 | gamma | weight on the reward one step later |
| γ to the power 2 | gamma squared | weight on the reward two steps later |
| the sum | plus | add all the weighted rewards together |

**In plain words:** return = this step's reward + γ × next step's reward + γ squared × the step after that, and so on to the end of the episode.

**With the real numbers.** As Figure 18-6 below shows, if an agent executes three consecutive steps resulting in immediate rewards of +10, 0, and -50, setting a discount factor of γ = 0.8 yields a return for the first step equal to 10 + 0.8 × 0 + 0.8 squared × (-50) = -22.

Working the other two out the same way:

1. **Step 3** has nothing after it, so its return is just -50.
2. **Step 2** sees 0 now and -50 one step later. The return of the second step is 0 + 0.8 × (-50) = -40.
3. **Step 1** sees +10 now, 0 one step later and -50 two steps later: 10 + 0 + 0.64 × (-50) = -22.

A **positive** immediate reward of +10 still produced a **negative** return, because the disaster two steps later was only discounted to 0.64 of its size. That is the point of the return: it judges an action by what followed it.

### 3 · What γ actually controls

| γ | Effect |
|---|---|
| close to 0 | distant rewards contribute very little |
| close to 1 | distant rewards count almost as much as now |

A discount factor close to 0 means future rewards will not count for much compared to immediate rewards; a discount factor close to 1 means rewards far into the future will count almost as much as immediate rewards. Typical discount factors vary from 0.9 to 0.99. With a discount factor of 0.95, rewards 13 steps into the future count roughly for half as much as immediate rewards, while with 0.99 it takes 69 steps to halve. In the CartPole environment, actions have fairly short-term effects, so a discount factor of 0.95 is reasonable.

### 4 · From return to advantage

A single sequence of rewards can still be noisy because a helpful step might be followed by several blunders — the book's version is that a good actor may sometimes star in a terrible movie.

To reliably separate effective decisions from poor choices, the agent runs many training episodes and computes the **action advantage**. The advantage estimates how much better or worse an action is compared to the other possible actions, on average. This metric normalizes returns by subtracting the overall mean return and dividing by the standard deviation.

**Standard deviation** is the usual measure of spread, so dividing by it puts every action on the same scale no matter how big the raw rewards were. Actions with a positive advantage are treated as beneficial choices, whereas actions with a negative advantage are classified as detrimental choices.

The essential insight to remember is that discounting future rewards measures total long-term impact, while normalizing these returns into action advantage reveals whether a step performed better or worse than average.

**One-liner for your notes:** the return is an action's discounted future rewards, the advantage is that return minus the batch mean divided by the standard deviation, and γ is the knob deciding how far ahead the agent cares.
