blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

# List all physical GPU devices available to TensorFlow
physical_gpus = tf.config.list_physical_devices("GPU")

# Display detected devices
print(physical_gpus)
```

items.term: Why the stack has two libraries and not one
items.text: CUDA is the general programming model for the card: memory, kernels, streams. cuDNN is a library of hand-tuned implementations of a short list of operations that deep networks spend nearly all their time in. The split is the classic one between a platform and an optimised library on top of it - anyone can write a convolution in CUDA, almost nobody can write one that beats the vendor's, because the fast version depends on the exact cache sizes and instruction mix of each card generation. Framework authors therefore write against cuDNN and get new-hardware speed for free when the library is updated.

items.term: Version pinning is the real operational hazard here
items.text: Driver, CUDA toolkit and cuDNN each have versions, and TensorFlow supports one narrow combination at a time. Mismatch usually does not announce itself clearly - you get a library-not-found error, a silent fallback to the CPU, or a crash inside a kernel. This is why the containerised route exists: the image pins the whole chain and the host only has to supply a driver new enough. Treat the version matrix as a hard dependency of the job, the way you would treat a JDBC driver version against a database.

items.term: Two commands, two different questions
items.text: nvidia-smi asks the operating system and the driver whether the hardware is present and healthy. tf.config.list_physical_devices asks TensorFlow whether it can reach it through CUDA and cuDNN. The interesting case is the one where the first succeeds and the second returns an empty list, because it localises the fault precisely: the card is fine, the layer between it and the framework is not. Building that ladder deliberately - check each layer from the bottom - is worth more than any single command, and it is exactly what you do when a query engine cannot see a healthy storage node.

blocks.title: Key points
items: GPUs significantly accelerate deep learning model training compared to traditional CPUs.
TensorFlow requires Nvidia graphics cards with CUDA Compute Capability 3.5 or higher.
The software stack requires installing system drivers, the CUDA Toolkit, and the cuDNN library.
System installations are verified using the nvidia-smi command-line tool.
TensorFlow detects visible hardware using the tf.config.list_physical_devices function.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The book says to weigh memory, bandwidth, core count and cooling when buying a card, but does not say how those weights change by workload. Which of them actually binds first for a given kind of model?
Look up: Tim Dettmers' blog post on which GPU to buy for deep learning, which the book cites here by name.

items.term: Managing GPU RAM in TensorFlow

blocks.content:
TensorFlow takes almost all the GPU memory on its first computation, so running two jobs on one machine means telling it, explicitly, to take less.

**The question this lesson answers:** your training script works. You start a second notebook on the same machine and it dies with an out-of-memory error, even though the GPU looks half idle. Why, and what do you set?

### The big picture

| Option | What you set | Result |
|---|---|---|
| split the cards | CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES | each process sees its own cards |
| cap the memory | a logical device memory_limit | both processes share every card |
| grow on demand | memory growth | takes what it needs, never gives it back |

### 1 · The default, and why it exists

When TensorFlow runs its first computation, it automatically allocates almost all available RAM across every visible GPU. The framework does this to reduce **memory fragmentation** — the state where free memory exists but is broken into pieces too small to satisfy a request, so grabbing one big block up front avoids it.

But this aggressive pre-allocation prevents other processes from using the hardware. If you attempt to run a second program, such as a separate training job or an additional interactive notebook, that process will immediately fail with an out-of-memory error. The memory is not in use; it is reserved. That distinction is the whole lesson.

### 2 · Give each process its own cards

To share GPU resources, you must manage how memory is allocated. One direct method isolates hardware per process by configuring the `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` and `CUDA_DEVICE_ORDER` environment variables. As Figure 19-8 below shows, a machine with four physical GPUs can run two distinct programs concurrently by assigning cards 0 and 1 to the first program, and cards 2 and 3 to the second. In this setup, each script only sees its designated subset of cards.

Setting `CUDA_DEVICE_ORDER` to `PCI_BUS_ID` ensures that each ID always refers to the same GPU card — without it the numbering can shift between runs, and a card number that does not mean the same card twice is worse than no numbering at all.

Inside each program, the visible cards are renamed in the order they are listed, starting from 0. So if Program 2 is launched with `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=3,2`, physical GPU #3 is named `/gpu:0` because it is the first card listed in the variable, and physical GPU #2 becomes `/gpu:1`. The card below works this through.

### 3 · Or cap how much of each card a process takes

Alternatively, you can allow multiple programs to share the same physical cards by capping process memory. Through `tf.config.set_logical_device_configuration()`, you create a **logical GPU** on each physical device with a fixed memory limit — a logical GPU is a slice of a real card that TensorFlow treats as if it were a whole device.

For instance, on a machine with four GPUs containing at least 4 GiB of RAM each, you can configure TensorFlow to limit each card to 2,048 MiB (2 GiB). As illustrated in Figure 19-9 below, two programs configured this way can run simultaneously across all four cards, each occupying only 2 GiB per card.

The same mechanism has a second use: a developer with only one physical GPU can simulate a multi-GPU training environment by defining multiple `LogicalDeviceConfiguration` entries on that single physical device, which splits it into `/gpu:0` and `/gpu:1`. That is how you test a multi-GPU code path on a single-GPU machine.

### 4 · Or let it grow

A third technique enables **memory growth** using `tf.config.experimental.set_memory_growth()` or the `TF_FORCE_GPU_ALLOW_GROWTH` environment variable. Instead of grabbing all memory upfront, TensorFlow allocates memory on demand but never releases it until termination — it keeps whatever it has claimed until the process exits, again to avoid fragmentation.

This is convenient for a machine running several notebooks and bad for production, because one program's peak can starve another at an unpredictable moment.

The central takeaway is that TensorFlow's default behavior assumes complete ownership of all GPU memory, so concurrent workloads require explicitly isolating physical cards or defining logical memory bounds right after importing the library.

**One-liner for your notes:** the GPU is not busy, it is reserved — split the cards with `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES`, cap them with a logical device limit, or allow growth and accept that nothing is ever handed back.

blocks.title: Worked out: GPU names, and splitting one GPU
blocks.content: With four GPU cards, you can run two programs in two terminals: `CUDA_DEVICE_ORDER=PCI_BUS_ID CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1 python3 program_1.py` and `CUDA_DEVICE_ORDER=PCI_BUS_ID CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=3,2 python3 program_2.py`. Setting `CUDA_DEVICE_ORDER` to `PCI_BUS_ID` ensures that each ID always refers to the same GPU card. Inside each program, the visible cards are named in the order they are listed, starting from 0. Program 1 sees cards 0 and 1 as `/gpu:0` and `/gpu:1`. Program 2 lists card 3 first, so card 3 becomes `/gpu:0` and card 2 becomes `/gpu:1`. If you have only one physical GPU but want to test a multi-GPU algorithm, pass two `LogicalDeviceConfiguration(memory_limit=2048)` entries for `physical_gpus[0]`: this splits GPU #0 into two logical devices with 2 GiB each, named `/gpu:0` and `/gpu:1`.

items.term: Reserved is not used, and every shared resource has this confusion
items.text: The GPU shows almost no free memory and almost no utilisation at the same time, and both readings are correct: one process claimed the memory and is not currently computing. Anyone who has watched a cluster scheduler hold containers for a job that is waiting on input has seen the same picture. The lesson that transfers is that capacity dashboards measure allocation, not work, and the two only agree when nothing is over-claiming.

items.term: Three sharing models, and the one that does not belong in production
items.text: Partition the cards, partition the memory, or let each process take what it needs. The first two are static: a process cannot exceed its share, so a bad neighbour cannot starve a good one, and you find out at configuration time rather than at three in the morning. Memory growth is dynamic and therefore non-deterministic - the job that crashes is whichever one asked second, which varies run to run. That is the right trade for a workstation running several notebooks and the wrong one for anything with a schedule, and it is the same argument as static versus elastic resource pools on a shared cluster.

items.term: Logical devices make a multi-device code path testable
items.text: Splitting one card into two logical GPUs exercises the real distribution code - variables are mirrored, batches are split, gradients are reduced - on hardware you already have. What it cannot test is the part that actually bites at scale: the interconnect. Two logical devices on one card have no cross-device transfer cost, so a bandwidth problem is invisible until the code meets real cards. Useful for correctness, useless for performance, and knowing which of the two you are testing is the point.

blocks.title: Key points
items: TensorFlow defaults to claiming almost all available GPU RAM upfront to mitigate fragmentation.
The CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES environment variable isolates specific physical GPUs to individual processes.
Setting a memory_limit via logical device configurations caps the exact GPU RAM TensorFlow can consume.
Enabling memory growth allocates RAM dynamically, but TensorFlow retains claimed memory until process exit.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Splitting one card between two processes divides its memory, but both processes still submit work to the same execution units. What actually happens to throughput when two jobs compute on one GPU at the same time?
Look up: Nvidia's documentation on the Multi-Process Service (MPS) and on Multi-Instance GPU (MIG), which are the two supported ways of sharing one card.

items.term: Placing Operations and Variables on Devices

blocks.content:
TensorFlow decides for itself which device each variable and operation lands on, and the default is usually right: network maths on the GPU, everything else on the CPU.

**The question this lesson answers:** you never wrote a line about devices, yet some of your tensors are on the GPU and some are on the CPU. What rule decided that, and when should you override it?

### The big picture

```
CPU  /cpu:0   data, preprocessing, integer tensors
GPU  /gpu:0   float network operations  <- the default
      transfers between them are the expensive part
```

### 1 · Why the split is not arbitrary

When training deep learning models, developers often need to manage where computations and data are stored across hardware components. The main challenge arises from resource constraints: **GPU RAM** is expensive and limited, and transferring data between hardware devices consumes valuable communication bandwidth. Placing heavy input preprocessing on a GPU can waste its memory and slow down overall training.

So the guidance has a reason behind it: GPU RAM is an expensive, limited resource that should be reserved for neural network operations, while data preprocessing and large dataset storage typically belong on the CPU. Adding CPU RAM to a machine is cheap; GPU RAM is fixed when you buy the card.

You have met the shape of this before — keeping the heavy scan where the data already sits, rather than shipping it somewhere to be scanned.

### 2 · The default placement rule

By default, TensorFlow places all supported floating-point variables and operations on the first GPU device, known as `"/gpu:0"`. If a specific operation lacks a GPU implementation — such as computations involving integer tensors — TensorFlow automatically places that operation on the primary CPU device, designated as `"/cpu:0"`.

The word for an operation's implementation on one device and data type is a **kernel**. There is a GPU kernel for float multiplication and none for integer variables, which produces exactly this behaviour:

| Written | Lands on | Why |
|---|---|---|
| tf.Variable of 1.0, 2.0, 3.0 | /gpu:0 | float32 has a GPU kernel |
| tf.Variable of 1, 2, 3 | /cpu:0 | integer variables lack GPU kernels |

So TensorFlow places integer variables on the CPU because integer operations lack GPU kernels — not because integers are small or unimportant.

### 3 · One CPU, however many cores

All CPU cores on a machine are treated as a single unified device named `/cpu:0` that runs multithreaded kernels. This catches people out: eight cores do not appear as eight devices. Parallelism across cores still happens, but it happens *inside* an operation, through its multithreaded kernel, rather than by placing different operations on different cores.

### 4 · Overriding it, and what happens when you are wrong

Developers can also override default placements using the `tf.device()` context manager. Placing a floating-point variable inside a `with tf.device("/cpu:0"):` block forces it onto the CPU, allowing developers to conserve precious GPU memory for matrix computations.

And if you ask for a device that is not there? The card below records the behaviour: TensorFlow silently falls back to the default device placement rather than raising an error. That is deliberate, so the same script runs on machines with different numbers of GPUs — but it also means a placement you thought you had made may have quietly not happened. Run `tf.config.set_soft_device_placement(False)` if you would rather get an exception.

The key insight to remember is that neural network operations belong on the GPU, whereas data preprocessing and datasets belong on the CPU, because GPU RAM is limited and data transfers into and out of the GPU should be kept to a minimum.

**One-liner for your notes:** floats go to `/gpu:0`, anything with no GPU kernel falls back to the single `/cpu:0`, and `tf.device()` overrides it — silently, if the device you named does not exist.

blocks.title: Placing an operation on a missing device
blocks.content: If you explicitly try to place an operation or a variable on a device that does not exist, or on a device for which there is no kernel, TensorFlow does not crash: it silently falls back to the device it would have chosen by default. This is useful when you want to run the same code on different machines that do not have the same number of GPUs. If you prefer to get an exception instead, you can run `tf.config.set_soft_device_placement(False)`.

blocks.caption: TensorFlow assigns floating-point operations to the GPU by default while reserving the CPU for data preprocessing and integer tensors.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

# Default placement for float32 goes to GPU:0
a = tf.Variable([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
print(a.device)

# Default placement for integer variables falls back to CPU:0
b = tf.Variable([1, 2, 3])
print(b.device)

# Explicit device placement using a context manager
with tf.device("/cpu:0"):
    c = tf.Variable([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
print(c.device)
```

items.term: Placement is a data-movement problem wearing a scheduling costume
items.text: The rule is not 'the GPU is faster, put everything there'. Moving a tensor across the bus costs time, so an operation only belongs on the GPU if the work it does there outweighs the cost of getting the data in and the result out. Preprocessing loses that comparison badly: it touches a lot of bytes and does little arithmetic per byte. Matrix multiplication wins it easily. This is the same arithmetic-intensity test that decides whether to push a computation to storage or pull the data to a compute node.

items.term: A kernel is the unit of support, which is why coverage is uneven
items.text: An operation is supported on a device only if someone wrote and compiled an implementation for that operation and that data type. There is no general translation layer. So 'the GPU cannot do integers' is not a hardware claim - GPUs do integer arithmetic constantly - it is a claim about which kernels were written, because integer variables are rare in the inner loop of a neural network and nobody invested there. Expect this pattern in any accelerator: fast paths for the common cases, silent fallbacks for the rest, and a performance cliff between them.

items.term: Soft placement trades a loud failure for a quiet one
items.text: Falling back silently is what lets one script run unchanged on a four-GPU box and a laptop, and it is genuinely useful. The cost is that a placement you believed you had made may not have happened, and the symptom is a performance mystery rather than an error. The professional habit is to assert rather than assume: read back the device attribute, or turn soft placement off in the environments where a wrong placement would matter. Fail-open defaults deserve an explicit check wherever the open case is expensive.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Data preprocessing and large datasets are best placed on the CPU, while neural network operations belong on the GPU.
TensorFlow automatically assigns supported variables and operations to the first GPU device by default.
Operations without GPU kernels, such as integer tensor operations, automatically fall back to the CPU.
All CPU cores on a system are treated as a single device named /cpu:0 that executes tasks using multithreading.
Developers can explicitly control device placement for operations and variables using the tf.device() context manager.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The rule says preprocessing on the CPU, but then the GPU can sit idle waiting for batches. How do you tell whether your training run is actually input-bound rather than compute-bound?
Look up: the TensorFlow guide "Analyze tf.data performance with the TF Profiler", which covers the input pipeline bottleneck analysis.

items.term: Parallel Execution Across Multiple Devices

blocks.content:
Inside one TF function, TensorFlow runs whatever is ready: it counts each operation's dependencies and queues an operation the moment its count hits zero.

**The question this lesson answers:** you never wrote any threading code. How does TensorFlow decide what runs at the same time across your CPU cores and GPUs, and what has to wait?

### The big picture

```
count dependencies -> zero? -> that device's queue -> run
   finishing an op decrements everyone downstream
```

### 1 · The scheduler is a counter

Modern hardware features multiple CPU cores and GPUs, but managing parallel execution manually across these computing resources is difficult. TensorFlow solves this problem by using a **computation graph** to schedule operations across available devices automatically based on their mathematical dependencies.

When executing a **TF function**, TensorFlow counts the dependencies for every operation in the graph. Operations with zero dependencies, known as source operations, are placed directly into the evaluation queue of their assigned device. As each operation finishes computing, TensorFlow decrements the dependency counter for any downstream operations. An operation enters its device's evaluation queue when its dependency counter reaches zero.

A **TF function** is a Python function TensorFlow has captured as a graph rather than running line by line. If you have looked at a query plan, this is the same object: a DAG of operations whose edges are data dependencies, executed by whatever is ready.

### 2 · Two thread pools on the CPU

On the CPU side, independent operations are handled by an **inter-op thread pool**, while heavy individual operations split their work across an **intra-op thread pool**.

| Pool | Runs | Grain |
|---|---|---|
| inter-op | different operations at the same time | whole operations |
| intra-op | pieces of one multithreaded operation | suboperations |

The primary role of the CPU inter-op thread pool is executing independent graph operations concurrently — it is what turns "these three ops have no dependencies" into three cores actually busy.

### 3 · The GPU does it differently

On the GPU side, operations execute sequentially from the queue, but internal kernels utilize underlying libraries like **cuDNN** to flood GPU threads with parallel sub-computations.

So there is no inter-op pool for a GPU, and the reason is not an omission: individual GPU operations use libraries that already saturate the GPU threads, so running two operations side by side would win nothing. One operation is already using the whole card.

### 4 · Figure 19-10, step by step

As Figure 19-10 below shows, consider a graph where operations A and B run on the CPU while operation C runs on GPU #0. Since A, B, and C have zero dependencies, they run simultaneously. Operation A uses the intra-op thread pool to split its work across CPU cores.

Operations D and E on GPU #0 depend solely on C. Once C finishes, both D and E are queued and executed sequentially on GPU #0 — and C is evaluated only once, even though two operations need its result.

Operation F requires inputs from A, B, D, and E. Operation F has a dependency counter of 4 and must wait for A, B, D, and E; the counter decrements as each predecessor finishes, and only when all four complete is F queued and evaluated on the CPU. The card below follows the same run in order.

One extra guarantee is worth knowing: stateful operations like variable updates are automatically executed in program order, so two writes to the same variable cannot be reordered even though nothing in the graph forces an edge between them.

### 5 · Turning the dial down

A developer can restrict TensorFlow to use only a specific number of threads for running independent CPU operations by calling `tf.config.threading.set_inter_op_parallelism_threads()`, and `set_intra_op_parallelism_threads()` does the same for the other pool. Useful when the machine is shared and you do not want TensorFlow taking every core.

**One-liner for your notes:** dependency counters drive the schedule — zero means queue it, the CPU has two thread pools, and the GPU needs only one because each operation already fills the card.

blocks.title: Worked out: the order of events in Figure 19-10
blocks.content: A, B and C are source operations, so they start at once: A and B go to the CPU's queue and the inter-op thread pool, while C goes to GPU #0's queue. Suppose C finishes first. The dependency counters of D and E drop to 0, so both are pushed to GPU #0's queue and run one after the other; C is evaluated only once, even though both depend on it. Suppose B finishes next. F's counter drops from 4 to 3, which is not 0, so F does not run yet. Once A, D and E are finished, F's counter reaches 0 and F is pushed to the CPU's queue. A GPU needs no inter-op thread pool, because each GPU operation's multithreaded kernel, for example one that uses cuDNN, already floods most of the GPU threads.

blocks.title: Figure 19-10
blocks.caption: Parallelized execution of a TensorFlow graph
blocks.alt: Figure 19-10: Parallelized execution of a TensorFlow graph

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

# Configure CPU thread pools for parallel execution
tf.config.threading.set_inter_op_parallelism_threads(2)
tf.config.threading.set_intra_op_parallelism_threads(4)

@tf.function
def parallel_graph(a, b):
    # Independent ops can execute in parallel
    c = tf.matmul(a, a)  # Executed on available inter-op thread
    d = tf.matmul(b, b)  # Executed concurrently with c
    return c + d         # Dependency counter reaches 0 after c and d finish
```

items.term: Dependency counting is the same scheduler you already run
items.text: Count incoming edges, run anything at zero, decrement downstream as each finishes. That is a DAG scheduler - the same algorithm behind a workflow orchestrator's task graph and behind a query engine's operator pipeline. Two properties come free from that shape and are worth naming: the schedule adapts to how long things actually take rather than to a plan made in advance, and the critical path, not the total work, sets the wall-clock floor. Adding cores cannot beat the longest chain of dependencies.

items.term: Two levels of parallelism, and why mixing them up wastes cores
items.text: Between operations is one axis; inside an operation is another. A graph of many small independent operations needs the inter-op pool and gains nothing from more intra-op threads. One enormous matrix multiply is the opposite. Setting both pools to the core count on a shared machine is how you end up with far more runnable threads than cores, and the contention costs more than the parallelism returns. The same mistake appears whenever a per-task thread pool sits inside an already-parallel executor.

items.term: Data dependencies are not the only ordering constraint
items.text: Two writes to the same variable have no edge between them in the graph, yet reordering them changes the result. TensorFlow therefore forces stateful operations to run in program order regardless of the counter. This is the general limit of dependency-driven execution: it can only reorder freely where the values are immutable, and every piece of mutable state needs an ordering rule bolted on beside the graph. It is exactly why a query planner can shuffle pure projections at will and has to be careful the moment side effects appear.

blocks.title: Key points
items: TensorFlow schedules computational graph operations dynamically using a dependency counter system.
Operations with zero pending dependencies are pushed immediately to device evaluation queues.
CPU parallelism relies on an inter-op thread pool for distinct ops and an intra-op thread pool for suboperations.
GPU queues run operations sequentially, but single operations utilize multithreaded libraries like cuDNN to maximize thread usage.
Stateful operations like variable updates are automatically executed in program order to preserve correctness.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: If the schedule is driven by dependencies, the longest chain sets the floor on how fast a step can run. How would you find that chain, and see which device was idle while it ran?
Look up: the TensorFlow Profiler guide and its trace viewer, which shows per-device operation timelines for a training step.

items.term: Model Parallelism Across Multiple Devices

blocks.content:
Model parallelism cuts one network into pieces and puts each piece on a different device — and for most architectures the communication between the pieces costs more than the parallelism saves.

**The question this lesson answers:** your model is too big for one GPU. Can you just split it across four, and what does the network's shape have to do with the answer?

### The big picture

| Architecture | Split that helps | Why |
|---|---|---|
| fully connected | none of them, really | every part needs every other part |
| convolutional | by chunks, naturally | layers are only partially connected |
| deep recurrent | horizontally, over time | later steps fill up the pipeline |

### 1 · The idea, and the catch

Training large neural networks on a single hardware device presents significant memory and processing bottlenecks. To overcome this, **model parallelism** divides a single neural network into separate sub-networks or chunks and assigns each chunk to a distinct computational device, such as a GPU.

The efficiency of model parallelism depends heavily on the architecture of the network. That sentence is the lesson. The split is not a scheduling decision you can make in the abstract; it is determined by which parts of the network need to talk to which.

### 2 · Fully connected networks: both splits fail

In **fully connected** neural networks — where every unit in a layer feeds every unit in the next — placing each layer on a separate device fails because each layer must idle until the previous layer completes its calculation. The devices take turns, which is not parallelism at all.

Alternatively, splitting fully connected layers vertically allows parallel computation within a layer, but introduces severe cross-device communication delays, as Figure 19-11 below illustrates. The primary drawback of vertically splitting fully connected layers across multiple GPUs is that the high cross-device communication overhead cancels out parallel speedups: each half of the next layer needs the output of both halves of this one.

In Figure 19-11 those transfers are drawn as the dashed arrows, which represent data transfers across different device boundaries during execution. The card below explains them further. Cross-device communication is slow, and slower still when the devices sit on different machines.

### 3 · Where it does work

Conversely, partially connected architectures like convolutional neural networks partition much better, as shown in Figure 19-12 below. A **convolutional** layer connects each unit only to a small neighbourhood of the layer below, so a chunk of the network can be computed with only local information — convolutional neural networks with partially connected layers are the architecture that naturally splits across devices.

Deep recurrent neural networks can also utilize horizontal splitting across devices, achieving parallelism through sequential pipelining as input signals propagate over time. A **recurrent** network processes a sequence one step at a time, carrying state forward.

### 4 · The pipeline, and the verdict

As Figure 19-13 below shows, as a sequence progresses through time steps, devices fill up sequentially like a pipeline until all layers run concurrently. Consider a deep recurrent neural network with four stacked LSTM layers distributed across four separate GPUs. At time step 1, only GPU 1 works on the first input item. By time step 4, GPU 1 processes item 4, GPU 2 processes item 3, GPU 3 processes item 2, and GPU 4 processes item 1.

While this pipelined execution activates all devices simultaneously, the inter-device communication overhead often means a single fast GPU still outperforms this multi-GPU setup in practice.

Ultimately, **model parallelism** is effective only when network connectivity minimizes cross-device communication overhead relative to local computation. The next lesson takes the other route: leave the model whole and split the data instead.

**One-liner for your notes:** splitting one model across devices only pays when the layers are sparsely connected — for dense stacks the cross-device chatter eats the gain, and one fast GPU wins.

blocks.title: The dashed arrows in Figure 19-11
blocks.content: Figure 19-11 shows two ways to split a fully connected network. Placing each layer on a different device does not help, because each layer must wait for the output of the previous layer. Slicing the network vertically, with the left half of each layer on one device and the right half on another, lets both halves of a layer work in parallel, but each half of the next layer needs the output of both halves. That cross-device communication is drawn as the dashed arrows. Because it is slow, and even slower when the devices sit on different machines, it is likely to cancel out the benefit of the parallel computation.

items.term: Partitioning quality is a property of the graph, not of the partitioner
items.text: The question 'can this be split across machines?' is always the same question: is there a cut through the graph that severs few enough edges? A fully connected layer is a complete bipartite graph - every cut severs almost everything - so no clever placement rescues it. A convolutional layer only connects each unit to a small neighbourhood, so cuts exist that sever little. This is the identical criterion that decides whether a join distributes cheaply or forces a broadcast, and it is why you look at the connectivity before you look at the hardware.

items.term: Pipelining converts idle devices into latency you have to hide
items.text: Splitting a recurrent network by layer fills the devices gradually: one busy at the first time step, all of them by the time the signal reaches the output. Steady-state utilisation is good; the fill and drain at the ends are pure waste, and the shorter the sequence the larger that fraction. Every pipeline has this shape - a CPU instruction pipeline, a staged ETL job - and the standard answer is the same, keep the pipeline full by having more work in flight than stages.

items.term: Why the honest answer is often 'use one GPU'
items.text: The book's verdict on a stack of LSTM layers is that a single GPU is much faster in practice, despite the theory of pipelining being sound. That is worth carrying beyond this chapter: distribution has a fixed overhead, and any technique whose benefit scales slower than its communication cost has a size below which it loses. Measuring the single-device baseline before distributing is not a formality, it is the only way to find out which side of that line you are on.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Model parallelism splits a single neural network across multiple computing devices.
Fully connected networks suffer high cross-device communication overhead when split vertically or horizontally.
Partially connected networks like CNNs lend themselves more naturally to model parallelism.
Deep recurrent neural networks achieve pipeline parallelism across time steps when split horizontally across GPUs.
High communication penalties often make single-device execution faster for standard stacked architectures.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Modern language models are far too large for one device, so model parallelism clearly does work at some scale. What changed - the architectures, the interconnect, or the way the split is chosen?
Look up: Mesh TensorFlow, which the book cites here as the next step for model parallelism.

items.term: Data Parallelism in Neural Network Training

blocks.content:
Data parallelism keeps the model whole, puts a copy on every device, feeds each copy a different slice of the batch, and then has to agree on one set of gradients.

**The question this lesson answers:** model parallelism mostly did not pay. What is the approach that does, and what stops it from scaling for ever?

### The big picture

```
batch -> split -> GPU1 GPU2 GPU3 (same model on each)
                    \    |    /
                    average the gradients -> update all
```

### 1 · The idea

Training deep learning models on large datasets can take days or weeks when executed on a single GPU. To accelerate this process, **data parallelism** (also known as single program, multiple data or SPMD) replicates the entire model across multiple processing units, such as GPUs. Each replica processes a distinct mini-batch of training data in parallel.

A **mini-batch** is the small group of training rows processed in one step, and a **gradient** is the direction each parameter should move to reduce the error for that group. This is the shape you already run every day: same program, different partition of the data, results combined at the end.

### 2 · The mirrored strategy

There are two main architectural strategies for managing parameters: the **mirrored strategy** and centralized parameter servers. In the mirrored strategy, identical copies of all model parameters reside on each GPU. During each training step, as Figure 19-14 below demonstrates, every GPU computes gradients on its mini-batch.

An **AllReduce** algorithm then calculates the mean of these gradients across all devices and updates every replica identically to keep them perfectly in sync. So the primary function of an AllReduce algorithm in the mirrored strategy is to calculate the average of gradients across all GPUs and sync the results. In Figure 19-14 that step appears as a cooperative mean operation executed across all replicas — it takes gradients from every GPU and sends one identical result back.

"Cooperative" is doing real work in that phrase: no single node collects everything, the nodes collaborate so that all of them end up holding the same answer.

### 3 · Centralized parameters, and the synchronous choice

Alternatively, parameters can be hosted centrally on parameter servers, as shown in Figure 19-15 below. This setup supports synchronous or asynchronous updates.

| | Synchronous | Asynchronous |
|---|---|---|
| Update happens | after all replicas report | as soon as one replica reports |
| Waiting | fast devices wait for slow ones | none |
| Risk | the slowest device sets the pace | stale gradients |

Synchronous updates aggregate gradients from all replicas before updating parameters, which can create bottlenecks if some GPUs are slower than others.

### 4 · Stale gradients, and how to blunt them

Asynchronous updates allow each replica to update parameters immediately upon finishing its batch. However, as Figure 19-16 below illustrates, asynchronous steps risk introducing **stale gradients**, where updates based on outdated parameters push the optimization in an incorrect direction. Figure 19-16 shows the consequence: applying stale gradients after other updates shifts the parameter path uphill, into worse rather than better territory.

Stale simply means computed against parameter values that have since been replaced by other replicas' updates. The card below lists the book's four mitigations; the one worth remembering is that starting training with a single replica during an initial warmup phase helps, because stale gradients do the most damage at the beginning of training, when gradients are large and different replicas may push the parameters in quite different directions.

### 5 · The ceiling: bandwidth

As a practical example, consider training an image classification model across 50 GPUs. Using data parallelism for dense models typically yields speedups of 25× to 40×, while sparser models like RankBrain can scale up to a 300× speedup across 500 GPUs.

The primary limitation to linear scaling is **bandwidth saturation**, caused by transferring parameters and gradients between devices — the point where adding one more GPU moves more data than it saves in computation. Large sparse models achieve higher scaling speedups than large dense models because sparse model gradients contain mostly zeros and require less network transfer. Figure 19-17 below comes from research aimed at pushing that ceiling further; this lesson does not cover it.

The essential insight is that data parallelism speeds up training by splitting batches across identical model replicas, but network communication overhead and synchronization bottlenecks limit scaling efficiency.

**One-liner for your notes:** copy the model to every device, split the batch, average the gradients — and expect bandwidth, not compute, to be what stops you scaling.

blocks.title: Fighting stale gradients, and why sparse models scale
blocks.content: The book lists four ways to reduce the effect of stale gradients: reduce the learning rate; drop stale gradients or scale them down; adjust the mini-batch size; and start the first few epochs using just one replica, which is called the warmup phase. The warmup helps because stale gradients do the most damage at the beginning of training, when the gradients are large and the parameters have not settled into a valley of the cost function yet, so different replicas may push them in quite different directions. Bandwidth saturation is more severe for large dense models, which have a lot of parameters and gradients to transfer. It is less severe for large sparse models, because their gradients are typically mostly zeros and so can be communicated efficiently.

items.term: AllReduce avoids the coordinator that a naive design would need
items.text: The obvious way to average gradients is to send them all to one node and broadcast the result - and that node's link then carries traffic proportional to the number of replicas, so it becomes the bottleneck the moment you add devices. AllReduce algorithms arrange the exchange so every node sends and receives a bounded amount regardless of how many participate, and all of them finish holding the same answer. It is the same reason a distributed aggregate is computed as a tree or a ring of partial results rather than pulled to one place.

items.term: Synchronous versus asynchronous is consistency versus throughput
items.text: Synchronous keeps every replica on identical parameters and pays for it by running at the speed of the slowest device at every step. Asynchronous never waits and pays in correctness: a replica computes its gradient against parameters that others have already replaced, so the step it proposes points somewhere the model no longer is. The book reports that a 2016 benchmark found synchronous updates with a few spare replicas beat asynchronous, converging faster and producing a better model - which is a useful reminder that the option with no waiting is not automatically the fast one.

items.term: The scaling ceiling is bandwidth, and it is predictable
items.text: Every step moves gradients proportional to the parameter count, whatever the batch size, so communication per step is roughly fixed while computation per device shrinks as you add devices. There is therefore always a device count at which the transfer dominates, and past it another GPU makes training slower. That is why the same technique gives 25 to 40 times on 50 GPUs for dense models and 300 times on 500 for sparse ones whose gradients are mostly zeros: the difference is bytes on the wire, not arithmetic.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Data parallelism replicates the full model across multiple devices, processing different mini-batches simultaneously.
The mirrored strategy uses an AllReduce algorithm to average gradients across all GPUs synchronously.
Centralized parameter servers store weights externally and support both synchronous and asynchronous updates.
Asynchronous updates avoid idle waiting time but can suffer from stale gradients that destabilize convergence.
Bandwidth saturation from transferring weights and gradients limits scaling, making sparse models scale better than dense models.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The book reports that synchronous updates with a few spare replicas beat asynchronous updates in one 2016 benchmark. What was actually measured there, and does the conclusion still hold at today's cluster sizes?
Look up: Jianmin Chen et al., "Revisiting Distributed Synchronous SGD", arXiv:1604.00981 (2016), which is the paper the book cites for this result.

items.term: TensorFlow Distribution Strategies API

blocks.content:
The distribution strategies API turns multi-GPU data parallelism into two extra lines: build the model inside a strategy scope, then train normally.

**The question this lesson answers:** the previous lesson explained mirrored data parallelism. What do you actually type to get it, and what changes about your training code?

### The big picture

```
strategy = MirroredStrategy()
with strategy.scope():
    build model; compile model
model.fit(...)          # batch split across GPUs for you
```

### 1 · What the API hides

When training deep learning models on large datasets, a single processor often suffers from long execution times. To accelerate this process across multiple hardware devices on one machine, TensorFlow provides the **Distribution Strategies API**. This API abstracts the underlying hardware complexity, allowing developers to scale model training without refactoring core neural network logic.

A **scope** here is a Python context manager — a `with` block. Inside it, Keras knows it must create variables in replicated form rather than singly, which is why model creation has to happen inside and training does not.

### 2 · What MirroredStrategy does per step

The API uses **data parallelism** through strategies like `tf.distribute.MirroredStrategy`. Under this approach, TensorFlow replicates the entire model architecture onto every available device, such as multiple graphics processing units. Each device holds a mirror of the model parameters, called a **MirroredVariable**.

During each training step, TensorFlow automatically splits each input batch into smaller equal sub-batches, assigning one sub-batch to each device replica. Each device processes its sub-batch, calculates gradients locally, and uses an efficient reduction algorithm — such as the NVIDIA Collective Communications Library — to compute the mean gradient and update parameters synchronously across all devices. So the primary function of MirroredStrategy is that it replicates model variables across GPUs and splits training batches evenly.

That default reduction backend is worth naming: MirroredStrategy uses the NVIDIA Collective Communications Library by default, through the `tf.distribute.NcclAllReduce` class, which is usually faster. The card below lists the alternatives and when to try them.

### 3 · The one number you have to get right

For example, consider a machine equipped with 4 GPUs. A developer instantiates a `MirroredStrategy` object and creates a Keras model within the `strategy.scope()` distribution context. If the developer specifies a total training batch size of 100 samples, TensorFlow divides the batch evenly, distributing 25 samples to each GPU per step.

The batch size should be divisible by the number of GPU replicas because it allows TensorFlow to allocate equal sub-batch sizes to all available devices. An uneven split means one replica does more work per step than the others, and since the update is synchronous everyone waits for it.

### 4 · Saving, and getting the parallelism back

After training, saving the model produces a standard single-device file. Reloaded normally, it runs as a regular model on a single device like GPU #0 or the system CPU — the distribution is a property of how you *ran* it, not of the artifact. Reloading it inside a `strategy.scope()` block allows parallel prediction across all 4 GPUs.

### 5 · The centralized alternative

For data parallelism with centralized parameters, use `tf.distribute.experimental.CentralStorageStrategy()` instead. CentralStorageStrategy stores all model variables on the CPU or on GPU #0 if only one GPU exists, while the GPUs do the computing — the `parameter_device` argument names that storage device, and the `compute_devices` argument lists the workers, defaulting to all available GPUs.

The key insight is that wrapping model creation inside a distribution context automatically manages cross-device variable replication, batch partitioning, and gradient synchronization with minimal code changes.

**One-liner for your notes:** build inside `strategy.scope()`, keep the batch size divisible by the replica count, and remember the saved model comes back single-device unless you reload it in a scope.

blocks.title: MirroredStrategy defaults and CentralStorageStrategy
blocks.content: By default, `MirroredStrategy` uses the NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) for the AllReduce mean operation, through the `tf.distribute.NcclAllReduce` class, which is usually faster. You can change it by setting the `cross_device_ops` argument to an instance of `tf.distribute.HierarchicalCopyAllReduce` or `tf.distribute.ReductionToOneDevice`; the best choice depends on the number and types of GPUs, so the alternatives are worth a try. For data parallelism with centralized parameters, use `tf.distribute.experimental.CentralStorageStrategy()`. Its `compute_devices` argument lists the worker devices, which by default are all available GPUs, and its `parameter_device` argument sets the device that stores the parameters, which by default is the CPU, or the GPU if there is just one.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

strategy = tf.distribute.MirroredStrategy()

with strategy.scope():
    model = tf.keras.Sequential([
        tf.keras.layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"),
        tf.keras.layers.Dense(10)
    ])
    model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="mse")

batch_size = 100
model.fit(X_train, y_train, epochs=10, batch_size=batch_size)
```

items.term: Why the scope has to wrap creation and not training
items.text: Variables are replicated at the moment they are created, so the strategy must be in force then. fit() only reads what already exists and can be called outside. This is why the API is a context manager rather than a flag on fit, and it is the source of the classic error: build the model first, wrap fit in the scope, and the variables are ordinary - the code runs, uses one GPU, and reports nothing wrong. An API that depends on where an object was constructed will always have this failure mode.

items.term: The batch size means two different things once you distribute
items.text: The number you pass is the global batch; each replica sees that divided by the replica count. So moving from one GPU to four with the same batch size quarters the per-replica batch, which changes batch-normalisation statistics and the effective noise in each step - the learning dynamics are not identical, even though the code did not change. Going the other way and holding the per-replica batch fixed grows the global batch, which usually requires the learning rate to be raised to match. Distribution is not transparent to the maths, only to the plumbing.

items.term: Distribution is a property of the run, not of the artifact
items.text: A model saved from a mirrored run is an ordinary single-device model; the replication existed only while it ran. That is the right separation - it means an artifact trained on eight GPUs can be served on a CPU, and the serving topology is chosen independently of the training one. The cost is a small trap in the other direction: loading it and expecting parallel prediction silently gives you one device unless the load happens inside a scope.

blocks.title: Key points
items: The Distribution Strategies API handles hardware complexity when scaling models across multiple devices.
MirroredStrategy replicates model variables as MirroredVariable instances across available GPUs.
Training batch sizes should be divisible by the total replica count to ensure equal workload distribution.
Saved models revert to standard single-device execution unless reloaded inside a distribution scope.
CentralStorageStrategy keeps variables on a central device like the CPU while distributing computation.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: MirroredStrategy defaults to NCCL for the gradient averaging, and the book says the alternatives are worth trying because the best choice depends on the number and types of GPUs. What in the hardware topology actually decides that?
Look up: Sylvain Jeaugey's post on massively scaling deep learning training with NCCL, which the book cites for AllReduce implementation detail.

items.term: Training a Model on a TensorFlow Cluster

blocks.content:
Once the GPUs live on different machines, the strategy needs a map of the cluster, and that map arrives in one environment variable.

**The question this lesson answers:** MirroredStrategy scaled across the GPUs in one box. What changes when the workers are separate machines, and how does each process learn who it is?

### The big picture

```
Machine A  ps 0     :2221
Machine A  worker 0 :2222   <- chief
Machine B  worker 1 :2222
each process reads TF_CONFIG to learn the map + its role
```

### 1 · A cluster is a set of tasks with roles

When a neural network model or training dataset becomes too large for a single machine, you must scale computation across multiple nodes. A **TensorFlow cluster** addresses this by enabling a group of parallel processes, called tasks or TF servers, to coordinate execution and weight updates over a network connection.

Each task in a cluster operates with a specific role, such as a **worker**, **chief**, **parameter server**, or **evaluator**.

| Role | Does |
|---|---|
| worker | the model computations, usually on a machine with GPUs |
| chief | worker computation plus logs and checkpoints |
| parameter server | holds variable values, usually on a CPU-only machine |
| evaluator | evaluation; not used often |

Workers perform heavy model computations, while the chief worker handles extra administrative duties like writing logs and saving checkpoints. The primary distinction is therefore that the chief task performs standard worker computations while also handling tasks like checkpointing and logging — it is a worker with a second job, not a coordinator that sits above the others. There is a single chief in a cluster, and the card below notes that if no chief is specified explicitly, the first worker is the chief by convention.

### 2 · The map itself

As Figure 19-18 below shows, tasks map to network addresses defined by IP addresses and ports. A single physical machine can host multiple tasks if they run on different ports. In the figure, Machine A runs a parameter server on port 2221 and worker 0 on port 2222, while Machine B runs worker 1 on port 2222 — so Machine A runs two separate TF server tasks on different TCP ports, while Machine B runs one TF server task.

To configure communication, every process must be given a cluster specification prior to starting TensorFlow. This is accomplished by setting the **TF_CONFIG** environment variable, which contains a JSON dictionary detailing the cluster layout and the specific task's role and index. A process in a TensorFlow cluster learns about the cluster layout and its own identity by reading the cluster specification and task details from the TF_CONFIG environment variable.

Setting it outside Python is the norm, and for a good reason: every machine then runs byte-identical code and only the environment differs. That is the same discipline as keeping connection details in the environment rather than the job.

### 3 · Training across machines

During synchronous training using `MultiWorkerMirroredStrategy` — the distribution strategy designed for synchronous data-parallel training across multiple worker machines — workers calculate gradients on local data subsets and synchronize them using **AllReduce** algorithms such as RING or NCCL.

Consider a training scenario with two worker tasks. Worker 0 acts as the chief, while worker 1 acts as a secondary worker. Both run identical script code wrapped in the distribution strategy scope.

### 4 · The rule that looks wrong and is not

When saving the final model, worker 0 writes the permanent checkpoint, whereas worker 1 writes to a temporary directory that it immediately deletes. Writing a file only to delete it looks like waste, and it is not: non-chief workers must execute model saving code because collective network operations like AllReduce require all workers to enter synchronization steps together. Saving can trigger those collective operations, so a worker that skips the code path stops stepping in time with the others and the whole job stalls.

The essential insight to remember is that all participating workers must execute collective network operations synchronously, requiring identical script steps across all workers even when secondary workers discard their saved outputs.

**One-liner for your notes:** a cluster is roles plus addresses handed to every process in TF_CONFIG, and under MultiWorkerMirroredStrategy every worker runs every step — including the save it is going to throw away.

blocks.title: Other task types and strategies in a cluster
blocks.content: A parameter server only keeps track of variable values, usually on a CPU-only machine, and this task type is only used with the `ParameterServerStrategy`. If you prefer asynchronous data parallelism with parameter servers, you change the strategy to `ParameterServerStrategy`, add one or more parameter servers, and set `TF_CONFIG` for each task; the workers then work asynchronously, although the replicas on each worker work synchronously. An evaluator task takes care of evaluation and is not used often. If no chief is specified explicitly, the first worker is the chief by convention. With `MultiWorkerMirroredStrategy`, the first workers to start stay blocked at the AllReduce step, and training begins as soon as the last worker starts up.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import os, json, tempfile, tensorflow as tf

strategy = tf.distribute.MultiWorkerMirroredStrategy()
resolver = tf.distribute.cluster_resolver.TFConfigClusterResolver()

with strategy.scope():
    model = tf.keras.Sequential([tf.keras.layers.Dense(10)])
    model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="mse")

model.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=5)

if resolver.task_id == 0:
    model.save("my_model", save_format="tf")
else:
    tmpdir = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    model.save(tmpdir, save_format="tf")
    tf.io.gfile.rmtree(tmpdir)
```

items.term: Identical code plus differing environment is a deployment pattern, not a convenience
items.text: Every task runs the same script; TF_CONFIG tells each one which task it is. That means one artifact to build, test and ship, and the topology becomes configuration rather than code - the same reason a stateless service takes its role and its peers from the environment. It also means a wrong TF_CONFIG is a runtime failure with a confusing shape: processes that cannot find each other simply block, because from inside the code there is nothing to distinguish 'the last worker has not started yet' from 'the last worker never will'.

items.term: Collective operations make every participant load-bearing
items.text: AllReduce is a rendezvous: it completes only when all participants arrive. Any branch that causes one worker to skip a collective hangs the job rather than degrading it, which is why a non-chief worker saves a model it is about to delete. The general rule for collective code is that control flow must be identical across participants - conditional logic may change what is written to disk, never how many collectives are entered. The failure mode is a stall with no error, which is far harder to diagnose than a crash.

items.term: Why the chief is a worker with extra duties rather than a separate coordinator
items.text: Making the chief a full participant means there is no idle node and no separate code path for the common case. The cost is a single point of responsibility for checkpoints and logs: lose the chief and you lose the write, not the computation. Contrast the parameter server, which genuinely is a different role because it holds state and does no gradient work - and note that it only appears with ParameterServerStrategy, because synchronous mirrored training has nowhere to put it.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A TensorFlow cluster consists of tasks running on specific IP addresses and ports with roles like worker, chief, or parameter server.
The TF_CONFIG environment variable specifies both the full cluster layout and the individual process role and index.
The chief worker performs training computation while also handling administrative work such as saving checkpoints.
When using MultiWorkerMirroredStrategy, all workers must execute matching steps to keep collective operations like AllReduce synchronized.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: If one worker dies mid-run, the collective never completes and the job stalls. What does recovery look like for a synchronous multi-worker job, and what has to be in place beforehand?
Look up: the TensorFlow guide "Multi-worker training with Keras", specifically its section on fault tolerance and the BackupAndRestore callback.

items.term: Running Custom Training Jobs on Vertex AI

blocks.content:
Running the same distributed script on Vertex AI means changing one thing: where the chief writes its outputs, and how it knows it is the chief.

**The question this lesson answers:** you have a working `MultiWorkerMirroredStrategy` script. What do you edit before handing it to a managed service that provisions the machines for you?

### The big picture

| On your own cluster | On Vertex AI |
|---|---|
| chief is worker index 0 | chief is the task whose type is chief |
| outputs go to a local path | outputs go to GCS paths in env variables |
| you start each machine | job.run() provisions them |

### 1 · Why hand it over

When training deep learning models on large datasets, local computing resources often lack sufficient GPU capacity and storage bandwidth. Cloud platforms solve this problem by managing clusters of virtual machines dynamically. **Vertex AI** provides a managed environment where you can execute custom TensorFlow training scripts across distributed compute nodes without manually configuring the underlying infrastructure.

Almost all of the training code is unchanged. What changes is the plumbing around it.

### 2 · Outputs move to cloud storage

To run a script on Vertex AI, you must adapt how output paths and worker roles are resolved. Instead of writing checkpoints and logs to local folders, the **chief node** must save artifacts to Google Cloud Storage using environment variables provided by the service.

| Variable | Holds the path for |
|---|---|
| AIP_MODEL_DIR | the final saved model |
| AIP_CHECKPOINT_DIR | training checkpoints |
| AIP_TENSORBOARD_LOG_DIR | TensorBoard logs |

So a TensorFlow script running on Vertex AI should determine the storage location for the final model by reading the path stored inside the `AIP_MODEL_DIR` environment variable, rather than hardcoding one. The service injects these, which is what lets the same script run in any job.

Non-chief workers write temporary files locally to prevent storage collisions — writing from multiple nodes to the same GCS destination causes file conflicts, and this is the same rule as the previous lesson's throwaway save, now with a storage reason on top of the synchronisation one.

### 3 · Identifying the chief

Furthermore, the chief task must be identified by checking whether `resolver.task_type == "chief"` rather than relying on task indices, ensuring robust coordination across cluster nodes. Vertex AI sets the task type explicitly, so the recommended condition for identifying the chief node in a Vertex AI custom training script is checking if `resolver.task_type == "chief"`. On your own cluster the first worker is the chief by convention; here the service says so directly, and the index check would be guessing.

### 4 · Reading the training data

Data input pipelines on GCS rely on `tf.io.gfile` to stream files directly into TensorFlow datasets, so a dataset can take a `gs://` path as if it were a filename. **gfile** is TensorFlow's file-access layer, and it handles both local files and cloud storage, which is why no download step appears in the script.

### 5 · Submitting the job

Consider a scenario where you launch a custom job using `aiplatform.CustomTrainingJob`. You specify the Python script path, the base training container image, a serving container image for deployment, and a Cloud Storage staging bucket. When executing `job.run()`, you request two worker machines, each equipped with two GPUs. Vertex AI provisions the virtual machines, injects the necessary environment variables, reads training data directly from Cloud Storage using `tf.io.gfile`, and executes the distributed strategy.

Hyperparameter values can be passed directly to a standard custom training script by setting the `args` parameter during the execution of the `run()` method, or as environment variables through the `environment_variables` parameter. The card below notes that for a large search the book points to Vertex AI's tuning service instead — the subject of the next lesson.

The essential takeaway is that Vertex AI standardizes cluster orchestration by passing storage locations through dedicated environment variables and managing node provisioning automatically.

**One-liner for your notes:** same distributed script, three `AIP_*` paths instead of local folders, and `resolver.task_type == "chief"` instead of index zero.

blocks.title: Passing hyperparameters to a training job
blocks.content: To try out a few hyperparameter values with a custom training job, one option is to run multiple jobs. You can pass the values to your script as command-line arguments by setting the `args` parameter when calling the `run()` method, or you can pass them as environment variables with the `environment_variables` parameter. In the book's example, `run()` uses `replica_count=2` and `accelerator_count=2`, which gives two workers with two GPUs each. Once the job is complete, `run()` returns a trained model that you can deploy to an endpoint or use for batch predictions. For a large search, the book recommends Vertex AI's hyperparameter tuning service instead.

blocks.content:
```python
if resolver.task_type == "chief":
    model_dir = os.getenv("AIP_MODEL_DIR")
    tensorboard_log_dir = os.getenv("AIP_TENSORBOARD_LOG_DIR")
    checkpoint_dir = os.getenv("AIP_CHECKPOINT_DIR")
else:
    tmp_dir = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
    model_dir = tmp_dir / "model"
    tensorboard_log_dir = tmp_dir / "logs"
    checkpoint_dir = tmp_dir / "ckpt"

callbacks = [tf.keras.callbacks.TensorBoard(tensorboard_log_dir),
             tf.keras.callbacks.ModelCheckpoint(checkpoint_dir)]
```

items.term: Injected paths are how a job becomes portable
items.text: The script does not know or care where its outputs go; the platform tells it at launch. That is what lets one script run in a test job, a production job and a tuning trial with no edit, and it is why every mature job runner does the same thing - the alternative, a path in the code, forces a code change for every environment and guarantees that someone eventually overwrites production output from a test run. The discipline generalises: anything that differs between environments belongs in the environment.

items.term: Convention breaks when a platform gets an opinion
items.text: On your own cluster the first worker is the chief by convention, so index zero is a safe test. Vertex AI assigns the role explicitly, so the index and the role are independent facts and testing the index is testing the wrong thing. This is a small instance of a general hazard: code that relies on a convention keeps working right up until it meets a system that makes the same information explicit and orders things differently. Ask for the property you actually need, not for something that usually correlates with it.

items.term: A filesystem abstraction over object storage is convenient and not free
items.text: tf.io.gfile lets a gs:// path stand in for a filename, so the dataset code is unchanged. Underneath it is HTTP against an object store, which behaves differently from a local disk in ways that show up under load: first-byte latency is far higher, seeks are expensive, there are no real directories, and listing is a paged API call rather than a syscall. The practical consequence for training is that many small files hurt badly and large sequential reads are fine - the same guidance you already apply to file sizing in a lake.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Vertex AI injects environment variables like `AIP_MODEL_DIR` to specify Cloud Storage paths for saving models and logs.
The chief task node must be identified using `resolver.task_type == "chief"` rather than checking for index zero.
Non-chief worker nodes write temporary output files to local directories to avoid overwriting the chief output.
Data input pipelines on GCS rely on `tf.io.gfile` to stream files directly into TensorFlow datasets.
Custom training jobs are executed using `aiplatform.CustomTrainingJob` by specifying script paths, containers, and compute hardware.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: The script reads training data straight from object storage over the network. At what point does that input pipeline become the bottleneck rather than the GPUs, and what is the usual fix?
Look up: the TensorFlow guide "Better performance with the tf.data API", in particular its sections on interleave, prefetch and file sharding.

items.term: Hyperparameter Tuning on Vertex AI

blocks.content:
Instead of running one training job, you declare a search space and let Vertex AI run many trials, each one choosing its settings from what the earlier trials scored.

**The question this lesson answers:** you do not know the right learning rate or layer width. How do you get the cloud to search for them instead of running jobs by hand?

### The big picture

```
script reads args -> trains -> reports metric (hypertune)
          ^                                  |
          +---- service picks next values <--+
        one run = a trial   all runs = a study
```

### 1 · What the service does

Finding optimal hyperparameters like learning rates and layer counts manually is time-consuming and inefficient. **Vertex AI** solves this problem by providing an automated hyperparameter tuning service driven by a Bayesian optimization algorithm. This service automatically explores a defined parameter space to discover configurations that maximize or minimize a specific model evaluation metric.

A **hyperparameter** is a setting you fix before training rather than one training learns — the closest thing you already use is a `--conf` value passed at submit time. **Bayesian optimization** means the search builds a model of which settings look promising from the results so far, and spends its next trials where that model expects the most gain. It is therefore not a grid and not random: order matters, because later trials use earlier results.

### 2 · What the script must do

To use this service, you must create a standard Python training script that accepts hyperparameters as command-line arguments using libraries like `argparse`. Inside the script, you build and train your model using the received arguments.

Crucially, the training script must report its evaluation metrics back to the service using the `hypertune` library — a training script passes performance results back to the Vertex AI hyperparameter tuning service by calling the report method from the hypertune library. Without that call the service has no signal and the search degenerates into unrelated runs.

The metric name you report has to match the metric name the job is told to optimise; they are joined by that string alone.

### 3 · Trials and studies

Each individual training execution with a specific hyperparameter configuration is called a **trial**, and the complete collection of trials makes up a **study**. Put plainly: a trial is one run with specific parameters, and a study is the set of all trials.

### 4 · Declaring the search space

In a typical scenario, a user configures a template using `CustomJob.from_local_script` to define the training environment and GPU requirements. They then launch a `HyperparameterTuningJob` by specifying search boundaries.

| Parameter | Spec | Range | Scale |
|---|---|---|---|
| learning_rate | double | 1e-3 to 10 | log |
| n_neurons | integer | 1 to 300 | linear |

The example also sets `max_trial_count` to `100` with `parallel_trial_count` set to `20`. Vertex AI runs these trials in parallel, continuously collecting metric reports.

A **log scale** on the learning rate means the search treats 0.001 to 0.01 as the same size of step as 0.01 to 0.1, which is how learning rates actually behave. A linear scale on a neuron count treats every unit the same.

### 5 · The parallelism trade-off

The key insight to remember is that higher parallelism speeds up total execution time, but because initial parallel trials cannot benefit from early feedback, you must increase the total trial count to maintain search quality. Search completes faster, but early trials cannot learn from previous results.

The book gives the numbers: raising `parallel_trial_count` from 20 to 60 can cut the total search time by a factor of up to 3, but the first 60 trials all start without the other trials' feedback, so it suggests raising the maximum number of trials from 100 to about 140. You are buying wall-clock time with extra trials.

The card below covers the alternative — running Keras Tuner on Vertex AI machines, where one machine is the chief and the rest are workers. That only requires setting three environment variables on each machine: `KERASTUNER_TUNER_ID`, `KERASTUNER_ORACLE_IP` and `KERASTUNER_ORACLE_PORT`.

**One-liner for your notes:** a trial is one run and a study is all of them — report the metric with hypertune, declare the ranges, and buy speed with parallel trials by raising the trial count to pay for the lost feedback.

blocks.title: Keras Tuner on Vertex AI, and more parallel trials
blocks.content: Instead of the tuning service, you can run Keras Tuner on Vertex AI VMs. One machine acts as the chief (the oracle) and the others act as workers: each worker asks the chief which hyperparameter values to try, trains the model, and reports its performance back. This only requires setting three environment variables on each machine: `KERASTUNER_TUNER_ID` ("chief" on the chief, or a unique ID such as "worker0" on a worker), `KERASTUNER_ORACLE_IP` (the chief's IP address or hostname), and `KERASTUNER_ORACLE_PORT` (the TCP port the chief listens on). For the tuning service itself, raising `parallel_trial_count` from 20 to 60 can cut the total search time by a factor of up to 3, but the first 60 trials start without the other trials' feedback, so the book suggests raising the maximum number of trials from 100 to about 140.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import hypertune
from google.cloud import aiplatform
from google.cloud.aiplatform import hyperparameter_tuning as hpt

# Report metrics inside the training script
tuner = hypertune.HyperTune()
tuner.report_hyperparameter_tuning_metric(
    hyperparameter_metric_tag="accuracy",
    metric_value=0.9774,
    global_step=1000
)

# Configure parameter search space in job submission
parameter_spec = {
    "learning_rate": hpt.DoubleParameterSpec(min=1e-3, max=10, scale="log"),
    "n_neurons": hpt.IntegerParameterSpec(min=1, max=300, scale="linear")
}
```

items.term: Why a sequential search resists parallelism by construction
items.text: Bayesian optimisation earns its advantage by choosing each trial in light of every finished trial. Running sixty at once means sixty choices made with the same stale information, so parallel trials are individually worse than sequential ones - which is exactly why the book raises the trial budget from about 100 to about 140 when parallelism goes from 20 to 60. You are not getting the same search faster; you are buying wall-clock time with extra compute. Any adaptive algorithm has this shape, and it is the opposite of a grid search, which parallelises perfectly because it never learns.

items.term: A log scale encodes a belief about the parameter
items.text: Searching a learning rate from 0.001 to 10 on a linear scale would put almost every sample above 1, where training simply diverges - the interesting region occupies a sliver of the range. A log scale makes each multiplication of the value an equal step, which matches how learning rates behave. A neuron count is different: 200 versus 210 is a small change and 1 versus 11 is a large one, so linear is right there. Choosing the scale is a modelling decision about the parameter, and it usually matters more than widening the bounds.

items.term: Optimising a metric means the metric had better be the right one
items.text: The service maximises the number your script reports, and it will exploit any looseness in it. Report training accuracy and it will find the most overfitted configuration available. Report validation accuracy from a single small split and it will find the configuration best suited to that split's noise, which is tuning on the test set by a slower route. The defence is the ordinary one - a validation set the search may see and a held-out set it never does, so the winning trial can be checked against data that had no vote.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Vertex AI uses Bayesian optimization to discover optimal hyperparameter combinations efficiently.
Training scripts accept hyperparameter values via command-line arguments and report metrics using the hypertune package.
A single execution with specific hyperparameter values is a trial, while the full set of trials is a study.
Increasing parallel trial counts speeds up overall search time but reduces the benefit of sequential trial feedback.

blocks.title: Look it up
items: Bayesian optimisation is one search strategy among several. When does a cheaper method that kills bad trials early beat it, given a fixed compute budget?
Look up: the Keras Tuner documentation's comparison of its Hyperband, Bayesian optimisation and random search tuners.

False
