quizData.question: In the spam filter example of Mitchell's definition, what plays the role of the experience E?
options: The emails users have already flagged as spam or ham
The ratio of emails that the filter classifies correctly
The rules a programmer writes to detect spam words
The task of flagging new incoming emails as spam
explanations: The lesson names the emails that users have already flagged as spam or ham as the experience, because they are the training data the filter learns from.
The ratio of emails classified correctly is the performance measure P, not the experience. It is how the filter is judged, not what it learns from.
Hand-written rules belong to traditional programming, where rules produce answers. In machine learning the experience is data, and the rules are what the learning produces.
Flagging spam is the task T in the spam filter example. The task is what you want done, while the experience is the data the system learns from.

quizData.question: What does the lesson say you have if you cannot name the task, the experience and the performance measure?
options: A well-posed problem that only lacks more data
A learning problem under Samuel's informal definition
A wish, not yet a machine learning problem
A learning problem, since having data is enough
explanations: A well-posed learning problem needs a named task, experience and performance measure. Adding more data does not supply the missing pieces.
Samuel's definition is the informal one, but the lesson never says it turns a vague goal into a learning problem. Without the three named parts, the lesson calls the goal a wish.
The lesson states that if you cannot name all three, you do not yet have a machine learning problem, only a wish. Naming them is what makes the problem well posed.
The lesson says data alone is not learning, as the example of downloading every Wikipedia article shows. Without a task and a performance measure, having data is not enough.

quizData.question: How does the lesson contrast traditional programming with machine learning?
options: Traditional code turns answers into rules; machine learning turns rules into answers
Both turn rules into answers, but machine learning is given far more data
Traditional code learns from experience; machine learning follows fixed rules
Traditional code turns rules into answers; machine learning turns answers into rules
explanations: This option reverses the two approaches. In traditional programming a programmer supplies the rules, and in machine learning the rules are what gets produced from the answers.
Machine learning does not take rules as its input. The lesson says it takes answers and produces the rules, so the difference is not just the amount of data.
Learning from experience is what machine learning does, according to Mitchell's definition. Traditional code follows the rules that a programmer spells out.
The lesson says the arrow turns around: traditional code takes rules and produces answers, while machine learning takes answers and produces the rules.

quizData.question: Why does the loop of hand-writing spam detection rules never really end?
options: Each rule must be retrained on every new email that arrives
The learning algorithm needs a new training step for each word
The rules cannot be tested until the whole list is written
The rules are written by hand while spam keeps changing
explanations: Rules are not retrained; they are written and patched by a person. Retraining on data is what the machine learning route does instead.
A learning algorithm and a training step belong to the machine learning route, not to the rule-writing loop. The hand-written loop has no training step at all.
The traditional loop tests the rules after writing them and then repeats. The lesson says the loop continues because the world keeps moving, not because testing has to wait.
The lesson explains that the loop never ends because the rules are hand-written and the world keeps moving. Every time the spam changes, a human has to update the rules.

quizData.question: In the machine learning route to building a spam filter, what replaces the step of writing detection rules?
options: A testing step that checks each rule against new mail
A training step that learns from spam and ham examples
A shorter list of rules that only its author maintains
A data mining step that lists every suspicious word
explanations: Testing rules is part of the traditional loop. The machine learning route removes the hand-written rules and trains on examples instead.
The lesson says the machine learning route replaces rule-writing with a training step. A learning algorithm is fed examples of spam and ham and works out which patterns predict spam.
A list of rules that only its author can maintain is the problem with the traditional approach. The machine learning route drops hand-written rules in favour of training.
Data mining is the practice of inspecting what a trained model learned to find unexpected correlations. It is not the step that replaces writing rules.

quizData.question: Speech recognition is the book's standard example of which situation where machine learning earns its place?

A problem solved today by a long list of hand-tuned rules
A fluctuating environment where the data keeps changing
Gaining insight into a large or complex dataset
explanations: The lesson uses speech recognition for problems with no good traditional solution, because no reasonable set of hand-written rules can tell "one" from "two" across every speaker.

Problems already handled by a long list of hand-tuned rules are a separate situation, where machine learning shortens the code. Speech recognition is described as having no good rule-based solution at all.
Fluctuating environments are illustrated by spammers changing "4U" to "For U". Speech recognition is used for a different situation in the lesson.
Gaining insight into large datasets is the data mining situation. The lesson does not use speech recognition as its example of that.

quizData.question: Spammers switch from writing "4U" to writing "For U". What does a spam filter that is retrained on recent mail do?
options: Waits for a human to notice the change and patch it
Picks up the new pattern and flags it automatically
Keeps missing the phrase until its code is rewritten
Flags only the old "4U" spelling it was trained on
explanations: Needing a human to notice the change and patch it describes a rule-based filter. The retrained filter learns the new pattern from fresh data without anyone writing a rule.
The lesson says a filter retrained on recent mail picks up the new pattern and flags it automatically. That ability to adapt is described as the sharpest advantage over rules.
Rewriting code is how a rule-based filter would be fixed. A filter retrained on recent mail learns the new phrasing from the data instead.
The filter is retrained on recent mail, which contains the new "For U" spelling. It therefore learns the new pattern rather than staying stuck on the old one.

quizData.question: What guarantees that the k-means labeling/re-centering loop eventually stops?

The mean squared distance between instances and their centroids can only decrease or stay the same each step, and it cannot go negative
Scikit-Learn stops it after exactly 3 iterations
The centroids are frozen after the first labeling step
explanations: Review the chapter explanation: Each alternation (relabel, then recompute centroids) can only make the total squared distance from instances to their assigned centroid go down or stay flat, never up. A quantity that keeps shrinking (or holding steady) but is bounded below by zero has to stop changing eventually, which is what guarantees convergence — though not necessarily to the best possible clustering.

quizData.question: What action should you take if you decide to change the batch size of your model?

quizData.question: Which three activation functions replace the step function in multilayer perceptrons so that backpropagation can train them?
options: Sigmoid, tanh, and ReLU

Softmax, sign, and Heaviside
Softplus, softmax, and sign
explanations: Correct. "Multilayer Perceptrons and Backpropagation" names the sigmoid $\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$, the hyperbolic tangent and the rectified linear unit $\max(0, z)$ as the activations that replaced the step function. The sigmoid has a nonzero derivative everywhere, so gradient descent can always make progress; ReLU is not differentiable at $z = 0$ and has a zero derivative for $z < 0$, yet it works very well in practice and has become the default.

Heaviside and sign are the step functions of Equation 10-1 in "The Perceptron", so they are what was replaced. Their flat segments give zero derivatives, which block gradient descent from updating the weights.

Softmax is the output activation for multiclass classification, and sign and Heaviside are step functions with flat segments. This set does not describe the three functions that replaced the step function.

Softplus keeps regression outputs positive, softmax turns output scores into class probabilities, and sign is itself a step function. This set mixes output activations with the very function that was being replaced.

explanations: Adding two separate layer outputs treats the layers as parallel branches that both read $\mathbf{X}$. In the feedforward MLP of "Multilayer Perceptrons and Backpropagation", data flows through the hidden layer first, so the output layer reads the hidden layer's result rather than the raw inputs.

This equation applies the output layer's weights to the raw inputs and the hidden layer's weights last. In a feedforward MLP, as "Multilayer Perceptrons and Backpropagation" describes, data moves from the input layer through the hidden layer to the output layer, so the order is reversed here.

Correct. Equation 10-2 in "The Perceptron" computes a dense layer as $\phi(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W} + \mathbf{b})$, and "Building Sequential Models with Keras" passes each layer's result on to the next layer. Applying the equation to the hidden layer and feeding that result into the output layer gives this nested form.

Multiplying $\mathbf{W}_h$ and $\mathbf{W}_o$ together skips the hidden layer's ReLU. The lesson "Multilayer Perceptrons and Backpropagation" explains that stacked layers without a nonlinearity between them collapse into a single linear function.

quizData.question: Which output-layer activation functions suit three tasks, in this order: classifying an email as spam or ham, recognizing MNIST digits 0 to 9, and predicting a house price?

The first two choices are right, but a sigmoid on the price output would squeeze every prediction between 0 and 1. "Building a Regression MLP Using the Keras Sequential API" leaves the regression output without an activation so that it can take any real value.

A digit classifier with no activation would output unconstrained numbers instead of class probabilities. Softmax produces probabilities that sum to 1, which suits the multiclass digit task in "Classification Multilayer Perceptrons", not a single continuous price.

quizData.question: What is likely to happen when SGD with momentum uses a momentum hyperparameter $\beta$ extremely close to 1, such as 0.99999?

explanations: Correct. In "Accelerating Training with Momentum Optimization", $\beta$ acts as friction, from 0 (high friction) to 1 (no friction), and the terminal velocity is $\frac{1}{1-\beta}$ times the plain step, which is 100,000 for 0.99999. "Nesterov Accelerated Gradient" notes that momentum already tends to overshoot the minimum and oscillate, and almost no friction makes that much worse.

Plain gradient descent corresponds to $\beta = 0$, where Equation 11-5 keeps none of the previous momentum vector. A value near 1 keeps almost all of it, so past gradients dominate the update instead of being ignored.

This reverses the scale. "Accelerating Training with Momentum Optimization" places high friction at $\beta = 0$ and no friction at $\beta = 1$, so a value near 1 lets the momentum grow rather than stopping the updates.

In Equation 11-5, $\beta$ scales the previous momentum vector before the new gradient term is combined with it, so with a steady gradient the steps grow toward a terminal velocity of $\frac{1}{1-\beta}$ times the plain step. As "Accelerating Training with Momentum Optimization" shows, the steps grow rather than shrink.

quizData.question: A CNN has three convolutional layers with 3 × 3 kernels, stride 2 and "same" padding, which output 100, 200 and 400 feature maps from a 200 × 300 RGB image. How many trainable parameters do the three layers hold in total?

7,000 parameters
903,400 parameters
19,600 parameters

A total of 7,000 ignores the depth of the input, but a neuron's receptive field spans every channel or feature map of the previous layer, so each kernel holds 3 × 3 × depth weights.

Each filter has one weight per kernel position for every input channel plus one bias, so the layers hold (3×3×3+1)×100 = 2,800, (3×3×100+1)×200 = 180,200 and (3×3×200+1)×400 = 720,400 parameters, which add up to 903,400. quizData.question: A CNN runs out of GPU memory during training, but the mini-batch size must stay the same. Which change to the architecture reduces memory use?

Use a larger stride in some convolutional layers
Switch the convolutional layers from valid to same padding
Give each convolutional layer more filters

quizData.question: Which pairing correctly matches a CNN architecture with the main structural innovation it introduced?

Skip connections that add a block's input to its output are the innovation of ResNet, not SENet; the contribution of SENet is the SE block that recalibrates the channels.

The lesson "Fully Convolutional Networks" teaches this conversion.
A convolutional layer contains no pooling step; each filter computes a weighted sum over its receptive field, which in this case is the whole feature map.
Valid padding adds no zeros at all; the equivalence holds because each filter covers the entire feature map, not because of a border.
The converted filters are H × W, the same size as the feature map; a 1 × 1 filter would look at only one location at a time and could not reproduce a dense neuron.

Convolutional layers share their kernels across all positions and can process images of any height and width; only dense layers force a fixed input size.

The weights are not equal. The alignment model scores how relevant each encoder output is to the current decoder step, which is why the output for 'soccer' receives 85% of the weight in the lesson's example.

The weights are not used to pick one output and throw the others away. Every encoder output contributes to the weighted sum, even when one of them, such as the output for 'soccer', receives most of the weight.

Passing only a final hidden state is how a basic encoder–decoder works, and it is the short-term memory bottleneck that attention was designed to remove. With attention, the encoder sends all of its step outputs to the decoder.

By sampling pixel intensity distributions directly from the real training set

quizData.question: What is the theoretical Nash equilibrium point for a trained Generative Adversarial Network?
options: The generator produces perfectly realistic images while the discriminator accuracy drops to fifty percent.
The discriminator accuracy stabilizes at zero percent while the generator stops updating its parameters.
The discriminator reaches one hundred percent accuracy, completely rejecting all fake images.
The generator produces identical perfect copies of training samples to completely bypass the discriminator.
explanations: Correct. At Nash equilibrium, generated images are indistinguishable from real ones, forcing the discriminator to guess randomly with 50% probability.
Incorrect. Discriminator accuracy of zero percent implies the discriminator actively misclassifies everything, which is not equilibrium.
Incorrect. If the discriminator reaches 100% accuracy, the generator has failed to produce realistic images.

quizData.question: What happens during the process of mode collapse in GAN training?
options: The discriminator continuously overfits to real images and refuses to process fake samples.

The learning rates of both models decay to zero automatically due to game instability.

quizData.question: Why are GANs exceptionally sensitive to hyperparameter choices during optimization?

The dual competing networks create complex dynamic interactions that easily oscillate or diverge.
explanations: Incorrect. Unsupervised GAN training generates its own labels (real/fake); dataset labels do not change dynamically.

Incorrect. The relative size of the networks is not the main reason for dynamic instability.
Correct. Because both networks push against each other in a game, parameters can oscillate wildly, making training dynamic and sensitive to hyperparameters.

Incorrect. Standard GAN training does not rely on validation labels for experience replay.

quizData.question: What primary purpose does mini-batch discrimination serve in GAN architectures?

Incorrect. The scaling factor is smaller than 1, which reduces signal intensity rather than maximizing brightness.
Incorrect. The noise variance added at step $t$ is explicitly set to $\beta_t$, which is non-zero.

It calculates the deterministic loss metric used to evaluate output pixel intensity.

quizData.question: Which group of tasks are autoencoders commonly used for?
options: Turning a latent vector z into an intermediate style vector w for a generator
Dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, denoising, and pretraining
Predicting the Gaussian noise that was added to an image at a given time step
Judging whether each input image is real or generated, like a GAN discriminator
explanations: Turning a latent vector z into an intermediate style vector w is the work of the mapping network in the StyleGAN generator. It is not one of the tasks that autoencoders are used for.

This is right. The lesson Overview of Generative Unsupervised Models names dimensionality reduction, the lesson Stacked Autoencoders shows trained encoder layers being reused to pretrain a classifier when labels are scarce, and the lesson Denoising Autoencoders lists image denoising, unsupervised pretraining, and feature extraction.
Predicting the noise added at a time step is how a diffusion model is trained. An autoencoder is trained with a reconstruction loss that compares its outputs with its own inputs.

Classifying images as real or fake is the job of the discriminator in a generative adversarial network. An autoencoder does not classify its inputs; it compresses them into codings and reconstructs them.

quizData.question: Why is an autoencoder that reconstructs its inputs perfectly not necessarily a good model?
options: Perfect reconstruction means the coding layer is too small to hold useful features
Perfect reconstruction happens only when the reconstruction loss is misconfigured
Reconstruction is not part of training, so it says nothing about the model
It may just have copied its inputs without learning any useful patterns
explanations: A small coding layer is what forces an autoencoder to compress and find patterns, which makes perfect copying harder. The risk of simply memorizing inputs comes from too much capacity, not too little.

A correctly configured reconstruction loss is exactly what pushes outputs toward inputs, so a close match is expected rather than a sign of a bug. The real question is what the network learned in order to achieve it.

Reconstruction is central to training: an autoencoder is trained with a reconstruction loss that penalizes differences between its inputs and outputs. The issue is that a low loss alone does not show that useful features were learned.

This is right. The lesson Denoising Autoencoders warns that an autoencoder whose hidden layers have too much capacity can memorize its inputs without learning meaningful representations, and the lesson Efficient Data Representations in Autoencoders explains that capacity limits exist to force the network to find patterns instead.

quizData.question: In a stacked autoencoder with tied weights, how is each decoder weight matrix defined?
options: As the matrix inverse of the matching encoder weight matrix
As an exact copy of the matching encoder weight matrix
As the transpose of the matching encoder weight matrix
As a separately trained matrix averaged with the encoder's
explanations: Weight tying uses the transpose, not the matrix inverse. The lesson's rule is simply that each decoder matrix equals the transpose of the corresponding encoder matrix.

The decoder mirrors the encoder and goes from fewer neurons to more, so its weights are tied to the transpose of the encoder's matrix rather than to an identical copy. The rule in the lesson is $W_{decoder} = W_{encoder}^T$.

This is right. The lesson Stacked Autoencoders explains that weight tying forces each decoder weight matrix to equal the transpose of its corresponding encoder weight matrix, $W_{decoder} = W_{encoder}^T$, which roughly halves the number of parameters.

With tied weights, the decoder matrix is not trained as a separate set of parameters at all. It is defined directly from the encoder's matrix, which is why tying cuts the parameter count roughly in half.

quizData.question: What is a generative model, and which kind of autoencoder is one?
options: A model that restores clean inputs from corrupted versions of them; a denoising autoencoder
A model that compresses its inputs into much smaller codings; an undercomplete autoencoder
A model that generates new instances resembling its training data; a convolutional autoencoder
A model that generates new instances resembling its training data; a variational autoencoder
explanations: Reconstructing clean inputs from corrupted ones describes a denoising autoencoder. Removing noise from a given input is not the same as generating brand new instances that resemble the training data.
Compressing inputs into smaller codings describes an undercomplete autoencoder, which is used for dimensionality reduction. Compression alone is not what makes a model generative.

The definition is right, but a convolutional autoencoder is still a deterministic autoencoder whose latent space can contain gaps, so decoding random vectors tends to give nonsense. The variational autoencoder is the variant that becomes a generative model.

This is right. The lesson Variational Autoencoders explains that standard autoencoders cannot easily generate novel instances that resemble the training data, and that a VAE turns the autoencoder into a probabilistic generative model whose decoder produces new samples from random normal noise.

quizData.question: What makes training a generative adversarial network difficult in practice?
options: Mini-batch discrimination makes each batch too diverse for the discriminator to learn
Experience replay pushes the generator to keep producing images of only one class
Its discriminator must reach 100% accuracy at equilibrium, which rarely happens
It may never reach equilibrium, and the generator can collapse onto a single class
explanations: Mini-batch discrimination does the opposite: it penalizes batches that lack diversity, which discourages the generator from collapsing onto a single mode.
Experience replay is a remedy, not a cause. It trains the discriminator on a buffer of previously generated images, which helps stabilize training instead of making the generator fixate on one class.

At the Nash equilibrium the generator's images are perfectly realistic, so the discriminator can only guess randomly with about 50% accuracy. A discriminator at 100% accuracy would mean the fakes are still easy to catch.

This is right. The lesson Understanding Difficulties in GAN Training explains that standard optimization methods do not guarantee that a GAN ever reaches its Nash equilibrium, that mode collapse can make the generator produce one class and cycle between classes, and that parameters can oscillate and make training unstable.

quizData.question: What is the primary objective of a reinforcement learning agent?

To minimize the total number of actions executed within its environment.
To predict exact future state observations without receiving feedback.
To memorize every single state transition present in the training set.
explanations: Reinforcement learning agents aim to maximize cumulative rewards across sequential decisions.
Minimizing the number of actions is not a general objective unless specified by negative rewards per step.
Predicting future observations is not the main goal; optimizing action rewards is the primary target.
Agents do not memorize static states; they learn optimal action strategies through interaction.

quizData.question: In a maze-solving application, how can negative rewards be effectively utilized?

By penalizing the agent only after it successfully reaches the target destination.
By rewarding the agent only when it moves backward toward the start point.
By setting all step rewards to zero so the agent moves completely randomly.
explanations: Receiving a negative reward per time step forces the agent to optimize for speed to avoid continuous penalties.
Penalizing success would discourage the agent from completing its objective.
Rewarding backward movements prevents the agent from completing the maze.
Zero rewards provide no incentive for the agent to reach the exit efficiently.

quizData.question: Which component in the reinforcement learning framework emits observations and rewards?
options: The policy gradient.
The software agent.
The neural network.
The environment.
explanations: Policy gradients are an optimization technique, not an environment component.
The software agent generates actions based on the feedback it receives from the environment.

quizData.question: Based on Figure 18-1, which scenario represents a reinforcement learning system applied to dynamic resource control?
options: The robotic rover selecting physical motor commands to navigate terrain.
The Ms. Pac-Man video game agent responding directly to visual Atari pixel inputs.

quizData.question: After a long episode ends in failure, which technique helps a reinforcement learning agent judge how much blame each earlier action deserves?
